articleTitle: Attention-Based Network for Cardiac Systolic Abnormality Segmentation in Catheterization X-ray Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study delves into the domain of automated cardiac imaging analysis, with a specific focus on semantic segmentation of cardiac systolic abnormalities in catheterization X-ray images. We thoroughly evaluate the effectiveness of attention-based network methods in this regard, utilizing a dataset comprising 1717 cardiac catheterization X-ray images. Attention-based learning methods are rigorously examined for their efficacy in medical image segmentation. Sixteen distinct models are constructed, employing UNet and ResNet architectures, each integrating eight different loss functions: MSELoss, BCELoss, FocalLoss, DiceLoss, DiceBCELoss, HybridLoss, BinaryLovaszLoss, and LovaszBCELoss. Our objective is to investigate the impact of these loss functions on segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we augment our investigation by incorporating 56 attention-based models from prior studies, encompassing a variety of architectures including ResUnetPlus, Vnet, Unet, DoubleUnet, R2AttU_Net, AttU_Net, MultiResUnet, and R2Unet. Our results unveil the notable precision and efficacy of select models, notably the ResNet model with FocalLoss achieving an accuracy of 98.35% and a dice coefficient of 95.27%. Additionally, our study demonstrates the superiority of the MultiResUnet model with FocalLoss, an attention-based network, surpassing these benchmarks with an accuracy of 98.68% and a dice coefficient of 96.44%. These findings underscore the potential of the AttU_Net model in automated cardiac imaging analysis, offering promise for enhanced clinical diagnosis.

articleTitle: Ensemble Learning Framework for Cardiac Systolic Abnormality Segmentation in Catheterization X-ray Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The integration of automated cardiac imaging analysis holds significant promise for expediting clinical diagnosis and enhancing patient outcomes. This study focuses on segmenting cardiac systolic abnormalities using a dataset comprising 1717 cardiac catheterization X-ray images. We investigate the effectiveness of ensemble learning methodologies in this task. Specifically, we explore the utilization of six diverse loss functions, including MSELoss, FocalLoss, BCELoss, DiceLoss, DiceBCELoss, HybridLoss, LovaszBCELoss, and BinaryLovaszLoss, across 16 distinct models constructed on UNet and ResNet architectures. Ensemble learning techniques involve amalgamating these models through six different strategies: Simple Average, Majority Voting, Bitwise AND, Bitwise OR, Stacking, and Weighted Average. Our study findings unequivocally demonstrate that the implementation of ensemble learning substantially improves segmentation accuracy. Notably, the SimpleAverageModel achieved an accuracy of 98.52% and a dice coefficient of 95.85%, outperforming individual models such as the ResNet model with FocalLoss, which attained an accuracy of 98.35% and a dice coefficient of 95.27%. This research contributes to advancing automated interpretation systems for cardiac imaging, potentially enhancing diagnostic efficacy and reducing reliance on subjective human judgment.

articleTitle: Fast Energy-Based Scatter Correction for 3D TOF-PET on NeuroExplorer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The NeuroEXPLORER (NX) system has recently been developed as a high-resolution and high-sensitivity PET scanner dedicated to brain research. A long axial field-of-view (FOV) of 50 cm and excellent sensitivity-boosting time-of-flight (TOF) was used to improve the quantification in the brain region. However, a remaining challenge is robust and rapid TOF scatter estimation, especially in low-activity regions.This work uses a hybrid method to extend the model-based single scatter simulation (SSS) on TOF bins based on energy information. We take advantage of the marked difference between the energy spectra of the trues and scatters, and use the detailed energy information in the list-mode data to estimate the scattered events distribution across TOF bins. The TOF-specified distribution is pre-calculated with measured 2D energy spectra, and can be directly implemented into the scatter estimation during OSEM reconstruction. The method’s effectiveness is evaluated with a line source, scatter phantom, uniform phantom, and a dual-isotope contrast phantom for low-activity quantification. Images were reconstructed using in-house SSS estimation with Energy-based (EB-) and a simplified prompt-based (SP-) scaling, then compared with full TOF-SSS and Monte-Carlo scatter estimation (MCS).Results show that EB-SSS reduces or eliminates the artifacts in SP-SSS images, and presents improved contrast and decreased bias for low-activity regions by $\sim 40 \%$ with 5:1 and 9:1 contrast. Our method achieves comparable quantification and image quality with $4 \times$ fold acceleration compared to the full TOF-SSS. However, the quantification in low-activity regions requires additional improvement compared to MCS. Future work will focus on the trade-off between count statistics and acceptance of scatter to address multiple-scatter and high-energy scatters, bypassing the SSS modeling.

articleTitle: Semi-monolithic detectors for Ultra-High performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) scanners dedicated to organ imaging demand exceptional spatial resolution. To achieve this, precise estimation of the impact position and high temporal resolution are required. In line with this objective, the ultra-high-performance brain PET scanner (UHB-PET) will be based on semi-monolithic arrays of LYSO crystals, as this configuration has been shown to provide an excellent compromise between timing and positioning capability. In addition, each detector module will have a trapezoidal shape to minimize transaxial gaps and improve the sensitivity of the system. The first results about the characterisation of such a detector module read out with TOFPET2 ASIC from PETsys report a time resolution below 300ps. The positioning performance was evaluated using neural network techniques resulting in 2.9mm and 4.2mm FWHM along the monolithic and DOI coordinate, respectively.

articleTitle: Perovskite CsPbBr3 Room Temperature Radiation Detectors in Electron Collection Mode
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: All inorganic CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> perovskite crystals have garnered significant attention over recent years due to its distinctive properties, including room-temperature semiconductor characteristics, easy manufacturing process, relative defect tolerance, and cost-effectiveness against CdZnTe and CdTe detectors. Notably, energy resolutions are enhanced with breaking record values, $1.08 \%$ for ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ (662 keV), without any signal correction process. Additionally, crystal yield over $90 \%$ has been achieved. Even though high energy resolutions were obtained with CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> crystals, the operation relies on the collection of holes due to the difference between hole and electron mobility-lifetime product, favoring holes. In this study, we have investigated electron transport properties for $\mathrm{CsPbBr} r_{3}$ crystals grown with the Bridgman technique. Remarkable energy resolution was achieved with the figures of $2.5 \%$ for ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}(662 \mathrm{keV}), 4.2 \%$ for ${ }^{57} \mathrm{Co}(122 \mathrm{keV})$, and $7.8 \%$ for ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}(59.5$ keV). When spectral performance was compared with holes, comparable results were obtained. Mobility-lifetime product for electrons calculated as $1.03 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}$, more than 2-fold higher than holes. Furthermore, mobilities estimated through rise time analysis yielded similar values for both electrons and holes, surpassing those of undoped crystals.

articleTitle: Study of a SPECT Detector for BNCT Applications Through Monte Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) exploits B-10 based drugs and epithermal neutron beams to target cancer cells while sparing healthy tissues. The detection of the 478 keV gamma rays emitted by the B-10 neutron capture could face the challenge of a real-time dose monitoring in BNCT. On the other hand, BNCT facilities are characterized by a high gamma ray background (e.g. neutron capture on borated shielding) which would prevent the detection of the 478 keV photons coming from the patient. This work focuses on the study and the optimization of a SPECT system based on a $\mathrm{LaBr}_{3}(\mathrm{Ce}+\mathrm{Sr})$ scintillator at the Nagoya BNCT facility (Japan). An extensive work based on FLUKA simulations has been carried out to design a proper detector shielding for minimizing the background signal. The designed structure is based on lead, polyethylene and cadmium shielding. This setup enhances the detection of 478 keV gamma rays from B-10 neutron capture on the patient, allowing measurement of Boron concentrations down to 100 ppm.

articleTitle: Synergistic PET-Compton Reconstruction for Whole Gamma Imaging of Positron Emitters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI), which is a hybrid of positron emission tomography (PET)-Compton imaging, is attracting attention for simultaneous imaging of positron emitters and single-gamma emitters. For the imaging of positron emitters, WGI has a potential to improve sensitivity by using single gamma rays that fail to be detected in the coincidence detection for imaging, but with the energy resolution currently achieved in WGI prototypes, Compton imaging for 511 keV photons is inferior to PET. Therefore, the question to answer in this work was whether it is possible to improve PET by adding inferior information of Compton imaging. We proposed a synergistic PET and Compton image reconstruction method for improving the PET image quality by adding inferior information of Compton imaging. We defined the relationship between PET and Compton images as prior information and we synergistically integrate it into both image reconstruction processes to obtain both PET and Compton images separately in three alternating steps: (1) reconstruct the PET image using the maximum a posteriori expectation maximization (MAPEM) algorithm; (2) reconstruct the Compton image using the MAPEM algorithm; and (3) update the energy function for the correlations between PET and Compton images. We evaluated the proposed synergistic image reconstruction method using Monte Carlo simulation data of a WGI system and compared the results with those of the ordered subset EM (OSEM) algorithm. The results suggested that the proposed reconstruction method could push the limit of spatial resolution while reducing statistical noise compared to the OSEM algorithm. In conclusion, the answer to our question was yes: PET image quality could be improved by adding inferior Compton imaging data in WGI for positron emitters.

articleTitle: Investigation of the time resolution of an ultra-compact sampling calorimeter (RADiCAL) module at EM shower maximum over the energy range 25 GeV ≤ E ≤ 150 GeV
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The RADiCAL Collaboration is conducting R&D on high performance electromagnetic (EM) calorimetry to address the challenges expected in future collider experiments under conditions of high luminosity and/or high irradiation: FCC-ee/hh, 10 TeV pCM, muon collider and fixed target/forward physics environments. Under development is a sampling calorimeter approach, known as RADiCAL modules, based on scintillation and wavelength-shifting (WLS) technologies and photosensor readout, including SiPM and SiPM-like technology. The modules discussed here consist of alternating layers of very dense (W) absorber and scintillating crystal (LYSO:Ce) plates, assembled to a depth of $25 \mathrm{X}_{0}$. The scintillation signals produced by EM showers in the region of EM shower maximum (shower max) are transmitted to SiPM located at the upstream and downstream ends of the modules via quartz capillaries which penetrate the full length of the module. The capillaries contain DSB1 organic plastic WLS filaments, or LuAG:Ce ceramic WLS filaments, positioned within the region of shower max, where the shower energy deposition is greatest. The capillaries are filled and fused with quartz rod elsewhere. The wavelength shifted light from the spatially-localized shower max region is then propagated to the photosensors. This paper presents the results of measurements of the time resolution of a RADiCAL module over the energy range $25 \mathrm{GeV} \leq \mathrm{E} \leq 150 \mathrm{GeV}$ using the H 2 electron beam at CERN. When using the DSB1 wavelength shifter, the data indicate an energy dependence of the time resolution that follows the functional form: $\sigma_{t}=a / \sqrt{ } E \oplus b$, where $a=256 \sqrt{ } \mathrm{GeV}$ ps and $b=17.5 \mathrm{ps}$. And for DSB1, the time resolution measured at the highest electron beam energy for which data was currently recorded ($\mathrm{E}=150 \mathrm{GeV}$) was found to be $\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}=27 \mathrm{ps} \pm 2 \mathrm{ps}$. For the LuAG:Ce wavelength shifter, the corresponding measurent was $\sigma_{\mathrm{t}}=30 \mathrm{ps} \pm 3 \mathrm{ps}$ at $\mathrm{E}=150 \mathrm{GeV} / \mathrm{c}$. Analysis details will be presented.

articleTitle: The ADRIANO3 Triple-Readout Calorimetric Technique
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Hadron calorimetry at collider experiments has been particularly problematic due to the large fluctuations in the electromagnetic and neutral components of the hadronic showers. In order to address the existing issues, a novel, high-granularity triple readout calorimeter with fast timing was developed: ADRIANO3. ADRIANO3 is composed of a sandwich of heavy-glass tiles, plastic scintillator tiles, and thin resistive plate chambers, assembled as a single readout layer. The heavy glass is mostly sensitive to the fast electromagnetic component of the shower above the Cherenkov threshold. The plastic scintillator is sensitive to all the ionizing particles (and to neutrons to a limited extent). The resistive plate chambers based on heavy gases and Gd-doped glass, are sensitive to all the ionizing particles as well as to neutrons. The individual components of ADRIANO3 were constructed as small prototypes and extensively tested in various beam test campaigns. Here we report on the development of the ADRIANO3 concept and its components, the construction and testing of the dedicated prototypes, and discuss the current findings and future directions.

articleTitle: Thermal Tests of a Mock-Up Detector-Module for an HPGe Planar Detector Operated with a LN2 Cryostat
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the test results of a mock-up detector-module modelling the configuration of a High Purity Germanium (HPGe) planar detector coupled to room temperature electronics. The mock-up detector-module was designed, fabricated and tested inside a liquid nitrogen (LN2) cryostat.The mock-up module and the related test results provide a reference layout and dataset that can be used to de-risk the adaptation of the design to project specific needs.The tests performed on the mock-up detector-module include measurements of the thermal flow across the components, assessment of the effect of the infrared load on the internal mechanics, calculation of parasitic thermal losses via quantification of the boil-off rate of LN2.

articleTitle: Towards artificial data generation for accelerated PET detector ML-based timing calibration using GANs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In PET systems, TOF scanners require dedicated time skew calibration of the individual detectors, which is commonly performed by analytical approaches. In previous research, we demon-strated that performing timing calibration of detectors with a machine learning (ML) approach yields superior results. However, this method demands an extensive data acquisition due to its reliance on supervised learning. Our current research introduces initial advancements in the data gathering approach by augmenting measurement data obtained from detectors using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). GenAI excels at learning the data distribution of complete multidimensional samples, thereby preserving correlations between features and ensuring high-quality representation of individual feature distributions. We compare our approach with an analytical baseline, where we linearly interpolate the data between different measured positions. In our study, we leverage an adapted version of the conventional Fre’ chet inception distance (FID) score, a dissimilarity measure, to evaluate the quality of the generated data. Utilizing generative adversarial network (GAN) as our GenAI model, we benefit from its well-documented efficiency in tabular data setups. The adjusted FID score demonstrates a notable enhancement, with interpolated data scoring 12.05 and generated data scoring 1.56, while the comparison of subsets of measurement data results in 0.02. The cumulative Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) of generated data with GAN shows slightly worse performance with a value of 7.68 in comparison to linearly interpolated data of 3.75, with measurement data scoring 0.04. However, the influence of FID score improvement significantly overcomes the decrease in the KLD performance, as we show strikingly similar correlations between the features of GAN-generated data and measurement data, in contrast to predominantly zero correlations observed in linearly interpolated data.

articleTitle: The Lunar OutpOst Neutron Spectrometer (LOONS)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutrons constitute an important component of the cosmic radiation, accounting for a significant amount of the radiation dose received by air/spacecraft crews. They are generated in the interactions of galactic and solar cosmic rays (CRs) with planetary atmospheres/surfaces, as well as spacecraft materials, posing a considerable hazard to satellite electronics and human health. The detection and monitoring of neutrons of lunar origin is particularly relevant for near-future manned missions to the Moon. In fact, apart from representing a considerable component of the lunar radiation environment, they can be used to characterize the surface chemical composition, especially the hydrogen content (e.g., associated with water ice). Neutrons are also produced in solar flares; their measurement provides a unique opportunity to investigate particle acceleration mechanisms at the Sun, complementing the observations based on $\gamma$ rays and charged CR species. The Lunar OutpOst Neutron Spectrometer (LOONS) is a new detector concept, as part of a low-Moon orbit or lunar-lander opportunity, designed for the measurement of neutrons of solar, terrestrial and lunar origin over an unprecedented and comprehensive energy range (up to $\sim 150$ MeV) including thermal, epithermal and fast components. Its capabilities also include $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy between 0.1 and 20 MeV. LOONS is a compact and robust instrument based on state-of-the-art techniques for neutron detection, using segmented organic scintillators coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), and subsequently processed with modern ASICs. In this work we describe the detector development and performance, and the future plans to integrate a flight-ready instrument.

articleTitle: Use of the CERN picoTDC for timing application in particle therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we explore the feasibility of measuring the ion crossing time in particle therapy using thin silicon sensors [1], a custom ASIC front-end and the CERN picoTDC evaluation board [2]. An ion counter based on a 144 strips sensor of $2.7 \times 2.7 \mathrm{~cm} 2$ area, developed at the INFN and University of Turin and named ESA_ABACUS [3], was first characterized at the Italian CNAO facility with the carbon ion beams in the clinical energy range, showing good particle counting capability and providing a beam lateral profile in agreement with the expectation. Later, 8 of the 144 channels of the board were integrated with the CERN PicoTDC allowing for the ion arrival time determination with 3 ps of the time bin width. The new system was characterized in the laboratory using a picosecond pulse generator, and at the CNAO therapy center with carbon ion beams of different energies and clinical intensities. A temporal resolution of the system of about 100 ps was measured using pulse injection. The high rate readout capabilities allowed to measure the CNAO beam time structure and particle distribution, highlighting the beam bunched structure determined by the accelerator’s radiofrequency. Ongoing work explores the system applicability for various timing application as beam commissioning and range verification based on prompt gamma timing techniques.

articleTitle: Practical Gamma-Ray Imager Performance Characterization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-ray imagers have achieved widespread adoption in recent years and a recent ANSI standard, N42.62, aims to quantify performance. This work summarizes a set of tests that can be used to characterize the radiological performance of gamma-ray imagers of different modalities so that design and procurement decisions can be made for various applications. The tests are designed to quantify performance in an application-agnostic way, yet to measure performance that might be expected in various applications with test designed to be as easy as possible to perform with common radiation sources. Tests do not measure detector parameters such as dead time or efficiency directly. The base set of tests quantify the ability to locate point sources, with additional tests for determining the extent of distributed sources and directional isotope identification. These tests are compared with the ANSI N42.62 tests. Comparison will be made between several commercially available detectors.

articleTitle: A Large-Area 2X4 Monolithic SDD Array Detector For Lab-Based XAS Instrument
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the recent past, the interest to perform X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) experiments with laboratory sources has increased. Within this context, the LabXAS project aims to develop a new table-top in-lab XAS instrument to investigate fundamental atomic properties in new freshly synthesized materials. Here we report about the detector system designed to comply with the requirements of the lab-based XAS spectrometer under construction at the Physics department of the Politecnico di Milano. The main components of the detection and readout chain are: one 2 x 4 monolithic SDD matrix, eight CUBE preamplifiers and a DANTE Digital Pulse Processor (DPP). The readout system is composed of two main boards: one housing the SDD and the CUBE preamplifiers and the other one dedicated to generate SDD bias voltages. At the end of the readout chain, a DANTE DPP system is installed outside of the vacuum chamber. In this summary, the preliminary spectroscopy results performed with the first version of detector system are presented.

articleTitle: A Dual-Channel Spectrometer Based on 1mm-Thick SDDs for the Study of Nuclear Beta Decays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the ASPECT-BET project developing a dual-channel SDD-based spectrometer designed to achieve high-precision measurements of beta decays across a broad energy range (spanning from 10 keV to 1 MeV). The adoption of SDDs in electron spectroscopy represents a relatively novel approach, with promising preliminary results already observed in the TRISTAN project, which focuses on accurate beta spectroscopy of Tritium decay. The primary objective of ASPECTBET is to extend the research, including more energetic radioactive sources to study allowed and forbidden nuclear beta decays. To achieve this goal, we have incorporated larger (8 mm diameter) and thicker (1 mm-thick) detectors to enhance the absorption capability of the spectrometer, and a CSA featuring a larger feedback capacitance. Furthermore, by utilizing two SDDs arranged one in front of the other, post-acquisition data processing can be applied to eliminate partial energy depositions in detectors caused by undesirable effects such as electron backscattering or escape of characteristic X-rays. An assessment of the energy resolution achieved at the Mn-K$\alpha$ (5.9 keV) fluorescence line, obtained by exposing the spectrometer to a 55Fe calibration source, is presented. A FWHM below 200 eV is achieved under conditions of a 1 μs peaking time and cooling at -23 °C, indicating the potential suitability of the spectrometer for high-energy beta decay studies.

articleTitle: Performances Study on TDC Timing Samples Resolution in a MVT Chip
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Previously, we proposed a multi-voltage threshold (MVT) sampling method for digitizing PET scintillation pulses. This method involves acquiring the time samples of an event pulse through a series of preset voltages. Several PET detectors and imaging systems based on discrete components have demonstrated the feasibility of this method in time-of-flight (TOF) measurement. Subsequently, we developed a MVT integrated circuit (IC) for better timing performance and a more compact structure. Each time sampling channel in the MVT IC employs a two-stage time-todigital converter (TDC), which consists of a delay-locked loop (DLL) and a vernier delay line (VDL). As the energy and timing information is picked up by analyzing the timing samples obtained by the MVT method, precision measurement of the timing samples will result in a better performance. In this paper, we simulated the time samples digitizing with the TDC having different DNL and average bin size. Our results indicate that the timing samples resolution could be 50 ps (FWHM) when the maximum DNL of the DLL is 0.12 LSB, the maximum DNL of the VDL is 1.2 LSB, and the average bin size of the VDL is 38 ps. When improving the maximum DNL of the DLL stage from 0.12 LSB (150 ps) to $0.02 \mathrm{LSB}(25 \mathrm{ps})$, the maximum DNL of the VDL stage from 1.2 LSB (46 ps) to $0.25 \mathrm{LSB}(10 \mathrm{ps})$, and keeping the same bin size, the timing samples resolution improves to 22 ps (FWHM). While keeping the maximum DNL of the DLL as 0.02 LSB, the maximum DNL of the VDL as 0.25 LSB, and further improving the average bin size of the VDL to 20 ps, the timing samples resolution improves to 16 ps.

articleTitle: Simulation of CMOS-based Amorphous Silicon Microchannel Plate Detectors for Metascintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CMOS-based Amorphous Silicon Microchannel Plate (CAMCP) detectors are devices built on and read-out by a multi-channel CMOS tile, using a PLANACON photocathode and a hexagonal grid of high aspect ratio micro-channels. Metascintillators are combinatory scintillators comprising more than one type of material, exploiting the electron leakage from a dense scintillator to a fast one. The two structures were simulated together using GATE. The scintillator had dimensions of $24 \times 9.6 \times 7.7 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, made of 22 slabs of LYSO:Ce ($24 \times 9.6 \times 0.25 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$) and PEA<inf>2</inf> PbBr<inf>4</inf> perovskites $\left(24 \times 9.6 \times 0.1 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right)$. The CAMCP was modeled, based on prototypes, with $1.5 \mu \mathrm{m}$ diameter channels of $40 \mu \mathrm{m}$, organized to be read out by $15 \mathrm{x} 15 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ channels, with 6 ps timing resolution. The study focuses on the single photon detection capabilities of the CAMCP and uses machine learning to reconstruct the characteristics of the scintillation event, such as interaction energy and x-y-z-t onset. It is demonstrated that with this structure, it is possible to achieve down to 1 mm spatial, $\sim 8 \mathrm{~mm}$ depth-of-interaction and 89 ps timing resolution for gamma interaction. Event analysis and timewalk corrections further improve the characteristics of this architecture.

articleTitle: Semi-Monolithic Crystals in Preclinical PET: A Leap Forward in TOF and DOI Technologies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Semi-monolithic crystals have the potential of combining the timing capabilities of pixelated crystals and the 3D positioning accuracy of monolithic crystals. We present here a preclinical PET scanner consisting of 2 rings with an inner diameter of 106 mm, and an axial length of 52 mm. Each ring consists of 14 semi-monolithic arrays of 22 slabs of $25.6 \times 12 \times 0.97 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ each, coupled to $8 \times 8$ SiPMs arrays. A timestamp averaging method, including time skew and time walk corrections, was applied, achieving a detector time resolution as good as 178 ps FWHM. A neural network technique based on a multilayer perceptron architecture has been implemented for the prediction of the annihilation photon impact position inside each detector module along the monolithic direction. The depth of interaction has been determined using the Energy/$I_{\max}$ estimator and calibrated using a Voronoi method. A full NEMA protocol evaluation has been carried out. A spatial resolution of $0.96 \pm 0.07 \mathrm{~mm}$ was achieved at ¼ of the axial Field of View. The sensitivity at the center of the scanner was 3.1% with an energy window of 30%. A NECR value of 10 kcps at a $280 \ \mu \mathrm{Ci}$ was achieved. The Recovery Coefficients (RCs) and Spill-Over-Ratio (SOR) values were obtained for the image quality phantom. RCs of 0.27, 0.71, 0.90, 0.98 and 0.99 were achieved for the 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 mm rods, respectively. The SOR values were 0.18 for air and 0.27 for water.

articleTitle: Point-supervised Brain Tumor Segmentation with Box-prompted Medical Segment Anything Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Delineating lesions and anatomical structure is important for image-guided interventions. Point-supervised medical image segmentation (PSS) has great potential to alleviate costly expert delineation labeling. However, due to the lack of precise size and boundary guidance, the effectiveness of PSS often falls short of expectations. Although recent vision foundational models, such as the medical segment anything model (MedSAM), have made significant advancements in bounding-box-prompted segmentation, it is not straightforward to utilize point annotation, and is prone to semantic ambiguity. In this preliminary study, we introduce an iterative framework to facilitate semantic-aware point-supervised MedSAM. Specifically, the semantic box-prompt generator (SBPG) module has the capacity to convert the point input into potential pseudo bounding box suggestions, which are explicitly refined by the prototype-based semantic similarity. This is then succeeded by a prompt-guided spatial refinement (PGSR) module that harnesses the exceptional generalizability of MedSAM to infer the segmentation mask, which also updates the box proposal seed in SBPG. Performance can be progressively improved with adequate iterations. We conducted an evaluation on BraTS2018 for the segmentation of whole brain tumors and demonstrated its superior performance compared to traditional PSS methods and on par with box-supervised methods.

articleTitle: Prototype of Front End Electronics based on FPGA-ADC for PET Detector Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is an advanced clinical examination imaging technology in the field of nuclear medicine. We will describe a novel PET module using a soft-core analog-todigital converter (ADC) based on time-to-digital converter (TDC). The soft-core ADC is implemented in an FPGA. In the hardware design, the FPGA-based ADC (FPGA-ADC) only requires one resistor and an FPGA. FPGA-ADC allows users to program the sampling rate and adjust the dynamic range of the ADC with small modifications. This design is characterized by flexibility and high density, which can greatly reduce the size of readout circuits for the PET module. In this PET Prototype, detector part used two detection units. Each unit contained a $3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}$ LYSO bar and a SiPM (J-series, ONSemiconductor). The FPGA-ADC served as the main part of the data acquisition (DAQ) system. It is possible for the FPGA-ADC to digitize waveforms from SiPM detector. The energy resolution of the two units is 16.8% and 14.5%, respectively. The coincidence timing resolution of the PET detector Prototype is about 520 ps.

articleTitle: Respiratory Motion Correction Using FastPET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Respiratory motion correction often encounters prolonged processing times due to iterative reconstruction processes. The emergence of the deep learning framework FastPET presents a promising solution, offering rapid reconstruction while maintaining high quality quantification. In this study, we develop a FastPET-based respiratory motion correction method and validate its efficacy through Monte Carlo simulations with the XCAT phantom. The results show that the FastPET-based motion correction effectively recovers motion blurring in liver and lung tumors. This application and validation of FastPET in motion correction represent significant progress. Future studies will explore various approaches to further optimize the motion estimation and correction techniques.

articleTitle: Gain Characterization of LGADs by Means of Transient Current Technique
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Detectors, LGADs, are widely considered for fast-timing applications in high energy physics, nuclear physics, space science, medical imaging, and in precision measurements of rare processes. Such devices are silicon-based and characterized by an intrinsic gain thanks to a p+-doped layer that allows the production of a controlled avalanche of carriers, with a multiplication in the order of 10-100. In contrast with p-in-n diodes, whose collected signal does not change significantly as a function of the bias voltage, once fully depleted, LGADs have a gain that is strongly dependent on the bias voltage, particularly for values close to breakdown voltage. The gain of LGADs is studied not only as a function of the bias voltage but also as a function of the injected charge. Such study allows to expand the characterization of LGAD’s performance from the case of minimum ionizing particles to the case of highly-ionizing particles, which is relevant for several future scientific applications. Tests were performed with an infrared laser and a beta source to characterize the gain of LGAD sensors as a function of bias voltage and injected charge.

articleTitle: The investigation of hybrid collimator to improve image quality for cardiac SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multi-pinhole collimator based on clinical dual-head detector has been applied for myocardial SPECT imaging. Previous work showed the flat detector with large area, especially the detector corner, cannot be fully utilized with multi-pinhole collimator. Recently, we designed a new hybrid collimator, composed of seven pinholes and four coded apertures, aiming to enhance image quality by utilizing the projection of the coded aperture as supplemental information in addition to the projection of the multiple pinholes. We developed an Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm to model the projection of the coded aperture as a constraint term during image reconstruction. We adopted the analytical simulation with NCAT phantom for performance evaluation. We quantified the recovery coefficient (RC) of the myocardium and the image noise by the normalized standard deviation (NSTD) of the liver. Meanwhile, the conventional MLEM algorithm, which just uses the projection from the multiple pinholes, was used for comparison. The results showed a superior performance with ADMM than MLEM in terms of the RC versus NSTD curve. When compared with MLEM algorithm, ADMM algorithm can improve more than $10 \% \mathrm{RC}$ while maintaining the same image noise level. Our results demonstrated that the image quality of the cardiac SPECT scanner can be improved when including additional code aperture collimators and applying ADMM algorithm for image reconstruction.

articleTitle: Using MLAA and registration to estimate attenuation of a flexible body matrix coil in nonTOF PET/MRI
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The attenuation of PET gamma photons caused by magnetic resonance (MR) hardware (HW) is often overlooked for flexible coils, potentially resulting in an underestimation of patient activity and reduced reproducibility. This study compares the application of a maximum likelihood algorithm that updates activity and attenuation using emission data only (MLAA) alone to its application combined with registration of a pre-acquired CT-derived template μMap of the coil on full count data as well as a sixth of the data to simulate gated PET data. NonTOF PET/MR scans of a patient were performed, where the MR body coil was placed on the patient torso. The data was then reconstructed using MLAA with known patient attenuation, but unknown HW attenuation. A template μMap was created from a CT-scan of the same coil wrapped around a NEMA Body phantom. This μMap was projected along the vertical axis, registered to the projected MLAA output and shifted to align with the patient outline in vertical direction. All μMaps were then used in final maximum likelihood expectation maximisation (MLEM) reconstructions of the PET data. This procedure was repeated for a sixth of the acquired counts to investigate the applicability of these methods on gated PET data. The highly attenuating preamplifiers were on the whole moved to the right position by registration and vertical shifting, although the coil deformation was not represented accurately by the current method. This remains the case when using a sixth of the data. When a background-prior was used, the step-size of MLAA had to be reduced to reach a converged μMap. The activity images reconstructed with the obtained HW μMaps show an increased activity uptake with respect to the reference scan with patient attenuation correction only.

articleTitle: Investigation of Microchannel Plate PMT Integrated with Barium Fluoride
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Precise timing measurements are indispensable for ultrafast applications such as high energy physics experiments and time-of-flight positron emission tomography. Barium Fluoride (BaF<inf>2</inf>) scintillator is one of the most attractive materials for such ultrafast applications owing to its fast decay time of 600 ps prior to its slow component of 600 ns. However, the wavelength of the fast emission is in a vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) region of $\sim 220 \mathrm{nm}$, making it difficult to efficiently extract photons to photodetectors because VUV photons are easily absorbed by optical greases. Therefore, in this study, we developed a microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (MCP-PMT) integrated with a BaF<inf>2</inf> scintillator as a window face plate as a potential detector for the ultrafast applications. The BaF<inf>2</inf>-windowed MCP-PMT allows us to efficiently detect VUV photons because there are no optical boundaries from emission point to the photocathode. Hence, high timing performance can be highly expected owing to the good transit time spread of the MCP-PMT while having an energy information. In this presentation, we report fundamental physical properties of the BaF<inf>2</inf>-windowed MCP-PMT, such as single photon response, gain, detection efficiency, energy and timing resolutions.

articleTitle: A Dual-domain Spectral Projection Completion Scheme for Fast kV-Switching Cone-beam CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fast kV-switching (FKS) technology has been actively studied as one of the promising dual-energy solutions for flat-panel-detector (FPD) based cone-beam CT (CBCT) spectral imaging. One of the typical issues for FKS is the misalignment between the low- and high-energy projection. A projection interpolation scheme is required if a projection-domain material decomposition is applied. In this work, we proposed a dual-domain spectral projection completion scheme to compensate for the slightly angular mismatch between low- and high- projections in FKS CBCT spectral imaging, where the reconstruction process involves two steps of material decomposition, one enhancing the image quality in image domain and the other applying material decomposition on completed projection to obtain the basis materials projection. We demonstrated its feasibilityon the tabletop CBCT system with FKS developed, where the multi-energy phantom was scanned with 80/105/130 kVp pair and projection data was obtained by the FPD with 550-um thickness of Cesium Iodine (CsI) scintillator. The preliminary physical experiment results validate the feasibility of the dual-domain spectral projection completion scheme in FKS CBCT spectral imaging.

articleTitle: Monte Carlo Simulation Model of the Dingo Thermal Neutron Imaging Beamline at ANSTO
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents an experimentally validated Monte Carlo simulation model of the Dingo thermal neutorn beamline at the Austrlian Centre for Neutron Scattering (ACNS). The model was constructed using CAD drawings of the entire beam transport system and its material composition. The neutron spectrum was refined using in-beam nuetron activation analysis and outof-beam Bonner sphere spectroscopy. A sapphire filter was implemented and evaluated against experimental results. The model achieved good agreement with experimental data, with simulated neutron beam profiles within 2.3% and 1.6% of gold wire measurements at the tertiary sutter and sample stage, respectively. The refined neutron spectrum consists of 63.5% thermal, 16.2% epithermal and 20.2% fast neutrons, while the beam filtered by the sapphire filter constitutes 981% thermal neutron, and a decreased the thermal neutron flux by approximately 45%. Out-of-beam neutron spectra and counts root mean square errors (RMSE) were within $5.0+/-1.4 \%$ and $9.1+/-0.5 \%$, respectively. The model’s accuracy and flexibility offer advantages to Dingo users and the neutronics community.

articleTitle: NUV-sensitive Deep-junction (NUV-DJ) SiPMs, a new technology optimized for fast timing applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK, Trento, Italy) has developed several Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) technologies, particularly for applications such as time of flight-positron emission tomography (ToF-PET) where fast timing is crucial. This work presents the latest development at FBK, the Near-Ultraviolet, Deep-junction (NUV-DJ) SiPM technology, providing improved Photon Detection Efficiency (PDE) and Single Photon Time Resolution (SPTR) with respect to the state-of-the-art SiPMs. TheNUV-DJ microcell has a $40 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pitch and features a modified design with the high-electric field region placed deeper inside the epitaxial layer, enabling an increased avalanche triggering probability even with longer-wavelength photons. The PDE showed outstanding values of 70% at 420 nm (with a nominal microcell fill factor of 80.8%). At 65% PDE, DCR of $80 \mathrm{kcps} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ and Optical Crosstalk probability below 2% were measured. Using a high-frequency readout, SPTR of 36 ps FWHM and of 65 ps FWHM were measured on 1x1 $\mathrm{mm}^{2}$ and $4 \mathrm{x} 4 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPMs, respectively. Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR) of less than 100 ps FWHM in the readout of $2.76 \times 2.76 \times 18 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LYSO:Ce crystals was achieved with a high frequency readout, while aCTR of 115 ps FWHM was measured using standard readout electronics. These findings represent cutting-edge advances in timing and PDE performance and are very promising for TOF-PET and high-energy physics applications employing LYSO, LSO, BGO, and LaBr<inf>3</inf> crystals, in scenarios where a high PDE in the NUV range combined with excellent timing is needed.

articleTitle: Event coincidences in 3D gamma ray semiconductor detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work investigates event coincidences in a three-dimensional semiconductor detector for gamma rays with energy 140 keV and 510 keV using GEANT4 for activities ranging from 5 MBq to 500 MBq. The semiconductor detector is assumed to have an area of $400 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ and a thickness of either 2 cm or 5 cm. We further assumed a point like source 15 cm from the detector embedded in a water cylinder with diameter 30 cm, while the voxel size in the semiconductor detector was set to be $25 \times 25 \times 700 \mu^{3}$. Given the recoil electron track estimations, it was also possible to estimate in each interaction the corresponding hit map for the voxels. The events used for the analysis in this work are determined by a gamma ray interacting at least once in the detector, concluding its track with either a photoabsorption or an escape. Each event volume was approximated with a sphere centered in the centroid of the interaction points, having as radius the distance between such center and the furthest interaction from it. Then each temporal coincidence of two events was divided in three different cases: overlap of the volumes, surface of the spheres closer than 2 cm, or than 5 cm. This was done to estimate how many temporally coincident events could be spatially separated as distinct events with a future algorithm and kinematic considerations. The resulting number of events not resolved due to temporal coincidence remained below $26 \%$ even at 500 MBq, while this percentage can be further reduced up to less than $4 \%$, with the spatial volume analysis. The results are important input to future hardware development of three-dimensional gamma ray detectors.

articleTitle: 6LiInP2Se6 Semiconductor: Advancements in Crystal Growth for Thermal Neutron Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The growth of $2 \mathrm{D}^{6} \mathrm{LiInP}{ }_{2} \mathrm{Se}_{6}$ (LIPSe) semiconductor, vital for direct thermal neutron detection, has been advanced through the combined use of chemical vapor transport (CVT) and the Bridgman-Stockbarger method. Devices were fabricated using CVT-grown and Bridgman-Stockbarger single crystals. They showed improved photoresponse and alpha particle response to $\mathrm{a}^{241} \mathrm{Am}$ source. Our study contributes to refining the efficacy of CVT and Bridgman-Stockbarger methods in controlling growth parameters and device fabrication, furthering the potential applications of $2 \mathrm{D}^{6}{ }^{6} \mathrm{LiInP}{ }_{2} \mathrm{Se}_{6}$ semiconductors in direct thermal neutron detection.

articleTitle: Study for the Upgrade of the Front-End DAQ of the DSSC Megapixel Camera for a Potential New Generation of Detectors at the European XFEL
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Within the Data Acquisition (DAQ) system of the 1 Mpixel camera based on DEPFET Sensor with Signal Compression (DSSC) at the European X rays-Free Electron Laser (EuXFEL), the DEPFETs are read-out by two Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) stages: the Input Output Board (IOB), which currently houses an End-of-Life (EoL) low-area and low-power Xilinx 45-nm 6-Series Spartan-6 (i.e., XC6LX45T), and the Patch Panel Transceiver (PPT) with an high-performance Xilinx 28-nm 7-Series Kintex-7 device. The IOB is the first acquisition stage located near the detector, housed within a vacuum-sealed metallic container, and operates at low temperature (i.e., -20°C). This specific working environment imposes significant constraints on the physical size of the board and compliance with thermal and current budgets. At EuXFEL a new detector development program is in the definition phase. This paper reports feasibility studies performed on the IOB, in order to provide, on one side spare parts for the existing installed detectors, and on the other, to check which kind of system could be compatible also for future operation. It is necessary to begin with a redesign of the IOB because the Spartan-6 FPGA it hosts is at End-of- Life (EOL). Moreover, using newer and more advanced FPGAs makes it natural to introduce features that can be compatible with future upgrades of the detectors at the European XFEL; e.g., higher pixel count, self-trimming, and pre-calibration. In this regard, two different models of Xilinx FPGAs at 16 nm, the SU65P Spartan UltraScale+ and the AU15P Artix UltraScale+, compatible with the current Spartan-6 in terms of package size, number of I/Os, amount of logic, and availability of transceivers, have been selected. This preliminary analysis covers aspects related to the estimation of resource usage, power consumption, operating frequency, and bandwidth, considering the current Spartan-6 FPGA and its firmware as reference.

articleTitle: Atomic-level Mapping of Cd0.9Zn0.1Te Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The presence of precipitates in the Cd\textsubscript{0.9}Zn\textsubscript{0.1}Te (CZT) semiconductors can play a key role in shaping the performance of CZT-based detectors. These precipitates range from nanometers to tens of nanometers, as it has been extensively reported in literature using transmission electron microscopy. Herein, we introduce laser-assisted atom probe tomography (APT) to map in atom-by-atom basis the three-dimensional of CZT crystals. The investigated crystals were grown by Travelling Heater Method. APT is an ideal method to investigate the distribution and local composition of individual precipitates. Our investigations focused on both as-grown CZT crystals and post-growth annealed crystals. APT specimens were prepared using a Focus Ion Beam (FIB) with Gallium ions. The preservation of the crystal structure was verified after FIB preparation by electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD). First APT results show no precipitation of Tellurium or Cadmium at the nanoscale. The structural integrity of the investigated CZT crystals has therefore been confirmed showing that homogeneous CZT structure down to the sub-nanometerscale on the scale of the micrometer-sized volumes APT explores.

articleTitle: Generation of lateral cephalometric radiographs from 3D CBCT dental images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Conventional lateral cephalometric radiographs are widely used in orthodontics and oral maxillofacial surgery. However, it suffers often from structural overlap and inadequate positioning of the head of the subject during the scan, limiting its diagnostic utility and affecting treatment decision-making. In this work, we propose a new method to produce digital lateral cephalometric radiographes from 3D head images acquired with dental CBCT, which is becoming widely available in dental clinics. Preliminary results reveal that the method proposed can yield digital lateral cephalometric radiographs with improved contrast and landmarks of clinical relevance.

articleTitle: Synthesised PET Image Reconstruction with Kernel Methods and the Deep Image Prior for Post-Reconstruction Image Enhancement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Advanced iterative image reconstruction methods, for example using the kernel method and the deep image prior, have improved the quality of positron emission tomography (PET) images. To realise the benefits of such approaches, raw PET data are needed in order to perform an image reconstruction. However, raw data may not always be available, and even when it is, there are complex scanner-specific data corrections (e.g. scatter, attenuation and normalisation) as well as the need for a fully 3D forward and back projector. In this work we take the benefits of both the kernel method and the deep image prior (DIP) and introduce them to our methodology of synthesised image reconstruction, a framework specifically designed to allow image-reconstruction improvements to be applied to images already reconstructed by scanner-specific software with all data corrections already accounted for. This approach has already shown success for spatial resolution recovery, delivering improvements compared to conventional post-reconstruction image-space based methods. Specifically, synthesised image reconstruction creates a new reconstruction problem from a standard reconstructed image. This present work takes the synthesised reconstruction framework further by introducing DIP with the kernel method, and corresponding image quality improvements are obtained. This finds application in a number of settings where there is no access to the original raw PET data, or no access to the projector and scanner geometry information, hence making state of the art methods more accessible to a wider range of applications.

articleTitle: Low Power, Dual Mode Detectors for Nuclear Security Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The detection of special nuclear material remains a matter of utmost importance due to potential security issues. Current neutron detection relies upon a combination of a ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ detector and a plastic scintillator. ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ is a rare material with decreasing global supply, so an alternative solution needs to be developed. This solution should be both low power and robust, in order to be deployed in field situations. This is possible using dual mode scintillators, which can use pulse shape discrimination (PSD) methods to separate between neutron and gamma species present due to their different timing characteristics. The scintillator materials selected for investigation are, CLLBC, an inorganic scintillator made of Cerium, Lanthanum, Lithium and BromoChloride. As well as EJ-276, an organic plastic scintillator. These materials are paired with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPM’s), which meet the requirements of being robust and having a low operating voltage, along with single photon sensitivity. Initial tests have taken place with these materials and photomultiplier tubes (PMT’s), which were chosen to begin with due to a lower room temperature dark count than SiPM’s. Results taken using CLLBC have demonstrated a 5% gamma energy resolution at 662 keV. The investigation has now transitioned towards SiPMs due to their robust and low power characteristics when compared to PMTs. Simulation work is ongoing with both GEANT4 and LTSpice simulations to test designs and provide idealised results. This work has led to the design of bespoke printed circuit boards (PCBs) with analog electronics to meet initial low power requirements. Work is currently underway to replicate accurate gamma and neutron species separation using PSD algorithms replicated in hardware, with the goal of creating a robust analog system that can perform as well as a digital PSD system at a fraction of the power requirements.

articleTitle: Concept of a Di-modal Metabolic Imaging System Combining PET and Sodium (23Na) MRI
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET is the state-of-the-art device to measure the cellular metabolism of the diseases, such as cancer and dementia. On the other hand, sodium (<sup>23</sup>Na) MRI also enables measuring cellular viability of the diseased area, as sodium is involved in the process of the energy metabolism in the cell. A simultaneous PET and <sup>23</sup>Na MRI metabolic imaging may provide additional complementary information of the diseases for improved treatment in the future. In this study, we developed a combined proton (<sup>1</sup>H) and <sup>23</sup>Na RF coils compatible for an extremity PET to be used with a 3T clinical MRI system (Siemens Prisma, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany). The <sup>1</sup>H RF coil was a 4-channel microstrip coil that integrated the RF shield cages of PET detectors as an integral part of the coil. We call it an MS PET coil. The <sup>1</sup>H MR images are to be used as a reference image for the <sup>23</sup>Na MR images. A rectangular loop <sup>23</sup>Na RF coil was developed as a separate coil. The <sup>23</sup>Na coil was positioned just below the 4-channel MS PET coil, so that both <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>23</sup>Na imaging become possible in one bed position. A cylindrical homogeneous phantom (NaCl + NiSO<inf>4</inf> × H<inf>2</inf>O) imaging was performed for a gradient-echo (GRE) sequence for both the cases of individual and combined RF coil configurations. The signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) of the <sup>1</sup>H coil for the gradient-echo (GRE) images were 18.7 and 35.6 respectively for individual <sup>1</sup>H coil and combined coil configurations, and similar respective values for the case of <sup>23</sup>Na coil were 14.3 and 10.8. Overall, the combined multi-coil device did not show worse performance than the separate coils.

articleTitle: Impact of Inter-crystal Scattering on Highresolution Small Animal Brain PET System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Inter-crystal scattering (ICS) is a common occurrence in pixelated PET detectors, during which gamma photons deposit energy in different crystals. This phenomenon can lead to mis-positioning of single events in light-sharing detectors thereby degrading performance and image quality of the system. In nine-to-one coupled light-sharing PET detector with light guide, the energy of single events is assessed using outputs from all 10 SiPMs (Silicon Photomultipliers). Traditional methods employ a narrow energy window to distinguish between ICS events and photoelectric (PE) events. However, in this study, we utilize a flood-map contour-based approach for ICS rejection. We also employ a wider energy window to partially compensate for the loss of sensitivity. After removal of ICS events, 2D filtered back projection (FBP) results reveals an improvement in spatial resolution, and iteratively reconstructed phantom imaging shows enhancements in image contrast, peakvalley-ratio (PVR), and lesion detectability. The application of contour-based ICS rejection method to small animal brain PET has led to notable improvements on both spatial resolution and image quality. By applying wider energy window, the removal technique has significantly enhanced system performance and image quality with a trade-off of a $50 \%$ reduction in sensitivity.

articleTitle: Understanding of Reconstruction-Free Anatomical Imaging Based on Compton Scattering
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Although direct positron emission imaging (dPEI) has been experimentally demonstrated, a practical imaging method compatible with dPEI is preferable to provide the anatomical information of the imaging objects required for attenuation correction. Recently, a reconstruction-free anatomical imaging method, which localizes the Compton scattering point of annihilation gamma rays within an object using ultrafast time-of-flight information on an event-by-event basis and generates an anatomical image without image reconstruction, has been proposed. However, the Compton scattering positions were calculated approximately, and the spatial performance of the generated images is not fully understood. This study introduces a theoretical understanding of the Compton scattering-based reconstruction-free anatomical imaging. We provide the exact algebraic solution at first. Once the algebraic solution is obtained, the spatial performance can be quantitatively estimated by total differentiation. It showed that the differences in the Compton scattering angle in the object impact the spatial resolution of the generated anatomical image. Monte Carlo simulations confirmed that the spatial resolution of the generated images was improved by selecting events with large Compton scattering angles using energy information. In addition, the use of energy information helped enhance the image quality by eliminating multiple scattering events in the object.

articleTitle: Thermal-Neutron Photon Spectroscopy for Passive Confirmation of High Explosives
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An often-employed definition for warhead dismantlement in an arms control context is the separation of fissile material from high explosives (HE). Therefore, a key aspect of dismantlement verification is the ability to confirm the absence or presence of HE. This summary looks at the feasibility of using gamma-ray signatures induced in HE by the intrinsic neutron population emitted by plutonium-containing items for this purpose. This work focusses on characteristic gamma-rays produced when neutrons are captured by elements that are commonly found in HE (H, N, Cl). We compare the gamma-ray spectral shapes in a few regions of interest (ROIs) to compare the expected spectrum from known high explosive compositions to measured spectra. Feasibility of the techniques were validated with data obtained from the plutonium “BeRP” ball surrounded by various thicknesses and compositions of mock HE at the National Criticality Experiments Research Center (NCERC). Configurations were successfully differentiated between bare plutonium and surrounded by three mock HE compositions with a reduced chi-squared template matching method over the ROIs (2.1-2.3 MeV and 9-11 MeV).

articleTitle: Performance of small-diameter muon drift tube chambers with new fast readout ASIC at high background rates
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Experiments like ATLAS at the HL-LHC or detectors at future hadron colliders need muon detectors with excellent momentum resolution at the percent level up to the TeV scale both at the trigger and the offline reconstruction level. This requires muon tracking chambers with high spatial resolution even at the highest background fluxes of ${\$}$\gamma${\$}$-photons and neutrons. Drift-tube chambers are the most cost effective technology for the instrumentation of large-area muon systems providing the required high rate capability and three-dimensional spatial resolution. Thanks to the advances in analog and digital electronics, the new generation small-diameter Muon Drift Tube (sMDT) detectors with 15 mm tube diameter can be used in stand-alone mode up to the background rates as high as expected at future hadron collider experiments, providing event times and second coordinates without the necessity of additional trigger chambers. A new amplifier-shaper-discriminator (ASD) chip in 65 nm TSMC CMOS technology with increased sensitivity and faster baseline recovery has been developed to cope with very high background fluxes by suppressing the pile-up effect, which could mask or distort the muon pulse. It has been tested on sMDT chamber in a muon beam at the CERN Gamma Irradiation Facility (GIF++) at the background counting rate up to 1 MHz. The first results show a significant improvement of the muon detection efficiency at the highest counting rate as desirable for future collider detectors.

articleTitle: Optimization of an indirect conversion X-ray photon counting module for irradiation of X-ray photon flux over 100 Mcps/mm2
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray photon counting (XPC), a low-noise method of detecting transmitted X-rays and binning them into multiple energy regions, is highly promising in fields such as medical imaging, in-line inspection, infrastructure inspection, and cargo inspection. The indirect conversion type XPC detector that combines a scintillator and a Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC) has excellent characteristics such as high inter-channel separation characteristics, high stopping power, and low drive voltage, which are important in these applications. However, the conventional indirect conversion sensor has the serious problems of low maximum count rate and high power consumption of the MPPC. Recently, we reported a Fast-pulse Enhanced MPPC (FE-MPPC) that has very low power consumption and high speed, which can solve these problems. However, the energy resolution and maximum count rate are still insufficient for use with X-ray flux of over $100 \mathrm{Mcps} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$ input count rate. We report the optimization of the parameters of the sensor and the signal processing circuit to solve these problems.

articleTitle: Enhancing Scintillation Efficiency of Scintillator Nanocomposites
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the quest for advanced scintillating materials capable of high-resolution and rapid-response detection, the European Pathfinder project Unicorn proposes to develop novel composite materials consisting of nanoparticle scintillators for radiation detection. This work explores the scintillation properties of scintillator nanocrystals in polymer matrices, aiming at applications in gamma and beta decay detection. The production of such a composite requires to estimate the effect of two specific optical parameters on the performance of the final system: absorption length and Rayleigh scattering. This contribution shows how to experimentally measure these two parameters and investigates their influence on light collection via numerical simulations. The absorption and scattering processes within the material are disentangled by transmittance measurements using a plug-in integrating sphere.

articleTitle: Automatic bed removal from small animal CT images using deep learning based segmentation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Numerous medical imaging applications necessitate removing the subject’s bed from X-ray computed tomography (CT) images. Here we propose and explore a novel automatic approach for bed removal in small animal CT scans. The solution uses a 2D neural network for semantic segmentation of the rats. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time a CNN approach has been used for bed segmentation/removal. The entire dataset used for this study included whole-body CT scans of thirteen rats taken in two different sites by the same scanner model but with different beds designs. After finding the most suitable network architecture, loss function, and training duration (epochs), we performed a 5-fold cross-validation on the remaining dataset acquired at the first site. The results demonstrated high compatibility between the network output and the ground truth labels, with an intersection over union (IoU) value of 0.943 and a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) value of 0.969. However, when training on datasets acquired on the first site and testing on the dataset taken at the second site, the suggested solution didn’t work as well, most likely due to the differences between the datasets.

articleTitle: Development of 3D diamond detectors for application in future particle physics experiments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Chemical Vapour Deposition (CVD) diamond is a wide band-gap material which features high radiation hardness and low leakage current, making it suitable for building solid state detectors for high energy physics and radiotherapy dosimetry applications. 3D diamond detector is a relatively new concept that is characterised by an electrode array fabricated inside a CVD diamond plate using a femto-second laser, resulting in electrically conducting graphitic paths. This fabrication method allows for various complicated electrode structures, making it possible to design novel electrode geometries and optimise the temporal/spatial performance of 3D diamond devices. In this paper, multiple 3D diamond detector structures are modelled. Their electric fields are simulated using Sentaurus TCAD, and the signal response is simulated with Monte Carlo method using Garfield++. Utilising these simulation tools, the performance of different 3D diamond detector structures are analysed. To test the detector performance experimentally, detector prototypes with various structures are built with a femto-second laser equipped with an optical correction using Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs). The Two Photon Absorption (TPA) technique is used to generate point-like charge distributions inside 3D diamond sensor, so that the detector response can be examined with high spatial and temporal resolution.

articleTitle: Unsupervised Tau PET Image Super-Resolution Using Cross-Domain Diffusion Posterior Sampling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography images are often hindered by poor spatial resolution, impacting diagnostic accuracy and quantitation. In this paper, we propose an innovative unsupervised learning framework utilizing diffusion models to enhance the spatial resolution of PET images. Our method leverages a pre-trained diffusion model as a prior to inverse uniform degradation processes like Gaussian blur. By integrating cross-domain autoencoders, we enable the transfer of images between an unknown low-resolution dataset and a Gaussian blur dataset for effective posterior sampling. This framework was trained and validated on unpaired ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-Flortaucipir PET images from Siemens HR+ and GE Discovery MI scanners. We demonstrate that our approach reduces the Fréchet Inception Distance between super-resolved images and actual high-resolution images and improves the spatial resolution of PET images from legacy scanners. These results indicate that our method is promising for addressing super-resolution as well as general PET inverse problems, enhancing the utility of PET imaging in neurodegenerative disease research.

articleTitle: From Radiomics to Deep Learning: Leveraging Gramian Matrix Features in CNNs for NSCLC Survival Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning has demonstrated effectiveness in PET-CT lesion detection [1] and interpreting complex glycotic uptake distributions [2]. Our prior work [3] pioneered the use of Gramian matrices to characterize and synthesize PET tumour heterogeneity. This study employs our “Titanium” features derived from the activation functions within the pretrained VGG-19 convolutional neural network (CNN). From this diverse feature set, we present our survival prediction model and validate the superior efficacy of “Titanium” features in enhancing predictive modeling of 2-year survival for non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients compared to traditional IBSI Radiomic Features. The model was evaluated on 381 NSCLC patients, expertly segmented and split into 80% training, $10 \%$ validation, and $10 \%$ testing sets. “Titanium” features were computed from activation functions across five CNN layers on three orthogonal tumor slices, providing a comprehensive 2.5D representation. This yielded 150 complex textural descriptors. Contrastingly, 203 traditional IBSI radiomic features were derived. Preprocessing included standard scaling, polynomial expansion, and L1-regularized logistic regression for feature selection. Data transformations and feature selection were determined solely from training the set to prevent data leakage. Prediction involved optimizing a multilayer perceptron on the validation set using cross-validation followed by independent testing on the held out set. Our results revealed that the “Titanium” model achieved a Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Area Under the Curve (AUC) of 0.83, significantly outperforming the traditional radiomic approach, which only achieved an AUC of 0.54. This $53.7 \%$ improvement in predictive power highlights the effectiveness of “Titanium” features in capturing more nuanced and predictive information and presents a sophisticated analytical technique for clinical predictive modelling of oncological outcomes.

articleTitle: A CdTe Timepix3-based Sub-micron XCT System for Non-Destructive Testing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The presented work shows results of spectroscopically-enhanced X-ray Computer Tomography (XCT) system, using a nanofocus X-ray source, and a spectroscopic photon-counting detector (SPCD) Timepix3 ASIC, bump-bonded to a 1 mm thick CdTe sensor, for sub-micron nondestructive sample characterization. SPCDs offer capabilities not available in current widespread X-ray detector technology. Their acquisition architecture offers the possibility to simultaneously count each individual photon, and its energy. Access to this information allows a variety of post-acquisition processing techniques that rely on differences in the materials’ attenuation properties and their energy dependence. Successful applications of this approach have been experimentally proven, with the photon energy leveraged to increase material contrast in 2D X-ray attenuation images, which allow for highlighting and segmentation from other background materials. By using the high attenuation semiconductor CdTe, a 100% efficient photon absorption detection scheme is possible, thus simultaneously reducing acquisition time and allowing for visualization of high-density materials with X-ray energies up to 80 keV. The use of a nanofocus X-ray source furthermore extends the system’s capabilities, by removing object unsharpness at high magnification, beyond what is possible with a rotating-anode ($100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ focal spot size) or a microfocus ($10 \mu \mathrm{m}$ focal spot size) X-ray source, achieving spatial resolutions below $1 \mu \mathrm{m}$ with the $55 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pixel pitch Timepix3. Combining the mentioned technical characteristics, along with a bandwidth-efficient data acquisition algorithm to substantially reduce the acquired dataset sizes, results in an innovative XCT system that allows to obtain high-spatial resolution, energy-enhanced 3D reconstructions of heterogeneous samples for non-destructive testing, material research, medical diagnostics, industrial settings, and more.
