articleTitle: Commissioning of the CGEM Inner Tracker
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The extension of the BESIII experiment (IHEP, Beijing) till 2030 prompted a program to improve both the accelerator and the detector. In particular, the current inner drift chamber suffers from aging and it is proposed to replace it with a detector based on cylindrical GEM technology. The CGEM tracker consists of three coaxial layers of triple GEM. The tracker is expected to restore efficiency, improve z-determination and secondary vertex position reconstruction compared to the current inner tracker, with a resolution of $130 \mu \mathrm{m}$ in the xy-plane and better than $300 \mu \mathrm{m}$ along the beam direction. A special readout system was developed for data acquisition. The signals from the detector strips are processed by TIGER, a custom 64-channel ASIC developed in CMOS 110 nm UMC technology, providing analog charge readout via a fully digital output with linear charge readout up to about 50 fC and less than 3 ns jitter. TIGER continuously transmits data across the threshold in triggerless mode to an FPGA-based readout module, the GEM Read Out Card, designed specifically for this system. The module configures the ASICs and organizes the incoming data by creating the event packets when the trigger arrives. The three layers were assembled in October 2023, and a cosmic ray data collection campaign is underway to evaluate the performance of the CGEM tracker before installation.In this presentation, the general status of the CGEM-IT project will be presented with a particular focus on the first results from cosmic ray detection.

articleTitle: Semi-Supervised and Unsupervised Deep Learning Combination for Automated PDL-1 Status Prediction in Lung Cancer with Multi-modal PET/CT Fusion
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Improving the amount of labeled information and the quality of labels is essential for any deep neural networks (DNNs) based classification task using PET/CT images. In addition, high-quality annotation depends on the experience of imaging specialists, introducing a certain variability in the quality level of achieved annotations. In this context, our aim was a combination of semi-supervised and unsupervised deep neural networks using early fusion multi-modal PET/CT images for the prediction of programmed death ligand-1 (PDL-1) status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Models were assessed using areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) considering 95% confidence intervals (CI). Compared with current methods, the proposed methodology enhances the robustness of the model and reduces the influence of outliers. The framework also yielded better performance when compared to current methods for PD-L1 classification, consistently outperforming current methods when using different levels of unlabelled PET/CT images. The results show the effectiveness of combining supervised and unsupervised DNNs for handling data with heterogeneous levels of labelled information.

articleTitle: Multi-Subject Image Synthesis as a Generative Prior for Single-Subject PET Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Large high-quality medical image datasets are difficult to acquire but necessary for many deep learning applications. For positron emission tomography (PET), reconstructed image quality is limited by inherent Poisson noise. We propose a novel method for synthesising diverse and realistic pseudo-PET images with improved signal-to-noise ratio. We also show how our pseudo-PET images may be exploited as a generative prior for single-subject PET image reconstruction. Firstly, we perform deep-learned deformable registration of multi-subject magnetic resonance (MR) images paired to multi-subject PET images. We then use the anatomically-learned deformation fields to transform multiple PET images to the same reference space, before averaging random subsets of the transformed multi-subject data to form a large number of varying pseudo-PET images. We observe that using MR information for registration imbues the resulting pseudo-PET images with improved anatomical detail compared to the originals. We consider applications to PET image reconstruction, by generating pseudo-PET images in the same space as the intended single-subject reconstruction and using them as training data for a diffusion model-based reconstruction method. We show visual improvement and reduced background noise in our 2D reconstructions as compared to OSEM, MAP-EM and an existing state-of-the-art diffusion model-based approach. Our method shows the potential for utilising highly subject-specific prior information within a generative reconstruction framework. Future work may compare the benefits of our approach to explicitly MR-guided reconstruction methodologies.

articleTitle: Novel Polycrystalline Perovskite Materials for Radiation Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Solid-state detection of high energy $\gamma$-rays is traditionally constrained to single crystal materials, which are costly and limited in areal extent due to complex fabrication. We aim to utilize polycrystalline manufacturing methods to broaden the options for detector materials by exploring novel compounds that offer high carrier mobility, effective attenuation, and easier processing. This study introduces preliminary findings on the synthesis and optimization of two candidate materials: KTaO<inf>3</inf> and NaTaO<inf>3</inf>, assessing their capabilities in detecting radiation. We present preliminary response measurements to Am-241 and highlight the critical influence of process parameter optimization on enhancing detector performance. In KTaO<inf>3</inf>, successfully balancing potassium incorporation, which facilitates grain growth, and grain pull-out during mechanical polishing led to improved detector stability and pronounced spectroscopic response. NaTaO<inf>3</inf> samples that underwent densification via Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) showed reduced leakage current compared to KTaO<inf>3</inf>. The samples were able to be biased to at least 400 V and showed significantly larger pulse amplitudes. Further characterization of these samples will be conducted to elucidate how distinct processing parameters influence detector efficiency.

articleTitle: Dynamic PET Image Reconstruction Using Deep Kernel Pretraining from a Total-Body PET Dataset
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The conventional kernel methods in PET image reconstruction integrate image prior information into the forward model using an empirically defined kernel representation. By extending the kernel representation into a trainable neural-network model, the deep kernel method enables a learned kernel representation for improved PET reconstruction. However, the existing deep kernel method focuses on single-subject learning and requires online training for each subject, which increases computational cost. Furthermore, its performance may be impacted if the prior images suffer from noise. In this work, we propose a pertaining strategy for the deep kernel model using a unique training database collected from the ultrahigh-sensitivity uEXPLORER PET scanner. The learning process of deep kernel representation seeks an optimal mathematical formulation for calculating the kernel matrix and is expected to be independent of a specific dataset. Once trained, the deep kernel representation model can be directly applied to other scans to generate patient-specific and scanner-specific kernels from the corresponding image prior data. To demonstrate proof-of-concept, real data evaluation for an older GE DST scanner (2004 model) was conducted. The results show that the proposed population-based learning outperforms the single-subject learning for the deep kernel method for high-temporal resolution dynamic PET image reconstruction.

articleTitle: A new modular device for automatic radiological mapping using visual-based reconstruction algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the context of Dismantling and Decommissioning activities, the establishment of a precise radiological map is essential, as it facilitates the detection of contaminated areas. This task mainly relies on manual labor executed by radiation protection operators. Nonetheless, this conventional approach is prone to human errors, physically taxing for operators, and exposes them to potentially hazardous environments. Consequently, the literature is exploring alternative methodologies, such as integrating radiological measurements with Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) techniques, enabling concurrent mapping of the environment while determining sensor location, independent of GPS or GNSS systems, which are typically ineffective within indoor nuclear facilities. However, existing solutions in the literature often have limitations, such as focusing on specific types of nuclear measurements, being cumbersome in design, and necessitating post-processing steps. To address these limitations, we developed a new modular device for real-time 3D environment reconstruction and localization of radioactivity measurements, based on the Visual Inertial Semi-direct Visual Odometry (VI-SVO) algorithm, which is the most suitable algorithm to operate in a nuclear facility undergoing dismantling, as demonstrated in recent works in the literature. To evaluate the ability of the VI-SVO to correctly identify the radioactivity measurements, we conceived newly datasets with the device: in the laboratory with punctual $\gamma$ and $\beta$ sources and in a real environment undergoing dismantling. As far as we know, this is the first time in the literature a single device is able to correctly localize different types of radiation, thanks to its modularity, being able to be coupled to different radiological sensors. The algorithm takes into account real-world constraints and was able to correctly identify $\gamma$ and $\beta$ count rates from different radiological sources in a real and laboratory environments.

articleTitle: PSIROC: A 64-channel Fully Configurable Read-Out Chip for Low-Gain Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Psiroc is a 64-channel front-end ASIC designed to readout PIN diodes, silicon strips, LGAD and GEMs, handling detector capacitances ranging from 0 up to few hundreds of pF for both input polarities. Psiroc allows triggering down to 0.5 fC on sub-20pF detector capacitances and provides dual-gain energy measurement with excellent Signal-to-Noise Ratio on the high gain (SNR over 10 for 0.5 fC) and large dynamic range on the low gain. For input signals over few pC a channel-wise TOT output is also available. Psiroc can be programmed to output the shapers high/low gain, individual triggers or ToT signals (two output pins per channels). The preamplifier gain is adjustable from 125 mV/pC up to 8 V/pC. Charge measurement is done with rail-to-rail peak detectors that can also be used in a track & hold mode. Analogue data are outed on two multiplexed analogue outputs and can be read-out with an external ADC. Shaping time can be adjusted from 20 ns to $3 \mu \mathrm{s}$ with a step of 20 ns up to 300 ns and a step of 200 ns up to $3 \mu \mathrm{s}$. Channel-by-channel calibration on the trigger thresholds for time trigger and TOT can be done with individual 6-bit DACs. Power consumption of the whole ASIC is 350 mW (under 5.5 mW/channel) and unused blocks can be shut down individually to lower power dissipation.

articleTitle: Simulation of SPECT Imaging for Targeted Alpha-Therapy with Surrogate
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes a simulation workflow of SPECT imaging of targeted alpha-therapy with surrogates for use in imaging-system development and to aid in dosing studies for both target and off-target organs. Targeted alpha therapy isotopes emit alpha particle to treat cancerous regions within the body. Many of the isotopes also emit gamma photons; however imaging with these gamma-ray emissions is difficult due to low injected doses. In addition, these high-energy emissions leads to large levels of scattering in the patient and imaging system, as well as difficulties with collimation. This motivated the recent application of imaging surrogates in target-alpha therapy. Imaging surrogates are isotopes with similar chemical properties to alpha-emitting therapeutic isotopes, but have lack alpha decay and further emit lower-energy gamma rays that are easier to image. To verify the feasibility of imaging alpha therapy with surrogates, we proposed a workflow of calculating the decay and pharmacokinetics of both therapeutic and surrogate isotopes, and a Monte-Carlo simulation of a SPECT system to evaluate imaging performance. We simulated the biodistribution of PSMA-11 tracer with $\mathrm{Pb} 212 / \mathrm{Pb} 203$ therapy/surrogate pair in a human body. With reported two-tissue compartment model of PSMA-11, time activity curves of Pb 212 and progeny and Pb 203 are calculated, allowing us to assess dose and photon emissions under realistic image-acquisition conditions. A collimator-based SPECT system and XCAT human phantom were implemented in the Monte-Carlo model to generate output images. The model simulated photon attenuation and scattering inside the phantom and imaging system. The results showed that imaging of alpha-therapy is feasible by utilizing Pb203 surrogate with low energy emission peak (72.9 keV). Our results demonstrated the utility of our workflow to evaluate the feasibility and performance of imaging targeted alpha therapy with surrogates.

articleTitle: Noise Analysis of the CMOS-DEPFET Front-End of the DSSC Imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The DEPFET sensor with signal compression (DSSC) is a 1-megapixel imager developed for the European XFEL. It is designed to detect X-rays with photon energies between 250 eV and 6 keV, and provides a peak frame-rate of 4.5 MHz. The smallest independent unit of the detector, called module, is composed by two sensors, forming a matrix of 512 by 128 active DEPFET pixels, bump-bonded to 16 readout ASICs. The in-pixel electronics comprises a trapezoidal-shaping filter with programmable gain and timing, an ADC with finely tunable gain and offset, and an 800-word long memory. The characterization of the first CMOS-DEPFET based prototype modules showed equivalent noise charge (ENC) better than $10 e^{-}$rms at megahertz frame-rate and room temperature. In this work, we present the results of a measurement campaign carried out to disentangle the noise contributions of the acquisition chain. We exploited the front-end capabilities and measured the ENC using the knife-edge method, varying the gain of single stages at a time. The measured ENC vs gain were fitted and the gain-dependent and -independent components extracted, and the contributions at key points of the acquisition chain presented.

articleTitle: Super-converged iterative reconstruction via CNN-aided Leap-Frogging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Maximum likelihood expectation-maximization (MLEM) and it is variant ordered-subsets EM (OSEM) have to be terminated in early iterations to reduce noise. Maximum a posteriori (MAP) reconstruction can reach convergence with improved image quality, but it is time consuming. In this study, we trained a conventional convolutional neural network (CNN) as a smart postreconstruction filter to transform the clinical OSEM reconstructed images to converged MAP reconstructed images, using relative difference as penalty function. Quantitative comparisons show that the method can improve lesion contrast as well as reduce background noise.

articleTitle: The DESY II Test Beam Facility - Current Status and Future Plans
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Test beams are an essential tool for detector characterization for detectors used in particle physics, nuclear physics and adjacent fields. By providing multi-GeV particles with precise timing and momentum they enable unique test opportunities for detectors. Such test beams are for example available at CERN, Fermilab and DESY. The DESY II Test Beam Facility provides three beam lines with electrons/positrons with an energy range of 1-6 GeV. Between 400 - 700 users each year are using the test beams at DESY. The test beam remains a very important infrastructure to train the next generation of instrumentation experts, as close to 60% of the users are graduate students and postdocs. All the beam lines are equipped with pixel-beam telescopes that provide the users with reference tracks with a few micron resolution. These telescope are being used by four ut of the five groups at the test beam. DESY II is mainly operated to provide beam to the synchrotron light source PETRA III. As PETRA III is going to be replaced by a next-generation light source called PETRA IV, this will also affect the injector. A status of the current capabilities of the facility will be presented together with the potential upgrade options for the next decade.

articleTitle: ALICE ITS3 Upgrade and First Experiences with the Large Scale Stitched Sensors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ALICE Experiment will upgrade the innermost three layers of its Inner Tracking System (ITS) during the next LHC Long Shutdown (LS3). It will replace the existing conventional setup using individual chips on staves by a novel concept, where wafer-scale sensors are bent to half-cylinders allowing for a tracker with an extraordinarily low material budget of $0.07\% \mathrm{X}_{0}$ per layer. The sensor chip will be based on Monolithic Active Pixels and fabricated in 65 nm CMOS technology exploiting stitching. Six individual sensor chips with dimensions of up to $26.6 \mathrm{~cm} \times 9.8 \mathrm{~cm}$ form three cylinders with radii of 19, 25, and 32 mm surrounding the beam pipe. During R&D, two stitched sensor prototypes, MOSS and MOST, were designed, where the first is sparsely designed and the latter follows a densely integrated in-pixel layout combined with a coarse power grid and granular power switches in the matrix. In the case of in-pixel short circuits, small regions of the matrix can be disconnected from the power grid restoring the remaining part of the overall functionality. The MOST readout is based on global high-speed lines spanning the entire approximately 25 cm long chip, which have successfully been operated. The yield of MOSS is extensively studied with impedance measurements, powering tests, and functional tests, preparing to finally select the final ITS3 chips already on the wafer. For MOSS, it is measured, that 67% of the wafers can be operated with less than 2% powered-off area. A large fraction of shorts can be traced down to anomalous cross-connections in the power grid by thermal imaging. Overall, these results are key milestones toward the realization of the large-scale sensor chip needed for the ITS3 upgrade. This contribution gives an overview of the two large-scale prototypes, outlines results that led to the ITS3 Technical Design Report (TDR), and presents the most recent results after the publication of the TDR.

articleTitle: Determination of active gamma background in a neutron interrogation system for cargo inspection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma ray signatures produced during active neutron interrogation of cargo can be used to detect the illicit diversion of shielded contraband including explosives, chemical weapons, and drugs. Understanding the active gamma background produced in the interrogation setup is essential for the rapid and reliable detection of the gamma signatures produced by the contraband, especially when they are well shielded. In this work, we investigate the active gamma background produced by the interactions of 14 MeV neutrons from a pulsed Sodern Genie 16 D-T generator with our interrogation cell and surrounding environment using $3^{\prime \prime} \times 8^{\prime \prime}$ NaI(Tl) detectors operated in coincidence. We conduct coincidence timing experiments with the NaI(Tl) detectors and identify an appropriate coincidence timing window of 15 ns to sum the partial energy depositions of high energy gammas across several detectors to improve the full energy deposition sensitivity of the array at energies up to 11 MeV. We use results from the coincidence-summed active background measurements with two unshielded NaI(Tl) detectors to inform the shielding design for measurements with the large detector array to interrogate contraband shielded in various cargo including paper and steel.

articleTitle: PET tracers surgical radio-guidance with using a small Compton-angles collimation probe
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: While effective detection of beta emitters could help localise positron emission tomography (PET) tracer-labelled tumours during surgery, current commercially available heavy and cumbersome surgical probes have imprecise directional capabilities and low ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ beta sensitivity, which overall lack relevance for clinical use. In this work, we explored an innovative approach based on small Compton-angles collimation. With 5 times greater directionality, comparable sensitivity and a significantly smaller probe diameter than basic mechanical collimation, small Compton-angles collimation can enable minimally invasive procedures to improve tumor detection during surgery.

articleTitle: Development of next generation MPPC for 150ps TOF applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In time-of-flight (TOF) applications such as TOF positron emission tomography (PET) and several high energy physics experiments, a better time resolution is important for precise identification of the position where radiation is generated. In recent commercial TOF-PET scanners, a TOF resolution of 178 ps has been achieved, and it is expected to reach 150ps in the near future. To improve the time resolution of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), it is necessary to increase the photon detection efficiency (PDE); improve the single photon time resolution (SPTR); and reduce dark noise such as dark count, crosstalk, and afterpulse.We have developed various types of SiPMs, which we call Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs), over the years. We recently developed a new MPPC with an improved structure, which has achieved better coincidence time resolution (CTR) compared to the conventional MPPC, and in this paper we report the new MPPC’s characteristics.

articleTitle: FastIC+: An Analog Front-End including on-chip TDCs for fast timing detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents the 8-channel FastIC+, a low-power consumption and highly configurable multi-channel front-end ASIC with internal digitization, for the readout of photo-sensors with picosecond time resolution and intrinsic gain. This 65 nm technology ASIC can readout positive or negative polarity sensors and provides a digitized measurement of the arrival time and energy of the detected events with a power consumption of 12.5 mW per channel. When connected to FBK NUV-HD LF2 M0 SiPMs, the analog processing achieves a Single Photon Time Resolution of (151 ± 3) FWHM and a Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR) of (127 ± 3) ps, coupled to LYSO:Ce:0.2% Ca scintillators measuring 3.13 × 3.13 × 20 mm<sup>3</sup> (without the digital contribution). On-chip digitization is executed by a Time-to-Digital Converter driven by a Phase-Locked Loop generating a 1.28 GHz clock. Preliminary evaluation of the TDC, conducted on a packaged ASIC within a socket board, yielded a time resolution of 34 ps FWHM with a power consumption of 3.3 mW per channel, demonstrating minimal impact on the analog readout.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of cross-tracer neural network training methods for PET image enhancement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Supervised learning technologies are effective in improving PET image quality when training dataset and test images have similar uptake distributions. However, the diversity of radiopharmaceuticals used in clinical PET imaging significantly increases the challenge of acquiring high-quality training data. In this work, we aim to evaluate how varied training datasets with different radiopharmaceuticals injected and obtained from different PET scanners affect network performance to improve image quality of ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}$-PSMA images. Three cohorts were collected for training, including 126 patients injected with ${ }^{68}$ Ga-PSMA scanned on uMI 550 or uMI 780, 134 patients injected with ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-PSMA scanned on UEXPLORER, and 72 patients injected with ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG scanned on uEXPLORER. The raw data were down-sampled and reconstructed to generate input-target image pairs. The counts ratio for ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}$-PSMA dataset was 1:4 and 1:6, for ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ PSMA and ${ }^{18}$ F-FDG dataset it was 1:5, 1:7.5 and 1:10, respectively. A feedback network architecture was used to train eight networks. Additionally, 10 patients injected with ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}$-PSMA scanned on uMI 550 or uMI 780 served as test data. Network performance was assessed based on liver SNR and lesion SUVmax of the inferred images. Preliminary results indicated that networks trained with the ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG dataset can generate high-quality images comparable to those with the ${ }^{68}$ Ga-PSMA dataset. A comparison between networks trained with ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}$-PSMA and with ${ }^{18}$ F-PSMA datasets revealed that higher quality images were obtainable using higher quality training data from uEXPLORER.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of S-PET, a compact, high sensitivity and high resolution small animal PET prototype
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: S-PET is a compact, high sensitivity and high resolution small animal PET prototype developed at Shenzhen Bay Laboratory. The prototype system is currently being evaluated at Cancer Hospital Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Shenzhen Center. The prototype consists of twenty detector modules arranged in two rings. The system diameter is 80 mm and the axial field of view (FOV) is 104.5 mm. Each detector module is comprised of a two-layer LYSO/BGO pixelated scintillator array and two pieces of 8×8 Hamamatsu S14161-3050HS MPPCs. All MPPC channels were readout by PETsys TOFPET2 ASICs. The inner layer is a 30×60 array of 0.79×0.79×5 mm<sup>3</sup> LYSO crystals. The outer layer is a 20×40 array of 1.22×1.22×7.5 mm<sup>3</sup> BGO crystals. The peak absolute sensitivity was 14.4% including cross-layer crystal scatter (CLCS) events and 11.2% excluding CLCS events at the center of the FOV. The average detector energy resolution derived by averaging the individual crystal spectra was 11.5 ± 2.9% for LYSO and 26.2 ± 3.0% for BGO. The coincidence timing resolution was 0.76 ± 0.08 ns, 2.06 ± 0.25 ns, and 3.17 ± 0.46 ns for LYSO-LYSO, LYSO-BGO and BGO-BGO coincidences, respectively. The image spatial resolution of a point source reconstructed by maximum likelihood expectation maximization with a spatially variant point spread function modeling has an average value of 0.70 ± 0.09 mm. The peak noise equivalent count rate and scatter fraction were 124 kcps at 6.3 MBq and 7.2% for the mouse-sized phantom, and 80 kcps at 7.2 MBq and 12.6% for the rat-sized phantom. For the NEMA image quality phantom (120μCi), the uniformity was 8.2%, and the spillover ratios measured in the water- and air-filled cold region chambers were 24.9% and 3.6%, respectively.

articleTitle: An Open Source General Purpose DMA Engine For DAQ Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a description of a high-performance direct memory access (DMA) engine and kernel driver for data acquisition systems. The DMA engine is designed to support multiple incoming interleaved data channels simultaneously. The kernel driver enables multiple user-space clients to access the DMA engine for receiving or transmitting data, with the ability to create a memory map in the user space to the underlying DMA buffers to minimize the number of data copies required during data recitation or transmission. The DMA engine and kernel driver combination have been deployed in multiple data acquisition systems, including on PCI-Express cards, Xilinx ZYNQ SOC devices, and the Xilinx RFSOC platform, with the platform fully utilizing the bandwidth of the host PCI-Express bus. Recent work on this engine/driver supports direct to GPU and AI accelerator DMA transactions.

articleTitle: Motion Correction for PET Brain Studies using a Marker-less Structured-light Infrared Optical System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Robust and clinically translatable correction for head motion during brain PET studies remains a challenge, especially for longer duration scans and as scanner spatial resolution improves. Here we present results from a marker-less approach that uses a structured-light infrared system that can construct a three-dimensional point-cloud of the surface of the head, providing estimates of rigid body motion at 30 frames per second. The optical United Imaging Healthcare Marker-less Motion tracking system (UMT, version 2) is implemented on a uMI 550 PET/CT scanner at Stony Brook University. We first developed a positioning fixture and optimized the position of the system - on the PET side, facing the patient table, 22 cm from the head. Position accuracy was determined to be about 0.2 mm using a phantom. We have so far collected motion data during 16 human research scans in the supine position including both head-first and feet-first orientations, and for durations up to 90 minutes. The head-first supine orientation is most clinically relevant and demonstrated the most robust results. The feet-first orientation is used for better access for arterial sampling and was found to be more sensitive to changes in facial expression. Improvements in overall PET image quality will be demonstrated in various clinical and research applications. The results suggest that this is a promising approach for accurate and clinically feasible motion correction for brain PET studies.

articleTitle: Performance of a second generation of the Fermilab Constant Fraction Discriminator ASIC for time-stamping long-strip AC-LGAD sensors.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the design and performance characterization results of the second generation of the novel Fermilab Constant Fraction Discriminator ASIC (FCFD) developed to readout AC-coupled low gain avalanche detector (AC-LGAD) sensors. This study presents the performance of the ASIC which was optimized specifically for reading out strip AC-LGAD sensors designed for ePIC experiment at EiC. Performance was measured using charge injection and particle beams with prototype AC-LGAD sensors wirebonded to the FCFD ASIC.

articleTitle: SiPM saturation, depth estimation, and inter-crystal scatter recovery: a simulation study in light-sharing PET detector modules
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET detector modules based on Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) suffer from limited dynamic range due to saturation effects, particularly when bright scintillators with finely pixelated crystal elements are utilized. The saturation effects are exacerbated when light-sharing between scintillator crystal elements is confined or minimized, as a large fraction of the emitted optical photons impinge on a small number of photodetector elements. Such designs, however, have demonstrated superior potential as high-performance, low-cost imaging platforms. We have, therefore, developed a Monte Carlo detector response simulation that incorporates SiPM saturation effects in addition to scintillation and optical photon transport processes. Parameters of the simulation are tuned to the specifications of our Prism-PET detector modules, which incorporate finely-pixelated scintillator crystal elements coupled to a segmented light guide for confined, deterministic light-sharing. The simulation results are in agreement with previous analytical models of SiPM saturation and demonstrate significant non-linearity in the detector response as energies exceed 300 keV. Additionally, saturation effects are shown to have a dramatic effect on the depth-estimation parameter and its distribution, with profound consequences for depth calibration and recovery of inter-crystal scatter events.

articleTitle: High Temperature Detector for Material Accounting in Advanced Reactors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-temperature-capable detectors are essential for nuclear material accounting in advanced fuel cycles like Molten Salt Reactors (MSRs). Dual-mode scintillators, capable of detecting gamma-rays and neutrons simultaneously, are highly advantageous for such environments. They enhance measurement accuracy and efficiency. $\mathrm{Cs}_{2} \mathrm{LiLa}(\mathrm{Br}, \mathrm{Cl})_{6}$ (CLLBC) is a notable dual-mode scintillator, renowned for its excellent gamma detection and ability to discriminate gamma-rays from neutrons. It’s readily available commercially from RMD. At room temperature, CLLBC shows a $3.0 \%$ energy resolution at 662 keV and a light yield of approximately $45,000 \mathrm{ph} / \mathrm{MeV}$. Its gamma-neutron pulse shape discrimination figure of merit stands at about 3.5 at room temperature. A high temperature (HT) detector was designed and manufactured using the CLLBC scintillator and a high temperature PMT (R1288AH-27) from Hamamatsu. The detector was characterized from $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $175^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ with various gamma sources and digital pulse processing MCA. The 662 keV energy resolution was measured to be $5 \%$ at RT and $7.8 \%$ at $175^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. We were able to resolve gamma energies from 60 keV to 1.5 MeV when a combination of multiple sources was used. In this presentation we will discuss the data and the significance of radioisotope identification and quantification for NMA applications at high temperatures and count rates.

articleTitle: High Granularity Readout Time Projection Chamber technology development for the future lepton collider
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A worldwide community of physicists specializing in Lepton Collider Time Projection Chambers is working to realize an exceptional physics program at the energy frontier, focusing on electron-positron collisions, particularly for the International Linear Collider (ILC) and the Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC). The International Large Detector (ILD) is one of the proposed detector concepts for the next e+e-collider. The Time Projection Chamber (TPC) is a promising technology as a central main tracker, along with silicon tracking detectors inside and outside the TPC, all embedded in a 3T solenoid field. After the last few years, an extensive R&D for the track detector have been developed within the collaboration of LCTPC. A large prototype TPC in a 1.0 T magnetic field, which allow accommodating up to seven identical Micro Pattern Gaseous Detector (MPGD) readout modules, is being studied using the 5GeV electron beam at DESY. The performance of the drift velocity, spatial resolution, the dE/dx resolution has been measured in several successful beam test experiments with the different readout concepts (GEM, Resistive Micromegas and GridPix) with monolithic cooling plate in a 2-phase CO2. In the updated CEPC Physics and Detector Technology Design Report (TDR), the TPC will be a cylindrical drift volume with an inner radius of 0.6 m, an outer radius of 1.8 m, and a half-length of 2.9 m, which can enlarge the tracking acceptance (cosθ~0.98). It can provide up to thousands of 3D space points, and the single hit resolution can achieve approximately 100μm in the r-φ plane. There are two options of the pad and pixel readout structure, and it can be a potential technology, especially at the high luminosity Z-pole. In this talk, we will present the track reconstruction performance results and summarize the next steps of the pad/pixelated TPC technology for the future lepton colliders.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of a High-Sensitivity Small-Animal PET/CT System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The performance of a high-sensitivity small-animal PET/CT system was evaluated using the NEMA NU-4 standard. The system achieved a spatial resolution of better than 1 mm (full width at half maximum) within the central 50 mm field of view. The absolute sensitivity was measured to be 13.3%; image noise level 4.1%; recovery coefficients 0.10,0.60,0.89,0.96,0.92 for the 1-5 mm cylindrical rods, respectively; spill over ratios for water and air cold regions 5.6% and 4.5%, respectively. On the PET image of a Micro Derenzo phantom the 0.9 mm rods were clearly resolvable. A study on SD rats demonstrated that the system is suitable for performing whole-body dynamic imaging in a single bed, with a short scan time (2-5 mins) or a low dose injection ($40 \ \mu \mathrm{Ci}$). In all cases, the PET images acquired from the system were free of artifacts with accurate quantification in tracer uptake. In short, this system is capable of quantitative small animal imaging studies.

articleTitle: Development of an 18-Picosecond Resolution, 64-Channel TDC, embedded in a Xilinx Field-Programmable Gate Array
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) play a critical role in numerous high-precision applications across the fields of nuclear science, biomedical engineering, and digital communication systems, including Time-of-Flight (ToF) ranging, Positron Emission Tomography (PET), and All-Digital Phase-Locked Loops (ADPLLs). The demand for flexible architectures providing higher timing precision for an increased number of channels has become a focal point due to the limitations of traditional single-channel TDCs which suffer from low bitrate and resolution. This paper presents the design, implementation and commissioning of a 64-channel TDC using the latest Xilinx Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) technology, aimed at overcoming these challenges and significantly enhancing measurement capabilities. The design is based on a combination of Tapped Delay Line (TDL) and Coarse Counter techniques to optimize both precision and dynamic range. The implementation achieved a remarkable temporal resolution of 18 picoseconds in an exemplary multi-stop implementation providing a sequence of nine time stamps in each cycle. This paper details the system architecture, the implementation challenges and the performance evaluation.

articleTitle: Posterior Parameter Estimation in Compartmental Models from Dynamic PET: a Simulation Study of Feedback-enhanced CVAE
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This research introduces a feedback-enhanced Conditional Variational Auto-encoder (Feedback-CVAE) for estimating posterior parameters in compartmental models from dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) imaging data. By integrating a corrective feedback signal to the latent space in the CVAE architecture, our approach enhances the reliability and accuracy of posterior estimates. The study uses simulation datasets to compare the performance of Feedback-CVAE against existing methods, including traditional Approximation Bayesian computation (PET-ABC) and the existing CVAE-dual-encoder. Our findings indicate that Feedback-CVAE is approximately 3000 times faster and exhibits significantly reduced uncertainty in posterior predictions than PET-ABC. The Feedback-CVAE outperforms CVAE-dual-encoder in terms of the prediction reliability. Specifically, Feedback-CVAE shows reduced bias in the predicted posterior distribution for four out of five kinetic parameters within the two-compartment model, compared to the CVAE-dualencoder. These results highlight the effectiveness of feedback mechanisms in improving CVAE models in the posterior estimation in dynamic PET imaging and encourage further exploration of Feedback-CVAE’s application to real dynamic PET imaging dataset.

articleTitle: Prism-PET super module with tapered crystals for high-resolution TOF-DOI brain PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Brain-dedicated positron emission tomography (PET) scanner with time-of-flight (TOF) and depth-of-interaction (DOI) capabilities has transformative potential for advancing diagnosis and research in neurology. We recently introduced a novel singled-ended TOF-DOI Prism-PET detector module with tapered crystals to minimize light leak, enhance energy, DOI, and timing resolutions, and enable the first experimental report of optical photon TOF (oTOF)-based depth encoding at the detector module level. In this study, we developed the 2×2 Prism-PET super module by fabricating four tapered Prism-PET modules into a 2×2 array with interleaved multiplexing (iMux) scheme to alleviate the saturation effects for silicon photomultiplier (SiPMs) at edges and corners and mitigate a large number of readout channels. The super module consists of a 32 × 32 array of 1.5 X $1.5 \mathrm{X} 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ lutetium yttrium oxyorthosillicate (LYSO) crystals which were tapered down to 1.2 X $1.2 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ at the crystal-readout interface and coupled 4-to-1 to a 16 × 16 array of $3 \mathrm{X} 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPM pixels on one end and to a prismatoid light guide array on the opposite end. All crystals in the 2×2 super module are clearly resolved from the flood histogram result. The full width at half maximum (FWHM) energy, energy-weighted DOI, oTOF-weighted DOI, and timing resolutions are $7.76+/-1.18 \%, 2.28+/-0.48 \mathrm{~mm}, 5.81+/-1.24 \mathrm{~mm}$ FWHM, and 311 ps respectively.

articleTitle: The micro-GPD, a Gas Pixel Detector with a new electron multiplier structure monolithically integrated on top of a finely pixelated readout ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We describe the design, fabrication and initial testing of a new generation of Gas Pixel Detectors, that we dubbed micro-GPD(u-GPD). The u-GPD is a monolithic device comprising a 50 um pitch, large area, analog readout ASIC with hexagonal pixels, combined with a very fine pitch (43.3 um) 1-D or 2-D gas proportional charge amplifying structure based on the concept of the micro-gap chamber. The charge multiplying structure is built directly on the top metal of a custom 180 nm CMOS pixelated readout ASIC, i.e. on the metal pads which act as the charge collecting electrodes each connected to the input stage of their respective individual pre-amplifier. This is achieved by adding, to the already developed readout ASIC, two finely patterned layers, one insulator and one metal, as a post-processing micro-fabrication step at a specialized foundry. The 2 um thick, high dielectric strength insulator sits in between the additional metal layer and the one on top of the pixels. These three layers together, constitute the anode-cathode gap of a microgap like charge multiplication structure. A moderate high-gain, of the order of 300, is obtained with a relatively low bias voltage. Such a gas gain is more than enough to image the photoelectron track and reconstruct the position, energy, time of arrival and polarimetric parameters of 2-10 keV energy X rays. Indeed, because the micro-gap anode-cathode distance is only 2 micrometers, the charge collection at the pixels is extremely fast and efficient. Test results on several geometries 1-D (strips) and 2-D (mesh) are presented.

articleTitle: Anomaly Detection in Brain Tumor Imaging: Few-Shot Learning with Generative Models and Knowledge Transfer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Anomaly detection plays a vital role in the early identification of brain tumors in MRI scans, and it directly impacts diagnostic accuracy and patient outcomes. Despite its importance, current methods often fall short in handling sparse labeled data and precisely localizing anomalies. In this study, an innovative method that integrates Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) with few-shot learning and transfer learning techniques, offering a new perspective in handling scarce labeled data in medical image analysis. At the core of the proposed method is a Vision Transformer-based generator, showcasing the dedication to advancing medical diagnostics technology. This generator, paired with a uniquely adapted discriminator benefiting from a pre-trained VGG16 network, enhances the model’s efficiency and accuracy in anomaly detection. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through its ability to distinguish between normal and patho- logical brain images obtained from a public dataset. In our study, the model achieved anomaly scores of approximately $0.14 \pm 0.18$ for normal images and $0.23 \pm 0.76$ for abnormal images. The enhanced precision achieved in anomaly detection and localization signifies a notable advancement beyond current methodologies. These outcomes pave the way for the creation of increasingly sophisticated and dependable diagnostic instruments, thereby facilitating more precise detection of brain tumors.

articleTitle: Super-gq DePFET put to the Test
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The development of DePFET (Depleted P-channel Field Effect Transistor) based sensors has gained significant momentum in recent years. Be it the PXD for the Belle II experiment, the DePFET based MIXS sensor aboard the planetary science mission BepiColombo, that will soon reach Mercury, the development of ultrafast real-time imagers for direct electron detection (EDET) at TEMs or the development of the Wide Field Imager (WFI) of the next generation X-ray telescope Athena. These sensors have been customized according to specific application requirements, including high frame rates, accurate position resolution, Fano-limited energy resolution, or maximized dynamic range. One of the development endeavors has resulted in the super- $\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{q}}$ DePFET technology. This technology achieves significant improvements in signal-to-noise ratio by shrinking the internal gate while keeping the external gate untouched, effectively avoiding short channel effects. Charge generated in the fully depleted bulk is collected in this so called internal gate below the channel, whereby the conductivity of the transistor is modulated, and the number of signal electrons can be determined. Simulations predict a considerable increase in charge gain by a factor of three ($1.7 \mathrm{nA} / \mathrm{e}-)$ and white noise of less than one e- ENC, while limiting impact ionization near the drain end of the channel. These improvements make super- $\mathrm{g}_{\mathrm{q}}$ DePFETs potentially capable of reaching sub-electron noise levels with a single readout. Based on these findings a test production has been initiated and recently completed. Studies on energy resolution, gain improvement, noise as well as optimal operation parameters are carried out in a specially designed test setup that caters to the unique requirements of the DePFET sensors. It ensures reliable characterization under the conditions encountered in various conceivable applications. Moreover, the setup allows investigations down to cryogenic temperatures for the first time on matrix level.

articleTitle: Exploring high-entropy design in rare-earth aluminum garnet scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cargo inspection via high-energy X-ray radiography is an important imaging modality for national security applications where 2-9 MeV X-rays are used to identify contraband through non-intrusive inspection. CdWO4 single crystal scintillator is a common detector material for this application, however, it suffers from a relatively low light yield and toxicity. As the need for this imaging capability grows, a search for new scintillator materials for this application is ongoing. In this work, single-component, multi-component, and high-entropy aluminum garnet ceramics are synthesized to investigate the effect configuration entropy has on the scintillation properties. In addition, the composition (Y,Gd,Tb,Lu)<inf>3</inf>Al<inf>5</inf>O<inf>12</inf>:Ce is investigated for use in high-energy X-ray radiography applications. Aluminum garnet powders are synthesized via a wet chemistry method and are densified into ceramics via uniaxial hot pressing. XRD measurements are done to confirm the phase purity of powders and ceramics. Scintillation properties such as light yield, decay time, and afterglow are evaluated. Radiation hardness is evaluated through the measurement of scintillation properties before and after irradiation with a ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ source. It is found that afterglow is suppressed in the compositions with greater configurational entropy.

articleTitle: A Study on Inference Method of Minimum Detectable Activity for Measurement of Liquid Radioactive Waste
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: These The dismantlement of the Kori Nuclear Power Plant Unit 1, decommissioned in 2017, is projected to generate approximately 14,500 drums of medium and low-level radioactive waste, necessitating stringent safety and classification measures. This study focuses on employing Gaussian Processes (GP) for the precise calculation of the Minimum Detectable Activity (MDA) to ensure accurate assessment of low-activity radioactive waste. Assuming that the point source activity was 10 Bq, the MDA was calculated when each was measured at 0.5 to 45 hours with 8 points. At a depth of 1 and 5 cm in the water phantom, the MDA can be reached with a true value that can be measured after roughly 55 and 71 hours, respectively. To infer the MDA, at least five data points must be measured. Radioisotopes can be detected accurately by employing inferred MDA, and worker doses can be calculated with precision.

articleTitle: Rad-Hard FPGAs in Digital Instrumentation & Control Infrastructure Modernization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A comprehensive evaluation of the radiation resistance of field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) is essential to enable digital instrumentation and control (I&C) upgrades in operating nuclear power plants (NPPs). In this study, we explored various testing methodologies to evaluate the single-event upsets (SEUs) and TID effects affecting the configuration memory of static random access memory (SRAM) based FPGAs. Methods aimed at quantifying the radiation upset sensitivity of SRAM-FPGAs in terms of SEU cross section are identified. Here, we present results from our preliminary study aimed at establishing FPGA programming and verification capabilities that are required towards demonstrating such methods. We have successfully developed, tested, synthesized, and implemented a ‘test’ design on an SRAM-FPGA. Radiation-induced upsets in the configuration memory of the FPGA was emulated manually to develop an understanding of bitstream verification through FPGA configuration memory readback and bit-pattern comparison. Our preliminary tests effectively demonstrated the methodology to identify the total number of radiation-induced bit-flips and determine the SEU cross section of the FPGA.

articleTitle: Design and Optimization of Integrated Analog Neural Network for In-Sensor Processing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new approach in signal processing involves integrating Analog Neural Networks (ANN) directly into the frontend ASICs utilized for signal processing tasks, such as those handling sensor arrays in PET and SPECT applications. This approach, which eliminates the necessity for an Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC) and FPGAs, aims to mitigate power consumption challenges commonly encountered in digital solutions, especially with a growing number of channels. A first prototype of an ASIC was previously designed and tested. This study introduces a novel neuron topology tailored to surmount limitations observed in prior designs. Computation is executed with 5-bit precision (1-bit sign, 4-bit data) employing a C-2C Digital-to-Analog-Converter (DAC). Compared to previous iterations, this implementation showcases a substantial 90% reduction in the capacitive bank’s footprint, alongside a remarkable enhancement in energy efficiency, estimated at 3.5 trillion operations per watt (TOPs/W).

articleTitle: Dry processing of perovskite films and composites for ionizing radiation detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskites are increasingly studied for the detection of high energy photons, and have already demonstrated their potential in thin-film dosimetry and even imaging, when the prepared as single crystals. In both cases and in most of the literature perovskite are prepared from solutions of the lead halide precursors, which implies issues in terms of scalability, substrate integration, among others. In this paper we discuss the potential of dry synthetic methods in the preparation of perovskite detectors. Perovskite thin film detectors can be prepared with physical vapor deposition (PVD), methods that are already in place in the industry. Moreover, these processes allow for the deposition of perovskite films with high purity, finely controlled thickness, and their integration in multilayer devices. [1] We show PVD-processed detectors with low dark and noise current, stable at reverse bias, and with X-ray sensitivity $\gt30 \mu \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{Gy} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. For the fabrication of thick perovskite materials, we show a dry synthetic route to prepare free-standing perovskite-polymer composite disks with thickness tunable from 25 to $250 \mu \mathrm{m}$. [2] These composite disks can be laminated on rigid and flexible substrates leading to functional detectors, with high environmental stability and promising limit of detection.

articleTitle: Development Status of Combination X-ray Luggage Scanner with Automatic AI Detection for National Security Facilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Korea Customs Service is a national agency launched to secure national fiscal revenue by managing the export and import customs clearance order at Korea’s borders and to perform the mission of protecting domestic industries through crackdowns on smuggling. However, as the customs administration environment changes, such as national economic development, and global trade liberalization, the role and duties of the Korea Customs Service have expanded into new fields, and currently include management of customs clearance for travelers, securing financial revenue through the imposition of tariffs and domestic taxes on imported goods, crackdown on smuggling, and other activities [1].The baggage scanners used by traveler, express, and postal customs offices are entirely made of foreign products. Because foreign baggage scanners use a single energy of 160 kV to inspect cargo, they have the disadvantage of being completely transparent to very thin objects, making it impossible to check their contents, and the original data files containing radiographic information are locked by the manufacturers with a lockdown function. It is difficult to obtain.In this study, we aim to introduce the current status of development of a domestically produced baggage scanner that can identify hazardous goods with an AI automatic reading function while resolving the problems that have arisen while using foreign baggage scanners at customs sites in the Republic of Korea together with the Korea Customs Service starting in 2021.

articleTitle: 131I imaging with MACACO Compton camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The IRIS group of IFIC-Valencia has developed a Compton camera prototype for medical imaging. The prototype MACACO is being tested for radiopharmaceutical imaging. First tests with different medical radiotracers in phantoms and patients pointed out the necessity of a detector with improved detection efficiency. For this purpose, MACACO III+, a new prototype version with an enlarged second detector area, has been assembled. Recently, experimental tests with the improved system have been conducted in the hospital La Fe with<sup>131</sup> I-MIBG using two different phantoms. Results of functional tests performed in the laboratory, as well as reconstructed images of the phantoms filled with the medical radionuclide are presented.

articleTitle: Proton irradiation on Hydrogenated Amorphous Silicon flexible devices
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiation damage test in hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si H) flux and dose-measuring flexible devices has been performed with a 3 MeV proton beam to evaluate combined displacement and total ionizing dose damage. The tested devices had two different configurations and thicknesses: The first device was a $2 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick $\mathbf{n - i}-\mathbf{p}$ diode having a $5 \mathrm{~mm} \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}$ area. The second device was a $5 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick charge selective contact detector having the same area. Both the devices were deposited on a flexible Polyimide substrate and were irradiated up to the fluence of $10^{16} \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{eq}} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. The effect of annealing for partial sensitivity recovery at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for 12 hours was also studied, and a final characterization of the annealed devices was performed. This test is the first combined displacement and total ionizing dose test on flexible a-Si:H devices.

articleTitle: ADA5Dv0, an Analog Front-End Prototype for the Readout of LGAD Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents an analog front-end channel for the readout of Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) based particle detectors for the next generation of space-borne experiments. The circuit has been designed in a 65 nm CMOS technology. The charge generated by the detector is integrated by a Charge Sensitive Amplifier (CSA) with dynamic signal compression features to achieve improved noise performance, along with enhanced time resolution capabilities over the wide range of input charge to be detected (from 38 fC to 16 pC). An RC-CR shaper with selectable shaping time, a fast discriminator and a Time-to-Amplitude Converter (TAC) complete the readout circuit. An SNR around 300, together with a time resolution of slightly below 50 ps, is achieved in post-layout simulations.

articleTitle: A Comparative Study of Various Scatter Estimation Methods in PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Several scatter correction strategies in PET have been compared in this study. Namely, we studied single-scatter simulation or SSS without scaling (’absolute’), SSS with scaling using conventional tail-fitting (TF), SSS with scaling using maximum likelihood scatter scaling (MLSS), energy-based scatter (EBS), and Monte Carlo (MC) scatter estimation methods. Two phantoms, a NEMA NU-2 image quality (IQ) phantom and a large elliptical uniform phantom, were used in the evaluation of the studied methods using a clinical PET/CT scanner (Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT). Results suggest that the absolute method can underestimate scatter due to the lack of accounting for multiple scatter or outside field-of-view activity. Similarly, the studied MC approach appeared to underestimate the scatter, especially when there is activity present outside the field-of-view. Studying the NEMA IQ images, TF, MLSS and EBS resulted in comparable images with an average contrast recovery coefficient (averaged over all hot spheres) of, respectively, 87.5%, 88.1%, 87.8% better than the absolute (average CRC 83.0%) and MC scatter (average CRC 86.1%) while the average background variability of images were similar (2.4% to 2.5%) regardless of the scatter correction method. The large elliptical phantom images also were similar for TF and MLSS while EBS showed a slightly lower global activity due to higher scatter fraction and absolute and MC scatter estimates led to nonuniform images due to scatter underestimations.

articleTitle: Enhancing timing of Ce-doped garnet scintillators by complex codoping
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The work deals with timing characteristics of garnet scintillation materials, especially for applications like time-of-flight PET or future collider experiments. While cerium-activated oxide scintillation single crystals are known for their fast performance due to rapid d-f relaxation in Ce<sup>3+</sup>. Meanwhile, the extended scintillation decay time of Gd<inf>3</inf>(Al,Ga)<inf>5</inf>O<inf>12</inf>:Ce (GAGG:Ce), the brightest oxide scintillator, still does not meet the requirements for the upgrade 2 of the central part of the LHCb electromagnetic calorimeter in CERN. Additionally, GAGG:Ce and other Ga-containing scintillators are typically grown in large sizes exclusively in Ir crucibles. Attempts to substitute Ga with Sc in the gadolinium garnet Gd<inf>3</inf>(Al,Sc)<inf>5</inf>O<inf>12</inf>:Ce (GSAG:Sc,Ce) grown from Mo crucibles resulted in a significant decrease in light yield compared to GAGG:Ce, although without a notable improvement in timing.The results obtained in this work certify that tuning the doping concentrations of Ca2+ and Mg2+ ions provides the enhancement of timing performance of Ce-doped YAG and GAGG scintillators due to elimination of carrier traps and acceleration of carrier transport to luminescence centers, independently on the host composition. Apart of that, YAG is more promising as host, because it can be obtained in cheap W/Mo crucibles in contrast to GAGG and other Ga-containing crystals. Due to the synergy between Ca2+ and Mg2+ dopants in garnets hosts, we demonstrated that improved combination of light yield and decay time can be achieved in Ce-doped garnets, i.e. larger number of prompt photons can be generated for fast-timing applications. At the same time, Sc,Ca codoped YAG:Ce is another promising approach to get fast scintillation crystals with a high light yield that may be grown by a cheap technology from W crucibles.

articleTitle: The CSES-Limadou Mission and the HEPD-02 Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The CSES-Limadou program is a scientific collaboration between the Italian Space Agency and the China National Space Administration. The program aims to realize a constellation of multi-instrument satellites, monitoring ionospheric parameters probably related to earthquakes. The goals of this mission are the development of new models to study the litho-ionospheric coupling, the monitoring of solar activity and its interaction with the magnetosphere, and the study of the energy spectrum of cosmic rays at low energies, extending data from experiments like PAMELA and AMS. The launch of the second satellite will take place on December 12, 2024. The enhancements made on the High-Energy Particle Detector (HEPD-02) allow the satellite to acquire data along the whole orbit and for different physics cases at the same time, thanks to a redesigned trigger system providing prescaled and concurrent triggers. Trigger capabilities have been extended for Gamma Ray Burst detection, adding dedicated trigger masks and rate meters. HEPD-02 is the first space detector employing Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) as a tracker, featuring increased spatial resolution, better power consumption and lower noise compared to HEPD-01. A campaign of tests has been conducted, in compliance with the space qualification standards, to ensure the correct operation of HEPD-02 in the space environment and its resistance to mechanical stresses. Beam tests with different particle species and energies allowed the evaluation of the detector’s scientific performance. To enhance performance and fully exploit the correlations within signals, a deep learning-based event reconstruction chain was developed. The results were tested and validated using both simulated data and test-beam measurements. This contribution will discuss the innovations made to HEPD-02, the space qualification tests and the current status of the CSES-02 mission.

articleTitle: Advancements in Deep Cryogenic Electronics Utilizing Field-Programmable Gate Arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Electronic systems capable of operating cold at deep cryogenic temperatures, sometimes close to absolute zero are in growing demand. New developments in high performance instrumentation, quantum computing, experimental physics, and spaceborne systems are increasing the need for this kind of electronics. Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) are a good option for providing the circuitry solution to support these applications. In this work we describe requirements for the reliable operation of digital circuits and analog to digital converters utilizing commercially available deep submicron FPGAs. We will analyze and characterize devices based on 28 nm HPL process offered by TSMC and widely available on commercially available as off-the-shelf (COTS) devices. The characterization of these devices is focused mainly on power dissipation, speed performance, and non-uniform heat distribution at temperatures ranging from 4.2K to 77K.

articleTitle: Collimator-less Imaging Method for Anterior View of Thyroid Scintigraphy using U-Net Model: Monte-Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thyroid scintigraphy is pivotal for detecting thyroid function irregularities, often utilizing gamma cameras and ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}}$ Tc Pertechnetate as a tracer. We employ deep learning method in thyroid scintigraphy to reduce measurement time and dose. We utilize a Monte Carlo method and a XCAT phantom to simulate thyroid scintigraphy. Our deep learning system effectively distinguishes normal thyroids, hot and cold nodules, hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism. The images reconstructed by deep learning method exhibit an eight-fold improvement for signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in a tenth measurement time compared to that of conventional methods. This demonstrates the potential for deep learning-based systems to increase efficiency and reduce patient radiation exposure in thyroid scintigraphy.

articleTitle: Accelerated Direct PET Attenuation and Scatter Corrections Using Generation-Prior Diffusion Model (GPDM)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation and scatter corrections play pivotal roles in PET image processing for accurate quantification. While CT-based corrections are conventional, they encounter limitations such as respiratory motion and metal artifacts. Recent advances in generative deep neural networks offer promising alternatives by directly estimating attenuation and scatter-corrected (ASC) PET from non-attenuation and non-scatter-corrected (NASC) PET. In GAN-based methods, the generator typically learns to map input data to the desired output (e.g. NASC PET to ASC PET) in one step. While this approach can be effective in generating realistic images, it often encounters significant challenges, such as unstable training and mode collapse. On the other hand, Denosing Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), a recent innovative solution based on probability theory, has emerged to address these issues, and gradually refines the image over numerous steps (e.g., 1,000 steps). In our previous study, a conditional DDPM (cDDPM) model, where the diffusion process was conditioned with NASC PET to generate ASC PET, outperformed conventional CycleGAN and conditional GAN (cGAN) approaches in the direct PET attenuation and scatter corrections [1]. However, the high computational complexity is one of the main drawbacks of DDPM. The training and inference steps of DDPM can be computationally intensive, requiring significant resources in terms of time, memory, and hardware. To overcome these problems, this study proposes a new acceleration method for the fast learning and sampling process of DDPM. In this method, named Generation-Prior Diffusion Model (GPDM), cDDPM is conditioned with prior variables obtained by applying a U-NET or cGAN to generate ASC PET from NASC PET. GPDM can significantly reduce the sampling steps owing to the high similarity between conditioned images and ASC PET. Consequently, computational complexity can be effectively decreased.

articleTitle: Compact Lidar Digitizing Receiver (CoLiDR) Benchtop Measurements with the HDSoCv2 Waveform Digitizing ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this report we describe a novel benchtop installation of the Compact Lidar Digitizing Receiver (CoLiDR) system, which is capable of measuring the time domain waveform induced by a laser impulse on all elements of a 64 element pixelated Silicon Photomultiplier array simultaneously; while meeting a size, weight, and power requirement that is suitable for space missions on cubesats or planetary/lunar mapping projects. We will report measurements of the novel digitizing ASIC HDSoCv2, using its internal current amplifier circuit, coupled to an Onsemi 8x8 SIPM array measuring a pulsed laser synchronized to the digitizer system.

articleTitle: Optimising Charge Transport Properties in FAPbBr3 Single Crystals for Direct Radiation Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskite single crystals have demonstrated potential as excellent direct radiation detectors. However, the growth of high quality perovskite single crystals is challenging due to long growth times and spontaneous nucleation. In this study, we demonstrate the growth and optimisation of bulk charge transport properties in FAPbBr<inf>3</inf> single crystals (FPB SCs) with the use of the sulfonic zwitterionic additive 3-(Decyldimethylammonio)propanesulfonate inner salt (DPSI). A DPSI concentration of 10% was found to be ideal for growing high quality FPB SCs. The FPB SCs synthesised using 10% DPSI show a relatively high electron and hole mobility of 84 cm<sup>2</sup> V<sup>-1</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> and 30 cm<sup>2</sup> V<sup>-1</sup> s<sup>-1</sup> respectively and a high carrier mobility lifetime product of 2.9 ×10<sup>-3</sup> cm<sup>2</sup> V<sup>-1</sup>. A high X-ray sensitivity of 1.1 × 10<sup>3</sup> μC Gy<inf>air</inf><sup>-1</sup> cm<sup>-2</sup> is obtained from these devices when irradiated with a 50 kV X-ray source at an applied electric field of 100 V cm<sup>-1</sup>. The device showed a low detection limit of 72 nGy s<sup>-1</sup> and a low and stable leakage current of 30 nA cm<sup>-2</sup> (2.7 nA). Preliminary α spectroscopy measurements carried out from a <sup>241</sup>Am α source show a resolvable α peak from 10% DPSI FPB SCs at -130 V and a mean rise time of 1.3 μs under a bias voltage of -30 V. Therefore, these devices show great potential to be used as high resolution α and γ-ray spectroscopic detectors.

articleTitle: A 16-channel 14-Bit, 1.2-Msps/channel, Three-stage Hybrid ADC with SAR/SS/TDC Architecture for Dark Matter Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Energy-efficient front-end electronics plays an important role to construct space-bone γ-ray radiation detector systems for the next-generation dark matter detection mission of China. A multichannel analog-to-digital converter (ADC) application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is required to digitize the analog signals represented charge quantity from a PMT detector with the plastic scintillator. The challenges of the ADC lie in multiple channels, a resolution of 14 bits, a sampling rate of large than 1 Msps with a low power condition. Two hybrid-architecture ADC prototype chips that combines successive approximate register (SAR), single-slope (SS) ramp, and a flash time-to-digital converter (TDC) have been designed by our group in the last three years. Both typical topologies and fabricated process have been verified. However, the developed ADCs cannot meet the engineering application of front-end electronics. In this paper, we propose an improved version of ADC to enhance the channel numbers and to improve the overall performances. A 16-channel ADC prototype chip has been designed and fabricated in 0.18-μm CMOS technology with a 1.8/3.3V power supply. The die size is 2.85 mm × 3.35 mm. With a clock frequency of 50 MHz, the simulated ENOB and the sampling rate are 12.87 bits and 1.27 Msps, respectively. The power dissipation is 3.9 mW/channel. The 16-channel ADC chip is currently under testing, and preliminary results have been obtained. For future work, the ADC circuits will be integrated into a multichannel front-end readout ASIC together for all-digital data output.

articleTitle: Characterisation of the Effects of Radiation Damage on Low Gain Avalanche Diodes for Low-LET Microdosimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low gain avalanche diodes have become of recent interest to their intrinsic gain and superior timing characteristics. These have been investigated for use in radiation dosimetry to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of silicon microdosimeters in response to low-LET radiation. In this study, LGADs irradiated with different levels of radiation damage were assessed for different proton energies. Spatial, temporal and energy domain masking techniques were applied to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the detectors. The gain of the LGADs studied showed a significant decrease in the gain along with a decrease in the variation in gain due to different LET radiation. This makes direct application of LGADs for radiation dosimetry difficult due to the radiation type and LET dependence of the LGAD response and thus requires further investigation and modelling.

articleTitle: A Geometric Calibration Method for a Multi-Source and Multi-Detector CT System
