publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A high temporal resolution of the CT system is necessary for dynamic imaging. Increasing the scan arrangement by increasing the number of X-ray sources and detectors is a way to improve the temporal resolution of CT system, but more sources and detectors will bring difficulties to the geometric calibration work of the CT system. This paper proposes a geometric calibration method for multi-source and multi-detector CT system. We design a calibration phantom with a specific arrangement of bear balls. The geometric parameters are iteratively optimized by an objective function based on the projection matrix relationship between the ball position and the ball projection positions. In the process of parameter calculation, the geometric parameters of coupled X-ray sources and detectors are firstly calculated, followed by the calculation of the parameters of uncoupled X-ray sources. We apply the proposed method to the multi-source and multi-detector CT system built in our laboratory, and validate the calibrated geometric parameters in image reconstruction. There are no obvious artifacts from geometric mismatch in the reconstructed images, which indicates that our method can accurately estimate the geometric parameters in multi-source and multi-detector CT systems.

articleTitle: QUANTOF: multi-GPU-based list-mode fully quantitative TOF PET image reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) plays a pivotal role in the early detection and precise diagnosis of various diseases, including cancer, neurological disorders, and heart conditions. Ordered subset expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithm is the most commonly used image reconstruction algorithm. To address the high computational costs associated with this algorithm, numerous studies have explored the effectiveness of GPU acceleration. However, these studies have predominantly focused on the forward and backward projection components of iterative algorithms, neglecting correction techniques which are essential for PET image reconstruction, such as scatter correction. This work introduces a multi-GPU-based list-mode fully quantitative Time-of-Flight (TOF) PET image reconstruction technique, named QUANTOF, that integrates all corrections during PET image iterative reconstruction on GPUs. Additionally, optimizations have been applied to the backprojection algorithm, resulting in a two-fold increase in speed compared to the pre-optimized version. Validation using experimental datasets from a Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner demonstrates that this technique significantly reduces reconstruction time costs while achieving exceptional quantitative accuracy.

articleTitle: Feasibility of a α/β/γ camera for the detection of activity from different radioisotopes in microdroplets
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Development and validation of new imaging and therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals takes years of research due to the complexity, cost and limited throughput of conventional radiochemistry. To address this limitation, we devised a high-throughput radiochemistry system for rapid development of radiotracers for imaging and radiotherapeutics for cancer therapy. The core of the system is a silicon wafer that contains a 4 x 4 array of 3 mm diameter microdroplet reaction sites allowing simultaneous droplet-based radiosynthesis. A critical requirement for these systems is that the activity of the droplets must be repeatedly measured to monitor the efficacy of each radiosynthesis step. Last year we presented at this conference a method to rapidly measure radioactivity for positron imaging isotopes. Quantification of radioactivity in droplets is complicated by variations in overall positron energy deposition depending on the stage of synthesis, including the height of the droplet. We showed that we could determine the activity in the droplets, but required measuring both the intrinsic but weak Cerenkov light produced by positrons inside droplets and measuring the stronger scintillation light generated above the reaction sites from positrons that exit the droplets and interact in a scintillator. From these, the volume of the droplets could be inferred leading to activity determination. Here, we extend our previous work to investigate therapeutic isotopes to determine what modifications to our device are necessary to monitor the activity during radiosynthesis. We simulated water droplets containing Ac-225 and Lu-177, which produce $\beta-, \gamma$, and for Ac-225, $\alpha$. For this first step, we allow time for the isotopes to come into secular equilibrium to observe all decay products that may be present. Ultimately, we plan to investigate these isotopes on shorter time frames and to address questions that will help guide the design of the collimator/scintillator in order to quantify the activity.

articleTitle: TRISTAN Phase-1: an Array of Nine 166-Pixel SDD Detectors for Sterile Neutrino Search
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An array of 9 detectors based on monolithic arrays of 166 Silicon Drift Detectors (SDD) will be installed in 2026 in the KATRIN experiment for the search of sterile neutrinos in the keV mass range by means of high-accuracy beta spectroscopy. With a total of 1494 pixels, this instrument represents the largest spectroscopic system based on SDD ever realized. This intermediate milestone (Phase-1) preludes to the full format detector composed of 21 modules (Phase-2). Here we report on the development of the array, discussing the challenges of implementation of such a high-density system and showing the characterization of several detectors (∼10) in different setups. As here reported, after an optimization of the cleaning of the silicon surface (critical when detecting electrons) and a delicate assembly procedure, faulty pixels are limited to a few % per array. Detectors are preliminary characterized with X-ray photons (at 5.9 keV, showing a typical energy resolution of ∼150 eV FWHM) and electrons, here generated by calibration e-guns at 5 and 10 keV (resolution of ∼200 eV) in vacuum setups, including a dummy system which replicates the KATRIN detector chamber hosting the tower with 9 detectors. The latter provides similar levels of vacuum (∼10<sup>-8</sup> mbar, requiring special vacuum shields around the detectors) and magnetic fields (∼1 T) which allow to study the behaviour of the detectors in realistic operating conditions, prior to commissioning in KATRIN for the search of the sterile neutrino, after the conclusion on the ongoing data taking focusing on the mass of the active neutrino.

articleTitle: Quantitative Imaging with Multiple Compton Imagers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-ray imaging is a powerful tool for quantifying the amount of radioactive material. One gamma-ray imaging technique, Compton imaging, uses the kinematic reconstruction of incident gamma rays to determine possible origins of detected radiation. Compton imagers are able to isolate sources of interest from background within a wide band of relevant energy ranges and in a full ${\$}$4 \pi${\$}$ angular distribution. In the case where the geometry of material is unknown, such as monitoring holdup, this position information can be used to provide additional constraints on the activity of a sample. An array of multiple imagers, each with a known position and orientation, can provide additional resolution by combining their responses to triangulate radioactive material. This work uses multiple fixed H3D, Inc. H420 Gamma Imagers with known position and orientation to demonstrate a quantitative reconstruction of ${\$}$^{239}${\$}$Pu source activity.

articleTitle: Utilizing Deep Learning for Enhanced Tritium Monitoring
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study explores the use of charge-coupled devices (CCDs) for detecting the low-energy betas from tritium, linked to nuclear safety and environmental monitoring. We compare a traditional cut-and-count method of classifying CCD particle tracks from tritium versus background radiation with a variety of deep learning methods. These include supervised methods trained on both tritium and backgrounds, like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), and unsupervised methods, including an autoencoder, which are trained only on tritium signals. Results demonstrate that the CNN outperforms other methods, offering accurate classifications. However, unsupervised methods show potential for scenarios where the background radiation is unknown. This work underlines CCDs’ potential in enhancing tritium detection for field applications.

articleTitle: Range verification in carbon ion therapy: Compton imaging of 718 keV gamma-rays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging is one of the most investigated methods for range verification in carbon ion therapy. ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}$ (halflife of 19.3 s) is one of the important positron-emitting nuclides produced inside tissues during carbon ion therapy. This nuclide emits a 718 keV gamma ray almost simultaneously with the positron decay, and it can be detected using PET and Compton imaging even for a short time scan of 1 min. We have shown the feasibility of ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}$ direct localization based on the $\beta^{+}$-gamma coincidence by our whole gamma imaging (WGI). The WGI is a combination of a PET and Compton camera. The feasibility of Compton imaging, which is not influenced by the positron range of positron-emitting nuclides produced inside body, has not been investigated for treatment verification in carbon ion therapy. In this work, we focused on the feasibility of Compton imaging for range verification in carbon ion therapy using PHITS Monte Carlo simulation. The shifts of the dose peak and Compton peak of ${ }^{10} \mathrm{C}$ nuclide produced in irradiated polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) and polyethylene (PE) phantoms with ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}$ ion beams of 170,250 and $310 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{u}$ were less than 3.5 mm for scan times of $1,4,10$ and 20 min, respectively. The shifts of the dose peak and all $\beta^{+}$produced in both phantoms for all ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}$ ion beams were less than 3.0 mm for all scan times. The WGI was modeled by Geant4, Compton and PET images of an irradiated PMMA phantom with a ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}$ ion beam of $310 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{u}$ were reconstructed. The shift of the dose peak and Compton peak of 718 keV was 4.25 mm for all scan time. The shifts of the dose peak and PET peak positions were less than 3.3 mm for all scan times. The shifts of dose peak and Compton peak positions were constant for different scan time duration; however, the shifts of dose peak and PET peak positions were decreased as the scan time increased. The results demonstrated the capability of Compton imaging for range verification in carbon ion therapy even for 1-min scan.

articleTitle: Enhancing Analysis Sensitivity of Low-Level Tritium through Channel Region Optimization in Liquid Scintillation Counters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Tritium is an important radioactivity monitoring nuclide that exists in nature and is produced by nuclear power plants. In the environment, the concentration of tritium is at ultra-low-level, making it difficult to detect. This research focuses on developing an automatic analysis program suitable for low-level tritium analysis to lower Minimum Detectable Activity (MDA) and improve analytical accuracy and precision. The program automatically optimizes the channel regions in the tritium beta spectrum, reducing MDA and improving analytical accuracy and precision for low-level tritium samples. The analysis program is applicable to three Liquid Scintillation Counters (Quantulus 1220, GCT 6220, and HIDEX 300SL) and is suitable for analyzing a number of samples at once. By adjusting the channel region in the tritium beta spectrum, Figure of Merit (FOM) improved by approximately 44-62%, the MDA reduced by approximately 11-18%, the analytical accuracy improved and precision improved by approximately $5-15 \%$. The developed program is expected to ensure better data management and nuclear safety regulations by analyzing ultra-low-level radionuclides in the environment.

articleTitle: Advancing Space Telescope Capabilities: SiPM-based UV-Light Detection for Cosmic Ray Studies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The SiSMUV project aims to develop a compact modular UV detector based on SiPMs for use in space telescopes, targeting the study of fluorescence and Cherenkov signals produced by Ultra-High Energy Cosmic Rays (UHECRs). SiSMUV has the objective of incorporating into a monolithic block, state-of-the-art sensors and low-power read-out electronics, creating a complete end-to-end system, which can be easily interfaced with a PC for standalone operation or back-end electronics in the case of a more complex system. The Monolithic Photo-detection Block is composed of a matrix of SiPMs, signal processing front end electronics, and a local intelligence. In this contribution, we will show the functional characterization of the first of the detector unit prototype performance using an integrating sphere coupled with an LED, and the study of the dynamic under dark condition examining signal shape, gain, crosstalk, and afterpulses to assess both PDE and timing performance.

articleTitle: Exploring Several Novel Strategies to Enhance Prediction of Lung Cancer Survival Time
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This research evaluates several strategies to predict Lung cancer (LCa) survival: i) comparing PET vs. CT imaging; ii) handcrafted vs. deep radiomic features (HRF vs. DRF); iii) semi-supervised vs. supervised learning; iv) sets with clinical features (CF) vs. HRF alone and DRF alone; and v) 3 different masks-whole, cropped ($32 \times 32 \times 32 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$), and segmented PET/CT images, vi) 3 regression algorithms (RA). Our analysis included 199 LCa patients (just 99 with existing death time). We extracted HRFs and DRFs by PySERA and a 3D Autoencoder within the ViERA software (visear.ca), applying them in both supervised and semi-supervised frameworks to predict LCa survival. In the supervised model, we used Principal Component Analysis (PCA) followed by 3 RAs, applied to various combinations of CFs, HRFs, and DRFs. Additionally, the semi-supervised model augmented our dataset by pseudo-labeling patients with missing outcomes. The models were evaluated via 5-fold cross-validation and external nested testing. This study showed that i) PET significantly outperformed CT images with an averaged mean absolute error (MAE) $\sim 0.57 \pm 0.27$ [outcome range 0.1 to 6.6 years] using semi-supervised approach+HRF extracted from PET+PCA+ Multilayer Perceptron Regressor (MLPR); ii) HRFs outperformed DRFs with averaged MAE~0.57 $\pm \mathbf{0 . 2 7}$ using above ML; iii) Semisupervised significantly outperformed supervise learning with averaged MAE~0.52±39 using sole CF the above ML; and iv) combinations with CFs outperformed combinations without CFs, with averaged MAE~0.52 ±0.39 using semi-supervised learning, sole CF and above ML; and v) whole mask outperformed others with averaged MAE~0.59 ±0.27 using semi-supervised learning+DRFs extracted from whole CT images +CF+ above ML, vi) MLPR outperformed other algorithms with a averaged MAE of $0.52 \pm 0.39$ using sole CFs and semi-supervised learning.

articleTitle: Absolute Scatter Scaling for Transmission Source Enhanced Attenuation Correction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Data-driven attenuation correction (AC) methods are valuable for brain imaging on standalone PET systems. We have developed a CT-less AC scheme, termed transmission-aided μ-map reconstruction (TRU-AC). The method combines counts from a low-activity transmission (TX) source and the patient to reconstruct μ-maps using physics alone. PET quantification with TRU-AC is impacted by performance of the TX source scatter correction. The current tail fitted scaling scheme, based on matching simulated to experimental scatter outside the patient, is sensitive to motion and noise. Our objective is to develop a new absolute scaling algorithm, for TX source counts, and compare it to tail fitted scaling and reference standard CT-AC results. For both scaling schemes, unscaled scatter is generated with a fully 3D single scatter simulation. Absolute scatter scaling utilizes PET and CT-AC data from a brief ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ge}$ phantom scan, and a reconstruction of the TX source activity. We input data into an iterative optimization algorithm, maximizing the log-likelihood of TX counts, to find scaling factors for all sinogram slices. During TRU-AC, scatter is iteratively refined from attenuation map reconstructions using TX counts alone. For evaluation, three human subjects were injected with ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG, underwent uptake, and were imaged with a sparse helical geometry TX source (fill activity $=14 \mathrm{MBq}$ of ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$) placed on a whole-body PET/CT. Line profiles from PET images with absolute scaling showed better agreement with CT-AC than tail fitted results. VOI analysis, of cortical and deep brain structures, demonstrated <3.9% absolute bias in activity concentrations for absolute scaling compared to CT-AC. Tail fitted scaling produced absolute bias up to 12%. TRU-AC using absolute scatter scaling enables quantitative PET during human neuroimaging. The method may particularly benefit dedicated brain PET imaging for radiotracer development or studies with unique patient cohorts, where training data is limited.

articleTitle: System Design and Validation for Treatment Monitoring for BNCT by using Tomographic Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) is a cancer treatment that combines the power of radiation therapy with targeted therapy by radiating 10B, a non-radioactive isotope of boron with thermal neutrons, to deliver high-energy particles selectively to cancer cells. This work aims to establish feasible conditions for conducting tomographic imaging measurements for Boron NeutronCapture Therapy (BNCT). In previous work, we developed a detector, a vhannel-edge pinhole collimator and an Artificial Neural Network to detect and localize γ-rays at 478 keV emitted from boron neutron capture reactions. Here we report measurements conducted in LENA neutron facility in Pavia, Italy, showing the system capability to distinguish boron radiation sources from background noise, even in the presence of water. In addition, we show the feasibility of 3D image reconstruction using a new implementation of the channel-edge pinhole modelling in STIR (Software for Tomographic Image Reconstruction). Using realistic simulations with ANTS2, we then investigate system configurations for experimental measurements in the LENA facility, considering space limitations given by the irradiation room. We end up reporting the system configuration that allows us to reconstruct with good precision a simulated boron source of radiation with a minimum number of required projections.

articleTitle: Combining the basis-region data mode with the volume conservation constraint for reconstructing multiple basis materials from DECT data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we investigate the combination of the volume conservation constraint with the basis-region data model for reconstructing multiple (${\$}$\ge 3${\$}$) basis images directly from DECT data. Based on the observation that basis materials of interest are often confined within spatial supports smaller than the image array, we have previously proposed and investigated a basis-region data model for reconstructing multiple basis images directly from DECT data, while it is assumed that each basis region can contain up to 2 basis materials. In this work, we aim to relax such condition by allowing up to 3 basis materials in each basis region and incorporate the volume conservation constraint into the optimization-based image reconstruction, to alleviate the impact of the increased number of unknowns. A modified NCPD algorithm has been developed to numericalling solve the optimization problem with the added constraint. Using simulated and real DECT data, we reconstruct basis-region images and subsequently obtain basis images on the full image array and VMIs. Results suggest that the algorithm developed can accurately and robustly reconstruction multiple basis images directly from DECT data, while allowing for up to 3 basis materials in each basis region. The work may engender insights into the development of practical procedures for reconstructing multiple basis images, VMIs, and physical quantities directly from DECT data in applications.

articleTitle: Direct Generation of Attenuation and Scatter Correction of Brain PET Data Using a Conditional Latent Diffusion Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon attenuation and scatter correction (ASC) are crucial for accurate PET images. Current literature on ASC mainly relies on generative adversarial network (GAN) architectures to obtain PET images corrected with synthetic CT data. Despite their potential, the generation of synthetic CT images through GAN models remains challenging, primarily due to factors such as inferior image quality and constraints related to tissue heterogeneity, patient-specific anatomical variations, and underlying pathologies. In this work, we propose an alternative method based on a conditional Latent Diffusion Model (LDM) to obtain accurate ASC PET data directly from non-attenuation and non-scatter-corrected (NASC) images without requiring any anatomical prior information. Retrospective 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) full-body PET/CT and PET/MR images from 32 subjects were collected and analyzed. We trained a conditional LDM to map NASC images to ASC PET images. As a baseline, we used two state-of-the-art GAN-based models: Pix2Pix and CycleGAN for direct generation of ASC PET data. The conditional LDM resulted in accurately corrected PET images close to the groundtruth. The average peak signal-to-noise ratio, normalized root mean square error (NRMSE), and structural similarity index for the conditional LDM were 35.3, 0.05 and 0.94 versus 34.7, 0.05 and 0.92 for Pix2Pix, and 31.2, 0.07 and 0.86 for CycleGAN, respectively. Conditional LDM was demonstrated to be a promising alternative to GAN models for direct generation of ASC brain PET image data.

articleTitle: Comparison of an OGS/Polystyrene scintillator (BSO-406) with pure OGS (BSO-100), EJ-276, EJ-309, and M600 scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we present an investigation into the scintillation properties and pulse shape discrimination (PSD) performance of the new BSO-406, which is a blend of organic glass scintillator and 60% polystyrene. We tested a cylindrical sample with dimensions of 2 × 2 inches. The study includes measurements of neutron-gamma discrimination capability, emission spectra, photoelectron yield, and analysis of light pulse shapes originating from events related to gamma-rays and fast neutrons. The results were compared to data previously recorded using a pure Organic Glass Scintillator (BSO-100), EJ-276 plastic scintillator, an EJ-309 liquid scintillator, and an M600 polyurethane-based plastic scintillator.

articleTitle: Implementation of a Digital Gaussian Filter to Restore Resolution of the PLATYPUS Reflectometer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Following its commissioning in 2019, the PLATYPUS reflectometer at the Australian Centre for Neutron Scattering, ANSTO, demonstrated a significant degradation in detector resolution from <2 mm to >7 mm full-width half-maximum. The PLATYPUS reflectometer uses a Monoblock Aluminium Multitube detector that was designed and fabricated at Institut Laue-Langevin and uses the charge division method for positional determination. After the cause of degraded resolution was determined to be electrical noise, a digital fourth-order low-pass Gaussian filter was applied to pre-processed preamplifier signals to remove high frequency components. The digital filtering method, also devised at Institu Laue-Langevin, was implemented purely in firmware and software and was successful at improving the resolution to 4 mm full-width halfmaximum. The results indicate the technique has limitations but also highlight the convenience and flexibility of the digital approach to pulse-processing.

articleTitle: Assessing the Performance of CT Image Denoisers using Laguerre-Gauss Channelized Hotelling Observer for Lesion Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The remarkable success of deep learning methods in solving computer vision problems, such as image classification, object detection, scene understanding, image segmentation, etc., has paved the way for their application in biomedical imaging. One such application is in the field of CT image denoising, whereby deep learning methods are proposed to recover denoised images from noisy images acquired at low radiation. Outputs derived from applying deep learning denoising algorithms may appear clean and visually pleasing; however, the underlying diagnostic image quality may not be on par with their normal-dose CT counterparts. In this work, we assessed the image quality of deep learning denoising algorithms by making use of visual perception- and data fidelity-based task-agnostic metrics (like the PSNR and the SSIM) - commonly used in the computer vision - and a task-based detectability assessment (the LCD) - extensively used in the CT imaging. When compared against normal-dose CT images, the deep learning denoisers outperformed low-dose CT based on metrics like the PSNR (by 2.4 to 3.8 dB) and SSIM (by 0.05 to 0.11). However, based on the LCD performance, the detectability using quarter-dose denoised outputs was inferior to that obtained using normal-dose CT scans.

articleTitle: Subject-aware PET Denoising with Contrastive Adversarial Domain Generalization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent advances in deep learning (DL) have greatly improved the performance of positron emission tomography (PET) denoising performance. However, DL model performance can vary a lot across subjects, due to the large variability of the count levels and spatial distributions. A generalizable DL model that mitigates the subject-wise variations is highly expected toward a reliable and trustworthy system for clinical application. In this work, we propose a contrastive adversarial learning framework for subject-wise domain generalization (DG). Specifically, we configure a contrastive discriminator in addition to the UNet-based denoising module to check the subject-related information in the bottleneck feature, while the denoising module is adversarially trained to enforce the extraction of subject-invariant features. The sampled low-count realizations from the list-mode data are used as anchor-positive pairs to be close to each other, while the other subjects are used as negative samples to be distributed far away. We evaluated on $97{ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-MK6240 tau PET studies, each having 20 noise realizations with $25 \%$ fractions of events. Training, validation, and testing were implemented using 1400, 120, and 420 pairs of 3D image volumes in a subject-independent manner. The proposed contrastive adversarial DG demonstrated superior denoising performance than conventional UNet without subject-wise DG and cross-entropy-based adversarial DG.

articleTitle: New GATE Digitizer Unit for versions post v9.3
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Gate Digitizer Unit (GDU) is a critical component within the Geant4 Application for Tomographic Emission (GATE), a platform used extensively in medical imaging and radiotherapy simulations. This unit is responsible for simulating the response of photodetection components using a combination of analytical and semi-analytical models. Originally developed approximately 20 years ago for the first version of GATE, the GDU has since grown into a complex and challenging-to-maintain codebase. Over time, parts of the code became redundant or unused. As a result, updating the GDU has become imperative to incorporate the latest advancements in Geant4, improve its current version, and introduce new features. This work presents the implementation of the new GDU starting from version 9.3. It discusses the newly added functionalities, the impact of these changes on users, the current progress of the update, and future perspectives.

articleTitle: Geometric Optimization of High-Resolution Small-Animal PET Scanner Utilizing a Sparse Detector Arrangement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, the development of small-animal Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners with long axial fields-of-view (FOV) has gained significant interest. However, the cost of these scanners has also risen. Using sparse detector configurations offers a potential cost reduction but introduces greater dead spaces, leading to reduced sensitivity and, more importantly, increased sensitivity variation across the FOV. This study examined the effect of different detector arrangements on sensitivity distributions across the FOV, focusing on a high-resolution scanner with an 188 cm axial FOV. Four scanners with different sparse detector configurations were investigated, each with 128 detectors arranged into 8 rings but with neighboring rings rotated by $0^{\circ}, 11.25^{\circ}, 5.625^{\circ}$, and 2.8125° in the tangential direction for the four systems, respectively. The results showed that scanners with rotational offsets between neighboring detector rings significantly enhanced the uniformity of sensitivity across the FOV. The standard deviation improvement (measure of uniformity) of the scanner with 2.8125° rotation between neighboring detector rings was as high as 73% in the axial projection while maintaining overall sensitivity.

articleTitle: Timing Characterization of 1 cm2 LGAD Pad Sensors for Space Experiments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Experiments that study charged cosmic rays in space using a tracker and calorimeter are affected by secondary particles created in the calorimeter entering the tracker. To distinguish between primary and secondary hits, timing measurements of each hit in the tracker are crucial. The Low Gain Avalanche Diodes (LGADs) are silicon detectors that use the impact ionization process to achieve gain values of about O(10). One of the important factors to consider when using LGADs for experiments studying charged cosmic rays in space is their timing performance. While conventional silicon micro-strip sensors only provide spatial information of the charged particles passing through the tracker, LGADs can provide additional timing information with a few tens of picoseconds resolution. This study demonstrates that an LGAD, with an active area of approximately $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, can achieve a jitter of less than 40 ps. The devices used in this study consist of pad sensors with three different thicknesses. Each thickness contains three different active areas and three layout designs for each area. The timing performance of these devices is evaluated using a pulsed infrared laser. Different layout designs and gain layers are compared to determine the best time resolution. The timing performance is estimated in terms of signal uniformity, gain, noise, and jitter.

articleTitle: Multi-PMT modules for the WCTE, IWCD and Hyper-Kamiokande experiments.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Hyper-Kamiokande experiment represents a significant advancement in underground water Cherenkov detection, building upon the success of the Super-Kamiokande experiment. It serves as the far detector for a long baseline neutrino experiment using the J-PARC neutrino beam, primarily determining CP violation. Additionally, it functions as a detector capable of observing proton decay, atmospheric neutrinos, and neutrinos from celestial sources [1]. Many systematic uncertainties are tied to neutrino-nucleus interactions, which can be mitigated by placing a detector near the beam production point. Thus, the Hyper-Kamiokande long-baseline program includes an Intermediate Water Cherenkov Detector (IWCD) and a 500-ton Cherenkov detector 1 km from the beam production point. This detector can vary its position within a vertical shaft, covering off-axis angles 1 to 4 degrees relative to the beam [2]. The Water Cherenkov Test Experiment (WCTE) conducted at CERN aims to evaluate multi-PMT technologies and techniques pertinent to water Cherenkov detectors. It comprises about 100 multi-PMT photosensors arranged in a water tank (3.8 m in diameter, 3.6 m in height, with a total water mass of about 41 tonnes). Each multi-PMT unit includes nineteen 3” PMTs with front-end electronics enclosed in a water-tight pressure vessel. This presentation will delve into the design and production of the multi-PMT system, detailing assembly procedures, quality assurance protocols, and initial testing results. The talk will encompass characterization studies of the 3” PMTs, including Transit Time Spread and afterpulse investigations. It will also cover the electronics architecture, signal paths, and pulse detection algorithms. The assembly process and quality assurance measurements will be outlined, followed by insights and outcomes from the testing station build of four multi-PMT modules.

articleTitle: GATE Simulation of an Ultra-Sensitive Total-Body Small-Animal PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we present validation of the GATE Monte Carlo simulation results to actual experimental results of the total-body small animal positron emission tomography (TBS-PET) scanner. We aimed at characterization of the TBS-PET scanner, which has a 155 mm ring diameter and an axial FOV of 325.6 mm. The TBS-PET scanner consists of 6 rings each of which has 10 depth-of-interaction (DOI) detectors. Each DOI detector has a 4-layer GSOZ crystal array which results in a 30 mm total thickness and 2.9 mm crystal pitch. The axial sensitivity profile was evaluated using a ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source with a step interval of 14 mm. For spatial resolution evaluation,<sup>22</sup> Na Derenzo-like phantom having different rod diameters (1.6, 2.2, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, and 6.0 mm) was scanned at the center of the field-of-view. For image reconstruction, the maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (ML-EM) algorithm was applied. An energy window of 400-600 keV was used. The simulated peak axial sensitivity (20.2%) showed good agreement with that of the experimental data (21.9%). The average differences of the spatial resolution between the simulation and experiment were 0.58 mm, and 0.36 mm for the filtered back projection (FBP) and ML-EM algorithms, respectively. The peak-to-valley ratio of the Derenzo-like phantom obtained with the simulation was 1.96 times higher than the experimental data. We attributed the difference between the experimental data and the simulation results as mainly being due to the crystal decoding error of the actual DOI detectors. In the future, we plan to include the crystal decoding error in the simulation for a more accurate modeling of the TBS-PET scanner especially for spatial resolution. At the conference, we will also present the count rate performance and NEMA NU4 image quality phantom analysis results.

articleTitle: X-ray Dark-field Imaging of Anisotropic Rod-shaped Magnetic Iron Oxide Particles
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dark-field (D-F) contrast is one of the mechanisms that may make the grating interferometry-based X-ray imaging more capable in preclinical and clinical applications. With resort to Fresnel-Kirchhoff analysis, we extended the definition of D-F contrast in grating interferometry-based implementation from a real metrics to a complex one. In general, both the real and imaginary parts of complex D-F contrast can be employed for Imaging. In this work, we explore the potentials of using the real part of complex D-F contrast of anisotropic rod-shaped magnetic iron oxide particles for clinical and preclinical applications. The obtained data show that the D-F contrast generated by anisotropic rod-shaped magnetic iron oxide particles is much stronger than its counterpart by attenuation and varies radically over particles’ orientation. Hence, there can be a good chance for X-ray D-F imaging, especially its concerted interplay with novel and bio-safe contrast agents such as the anisotropic rod-shaped magnetic iron oxide particles, to play significant roles toward advanced clinical and preclinical applications.

articleTitle: Reducing trade-off between TOF capability and sensitivity using scalable DOI detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time of flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) establishes its importance in nuclear medicine. Coincidence time resolution (CTR) of TOF-PET is a representative metric of system performance and has been improved owing to technological advancements including scintillators, photodetectors, and readout electronics. However, achieving a CTR of 100 ps full width at half maximum (FWHM) is still challenging because a TOF-PET generally requires a sufficiently thick scintillator of approximately 20 mm, otherwise the sensitivity of TOF-PET system is insufficient. However, photon transit time spread in such a long scintillator is not negligible to achieve the CTR of 100 ps and thinner scintillators are preferable in terms of an improved CTR. To overcome this trade-off, in this study, we propose a readout scheme of PET detectors. Orthogonally stacked two 1D-PET detectors of which one longitudinal side is not covered by a reflector and faces to each other allow us to reduce the thickness of scintillators shorter than 13 mm without compromising the detector sensitivity by stacking the detectors along a depth-of-interaction (DOI) axis of a PET scanner. The CTR of 100 ps FWHM can be practically expected with such a thin scintillator using the state-of-the-art scintillators, photodetectors, and readout electronics. Furthermore, the proposed PET detector can simultaneously extract a DOI information. We will investigate and show the energy, 3D-spatial, timing resolutions of the proposed detector.

articleTitle: Multiple material decomposition with a combined X-ray spectral and phase imaging system
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The combined approach of X-ray spectral and phase contrast imaging brings complementary advantages for comprehensive imaging and analysis of complex samples thanks to the simultaneous visualization of structural features and elemental composition for quantitative multimodal characterization of materials with diverse compositions and properties. This integration offers a dual advantage; it enhances the visibility of soft tissues while effectively isolating high-Z materials, thus augmenting the capabilities of X-ray imaging system. Its potential impact is notable for instance in medical imaging, materials science, and cultural heritage. We have developed a novel X-ray imaging system that yields spectral information and retrieves the phase simultaneously in a single acquisition procedure. The spectral information is obtained utilizing a bent Si Laue crystal, which energetically disperses a polychromatic synchrotron X-ray beam focused into narrow line where the sample is placed. The system can be tuned such that multiple absorption edges can be captured simultaneously in the vertical direction of a 2-D detector allowing multi-material decomposition at the mg/ml level or recording spatially resolved X-ray absorption fine structures in a single shot. On the other hand X-ray phase contrast is capable of enhancing soft tissue visibility since it is based on material refractive properties rather than attenuation. Here it is achieved through the beam tracking technique exploiting beamlets generated by an absorption mask upstream the crystal, providing absorption, refraction, and dark field images. Moreover introducing the phase image into the material decomposition algorithm allows retrieving an additional material while keeping high phase contrast sensitivity in low density samples. Here we will present our combined X-ray spectral and phase system showing preliminary imaging results on dedicated phantoms and biological samples that highlight the potential of the method.

articleTitle: Dead-Layer-Free Semiconductor Detectors via Highly Charged Dielectrics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The entrance window of semiconductor particle detectors typically contains undepleted regions that the impinging particles pass through before reaching the sensitive area of the device. These so-called dead layers pose a fundamental limitation for achievable energy resolutions and are unavoidable in externally doped pn-junction detectors. Here, we fabricate a silicon particle detector using an alternative method for creating the charge-collecting junction that depletes the whole surface and minimizes the dead layer. The junction is realized by inducing an electric field at the surface of the detector using a charged thin film, which consequently forms an inversion layer. Such approach has previously been implemented in photodiodes, which have demonstrated efficient collection of charge carriers from the very surface of the devices. Utilizing the same method in a particle detector could thus allow a device without junction-originated dead layer. Our device is characterized using detection of alpha particles as a case example. We achieve energy resolutions and leakage currents that are, already without extensive device optimization, on the same level with commercial externally doped silicon particle detectors. We also demonstrate the excellent charge collection capability extending all the way to the device surface. Finally, we discuss the applicability of the device in detection of other charged particles in addition to alpha particles, which may benefit from the design even more.

articleTitle: Development of Hybrid Gaseous Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gaseous detectors are crucial components of the current and future collider experiments from tracker to muon chambers and even calorimeters. One of the major challenges for the future implementation of gaseous detectors is the limitations on the usage of some common detector gases. In order to address this issue, our team has developed the concept of “hybrid gaseous detectors” where part of the electron multiplication is transferred from the gas layer to a solidstate layer applied directly on the in-chamber anode surface. The concept was tested with the Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) and was validated to relax the operating conditions considerably enabling the consideration of alternative gases and flow schemes. Recently the concept was also applied to drift tubes by coating the central anode wire with high secondary emission yield materials. The hybrid drift tubes were mainly developed to be utilized as beam loss monitors at the Turkish Accelerator and Radiation Laboratory in Ankara, Turkey. Here we report on the details of the concept of hybrid gaseous detectors, present the results from laboratory and beam tests, and discuss future directions.

articleTitle: Trapezoidal Pulse Height Method Using Deep Learning for Pile-Up Correction in High Radiation Environments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate peak detection is paramount in high radiation environments where gamma-ray spectroscopy is compromised by significant signal pile-up. This study introduces an enhanced peak detection method for trapezoidal pulses, focusing on overcoming the challenges of spectral distortion due to overlapping peaks. The introduced method employs a technique of differentiating and precisely slicing piled-up signal, allowing for the reliable identification of individual peaks within piled-up signal. Tested against synthetic signals generated from a LaBr3 detector, the method showed superior accuracy in detecting both single and piled-up peaks. The method’s effectiveness was further validated through extensive empirical tests, demonstrating its potential to dramatically improve spectral analysis in environments with high radiation levels. This approach sets a new standard for peak detection, offering significant improvements over traditional methods in both accuracy and reliability. The versatility of the method also enables it to be adapted for various types of radiation detectors, enhancing its applicability across different nuclear science fields. Ultimately, this method provides a robust solution for accurate spectral data interpretation, crucial for effective radiation monitoring and safety assessment.

articleTitle: Optical and photoelectric properties of surface barrier diodes based on n-Hg3In2Te6
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The electro-physical properties of Cr/Hg<inf>3</inf>In<inf>2</inf>Te<inf>6</inf>/Cr surface-barrier diodes, which were made on Hg<inf>3</inf>In<inf>2</inf>Te<inf>6</inf> single crystals after annealing under an overpressure of their own components, were studied. As a result of this treatment, the specific resistance of the semiconductor material significantly decreased - from r »5×10<sup>3</sup> to r »2×10<sup>2</sup> Ohm×cm. It is important that such a significant decrease in resistivity did not lead to deterioration of the optical transmittance in the Urbach region, and in some cases even improved it. The reduction in resistivity also resulted in a significant improvement in the dynamic range of the linear region of the watt-ampere characteristic. It is important that the rectification coefficient K increased by approximately 10 times at a voltage of U=1 V, and for the best diodes the rectification coefficient was equal to K»10<sup>3</sup>. A significant decrease in the dark current was observed, which was measured at voltages of U=1 and U=10 V. Considering the high radiation resistance of n- Hg<inf>3</inf>In<inf>2</inf>Te<inf>6</inf>, rectifier diodes and photodiodes based on it can have an important application under conditions of high exposure to ionizing radiation.

articleTitle: Self-Organised Polylinear Regression Maps as a Method of Resolving HPGe Detector Responses
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Within the field of Nuclear Instrumentation, the technique of Pulse Shape Analysis (PSA) is used to apply bespoke timing and energy corrections for detectors by interrogating the signal profiles corresponding to their spatial response. Parametric PSA methods are suitable for high-rate applications but rely on human-interpretable corrections and are often limited in their accuracy and application to multi-interaction signals. Non-parametric PSA methods such as the gamma-ray localisation used in the Advanced Gamma Tracking Array (AGATA) provide excellent prediction accuracy but are rate-limited and can only operate at a few kHz. In this work we propose a pseudo-parametric method using Self-Organising Maps (SOMs) for generating a human-interpretable approximation of the underlying detector response. These SOMs can be experimentally trained for accurate analytical regression of a variety of parameters from radial and cartesian position to timing. This method provides an efficient and tuneable way for the prediction of signal characteristics when a detector exhibits complex non-linear behaviour whilst capable of being implemented real-time on conventional digitiser hardware.

articleTitle: Energy-Dependent Spatial Resolution and Uniformity Measurements on Large-Volume Pixelated CdZnTe using Modified Subpixel Corrections
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Systems based on large-volume, pixelated CdZnTe detectors are becoming commonplace across research and industry. Historical subpixel event reconstruction algorithms, which enable interaction localization to finer than a pixel pitch, have been limited to a few key photon energies on M400 detectors. Furthermore, the historical algorithm was observed to leave non-physical gaps between crystal anodes. As such, an updated subpixel sensing algorithm has been implemented to mitigate gaps and enable arbitrary-energy subpixel sensing for a wide range of special nuclear material and novel medical isotopes. M400 device uniformity and position resolution will be benchmarked using far-field flood and edge-spread function measurements across energies ranging from 122-511 keV. These values can be used to estimate limiting spatial resolution and signal-to-noise-ratio in common imaging system relying on occlusion like SPECT and coded aperture.

articleTitle: Using Residual Physics to reach near-200 ps CTR with TOFPET2 ASIC Readout and Clinical Detector Blocks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Last year’s SNMMI, Siemens Healthineers presented the Biograph Vision.X PET/CT scanner, currently delivering the industry’s leading time-of-flight (TOF). Although recent TOF-research explores novel materials, electronics, and calibration concepts, system developments are often evaluated against the Biograph Vision.X benchmark. In this work, we explored what coincidence time resolution (CTR) can be achieved with conventional readout electronic (TOFPET2c ASIC) and clinical detector blocks using our previously established residual physics timing calibration. It is the first time we apply the concept to a detector read out with analog SiPMs and the TOFPET2c ASIC. Our method relies on channel-individual information in combination with machine learning (ML) models, which we characterized in this work regarding their functionality and capability to improve the detectors’ CTR. We compare the timing performance against an approach based on a purely analytical calibration as it is applicable to general system architectures. The results show that the residual physics calibration concept offers significant advances demonstrated by the improvement of CTR from $335 \pm 5 \mathrm{ps}$ (analytical cal) to around $219 \pm 1 \mathrm{ps}$ (analytical cal + ML) for coincidences within an energy window from 300 keV to 700 keV.

articleTitle: PET Image Denoising based on Diffusion Schrodinger Bridge Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging is an important modality that provides quantitative insights into molecular and physiological processes. PET denoising has been widely studied due to the high noise levels inherent to PET imaging, which can significantly impede accurate scan interpretation and analysis. With recent advances in generative artificial intelligence, particularly diffusion models, diffusion model-based PET denoising methods have shown performance improvements. However, these models often generate over enhanced signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) PET images from the random Gaussian noise via iterative sampling, which does not fully consider the informative priors of low-dose PET imaging during diffusion sampling. Our PET denoising method using the Diffusion Schrödinger Bridge model (DSBM) addresses these challenges through the Schrödinger Bridge framework, enhancing the sampling process while preserving the priors of low-dose PET imaging by starting diffusion sampling from low-dose PET images. Additionally, the DSBM maintains spatial coherence and anatomical detail by utilizing an anatomical MR image prior. We demonstrate that the DSBM provides superior denoising performance for unseen data, outperforming state-of-the-art methods while preserving image details.

articleTitle: Preliminary CT Results Using a Simultaneous Photon-Counting and Energy-Integrating Prototype Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The HPIX-detector used in X-ray imaging enables simultaneous acquisition of energy-integrating and photon-counting information, offering great potential in the field of spectral CT imaging. This paper introduces CT imaging tests using a four-module prototype HPIX-detector and presents the corresponding preliminary reconstruction results. In addition to individual bad pixels caused by factors such as fabrication process and digital interference, severe spectral inconsistencies across pixels in the photon counting channel directly lead to obvious ring and band artifacts in the original reconstructed images. Following interpolation to address bad pixels in both channels, a spectral inconsistency correction method was applied to photon-counting data. After data preprocessing, the ring artifacts in both channels were significantly reduced and the reconstructed image quality is improved. Preliminary CT results from this study on the prototype indicate that the HPIX-detector is promising to perform simultaneous energy-integrating and photon-counting CT imaging.

articleTitle: A new combined hardware and software tools for X-ray in-depth and non-destructive analysis of metal deformation processing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The aim of COHeSIA project is to project and build an X-ray-based tool, composed of a hardware instrument with double silicon and CdZnTe detector and a dedicated software, capable measure and analyze angle-energy map with diffraction and fluorescence signals on a wide energy range. This tool will be capable to provide an in-depth characterization, from atomic to the macro scale, of the deformation process typical of metal processing (like rolling, deep drawing or even machining) under investigation. This kind of instrument can be fundamental for monitoring the manufacturing process at industry level and can be implemented into feedback-based control systems

articleTitle: Influence of Self-Absorption on Pulse Shape Discrimination in Organic Glass Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper we report on the scintillation properties and neutron-gamma pulse shape discrimination (PSD) performance of organic glass scintillator (OGS) compared to trans-stilbene. 25.4 mm diameter cylindrical OGS samples of heights from 25 mm to 125 mm were measured with PuBe neutron source, as well as $25.4 \mathrm{~mm} \times 25.4 \mathrm{~mm}$ stilbene cylinder. To improve comparison reliability we analyze raw pulse data from a digitizer to obtain the highest Figure of Merit (FOM) value and estimate the optimal parameters in Charge Comparison Method (namely a short and a long gate). Best FOM values of OGS range from 1.38 at 100 keVee to 3.28 at 1000 keVee. Measured photoelectron yield of OGS decreases with the height of the scintillator due to light self-absorption. Discrimination capability follows this trend, with FOM decreasing from 1.65 (height 25 mm) to 1.43 (height 125 mm) for a wide energy range 100-1000 keVee.

articleTitle: Development of Benchmark Experimental Method of Large Angle Scattering Reaction Cross Section at 14 MeV for Compound Targets
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In high energy and intensity neutron environments in the fusion reactor, large angle scattering reactions play a pivotal role in neutronics calculations, since the reactions can particularly impact assessments of the fusion reactor blanket. Discrepancies identified by C. Konno’s group in Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) underscore the necessity for benchmarking large angle scattering cross sections. In the previous study, the authors’ group developed a benchmark experimental system utilizing the foil activation method to validate large angle scattering reaction cross sections. Four experiments for a certain sample were conducted using two shadow bars composed of conical irons with and without the sample to deduce the large angle neutron scattering cross section. Despite previous benchmark experiments on various elements, gaseous samples like fluorine have not yet been validated. The present study proposes a novel benchmark experimental approach for benchmarking fluorine’s large angle scattering cross sections using a compound sample as the target. We selected PTFE as the sample. MCNP 5 was employed to evaluate the ratio of carbon reaction rate to that of PTFE in the PTFE sample in advance. Two benchmark experiments were carried out using the PTFE or graphite samples as the targets to obtain their reaction rates and subsequently the fluorine’s reaction rate was derived from the measured reaction rates using the results by MCNP. Furthermore, the benchmark experiments were simulated by MCNP and the calculated results were compared with those obtained from the experiments. The comparison exhibited an excellent agreement with the calculation results for ENDF/B-VIII and JEFF-3.3. In future we will focus on reduction of experimental errors and feedback mechanisms to enhance nuclear data quality.

articleTitle: Impact of respiratory motion-matched attenuation correction for different lesion locations in dual-gated SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cardiac and respiratory dual-gated single-photon emission computed tomography (D-SPECT) is a promising technique for minimizing the motion artifacts in myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI). However, attenuation correction (AC) for dual-gated SPECT using an attenuation map averaged over the respiratory cycle may lead to mismatched attenuation correction artifacts. In this study, we propose a respiratory motion-matched attenuation correction (RMM-AC) to further improve dual-gated SPECT. For each respiratory gate, RMM-AC uses an attenuation map that matches the SPECT image in a 4D reconstruction framework. 4D reconstruction with the attenuation map averaged over all respiratory gates (AVE-AC) are used for comparison. We used the NCAT phantom and SIMIND Monte Carlo simulation to simulate dual-gated cardiac SPECT using ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-sestamibi. An ischemic lesion with 20% uptake reduction at four locations of the left ventricular myocardium is used for a channelized Hotelling observer (CHO) study. Two AC methods are quantitatively evaluated using the root mean squared error (RMSE) and the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve $\left(\mathrm{A}_{Z}\right)$ of CHO. RMM-AC outperforms AVE-AC in both metrics for all four lesion locations, which reflects improvements on both reconstruction accuracy and lesion detectability. The preliminary results show that the biggest difference occurs in the anterior and posterior direction of the short-axis images.

articleTitle: Performance of the prototype of an ultra-low-dose stationary tomographic Molecular Breast Imaging (ULDMBI) camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A prototype of an ultra-low-dose stationary tomographic Molecular Breast Imaging system (ULDMBI) has been developed and built by Kromek. The system combines superior energy, position, and depth of interaction (DOI) resolution of CZT detectors, wide range angular sampling of multi-pinhole (MPH) collimators and novel demultiplexing image reconstruction, to mitigate the MBI drawbacks (higher than mammography patient dose and long imaging time of 40 min) without compromising diagnostic content. The initial feasibility study of this new technology was conducted by Kromek and University College London. It indicated that it is possible to achieve a dose/time reduction of a factor of seven compared to the current MBI clinical practice. The new dual-head prototype has field-of-view of $132 \mathrm{~mm} \times 88 \mathrm{~mm}$ which is large enough to allow clinical evaluation with phantoms. Each head is made of a 6x4 array of Kromek’s $5 \mathbf{~ m m}$ thick CZT detectors with 2 mm pixels. The raw detector data is analysed using a novel machine-learning-based model which provides strong improvement in the sub-pixel position resolution and depth-of-interaction information. Preliminary evaluation of the model performance using planar imaging has demonstrated significant increase in the detector position resolution allowing achievement of $5 \times 5$ sub-pixelisation of 2 mm pixels producing images equivalent to $400 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pixel pattern. These results surpass any previous demonstration by a SPECT or MBI system with $\sim 2 \mathrm{~mm}$ pixel CZT detectors. This high-resolution data is used in tomographic image reconstruction allowing results of the prototype performance evaluation with $^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-filled phantoms and further studies of the dose/time reduction to be presented and discussed.

articleTitle: A new integrated image reconstruction method for muon tomography to improve material identification and image quality
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Non-destructive testing (NDT) methods using cosmic ray muons, known as muon tomography, have been studied and used for decades to monitor a variety of large and dense objects. In this study, we propose a new image reconstruction method for muon tomography using the point of closest approach(PoCA), the kinetic energy of muons and the Highland-Lynch-Dahl formula to improve material identification and image quality. A muon tomography system with four 2D detectors arranged in the top and bottom layers, and 20 X 20 X 10 cm3 of aluminum and uranium target materials were modeled for the GEANT4 simulations. For each of the 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 3 GeV energy ranges, 400,000 muon particles were vertically irradiated to the system to obtain incoming and outgoing muon trajectories. First, 3D reconstructed images for each energy range were obtained using scattering points and scattering angles calculated through the PoCA algorithm. Then, the edge rise distances at 10%, 50%, and 90% from the z-axis scattering angle profile curve were measured for each energy range. The edge rise distance obtained at 90% with the 0.5 GeV muons was chosen as the closest target material thickness. The radiation length value was calculated by substituting the target thickness, muon energy and the standard deviation of the scattering angle for each energy into the Highland-Lynch-Dahl formula. The target images were re-reconstructed using the calculated radiation length instead of the scattering angle. The ratio of the standard deviation and mean of the radiation length obtained by the proposed method was smaller than that of the scattering angle obtained from the PoCA image. The results demonstrated that the proposed method could improve material discrimination and image quality in muon tomography.

articleTitle: Diffusion-based Bayesian posterior distribution prediction of kinetic parameters in dynamic PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging non-invasively study molecular processes in neurodegenerative diseases, such as tau protein aggregates in Alzheimer’s diseases. Tracer kinetic modeling is crucial for quantitative analysis of dynamic PET data, e.g., tau’s density and cerebral perfusion. Yet, noise in PET images causes uncertainty in the estimated parameters. Bayesian inference (BI), traditionally through Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), can estimate posterior distributions, but demands heavy computation. This work presents an efficient deep learning-based approach to estimate Bayesian posterior distributions using an improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model. The network is trained on data drawn from an explicit, data-driven, prior distribution of kinetic parameters. During inference, samples are then drawn from the approximated posterior distribution given PET time-activity curves. The proposed method was tested and validated on an [18F]MK6240 study using 48 regions-of-interest covering most of the brain, comparing it to Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) and Metropolis-Hasting MCMC as reference. Our approach significantly reduced computation time (over 230 times faster than MCMC) with less bias than CVAE, consistently providing accurate (mean error $\lt0.58 \%$) and precise (standard deviation error $\lt9.92 \%$) posterior distributions.

articleTitle: Comparative Experimental and Simulation DOI Analysis on Semi-Monolithic Metascintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study compares the depth of interaction (DOI) performance of semi-monolithic metascintillators (SMMS) with dimensions of $25.4 \times 25.4 \times 24 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ and standard semi-monolithic scintillators (SMON) of $25.4 \times 25.4 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$. The SMMS comprises LYSO:Ce interleaved with EJ232 organic scintillators, while the SMON contains eight slabs of LYSO:Ce. The experimental findings demonstrated comparable behaviors regarding centroid positions and Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM) of the DOI distributions. Indeed, using linear interpolation over the centroid positions, the average DOI resolution computed resulted in 2.6 mm for SMMS and 2.1 mm for SMON. On the other hand, using exponential interpolation, the average DOI resolution results change to 6.3 mm for SMMS and 6.1 mm for SMON. Moreover, simulation results indicate a close correlation with experimental data, especially in the exponential behavior of the DOI distribution centroid positions, while showing a discrepancy in the FWHM. From the timing perspective, simulation results show significant improvement in timing through DOI-time walk correction enhancing an initial 136 ps up to 98 ps after correction, thus staging a 28\% CTR improvement. These results validate SMMS for PET imaging, matching traditional structures. Future metascintillators could enhance timing and DOI capabilities by exploiting this architecture.

articleTitle: Pushing the performances of DOI-capable TOF-PET modules using Low-Noise HighFrequency Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-frequency (HF) front-end electronics are an attractive solution for exploiting fast light production mechanisms in crystals and achieving excellent performance in TOF-PET applications. Moreover, the combination of this readout with novel technologies, such as heterostructured scintillators made of layers of two materials with complementary properties, high stopping power (BGO) and ultrafast timing (plastic), has shown excellent results. However, layering is a limiting factor for the best achievable time resolution, as it worsens light transport. This effect can be mitigated by retrieving depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. To address this issue, a matrix of scintillators with a light guide on top can be employed to identify the DOI and correct the induced bias. For the light-sharing method to work, readout integration in a multi-channel scheme is required. We present the achievement of $124 \pm 3$ ps coincidence timing resolution (CTR) as full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) integrating a standard matrix made of 16 pixels of $3.1 \times 3.1 \times 15$ $\mathrm{mm}^{3}$ LYSO: Ce coupled to a Broadcom MT SiPM array to a 16 -channel low-noise low-power high-frequency development board. Moreover, using the light-sharing method and depolishing of the lateral surfaces of the crystals, the detector proves a DOI capability of $2.4 \pm 0.2 \mathrm{~mm}$ and CTR of $146 \pm 4 \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM. Finally, we outline the steps toward implementing this readout to a matrix made of BGO and heterostructured scintillators.

articleTitle: Investigation of Charge Transport in CdTe Detectors Using Edge-Transit Current Technique
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study explores the charge transport properties of Cadmium Telluride detectors, employing the transient current technique with red laser light with a beam waist of $6 \mu \mathrm{m}$ FWHM. The beam was aligned parallel to the detector surface and perpendicular to the metal electrodes to generate electron-hole pairs at known depths. The CdTe crystals were configured into a planar diode structure with Titanium on the Tellurium-terminated side and Gold on the Cadmium-terminated side, creating a Schottky barrier. The dimensions of the samples were $3 \times 3 \times 0.95 \mathrm{~mm}$, with equal metallization of $2.5 \times 2.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ on both sides. Our study systematically varied the laser beam’s position to modulate the depth of carrier generation and applied different voltages, including both polarities at the tellurium-terminated electrode which served as the collection electrode. Charge movement through the bulk and across crystalline defects was reconstructed, and electrical field profiles were determined from recorded waveforms. Via the Hecht equation the $\mu \tau$ product was extracted. Our findings provide insights into the mechanisms of charge transport and the impact of structural anomalies on detector performance.

articleTitle: KETEK’s Next Generation Analytical X-Ray Acquisition System AXAS 3.0
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: KETEK, the leading manufacturer of Silicon Drift Detectors, presents the next generation 3.0 electronics system. Key elements of the new platform are an optimized front-end electronics with excellent temperature stability, increased throughput capability and KETEK’s new, proprietary high-performance digital signal processor DPP 3.0. The modern AXAS 3.0 analytical x-ray acquisition system features all benefits of the new technology platform. It supports VITUS SDDs from $7 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ up to $50 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ collimated area, all equipped with KETEK’s outstanding first stage ultra-low noise charge sensitive amplifier CSA and KETEK’s proprietary CH- or CL-Graphene windows with excellent x-ray transmission from 0.1 keV (CL-type) upwards. The system has a very compact form factor of $80 \times 60 \times 36 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ and further provides two user interfaces (ethernet and USB) as well as a dedicated mapping mode for ultra-fast scanning of samples e.g. in SEM applications. Due to shortest DPP peaking times down to 25 ns, super-high input count rates up to 4 Mcps at less than 60% dead time yield in output count rates close to 2 Mcps. On the other side an excellent energy resolution down to 123 eV ($\mathrm{Mn} \mathrm{K} \alpha$-line) can be achieved at $1 \mu \mathrm{s}$ peaking time. We will present performance data, focusing on the specific needs of SEM and benchtop XRF applications.

articleTitle: Establishment of an irradiation field with a wide range of dose rates for the development of gamma-ray detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dose rates at each position in an irradiation facility have been derived using an ionization chamber. On the other hand, the energy spectrum of gamma-rays at the irradiation positions has not been evaluated. Recently, irradiation tests have been conducted to evaluate the characteristics of gamma-ray detectors, but the energy dependence of some detector materials makes it impossible to accurately evaluate the detector response. Dose evaluations that take into account the energy spectrum at the irradiation location are desired. Furthermore, it is desired that the dose rate in a wide dynamic range from mGy/hr to kGy/hr for the irradiation in the development of gamma-ray detectors. Therefore, the objective of this study is to establish a gamma-ray irradiation field with a wide range of dose rates with energy spectrum evaluated. Dose rates were measured using a high-precision electrometer and an ionization chamber, and the energy spectrum at the irradiation position was evaluated by simulating an irradiation room using a gamma-ray transport Monte Carlo simulation. In the irradiation positions where the gamma-ray source was directly visible, the contamination of scattered gamma-rays in the walls and water phantoms was confirmed. In addition, the contribution of low energy gamma-rays to the energy dependence of the detector was found to be larger at irradiation positions with low dose rates. We were able to establish a gamma-ray irradiation field that reveals the energy spectrum with a wide range of dose rates for the development of gamma-ray detectors.

articleTitle: Dose-aware Diffusion Model for 3D Low-count Cardiac SPECT Image Denoising with Projection-domain Consistency
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: SPECT imaging has been widely used in cardiology studies. Since SPECT scans are accompanied by radiation exposure, reducing the injected dose in SPECT scans is an important topic. Deep learning techniques have been investigated for low-dose SPECT imaging. However, previous neural networks proposed for low-dose SPECT imaging have limited generalizability to other noise levels due to different noise amplitude and variances. Recently, diffusion model demonstrated its potential for superior medical image denoising performance and generalizbility to different noise-levels. However, the stochastic nature of diffusion models results in distorted anatomical structures in challenging cases. Here, to address these limitations, we developed DDSPECT-3D, a dose-aware diffusion model for 3D low-count SPECT image denoising. During model testing, we proposed to incorporate MLEM iterative reconstruction updates within the reverse sampling steps to enforce a projection-domain consistency. Tested on 100 patient studies with low-count levels ranging from 5% to 50%, presented results showed that DDSPECT-3D can consistently produce promising denoised results regardless of input noise-levels.

articleTitle: CBCT-MOTUS: Model-Based Non-Rigid Motion Estimation and Correction for CBCT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) imaging has many applications including position verification in radiotherapy. However, patient motion introduces artifacts in the reconstructions, degrading their quality and resolution.
