To this end, we have developed a framework for joint non-rigid motion estimation and correction from reference images and projection data (CBCTMOTUS). Deformation vector fields are estimated through a spline-based motion model and spatial regularization, reducing the number of parameters to optimize. It is validated in silico and applied on clinical acquisitions. The framework can estimate and correct periodic and random motion with high temporal resolution (182 ms), where the motion-corrected reconstructed images show improved image quality for both experiments, such as deblurring and removal of contour artifacts. In conclusion, we estimate and correct non-rigid motion through CBCT-MOTUS by parametrization of spatially smooth motion.

articleTitle: Cyber-Nuclear-Security: Anomaly Detection of Latent Cyber Attacks on Spectroscopic Systems using Unsupervised Autoregressive Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The paper presents an anomaly detection approach for cyber attacks on radiation detectors, based on autoregressive machine learning techniques. It uses specifically trained Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM) and Autoencoders (AE). Radiation detectors are relevant for various security missions. Some of them are integrated in networks and therefore prone to cyberattacks. The latter is a threat of high interest, as latest conflicts and wars show an increasing amount hybrid attacks [1] taking place. While cyber attacks are often associated with pure Information Technology (IT) related solutions, recent attack vectors on process industry, hospitals, critical infrastructure and security systems suggest that fortification on the layer of Operational Technology and the sensorial itself yields reasonable success to detect and mitigate such attacks [2]. In 2023, a blockchain based safety mechanism against intentional sabotage of nuclear security data was shown in [3], a technique focusing on handheld instruments that rarely connect to networks and have a low amount of communication overhead. The present paper extends these ideas to the application of RBM and AE to actively encrypt measurement data of spectroscopic detectors. The encrypted data accompanies the original data stream. As online systems are more vulnerable to intentional attacks, the approach utilizes the inherent stochasticity of SNM measurements to prevent attackers from reconstructing the machine learning model from own data records. The method is tested on real data streams from smart portal detectors, that were intentionally hacked to manipulate their data and test the capabilities of the presented algorithms.

articleTitle: FastPET: Histo-Projections Approach
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep Learning (DL) PET reconstruction offers a promising alternative to full model iterative reconstructions when computational resources are limited. Previous work introduced the FastPET network, utilizing histo-images instead of projection data as DL network input, allowing for efficient network parameter optimization. However, subsequent investigations indicated that for optimal image representation, normalization and attenuation corrections should be applied to these data, and multi-view histo-images may be necessary. This raises the question of whether highly compressed TOF projection data, used in full model reconstruction, can serve as DL network input. This study explores the feasibility of using histoprojections, compressed TOF data, as DL network input, specifically in the context of Siemens reconstruction software and its highly optimized histo-projections data format. Initial results suggest that while backprojected images from histo-projections may be smoother compared to histo-images, they can be effectively deblurred to a gold standard image using the original FastPET network.

articleTitle: Progress on Development of the Electron Spectrometer Telescope
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Pitch REsolving Spectroscopy for Electron Transport (PRESET) mission aims to measure the pitch-angle dependent electron spectrum in the outer Van Allen Belt’s. This will provide high angular resolution measurements of the electron spectrum within the loss cone for use in development of ionospheric-atmospheric models. To this end the Electron Spectrometer Telescope (EST) is being developed. The EST is a small form factor electron spectrometer based on silicon strip detectors in a telescopic configuration, read out using a set of VATA460.3 ASICs. In this paper we discuss development and testing of the EST hardware. The newly designed BB37(SS) silicon strip detectors are tested for energy and spatial resolution using a VATA460.3 ASIC designed for strip detector read-out. The results are compared with those collected using a commercial pulse processing system connected to the BB37(SS) detectors. The maximum number of strips per channel with acceptable energy resolution is determined to reduce power consumption and instrument cost. A prototype version of the EST containing the custom electronic read out is tested on a high altitude balloon flight. Performance of the current front-end and data acquisition modules and the spectra collected during the flight are discussed.

articleTitle: Neutron Spectrum Unfolding of Activation Foils Irradiated in JET’s Deuterium-Tritium Fusion Environment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron spectrum unfolding methods are an essential part of an analysis toolkit for the application of neutron diagnostics to fusion environments. As fusion research moves towards more powerful machines, there is a requirement for radiation-tolerant diagnostics for safety and operation, and activation foils combined with neutron spectrum unfolding remain one of the most robust tools for indirect neutron detection. Therefore, developing unfolding methodologies and testing them in real fusion environments, particularly deuterium-tritium (D-T), is critical in the path to delivering fusion. In this work, activation foils $\left(\mathrm{Cr}, \mathrm{Cu}_{89} \mathrm{Sn}_{11}, \mathrm{Nb}\right.$ and Al<inf>90</inf>Ce<inf>10</inf>, and In) were irradiated in two pulses, with the In foil being irradiated separately from the rest of the foils, during D-T operations at the Joint European Torus (JET). Gamma spectrometry was conducted using a High-Purity Germanium (HPGe) detector, and neutron spectra were extracted using SPECTRA-UF, a suite of unfolding tools developed by UKAEA. A JET MCNP model simulated a pure D-T pulse was used as an a priori for unfolding. Six radionuclide reactions, ${ }^{27} \mathrm{Mg},{ }^{52} \mathrm{~V},{ }^{94 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Nb},{ }^{114 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{In},{ }^{115 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{In}$ and ${ }^{116 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{In}$, were used in unfolding. Unfolded solutions varied significantly; the unfolded spectrum from the indium foil reactions was comparable to the a priori with a small increase in the lower-energy spectrum region corresponding to D-D and T-T neutrons. While the remainder of the reactions unfolded a solution that significantly increased the lower-energy flux while reducing the 14 MeV D -T neutron peak so it no longer dominated. JET neutron yield data gave neutron fluence of $1.43 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{n} \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and $1.06 \times 10^{12} \mathrm{n} \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$, while integrating the unfolded spectra gave neutron fluences of $1.90 \times 10^{12}$ $\mathrm{n} \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ and $8.74 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{n} \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$ for the indium reaction and reaction of the reactions, giving percentage differences of 28% and 170%, respectively. The level of agreement, approach accuracy, and observed discrepancies will be discussed.

articleTitle: Characterizing scintillation properties of CdSe/CdZnS core-shell nanocrystal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: There has been increasing interest in measuring radiation, such as X-ray or gamma-ray, using inorganic nanocrystals (NCs) as scintillators as alternatives to X-ray sensors in CT scanners and plastic scintillators in medical imaging and nuclear decommissioning, respectively. In this study, we prepared a highly luminescent CdSe/CdZnS type-I heterostructure NCs and proposed two different methods to observe their scintillation properties. First, the scintillation properties of NCs can be observed using hexane, rather than strong scintillating toluene, as a solvent. At low-level loading of NCs, because the mean free path of hot electrons is much larger than the NC size, most of the electron energy is likely deposited in the surrounding organic molecules. Consequently, the scintillation properties of NCs can be masked by the scintillating organics, such as toluene. Second, after evaporating the solvent, the photolithography process was used to fabricate neat NC films with a thickness of several hundred micrometers. Despite the bright light emission property of the direct bandgap NCs, previous studies on nanocomposite scintillators without organic dyes suffer from strong self-absorption of NCs (due to a small Stokes shift). The allowable thickness (around $200 \mu \mathrm{m}$) of the neat NC film was quantitively determined in accordance with the radiation measurement performance.

articleTitle: Sub-mm four-side butt-able plug-in multi-energy photon-counting semiconductor x-ray detectors for security screening
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We have fabricated direct conversion cadmium telluride (CdTe) and cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) semiconductor multi-energy x-ray detectors using custom application specific integrated circuits (ASICs). The detectors use a modular four-side butt-able geometry and can be tiled in two dimensions covering a large field of view (FoV). The CdTe and/or CZT semiconductor sensors have sub-millimeter pixel dimensions with a 0.68 mm pitch perpendicular to the scanning direction for high spatial resolution. The semiconductor sensors are guard ring free and detectors have been fabricated in a range of thicknesses for high detective quantum efficiency (DQE) within the different dynamic ranges required for different security screening applications. The mixed signal ASICs have four thresholds per pixel for up to four contiguous energy windows across a dynamic range from 25 keV to $160 \mathrm{keV}, 180 \mathrm{keV}$, and 220 keV from sensors that are $2.5 \mathrm{~mm}, 2.5 \mathrm{~mm}$, and 3 mm thick respectively. The ASICs and operate at a fast peaking time for high output count rates of up to 20 million counts per second per square millimeter ($\mathrm{Mcps} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$). We have also integrated field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), in addition to the ASICs, within the active area of the sensors. Using advanced interconnects, the vertically integrated sensors, ASICs, and FPGAs, produces a detector module with 100% active area that contains digital data processing capabilities which are normally performed in either a back-plane readout or computer. Multiple four-side butt-able detector modules, each with $3.5 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} ~\mathrm{FoV}$, have been tiled in one dimension in lengths of up to 17.5 cm suitable for demonstration use in stationary and rotating computed tomography (CT) security screening systems. We will report the output count rate capability, dynamic range, and the spatial and energy resolution, as well as the uniformity and stability under conditions for carry-on and checked baggage inspection screening lanes at airports.

articleTitle: Evaluation of the TID effects on a 28 nm CMOS technology for high-density front-end electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the analog characteristics, focusing in particular on the small-signal and noise parameters, of MOSFET devices belonging to a 28 nm commercial CMOS technology exposed to high levels of ionizing radiation. The results show the extreme radiation hardness of this particular technology node, proving its applicability in high energy physics experiments.

articleTitle: Optical Re-Excitation of Scintillator Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: One of the limiting factors for energy resolution of scintillator detectors is their light yield. Re-excitation of the activator ions within a scintillator is a theoretical pathway for amplifying the scintillator yield. $\mathrm{Lu}_{2(1-\mathrm{x})} \mathrm{Y}_{2 \mathrm{x}} \mathrm{SiO}_{5}$ (LYSO) and Lu<inf>3</inf> Al<inf>5</inf> O<inf>12</inf>(LuAG) co-doped with Ce and Ca are good candidate host-dopant pairings to verify the possibility of a re-excitation mechanism. Emission and excitation spectra of both Ce and Ce, Ca co-doped samples of LuAG and LYSO are collected using spectrophotometry to determine the impact of Ca on the valence state of the Ce activator atoms. The optical spectra indicate that co-doping with Ca converts the $\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ to $\mathrm{Ce}^{4+}$ which is necessary for the multiphoton generation experiment. A dual-beam optical and x-ray excitation experiment was designed to compare the signal amplitude of single- and dual-beam excitation using a chopper wheel and lock-in amplifier. The responses of LYSO:Ce, Ca and LuAG:Ce, Ca samples will be tested in this setup to verify the re-excitation amplification mechanism.

articleTitle: Generation of Synthetic CT (sCT) from MR using Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Networks and Image Registration
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Image registration refers to the process of aligning two or more different images into the same coordinate system. However, direct transformation of multi-modal images after preprocessing is challenging, and conventional image registration studies that rely on pixel-level comparisons, typically using MSE, have been considered inadequate to achieve consistent results in CT and MR image registration. To overcome these limitations, we study how to convert multi-modal images into single-modal images and use them to perform image registration. This system consists of two main steps: generation of synthetic CT (sCT) image and image registration. In the generation of sCT image step, MR images were converted to CT images (sCT) using Cycle-Consistent Adversarial Network (CycleGAN). In the image registration step, a transformation matrix between original CT images (fixed image) and sCT images (moving image) was generated based on VoxelMorph and applied it to the original MR images (warped image) for multi-modality image registration. The results show a PSNR of 19.82, and an NCC of 0.91. The registration results show similar patterns for the regions of interest, confirming that the registration is well-matched.

articleTitle: Camera-based Motion Correction for Positron Emission Tomography Brain Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents our camera-based motion correction (MC) solution’s latest experimental results by imaging cross-calibration (CC) and resolution phantoms using the 2nd generation PETcoil insert. Our proposed solution uses a camera to track a 3D marker attached to the object to be imaged. This data is then incorporated in the multiple acquisition frames (MAF) image reconstruction algorithm to compensate for motion. The CC phantom study measured the distance between the initial frame point source locations and the consecutive aligned frames point source locations, resulted in average and maximum Euclidean distance errors of 1.2 and 3.37 mm, respectively. These results signify that when aligning two static frames, the average alignment error is less than half the scanner’s intrinsic spatial resolution. The resolution phantom study compared a long static phantom scan, a short static phantom scan, and a combined scan of multiple short static scans, simulating a moving phantom scan with and without applying MC. While we got multiple spatially shifted replicas of the resolution phantom in the motion study’s image when our proposed MC solution was not applied, the motion-corrected image quality was similar to the static images, with similar peak-to-valley ratio (indicating no degradation in separation ability due to motion when applying our MC solution). Furthermore, we observed a 1.73-fold signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improvement when utilizing all frames in the motion study to generate a MC image, compared to using only the first frame. The context of the results presented is in PET imaging, but in principle, this motion compensation method could be used in other types of medical imaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

articleTitle: Interoperability of Deep Learning Denoising for Cross-Domain Emission Tomographic Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning (DL) denoising methods have been applied for noise suppression in reduced-dose studies in various medical imaging applications. While effective, a DL denoising network is typically trained specifically for a given application setting. In this work, we investigate the feasibility of employing a single DL denoising network for processing reduced-dose studies from different application domains in emission tomography. We acquired two sets of clinical image data with 500 cases each, one from cardiac SPECT imaging and one from pediatric renal imaging. We evaluated the performance of DL denoising on the two data sets with imaging dose reduced by a factor of four. The quantitative results indicate that through adequate choice of loss function a single DL network could achieve performance for both domains on par with (or even better than) optimizing for each specific domain, overcoming the disparity in data characteristics between two application domains.

articleTitle: Study of electro-physical properties of CsPbBr3 perovskite single crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, the electro-physical properties of the inorganic perovskite CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>, which can be used as optical, X-ray and gamma radiation detector, were investigated. Single crystals of these compounds were grown by the Bridgman method. The melt temperature was $580{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, the gradient at the crystallization front was $5 \mathrm{~K} / \mathrm{cm}$, and the ampoule lowering speed was $3 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{hour}$. Crystals for research were cut from the beginning and end of the ingot. The optical absorption spectra were measured depending on the crystal thickness and temperature, the differential resistivity $r_{\text {dif }}$ and the product $m \times t$ were determined from the I-V characteristics. It was established that $r_{\text {dif }}$ practically does not change for samples made from the beginning and the end of the ingot, and is $r_{\text {dif }} \gg 2 \times 10^{10} \Omega \times \mathrm{cm}$ at 100 V and 293 K. To determine the differential resistivity, a $\mathrm{Cr} / \mathrm{CsPbBr}_{3} / \mathrm{Ni}$ structure was formed. Chromium and nickel, 20-30 nm thick, were deposited on opposite faces of the single crystal by the resistive method in vacuum. The product $m \times t$, which we estimated from measurements of I-V characteristics according to [5], for single crystals in the middle of the ingot was equal to $m \times t \gg 8.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \times \mathrm{V}^{-1}$, and for single crystals at the end of the ingot it was approximately three times smaller and equal to $m \times t \gg 2.5 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \times \mathrm{V}^{-1}$. The band gap of single crystals was determined from measurements of fundamental absorption spectra, which for crystals from the middle of the ingot was $E_{\mathrm{g}}=2.355 \mathrm{eV}$, and for crystals at the end of the ingot $-E_{\mathrm{g}}=2.360 \mathrm{eV}$.

articleTitle: Performance of full system tests for the ATLAS Inner Tracker Strip Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The new ATLAS Inner Tracker (ITk) will replace the current tracking system in ATLAS to cope with the challenging conditions during the high-luminosity phase of the Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). The ITk is an all-silicon detector consisting of a pixel inner tracker and a silicon microstrip outer tracker.This contribution focuses on the full system tests of the strip sub-detector that are being developed to verify the design and evaluate the performance of detector components prior to production. Moreover, important lessons are learned on these large-scale system tests for the detector integration as well as operation of the full detector. Two setups at CERN and at DESY (Hamburg/Germany) target the design verification of the central barrel section around the interaction point and the end-cap section covering the forward region. In both setups, silicon sensors mounted on local support structures are connected to electrical, optical and cooling services. As such it is possible to validate the detector design, verify the detector DAQ and perform tests with the services, e.g. concerning the dual-phase CO${\$}${}_2${\$}$ cooling.In this contribution, we will give a general overview of the developed system tests for the ITk strip detector and will present a selection of results from performance measurements.

articleTitle: Energy-based scatter correction in PET, accounting for the position dependent energy spectrum of the true coincidences
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scatter correction (SC) is essential for obtaining quantitative images in Positron Emission Tomography (PET), and is routinely performed using tail-fitted single scatter simulation (SSS). While this method is usually robust and accurate, it can fail when there is a strong scatter contribution from activity outside the field of view (FOV) or when the attenuation map is not well aligned due to patient motion. As an alternative, energy-based scatter estimation has recently been proposed [1, 2]. Hamill et al. [2] model the joint photon energy histogram as a sum of nine basis functions. An iterative expectation maximization approach determines the coefficients and estimates the scatter. In this study, we investigate possible improvements to the approach by Hamill et al. including: (i) modeling the position dependence of the trues energy spectrum and (ii) invoking time-of-flight TOF to reduce the number of model parameters to 5. Using GATE simulations, we show that the trues energy spectrum depends on the photon incidence angle and therefore on position. We provide arguments for the parameter reduction; the evaluation of its effect on the final reconstructed image is ongoing.

articleTitle: EDM: Enhancing Quality Diversity of Medical Image Augmentation Under the User-specified Complex and Various Conditions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the medical domain, the scarcity of data leads to class imbalances and fairness issues, significantly impairing deep learning performance and leading to the underrepresentation of minority patient groups. To address these challenges, data augmentation techniques employing Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and diffusion models have been extensively explored, with diffusion models particularly noted for their ability to enhance data diversity and quality. Despite their achievements, it remains a challenging task to generate a diverse range of samples from limited datasets and to achieve precise generation of images that align with user intentions.To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework, EDM (Enhancing Quality Diversity of Medical image augmentation under the user-specified complex and various conditions), designed to generate diverse high-quality medical images under the various and complex multimodal conditions, representing age, sex, and diseases. Our framework comprises four steps. First, we propose a metric to quantize the necessity of data augmentation. Second, we prepare data augmentation. We generate medical sketch-image-text triplets using DiffSketcher from the real patients’ dataset. Then we employ these triplets to train ControlNet, enabling the generation of synthetic medical images from sketch data. Third, we generate synthetic medical images. We obtain multiple sketches for each image from a diversity-enhanced DiffSketcher, incorporating similarity loss. Using these sketches, we augment data from the fine-tuned ControlNet from the second step. Lastly, we introduce a metric to measure the diversity of the generated images, ensuring the effectiveness of our augmentation process.Our preliminary experimental results imply EDM can be the promising solution. Future experiments are planned to construct synthetic datasets of various modalities such as PET and CT for underrepresented patient groups.

articleTitle: Update on the Energy Resolution and DOI Performance of the Detector for the Human Dynamic Neurochemical Connectome Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our group develops the Human Dynamic Neurochemical Connectome Scanner (HDNCC), a high spatio-temporal resolution brain PET insert for a 7T MR Scanner. Sensitivity and spatial resolution are maximized by a spherical design combined with thin and long crystals. To maintain a high uniform spatial resolution, we developed depth-of-interaction (DOI) capable detectors [1]. In this study, we report the advances in optimization of operational parameters in the method for DOI determination and updated detector performance. The detectors are based on a modified version of the C13500 TOF-PET modules (Hamamatsu K.K.) with a 10×10 1.6×1.6×26 mm<sup>3</sup> LSO crystal block coupled to a 4×4 4×4 mm<sup>2</sup> SiPM. A 380 μm light guide on top of the crystal block enables a DOI-dependent light spread. We evaluated the impact on the performance of different ASIC parameters affecting signal gain, shape and time-over-threshold. A new method to extract the DOI information from the light spread employing a crystal-specific ratio of multiple SiPM signals was evaluated with a collimated coincidence setup with a translational stage to obtain ground truth information for interaction depths. Further, we assessed the impact of inter-crystal scatter (ICS) rejection on crystal identification. The optimization of the ASIC parameters resulted in an improvement of the energy resolution from 16.9±3.5% to 12.6±2.0% with a high crystal identification accuracy (peak-to-valley-ratio 3.7±2.0). The optimized settings in combination with the new method for DOI determination improved the DOI resolution from 12.8±9.0mm to 5.0±1.0mm. The ICS rejection method resulted in further improvements in crystal identification, and we are currently evaluating its impact on DOI and energy resolution. With the updated experimental setups, optimum ASIC parameters could be identified, which, combined with the new DOI method, could further improve the performance of the HDNCC.

articleTitle: DNA strands break by low energy electrons assessed with Monte Carlo GEANT4 at the atomic level
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiotherapy is the mostly used approach for cancer treatment and approximately accounts for $50 \%$ of all cancer therapies. The radiations frequently used are the photons (X-rays, gamma-rays) and others not widely used are the protons and heavy ions. Independently of its energy, any radiation interacts in general by ionizing the medium thus putting electrons in movement. The low energy electrons set in movement and the free radicals and ions are the main products causing damage to DNA. In the present work, we consider the interactions of low energy electrons on the DNA atoms, and by converting the energy deposit into absorbed dose, DNA strand breaks are estimated. The calculations are conducted with Monte Carlo simulation taking advantage of GEANT4 toolkit and by designing around 1000 nucleotides of DNA molecules. The generated electron beams were set to several energies between 2 eV till 500 eV with 10 million simulated electrons. The results show a great similarity with the experimental results for the interactions of excitation, dissociative electron attachment (DEA) and ionization. At 30 eV, ionization in DNA molecule was the dominant interaction type, followed by excitation then by DEA. While at low energy, 4 eV, DEA was found the most dominant, decreasing with increasing energy. The single and double DNA strand breaks were found maximum around 100 eV. In conclusion, such calculations provide more details than experimental results on the types of interactions and their effects on DNA damage, which is of great help specifically in selecting isotopes for internal radiotherapy.

articleTitle: Optimizing Proton Range Verification on Compton Camera Experimental Data with Neural Network Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a novel approach for signal event selection in Compton camera imaging, focusing on proton range verification. Experimental data were collected from a clinical cyclotron facility by employing the MACACO III Compton camera prototype. An event selection method based on neural networks was applied and compared with a traditional energy-cut method. Results demonstrate that the NN-based approach significantly enhances signal percentage and improves the precision in detecting millimetric shifts in depth-dose distribution. Ongoing work involves implementing the NN approach on experiments performed with an improved Compton camera prototype for further refinement and application in hadron therapy monitoring.

articleTitle: The End-of-Substructure card for the ATLAS ITk Strip Upgrade: Lessons learned from the full production
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)

authors.preferredName: A. F. Arranca Menezes Trigueiros Da Silva

abstract: The ATLAS Strip Tracker for HL-LHC consists of so-called modules that host the silicon sensors and the front-end electronics. These units are then mounted on mechanical structures, the so-called staves and petals, which are hosting up to 14 modules per side. An End-of-Substructure (EoS) card connects up to 28 data lines from the modules to and up to 12 lines from the lpGBT ASIC. The lpGBT then does (De-)Serialization and connects to the VL+ ASICs which then provides a 10 GBit/s optical data transmission to the off-detector systems respectively. The EoS is powered by a dedicated Dual-Stage DC-DC converter unit. As the both staves and petals host modules on both sides, two EoS are required for each stave and petal, however to reduce cabling, they are sharing a single voltage connector. While schematically the EoS cards are very closely related, especially for the barrel each layer requires a distinct layout, which adds complexity also for testing. As the EoS production of almost 2000 EoS cards and the accompanying 2000 DC-DC converters is going to be completed in fall 2024, we report on the production experience including detailed QC statistics. We conclude with a few lessons learned during the project duration.

articleTitle: Automatic segmentation of gray and white matter lesions in multiple sclerosis patients using isolines
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multiple sclerosis is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by the presence of lesions in brain tissues due to the inflammatory processes. The analysis of these lesions, visible through magnetic resonance imaging, is of great utility for the diagnosis and monitoring of the disease. In this work we propose a computerized procedure based on isolines to automatically segment the lesions caused by the disease, thus reducing the burden of physicians and removing human factor from the process. The proposed method calculates the isolines of all axial slices of the magnetic resonance image corresponding to a subject, selects those corresponding to points of higher intensity and triangulates the points of selected isolines, forming solid surfaces covering the proximities of the isolines. The process concludes by returning a 3D map containing all the lesions of a given subject in a standardized space that can be used to determine the volume of lesioned tissues or to perform quantitative analysis of molecular neuroimaging data to improve patient monitoring. This method has been evaluated using neuroimaging data from 16 patients and the results, similar to those obtained by manual segmentation, have been visually validated by experienced clinicians.

articleTitle: Large Volume Lu2O3 Ceramic Scintillators for HEP
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Future colliders that operate at high energies and luminosity require inorganic scintillators that are ultrafast and dense due to the very high event rates. In addition, the scintillators should be radiation hard to withstand the high accumulated doses of tens of million rads. There are only few scintillation mechanisms that provide ultrafast scintillation - one of them being the charge transfer luminescence (CT), in which the emission originates from an ion changing its charge state. $\mathrm{Lu}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}: \mathrm{Yb}$ is one of the densest hosts at $9.4 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cc}$, emission of which relies on CT luminescence. $\mathrm{Lu}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}: \mathrm{Yb}$ shows decay time faster than 2 ns and light yield as high as 500 photons $/ \mathrm{MeV}$. Since the melting point of Lu<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> is very high ($\gt2,000^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$) and its structure is cubic, the optically transparent material is manufactured using ceramic processes, which are very malleable for producing samples of various sizes and geometries. Samples of large sizes, including 1-inch cubes of Lu<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> doped with Yb were manufactured at RMD. The samples were characterized at both RMD and Caltech. The 1-inch square samples of few mm thickness show light yield as high as $500 \mathrm{ph} / \mathrm{MeV}$, while the 1-inch cubes show light yield of $\sim 100$ $\mathrm{ph} / \mathrm{MeV}$ due to reduced transparency. The light yield numbers are consistent with small samples for the 1-inch square samples. For the larger cubes we expect a higher light yield as the transparency of the samples is improved. The X-ray excited luminescence peaks around 370 nm and the scintillation decay time measured with a fast photomultiplier tube is around 2 ns. With its high density and ultrafast decay, Lu<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> ceramics are promising for future HEP calorimetry, time of fight (TOF) applications, and high energy resolved radiography. Optical and scintillation properties and radiation hardness studies for large volume samples will be presented.

articleTitle: A CNN-based demultiplexing method for an interleaved signal multiplexing readout with a TOF-DOI brain PET detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A prototype PET system for human brain-dedicated PET imaging (named N-PET) is being developed at Shenzhen Bay Laboratory, which uses multi-resolution TOF-DOI detectors. High resolution PET imaging systems require a significantly large number of readout channels, which increase the system complexity, power consumption, heat production, and cost. In this study, we investigate an interleaved signal multiplexing readout that utilizes the characteristic light-sharing pattern of depth-encoding N-PET detector modules. In this study, we proposed a demultiplexing method using a CNN model, which was trained by 16 channel synthetic multiplexed signals and 64-channel ground-truth data. The CNN model used in this work was a typical U-net model. We reduced the number of layers in the network and decreased the number of kernels in each convolutional layer for shrinking the paths. The CNN input is a $4 \times 4$ matrix representing the integrated charges of the 16 -channel outputs from the multiplexing circuit. The output is an $8 \times 8$ matrix representing the original 64 -channel demultiplexed data. By using the CNN predicted 64-channel data, all crystals could be clearly resolved in the flood images. Energy spectrum of the detector obtained by the sum of the multiplexed 16-channel data and the sum of the CNN predicted 64-channel data were similar. The average DOI resolution obtained by measured and CNN predicted data were 4.1 and 3.9 mm. In the future, timing resolution using this signal multiplexing circuit will be studied. The proposed demultiplexing method provides an alternative approach for the development of N-PET system, potentially bringing benefits in terms of commercial viability, power efficiency, and cost-effectiveness.

articleTitle: Spatial representation of die-cast defects by industrial 3D X-ray CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In inspections using 3D X-ray CT for industrial applications, along with improvements in CT technology and software performance, evaluation methods have improved, such as characterization using energy information and segmentation according to composition information and analysis using conventional transmission images and CT reconstructed images. On the other hand, in the conventional method of checking segmented three-dimensional voxel data with multi-section reconstruction (MPR) images, it is difficult to grasp the location of defects and cracks, and it is difficult to check the overlapped areas of segmented models in the 3D rendering method. In our previous research, a system that represents the internal structure of an object imaged by 3D X-ray CT using Mixed Reality (MR) and combines a spatial reality display and motion capture was proposed so that the internal structure can be grasped spatially with intuitive operation while viewing the object in 3D. This study attempts to represent the information easily spatially from these segmented 3D X-ray CTs. In the experiment, an aluminum die-cast sample was prepared, two surface-rendered models with threshold values suitable for displaying surface and internal defects, performed surface rendering, overlaid with translucent coloring, and pasted MPR images generated from DICOM onto the cross-section according to the position and angle of the surface with MPR images generated from DICOM.

articleTitle: CdZnTe surface conditioning using Ar plasma
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CdZnTe semiconductor direct conversion X-ray detectors are highly sought-after for applications in medical imaging and security due to their potential to deliver a high SNR at room temperature. However, the growth and subsequent processing of wafers induce a defective layer at the surface yielding a large density of trapping center thus reducing the charge collection and SNR. Whereas this layer is typically removed using a Br: MeOH wet etching, we investigate the use of Ar plasma for better repeatability and uniformity. The 400 W Ar plasma treatment is shown to increase the surface roughness to 10.9 nm (RMS) from 3.7 nm (RMS) for the chemical-mechanical-polished surface. Albeit this notable roughness, the etched contacts are shown to present a dark current of 2.5 nA, an increase of 1.5 nA from those on the chemical-mechanical-polish surface. The devices fabricated are still shown to present a dark current an order of magnitude lower than devices prepared by 5% Br:MeOH. This decrease in dark current is attributed to the maintenance of the surface stoichiometry, yet the increase in the surface roughness likely causes an increase in the surface state density. The plasma process is further found to remove the charge-trapping effects found in polished devices.

articleTitle: High-resolution brain phantom data, with flexible contrast: Validation on the NeuroExplorer (NX)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The goal of this work was to assess the quantitative accuracy and spatial resolution of our recently installed ultra-high-performance brain dedicated NeuroEXPLORER (NX) scanner, using a set of high-resolution 3D-printed occipital phantoms recently developed by our group. This was achieved by: 1) developing an easy and flexible technique of creating phantom data with different contrasts, via merging of separate listmode data, needed to test the quantitative accuracy of iterative reconstruction algorithms; 2) evaluating the spatial resolution of iteratively reconstructed PET images as a function of contrast. The advantage of using such phantoms is to characterize images that are more representative to those provided to physicians and researchers. These preliminary results show: 1) merging of separate list mode data sets offers the potential to easily customize phantom studies with different contrasts, without compromising quantitative accuracy; 2) using such phantoms deliver spatial resolutions ($\sim 2 \mathrm{~mm}$ FWHM) in both transaxial and axial directions, which are, not surprisingly, slightly higher than previously reported results (1.2-1.5 mm FWHM) for the NX using point sources, which emphasize the fact that resolution measurements using point sources do not necessarily match the resolution of the reconstructed images. Future analyses will investigate the use of other phantoms, and assess the effects of slight differences in attenuation properties on attenuation correction and scatter correction accuracy.

articleTitle: Imaging Performance of a Phase-contrast X-ray Imaging System with a Silicon-based Photon Counting X-ray Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present imaging performance of a phase contrast X-ray imaging system constructed by an innovative silicon-based photon counting X-ray detector and a microfocus X-ray tube. The developed propagation-based phase contrast imaging system without grating involves a super-large area flat-panel silicon based photon counting X-ray detector and a microfocus X-ray tube with a minimal focal size of five micron meter. According to the principle of coaxial phase contrast, phase differences of the imaging subject are generated by detection at specific detecting locations. The phase information is extracted from a series of back-projection images. The detailed phase contrast image is then acquired. To obtain high-resolution and high sensitivity phase contrast imaging, the system uses a up-to-date silicon base photon counting flat-panel detector, which pixel size is 70 micron, thickness of silicon x-ray sensitive layer is 700 micron, and the counting rate of pixels is $2.6 \mathrm{E}^{6}$. Comparing with conventional absorption-contrast imaging, the presented phase-contrast system has better performances and enhanced phase contrasting details, especially for imaging biological samples with soft issues of low densities.

articleTitle: Advanced Lymphoma Classification: Leveraging Radiomics and Machine Learning on 18F-FDG PET/CT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigated the potential of machine learning analysis on radiomic features extracted from baseline 18F-FDG PET/CT scans in combination with clinical data to aid in the diagnosis of lymphoma subtypes.Patients with initial/new pathology-confirmed diagnoses of Diffuse Large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL, n=34), Cassical HL (n=70), and other less common lymphomas ($\mathbf{n}=27$) were included in this study. All patients underwent 18F-FDG PET/CT scans with VUE Point FX reconstruction. Volumes of interest were delineated over the lesions and the liver. Radiomic features were extracted from the region of interest on co-registered 18F-FDG PET (for lesions and also liver) and CT images. Models were developed using radiomics (tumor-to-liver background ratio (TLR) radiomics and TLR with clinical data), with 2 different machine learning (ML) classifiers, to classify lymphoma type on a lesion-based approach.Radiomic features were extracted from both SUVmap and CT imaging modalities separately, along with 14 shape features, resulting in a total of 93 radiomic features from each imaging modality. While the radiomics-based Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) classifier achieved a micro average-AUC of 0.82, the multinomial logistic regression classifier using 200 radiomics features along with age and gender achieved the highest discrimination performance with a micro average AUC of 0.84. This study investigated the use of baseline 18 F -FDG PET/CT scan radiomic features for machine learning-based lymphoma subtype diagnosis. Strong discrimination was demonstrated by the results, particularly when using TLR Radiomics in combination with clinical data. The incorporation of demographic variables significantly improved the accuracy of lesion classification, which may improve lymphoma patients’ personalized treatment plans and diagnostic accuracy.

articleTitle: Advances in 3D Source Reconstruction Using Coded-Aperture Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-ray imagers are useful for identifying the angular location of radioactive sources. Although the typical angular resolution of a coded-aperture gamma-ray imager is quite good (approximately 5 degrees), depth information is uncertain in the near field and essentially unknown in the far field. Many applications are aimed at quantifying the amount of source material being imaged, and to that end, knowledge of the depth of a source is required. Depth information, and thus the full 3D location, of a source can be acquired by incorporating measurements from imagers with multiple lines of sight. Iterative methods, such as Maximum Likelihood, provide a framework for 3D source reconstruction using multiple imager views. This paper discusses recent advances in applying a Maximum Likelihood iterative method to reconstruct radioactive sources in 3D using coded-aperture gamma-ray imagers. Advances include data-driven convergence criteria, extended source reconstruction in 2D, background subtraction assessments for various signal-to-noise-ratios, and point source reconstruction in 3D.

articleTitle: Modeling intra-regional heterogeneity during projection-domain quantification for alpha-particle SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Methods to quantify absorbed dose in lesions and at-risk organs in alpha-particle radiopharmaceutical therapies (α-RPTs) are much needed. While SPECT does provide a mechanism for this quantification, due to the extremely low counts, imaging artifacts and complex isotope physics, the images have limited quality for quantification tasks. To improve this quality, there is a need to optimize SPECT systems and protocols. This optimization step requires the development of reliable estimators. Conventional quantitative SPECT (QSPECT) methods include reconstruction-based quantification (RBQ) methods, which calculate uptake from images reconstructed using SPECT projections, and projection domain quantification (PDQ) methods, which calculate uptake directly from the projections. However, both methods have disadvantages that lead to erroneous estimates. RBQ suffers from information loss during reconstruction, while conventional PDQ methods do not account for uptake heterogeneity. To address these issues, we developed and validated WIN-PDQ, a Wiener-estimator-based PDQ method that accounts for intra-regional heterogeneity. We evaluated its performance using clinically realistic simulation studies conducted with anthropomorphic phantoms of prostate cancer patients undergoing 223Ra-based α-RPT treatment and validated Monte Carlo-based SPECT simulation software. The method was compared with an RBQ method, and 2 PDQ methods that do not account for heterogeneity. The WIN-PDQ method demonstrated high reliability, showing normalized ensemble root mean squared error (NREMSE) of 12.43% averaged over all lesion sizes, and an NREMSE of 5.34% and 9.26% averaged over all heterogeneity levels in the kidney and lesion respectively, which was the lowest amongst all considered QSPECT methods. In conclusion, WIN-PDQ demonstrated reliability for SPECT-based regional uptake quantification in α-RPTs, supporting its potential in defining task-based optimization of SPECT systems and protocols.

articleTitle: Scintillating Glass for Future HEP Calorimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A novel homogeneous calorimeter concept is being pursued by CalVision: a collaboration of multiple universities and national laboratories for the proposed high energy physics (HEP) Higgs factory. Dense, UV-transparent and cost-effective inorganic scintillators are required for a longitudinally segmented precision electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) with multiple readout. Novel heavy inorganic scintillators, if cost-effective enough, may also be used for a homogeneous hadronic calorimeter (HHCAL) concept which promises a jet mass resolution at a level of $20\%;/\sqrt{E}$. We report an investigation on cerium-doped aluminoborosilicate (ABS) and cerium-doped DSB (BaO·2SiO2) glass samples. Optical and scintillation properties are characterized at room temperature, including X-ray excited emission, longitudinal and transverse transmittance, pulse height spectrum, light output, decay time, and light response uniformity for long samples. Their emission weighted quantum efficiency (QE) and photon detection efficiency (PDE) are calculated for photomultiplier (PMT) and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readouts respectively, and are compared to BGO, BSO and PWO crystals.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based scatter correction acceleration using view-grouped histo-images in long axial field-of-view PET system
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Benefited from the improved TOF resolution of modern PET scanners, the scatter correction (SC) algorithm based on the histo-image and deep neural network solves the problem of multiple iterations in a short AFOV system with $\sim 200$ ps TOF resolution. On the other hand, the method of feeding view-grouped histo-image into a 3D CNN as a multi-channel image is reported to recover finer structures of deep learning reconstructed images. We proposed a view-grouped histo-image based SC algorithm that improves the speed of SC for LAFOV PET/CT systems with $\sim 500$ ps TOF resolution. Compared with the SC by taking the clinical reconstructed image as the emission map, the organ-based NMAEs are less than 5%, except for the stomach, which is purely cold region. Although the worst case in stomach has 72% quantitative difference, its MAE was only 0.02 kBq/ml, proving that our proposed method is still quantitatively accurate while accelerating.

articleTitle: Calibration of the ALICE Inner Tracking System for the LHC Run 3
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The new ultra-light ALICE Inner Tracking System (ITS2) for the LHC Run 3 significantly enhances the resolution on the determination of the distance of closest approach to the primary vertex, the tracking efficiency at low transverse momenta, and the readout rate capabilities with respect to the previous tracker. It is equipped with silicon Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS) with a pixel size of 27${\$}$\times${\$}$29 ${\$}$\mu${\$}$m${\$}$^2${\$}$.. With a a total sensitive area of about 10 m${\$}$^2${\$}$, ITS 2 represents the largest scale application of the MAPS technology in a High-Energy Physics experiment. For stable operations during data taking, it is of crucial importance to calibrate the in-pixel thresholds and to mask any noisy pixel in order to keep the fake-hit rate below 10${\$}$^{-6}${\$}$ hits/event/pixel. The calibration of 12.6${\$}$\times${\$}$10${\$}$^{9}${\$}$ pixels powered from a distance of about 7 m, represents the main challenge addressed in this contribution.

articleTitle: MLTiming: A Machine Learning Framework for Gamma-Ray Pulse Time Pick-Up.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ability to obtain accurate timing characterization of detected radiation events in nuclear medicine has a number of increasing applications, especially in Positron Emission Tomography (PET). In PET, a good coincidence resolving time (CRT) between detector pairs provides useful Time-of-flight (TOF) information for each detected coincidence, which has been shown to improve the signal-to-noise ratio of the images. In this work, we propose a method that enables the training of machine learning (ML) models to assign accurate timestamps to incoming radiation signals in each detector. We used fully-connected dense neural network models trained with pairs of events: a measured one and a delayed version of it. The delay used served as a label in the training process. The proposed trained model was evaluated with data acquired with a 60Co point source with a pair of conic 2” LaBr3(Ce) detectors in coincidence mode connected to Hamamatsu R9779 PMTs sampled at $5 \mathrm{Gs} / \mathrm{s}$. An average of 149 ps CRT was achieved. These promising initial results are expected to be improved with more sophisticated ML models, but they already provide an efficient alternative way to analyze the timing of pulses in medical physics.

articleTitle: PR-PET: Design and Performance Evaluation of Partial Ring PET Based on GATE Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Traditional PET detectors utilize a full-ring structure, which can provide clearer and more effective imaging of the human body. However, this full-ring structure is costly and inflexible, making it inconvenient for certain specific applications, such as gamma therapy, due to limitations in imaging functionality. In this paper, we propose four partial-ring PET (PR-PET) structures with adjustable fields of view (FOV) and flexible positioning. The imaging performance of the PR-PET changes with the adjustment of the positioning. In this study, we conducted NEMA tests on the four structures with detectors placed at equal intervals and performed imaging analysis and comparison based on brain scans. By comparing the imaging performance of full-ring and partialring PET, we validated the performance of partial-ring PET. Overall, our contributions are as follows: (1) we proposed four partial-ring PET structures; (2) we validated the performance of partial-ring PET detectors based on NEMA tests; (3) we compared and analyzed the imaging performance of full-ring and partial-ring PET based on brain imaging. By proposing the partialring PET structure, we aim to reduce medical costs and promote the clinical application of gamma therapy.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Spatial Resolution Enhanced by the NeuroEXPLORER PET Insert through Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: NeuroEXPLORER (NX), designed for high-performance human brain imaging, has now been utilized in a variety of studies. However, higher spatial resolution in regions such as the carotid artery is highly desirable for precise extraction of the image-derived blood input function. To address this need, a PET insert panel with finer detector crystals (size: $0.92 \times 0.92 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$) was proposed for integration into the field-of-view of the cylindrical NX scanner (crystal size: $1.56 \times$ $3.07 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$) positioned 8.4 cm from the NX axis over the neck. This study utilizes simulation to estimate the spatial resolution enhancement introduced by the insert. The NX insert is a dual PET system having cylinder- (cy-) insert coincidences detected by the NX and the insert, and cy-cy coincidences detected by the NX only. Simulation was implemented using GATE with actual system parameters. Normalization of the NX insert involves two steps: normalizations for cy-insert coincidences using a planar source and for cy-cy coincidences using a cylinder source. Currently, spatial resolutions of the NX insert are evaluated at two points, positioned 2.8 and 5.6 cm from the insert panel center, respectively, based on isolated point sources reconstructed using the maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) algorithm and 0.4 mm voxels. Results reveal spatial resolutions of 1.4, 1.0 and 1.0 mm for the point closer to the insert, and 1.1, 0.9 and 1.1 mm at the point further from the insert, in radial, tangential and axial directions. A substantial axial spatial resolution enhancement compared to the NX scanner alone ($\sim 1.8 \mathrm{~mm}$ axially) was observed. The proposed PET insert is promising for spatial resolution enhancement in NX in various regions for improved quantification and enhanced visualization of microstructures.

articleTitle: Application of the Cohn-■ Method to Supercritical Assemblies of Bare Highly Enriched Uranium Metal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron noise measurements are a modality of nondestructive assay to measure fission chain kinetics. These noise measurements exploit the temporal fluctuations present in multiplying fissionable systems and can be used to monitor reactors for nuclear nonproliferation, criticality safety analysis, and nuclear data validation. Parameters such as the prompt neutron decay constant ($\alpha$) can be used to calculate the lifetime of prompt fission chains within a multiplying system. This new work analyzes data from a series of measurements on a fast, bare system of highly enriched uranium hemisphere shells known as the Measurements of Uranium Subcritical and Critical (MUSiC). A three-by-four array of 5.08-cm-length by 5.08-cm-diameter cylindrical trans-stilbene organic scintillators (OSCAR) was used to obtain the gamma-ray and fast neutron signals. Pulse shape discrimination was used to isolate the neutron time-series data. The data analyzed was from Configuration 8 of MUSiC, comprising 61 kg HEU (93% 235U). The Cohn-. method was used to infer the prompt neutron period of three supercritical perturbations. Linear extrapolation of Cohn-$\alpha$ results suggests this configuration has a prompt neutron decay constant (a) of $-8.11 \times 10^{5} \pm 5.28 \times 10^{4} 1 / \mathrm{s}$ at delayed critical. This result was compared to a high-fidelity MCNP6 KCODE simulation with an estimate of the prompt neutron period at delayed critical ($\mathrm{a}_{\mathrm{DC}}$) of $-9.80 \times 10^{5} \pm 3.44 \times 10^{3} 1 / \mathrm{s}$.

articleTitle: An Analytical System Response Model for Spatiotemporal Emission Reconstruction from Multi-Detector Prompt Gamma Timing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Particle therapy verification using induced prompt gamma radiation is a field of active research. We employ an iterative reconstruction algorithm to reconstruct the spatiotemporal emission distribution. Due to the fast emission of the prompt gamma radiation after the interaction, their spatiotemporal distribution can be used as a surrogate for the primary particle motion. Using a motion model, we extract the particle range and the stopping power, which should allow direct validation of expected values from treatment planning without additional imaging time. The reconstruction is based on Prompt Gamma Timing spectra from multiple detectors, i.e. the combination of primary particle time of flight before nuclear interaction and secondary photon time of flight until detection outside the patient. Reconstruction requires an accurate model of photon transport and detection, which we previously calculated using extensive Monte-Carlo simulations. Here, we present an analytical model that accelerates calculations by almost 200 times, while matching the Monte-Carlo implementation within 6% of the global maximum value for 99% of all non-zero entries. Furthermore, detection delay caused by secondary particles created by the photons in the detector is studied and its integration into the analytical model demonstrated. First reconstructions of spatiotemporal emission distributions from simulated data using both models show almost perfect agreement. The impact on range and stopping power estimates is currently under investigation.

articleTitle: The OxyFLASH project: overview and first measurements
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The recently started OxyFlash project is dedicated to in vitro and in vivo measurements of flash radiotherapy-induced effects on oxygen dynamics and radiobiological damage. Its primary goals are to measure simultaneously and in real-time the dose and oxygen distribution in healthy and tumor tissues irradiated with conventional and flash electron beams, and to correlate these prompt measurements with the radiobiological damage. Oxygen concentration is measured with Oxyphor PtG4, where the time information is measured with a fast photodetector while an optical imaging system samples the spatial heterogeneity of oxygen. The dose information is given by a combination of detectors, which we are testing for operation in the flash regime (e.g. a calibrated flash diamond detector, gafchromic films, plastic scintillators). The irradiated samples (both in vitro and in vivo) are then analyzed to assess the short- and long-term flash-induced radiobiological damage. This contribution will give a brief overview of the project and describe the first oxygen measurements performed to measure Oxyphor decay time and to image its light intensity.

articleTitle: An in silico imaging pipeline for the simulation and deep learning-based segmentation of photon-counting CT brain images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The combination of photon-counting CT and deep learning-based tumour segmentation can be of great benefit to radiotherapy treatment planning in neuro-oncology. We developed an in silico imaging pipeline for the simulation of photon-counting CT brain images. The reconstructed images are then used to train and test a 2D nnU-Net to automatically segment the tumour volumes and its performance is compared to conventional images acquired using an energy-integrating detector. Preliminary results demonstrate the capability of the pipeline to produce both photon-counting and conventional CT images, as well as images of different energy bins. We also demonstrate that the reconstructed photon-counting CT images are significantly more robust towards electronic noise as compared to the conventional CT images. Ongoing work focuses on the automatic tumour delineation and optimisation of image quality.

articleTitle: Post-Neutron-Tomography SPECT for 3D Isotopic Reconstruction in Bulk Samples
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The non-destructive assessment of interior elemental composition and spatial distribution in bulk samples (greater than a few hundred $\mu \mathrm{m}$) is essential across various fields of research including archaeometry, palaeontology and cultural heritage. Traditional neutron activation analysis (NAA) techniques offer elemental identification, but lack the 3D spatial context. Similarly, advanced imaging techniques like X-ray and neutron tomography provide 3D structural information but often fall short in extrapolating internal elemental distributions. To address this issue, we propose a novel method: Post-Neutron-Tomography SPECT. Using ANSTO’s thermal neutron imaging beamline (DINGO), samples are irradiated to induce temporary activation through neutron capture. The characteristic gamma lines from these decaying radionuclides can be used to identify the created isotopes. By performing single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) of the neutron-irradiated samples, the spatial distribution of resulting isotopes, determined using delayed gamma emission, can reconstructed through additional energy windowing techniques. Successful 3D reconstructions of copper (Cu-64) and gold (Au-198) samples demonstrate the method’s potential in providing 3D isotopic distributions of bulk objects. Simulation modelling can also be used to predict and inform irradiation time and which isotopes may be present in the collected gamma spectra. Combined with structural imaging modalities, this approach enhances our capacity to estimate elemental distributions in bulk samples of unknown compositions.

articleTitle: A front-end circuit for a Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor in 65-nm CMOS Technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents an analog front-end circuitry implemented in a monolithic active pixel sensor (MAPS) fabricated in a 65-nm CMOS imaging technology. It combines the low-capacitance collection electrode ($\lt 2 \mathrm{fF}$) and an analog processor featuring a charge-sensitive amplifier (CSA) driving a fast continuous-time threshold comparator. The CSA features a gain stage along with a Krummenacher-type feedback network. Its gain approximately amounts to $130 \mu \mathrm{V} / \mathrm{e}^{-}$and provides a rise time of 5 ns. The negative feedback provides leakage current compensation of the sensor diode and a continuous linear discharge of the feedback capacitor. This implements a time-over-threshold (ToT) measurement in combination with the comparator. Threshold voltage and Krummenacher-bias current can be adjusted pixel wise by using a 4-bit and 3-bit DAC, respectively. The prototype shows an input referred noise charge smaller than $35 \mathrm{e}_{\mathrm{rms}}$. It takes an overall area of $500 \mu{\mathrm {m}}^{2}$, the power consumption is less than $4 \mu \mathrm{W}$ at a power supply of 1.2 V. Beside design aspects electrical and spectral characterization of a small pixel matrix will be shown in this work.

articleTitle: Impact of Br-etching on surface and current-voltage characteristics of CZT detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CdZnTe (CZT) is widely recognized as a highly promising material for detecting X-rays and gamma-rays due to its notable advantages over traditional direct conversion detector materials like silicon and germanium, particularly its high density and resistivity, eliminating the need for cryogenic cooling. However, the performance of radiation detectors is significantly influenced by the surface characteristics of the CZT crystal. In this study, we investigate the impact of bromine methanol ($\mathrm{Br}: \mathrm{MeOH}$) etching on eliminating surface-related defects and enhancing the current-voltage characteristics of the CZT detectors. The preparation of CZT detectors often results in surface damage, leading to surface trap states and non-stoichiometry. Optical and atomic force microscopy measurements reveal prominent polishing lines and increased surface roughness of polished CZT wafers. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms the presence of tellurium oxide on the CZT surface. CZT devices treated with $\mathrm{Br}: \mathrm{MeOH}$ etching demonstrate improved carrier transport at the metal-semiconductor interface compared to untreated ones.

articleTitle: Beam test results for the Endcap Timing ReadOut Chip (ETROC2) for CMS ETL upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Endcap Timing ReadOut Chip (ETROC) for the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) Minimum ionizing particle Timing Detector (MTD) is designed to process Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) signals with a time resolution of 40-50ps per hit, with 30-35 ps per charged particle using twolayer detector. The ETROC2, is the first full size (16 x 16 pixels) and full functionally design that has been tested in hadron and electron beams at CERN and DESY (Sep 2023 - Aug 2024). Precision timing studies at these test beams are done using a self-referential beam telescope composed of up to 4 layers/chips. This talk describes the ETROC2 beam telescope and summarizes the performance of the ETROC2 chips bump-bonded to (16x16) Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) and Hamamatsu Photonics K.K. (HPK) LGAD sensors using results from recent test beams. The experiences and lessons learned during these test beams are also detailed in this talk.

articleTitle: Ultra low-mass pixel tracker for the Mu3e experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Mu3e experiment is on the frontier of charged lepton flavour violating searches as well as paving the way globally in terms of cutting-edge ultra low-mass detector technologies. The search for the elusive decay of the muon to three electrons demands excellent vertexing and momentum resolution (less than 1 MeV), which is achieved using two 6 -chip inner (vertex) and two 17 or 18chip outer pixel tracking layers in the central detector region, plus two additional outer pixel layers in each of the two re-curl regions. This pixel detector exploits ultra-thin custom-designed silicon High Voltage Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (HV-MAPS), known as MuPix. These 50 - 70 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ thick chips are mounted on low mass service flexible printed circuits (HDI), which then define the so-called “ladder” support structures of the Mu3e pixel detector. An additional $25 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick unidirectional carbon fibre layer is added to the 18 -chip outer pixel layers. The total mass of one ladder is less than 2 grams, and the total radiation length achieved is $\mathrm{X} / \mathrm{X} 0=0.115 \%$ per layer. This talk will present an overview of the Mu3e pixel detector, in particular, preliminary results of the construction of the first ladder objects will be discussed. The Mu3e detector is expected to start data-taking mid-2025. An overview of the production procedure and status of the pixel tracker readiness will also be presented.

articleTitle: Attenuation Correction for Phantom Images Acquired in the Second Generation PETcoil Insert for PET/MR Brain Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper proposes a geometry-based attenuation correction method for phantom PET scans using emission data alone. The method reconstructs the phantom image without attenuation and scatter correction, registers the image with the known phantom, and calculates the intersection of every line of response (LOR) with the registered phantom geometry. Knowing the attenuation per LOR allows us to manipulate the list-mode emission data accordingly and generate a list-mode data file with an enhanced number of coincidences per LOR according to the estimated attenuation.The approach yielded promising results when applied to a Hoffman brain phantom study using the second-generation PETcoil insert scanner. The intensity line profile generated by summing the signal intensity along the transverse and coronal axes looked more like the expected line profile without scatter correction, as expected. This approach can be easily generalized to any other phantoms and scanners.

articleTitle: A Detector Prototype for Prompt Gamma Imaging with Gamma Neutron Discrimination Capability
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the field of hadrontherapy, Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI) is a technique considered for range verification purposes. Prompt Gamma (PG) measurements are strongly affected by the presence of a neutron background, which can limit the possibility to perform range monitoring, especially in the framework of Carbon Ion therapy. A detector system based on Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) for neutron background reduction in Prompt Gamma range monitoring is here proposed. The detector, based on a $5 \mathrm{~cm} \times 5 \mathrm{~cm} \times 2 \mathrm{~cm}$ CLYC (Cs2LiY Cl6: Ce) scintillator crystal, read out by near-ultraviolet high density (NUV-HD) SiPM tiles and compact electronics, acquires and converts in real time the Pulse Shape Discrimination coefficients, allowing to discard during the acquisition the range uncorrelated signal caused by neutrons. The effectiveness of the discrimination capability of the crystal was confirmed with experimental measurements performed at CNAO (Centro Nazionale di Adroterapia Oncologica), with the detection of PG and neutrons following an RW3 phantom irradiation.

articleTitle: Radiation tests performed to the ATLAS Hadronic Calorimeter link and control Daughterboard for High Luminosity Upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a summary of the results of the radiation studies performed on the latest revision of the ATLAS Tile Calorimeter (TileCal) read-out link and control Daughterboard for the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). The Daughterboard serves as a hub that interfaces the off- and on-detector systems. CERN radiation hard GBTx ASICs, Microsemi ProASIC FPGAs and Xilinx Kintex Ultrascale FPGAs are combined in the design to receive configuration commands and configurable LHC synchronous timing, while simultaneously transmitting all the monitoring, physics and calibration front-end data. The Upgraded TileCal be powered by 896 Daughterboards that will provide continuous read out of the full calorimeter via 5376 optical multi-Gbps links. The design contains a diverse set of commercial off-the-shelf components that have been pre-selected and tested in radiation environments up to the expected radiation levels simulated for the entire HL-LHC lifetime. The Daughterboard features a double-redundant scheme that minimizes single points of failure induced by sensitivity to radiation damage. Any possible corruption on the data path is mitigated by means of Triple Mode Redundancy strategies, the Xilinx Soft Error Mitigation solution, and Forward Error Correction (FEC) in all the links. Radiation campaigns took place to study the impact that Total Ionizing Dose, Non Ionizing Energy losses and Single Event Effects will have in the Daughterboard performance.

articleTitle: The ATLAS ITk Pixel Detector. A great adventure from design to construction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: ATLAS-ITK Pixel Collaboration (the speaker to be selected by the ITk Speakers Committee after the contribution acceptance) For the HL-LHC upgrade the current ATLAS Inner Detector is replaced by an all-silicon system. The Pixel Detector will consist of five-barrel layers and a number of rings, resulting in about $14 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ of instrumented area. Due to the huge non-ionizing fluence ($1 \mathrm{e} 16 \mathrm{neq} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$) and ionizing dose (5 MGy), the two innermost layers, instrumented with 3D pixel sensors (L0) and $100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thin planar sensors (L1) will be replaced after about 5 years of operation.
