All hybrid detector modules will be read out by novel ASICs, implemented in 65nm CMOS technology, with a bandwidth of up to 5 $\mathrm{Gb} / \mathrm{s}$. Data will be transmitted optically to the off-detector readout system. To save material in the servicing cables, serial powering is employed for low voltage. Large scale prototyping programs are being carried out by all sub-systems. The talk will give an overview of the layout and current status of all the different aspects in the ITk Pixel Detector.

articleTitle: Crystal growth, scintillation mechanism, and radiation detection applications of Cs3Cu2I5:Tl single crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Materials for radiation detection are critically important and urgently demanded in diverse fields starting from fundamental scientific research to medical diagnostics, homeland security, and environmental monitoring. Low-dimensional halides (LDHs) exhibiting efficient self-trapped exciton (STE) emission with high photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) have recently shown a great potential as scintillators. Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf> based single crystals are one of the most promising LDHs for radiation detection applications. In this work, we study the growth of inch-sized $\mathrm{Cs}_{3} \mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{5}: \mathrm{Tl}$ single crystals, and address an overlooked issue of exciton-exciton interaction in Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf> host under ionizing radiation. Finally, we demonstrated a prototype of a highly sensitive all-solid-state radiation dose detector based on a highly efficient Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf>: Tl single crystal and a Si photodetector with a heterojunction structure, and a highly efficient nuclear battery device based on $\mathrm{Cs}_{3} \mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{5}: \mathrm{Tl}$ single crystal. Overall, we believe $\mathrm{Cs}_{3} \mathrm{Cu}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{5}: \mathrm{Tl}$ can serve as versatile scintillators covering a wide range of radiation energies for various applications

articleTitle: Sinogram-based Alignment Estimation of PET Detector Blocks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Mechanical inaccuracies in PET detector installation due to errors and imprecisions during manufacturing pose significant challenges to image quality. If unaccounted for gamma interaction positions and consequently resulting lines of response are mispositioned and lead to reduced signal-to-noise ratios in reconstructed images. We propose to optimize transaxial detector alignment parameters using stochastic gradient descent by matching a differentiable version of the sinogram with the analytical solution of the tracer line integral values. Our method conceptually allows for the usage of arbitrary tracer distributions, rendering the need for specialized phantoms and acquisition protocols obsolete, and paving the way towards the usage of clinically available phantoms for fast and regular detector alignment calibration. We utilize the Adam optimizer with an adaptive normalization strategy and convex hull regularization to incorporate prior knowledge on established mounting precisions. To deal with known phantoms placed in unknown positions, we incorporate a clustering procedure in the noisy reconstructed images to adaptively compute target tracer distribution and line integral values. Our study involved GATE simulations of multiple point sources with known and unknown positions inside a small animal PET scanner. The detector configuration was subsequently subjected to simulated alignment noise. Our method is able to estimate positions with ~300μm and axes with ~0.7° precision, even in cases where point source positions were unknown. Our research demonstrates that the fitting of sinograms proves a valid strategy for transaxial detector alignment with the potential for extension towards z-axis alignment.

articleTitle: Synchrotron-based Characterization Techniques for Radiation Detection Materials and Devices: An Overview
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-performance room-temperature radiation detectors (high energy resolution for spectrometers, high spatial resolution for imaging devices, and low defect-density for high flux applications) are needed for photon energies ($\gt 20 \mathrm{keV}$) that are not well suited for silicon detectors. Applications for such radiation detectors include nonproliferation, synchrotron, medical, astrophysics, and homeland security. Material- and device- characterization to understand and solve the limiting factors of radiation detection materials and devices is a core element of a radiation detector development R&D program. This presentation will give an overview on the two main synchrotron-based characterization techniques that have been employed by the authors in the last $\sim 20$ years: (1) White Beam X-ray Diffraction Topography and (2) Micron-scale detector mapping.

articleTitle: Understanding Precondition in Metal Halide Perovskites for Improved Gamma Ray Spectrum Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskites are promising candidates for room-temperature gamma ray spectroscopic detectors, but their capabilities in gamma ray detection have yet to reach their full potential. It is often observed that a preconditioning with constant bias is needed to remarkably enhance the spectroscopic performance of perovskite single-crystal detectors. In spectral measurements of fresh perovskite single crystal gamma-ray detectors, an initial poor response to gamma ray radiation with indistinguishable spectra was observed. However, after maintaining a voltage application over a period, we observed a gradual improvement in both charge collection efficiency and detection efficiency. Our work also shows that even for low-quality perovskite crystals that are defective, it is possible to significantly reduce defect density, improve crystal quality, and obtain appreciable gamma-ray responses by applying this simple precondition process. Furthermore, precondition has been shown to be applicable to a variety of perovskite components. By applying preconditioning strategy, we successfully optimized devices with initially poor responses into high-resolution, high-efficiency gamma-ray detectors, with our champion device achieving an energy resolution of less than $1 \%$ under 662 KeV Cs source. We will present our studies that will reveal the underlining mechanism for the preconditioning in enhancing the crystal quality in metal halide perovskites, and compare them with other room temperature detectors made of TIBr which also benefits from a preconditional process, and CdTe which suffer from the polarization effect.

articleTitle: The Single Event Error (SEE) test and analysis of the CMS Endcap Timing Layer readout chip
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ETROC2, the first full size and full functionality prototype chip for the CMS Endcap Timing Layer readout, is strategically designed to meet the SEE immunity requirements of detector operation with the low power constraint. The triplicated periphery and pixel I2C configuration registers are designed with self-correction feature. The pixel readout control is centralized in the global readout and fully triplicated. The pixel readout is not triplicated, instead protected with power-efficient one-bit correction Hamming code. The TMR protection of the on-pixel threshold calibration can be turned off allowing the detection of the beam spot during the beam test by checking the bit-flips of the internal memory cells. In the initial proton beam test in January 2024, the chip readout process did not hang throughout the tests. The Hamming code correction strategy works because the error corrected TDC data were observed in the data frames. The error-injection simulation is performed to analyze the small number of bit-flips in the configuration registers. We also performed SEE testing with a heavy ion beam in April and the data analysis is ongoing. The detailed design on the SEE immunity and the testing as well as simulation results will be presented, including follow-up SEE testing results in May and June 2024.

articleTitle: Constraints on Kinetic-Model Fitting that Yield Unique Solutions for 99mTc-Teboroxime
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Myocardial Perfusion Imaging studies commonly use ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-Sestamibi. We have previously used it to measure Myocardial Blood Flow in mice using dynamic imaging with 10-second frames. We have shown analytically and confirmed with simulation that the uptake constant to the myocardium, $K_{1}$, and blood volume fraction, V, can be determined uniquely when the recovery coefficients for the arterial and myocardial Volumes of Interest (VOIs) and the mixing coefficient $\left(F_{A}\right)$ for the contribution of the arterial VOI to the myocardial VOI (e.g., from resolution) and known and fixed in the model fit; the mixing from the myocardial VOI into the arterial VOI $\left(F_{T}\right)$ can be a fitting parameter. A challenge with ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-Sestamibi is the low extraction fraction, particularly in mice and at stress. By comparison, ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-Teboroxime offers higher extraction fraction, but washout has been observed $\left(k_{2} \neq 0\right)$, unlike in sestamibi. Herein, we re-evaluate the uniqueness requirements for the kinetic model with the extension $k_{2} \geq 0$. To determine if $k_{2}$ could be uniquely identifiable in addition to our other physical parameters ($K_{1}$ and V), we generated time-activity curves (TACs) for a 1-tissue compartment model simulation and fit them according to 5 different trials of given input parameters. We simulated noiseless TACs for 3 different $K_{1}, 11$ different $k_{2}$, and 5 different V in addition to 10 time-phase offsets. We measured the relative error, bias, and RMSE of each measured (fitted) output parameter. For trials where there was anomalously high bias or variance, we investigated for correlation between measured fit parameters. We found that fitting for either $F_{A}$ or $F_{T}$ does not provide for unique identification of all three physical parameters: $K_{1}, k_{2}$, and V.

articleTitle: PET Simulation Study of Quantum Entangled Annihilation Photons for Application in Gamma-Positron Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Leveraging quantum entanglement (QE) properties of annihilation photons is among new emerging techniques being investigated for improving spatial resolution and sensitivity in Positron Emission Tomography (PET). The double Compton scattering (DCSc) kinematics of coincident photons reveal the entangled annihilation photons via the polar and azimuthal scattering angles. This information can aid Gamma-Positron $(\beta+\gamma)$ imaging, which combines PET with the detection of prompt-gammas, in discriminating between annihilation photons and non-entangled promptgammas. Filtering annihilation photons from prompt-gammas using QE would reduce noise and improve spatial resolution in PET. In a GATE simulation of a Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) PET system currently undergoing system calibration and scale-up at UC Santa Cruz, we report results on its capability in capturing the scattering kinematics of entangled annihilation photons for use in QE filtering. Here, we demonstrate the linearly orthogonal polarization enhancement ratio in the azimuthal scattering difference of entangled photons ($\mathrm{R}=2.035 \pm 0.020$). We then report that each mm decrease in detector crystal resolution leads to a 23% reduction in the quantity of captured DCSc events. This increases the mean absolute error (MAE) of the computed azimuthal scattering angle difference from 6.8° to $9.5^{\circ}, 12.2^{\circ}$, and 15.3° for 1, 2, 4, and 8 mm resolution. Our result demonstrates the capability of our CZT system to take advantage of entangled photons for use in yet-to-be-developed QE filtering techniques for $\beta+\gamma$ imaging while experimental verification is in progress.

articleTitle: Fabrication and Characteristics of Low Gain Avalanche Detector for X ray Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A low gain avalanche detector (LGAD) provides a good timing resolution and moderate charge multiplication. Thus, it is studied as a device for the direct detection of X-ray. Considering an absorption length of X-ray and for easier charge multiplication, the LGAD is fabricated on a 400 $\mu$-thick p-type silicon wafer with a high resistivity $(8-10 \mathrm{k} \Omega \bullet \cdot \mathrm{cm})$. The LGAD has PIN structure for full depletion layer with reverse bias voltage. There is a multiplication layer (P-well) underneath a junction layer (N-junction), and an implantation condition for the P-well and N-junction are controlled to get a desired gain value. In this study, we present the electrical characteristics and gain test using Sr-90 radioactive source of fabricated six wafers with different fabrication parameters.

articleTitle: Development of the Front-end Electronics of a Diamond-Based Microfluidic Alpha Spectrometer in Molten Salt Reactors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper reports on the development of advanced readout electronics for a novel Diamond-Based Microfluidic Alpha Spectrometer (DiMAS), specifically designed for Material Control and Accountancy (MC&A) within Liquid-Fueled Molten Salt Reactors (LF-MSRs). Faced with harsh conditions inside containment of an LF-MSR. including high radiation levels and elevated temperatures, this paper focuses on designing suitable front-end electronics capable of operation within a hot cell inside containment. The board design employs Cremat charge-sensitive preamplifier and shaping amplifier chips, carefully optimized to ensure minimal electronic noise and enhanced signal integrity. Comprehensive testing, including temperature-dependent noise evaluations and radiation tolerance using a gamma-ray source, is conducted to confirm the electronics’ capability to withstand such harsh conditions while maintaining high performance.

articleTitle: Front-end Study for future European XFEL detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: New X-Ray pixel detectors are required to cope with the demanding requirements from XFEL (Xray Free Electron Laser) sources, in terms of high-speed and high dynamic range. Detectors have to provide also low electronics noise to allow single photon detection. In this work, we explore the feasibility of an alternative front-end (FE) based on a Charge Sensitive Amplifier (CSA) with Active Gain switching (AGC), and on a Flip-Capacitor Filter in a closed-loop configuration. The CSA can achieve either a single photon resolution and a high dynamic range by employing different feedback capacitances, configurable using a “predictive” AGC circuit. The predictive AGC circuit dynamically sets the proper gain by measuring the time needed for the signal to exceed a fixed threshold. The FE performs a fast trapezoidal filtering of the output CSA signal with an architecture based on a Flip-Capacitor Filter. We expect to present at the conference the final FE design and relevant simulations, considering a first prototype realized in 65 nm CMOS technology. The first version is optimized for low-noise readout of X-ray photons at 1 keV, but it can be adapted for the use with higher energies (>10 keV).

articleTitle: Intrinsic Fast neutron Efficiency Measurements of CLYC Scintillators of Various Sizes
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The paper reports on a fast neutron efficiency study with CLYC scintillators of different sizes useful for various fast neutron spectroscopy applications such as medical physics, security, space missions, and nuclear physics experiments. In nuclear physics experiments to study the collective properties of nuclei, neutron and $\gamma$ spectroscopy are required. CLYC scintillators are good candidates to build an array for such experiments, thanks to their ability to measure and discriminate both $\gamma$ rays and neutrons. This paper presents the results of fast neutron efficiencies of different sizes (1” x 1”, 2” x 2”, 3” x 3”) of CLYC scintillators in the energy range 0.8-10 MeV using an AmBe source with a continuous spectrum, in order to select the most suitable size for a future array. The found efficiencies were somewhat unexpected and did not scale with crystal volume. In this paper we give two explanations: i) neutrons lose energy in the crystal and are no longer detected, and ii) neutrons interact by scattering and escape from the lateral surface of the detector. We present the results of measurements to quantify and disentangle the effects. Furthermore, these results show that it is better to cover a large solid angle than to have a single long crystal.

articleTitle: Dual-Mode Range Verification for Ion Therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We developed a dual-particle scintillator array to measure the location of the Bragg peak of heavy-ion beams for range verification in ion therapy treatment. The detection system encompasses 30 Pulse-Shape-Discrimination (PSD)-capable organic scintillators to measure the secondary neutrons and gamma rays generated from the ion beam interaction with a water phantom. The spatial distribution of the detector responses can be used to determine the beam range, with a rationale similar to prompt-gamma range verification. The dual measurement is expected to result in a reduced uncertainty associated with the estimated range. The principle was demonstrated simulating a $150-\mathrm{MeV}$ proton beam interacting with a water phantom, and related detector responses, with FLUKA and MCNPX-PoliMi, respectively. The 90${\$}$%${\$}$ fall-off of the detected neutron profile ($35.8 \pm 0.1 \mathrm{~cm}$) agreed well with the 150 MeV proton beam range (35.8 cm). We designed the system encompassing 305 mmx5mmx5cm EJ-276D scintillators coupled with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout and tested it with a PuBe neutron/gamma-ray source and a collimated Cs-137 gamma-ray source. This preliminary characterization demonstrated the PSD capability and differential spatial response of the system, which will be used for range verification of the proton therapy unit at OSF HealthCare.

articleTitle: Comparison of Different Direct Deep Learning-based Attenuation Correction Schemes for Myocardial Perfusion SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning-based attenuation correction (DLAC) has been proven to improve the quantitative and diagnostic accuracy of myocardial perfusion SPECT (MP SPECT) as compared to non-attenuation corrected (NAC) MP SPECT. Previous studies have investigated various DLAC strategies using different NAC input, e.g., volume-of-interests (VOI) of whole thoracic volume-of-interest (wVOI) for conventional scanners, cardiac region (cVOI) for dedicated cardiac scanner, and 2D polar plots (pROI). This study aims to provide a direct comparison of these DLAC methods. Three hundred clinical patients scanned with standard one-day stress/rest <sup>99m</sup>Tc-sestamibi protocol are retrospectively recruited. 64 projections were acquired from RAO to LPO with 20 s/projection using a standard general-purpose dual-head SPECT scanner, and reconstructed with DEW scatter correction, with or without CTAC by 3D OS-EM algorithms with 48 updates. A conditional generative adversarial network was implemented to generated AC images from NAC images for 4 different inputs: 64×64×N wVOI, 24×24×24 cVOI, 24×24×24 short axis (SA) VOI, and 96×96 pROI. Both stress and rest scans were used, i.e., a total of 600 scans, dividing into 420, 60, and 120 for training, validation, and testing. After testing, all processed images were converted to polar plots for final comparison. Voxel-based bias and intraclass correlation analysis on extracted radiomics features were assessed using CTAC polar plots as reference. The training time for wVOI, cVOI, SA, and pROI was 2.5 hr, 1.0 hr, 1.0 hr, and 0.5 hr. We find that the inputs using all 3D VOIs have close quantitative and ICC results, while polar plot inputs are slightly worse. The use of wVOI input has the best ICC reliability with CTAC among all the VOIs. DLAC is robust for different types of NAC input.

articleTitle: Q-Wall, a Novel Quartz-Cherenkov Calorimeter Concept
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Calorimeters intended to operate in the heavily demanding radiation conditions of future collider detectors and the upgrades of existing large-scale experiments must possess significant radiation resistance and robustness to ensure consistent performance throughout the lifetimes of the experiments. In this context, a novel calorimeter design known as Q-Wall has been developed, utilizing quartz-Cherenkov calorimetry. The Q-Wall design employs a sampling calorimeter structure, alternating between absorber plates (e.g., Fe, Pb, W) and active layers. The active layers feature compact arrays of photomultiplier tubes with either thick quartz windows or fused silica pads optically linked to traditional photodetector windows. In these active elements, charged particles with $\beta\gt 0.685$ emit Cherenkov radiation which directly illuminates the photocathode. This innovative concept offers the potential for a rapid and finely detailed tracking calorimeter suitable for high radiation environments. Here we report on the development of the QWall concept, the construction of the first prototypes and the results of the beam tests with the prototype modules and compare them with electromagnetic shower development simulations with GEANT4.

articleTitle: Performance Effects of Organic Scintillator Bonding with Optical Cement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An experimental investigation into the effects of recombining Eljen EJ-200 Polyvinyl Toluene (PVT) blocks into a larger sample using EJ-500 optical cement has been conducted. The light collection efficiencies of 4-block and 16-block recombined samples have been compared to a solid control sample using the Compton edge energy observed when each sample is in the presence of a Cs-137 source. The use of optical cement is seen to contribute to a decrease in light collection efficiency, and this decrease is greater as more blocks are used. For a 4 -block sample, this decrease is of a magnitude comparable to the fluctuations observed between different samples of the same specification, and in this context the effect of optical cement can be considered minor. Little effect from the use of optical cement is noted on the spatial performance of a sample, which was tested by varying the location of the Cs-137 source and the PMT relative to the sample.

articleTitle: Large-Area Ultrahigh Resolution CZT Imaging Spectrometer with FPGA-Implemented Machine-Learning-based Spectral Enhancement for Clinical Spectral-SPECT Imaging Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we present the design and implementation of large area CZT imaging spectrometers for use in our Alpha-SPECT system, a superhigh-performance clinical SPECT system for spectral imaging of therapeutic radionuclides. To facilitate this application, we developed a modular and compact readout electronics comprising of a front-end circuitry and digital data acquisition system (DAQ). The design is fully expandable to accommodate CZT detectors of say $40 \times 40 \mathrm{~cm}$ area, offering a sub- 200 mm intrinsic resolution and an excellent energy resolution of about 2 keV at 140 keV. The analog front-end printed circuit board (PCB) is designed to offer low-noise, high-speed data digitization and signal amplification controls to each $2 \mathrm{~cm} \times 2 \mathrm{~cm}$ detector. The digital front-end board manages the power distribution to four such analog PCBs and transfers the data to a DAQ system at 80 Gbps using an SFP+ interface. The DAQ system can read the multiplexed raw data from up to 50 detector panels synchronously and store the data to a 20 Gbps fast NVMe storage. The preliminary experimental evaluation of a CZT detector using Am-241 and Co-57 point sources show good energy resolution across a broad range of medically relevant energies. However, due to increased charge sharing effects for thicker crystal, the full width at half maximum (FWHM) values are slightly degraded. We have employed machine learning charge-sharing correction models to correct for the charge loss and enhance the spectral resolution of the detector. In this work we will discuss the FPGA implementation of these machine learning charge correction algorithms for on-the-fly spectral enhancement.

articleTitle: Distribution of 99mTc-tetrofosmin in Real SPECT Image Reconstructions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The XCAT computational phantoms have been widely used for medical imaging research including Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT). However, these phantoms lack real statistical distributions for any given tracer. This research analyzes 10 reconstructed SPECT images to determine tracer distribution in 3 key regions of interests (ROIs): myocardium, blood pool, and liver. From these distributions we were able to generate XCAT phantoms which represented real tracer distributions.

articleTitle: Resolution Model with Asymmetric and Spatially-Variant PSFs for the S-PET System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A resolution model with asymmetric and spatially-variant point spread functions (asv-PSFs) was designed and implemented in the S-PET prototype system at Shenzhen Bay Laboratory (SZBL). The S-PET system consists of 20 detector modules arranged in a decagonal ring, with each module comprising two layers of crystals of different sizes: a top layer consisting of smaller LYSO crystals sized at $0.86 \times 0.86 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, arranged in a $30 \times 60$ array, and a bottom layer utilizing BGO crystals sized at $1.29 \times 1.29 \times 7.5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, arranged in a $20 \times 40$ array. We performed image reconstruction using a resolution model that incorporates asv-PSFs in the image space. This was done using convolution operations using the code from Customizable and Advanced Software for Tomographic Reconstruction (CASToR). The asv-PSFs model was compared with the isotropic and spatially-invariant PSF (isi-PSF) model, a built-in model in CASToR. Point source imaging experimental results show that at the axial center of the FOV and a 25 mm radial offset, the radial resolution was improved by 53% from 1.92 mm to 0.90 mm. Two Derenzo-style hot-rod phantoms of different sizes, were used separately in GATE Monte Carlo simulation and experimental measurement to evaluate the effectiveness of the asv-PSFs model. Both simulation and measurement demonstrate the efficacy of the asv-PSFs model in correcting the rod shape distortion caused by the depth of interaction (DOI) effect. Furthermore, the isi-PSF model was unable to distinguish among the 0.75 mm rod sources positioned approximately 20 mm from the center of the FOV, while the asv-PSFs model was able to differentiate among them.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of Photon-Counting Detector ASIC with Peak-Finding Counters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a simulation study of the application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) with peak-finding counters. As a critical component of the photon-counting detector (PCD), the ASIC counts photon events and records their energy. However, its performance degrades with events pile-up at high flux. To address this issue, a peak-finding counting mode is proposed. The ASIC working in this peak-finding mode can identify and measure individual signal peaks. By constructing a detector full-response model, the performance of the ASIC working in the peak-finding mode is compared with that of ASICs working in conventional paralyzable and non-paralyzable modes. Additionally, noise levels of ASICs are assessed to evaluate overall detector performance. Preliminary results demonstrate that the ASIC operating in peak-finding mode exhibits the least counting rate loss in high-flux scenarios, suggesting its potential for improving PCCT performance.

articleTitle: Integration of a continuously varying image-space PSF for a dual-panel ultra-high TOF-PET scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET), achieving high resolution and accurate image reconstruction is crucial for effective diagnosis and research applications. This study addresses the challenges posed by the parallel flat panel architecture of a novel high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) PET scanner. Despite its cost and size benefits, this architecture introduces significant anisotropic spread in point source distribution, particularly in the direction orthogonal to the panels. Furthermore, objects closer to one of the panels may exhibit a splitting into two components. To tackle these issues, we propose a methodology to estimate and apply a continuously spatially variant point spread function (PSF). Our approach utilizes Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) to fit the spread of simulated point sources. This fitting process followed by parameters interpolation through Gaussian process regression (GPR), accommodates the anisotropic and spatially varying nature of the spread. We implemented a continuous shift varying convolution that was integrated into a Maximum Likelihood Estimation Maximization (MLEM) algorithm. We simulated a clinically realistic count level to assess the ability of the method to correctly recover the PSF deformations, on a Derenzo resolution phantom and a brain phantom.

articleTitle: Growth and Scintillation Properties of Ce-Doped Bismuth Germanate Single Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Centering on the major application needs of the next-generation high-energy physics experiments in energy and intensity frontiers, bismuth germanate (Bi<inf>4</inf>Ge<inf>3</inf>O<inf>12</inf>, BGO) crystal is one of the most promising candidate crystals with high density. The high light output of BGO will cause reduced dynamic range for silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout, it is urgent to reduce its light output. In this study, we report the effective suppression of light output in BGO crystals by Ce doping. BGO single crystals doped with 0.05 wt% and 0.1 wt% CeO2 were grown by the Bridgman technique at Shanghai Institute of Ceramics, Chinese Academy of Sciences. The optical transmittance, radioluminescence and light output properties were measured. The results show that 0.1 wt% Ce doping reduces the light output of BGO crystals to 2198 ph/MeV, which is 25.5% of that of pure BGO.

articleTitle: Prototyping and evaluation of electronic components with radiation resistance and high temperature operation for severe accidents
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: As part of the development of electronic devices for use in containment vessels for severe accidents, we fabricated and evaluated resistors and capacitors that can be operated at temperatures ranging from room temperature to $500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Constantan (CuNi) and nichrome (NiCr), which have low temperature coefficient and high specific resistance, were deposited on sapphire substrates by sputtering method; stable operation from room temperature to $600{}^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ was successfully achieved. Capacitors were fabricated by aerosol deposition and atomic layer deposition using Al2O3 as the insulating material. Both capacitors were confirmed to operate from room temperature to $500^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. X-ray irradiation tests were conducted on the fabricated resistors and capacitors. The NiCr resistors and Al<inf>2</inf> O<inf>3</inf> capacitors fabricated by the ALD method remained sound even after an integrated dose of 5 MGy. A source grounded circuit was fabricated by combining the fabricated resistors and capacitors with radiation-resistant hydrogen-terminated diamond MOSFETs (RADDFETs), and was successfully operated continuously at $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ for 8 days..

articleTitle: POUR-Net: A Population-Prior-Aided Over-Under-Representation Network for Low-Count PET Attenuation Map Generation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low-dose PET offers a valuable means of minimizing radiation exposure in PET imaging. However, the prevalent practice of employing additional CT scans for generating attenuation maps (u-map) for PET attenuation correction significantly elevates radiation doses. To address this concern and further mitigate radiation exposure in low-dose PET exams, we propose an innovative Population-prior-aided Over-Under-Representation Network (POUR-Net) that aims for high-quality attenuation map generation from low-dose PET. First, POUR-Net incorporates an Over-Under-Representation Network (OUR-Net) to facilitate efficient feature extraction, encompassing both low-resolution abstracted and fine-detail features, for assisting deep generation on the full-resolution level. Second, complementing OUR-Net, a population prior generation machine (PPGM) utilizing a comprehensive CT-derived u-map dataset, provides additional prior information to aid OUR-Net generation. The integration of OUR-Net and PPGM within a cascade framework enables iterative refinement of u-map generation, resulting in the production of high-quality u-maps. Experimental results underscore the effectiveness of POUR-Net, showing it as a promising solution for accurate CT-free low-count PET attenuation correction, which also surpasses the performance of previous baseline methods.

articleTitle: The Whole-body Activity Monitor (WhAM) for Personalization of Radiopharmaceutical Therapies (RPT)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Purpose: We seek to develop portable whole-body radiation detector technology designed for at home use to assist in activity monitoring of patients that have received ${ }^{177} \mathrm{Lu}$-PSMA or ${ }^{177} \mathrm{Lu}$ DOTATATE radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT). The goal of the Whole-body Activity Monitor (WhAM) detector system is to help enable ${ }^{177} \mathrm{Lu}$-RPT treatment personalization based upon accumulated dose to a patient’s organs at risk (OAR) or tumors. Methods: The WhAM detector system will consist of 2-4 collimated detector assemblies that will translate on a lightweight rail assembly to scan a patient from head to mid-thigh. Each detector assembly consists of an 8 xN (where $\mathrm{N} \leq 30$) array of $6 \times 12 \times 6 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ pixelated GAGG crystals with tungsten septa at the endcaps and between the 8 columns of crystals. Additional more sparsely spaced septa will be placed between the N rows of GAGG crystals. Monte Carlo simulation is used to determine the sensitivity function between each voxel in the patient and each crystal element in the WhAM detector assembly. Full energy spectra information is acquired for each crystal element. For this optimization study, the patient activity and attenuation are modeled using the digital Zubal anthropomorphic phantom. The sensitivity functions for OAR and tumors with the detector system are formed by aggregating voxels of each structure. Organ and tumor activity estimation will be investigated using generalized matrix inversion; maximum likelihood expectation maximization and convolutional neural networks. A quantitative SPECT/CT of<sup>177</sup> Lu-RPT activity distribution in the patient will be available to provide starting activities in OAR and tumors and as a calibration data set for WhAM measurements. Results: Investigations are on going. Goals are to estimate time integrated activity for OAR and tumors $\gt3 \mathrm{~cm}$ diameter to within ±8%. Main optimization parameters are septa design, size of crystals, configuration of crystal array, and activity estimation methodology.

articleTitle: An FPGA-Controlled Analog Switching-Based Single-Readout Multiplexing Method for Pulse Mode Radiation Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: North Carolina State University developed a single readout multiplexing method for pulse mode radiation detectors that outputs a detector pulse from the first fired detector and a variable width logic pulse attached at the tail of the detector pulse. The width of the logic pulse encodes the identity of the fired detector. This method operates by switching on the first fired detector channel for a fixed duration while keeping all other detector channels switched off. For this purpose, individual analog switches for all detector channels are used. A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) was programmed to produce the switching pulse and the identification pulse when triggered by the arrival of first fired detector pulse. Output of the switches and the delayed identification pulse are fed to a fan-in circuit which produces the multiplexed output. To demonstrate the method, a prototype 8-to-1 multiplexer was built and tested with eight NaI(Tl) detectors. The performance of the multiplexer was investigated in terms of its ability to keep the original energy resolution, timing resolution, and pulse shape intact. The multiplexer showed minimal degradation of these parameters. The switching gate feature of the multiplexer ensures that the baseline noise from the inactive detector channels are not added to the multiplexed output when used in a large radiation detector network. This method is also capable of blocking accidental coincidences: it can isolate the first fired detector pulse from coincident pulses of other detectors in a single digitized record. These features make this method promising for use in positron emission tomography (PET), fundamental physics experiments, and neutron and gamma imaging systems.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Imaging of Plutonium and Thorium with Organic Glass System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A scatter-based imaging system using organic glass and CeBr<inf>3</inf> scintillators has been developed at the University of Michigan that is capable of imaging both gamma rays and fast neutrons. Various efforts in verification within the nuclear safeguards regime would greatly benefit from a system that can successfully locate different sources when they are in the same field of view. Gamma signatures can be used to distinguish sources of interest in a scenario where other gamma ray emitting sources are present, allowing for imaging capabilities that can focus on specific objects. In this work, a pair of hemishells containing plutonium oxide and a hemishell of thorium metal were simultaneously imaged using an organic glass-based system. The plutonium and thorium sources were separately imaged by using energy gates of $300-475 \mathrm{keV}$ and $500-600 \mathrm{keV}$ on the gamma coincidence spectrum, respectively. We applied a MLEM converging algorithm on the reconstructed images to demonstrate successful localization of the three hemishell sources in angular space.

articleTitle: Attention-Guided CNN Approach for Accurate Pulmonary Embolism Segmentation from Contrast-enhanced CT images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is the gold standard for Pulmonary embolism diagnosis. This study proposed an augmented U-Net architecture, incorporating Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and attention mechanisms, for improved pulmonary embolism segmentation in CTPAs. Two online datasets, CAD-pe and FUMPE, containing a total of 126 images of individual people were utilized. Both datasets included cases of pulmonary embolism with available binary masks for positive cases. Performance evaluation on positive cases using sensitivity, specificity, Sorensen-Dice similarity coefficient, and Jaccard coefficient demonstrates the efficacy of the proposed network for PE segmentation. The patient-wise Dice coefficient of $0.58 \pm 0.17$ (Mean ± SD) is slightly higher than the slice-wise $0.55 \pm 0.29$ (Mean ± SD), indicating that patient-wise segmentation is more accurate and consistent in this particular context. The higher value of slice-wise sensitivity (70%) indicates that the model may be more effective when examining slices individually than considering the entire patient’s scan (62%). The 100% specificity shows that the model can accurately identify all true negatives which indicates reducing the false-positive rate in detecting pulmonary embolism compared to other networks. These findings exhibit that the employed model has shown great performance in pulmonary embolism segmentation tasks.

articleTitle: A Neutron-Sensitive Detector Based on a 3D Printed Plastic Scintillator
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents results on a neutron-sensitive scintillating detector fabricated by additive manufacturing. 3D-printed sensors are produced using the Fused-Deposition Modelling (FDM) method. FDM uses a flexible filament to produce solid plastic objects, which are at the same time low-cost and custom shaped. Filaments were produced, using polystyrene as a base scintillator, doped with PTP and POPOP to ensure visible scintillation, as well as <sup>6</sup>LiF to enhance neutron sensitivity. 3D printed scintillators were then tested using a high spatial and temporal resolution TimePix3 camera. The response of each produced scintillator was also confronted with Geant4 simulations. We will discuss the additive manufacturing details and examine the response of the scintillating sensor to electrons, X-rays, and thermal neutrons.

articleTitle: Characterizing the Effectiveness of High Temperature Annealing for Correcting Radiation Damage in Cross-Strip Germanium Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We explore methods for restoring the spectral resolution of cross-strip germanium detectors after undergoing radiation damage from high energy protons. Our goal is to understand the potential benefits and impacts of annealing on the detectors to be flown on the COSI satellite mission. COSI will be irradiated by protons and neutrons in its low-Earth orbit. Irradiation damages the crystal structure of the germanium, increasing charge carrier trapping, and resulting in degraded spectral performance. Radiation damage effects to the detectors will be dominated by hole trapping induced by proton damage, causing broadened spectral resolution from hole-collecting electrodes. We irradiated a cross-strip germanium detector with a fluence of $2 \times 10^{8}$ proton $\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, which is several times larger than COSI’s expected fluence during its primary 2-year mission. After irradiation, we completed a series of incremental high temperature anneals on this detector with the intent of tracking progress towards restoring the original spectral resolution. In this work, we evaluate decrease in charge trapping, and resulting improvement in spectral resolution, by measuring the FWHM of the 662 keV gamma-ray line from a Cs-137 source. After completing six anneals at $80^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, we observe a full recovery of spectral resolution on hole-collecting strips. In particular, we find that the FWHM measurements of the Cs-137 line for the hole-collecting strips improves linearly with total time spent annealing at $100^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$.

articleTitle: Material Design of Eutectic Scintillators for Discrimination of Thermal Neutrons and Gamma-rays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, decommissioning as represented by the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (F1) has attracted worldwide attention, and market is also expanding. Tohoku University, the University of Tokyo, AIST, and JAEA are developing scintillator detectors for the F1 decommissioning with the support of the CLADS, “Problem Solving type Decommissioning Research Program”. In F1 reactors decommissioning, it is essential to detect n-rays emitted only from fuel debris under very high- $\gamma$ background. In order to sort mixed fuel debris, wastes and structures, the $\mathrm{n} / \gamma$-ray discrimination performance is particularly important for the radiation detectors. The selection of scintillator is important as it affects the performance of the detector, and high n-ray sensitivity, high light yield, fast decay, and enough n/$\gamma$-ray discrimination performance are required. In this study, we propose a new material design guideline to develop eutectics with excellent $\mathrm{n} / \gamma$-ray discrimination performance and thermal neutron sensitivity by combining a scintillator phase with excellent $\alpha / \gamma$ discrimination performance and a ${ }^{6} \mathrm{Li}$-containing phase. Here, T1:CsI, Tl:NaI, LaBr<inf>3</inf> (pure, $\mathrm{Ce}, \mathrm{Sr}$ co-doped), and LaCl<inf>3</inf> (pure, Ce doped) were selected as scintillator phase

articleTitle: Positronium Lifetime Measurement Using a Clinical PET for Quantification of Radicals In Vivo
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron sometimes forms positronium (Ps) before the positron-electron annihilation in vivo occurs. The Ps lifetime, the time at which Ps annihilates, changes depending on the surrounding electron density. We reported that the Ps lifetime is linearly correlated to the oxygen partial pressure in water and it is expected to act as a sensor for tumor hypoxia. Therefore, we are developing a Ps lifetime imaging technique, named quantum PET (Q-PET), based on whole gamma imaging (WGI). We also expect another application of Ps lifetime imaging is for the quantification of radicals (free radicals) in vivo. Previously, we observed the change of the Ps lifetime in aqueous solution containing radicals, using a pair of PET detectors. However, it is not well known to what extent statistics are needed to quantify the concentration of radicals. In this study, we investigated the relationship among the radical concentration, the accuracy of the lifetime value, and the counting statistics using a brain-dedicated clinical PET scanner, VRAIN. Pure water, 1 mM, and 2 mM TEMPOL (stable radical) aqueous solutions were prepared. The solutions were placed in contact with a thin ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ source (0.43 MBq), and measured individually. Time difference spectra were obtained with 1275 keV photon detection as the start and 511 keV photon detection as the stop, and lifetimes were analyzed. The counts of the spectra were 165 million counts for 12 hours of measurement data. These data were reduced to 6 hours (82 million) and 3 hours (41 million) and the change in accuracy of the lifetime values was compared. 165 million counts of data showed that the lifetime values at each concentration were separated with an error of $\pm 1 \sigma$, but the accuracy of the lifetime values degraded as the number of counts was reduced. The results suggested that differences in radical concentrations in aqueous solution of the order of a few mM could be quantified by Ps lifetime if the counting statistics are more than $10^{8}$ counts.

articleTitle: Subtraction of Single-Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) in Radioembolization: A Comparison of Four Methods
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Subtraction of SPECT images has several clinical applications, but can be challenging due to high noise levels and poor resolution. In this work, we compared four methods of obtaining a difference SPECT image. As a use case, we investigated the technical performance of SPECT subtraction to quantify the effect of angiotensin-II on the ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$-MAA liver distribution during hepatic radioembolization using an innovative hybrid C-arm scanner. The included methods were (i) straightforward image subtraction, (ii) projection subtraction, (iii) projection addition during iterative reconstruction and (iv) image addition during iterative reconstruction. Utilizing digital simulations (XCAT) and phantom studies (NEMA-IQ and anthropomorphic torso), we found that all methods were able to generate difference images. Image subtraction showed the best quantitative performance but the worst visual quality due to high noise levels. Image addition resulted in the best visual image quality but had a quantitative bias when the two images to subtract contained opposing features. Since quantitative accuracy is most important for the dosimetric investigation of angiotensin-II, we recommend using the image subtraction method for this purpose.

articleTitle: Measurements of Angular Energy and Flux Distribution of Neutrons Produced by DT Neutron Generator Using Diamond Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron generators can produce mono-energy fast neutrons by fusion reactions. The neutrons from the generators have angular energy and flux distribution. In this study, we measure the angular distribution of neutrons about energy and relative flux produced by DT neutron generator in KRISS (Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science) using the diamond detector. The carbon in the diamond undergoes a ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{n}, \alpha)^{9} \mathrm{Be}$ reaction with a fast neutron, producing an alpha particle whose energy is same as the incident neutron energy minus the Q value (5.702 MeV). For this reason, the diamond detector can directly measure the incident neutron energy without any difficult algorithm or large space for detection. The angle of the neutrons was set relative to the incident direction of the accelerated deuteron beam. Neutron energy was obtained at different angles by ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{n}, \alpha){ }^{9} \mathrm{Be}$ peak centroid. Subsequently, it was revealed that the neutron energy angular distribution follows the single-term cosine function. Furthermore, the variance of the neutron energy is larger with smaller angle of neutrons. Relative neutron flux was determined by ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{n}, \alpha)^{9} \mathrm{Be}$ peak area and normalized with the neutron flux at the 0°. Relative neutron flux decreased as the larger angle. With this study, DT neutron generator in KRISS can be calibrated about neutron energy and flux corresponding to the angle.

articleTitle: An Accurate Attenuation and Scatter Correction Method for PET/MR Scanners with Lutetium-based Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A novel method for attenuation and scatter correction of PET data in PET/MR is investigated in this work. Given the absence of an accurate attenuation map in PET/MR, the use of an activity and attenuation joint reconstruction algorithm such as TOF-MLAA is studied. To address issues in TOF-MLAA, a number of, improvements were investigated: 1) the use of background radiation from lutetium-based scintillators as a weak transmission source, 2) denoising attenuation maps with artificial intelligence, and 3) the use of an energy-based scatter method that does not require any prior anatomical knowledge. The proposed method is evaluated on PET data from a Siemens Biograph Vision Quadra scanner using phantom and patient data. Images of NEMA NU-2 image quality showed that the proposed method retains the contrast recovery and background variability of the PET images within 5% of the reference CT-based reconstructed PET images. Similarly, organ uptake in PET images using the proposed method showed an average of 5% error. In conclusions, the proposed reconstruction framework showed promising results towards quantitative CT-less PET suitable for PET/MR.

articleTitle: Simulation and Detector Measurements of a Small Animal PET System for Simultaneous Multi-Tracer Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is a method of measuring quantitative uptake of positron emitting tracers in vivo. Due to scanner limitations, it is not possible to measure more than one tracer’s biodistribution at a time using PET. However, many diseases would benefit from information provided by multiple tracers. We present Monte Carlo simulations of a small animal imaging system under development for imaging pure positron and positron + prompt gamma emitting radionuclides simultaneously in a new paradigm for simultaneously imaging multiple PET tracers in one scan. A detector submodule has been tested with $1.5 \times 1.5 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LYSO crystals to have an uncalibrated energy resolution of 9.8% +/- 0.9% and 9.0% +/- 2.0% at 511 keV and 1275 keV respectively. Simulation studies were conducted with positron + prompt gamma emitters ${ }^{44} \mathrm{Sc}$ and ${ }^{124} \mathrm{I}$ yielding a peak sensitivity of 7.3% and 2.2% for the 2-photon coincidences and 4.1% and 0.7% for the 3-photon coincidences with those two isotopes, respectively.

articleTitle: Development of a Neutron Diamond Detector Using Printed Wire Bonding Techniques
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This report summarizes the development of a neutron diamond detector using printed wire bonding technology [1]. The purpose of this study is to develop a neutron diamond detector for use in high $\gamma$-ray environments.One of the key issues in the development of the detector is the thinness of the diamond sensor. The thickness of diamond sensors is less than $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$, so crimp bonding methods (wire bonding, bump bonding, etc.) cannot be used. We have developed the printed wire bonding method using printed wiring with a new stencil printing technique [2]. This method enables the bonding of thin diamond sensors. The results of the evaluation of the neutron diamond detector using a neutron source and a $\gamma$-ray source showed that the neutron diamond detector using the printed wiring bonding technique satisfied the specifications.

articleTitle: Radioroc-picoTDC System: Improved Time Resolution for Medical and Scientific Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the performance of a new system combining Radioroc ASIC and picoTDC for scientific and medical applications. The integration of Radioroc’s detection capabilities and picoTDC’s precise time-stamping performance offers exciting potential for advancement in TOFPET medical imaging and physics experiments where time resolution is crucial. This study explores the performance of the Radioroc-picoTDC system, coupled with the most recent SiPM technologies available on the market (Hamamatsu, FBK, Broadcom), in various configurations. Preliminary results indicate that the Radioroc-picoTDC system provides improved time resolution compared to conventional TDC. Further study and optimization of this innovative integration to unlock its full potential are foreseen as the next steps.

articleTitle: One Linear Layer is all you Need for Positron Range Estimation and Correction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel approach to enhance the estimation of positron range for highenergy isotopes like Ga68 used positron emission tomography (PET) scans, which typically compromise image resolution. Traditional methods for correcting positron range (PR) effects are computationally intensive and often struggle with computing the transposes required for iterative reconstruction algorithms. Our method leverages a graph neural network (GNN) to simulate PR blurring effects using activity images and density maps, efficiently calculating the necessary transposes for iterative methods such as the maximum-likelihood expectation-maximization (MLEM) algorithm. This method offers a computationally efficient and accurate solution for voxelized positron range blurring simulations and positron range corrections.

articleTitle: Whole-Scene Backscatter X-ray Imaging with Coded Apertures
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Backscatter x-ray imaging is a well-known technique that can obtain radiographic-like images of an object’s internal distribution without requiring access to both sides of the object. It has been used in diverse security applications, from screening air-traffic passengers for weapons to searching for contraband hidden in internal compartments in vehicles. Typical system designs rely on rastering a collimated x-ray beam across the object of interest and using an omni-directional or collimated x-ray detector to measure the scattered x-ray signature as a function of beam location to create the overall image. This paper reports proof-of-feasibility results demonstrating that one can avoid the use of pencil beams or detectors with highly restricted fields of view to generate useful backscatter x-ray images. Instead, one can illuminate the entire object at once and create images with the backscattered x-rays using the coded-aperture technique. This is particularly useful for incident response scenarios where both sides of a suspect object may be inaccessible, and the field ability and penetration of commercial systems are inappropriate.

articleTitle: Detector Mechanisms for a Portable Nuclear Resonance Transmission Analysis Device
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron resonance transmission analysis (NRTA) is a neutron interrogation method used for identifying nuclear materials, with broad applications towards arms control, nonproliferation, and safeguards. This study extends previous efforts to develop a portable NRTA device capable of characterizing nuclear materials without the constraints of fixed, large facilities. This NRTA configuration utilizes a D-T generator enclosed by a moderator to generate epithermal neutrons, facing a detector made up of GS20 lithium glass scintillators. Prior research has shown that this NRTA setup can accurately detect several millimeters of uranium shielded by several millimeters of lead with an 80% accuracy rate. However, a critical limitation of GS20 scintillators is a lack of sufficient neutron-gamma discrimination capability. Attempts at shielding to reduce gammas also result in greater noise and require longer measurement times. This study therefore seeks to enhance the NRTA system by taking approaches to minimizing gamma background interference, allowing for potential applications in areas such as thorium fuel cycle materials and other high-gamma-emitting environments. This is achieved by optimizing the detector configuration and investigating detectors with reduced gamma sensitivities, such as boron-coated straws. By reducing the detected gamma background, the signal-to-background ratio of measurements can be increased, leading to broader applications of this method.

articleTitle: CDEM-based Random-triple Correction for Simultaneous Dual-isotope PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dual-isotope imaging holds significant promise in positron emission tomography (PET), offering a multi-dimensional characterization of tumors’ functional morphology. Although triple-coincidence-based approaches enable the simultaneous dual-isotope PET imaging, current techniques still face challenges due to contamination by interference signals from the other emitter, notably correlated random triples. To address this issue, we propose a novel correction method, the Consistent Delayed Expectation-Maximum algorithm (CDEM), based on a joint Poisson model and the irrelevance between decays of random coincidences. The consistent delayed window, which preserves the photon correlation within the same decay, enables unbiased estimation of random triples, while the Expectation-Maximum iteration guarantees efficient correction in cases of ultra-low count. Using a homemade preclinical PET system, we demonstrate the superior performance of CDEM through phantom and in vivo mouse experiments. In the ${ }^{124} \mathrm{I} /{ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ dual-isotope mouse imaging, the sharp decrease in the pixel value ratio of brown fat to thyroid indicates the effectiveness of CDEM in correcting random triples. Moreover, in single pure emitter scenarios, CDEM yields near-zero images of true triples with the structural similarity index measure between random triples estimated by CDEM and prompt triples exceeding 0.93 after denoising, highlighting CDEM’s robust performance. These findings underscore the potential of CDEM in enhancing the accuracy of dual-isotope PET imaging, contributing to its broader application prospects.

articleTitle: A PET daily quality control method using background radiation of LYSO crystal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the routine use of PET (Positron Emission Tomography), daily quality control (QC) plays a crucial role in the normal operation of the system. To facilitate more convenient and safer PET QC, in this article, we utilize the inherent radioactive isotope Lu176 in the scintillation crystal LYSO to detect and correct important stability indicators of PET systems, such as energy calibration status and time calibration status. To validate the effectiveness of this new method, we conducted verification on the PET/CT system uMI Panorama GS, produced by United Imaging Healthcare. The Panorama GS has an axial length of 148.2 cm, and traditional radioactive source QC methods require either an extremely long radioactive source phantom or multiple movements of the radioactive source, which is very inconvenient. We compared the results from background detection with those from radioactive source detection and subsequently corrected the system’s calibration status based on the background results. The results showed that the energy detection accuracy per crystal can reach ± 1 ADC channel at 511 Kev. The NEMA2018 time resolution improved from 251.5 ps to 189.5 ps, which is very close to the actual time resolution of 188.9 ps, demonstrating the high precision of this method. Our next step is to continue studying the effects of background correction on system sensitivity, image quality, and other factors.

articleTitle: The large area scintillator neutron detector based on the SiPMs readout in CSNS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Chinese Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) has successfully produced its first neutron beam on 28th August 2017. It has been running steadily from March,2018. According to the construction plan of the CSNS, the rest 10 neutron instruments will be built as the multidisciplinary platforms for scientific research between 2023~2028. Huge number of neutron detectors are needed for the program. Due to the 3 He gas shortage and the rapidly increasing price, the larger area scintillator neutron detectors as the alternative of 3He tubes are under development since 2011 in CSNS. The latest detector scintillator neutron based on the Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) readout was introduced in this paper. The detector was composed of oblique $6 \mathrm{LiF} / \mathrm{ZnS}(\mathrm{Ag})$ scintillator screens, SiPMs and electronics. The Monte Carlo simulation was done to study the neutron detection efficiency and the position resolution of the detector. The simulation results showed that when the oblique angle of the $400 \mu$ m-thick $6 \mathrm{LiF} / \mathrm{ZnS}(\mathrm{Ag})$ scintillation screens was set as 75°, the readout SiPMs with $3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}$ pixel size could rebuilt the incident neutron position resolution of 0.64 mm using the center-of-gravity method. And the detection efficiency of the detector can exceed $80 \%$ for thermal neutron which is comparable to that of $10 \mathrm{~atm}^{3} \mathrm{He}$ tube.

articleTitle: Radiation profile analysis of spent fuel bundles in wet storage using the Optical Fiber Probe System (OFPS): Monte Carlo study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Optical Fiber Probe System(OFPS), consisting of an optical fiber and p-terphenyl scintillators, is used for physical inventory verification(PIV) of spent nuclear fuel in wet storage. The OFPS measures radiation emitted from each spent fuel bundle as it scans between them, and generates a radiation profile based on this data to determine the presence or absence of a spent fuel bundle. In this study, the OFPS in wet storage was simulated to analyze and evaluate its performance. The Oak Ridge Isotope GENeration and depletion(ORIGEN) tool was used to calculate the gamma-ray source term emanating from CANDU 37 spent fuel bundles. In addition, a code was developed to update the intensity of gamma-ray emitted from the bundles depending on their storage period. The OFPS scanning geometry of the wet storage was modeled using GEANT4, and the contribution of energy deposition from each bundle on the detector was determined as a function of detector position. Then, the radiation profile was obtained by convolving the radioactivity of each bundle with the energy contribution for each detector position. These generated radiation profiles were used to develop a radiation profile analysis algorithm to help identify the location of missing bundles. The radiation profile analysis algorithm was evaluated by simulating a situation where a bundle was missing at a random location among the bundles stacked in the wet storage.

articleTitle: Photoresponse, X-ray response and electric fields in silicon carbide with graphene
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In our contribution, we demonstrate the possibilities of epitaxial graphene grown by thermal decomposition of hexagonal silicon carbide in terms of sensitivity to light and high-energy radiation. We present the concept of an optically gated graphene transistor that has the potential to work under extreme temperature and radiation conditions. We show that the modulated photoresponse of a single atomic graphene may vary by up to 20 percent due to changes in the electric field in a semiinsulating silicon carbide substrate. This effect occurs due to changes in the occupancy of a vanadium-related deep level with an activation energy close to 1 electronvolt. The occupancy of this level can be tuned by external illumination with wavelengths ranging between 400 and 1500 nm and under X-rays. In connection with this, we also demonstrate the generalization of the crossed polarizers method for the electric field measurements in any Pockels crystals.

articleTitle: 28 nm MOS Transistor SPICE BSIM Model based on Equivalent Gate Oxide Capacitance supporting Electrical Effects of 1-Grad Total Ionizing Dose
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: There is a lack information and simulation tools accounting for global-level simulations in SPICE environments for Pure Analog Design in 28 nm CMOS technologies for those analog stages superimposed to severe radiation doses and damages up to 1 GRad (pre HPC and HPC+ flavour). In this paper, we present a SPICE Model based on Gate-Oxide Capacitance variations to support variations of key electrical parameters due to 1 GRad dose in CAD/EDA environment. This model is so called RAD-BSIM, and is based on the evidence that radiation-induced charge traps phenomena localized at gate oxide, spacer, and shallow trench isolation layers induce a certain threshold voltage shift that at constant MOST amount of charge spread over the conductive channel, is fully equivalent to a variation in the gate capacitance per unit area (C’OX). This formulation is validated by comparing the electrical characteristics of the RAD-BSIM with experimental characteristics of the same MOST after 1 GRad exposure. Threshold voltage in nominal conditions (pre rad) is 386 mV, becoming 314 mV after 1 Grad dose absorption. RAD-BSIM simulations present 326 mV, resulting in only $0.63 \%$ deviation comparing rad model and measurements. Similar results have been achieved for off-state leakage current ($1.22 \%$ deviation).

articleTitle: PET Attenuation Map Generation from Virtual Monochromatic Images Obtained with Photon Counting CT Scanners
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction (AC) is essential for achieving artefact-free PET/MR images. Many previous studies have primarily relied on conventional CT scanners for AC. Currently, CT-derived PET attenuation maps are based on conversion schemes from conventional CT scanners with data from polyenergetic X-ray spectra and it is known that converting from these CT image data to monoenergetic 511 keV attenuation coefficients unavoidably introduces systematic errors in the attenuation coefficients employed for AC in PET imaging. To address this issue, we utilized spectral CT in order to obtain more accurate attenuation maps. Spectral CT offers advantages over conventional CT scanners by providing the possibility of material decomposition. Spectral CT systems also allow to reconstruct virtual monochromatic images (VMI) from the inherently multiple polyenergetic data sets of CT. VMIs can be used to obtain virtual non-contrast (VNC) images and bone mineral density measurements. In our approach, we plan to use angiographic spectral CT scans with an administration of iodinated contrast agents and to compute VNC images from the obtained dataset. The conversion scheme from monochromatic CT images to linear attenuation coefficients at 511 keV was obtained by acquiring spectral CT data for different tissue types using an electron density phantom developed for spectral CTs and a photon counting (PC) CT scanner.

articleTitle: Timing perspective with dual-ended high-frequency SiPM readout for TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With recent advancement in SiPM technology and fast readout electronics, one limiting factor on achievable timing performance of gamma-ray detectors for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) is light transport in the crystal. The effects of light transport manifest as depth-of-interaction (DOI)-dependent detection time jitter. For Cherenkov photons, the increase of optical path mitigates the intrinsic advantage of this prompt signature. For high aspect-ratio crystals with a single-ended readout, the information of about half the photons cannot be fully harvested as they initially travel in the direction opposed to the photodetector. Low-noise high-frequency dual-ended SiPM readout can contribute to mitigate the aforementioned challenges and, at the same time, has the potential to combine ultra-fast timing with highest gamma-ray detection efficiency. We have studied the timing properties of LYSO:Ce and BGO in a symmetric dual-ended SiPM readout configuration. Coupling $3 \times 3 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ polished BGO crystals to Broadcom AFBR-S4N44P014M SiPMs a CTR of 455 ps FWHM was measured for all photopeak events using the average of the front and back timestamp. Three optimization steps were used in the analysis: baseline correction, a novel adaptive timestamp weighting, and rise time correction. CTR values improved to 371 ps, 259 ps, and 232 ps, respectively, when all photopeak events were included. Additionally, for one third of the events per channel, the CTR could further be improved to 172 ps. Using polished 3x3x20 mm<sup>3</sup> LYSO:Ce crystals, we obtained CTR values of 112 ps after baseline correction, and upon applying a time-based DOI correction, sub-100 ps for all photopeak events. This comprehensive study employs various light-emitting materials and geometries and provides detailed insights on the role of light transport and the efficient usage of information, toward the fundamental physical timing limits in TOF-PET.

articleTitle: Imaging α/β Radiotherapy with Compton Tomography: Progress in Image Quality Using Event Filtering and Maximum-a-Posteriori Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Although the Compton camera has been studied for many years, it is still rarely used in nuclear medicine. The main rationale for this situation is the poor image quality and numerous artefacts at low statistics on Compton images. To address this issue, Damavan Imaging has developed a Compton camera with good spatial resolution and high signal-to-noise ratio on detected events thanks to a coincidence veto between the two plates. Using time and energy information, we can discriminate direct events from retro-diffused events. These features allow further cleaning of 3D images, but still distort their shape when reconstructed. To improve the quality of reconstructed images, we have developed a maximum a posteriori reconstruction algorithm with a Markov random filed prior based on the Bayesian inference. Especially, a simultaneous coordinate ascent scheme has been proposed to maximize the posterior function. Its simultaneous update of all coordinates makes the reconstruction algorithm particularly suitable for large-scale image, such as in 3D Compton camera imaging. Various comparative studies conducted with real Compton data provided by Damavan Imaging confirm that the developed reconstruction algorithm outperforms the classical LM-MLEM algorithm in both speed and accuracy.

articleTitle: Quantum entangled PET - recent progress and new insights
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Exploitation of the implicit quantum entanglement (QE) of the two gamma-photons in PET for improving image quality is a novel new methodology proposed only recently e.g [1]. However progress in this new area had been hindered due to lack of theoretical understanding or experimental constraint on how the initial QE can be dispersed to the envirionment through decoherence. Such processes will have significant role in PET imaging through scatter processes in the patient, bed or the detector crystals.
