The role of such processes will be significantly enhanced in next-generation fully body PET.Addressing this major gap in our knowledge of QE decoherence is a key aim of the new MeVQE collaboration, an interdisciplinary grouping of nuclear physicists, quantum information theorists and mathematicians based at the University of York. The first theoretical calculation of the decoherence of QE for PET photons will be presented [2]. Predictions from the new theory are challenged with a first detailed experimental determination of the triple Compton scattering of entangled gamma photons [3]. The work provides a paradigm shift in our understanding of QE decoherence for PET photons. In addition a further key measurement for the field will be presented, the first determination of the QE witness in a relistic preclinical scenario viz. 18-F source with gamma produced from annihilation in tissue (mouse heart). The future programme of MeVQE in establishing QEPET will also be outlined.

articleTitle: Exploring the light transport and timing characteristics of layered scintillators for TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Heterostructured scintillators are a novel solution for the trade-off between high sensitivity and fast timing in detectors used in time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). Here, two materials are combined through alternating layers in micrometer range, one has a high stopping power and the other has fast timing properties. Through energy sharing via recoil electrons with the fast scintillator, the timing properties of the detector improve. This layered structure however degrades the light transport, limiting the achievable timing resolution and photon detection efficiency. To mitigate this limitation a double sided readout can be used in which the scintillator is sandwiched between two silicon photomultipliers. In this way the amount of detected photons is increased and the depth of interaction (DOI) information can be additionally retrieved. In this work, we aim to enhance our understanding of heterostructured scintillators by examining the influence of layering on their timing and depth-of-interaction (DOI) properties. For this purpose, we focus on the single materials that make up the heterostructure. In particular we analysed a $3 \times 3 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ Bismuth Germanate (BGO) as bulk/polished crystal and as a layered structure ($250 \mu \mathrm{m}$ layers). We investigate the optimisation of the coincident time resolution (CTR) and the DOI information. Using the layered structure, it was possible to improve the CTR (FWHM) by 37% (439 ps to 275 ps) through the application of DOI-based correction methods. In addition, a DOI resolution (FWHM) of 8.1 mm to 9.2 mm was measured. The results are compared to measurements of the polished/bulk BGO crystal of the same dimensions.

articleTitle: HEXID: A finely pixelated readout ASIC for future hard X-ray space missions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents the Hyper-Spectral X-ray Imaging Device (HEXID) readout integrated circuit for future Hard X-ray space telescopes missions. Following the success of the NuSTAR (Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array) mission (launched in 2012), follow-up missions, such as the proposed: HEX-P, BEST, and FORCE, could perform a deeper black hole census providing a more refined measurements thanks to recent hard X-ray mirror technologies, where mirrors, made of monolithic silicon segments or shells, demonstrated the feasibility of making hard X-ray mirrors with angular resolutions of 5-10 arc-seconds Half Power Diameter (HPD) compared to the NuSTAR’s 1 arcminute HPD. Such a high angular resolution requires matched detectors (higher degree of segmentation) to fully benefit from the achievable improved spatial resolution. In this framework, a first prototype of the HEXID ASIC family, named HEXID65P1, has been developed and characterized. This prototype features a novel pixelated front-end tailored to reading out a finely segmented CZT sensor with a 150 um pixel pitch in a hexagonal arrangement. The prototype implements an array of 8 by 8 pixels and it employs the Event-based readout EDWARD. This readout ASIC is capable of processing the photon-generated charge over a large dynamic range (from 2 keV up to 180 keV), while keeping a low input noise (ENC < 20 e-) up to 18 keV. This work presents the characterization results of the spectroscopic performances of the ASIC in terms of noise, linear response over the defined energy range and its sparsified readout. Moreover, the plan for its future expansion into a larger detection area will be detailed.

articleTitle: Thin, Radiation Tolerant AlGaAs Solid-State Photomuliplier Prototype Development
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are a compact, high-gain photodetector that can be used in nuclear instruments for capturing photons from large scintillator crystals for spectroscopy or thin films for imaging. One limiting factor for SiPMs is that the devices can degrade rapidly in highradiation environments. Using aluminum gallium arsenide (AlGaAs), a solid-state photomultiplier (SSPM) can be designed to address the radiation tolerance. GaAs has a larger absorption coefficient than silicon, and therefore, less material is required to provide an equivalent quantum efficiency. A thinner device provides less volume to become damaged by incident radiation. For Geiger-mode operation required for a SSPM, a high internal electric field is required. To provide this large field within a thin device, multiple tiered mesa designs have been studied. Radiation damage from neutrons show minimal impact on dark currents for the AlGaAs devices up to $10^{9}$ $\mathrm{n} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$, while a noticable increase in silicon was measured. A prototype, triple mesa SSPMs have been produced for evaluation.

articleTitle: A high performance small animal PET/CT/MRI Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET, CT, and MRI are essential imaging technologies widely used in both clinical diagnostics and biological research. PET scans detect metabolic activity in the body and are commonly used for the diagnosis of cancer, cardiovascular diseases, and brain disorders. CT scans can identify structural abnormalities such as fractures, tumors, and internal bleeding, and are also the most effective method for attenuation correction in PET imaging. MRI is particularly effective for imaging soft tissues, such as the brain, spinal cord, muscles, and joints. We have developed a PET/CT/MRI tri-modality small animal imaging system that uses a mechanical arm to switch between imaging modes, ultimately achieving tri-modal imaging in mice. The PET component was developed in-house by our team. It features an imaging field of view with a diameter of 78mm and an axial field of view of 84mm. LYSO is used as the scintillator crystal. Image reconstruction is performed using the OSEM algorithm with five iterations, achieving a spatial resolution of approximately 0.7mm within the field of view. In the future, we plan to integrate these tri-modal systems to enhance image reconstruction, image correction, and support biological research.

articleTitle: MexSIC-TDC, A Mixed-Mode Readout ASIC for SiPM TDC Measurements with a 48.82 ps Resolution
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents a mixed-mode readout ASIC, the MexSIC-TDC, aimed at SiPM output time-todigital (TDC) measurements. The proposed ASIC is mainly composed of an analog front-end, a 48.82 ps resolution time-to-digital converter (TDC), and a digital back-end. The analog front-end converts the current delivered by the SiPM into a voltage using a $500 \Omega$ @ 100 MHz transimpedance amplifier. The resulting voltage is compared against an 8-bit controlled voltage reference to create a digital pulse, the width which is proportional to the voltage reference level and the SiPM’s current pulse duration. The digital pulse is used to trigger an edge detector which enables two up/down 6-bit hit registers that captures two digital words coming from a delay-line loop (DLL).These two words are the time stamp of the rising/falling events. The DLL consists of a 64stage Meneatis cell delay-line with a time reference provided by a 320 MHz clock that comes from a 1.28 GHz LC-tank phase-locked loop (PLL) and a 4 x frequency divider. The PLL uses a 40 MHz reference clock. The PLL, DLL, and hit registers conform the TDC. The digital back-end uses the up/down words and a 10-bit coarse counter for ToF calculations, leading to a maximum timewindow of $3.2 \mu \mathrm{s}$. All data is stored in two 7-bit depth 16-bit FIFO memories that send their content through a 80/160 MHz serializer. In addition, the digital back-end performs frequency/time corrections in the PLL and DLL during the calibration start routine using an $\mathrm{I}^{2} \mathrm{C}$ protocol. The MexSIC-TDC was designed in a 180 nm CMOS standard process and Cadence ${ }^{\circledR}$ software, it exhibits a $2.5 \mathrm{~mm} \times 2 \mathrm{~mm}$ silicon area, includes three fully functional channels and one calibration channel. The MexSIC-TDC is a fully integrated solution that eliminates the use of separate analog front-end integrated circuits (IC) and TDC ICs.

articleTitle: Updates on SiPMSiM, a standalone Monte Carlo simulation toolkit at the micro-cell level to mimic SiPMs signals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A free accessible Monte Carlo simulation toolkit that does not require GATE or Geant4 to be installed has been recently introduced and validated against experiments. It reads the 3D position, time and optionally energy ($\mathrm{X}, \mathrm{Y}, \mathrm{Z}, \mathrm{T}, \mathrm{E}$) of optical photons striking the SiPM surface and generates the corresponding signal. The SiPM class enables Monte Carlo simulations at a fine scale by generating signals and noise for each photon interacting with a micro-cell such as crosstalk and afterpulsing. Simulations outputs can be used to characterize one’s detector energy or timing resolution, or as input signal for machine learning. In this new version, new functionalities have been added and are presented: simulation of SiPM arrays, the ability to mimic the SiPM response variation with temperature or over-voltage, and the availability of simulation parameters for NUV-HD-MT SiPMs.

articleTitle: HPSoCv2 - design and testing of an improved prototype for high density sensor array 10GSa/s Waveform Digitizer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this article we describe the design and testing of the HPSoCv2, the second prototype in a sequence of planned family of integrated circuits aiming at high resolution readout (10 ps or better resolution) of fast and dense sensor arrays (e.g. LGADs) - servicing up to 100 channels per chip. HPSoCv2 is the second generation prototype (4 channel) that includes an improved input TransImpedance Amplifier and initial back end digital control logic to perform autonomous triggering and readout for each of its inputs. In this paper, we present the design, fabrication and testing of the digitizer prototype.

articleTitle: TlBr Spectral Detectors for SPRD Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report on recent advances in the development of TlBr detectors for spectral personal radiation detectors (SPRDs). TlBr has an appreciably higher absorption of gamma photons than CZT, enabling design of more compact instruments than is possible with CZT. We report on manufacturing advances that have resulted in significant yield of spectroscopic detectors and will discuss a TlBr-based SPRD capable of detecting the direction of the radioactive source.

articleTitle: 3D-FLOW OPRA for Level-1 Trigger: A Breakthrough Invention Capable of Extracting ALL Valuable Information from Radiation Providing a Very Powerful Tool to Discover New Particles, Reduce HEP Costs, Advance Science and Benefit Humanity
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The 3D-Flow OPRA Level-1 Trigger system is capable of extracting ALL valuable information from radiation, which can save taxpayers millions of dollars in HEP experiments. Unlike the traditional Level-1 Trigger algorithm implementation in “cabled-logic”, or the CERN-CMS approach of executing 128 algorithms, or the costly lower performant FPGA approach, the 3D-Flow architecture allows the execution of billions of different algorithms like a generic processor but has the advantage over any Pentium, Hypercube, or other processor/architecture in that it can execute specialized instructions (or “OPRA steps” for an optimized Object Pattern Real-Time Recognition Algorithm) to identify particles with the capability to execute at each “step” up to 26 operations in less than 3 ns. The 3D-Flow performance is further increased by its bypass switch and North East West South communication channels with neighbors. The 3D-Flow pyramid provides reduction from thousands of input channels to one or a few output channels. A 3D-Flow system with 10,485 Gbps input bandwidth, 8,192 electronic input channels, 43,000 x 3D-Flow processors and the capability to execute up to 40 “OPRA steps” on each processor is technology-independent, feasible in a 36 cm cube of electronics consuming less than 5 kW at a cost of less than ${\$}$10.70 per channel. The 3D-Flow conceptual design allows the input data rate and the complexity of the real-time algorithm to increase satisfying the most stringent requirements, and can be used for tracking applications. It was proven feasible and functional in hardware using two FPGA chips in 2001 and two modular electronic boards in 2003, suitable to build 3D-Flow systems for detectors of any size. The inventor has faced many adversities and suppressions that have delayed its implementation. This caused a monetary burden on taxpayers and curbed the advancement of science that calls for an investigation to fix science as stated in October 2018 issue of Scientific American

articleTitle: Efficient and cost effective “sum of rows and columns” readout for large numbers of SiPM arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In systems with many 1000 SiPM pixels and with one electronic channel per SiPM pixel, the total cost is usually dominated by the cost of the electronics. We present a simple and low-cost solution for reducing the cost of the electronics without significantly affecting the time and energy resolution. The method requires no active electronic components. We tested the method using the PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC and its readout system. The CTR time resolution is reduced by $12 \%$ compared to a readout with one electronic channel per SiPM pixel. We observed no measurable degradation of the energy resolution and negligible cross talk.

articleTitle: Adaptive Readout Technique for Spectroscopic CT with 1mm CdTe Timepix3 Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The recording of spectroscopic CT images with Photon Counting Detectors faces several challenges. A sufficient number of recorded photons is required in order to reconstruct the underlying energy spectrum per pixel. It leads to large amount of data that must be stored and processed. Additionally, the readout speed of the hardware is limited. The intensity of the X-ray source must be adjusted to avoid overflow errors for areas of high flux. This adjustment reduces the photon flux for the entire detector and leads to long acquisition times if a minimum number of photons per pixel is required. This is especially relevant in cases with high absorption variations through the absorbing object. A two-step recording method was developed to address these challenges, taking advantage of the different read-out options of the Timepix3 detector. These are the photon-counting Medipix mode and the event-based ToT+ToA Mode, where the position, recorded energy, and time of arrival of every photon is stored. This study shows a new approach for advanced and more efficient data handling for spectroscopic CT-Applications with a 1mm CdTe Timepix3 Detector. The new approach integrates the event-based readout with adaptive pixel masking and Medipix mode. Each CT scan projection starts by recording an intensity map in Medipix mode, followed by a ToT+ToA measurement that applies adaptive masking to each pixel. The intensity map serves as an intensity measure for the integrated spectra recorded per pixel, enabling adaptive masking, and allowing for variable X-ray intensity during the scan, significantly reducing measurement times. This work presents a comparison between the raw ToT+ToA mode measurements and the new measurement method. First results of spectroscopic CTScans will be presented taken with the new readout method, which makes fully spectroscopic CT-scans with PCDs feasible for real world applications.

articleTitle: Maximum-Likelihood Structural-Regularization Model and Fixed-Point Proximity Algorithm for SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: SPECT reconstruction is severely restricted by low count and high noise due to its unique mechanism. Most of the common SPECT Maximum-Likelihood (ML) reconstruction methods apply Universal Regularization (UR), which suppresses noise but meanwhile introduces artifacts at structure boundaries. Since functional imaging is often accompanied by high-resolution structural scanning, it should be beneficial to embed structural information into functional reconstruction as additional guidance. Based on this intuition, we propose Maximum-Likelihood Structural-Regularization (ML-SR) model, and apply Fixed-point Proximity (FPPA) algorithm to obtain MLFPSR algorithm with convergence theorem. Simulation study shows that ML-SR could greatly improve SPECT image quality comparing to ML and ML-UR models. Such multi-modal methodology could be easily applied to other functional reconstruction related to structure.

articleTitle: Towards 3D Proton Range Verification with a Compact and high-resolution PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work aims to demonstrate the applicability of an innovative, compact and high-resolution PET system - HadronPET (based on the easyPET technology) - for the quality assessment of proton beams in proton therapy facilities. The focus of the work lay in predicting accurately the 3D distribution of β+ emitters produced in a phantom after proton beam irradiation, and in detecting potential deviations in the proton beam characteristics. Monte Carlo simulations were employed to simulate the irradiation of homogeneous PMMA (Poly(methyl methacrylate)) phantoms with monoenergetic protons, as well as the corresponding acquisition with the easyPET based system of the material irradiation. The comparison between the generated β+ production map and the image acquired with the HadronPET system consistently demonstrated strong agreement, with a maximum discrepancy of less than 1%, thus indicating promising results. The system was also successfully tested in situ in the proton therapy center of Paul Scherrer Institut (PSI), Switzerland. The first 3D images acquired with the system in a real environment of a proton beam will be also presented and discussed.

articleTitle: Pulse Pile-up Correction of Objects with Various Atomic Numbers for Clinical Applications Using a Photon Counting Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Energy-resolving photon counting detectors (ERPCDs) that capture X-ray energy information are expected to derive quantitative information from objects. In clinical applications requiring high-count-rate radiation, quantitative analysis necessitates resolving distortions in X-ray energy information caused by the pulse pile-up effect. The aim of our study is to propose a novel pulse pile-up correction method that accounts for changes in the spectrum influenced by an object’s effective atomic number ($Z_{\text {eff }}$). The method converts the count rate measured with an ERPCD to the count rate expected in an ideal measurement. The novelty of our method lies in assuming the expected count rates for various experimental conditions by simulating the X-ray spectra detected by the ERPCD. Our method predicts the theoretical X-ray spectra based on experimental values obtained under low-count-rate conditions where pulse pile-up does not occur and calculates the theoretical X-ray spectra related to various high-count-rate conditions. In X-ray radiography, pixels with high and low count rates coexist in the same image, and our model handles this situation. Using the relationship between measured and expected count rates, the pulse pile-up effect can be corrected for each energy threshold. To demonstrate our method, we measured aluminum and polymethyl methacrylate having mass thicknesses of 1,5, and $10 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ using our prototype ERPCD system. We applied our correction method to each pixel in the count images and evaluated the $Z_{\text {eff }}$ images derived from the corrected count rate images. The $Z_{\text {eff }}$ values agreed well with the theoretical value regardless of $Z_{\text {eff }}$ and mass thickness, achieving an accuracy of $Z_{\text {eff }}+/-1$. Our correction method, which considers differences in $Z_{\text {eff }}$ of an object, can play an important role in precision analysis.

articleTitle: A SiPM array readout with high PDE and fast signal for compact high-performance scintillation detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: SiPM photodetectors present significant advantages over photomultipliers for the design of radiation detectors. When compared to photomultipliers, SiPM arrays are very compact, do not require high voltage, are insensitive to magnetic fields and photodetection efficiency can reach 63%. We developed a readout circuit for fast acquisition of SiPM signals and we are presenting a photodetector with a $20 \mathrm{mm} \times 20 \mathrm{mm} 4 \mathrm{x} 4$ array of high PDE (63%) SiPMs integrated with this fast readout. The unit includes an integrated amplifier with programable amplification and offset to suit a wide variety of configurations. The impulse response as measured with a 1 ns laser has a 10-90% rise time of 11 ns and a 90-10% fall time of 160ns, making this solution applicable for high count rate situations. This unit was tested with NaI:Tl and YAP:Ce scintillators with excellent resolution results. A 1 in diameter packaged NaI crystal is larger than the SiPM array but produced a resolution of 7% at 662 keV. We will present the performance results acquired with a variety of scintillator materials and sizes and the comparison with PMT based scintillation detectors and discuss the design advantages. A direct coupling to hygroscopic crystals inside a hermetic package with electrical feedthrough is an excellent compact high performance solution example.

articleTitle: An Expert-Driven Machine Learning for Medical Imaging-Based Diagnosis of Lesions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes an expert-driven, instead of data-driven, machine learning (EdML) to characterize in vivo tissues for medical imaging-based diagnosis of lesions. The presented EdML mimics experts’ performance by incorporating experts’ prior knowledge into analysis of data to accomplish a task that the data were acquired for. The experts’ prior knowledge for the task of lesion diagnosis include: (1) lesions are the outcomes of in vivo tissues’ biological changes from normal to abnormal; (2) lesion diagnosis is based on pathological conditions (malignant vs. benign) of the tissue biological changes; (3) lesion pathological conditions are described by tissue pathology and thus tissue pathology must be used as the ML training labels for the task; and (4) what tissue biological information is encoded inside the data by the imaging device. This study tested the EdML using low dose computed tomography (LdCT) imaging modality for the objective of early lung cancer screening. The challenge to achieve the objective is the diagnosis of those screening-detected pulmonary nodules, which are interpreted as indeterminate lesions (IDLs) by medical experts in the field. Current data-driven ML (DdML) cannot perform better than the medical experts. Because of the difficulty in diagnosing the IDLs, both experts and current DdML reached AUC (area under receiver characteristic curve) of 0.89. Two IDL datasets (sample sizes of 68 and 114) with their tissue pathological reports as ML labels were used to quantify the performances of EdML with comparison to DdML with AUCs of 0.90 s vs. 0.70 s. These experimental outcomes demonstrated an immense potential of EdML to overcome the challenge to achieve the objective of LdCT screening of early lung cancer.

articleTitle: Segmented OctaSiPM for Dual-ended Readout of BGO to Improve Timing Resolution in Time-of-Flight PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: BGO has been highlighted as a cost-effective option for hybrid scintillator/Cherenkov radiator. However, effectively utilizing its improved timing resolution is hindered by challenges in managing the high detection fluctuation of Cherenkov photons and their spectral overlap with scintillation photons. Our previous study showed that the dual-ended readout and an adaptive timestamp method could enhance the detection of quasi-isotropically and simultaneously emitted Cherenkov photons in BGO. The OctaSiPM, developed by FBK, features a single pixel active area of 2.5 × 1.4 mm<sup>2</sup> and a 2 × 4 SiPM arrangement, offering a total active area of 5.3 × 5.8 mm<sup>2</sup>. In our recent investigation, when one end of a BGO crystal was coupled to two segmented pixels of the OctaSiPM, additional information about the initial photon density of the corresponding event could be provided. Thus, we hypothesize that the combination of the segmentation scheme and the dual-ended readout can provide multidimensional information on gamma events in BGO TOF-PET detectors. In the experimental setup, a Teflon-wrapped polished BGO crystal was read out from both ends using OctaSiPMs, followed by low-noise high-frequency amplification. Coincidence detection of gamma rays was conducted between a BGO detector and an LYSO:Ce:Mg reference detector. Relationship between segmented pixel time differences and top-bottom time differences revealed a unique pattern correlating with Cherenkov photon events. By selectively adjusting time windows, time difference distribution converged towards a single Gaussian distribution, enabling the selection of pure Cherenkov-triggered events. This marks the first instance of achieving a single Gaussian fitting from BGO data, underscoring the novelty and importance of our findings. Moreover, the analysis of initial photon counts provided insights into the likelihood of prompt Cherenkov photon detection and its temporal density.

articleTitle: PET attenuation correction with multiplexed CT for delayed imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we proposed a direct generation method for PET attenuation correction of delay imaging using multiplexed CT images, which could significantly reduce the risk of ionizing radiation associated with multiple CT scans. We employed a 3D U-net network architecture to predict the attenuation-corrected delayed images using second non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET images and first multiplexed CT images. The proposed method is evaluated on a delayed PET dataset with 32 clinical patient data and 10 test patient data. The experimental results demonstrated excellent generation performance of visual and quantitative results, leading to significant improvements in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). Our proposed method has the potential to eliminate the radiation risk associated with multiple CT scans for delay imaging and to improve the accuracy and efficiency of PET attenuation correction. Future studies in larger patient datasets and with different tracers could further validate the effectiveness and generalizability of our approach.

articleTitle: Gaussian Splatting-Based Registration for PET Image Correction: A Proof-of-Concept Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dedicated, standalone PET scanners have been proposed for applications ranging from targeted field-of-view imaging to heavy-ion therapy verification. These scanners have limitations when it comes to acquiring transmission scans for attenuation correction. Previous approaches have used an averaged template CT based registration for attenuation correction. We propose a Gaussian splatting-based approach which aims to replace the registration between the template PET and patient’s PET to enhance the accuracy of registration over traditional methods which will, in turn, impact attenuation correction. This technique utilizes multiple Gaussians defined by their positions and covariances to represent both corrected and uncorrected template PET images, which are then fine-tuned to the patient’s uncorrected PET image. This approach enables accurate representation of the patient’s corrected PET image by accounting for both attenuation and scatter. Evaluation on six different template-patient combinations within our dataset yielded a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.9651 ± 0.008 and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 24.9699 ± 0.498. These results indicate the potential of Gaussian splatting in refining PET image corrections, offering a promising direction for further research in transmission-less PET imaging.

articleTitle: A Gain Compensation Scheme Based on Delta-Sigma Energy Measurement Electronics for SiPM Based PET Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography-magnetic resonance imaging (PET-MRI) systems, temperature fluctuations by MRI-induced eddy currents lead to variations in Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) gain. This study proposes a gain compensation scheme based on Delta-Sigma energy measurement electronics to compensate for SiPM gain variations caused by temperature. A Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) was added to provide a programmable reference voltage at the amplifier’s in-phase input of the Delta-Sigma energy measurement electronics. This adjustment changes the voltage at the SiPM cathode, thereby modifying the bias voltage across the SiPM. The proposed method was validated using a $3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}$ LYSO crystal coupled to a single-channel SiPM (MicroFJ-30035, SensL Inc.). The energy measurement circuit maintains good linearity even with changes in temperature and bias voltage. With compensation, the error in 511 keV peak position relative to the reference is reduced to 0.275 % ± 0.137 %. Furthermore, the energy resolution remains relatively consistent (9.285 % ± 0.556 %) with changes in temperature and bias voltage. This proves that the Delta-Sigma-based gain compensation scheme can accurately correct temperature-induced gain offset over a wide temperature range of $5-35{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, while maintaining high linearity and consistent energy resolution. In future studies, this method will be applied to MR-compatible PET detectors for temperature compensation.

articleTitle: Component-Based Normalization for a Multi-Resolution DOI PET System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A component-based normalization method was developed for a preclinical PET protype system (SPET) which employs multi-resolution DOI detectors. The detector consists of dual-layer pixelated scintillators, with LYSO crystals measuring $0.86 \times 0.86 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ arranged in a $30 \times 60$ array in the top layer and BGO crystals measuring $1.29 \times 1.29 \times 7.5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ arranged in a $20 \times 40$ array in the bottom layer. Compared to direct normalization, the proposed component-based normalization method addresses challenges in data acquisition and storage efficiency by transforming the original PET system into a configuration with uniform-sized pseudo crystals.Two simulated scans were performed using cylindrical and annular sources to calculate four normalization component factors. The axial block profile factor bax were obtained by considering only the direct sinogram planes, while the axial geometric factor gax were computed for all combinations. The intrinsic efficiency factor $\varepsilon u($ were computed using a 3D fan-sum algorithm, and the transverse factor frdtr were computed by considering the transverse differences in the direct sinogram planes. A simulation using a large uniform cylinder, along with experimental data acquired using the NEMA NU-4 image quality phantom (IQP), were used to evaluate the performance of the algorithm in improving image uniformity and reducing artifacts. Through normalization, uniform reconstructed images were obtained for both simulated cylinder data and experimental IQP data.In conclusion, the proposed component-based normalization method greatly contributed to the production of high-quality images. By effectively addressing challenges in a multi-resolution DOI PET system, this approach leads to reliable reconstructed images from both simulated and experimental data. Future reserch will focus on using experimental data to improve the accuracy of normalization and to optimize the performance of the small animal PET system in biomedical research and preclinical studies.

articleTitle: Optimising Subset Selection in Synergistic Emission Tomography Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates subset selection strategies for the synergistic reconstruction of Yttrium-90 PET/CT and SPECT/CT NEMA phantom data acquired on a triple-modality scanner. We previously introduced a smoothed directional total nuclear variation (TNV) prior, which extends the standard TNV prior with an anatomically informed, directionally dependent operator and can be used in gradient-based reconstruction algorithms. We used a modified block-sequential regularised expectation maximisation algorithm and its stochastic variants. Stochastic variance reduction improved convergence rates for PET but showed slower convergence in all but the smallest NEMA sphere for SPECT. Treating modalities as separate subsets yielded convergence rates comparable to joint updates, suggesting the number of subsets can be optimised for each modality. However, treating the prior as a separate subset was less effective, particularly for the largest sphere due to overshooting. This could be mitigated in future work with improved step size selection and preconditioning.

articleTitle: Comparison of Silicon and Scintillator Radiopharmaceutical Trackers by Monte Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical imaging at the microscale is a key capability, enabling measurement of radionuclide uptake at the cellular level, both for personalized nuclear medicine and for the development of new tracers and therapeutic agents. Conventional methods rely on the direct detection of charged particles emitted by radionuclides with autoradiographic films, or more recently using 2D active imaging techniques. We propose a novel detection concept for a 3D radiomicroscopy, tracking individual beta rays through multiple layers of position sensitive detectors. Track-based reconstruction of the source distribution in 3D enables more precise localization and dose estimates and enables more efficient imaging of thicker tissue volumes in a single sample. Two detector concepts to realize a tracking microscope are studied compared, using layers of scintillator detectors, or layers of pixelated silicon detectors. Quantification and optimization of the tracking resolution is performed, considering in particular the impact of multiple scattering. The ability to reconstruction extended sources in 3D is under investigation.

articleTitle: High Energy Resolution, Large FOV, Cylindrical Time-Encoded Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiation source localization can be achieved with non-pixelated detectors by using cylindrical time-encoded imaging (cTEI). A cylindrical coded aperture is rotated around a detector, modulating the observed count rate from a radiation source in the field-of-view (FOV). Typically, scintillation crystals on the order of 1 to 2 inches in diameter are used; however, using a high energy resolution detector such as high-purity germanium (HPGe) allows for more accurate source classification and improved image quality. A region-of-interest (ROI) can be selected around a photopeak region (i.e. 662 keV for Cs -137) to reduce modulation counts originating from scatter interactions and radiation background, effectively improving the mask’s modulation properties. Widening the ROI degrades the image quality by allowing the acceptance of low-angle scatter interactions in front of open apertures. These image quality effects are validated with a small diameter, 1D cTEI system while a larger FOV and diameter, 2D cTEI system is being constructed.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Chromium Compensated Gallium Arsenide Sensors Using Photon Counting Readout Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work summarizes the evaluation results of chromium compensated GaAs sensors manufactured by Advafab Oy and evaluated with different photon counting readout electronics. Flip chip bonded assemblies were evaluated to study the optimal sensor design and bias voltage; uniformity; sensor stability; energy resolution; charge transport properties and high X-ray flux operation. The presentation summarizes the GaAs performance results received from the contributing authors. It presents analytical comparisons to the formerly commercially available GaAs sensor material in terms of uniformity and spectral resolution and high flux operation. Advafab’s GaAs presents better uniformity, similar energy resolution and superior high flux tolerance. Furthermore, the presentation covers the latest development efforts to reduce the leakage current of the GaAs sensors by using new types of anode and cathode contacts. The presentation concludes that it is possible to manufacture radiation sensors of chromium compensated GaAs with high uniformity and a good energy resolution that can operate at high X-ray fluxes.

articleTitle: Optimizing the Multi-Angle Imaging Method for Planar Organ-Targeted PET Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Organ-targeted Positron Emission Tomography (PET) has demonstrated the potential to overcome limitations of conventional whole-body (WB) PET/CT systems, such as restricted axial field-of-view (AFOV), limited spatial resolution, and high radiation exposure. The AFOV in organ-targeted PET with planar detector heads can be adjusted to the organ of interest, minimizing unwanted signals from elsewhere in the body, improving signal collection efficiency, and reducing the dose of radiotracer administered. However, while planar detector PET technology allows for quasi-3D image reconstruction due to the separation between detector heads, a limited angular view degrades axial spatial resolution, affecting recovery coefficients (RCs) and causing object smearing in reconstructed images along the axial direction perpendicular to the detectors’ plane. Previously, we introduced a multi-angle imaging method to improve the quality of images acquired with a planar organ-targeted PET camera. Here, we determine the optimal number of acquisition angles and image reconstruction iterations suitable for brain imaging with a wide detector separation. For quantitative analysis, we use the NEMA NU4 2008 standard image quality phantom. Our results indicate that performing a 4 -angle scan, with 45° increment rotations of the detector heads, is an optimal detection scheme. Specifically, it achieves an image uniformity of 6.29%, recovery coefficients of 0.15,0.33,0.52, and 0.73 for the 2-, 3-, 4, and $5-\mathrm{mm}$ rods, and spill-over ratios of 0.23 and 0.18 for the air and water chambers, respectively, significantly exceeding performance metrics of the standard 1 -angle image. Moreover, increasing the number of image reconstruction iterations minimizes spill-over of activity within air and water chambers. Improved image quality was obtained using the same scan duration time in the 4 -angle composite image compared to the standard 1-angle image.

articleTitle: High quality X-ray and gamma ray CsPbBr3 sensors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we present our results of the single crystal growth of all-inorganic perovskite $\mathrm{CsPbBr}{ }_{3}$ using Bridgman method and preparation of CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>-ray and gamma ray sensors with high-energy resolution. We used polished and etched single crystalline samples for preparation of the radiation sensors applying chromium electrodes with the guard-ring structure. We identified twins or stacking faults defects in our single crystals, which significantly influence the charge transport in prepared sensors. Using guarded pulsed I-V characteristics we evaluated resistivity of as-grown CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> single crystals $\rho=3 \cdot 10^{8} \Omega \mathrm{cm}$ and we found that the surface current is 3 times higher than bulk current. Using pulsed bias laser-induced transient current technique we evaluated hole mobility of $\mu=25 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{V} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ and hole lifetime $\tau=600 \mu \mathrm{s}$ leading to the hole mobility-lifetime product $\mu \tau\gt1.510^{-2} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~V}^{-1}$, which is value comparable with the highest quality CdZnTe sensors. We irradiated prepared CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> sensors by X-ray radiation (8 keV) in the switch on/off mode and measured time evolution of the photocurrent density. We found that prepared single crystals are suitable for the fabrication of photocurrent non-spectroscopic sensors. Simultaneously, we observed strong and fast polarization of prepared sensors at DC bias, which does not yet allow using material for preparation of spectroscopic sensors operating at DC bias. The polarization is most probably caused by a non-optimal metallization or the existence of crystallographic defects and high concentration of shallow acceptors in the sensor material. In the presentation, we will demonstrate the effect of various types of metallization and purification of prepared single crystals on the charge collection efficiency of DC biased sensors.

articleTitle: ASAP110LF, a test platform for SPADs and dSiPMs in a 110 nm CMOS image sensor process
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A test chip, including arrays of SPADs and digital SiPMs, has been designed and fabricated in a 110 nm CMOS image sensor (CIS) process. Characterization of the main device features, including dark count rate (DCR), afterpulsing, cross-talk, photon detection probability, breakdown voltage dispersion and jitter, has been carried out, also taking advantage of purposely integrated structures. Comparison with other CMOS SPAD platforms emphasizes the strengths and advantages of the technology under test as a trade-off among integration density, timing accuracy and noise performance.

articleTitle: Impact of Film Thickness on High-Temperature Tolerance for BGaN Neutron Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the high-temperature gas-cooled reactors (HTGR), new neutron detectors are expected to be developed because the in-core temperature is over $600{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C} . \mathrm{BGaN}$, a wide bandgap semiconductor operating in harsh environments, is expected to be a new neutron detection semiconductor. In previous studies, a high-temperature tolerance of BGaN detectors is $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. In this study, we fabricated detectors with different BGaN film thicknesses and investigated their effect on high-temperature tolerance through neutron irradiation and high-temperature tolerance experiments. BGaN films are grown by MOCVD with BGaN thicknesses of 1 and $5 \mu \mathrm{m}$. Neutron detectors were fabricated using BGaN films, and $\alpha$-particles detection measurements were performed at high-temperatures. Neutron irradiation measurements were carried out at UTR-KINKI and at KUR. The crystallinity of BGaN was degraded with increasing film thickness by XRC measurements. The detection characteristics of $\alpha$-particles at high-temperature were evaluated using each BGaN detector. In case of the $5-\mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{GaN}$ detector, its high-temperature tolerance was $600{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. In case of the $5-\mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{BGaN}$ detector, the noise signals were increased at $300^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, and it was difficult to discriminate between the detection and noise signals. On the other hand, in the $1-\mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{BGaN}$ detector, increasing in the noise signals is suppressed at $400^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. These results indicate that the improvement of crystallinity has reduced defects and improved tolerance to thermal noise.

articleTitle: FAIR R3B-TRT: a MAPS-based Si-tracker
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the latest developments related to the production of the detector modules for the Si-tracker of the fixed target experiment called R3B at FAIR (DE). The evolutionary design of the R3B Target Recoil Tracker (TRT) currently envisages a Si-tracker which is fully populated with Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), thinned down to $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$. Specifically, the R3B experiment aims to deploy the ALPIDE sensor technology developed by the CERN-ALICE collaboration as part of the Inner Tracking System (ITS) 2. The UKRI-STFC Laboratories and the University of York are working collaboratively to manufacture the detector-modules required by the R3B-TRT. In the pre-project phase, the team produced a series of low technology readiness level (TRL) prototypes, electrically tested one single ALPIDE sensor and installed the pick-and-place machine (called ALICIA) required to position the ALPIDE chips during the production phase.

articleTitle: Prototyping an Si-GAGG Detector Unit for Whole Gamma Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Whole gamma imaging (WGI) is our original concept to combine PET and Compton imaging. The WGI consists of an inserted scatterer ring in a PET ring, which also works as an absorber in Compton imaging. Previously, we developed WGI prototypes using scintillators as the scatterer detector. However, such scintillators may have limitations for their use in WGI, in terms of energy resolution and Doppler broadening. Therefore, the purpose of this work is developing a Compton imaging system using a Si detector as a scatterer to improve imaging performance. In particular, for low energy gamma rays there is better energy resolution and higher Compton scattering efficiency of the Si detector compared to the scintillators. We constructed a prototype Compton imaging system using the Si scatterer we previously developed and added a PET detector as the absorber based on the scintillation detector. The active area of the Si scatterer was $\mathbf{1 8. 0}$ $\mathrm{mm} \times 18.0 \mathrm{~mm}$. Strip pitch was $450 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and the chip thickness was $600 \mu \mathrm{m}$. The number of strips was 40 channels for each side. The PET detector consisted of a stagger type GAGG scintillator array ($13 \times 13$ and $14 \times 14$). The GAGG crystal was $1.5 \mathrm{~mm} \times 1.5 \mathrm{~mm} \times$ 5.0 mm. The PETsys readout system (PETsys Electronics, Portugal) was used as a readout system of the PET detector. Because both systems were completely different systems, we developed the synchronization system for coincidence. Modified PETsys firmware was applied to generate the 25 MHz clock signal and the reset signal which was generated at the clock reset timing in the PETsys readout system. Both signals were sent to the Si detector and used as timing information. We conducted a performance evaluation of the coincidence measurement. In the evaluation of energy information, the energy spectra of Ba-133 were obtained with both detectors and sufficient performance values were obtained. In addition, the synchronization system worked well and sufficient timing resolution was obtained.

articleTitle: Correlation of NEC to Image SNR and Lesion Detectability in Clinical PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET) imaging, Noise Equivalent Counts (NEC) serve as a key indicator of overall system performance. Previous studies have established the relationship between NEC and signal-to-noise (SNR) for both non-time-of-flight (non-TOF) and TOF PET scanners employing filtered back-projection (FBP) algorithms. This study aims to explore the correlation between NEC and image SNR, as well as task-specific metrics, using iterative reconstruction with comprehensive TOF PET system modeling. The phantom, 35 cm in diameter to represent a patient with $\mathrm{BMI}\gt30$, featured 12 1-cm diameter spheres placed in an off-centered slice, and data were acquired across a wide range of activity levels using the PennPET Explorer. Multiple scans were generated via bootstrapping and reconstructed using list-mode TOF-ordered subset expectation maximization (TOF-OSEM) algorithms to obtain mean and standard deviation images. Image SNR was quantified as the ratio of mean values within a central volume-of-interest (VOI) across both images. Utilizing a generalized scan-statistic model, the area under the localization receiver operating characteristic (ALROC) was calculated for the spheres placed at the offset slice. NEC was computed using both conventional and TOF-adapted formulas from the original data. The results indicate that despite the linearity between SNR and NEC metrics, neither conventional NEC nor $\mathrm{NEC}_{\text {TOF }}$ metrics accurately represent the global image SNR when employing iterative reconstruction methods. Furthermore, our results show that although SNR is proportional to ALROC, it does not adequately represent the change in ALROC as TOF resolution improves.

articleTitle: FPGA based Time-To-Digital Converter for Time of Flight Computed Tomography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-Flight Computed Tomography (ToF-CT) is a novel research path to improve current CT scanners. By measuring the travel time for photons to reach the detectors and discriminating scattered photons from primary photons, we expect to be able to reduce the dose delivered during the procedure or to increase the image quality. Many challenging requirements must be met in order to build a first ToF-CT prototype scanner. One of them is the ability to digitize the energy and time information of the incoming X-ray photons with a high precision and managing the high data rate.This work focuses on a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) built in an FPGA to measure the time of flight of X-ray photons. These time measurements, combined with the energy measurement of the incoming photons, are used to generate ToF histograms for different energy ranges. The current implementation can measure energy with a Time-Over-Threshold scheme using 1 ns time resolution, and can measure time-of-flight with 10 ps FWHM precision in a 2 ns narrow dynamic range and a 16 ps FWHM precision on its full scale range of around 30 ns. Moreover, the TDC is capable of sampling all hits at a 25 Mhit/s rate, which is sufficient for current ToF-CT goals. This TDC is scalable for a multi-channel implementation for the first ToF-CT scanner.

articleTitle: Image Reconstruction Algorithms on an FPGA
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we successfully demonstrate the ability to implement and perform stand-off gammaray image reconstruction on the inexpensive and small Xilinx Pynq-Z2 evaluation board’s field programmable gate array (FPGA). We implemented and optimized two image reconstruction algorithms: filtered back projection (FBP) and maximum-likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM). FPGAs are customizable platforms with similar functionality to fast waveform digitizers while offering the capability to perform on-board advanced analysis, in real time. These characteristics make FPGAs an ideal platform for the development of advanced radiation detection systems for rapid source characterization and localization. We used High-Level Synthesis (HLS) to implement and optimize the image reconstruction algorithms directly on the FPGA hardware. Our optimized solution localizes a source in 20.35 seconds, which is a 5.96 x speedup over its nonoptimized counterpart. The truncation error due to the reduced precision did not degrade the image contrast significantly.

articleTitle: Extracting high accuracy of energy information in photon-counting Computed Tomography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting CT (PCCT) has recently been proposed and researched as the next-generation CT. A photon-counting detector can count X-ray photons, which provides multi-energy imaging and low-radiation-dose imaging. The PCCT, which was released as the first device for clinical use, achieved a reduction in the total radiation dose and high spatial resolution. However, whether the energy information in all energy bands acquired in the PCCT is accurate remains unclear. In particular, some previous studies have reported that the low-energy information in the PCCT is partly inaccurate owing to the miscounting of high-energy X-ray photons as low-energy photons. In this study, we investigated the accuracy of the CT values in the low-energy band using a PCCT system composed of a scintillation detector. The experimental results showed that the CT values in the low-energy band deviated widely from the theoretical values, mainly because of escape events. When high-energy X-ray photons enter the detector, some of them might be counted as low-energy X-ray photons owing to escape events, which is considered to lead to increased miscounts in the low-energy band and underestimation of CT values. Based on these results, a correction method to reduce the effects of escape events was devised and applied to the measured CT data. Consequently, the contrast of the CT images and CT values in the low-energy band improved. This correction method is independent of the phantom properties, which means it can be applied in various cases. Consequently, the proposed method can be effective in improving the accuracy of the low-energy information in PCCT, leading to expand clinical applications of PCCT, particularly its energy information.

articleTitle: Initial human study of an AWSM-PET Device for Augmented Whole-body PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Augmented Whole-body Scanning via Magnifying PET (AWSM-PET) device is a novel technology designed to improve the detectability of lesions in whole-body PET/CT imaging. We have developed a prototype AWSM-PET device that consists of two panels of high-resolution time-of-flight (TOF) PET detectors, integrated with the standard readout electronics and event processing architecture of the Biograph Vision (Siemens Healthineers). The system exhibits excellent spatial, energy and timing resolution, with an average coincidence resolving time of $\sim 217$ ps FWHM and an average energy resolution of $\sim 11 \%$ FWHM at 511 keV. Custom firmware and software have been developed to encode the large number of detector elements and to form coincidences between the AWSM-PET detectors and the Biograph Vision scanner. We have pioneered a specialized image reconstruction approach utilizing a GPU-based list-mode framework, which incorporates the system’s point-spread function (PSF) to optimize image quality and spatial resolution. Continuous-bed motion (CBM) whole-body imaging protocols have been implemented for the AWSM-PET operation to improve the uniformity of sensitivity across the patient’s body. Sensitivity enhancement was evaluated using a point source. The first human subject study was a head-andneck cancer patient scheduled for a standard-of-care (SOC) FDG PET/CT scan following treatment. Both the SOC-PET/CT images and the AWSM-PET images were acquired simultaneously for a total of 17 minutes using the CBM mode. Results show high-resolution and high-quality AWSM-PET images. We anticipate to image more patients in the summer, refine AWSM-PET image reconstruction parameters and correction techniques. Comparison between the AWSM-PET and the SOC-PET/CT will be presented at the 2024 IEEE MIC conference.

articleTitle: Large human cohort study of markerless head motion tracking for brain PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET is a widely used imaging modality in the study of brain function and metabolism. However, head motion during PET scans can degrade image quality and affect quantitative measurements. In this study, we evaluated the performance of the United Imaging Healthcare Motion Tracking system (UMT) with event-by-event (EBE) motion correction for brain PET imaging. A large human cohort study was conducted using 51 subjects with 5 different PET radiotracers. The UMT EBE method was compared to the Polaris Vicra system and post-reconstruction registration (PRR) method. Our results demonstrated that the UMT method achieved comparable results to Vicra, and surpassed PRR, both qualitatively and quantitatively for all tracers. The UMT method effectively eliminated motion blurring and yielded accurate quantitative PET images. Additionally, we found that UMT EBE exhibited smaller residual standard deviation in time activity curve (TAC) fitting compared to PRR. The UMT EBE method showed superior performance in large gray matter regions of interest analysis, producing a 1.39% higher average SUV than PRR and a 0.13% higher average SUV than Vicra, with lower variability (0.42%). This work provides valuable insights into motion correction techniques for brain PET imaging, highlighting the potential of UMT EBE to enhance the accuracy and quality of PET measurements. Future study will focus on applying the UMT EBE method to human studies using the NeuroeXplorer.

articleTitle: Tumor Segmentation for Noisy PET Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Tumor staging and the evaluation of treatment effects require the precise segmentation of lesions in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans. Manual segmentation is tedious and should be replaced by automatic methods that are robust to the noise of PET reconstructions. This paper proposes a statistical method that consists of non-local means filtering, energy histogram-based local threshold selection, adaptive voxel classification, and fast-marching to find groups of voxels forming lesions. The effectiveness of the proposed solution is demonstrated by reduced dosage sequences of PET scans. We show that similar clinical decisions can be made using even noisy data reconstructed from low-dose scans.

articleTitle: Development of the Optimized Solar Neutron Tracking (SONTRAC) Instrument
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Solar flares are known to accelerate charged particles up to high energies. If those particles precipitate downward toward the Sun, the accelerated ions can produce secondary neutrons via interactions with the dense plasma of the chromosphere and photosphere. Owing to their low interaction cross sections and brief lifetime, solar neutrons are among the least-measured products of solar flare acceleration. To fill this gap in measurement, we are developing the SOlar Neutron TRACking (SONTRAC) instrument, a novel imaging neutron spectrometer utilizing a scintillating fiber hodoscope read out by miniature silicon photomultipliers. In this presentation, we describe the refinement and optimization of the SONTRAC instrument based on lessons learned from the previous generation SONTRAC design. At the end of this development cycle, we plan to have a fully optimized instrument suitable for proposal to a variety of mission opportunities.

articleTitle: A One-ring Prototype of the Next Generation Hemispherical PET with TOF and DOI Measurement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We successfully commercialized the world’s first hemispherical brain positron emission tomography (PET) system Vrain to visualize functions and metabolisms in the human brain. Time-of-flight (TOF) resolution of 229 ps works well to increase sensitivity and reduce image noise, but there is room for further improvement of spatial resolution because the crystal pitch of 4.2 mm is not so fine for brain imaging and there is no capability for depth of interaction (DOI) measurement. DOI measurement helps mitigate the parallax error in the peripheral area and provides uniform spatial resolution in the whole field-of-view. Therefore, we are aiming at development of the next generation hemispherical brain PET with both TOF and DOI measurement in finer pitch crystals to achieve higher sensitivity and higher spatial resolution. Last year, we reported the feasibility for achieving 1 mm resolution by simulating a TOF-DOI brain PET system. Based on the results obtained for the simulated geometry, in this work, we have developed a one-ring prototype with our original crosshair light-sharing (CLS) detectors. The 30cm-diameter detector ring is composed of 36 detector blocks. The scintillator is fast-LGSO crystals with the element size of $1.45 \times 1.45 \times 15 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$. The energy resolution and the TOF resolution are 11.6% and 302 ps, respectively. The one-ring prototype successfully resolved 1.0 mm rods, which was consistent with the simulation results. DOI information effectively improved the rod separation capability at radial offset positions. In conclusion, we experimentally demonstrated 1 mm resolution for the prototyped brain TOF-DOI PET system with the CLS detectors.

articleTitle: Few-Shot Classification and Anatomical Localization of Tissues in SPECT Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate classification and anatomical localization are essential for effective medical diagnostics and research, which may be efficiently performed using deep learning techniques. However, availability of limited labeled data poses a significant challenge. To address this, we adapted Prototypical Networks and the Propagation-Reconstruction Network (PRNet) for few-shot classification and localization, respectively, in Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) images. For the proof of concept we used a 2D-sliced image cropped around heart. The Prototypical Network, with a pre-trained ResNet-18 backbone, classified ventricles, myocardium, and liver tissues with 96.67% training and 93.33% validation accuracy. PRNet, adapted for 2D imaging with an encoder-decoder architecture and skip connections, achieved a training loss of 1.395, accurately reconstructing patches and capturing spatial relationships. These results highlight the potential of Prototypical Networks for tissue classification with limited labeled data and PRNet for anatomical landmark localization, paving the way for improved performance in deep learning frameworks.

articleTitle: Development of Photon-to-Digital Converters -- A 3D Integrated Digital Single- Photon Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We develop 3D integrated photon-to-digital converters (PDC) aimed to replace PMTs and SiPMs in various radiation science applications. In previous years we reported on a CMOS readout electronics designed for low power consumption in large area systems such as noble liquid dark matter or neutrino searches, or fast neutron spectroscopy. System integration of these PDCs has also been demonstrated. We also reported on the development of the SPAD technology optimized for precise timing at wavelengths below 500~nm and specifically designed to be 3D integrated onto the CMOS readout. A comprehensive test platform allows performing all SPAD testing in Geiger mode on either dies or wafers was also demonstrated. A revised CMOS readout modified to ease large system integration was designed. Wafers of this readout were produced and we are presently characterizing them to study performance variations on and across wafers. We also discuss the challenges of resizing and matching patterns between TSMC wafers and our custom SPAD layer. Recently, we have completed key milestones with wafer-to-wafer bonding of mock-up SPAD wafers onto resized but otherwise unprocessed TSMC CMOS wafers. We are proceeding with the bonding of functional SPAD wafers onto CMOS readout wafers to complete the first lot of 3D PDCs. We will report on their fabrication, on the CMOS readout operation, and on the SPAD performance.

articleTitle: X-ray response of (BA)2PbI4 Polycrystalline Perovskite X-ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a study of the optical and electrical properties of (BA)<inf>2</inf>PbI<inf>4</inf> n=1 Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) phase polycrystalline perovskite X-ray detectors. (BA)<inf>2</inf>PbI<inf>4</inf> single crystals were prepared using a slow cooling method and were processed into a powder before being pressed into pellets. A X-ray detector was fabricated from the resulting polycrystalline perovskite pellet. Our preliminary results show that polycrystalline 2D perovskite (BA)<inf>2</inf>PbI<inf>4</inf> wafer-based X-ray detectors showed a high resistivity of 1.03 × 10<sup>11</sup>Ω·cm, leading to low dark current, making it an ideal candidate for use as an X-ray detector. In this study we will characterise the X-ray response of (BA)<inf>2</inf>PbI<inf>4</inf> polycrystalline X-ray detectors and compare their sensitivity with single-crystal perovskite devices. By optimising the polycrystalline material structure we will enhance the performance of our devices and create an ultra-sensitive and efficient X-ray detector.

articleTitle: Feasibility of Zirconium-89 Imaging with MERMAID, a small-fish PET scanner prototype
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET), radiolabelling of antibodies with Zirconium-89 ($\mathrm{t}_{1 / 2}=78.4$ hours) has opened the door to studying a variety of diseases, aka. immuno- PET). Due to its low branching ratio for positron emission ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$ poses some difficulties to PET imaging, e.g. low-count scans. Performance evaluation using phantoms filled with ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$ is not straightforward due to the Zirconium metallic nature that causes it to stick to the phantoms walls. Here we study the feasibility of ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$-based PET with MERMAID, a PET prototype dedicated to adult zebrafish and small aquatic animals To this aim, we have developed a 3D printing approach to create solid radioactive phantoms with ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$. The phantoms were used to study different aspects of MERMAID performance, from energy calibration to image quality. Images were compared to those obtained using ${ }^{18}$ F-FDG 3D-printed solid phantoms. Preliminary results show that MERMAID is capable to image ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$ but further adjustments are required.

articleTitle: An Approach to Reliable PET Image Denoising Using Deep Image Prior
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning is being studied a lot for positron emission tomography (PET) image denoising, but the general issue of uncertainty of deep learning caused by its black-box-like characteristics has not been resolved yet. Therefore, we proposed a concept for approaching reliable deep learning and implemented it into conditional deep image prior (DIP) denoising for PET images. DIP is recognized as an unsupervised deep learning technique, which can avoid the issue of domain shifts. In this work, we incorporated the idea of “stability information” of the optimization process of the conditional DIP denoising. We defined this stability as the standard deviation of the multiple moderate network outputs during network optimization. The proposed method operates so that the contribution of the ordered subset expectation maximization (OSEM) image increases at the areas (voxels) of low stability value. As a result, the reliability of the denoising algorithm can be improved because the denoised result of DIP is less likely to be used for such an unstable area. We evaluated the proposed method using low-dose clinical brain $\left[{ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}\right]$ FDG PET data measured with the brain-dedicated PET scanner VRAIN, and its results were compared with those of the OSEM and the conditional DIP denoising method. The comparison showed that the proposed method can mitigate the statistical noise while keeping brain structure details and contrast. Therefore, we concluded that the proposed method can improve the reliability of PET image denoising by incorporating the stability information of network optimization.

articleTitle: TOM: A Universal Tongue Optimization Model for Medical Tongue Image Segmentation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In computerized intelligent tongue diagnosis, tongue segmentation is usually used as an input for subsequent downstream tongue diagnosis tasks, and the accuracy of tongue segmentation directly affects the results of tongue diagnosis. Hence, tongue segmentation is of great significance for computerized tongue diagnosis. In this paper, we propose a universal tongue optimization model (TOM) for tongue segmentation. Our method has higher segmentation accuracy and segmentation speed than previous segmentation methods. Even in a complex tongue image dataset with artificially added noise, the TOM method still achieves 97.85% mIoU and saves more than 25% inference time. Moreover, we developed an online tongue segmentation tool (http://www.itongue.cn) based on TOM, which allows doctors to obtain tongue segmentation without coding.

articleTitle: Quantification of radioactivity from coincidence measurements: a hybrid method using simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the context of the Comprehensive nuclear-Test Ban Treaty, the CEA-DAM developed 10 years ago a system dedicated to the measurement of very low levels of particulate or gaseous fission products, named Gamma<sup>3</sup>. The system is composed of three high-resolution gamma-ray detectors (HPGe); low background noise is achieved through its optimized radiation shielding. Additional beta detectors, developed in the laboratory, can be integrated into the Gamma<sup>3</sup> for radioxenons samples. In addition to classical gamma spectrometry (1D), the Gamma<sup>3</sup> can operate in coincidence mode (2D) by detecting several particles in multiple detectors within a short time window. So far, the laboratory uses gamma/gamma and beta/gamma coincidences for qualitative purposes only. Algorithms have been developed to reconstruct coincidences from output list mode files. The low probability of coincidence events is compensated by high signal-to-noise ratio (a gain of 10 to 100 on direct spectrometry) and much lower detection limits. Difficulties come from the calculation of coincidence efficiencies needed to quantify activities. This work proposes a hybrid approach using Monte-Carlo simulations (MCNP) and experimental spectra to determine detection efficiencies in order to extract quantitative results from coincidence measurements. Simulation models have first been validated for direct spectrometry using radioactive sources; these validations ensure metrological connection between experiment and simulation. Then, coincidence detection efficiencies are retrieved from the Region Of Interest (ROI) method and used for the experimental results. Finally, this new method was tested using samples of fresh fission products.

articleTitle: Sino2Sino: deep learning-based direct sparse-view CT reconstruction with only sinogram data training
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Sparse-view computed tomography (CT) can reduce the total scan time and radiation dose by reducing the number of projections. However, employing analytical reconstruction algorithms with fewer projections causes severe streak artifacts on CT images. In recent years, numerous artifact reduction methods based on supervised learning using datasets containing pairs of noisy and clean CT images have been proposed. These methods require well-designed, clean CT images that serve as labeled data. This study proposes a deep learning-based direct sparse-view CT reconstruction method, Sino2Sino, which does not require clean CT images. The proposed Sino2Sino takes sparse-view sinograms as input and directly reconstructs CT image faster than conventional iterative reconstruction methods. In addition, we present a U-net-based architecture that integrates the physical model of the FBP operation into the skip connections to enhance convergence and image quality. The proposed network is optimized through comparisons between the sinograms obtained by applying forward projection to the predicted CT image and the full-view sinograms. In other words, it can be trained through optimization in the sinogram domain without involving the CT image domain. We evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed method using publicly available CT datasets. Experimental results showed that the proposed Sino2Sino demonstrated successful network optimization and streak artifact reduction without the need for labeled CT images. Thus, our proposed Sino2Sino has the potential to obtain desired CT images, which does not require refining reconstruction methods to produce labeled CT images.

articleTitle: A new method to solve the Inter-Crystal Scattering kinematics in DOI-capable PET modules based on Light Sharing
