publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To achieve high spatial resolution, commercial PET scanners often utilize detectors based on pixellated crystals with a shared readout. In this configuration, over half of the total coincidence events deposit energy in two or more crystals, Inter-Crystal Scatter (ICS) events, and are normally discharged. To achieve the best possible spatial resolution, without compromising sensitivity, a dedicated algorithm can be used to address the issue. Here we present a new algorithm, based on a detector made of small discrete scintillator elements with light sharing, to evaluate the temporal sequences of gamma interactions in the crystals and the most likely impact positions, removing the ambiguity in the determination of the line-of-response (LOR). The detector module already demonstrated 9% full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) energy resolution and 3 mm FWHM resolution on the depth-of-interaction (DOI) at 511 keV. The proposed algorithm is validated using Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations, demonstrating accuracy above 80% in assessing the first crystal of interaction and $\sim 4 \mathrm{~mm}$ FWHM resolution in determining the impact positions in the crystals. Final testing will involve experimental measurements and utilization of modules with increased segmentation and number of channels.

articleTitle: Comparison of Large, 5 × 5 × 10 Inch NaI:Tl Detectors with Light Readout by Means of R11833-100 and ET9390, 5 inch Photomultipliers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The performance of the large $5 {\mathrm {x}} 5 {\mathrm {x}} 10$ inch NaI:Tl scintillator coupled to the R11833-100 PMT was investigated in gamma spectrometry, in comparison with the well-known 5x5x10 inch $\mathrm{NaI}: \mathrm{Tl}$ crystal coupled to the ET9390 PMT. The tests included measurements of energy resolution up to 6.1 MeV andtime resolution was measured in coincidence experiments with 511 keV annihilation quanta from a ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ gamma source and 1173 and 1332 keV from a ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ gamma source.

articleTitle: Generative-Model-Based Fully 3D PET Image Reconstruction by Conditional Diffusion Sampling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Score-based generative models (SGMs) have recently shown promising results for image reconstruction on simulated positron emission tomography (PET) datasets. In this work we have developed and implemented practical methodology for 3D image reconstruction with SGMs, and perform (to our knowledge) the first SGM-based reconstruction of real fully 3D PET data. We train an SGM on full-count reference brain images, and extend methodology to allow SGM-based reconstructions at very low counts (1% of original, to simulate low-dose or short-duration scanning). We then perform reconstructions for multiple independent realisations of 1% count data, allowing us to analyse the bias and variance characteristics of the method. We sample from the learned posterior distribution of the generative algorithm to calculate uncertainty images for our reconstructions. We evaluate the method’s performance on real full- and low-count PET data and compare with conventional OSEM and MAP-EM baselines, showing that our SGM-based low-count reconstructions match full-dose reconstructions more closely and in a bias-variance tradeoff comparison, our SGM-reconstructed images have lower variance than existing baselines. Future work will compare to supervised deep-learned methods, with other avenues for investigation including how data conditioning affects the SGM’s posterior distribution and the algorithm’s performance with different tracers.

articleTitle: Rapid Shielding Prototyping for Portable X-ray Generators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Portable X-ray generating devices are used in a variety of field and laboratory applications. Time, cost, and/or spatial constraints can sometimes preclude the customization of radiation shielding. Here we investigate the applicability of Prusa Research W-doped filament, used with a commercially available 3D printer, to create custom geometry radiation shielding. Initial results show that a Golden Engineering XR-150 produces a bremsstrahlung output with a soft and hard component, both of which can be attenuated by PETG W-doped shielding, allowing for fine-tuning of the output dose. Additional work is underway to begin creating custom geometries for shielding and tuning the XR-150 output.

articleTitle: NeuroScope: An Ultrahigh Resolution Clinical Brain Scanner with hardwareImplemented Super Resolution Sampling Strategies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Brain-dedicated imaging systems with high sensitivity and high spatial resolution have become an urgent requirement to facilitate improved understanding of several neurological disorders like Parkinson’s Disease, epilepsy, Alzheimer’s Disease and so on. In this paper, we present the design and preliminary simulation studies of our ultrahigh resolution brain Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) scanner with a hardware-implemented sampling enhancement strategies. The system is designed with 3202 -mm thick cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) detectors, arranged in a cylindrical geometry with dual field of view capability of 20 cm and 5 cm diameter. The whole brain imaging will be performed by coupling the detectors with a 2-mm diameter pinhole collimator, whereas, the microscopic imaging will be facilitated by using a nonconventional micro-ring aperture design with 0.15-mm ring opening. The micro-ring design offers an ultrahigh intrinsic spatial resolution with a reasonably adequate sensitivity. The collimator apertures are designed to be mounted with a precise single linear motor to shift the apertures slightly to improve the non-redundant angular sampling and thereby enhancing the spatial resolution of the system. The preliminary simulation study yields a peak sensitivity of $\sim 0.13 \%$ for larger FOV and $\sim 0.19 \%$ for the smaller FOV using micro-ring apertures.

articleTitle: Plutonium Characterization Using Neutron-Scatter Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Plutonium exists in a variety of forms, including metal and oxide, and characterization amongst these forms is crucial for nonproliferation and international safeguards missions. Traditional approaches, such as gamma-ray spectroscopy can provide insight into the plutonium isotopic composition, but has difficulty discern between metal and oxide forms. On the contrary, the energy spectra of the neutrons emitted from metal and oxide plutonium forms are significantly different from one another. In this work, plutonium metal and oxide samples have been measured with a handheld array of organic glass scintillators. From these measurements, the energy spectrum of the incident neutrons can be determined using the kinematics of neutron elastic scattering. Results show that the reconstructed energy spectrum measured from the plutonium metal sphere are consistent with a Watt fission spectrum. At the conference presentation this spectrum from plutonium metal will be compared with that from other plutonium forms, such as oxide, and plutonium-based industrial sources such as PuBe.

articleTitle: In-vivo imaging of therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals with a developmental CZT-based SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The use of targeted radionuclide therapy has the potential to become one of the most significant revolutions in cancer treatment in the upcoming decades. Accessing the post-injection \textit{invivo} biodistribution of radiopharmaceuticals within the body poses a significant challenge in targeted particle therapy. Some of the promising therapeutic radioisotopes like ${\$}$ ^{177} Lu and ${\$}$ ^{225} ${\$}$ Ac (beta and alpha emitters, respectively) emit secondary gamma photons during their decay chain, that can be used for \textit{in-vivo} imaging. However, they typically emit more than one gamma-ray and some of these are relatively high energy, so their imaging with typical Single Photon Emission Tomography (SPECT) scanners is challenging. In particular, pre-clinical imaging and dosimetry of ${\$}$ ^{225} ${\$}$ Ac is specially demanding due to the extremely low injected doses, leading to a minimal number of detectable photons. We have developed a small-animal, multi-head CZT SPECT equipped with multipurpose tungsten collimators that extends the energy range to $\sim 250 \mathrm{keV}$. A flexible image reconstruction framework was implemented based on the one-step late algorithm, with a triple energy window-based scattering correction, with a pyramidal model for the system matrix, and with the possibility to include a Monte Carlo system matrix extracted from the GATE simulations. In this summary we demonstrate tomographic imaging of several photon emissions from ${\$}$ ^{225} ${\$}$ A c, ${\$}$ ^{177} ${\$}$ Lu, and ${\$}$ ^{99m} ${\$}$ Tc, independently and simultaneously. A final proof of principle will be presented with in-vivo images of mice injected with therapeutic radiopharmaceuticals.

articleTitle: PROTOTWIN-PET: Patient-Specific Deep Learning Models for 3D Dose Verification in Proton Therapy with PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we present PROTOTWIN-PET (PROTOn therapy digital TWIN models for dose verification with PET), a patient-specific GPU- and deep learning-based workflow to predict realistic dose deposition deviations in a proton therapy treatment with a PET scanner. Existing PET-based dose verification approaches do not consider realistic clinical deviations, are implemented in 1D or 2D with CPU systems, or lack reliable conversions from detected PET activity to deposited dose. To solve this, the proposed workflow begins with the simulation of realistic treatment plan deviations in patient positioning and physical parameters with GPU Monte Carlo software FRED. Then, the obtained activation images are transformed into the expected activity images with in-house GPU PET simulation and reconstruction software. Finally, a deep learning model is trained to predict the 3D dose deposition from the activity images. We demonstrate this workflow in an oropharynx cancer treatment. Using the SwinUNETR deep learning model, we improve the Gamma Passing Rate (1mm, 3%) from 61.2% to 99.8%. Furthermore, we implement a Deviation Predicting Branch (DPB) on the model that predicts the positioning displacement values within 0.2mm and 0.2°. The entire data generation and model training can be completed in the time interval between the treatment plan CT and the first treatment session, where it can be deployed to detect dose deviations in milliseconds from a PET scan

articleTitle: Photonic Crystals’ effect on Scintillation and Cherenkov photons in scintillator detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Optical photon propagation and collection inside the scintillator in radiation detectors provide important information for advanced scintillator detector development. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is an imaging technique for clinical and biomedical research applications using scintillation detectors. A PET scanner comprises many PET detectors. The improved PET detectors can improve PET imaging resolution and can make progress in the medical fields mentioned above. Scintillation and Cherenkov photons have separate roles in PET detectors, with Cherenkov detectors increasingly used to improve timing resolution. One of the challenges of PET detectors is optical photons trapped inside the scintillator due to the critical angle limit at the interface with the photodetector. Degradation of spatial and timing resolution can be attributed to trapped optical photons. Photonic Crystals (PhCs) are nanostructures with periodically varied refractive index. PhCs may have different effects on harvesting Cherenkov and scintillation photons because of their different emission distribution and wavelength, and the angular distribution of transmitted or reflected optical photons coming from PhCs does not follow specular transmission or reflection rules. Simulation tools like GATE, used for designing scintillation detectors, cannot simulate PhCs because GATE follows geometric optics principles rather than wave optics principles governing the optical photons’ behavior in PhCs. We built PhCs LUT and incorporated it into GATE. Finally, we investigate PhCs’ effect on both scintillation photons’ and Cherenkov photons’ harvest, as well as their momentum.

articleTitle: Commissioning of an X-ray irradiation facility to test HPGe sensors and to irradiate CMOS electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a new X-ray irradiation facility that was opened at the UKRI-STFC Daresbury Laboratory, UK.The facility supports the core-research at Daresbury Laboratory in two key areas. The first one is the development of High Purity Germanium systems for the detection of hard X-rays at accelerator based light sources. The second one is the development of radiation-hard electronics for collider experiments, starting with the R&D on CMOS sensors for the Electron Ion Collider. The facility also aims to support the wider community of innovators on the Daresbury Campus, like the UK, North-West, Space-Tech network of entrepreneurs. This contribution will describe the key features of the facility and the related commissioning results.

articleTitle: Coupled Gel/Seeded Growth of Cs2 AgBiBr6 Single Crystals for Radiation Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The all-inorganic lead free Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> perovskite represents a highly promising environmentally-friendly radiation detector material. The first attempt to grow Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> single crystals using the unique gel growth method is reported in this study. This technique enables controlled reagent diffusion in a gel medium at room temperature, fostering the growth of visible single crystals. It offers advantages over conventional methods, leading to fewer equilibrium and non-equilibrium defects and simplified execution. Interestingly, the as-grown crystals exhibited variations in size and colors within the gel matrix, indicating the influence of Bi solutes in Bi-poor and Bi-rich Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> crystals. After the crystals were confirmed by powder x-ray diffraction, a series of comprehensive material characterizations were performed. The resistivity of Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> single crystals was measured at $1.12 \times 10^{7} \Omega \cdot \mathrm{cm}$. Trap density analysis yielded a value of $2.82 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}$. The charge carrier mobility was determined to be $32.9 \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~V}^{-1} \mathrm{~S}^{-1}$, suggesting the suitability for radiation detector applications. Additional growth optimization is on-going, and further characterization will be reported during the presentation.

articleTitle: First Prompt Gamma Timing measurements with carbon ions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Prompt Gamma Timing (PGT) method provides the assessment of particle range by measuring the time of flight between the primary particle and PG detection. This non-invasive and real-time approach is a tool to monitor the therapy’s effectiveness and reduce uncertainties in treatment planning. We report the first PGT results obtained with carbon ion beams at the sub-clinical rate at the CNAO (Pavia, IT). The experimental setup relies on a silicon strip sensor to measure the transit time of the primaries and a detector based on a monolithic LaBr3-crystal coupled to a Silicon PhotoMultiplier matrix. Homogeneous and in-homogeneous phantoms have been irradiated with carbon ion beams of energy equal to $398 \mathrm{MeV} / \mathrm{u}$. The obtained results are promising, and further tests are foreseen to address clinical rates and prove the applicability of this approach to clinics.

articleTitle: Identification of γ-ray Nuclide in an Intense γ-ray Field for Nuclear Decommissioning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: As nuclear facilities are aging, nuclear decommissioning is attracting global attention. Most decommissioned nuclear facilities have left large quantities of radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel behind, which is an obstacle to decommissioning promotion. $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy assay is a supporting technique for managing and disposing radioactive waste and spent nuclear fuel. A $\gamma$ ray-spectroscopy system for intense $\gamma$-ray fields without radiation shields was developed using a small $\mathrm{LaBr}_{3-\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{Cl}_{\mathrm{x}}(1\lt \mathrm{x}{\lt}3)$ scintillator with dimensions of $5 \mathrm{~mm} \times 5 \mathrm{~mm} \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}$. The scintillator has suitable properties of fast decay time (${\lt}25 \mathrm{~ns}$) and high energy resolution (2.8%-3.5%). The scintillator was coupled to a photomultiplier tube covered with an aluminum case for shading and shielding electromagnetic noise. The anode pulse signals were digitized with $10^{9}$ samplings per second and 14-bit quantum resolution. The digital values were averaged over 8 ns and applied to a 10 ns digital low-pass filter integrated for $136 \mathrm{~ns}. \gamma$-ray nuclide identification of ${ }^{133} \mathrm{Ba}(6.45 \mathrm{MBq})$ was investigated in a ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ radiation field at varying dose rates. In the measured $\gamma$-ray spectra, full energy peaks (peak) of ${ }^{133} \mathrm{Ba}$ with primary emission ratios (emission ratio >5%) were detected at $0.0658 \mathrm{~Gy} / \mathrm{h}$. As the irradiation dose rate increases, peaks with low emission rates were not detected initially. This $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy system detected a low energy peak at 81 keV at 0.474 $\mathrm{Gy} / \mathrm{h}$ and ${ }^{133} \mathrm{Ba}$ at dose rates up to $1.07 \mathrm{~Gy} / \mathrm{h}$ using the peak with the highest emission ratio (356 keV).

articleTitle: Polarization Correction using Physics-guided Foundation Model for Photon-Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) represents a paradigm-shift advancement in CT technology. However, a significant challenge in PCCT is the polarization effect in photon-counting detectors (PCDs), especially in cadmium-based PCDs, which generate instable counting rate and inaccurate material decomposition results. In this paper, we introduce a polarization spectrum response model and propose a polarization correction method based on a physics-guided foundation model for photon-counting CT. Our approach is designed to accurately address the complexities of time-varying and dose-dependent polarization in PCDs. Preliminary results demonstrate accurate material decomposition that is free of significant band artifacts with proper polarization correction, underscoring the potential benefits in PCCT image quality.

articleTitle: High-resolution Twisted Clustered Pinhole for high-energy preclinical SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Advanced pinhole collimation geometries optimized for preclinical high-energy gamma imaging enable various applications including alpha and beta emitter imaging, simultaneous multi-isotope PET and PET/SPECT, and positron range-free PET. These geometries utilize clustered pinholes (CP) with small individual pinhole opening angles, ensuring high resolutions up to $\sim 1 \mathrm{MeV}$ (VECTor, MILabs BV). In previous research, we introduced a novel CP geometry, called Twisted Clustered Pinhole (TCP), which further reduces pinhole opening angles while maintaining the field-of-view (FOV) by twisting the pinholes around their cluster’s central axis. This adjustment reduces penetration at pinhole edges and improves sensitivity compared to CP when assessed at equivalent system resolution. Here we present an alternative TCP design, termed high-resolution TCP (HR-TCP), which prioritizes image resolution over sensitivity. Its performance was evaluated in a simulation study for high-energy prompt gamma imaging of ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}(909 \mathrm{keV}) \mathrm{comparing}$ it to CP. Sensitivity and system resolution were assessed alongside image resolution which was evaluated with a Derenzo phantom at low (12 MBq/mL) and high (190 MBq/mL) activity levels. HR-TCP achieved sensitivity across the CFOV equivalent to CP (0.17%), with a slight performance decrease ($\sim 6 \%$) observed over a mouse-sized phantom. At such comparable sensitivities, HR-TCP enhanced system resolution by $\sim 19 \%$ compared to CP, concurrently improving image resolution. At low activity, CP achieved 0.90 mm image resolution, whereas HR-TCP reached 0.80 mm; at high activity, resolutions of 0.70 mm for CP and 0.60 mm for HR-TCP were obtained. These results show improved image resolution, valuable for applications prioritizing resolution over sensitivity.

articleTitle: Development of readout electronics for the electromagnetic calorimeter in the DarkShine Experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The DarkShine experiment detects dark photons by measuring the energy loss of a single electron after scattering. Its electromagnetic calorimeter is primarily responsible for accurately reconstructing the energy of the recoil electrons and bremsstrahlung photons. The performance of the electromagnetic calorimeter is crucial, as its energy measurement precision directly determines the sensitivity to dark photons. The DarkShine electromagnetic calorimeter uses LYSO crystals to form a fully absorptive electromagnetic calorimeter. It utilizes SiPMs to detect scintillation light in the crystals, and its readout electronics system deduces the deposited energy in the crystals by measuring the number of photoelectric signals generated by the SiPMs. The DarkShine electromagnetic calorimeter operates at an event rate of 10 MHz, detecting energies ranging from MeV to GeV. These aspects pose challenges to the readout electronics. To meet the requirements of high energy measurement precision, a high event rate, and a large dynamic range, we have researched and designed a readout electronics system based on dual-channel highspeed ADCs. The front-end amplification section of this system uses low-noise trans-impedance amplifiers to achieve high-precision waveform amplification. It successfully achieves a dynamic range of up to a thousandfold through a double-gain readout scheme. The digital section uses 1 GSPS high-speed ADCs to achieve non-dead-time, high-precision waveform digitization. We have completed the design and evaluation test of the readout electronics prototype. Test results show a signal-to-noise ratio greater than 66 dBFS and an ENOB greater than 10.6 bits. Energy spectra measurements have been conducted using LYSO crystals and SiPMs, and an energy resolution of $5.96 \%$ at the 2.6 MeV gamma peak of Th-232 has been achieved.

articleTitle: Cell Flow PET Simulations for Validation of Cell Tracking Algorithms
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The tracking of cells using radioactively labeled cells is a topic of active research by many research groups. For development and validation of reconstruction algorithms capable of this, ground-truth data is needed that realistically depicts the flow of cells in a clinical situation. In this work, we present cell flow PET simulations (CeFloPS) that simulate realistic cell paths in the human body based on the organ and blood vessel structure of the XCAT phantom in combination with Monte-Carlo based simulations. The cell path simulations are divided into a blood flow part and an organ distribution part. Blood vessels are reduced to a node structure along which cells can move. The movement is directed by the blood flow which is calculated in each node using the Hagen-Poiseuille equation and Kirchhoffs’ laws assuming laminar flow. Organs are voxelized and movement of cell from artery entry to vein exit occurs via a biased 3D random walk. The probability of movement in organs is derived from rate constants of physiologically based compartment modelling. Raw PET data is generated using the Monte-Carlo based simulation framework GATE with cell paths as moving radioactive sources and the XCAT phantom providing attenuation data. As a proof-of-principle, the flow of eight “cells” is simulated with CeFloPS based on a ${ }^{18}$ F-FDG model. The generated PET data is reconstructed using a new cell tracking algorithm and compared with the ground-truth data for validation.

articleTitle: Validated Synthetic Datasets for Treaty Verification
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Nuclear treaty verification efforts will require a broad menu of negotiation options that can maintain treaty objectives while not releasing sensitive information about the items or introduce facility risk all while still being robust to potential cheating scenarios. The Enhanced Modeling for Arms Control Scenarios (EMACS) program, part of the Priority Research Objectives for Arms Control Technology Innovation, Verification and Evaluation (PROACTIVE) venture, seeks to aid in preparations for just such an eventuality through generating validated and physics-based synthetic datasets. The purpose of this work is to counter the requirement for large experimental campaigns, which are a difficult task within this application space. These datasets, based on experimental data and Monte Carlo N-Particle Transport Code (MCNP), are composed of source terms and detector response functions. The two may then be coupled with induced systematic and statistical variations representing a range of realistic scenarios that can in turn be used to benchmark detectors and algorithms that are still under development. Alterations could include items such as varying source strength, measurement times, as well as background rates and compositions, all without the need to obtain more data experimentally. The bulk of the work to date has occurred using data from the Spiral Zero experiment, wherein a treaty verification exercise was simulated. The exercises were performed with increases steps of complexity to demonstrate the relationship between confidence and sensitivity concerns as related to treaty accountable objects. The data from this experiment were in turn used to validate MCNP models which were used for synthetic data generation.

articleTitle: Characterization of the SIRMIO Spherical Small Animal PET toward Simultaneous Beam and Tracer Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We developed a small animal in-beam positron emission tomography (PET) scanner for accurate image-guided proton irradiation at clinical facilities within the project “Small animal proton Irradiator for Research in Molecular Image-guided radiation Oncology” (SIRMIO)”. The PET scanner is composed of 56 3-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) PET detectors arranged in a unique spherical shape with an inner diameter of 72 mm. Each DOI PET detector is composed of a LYSO scintillator block with a pixel size of 0.9 mm readout by an 8×8 SiPM array. A custom- made charge division circuit and an amplifier circuit board are used to reduce the 64 signals from the SiPM array to 4 signals. We employ the R5560 digitizer (CAEN, Italy). We succeeded to image the distribution of positron emitters generated by proton beams irradiated in PMMA targets with an energy range of 30-50 MeV using our novel SIRMIO beamline and the PET scanner at the Danish Centre for Particle Therapy (Aarhus, Denmark). Moreover, we are currently characterizing our scanner for imaging PET tracers, which could potentially enable us to image both the tumor and proton beam simultaneously with high resolution. In this study, we evaluated the performance of the count rate and the image resolution of a micro Derenzo phantom at the center pf the PET scanner. A Maximum Likelihood Expected Maximization algorithm was used for PET reconstruction. The count rate was linear with the activity in the investigated range up to 1.65 MBq. The peak-to-valley ratio along the radial direction was 1.5, 1.6, 1.6, 1.3 and 1.2 for the rods with diameters of 1.5, 1.2, 1.0, 0.9 and 0.8 mm, respectively, without any corrections. The 0.7 mm rod was not resolved. We confirmed that our PET scanner has 0.9 mm imaging and can be used for high resolution imaging both tumor and the beam simultaneously.

articleTitle: Upgrade for the Hyperion Detector Platform: Analog SiPM and TOFPET ASIC Integration
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Hyperion PET detector platform comprises sensor tiles, which are connected through flexible cables to the mainboards of the PET detector modules. The versatility of analog SiPM / ASIC combinations will be used to design sensor tiles for multiple PET/MRI projects. SiPMs and digitizing ASICs are integrated into the detector platform. The first implementation will have a form factor of $49 \times 49 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ and use 4-mm SiPMs. The resulting 144 SiPMs shall be read out by a single TOFPET ASIC with 64 input channels to improve the required space, power consumption and costs. Several channel compression schemes with a factor of at least 2.25 are under investigation: Row-column-sum and matrix-head circuits with active components such as amplifiers as well as different passive connection schemes using the light-spread of a crystal over multiple sensors. Simple patterns allow straightforward algorithms for crystal identification, whereas other more optimized patterns employ more advanced processing algorithms, like neural networks, for this task. Simulations show that the probability to find the correct crystal is only reduced by $1.6 \%$ to $4.6 \%$ compared to the uncompressed data from all 144 channels. Test PCBs were designed for SiPMs and for the compression schemes as interposing PCBs. At the same time, a sensor tile is being designed with a TOFPET2 ASIC and an FPGA on the electronics side and just two connectors for the SIPMs on the other side. As such, the digitizing ASIC, the compression schemes, and the SiPMs can be freely combined.

articleTitle: Investigating Nuclear Photovoltaic Batteries for Beyond μW Power Generation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Monitoring the operation and safety of nuclear power plants based on sensors is of utmost importance for reliable and sustainable plant operation. These sensors can still be powered in the case of an emergency shutdown by converting nuclear decay radiation, abundant in spent fuel pools, into electricity using the nuclear photovoltaic (NPV) battery concept. An NPV battery converts high-energy gamma rays into low-energy visible light using a scintillator. The scintillation lights are then captured by a photovoltaic cell, which generates electric power. The output power is relatively low, but with better PV cell and scintillator characteristics, enough power can be produced to power low-power consuming devices. In this study, a polycrystalline Schottky CdTe solar cell with an Au contact size of 1.3 cm x 1.3 cm was optically coupled with a 2 cm x 2 cm x 1 cm Gadolinium Aluminum Gallium Garnet (GAGG:Ce (HL)) scintillator, and the resulting device was tested using a high gamma fields of Cs-137 (1.5 kRad/h) and Co-60 (9.9 kRad/h) irradiators. The measurements with Cs-137 provided a maximum power output (P<inf>max</inf>) of ~288 nW, with a short circuit current density (J<inf>sc</inf>) of ~1.22 μA/cm<sup>2</sup>, an open circuit voltage (V<inf>oc</inf>) of ~340 mV, and a fill factor (FF) of ~ 41%, while the measurement with the Co-60 irradiator gave a P<inf>max</inf> of 1.5 μW, with a J<inf>sc</inf> of ~4.73 μA/cm<sup>2</sup>, a V<inf>oc</inf> of ~375 mV, and a FF of ~ 50%. A specially designed low-power clock, consuming ~0.8 μW, will be operated with the NPV battery using the Co-60 irradiator to showcase the concept’s potential. To enhance power generation, we will explore the geometric optimization of the coupling between CdTe and the scintillator, as well as investigate the connection of additional NPV batteries. Lastly, the NPV battery will be tested with very high gamma field (~100 kRad/h) of a research reactor.

articleTitle: Dual-energy Backscatter X-ray Imaging for Material Discrimination
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In many countries, transmission and backscatter X-ray inspection have been employed to investigate potential threats in the articles. The backscatter X-ray imaging system has a high sensitivity to organics, which are composed of low atomic number materials. Nevertheless, the backscatter imaging technique based on a single energy source is constrained in its capacity to accurately discriminate materials. In the present study, we proposed a dual-energy method for a backscatter X-ray imaging system that would provide a color image according to the effective atomic number. In order to obtain a backscatter X-ray image, a security scanner with a tunnel size of $62 \times 46 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ was modeled in the Geant4 simulation toolkit. The spectra of the dual-energy X-ray source were obtained using the SpekCalc software. To obtain a pseudocolored backscatter X-ray image, the ${\mathrm {R_{B}}}$ value was calculated for each pixel using the backscatter count. The differentiation of common organic materials and explosives in backscatter X-ray images is challenging due to their similar atomic composition. To address this challenge, energy windowing was employed as a means of summing the counts of specific energy regions in the detector’s energy spectra. It was demonstrated that pseudocolored backscatter images can be generated with improved discrimination for organic and inorganic materials. The energy-windowed image enabled the differentiation of organic and inorganic materials, as well as organic and explosive materials. It is anticipated that this dual-energy backscatter X-ray imaging for pseudocolor images will prove to be a more effective inspection method than that provided by a conventional grayscale backscatter X-ray imaging system.

articleTitle: TlBr Film Growth and Morphology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thallium bromide (T1Br) has garnered substantial attention due to exceptional properties, including high atomic number, wide bandgap, and excellent radiation detection capabilities. This paper explores the growth and morphology of TlBr thin films for hard X-ray imaging applications. The composition and morphology of TlBr thin films plays a pivotal role in determining performance characteristics. We can fine-tune the material composition to achieve the desired properties by controlling the deposition parameters and precursor concentrations. This involves precise manipulation of the stoichiometry to ensure optimal charge transport properties, radiation absorption efficiency, and stability. One key facet of optimization we explore is controlling the morphology of the film. Morphology control plays a pivotal role in minimizing defects and interfacial barriers at grain boundaries and interfaces within the film structure. Defects such as vacancies, dislocations, and grain boundaries can act as recombination centers or trap sites for charge carriers, leading to deteriorated device performance. These defects can be mitigated through optimized film morphology, resulting in enhanced device performance, stability, and reliability. The paper describes TlBr Film morphology and its correlation to the deposition conditions.

articleTitle: Modeling the Efficiency of a Compact ZnS:6LiF Neutron Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A GEANT4 model of a ZnS:<sup>6</sup>LiF neutron detector consisting of wavelength-shifting (WLS) plastic sandwiched by converter-layers was constructed in order to determine the intrinsic neutron efficiency as a function of energy over several orders of magnitude from 25 meV to 20 MeV. Energy deposited in the detector was converted to a simulated pulse-height spectrum using light-yield distributions and an optical-transport efficiency. Thresholds were placed on the pulse-height spectra corresponding to the estimated dark-current level, and the lower edge of the <sup>6</sup>Li peak. The absolute efficiency of the detector was subsequently modelled with a mono-energetic neutron beam and found to be 65% for thermal energies, decreasing exponentially to ~ 3 - 10% for fast neutrons. The efficiency is dominated by the <sup>6</sup>Li reaction at thermal and epithermal energies until approximately E<inf>n</inf> = 1 MeV, where the detector transitions to a plastic scintillator.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-based Scatter Estimation for Time-of-Flight PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate scatter correction is crucial for quantitative positron emission tomography (PET). While the gold standard, Monte Carlo simulation, is usually too slow to be used routinely, faster alternatives often come at the cost of lower accuracy. To avoid this trade-off between accuracy and computational performance, deep learning-based approaches have recently indicated great potential. Here, we focus on the latest generation of PET scanners and provide an extension of prior work that is dedicated to time-of-flight PET in long axial field-of-view scanners. In particular, we train a U-net-like neural network to reproduce the outcome of our in-house Monte Carlo (MC) simulation as a function of the TOF PET emission data and the CT-based PET attenuation correction factors. Trained on data of 23 patients and tested on another 3 patients, our deep scatter estimation (DSE) yields scatter distributions that differ by 6.4% from the MC ground truth and clearly outperform single-scatter-simulations (error of 21.3%). These errors translate to 6.7% (DSE) and 24.6% (SSS) for scatter-corrected PET reconstructions, demonstrating the potential of DSE for fast and accurate scatter correction in clinical practice.

articleTitle: Single Photon Response Deconvolution for Boosting an Understanding of BGO Emission
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Bismuth germanate (BGO) is expected to be utilized for time-of-flight positron emission tomography and ultrafast timing applications in terms of its Cherenkov emission properties although it has a slow decay time constant and low light yield. Cherenkov photons conveys timing information more precisely than scintillation photons, allowing significantly enhanced timing resolution. However, Cherenkov/scintillation separation to accurately explore the first Cherenkov photon can be challenging. In this study, we introduce a neural network optimization-based temporal photon resolving method from an analog waveform to boost a comprehensive understanding of BGO emission and help maximize the potential of Cherenkov photon. The proposed method can estimate a probability density function (PDF) of the BGO emission by deconvolving the single photon response from detector raw waveforms event-by-event using neural network framework. Experimental results showed that the proposed method can accurately estimate the PDFs and restores a sharper rising edge than the raw waveform. Furthermore, we experimentally recovered all the photon timestamp information by integrating a PDF obtained from an analog waveform. A more detailed and quantitative analysis using all photon timestamps, for example, distributions of time differences between the first and subsequent photons, will lead to boost our experimental understanding of the behavior of BGO emissions and potentially improve the time resolution.

articleTitle: Triple coincidence processing for the BrainPET-7T
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The extension of double coincidence processing to triple coincidence processing not only improves the compromise between sensitivity loss and quantitation accuracy for multiple coincidences, but facilitates the identification of true triples of isotopes emitting additional prompt gammas after the $\beta+$-decay. This is a prerequisite for dual-isotope imaging, exploiting the prompt gamma as a marker for the additional tracer applied simultaneously with a pure positron emitter and for positronium lifetime imaging, using the prompt gamma as a flag for the creation time of positronium. The recently developed BrainPET-7T insert is a high-performance PET insert for human neuroimaging compatible with UHF-MRI. Due to its high sensitivity, it is capable of detecting triple coincidences at acceptable noise level. The mentioned methods will further extend its possibilities for neuroscientific studies. In this work, we present studies on triple coincidences of pure positron emitters and prompt gamma emitters with the BrainPET-7T. The ratio between double and triple coincidences for an extended ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ source was 5% at 50 MBq. From simulations and measured double sensitivity a triple sensitivity of $\approx 1.5 \%$ is expected at the isocenter. The positronium lifetime of a ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ source in plastic was determinedto be ($2.02 \pm 0.03$) ns.

articleTitle: Gamma-ray Probe Endoscope using Phoswich structure & Pulse Shape Discrimination system
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study focuses on separation of gamma-ray signals, when a high density BGO is used in place of a light guide. The purpose of utilizing BGO instead of the light guide is to shield the GAGG scintillator from background radiation while also acting as a light guide. By using a 1.5mm BGO scintillator, over 87% of side/rear gamma rays were found to interact with BGO rather than GAGG. Gamma radiation interacting with GAGG from the front and the signals interacting with BGO from the side/rear can be separated using our pulse shape discrimination (PSD) method. In addition, unlike the conventional gamma-ray PSD method that processes with raw signals, our method can separate signals processed through CSA using rising time discrimination. By shielding side/rear gamma rays, the structural/spatial limitations of detectors such as the 3 mm diameter flexible gamma probe endoscope being developed by our research team, which limits the use shielding materials, can be overcome.

articleTitle: Neutron detection characterization of thick film BGaN detector for neutron imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In neutron imaging, the development of neutron detectors with high spatial resolution is expected. BGaN neutron semiconductor detectors have been proposed as new neutron imaging sensors. BGaN includes ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}$ elements with large neutron capture cross-section as constituent atoms and has low $\gamma$-ray sensitivity because of a constituent atom with a relatively small atomic number. In previous research, a neutron detection pulse signal was observed, but an energy spectrum could not be obtained. In this study, the influence of film thickness on neutron detection in BGaN devices was evaluated by simulation and experiment. The neutron detection energy spectrum for each film thickness was calculated by PHITS. In BGaN film thickness of over $1 \mu \mathrm{m}$, the dominant peak energy was 2.3 MeV. This result indicates that $1 \mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{BGaN}$ may have sufficient energy discrimination properties in neutron detection. Then, we fabricated BGaN detectors with film thicknesses of $1,3,5$, and $10 \mu \mathrm{m}$. The $1 \mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{BGaN}$ has the best crystallinity, and decrease in crystallinity was observed with increasing BGaN film thickness. On the other hand, the sensitive layer region becomes thicker as the BGaN layer becomes thicker, which is expected to improve the neutron capture sensitivity. In the neutron irradiation experiment results at UTR-KINKI, the neutron detection sensitivity was contributed by crystallinity rather than B content. Furthermore, neutron capture energy spectra of 5 and $10 \mu \mathrm{m}-\mathrm{BGaN}$ devices were obtained by irradiation experiments using long wavelength neutrons at MINE-1 in JRR-3. FWHM of energy peak by neutron capture was decreased with increasing BGaN thickness. The result suggests that some of the generated charged particles escaped outside the BGaN -sensitive layer.

articleTitle: Deep Equilibrium for Hyperparameter Estimation in Dynamic PET Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a functional quantitative medical imaging modality with main applications in oncology and treatment of neurodegenerative diseases. The reconstruction step solves a tomographic ill-posed inverse problem with Poisson noise, with particularly high intensity for dynamic protocols. The injected dose, radioactive tracer distribution, and noise level, are also varying across the exams, which requires to devise a sophisticated regularization scheme adapted to the protocol. In this work, we focus on constructing a parametric model of the dose-dependence with a large number of hyperparameters in regularized dynamic PET reconstruction. Our objective is to emphasize the interpretability of the learned parameters. Classical grid search becomes inefficient to explore such a high-dimensional space of hyperparameters. This work investigates a new approach based on the Deep Equilibrium (DEQ) framework. Starting from an iterative algorithm, DEQ performs learning on the fixed point of this algorithm seen as a (deep) sequence of parameterized iterations. The dose-dependence model is then built from a series of DEQ estimates obtained for a constant number of detected events. The proposed method is validated on a synthetic 2D+t database derived from acquired data of a dynamic PET protocol.

articleTitle: Design and Characterisation of a Compton-Polarimeter in Telescope Configuration for X-ray Energies up to 1 MeV
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Compton-polarimeters based on planar semiconductor detectors are successfully operated in experiments at particle accelerators (like GSI/FAIR) and synchrotron facilities (like DESY) to analyze the linear polarization of photons originating from various atomic or nuclear processes. More applications may be found in the field of medical and astrophysics. Within the SPARC collaboration (Stored Particles Atomic Physics Research Collaboration) we have built a Compton-polarimeter in telescope configuration from a 2D-Si(Li)- and a 2D-HPGe-detector. The first layer, the 2D-Si(Li), is optimized for polarization measurements in the energy range from 60 keV to 250 keV. The Compton scattering of the incident photon and the absorption of the scattered photon are detected simultaneously. This polarimeter configuration already measured fantastic results in QED experiments at the synchrotron facility DESY. To extend the applicability in physics we have to cover a wider photon energy range up to the 1 MeV regime. For this purpose we placed a 2D-HPGe as an absorber for higher photon energies behind the 2D-Si(Li). We will report on the design of the new Compton-polarimeter and present the results of the laboratory tests of the system.

articleTitle: In-Situ Estimation of Gamma-ray Sources Depths Using Coded-aperture Imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The in-situ methodology was developed for estimation gamma-ray source depth using gamma-ray imager. The equipment used in this research utilized the EPSILON-G gamma ray imager, which features a coded-aperture and is equipped with a GAGG(Ce) scintillator array for image reconstruction to locate gamma-ray source. For in-situ imaging, the minimum imaging count (MIC), which determines imaging with minimal count in the range of 59.54 to 1332 keV, was acquired using the MCNPX-PoliMi codes and measurements. Using the MIC, the minimum detectable activity (MDA) was calculated, which determines the lowest concentration of surface radioactivity that can be imaged. A depth estimation method was developed for in-situ detection of radioactive materials at specific depths on the surface during radiological emergency situations. The method was validated by comparing the calculated results using <sup>137</sup>Cs with the actual location of the gamma-ray sources in the images.

articleTitle: Characterization of a compact TDC unit with picosecond timing capabilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-precision time measurements are the latest trend for particle physics experiments and medical applications (such as PET). Compactness, scalability and applicability to thousands of channels is required for the readout electronics. CAEN A5203 board, part of a synchronizable and distributable Front-End Readout System (FERS), integrates the CERN picoTDC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC) into a small unit for high-resolution time measurements of Time of Arrival (ToA) and Time over Threshold (ToT). The performances of the A5203 unit, in terms of time resolution, walk correction, background reduction and signal amplitude reconstruction will be presented. The reported results come from laboratory tests with a signal generator and the A5256 CAEN Adapter, and from the unit application to the Picotech PET system.

articleTitle: A New Scheme for the Injection Veto System of the Belle II Experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Belle II experiment is a high-energy particle physics experiment using the SuperKEKB accelerator at Tsukuba-shi, Japan, an asymmetric electron-positron accelerator with the world’s highest luminosity. In the accelerator, a linear accelerator makes two beams of energetic electrons $(7 \mathrm{GeV})$ and positrons $(4 \mathrm{GeV})$, which are injected into a storage ring with a 3km circumference to store and collide the beams. Especially, SuperKEKB injects the beams even during the physics data taking is ongoing in Belle II, which maintains the beam current always maximally and realizes the highly efficient data taking of Belle II. However, we have inefficiency and loss of a part of the beams in the injection, which turns out background events for the Belle II detector. We adopt a veto system for the detector called “injection veto” to prevent the effects of the injection backgrounds. This system pauses the data acquisition system of Belle II at the time of arrival of the injection backgrounds at the detector along revolutions of the injected beams in the storage ring. The current injection veto scheme uses the beam injection signal and the revolution timing information only, which makes the redundant deadtime of about 15% at maximum for the data acquisition system of Belle II. To solve this problem, we developed a new scheme for the injection veto on the L1 trigger system implemented with FPGA. The scheme uses the information from a wire chamber and an electromagnetic calorimeter of Belle II, which are sensitive to charged particles and gammas. The injection backgrounds generate those particles many times more than the typical collision events. Thus, the new scheme issues the pausing signals to the detector only if the hit number from the subdetectors is above the threshold, in addition to the pausing signals from the current scheme. We began using the new scheme in 2024 and confirmed it halved the deadtime. We will discuss the details of this improvement in the presentation.

articleTitle: CT-Less Attenuation Correction for PET using Backward Inter-Crystal Scattered Events
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The probability of Compton interaction occurring between the 511 keV gammas and scintillation detectors is high. On one hand, the most likely scattering is in the forward direction. The forward inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events cause count loss in sensitivity and degradation in spatial resolution. On the other hand, the backward ICS events may pass through the object and finally be detected by another crystal on the opposite side. Therefore, the backscattered events can be used as a transmission source for estimating attenuation coefficients. In this study, a Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) toolkit with GPU acceleration for backward ICS simulation was developed and the potential of using backward ICS events for attenuation correction was studied using simulations and a real experimental dataset performed on NeuroEXPLORER (NX). The results demonstrate the feasibility of using backward ICS events for CT-less attenuation correction in PET.

articleTitle: Temporoc: A 64-channel SiPM read-out chip for time-of-flight measurement on monolithic crystal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: TEMPOROC is a 64-channel SiPM read-out chip designed in TSMC130nm technology for time-off-light positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). The ASIC aims at measuring both the energy and the time-of-arrival (TOA) of gamma photons in a monolithic crystal read-out by a SiPM matrix. In this study, we describe TEMPOROC architecture to readout monolithic crystal and report measurements of the analog front-end embedded alone. Coincidence experiments were conducted using BROADCOM NUV Metal in Trench SiPMs of $4 \times 4 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ and LYSO:Ce, Ca scintillating crystals from Taiwan Applied Crystals (TAC) of $2 \times 2 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$. A CTR of 83 ps FWHM was achieved at an overvoltage of 17 V. The single photon time resolution was also measured using a PbF<inf>2</inf> black coated crystal of $2 \times 2 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ and a FBK NUV-HD-LF M3 SiPM against a high-frequency readout electronics equipped with LYSO:Ce,Ca (TAC) of $2 \times 2 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ and the same FBK SiPM. A SPTR of 73 ps FWHM was achieved at an overvoltage of 7V.

articleTitle: 3D In-System Calibration of Advanced PET Detector Topologies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Research on PET systems is advancing quickly towards sophisticated detector designs. These designs aim to enhance performance but increase the complexity of integration. This is due to features like fast timing and continuous gamma interaction positioning. Individual detector calibration has shown attractive performance for those detectors using machine-learning-based models for, e.g., 3D positioning calibration that include the depth-of-interaction (DOI). However, data acquisition typically takes place in benchtop setups. A prerequisite for system integration is the fast acquisition of the training data and a practicable re-calibration and quality control which is hardly feasible in benchtop routines. We propose a new 3D in-system calibration with data acquisition inside the scanner by virtually collimating a radioactive point source combined with angular detector irradiation for DOI. Experiments were conducted with a point source mounted to a 3-axis motor and placed inside a proof-of-concept scanner (120mm diameter). The source was moved in front of one slab detector ((24×10×1)mm<sup>3</sup> slabs). By selecting orthogonally incident gamma rays, a planar calibration was conducted using Gradient Tree Boosting (GTB). Then, DOI was calibrated by selecting oblique angles and calculating the DOI label from the geometric ray path and the planar position estimate. For planar positioning, the results were within 1% of state-of-the-art calibration at 0.8mm MAE and 1.19 mm FWHM. For DOI, 1.13mm MAE and 2.47mm FWHM were achieved. The method’s applicability to different scanner geometries was analytically calculated and investigated. The proposed in-system calibration method is suitable for 3D-calibrating assembled PET systems.

articleTitle: Growth and Characterization of CsPbX3 Perovskite Semiconductor Crystals for Room Temperature Gamma-Ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper we will present the latest growth and characterization of CsPbX<inf>3</inf> crystals for room temperature gamma-ray detection and imaging. Material purification, synthesis, crystal growth from $16-\mathrm{mm}$ to $35-\mathrm{mm}$ diameter, sample preparation, and detector characterization will be presented. We have managed to grow single crystals, free of polarized planes, with resistivity $\gt$ $6.0 \times 10^{9} \Omega$-cm and $\mathrm{mt}_{\mathrm{h}}\gt2.0 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}$.

articleTitle: A 0.38 mm LYSO and GAGG checkerboard pattern detector with inter-crystal scatter identification capability for high-resolution mouse brain PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Ultra-high spatial resolution PET imaging, such as mouse brain imaging, is significantly influenced by detector’s intrinsic resolution (crystal size), position decoding accuracy, and the capability to identify inter-crystal scatter.In this work, a 0.38 mm LYSO and GAGG checkerboard pattern detector is proposed. The detector consists of a $28 \times 28$ array of $0.38 \times 0.38 \times 4 \mathrm{~mm} 3$ crystals, where each crystal is surrounded by crystals of different type. A 2 mm thick glass light guide was placed between the scintillator array and a 64-channel Hamamatsu MPPC. A PETsys TOFPET2 ASIC records both integrated charge (QDC) and time over threshold (ToT) for each MPPC channel to discriminate the LYSO, GAGG and inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events (ICS-QT). A Look-Up-Table based method was used to identify more ICS events (LYSO-Out and GAGG-Out).Flood images were acquired using a Na-22 point source. Majority of the 0.38 mm crystals were clearly resolved. The average peak-to-valley ratio (PVR) is 8.6 for GAGG and 6.8 for LYSO. A total of 37.6% of the measured events were identified as ICS events (ICS-QT + LYSO-Out + GAGG-Out).GATE simulation was used to investigate the fraction of the ICS events. The fraction of ICS events, which correspond to the events that interact with multiple crystals, is 68.0%. A simulated imaging study was also performed. By using a box-shaped scanner comprising four LYSO and GAGG checkerboard pattern detectors, 0.4 mm diameter hot rods can be resolved with an average PVR of 1.8.

articleTitle: BETA, a low-power, high-dynamic range, radiation-tolerant 64-channel ASIC for space applications and beyond
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) have the potential to be particularly suitable for space applications, where weight, volume and power consumption are strongly constrained. The SiPM signals recorded on board satellites, balloons or drones must be processed and digitized minimizing the size, cost and power consumption of the electronics. In this context we developed the BETA ASIC, a radiation-tolerant chip designed to amplify, shape and digitize the signal of up to 64 channels, with a power consumption of $\sim 1 \mathrm{~mW}$/channel. The ASIC provides a dual gain path, which allows resolving single-photoelectron (single-phe) events and achieving a large dynamic range of a few thousand phes. Each gain path can also be adjusted in order to optimize the ASIC performance for a given SiPM or application. BETA also provides a trigger output, with which it is possible to time tag events of a few phes with $\lt 1 \mathrm{~ns}$ resolution. We developed two different versions of the chip: BETA-64, which has 64 input channels; and BETA-16, in which each of the 16 inputs channels has its own trigger output, which can then be combined to define a more complex coincidence trigger logic. In this contribution we describe the main characteristics of the ASIC and the evaluation of its performance. We also introduce a few examples of applications planning to employ the BETA, like the development of a radiation monitor for ESA’s LISA large space mission.

articleTitle: Neutron Detector System with Diamond Sensor for Decommissioning of Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We have developed a prototype neutron detector system using a diamond sensor for nuclear decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant in Japan. The detector system consists of hundreds of sensor-diodes and dedicated analog/digital front-ends. The diamond sensors are covered by the Boron-10 membrane for converting the neutron-induced alpha-rays into electric charges. The analog circuit determines the neutron events by comparing with an externally set threshold value. However, the conventional readout circuit had a problem that the judgment result differed from channel to channel even for the same signal due to the large variation in the threshold. To compensate for the errors in each element and improve the consistency of signal judgment, we have newly included an auto-tuning circuit in the analog frontend. We also discuss the primary test results of the detector and its performance for on-site applications.

articleTitle: Experimental evaluation of Nano-pattern coating on scintillation crystals for enhanced light extraction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In a PET detector, a large number of photons are lost at the crystal-photosensor boundary due to the mismatched refractive index and the use of long and narrow pixelated crystals. In this study, we addressed this challenge by applying nano-pattern coating on the surface of scintillation crystals. Utilizing optimized pattern shapes obtained from previous simulation results, we fabricated line-type nano-patterns to coat the surfaces of GAGG and BGO crystals. Comparative experiments were conducted using two crystal sizes and two types of resin to evaluate their impact on light extraction. Our findings from the patterning tests revealed an enhancement of up to $\times 1.23$ and $\times 1.44$ in light extraction for $5 \times 5 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ GAGG and BGO, respectively. This enhanced light extraction can ultimately improve PET detector and system performance.

articleTitle: Brain MRI Synthesis from Amyloid PET/CT via Enhanced Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we presents a novel method for generating synthetic brain MRI images from amyloid PET/CT scans using an enhanced Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) conditioned with the joint probability distribution. We explored the use of early and late-phase 18 F -Florbetaben PET scans to guide the synthesis process within our DDPM framework, verifying that early-phase scans significantly improved the quality of synthetic MRI generation compared to other deep learning models. In addition, the proposed DDPMs using early-phase PET/CT suggest promising results, particularly for enhancing the accuracy of regional gray matter volume measurements and facilitating PET partial volume corrections in settings where traditional MRI is unavailable.

articleTitle: Characterization of SparkPix-RT1: A 48x48 charge-integrating X-ray pixel detector with on-chip compression
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: SparkPix-RT is a pioneer mixed-signal ASIC for the development of the next generation of high frame-rate X-ray detectors featuring continuous \textbf{r}eal-\textbf{t}ime on-chip data compression. The first prototype chip (RT1) contains a $48 \times 48$ array of pixels demonstrating capabilities of real-time image processing of 100,000 frames per second. The chip consists of a front-end pixel of size $100 \mu \mathrm{m} \times 100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and is designed to integrate the sensor charge into voltage. An on-chip Analog-to-Digital Converter (ADC), incorporated inside the matrix converts the output of each pixel into a digital value at $8 \backslash$ MSPS. At the periphery of the chip, a digitally implemented compressor runs various data compression algorithms (e.g., Poisson and Zero Suppression etc) to reduce the high-bandwidth frame rate data acquired from every cluster (12 x 6 pixels) columns, which is then sequentially processed by a Priority First-In-First-Out (FIFO) read scheme

articleTitle: Development of a Two-layer GAGG Compton Camera for High-accuracy Positioning of Gamma Sources
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Considerable attention has been directed at the GAGG-based Compton camera for the past few decades, especially since the Fukushima accident. Previous GAGG Compton cameras were mainly used to detect nuclear waste and had large pixel sizes and low position resolutions. In this study, we proposed and built a GAGG Compton camera prototype which was expected to be achieve high-accuracy positioning of gamma sources both in nuclear medical imaging and nuclear waste detection, such as nuclear waste, radiopharmaceuticals, and prompt gammas. Radioactive sources experiments were conducted to evaluate its performances on position, energy, and angular resolution. We used two $25 \times 25$ GAGG arrays, $8 \times 8$ silicon photomultipliers arrays, and corresponding capacitive multiplexing readout circuits to construct our Compton camera prototype. The pixel sizes of the GAGG arrays are $1.9 \times 1.9 \times 5 / 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ for the scatterer/absorber, and the size of silicon photomultipliers components is $6 \times 6 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. The double-coding structure consists of a light guide and a capacitive multiplexing readout circuit and transfers the 625-channel signals to 4 -channel outputs for each layer. Point-like ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ and ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ sources were used for detector calibration and imaging experiments. For the developed GAGG Compton camera, the energy resolutions of the two detectors were $10.80 \%$ and $11.85 \%$ at 511 keV, respectively. The detection efficiency was $6.29 \times 10^{-3} \text{@} 511 \mathrm{keV}$. Its angular resolution of a point-like ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ source at 5 cm was around 10 degrees. The study proposed and developed a GAGG Compton camera for positioning of radioactive sources. Its feasibility for applications in accurate spatial positioning of radioactive sources is verified. We expect such a prototype to meet the requirements of the nuclear industry and medical applications.

articleTitle: Synchronous Readout of Single-Pixel Mode and Charge-Summing Mode for Photon-Counting Detector Readout ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a synchronous readout approach for the application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) oriented to the photon-counting detector (PCD). By using this approach, the single-pixel mode and charge-summing mode can be simultaneously achieved. Compared to the case that only includes one mode, the synchronous mode can correct the charge-sharing effect while preserving the high resolution and high count rate. To validate the performance of the synchronous mode, the full-response model of detector is used to simulate the energy spectrums of the single-pixel mode, charge-summing mode, and the synchronous readout of both modes. Preliminary results indicate that the proposed synchronous mode exhibits the improvement in charge-sharing effect while ensuring resolution and count rate. Furthermore, utilizing the Cramer-Rao lower bound (CRLB), the optimization of pixel size is explored within the synchronous mode.

articleTitle: A Modular TOF-DOI Detector For OrganDedicated and Large Axial Field of View PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: For organ-dedicated and large axial field of view positron emission tomography scanners, depth-of-interaction (DOI) encoding is indispensable to correct parallax errors at oblique angles. The sensitivity of these systems can be boosted effectively by additionally taking advantage of the time-of-flight (TOF) gain in signal-to-noise ratio due to a high coincidence time resolution (CTR). Ultimately, TOF and DOI resolution can not be treated independently due to the DOI-dependent impact of the photon travel time spread (PTS) on the TOF resolution. With a sufficient DOI resolution, the impact of the PTS on the CTR can be corrected. We present a TOF- and DOIcapable detector block that maintains a high CTR while allowing for a DOI resolution of 3.4 mm to 4.7 mm (RMSE), which results in a binning of the crystal into at least two DOI layers. We report the CTR achieved with different system-applicable readout electronics (NINO and TOFPET2 ASIC) and provide benchmarks for the CTR improvement with custom high-frequency readout electronics. With these, the CTR of a single TOF-DOI unit of 141 ps (FWHM) can be maintained on the detector-block level.

articleTitle: MLEM Method for Estimating Spatial Sensitivity Coefficients for Simultaneous Multi-Tracer Positron Emission Tomography (mPET) Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography would benefit from being able to simultaneously image multiple biomarkers in a single scan. Imaging multiple isotopes in a single study will require a correction for the different sensitivities to each isotope in order to reconstruct quantitatively correct images. This presentation gives different methods to estimate the spatially varying sensitivity coefficients using a uniform calibration phantom. Results indicate the maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM) method performs the most accurate estimation of the sensitivity coefficients with a root mean square error of 0.0027. The main improvement of this method is more accurate multi-tracer quantification, with the MLEM achieving 7% overestimation as compared to $10.4 \%$ and $37 \%$ in the simple back projection and constant alpha estimation methods respectively.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Denoising with Edge-Preserving for Reduced-dose Cardiac SPECT Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to improve the detectability of perfusion defects in reduced-dose myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) with single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) by employing deep learning (DL) denoising techniques. Specifically, a 3D convolutional auto-encoder (CAE) model integrated with an edge-preservation mechanism is developed to mitigate the blurring effects often associated with denoising methods. The CAE is designed to suppress noise in reduced-dose SPECT-MPI scans while preserving important image-edge features for identifying subtle myocardial perfusion defects. In the experiment the proposed approach was demonstrated to improve the contrast in perfusion defects compared to a baseline DL denoising network, with up to a 5.2% increase in contrast level, and achieve significant noise suppression in reduced-dose images.

articleTitle: A fast detection system for Prompt Gamma Time Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In order to ensure the consistency of treatment delivery and treatment planning in hadrontherapy, we propose an on-line range monitoring technique called Prompt Gamma Time Imaging (PGTI) that is based on the exclusive measurement of Prompt Gamma Time-Of-Flight. For this, we are developing a high temporal resolution, multi-channel, gamma detector (TIARA for Tof Imaging ARrAy) read in time coincidence with a ion beam monitor [1]. The gamma modules are based on pure Cherenkov radiators (PbF2) coupled to SiPMs in order to optimize the time response and minimize the sensitivity to neutron background. Thanks to their small volume (~1 cm<sup>3</sup>) they can be placed all around the target/patient while allowing irradiations from multiple angles. A dedicated spatial reconstruction algorithm is also developed to combine the response of the 30 TIARA modules. PGTI accuracy is a compromise between the number of Prompt Gamma events acquired and the system time resolution. According to previous Monte Carlo simulations, we expect to reach a spatial accuracy of 1 mm at 2 σ under the hypothesis of a 235 ps FWHM coincidence time resolution and 10<sup>8</sup> incident protons [2]. In this work, we present the design and performances of an 8-channels prototype. With 63 MeV protons from the Medicyc cyclotron of the Centre Antoine Lacassane (CAL) in Nice, we obtained a coincidence time resolution of 254 ps FWHM, and we achieved an accuracy of 2 mm (at 2 σ) on the measurement of proton range with 3000 PGs, corresponding to the statistics expected for an irradiation spot of 10<sup>7</sup> protons. More recently, the TIARA response was tested through the irradiation of an anthropomorphic head phantom at the S2C2 synchro-cyclotron of the CAL, with 100 MeV protons directed at one of the sinuses. The two acquisitions performed with the sinus either empty (air) or filled with ultrasound gel resulted in significantly different Time-Of-Flight distributions, thus proving TIARA’s ability to detect anatomical changes.

articleTitle: Radiation Detection with Vertical Gradient Freeze Grown CdZnTeSe Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we report the growth of detector grade Cd<inf>0.9</inf> Zn<inf>0.1</inf> Te<inf>0.97</inf> Se<inf>0.03</inf> (CZTS) single crystals by a vertical gradient freeze (VGF) method. CZTS is a recently discovered quaternary semiconductor for high-resolution room temperature radiation detection. VGF is a comparatively low-temperature crystal growth method and avoids relative motion between the heater and the ampoule containing the precursor materials that helps minimize thermal drifts or temperature fluctuations. Planar detectors fabricated by deposition of gold contacts on a $4.0 \mathrm{mm}{ }^{\prime} 4.0 \mathrm{mm}{ }^{\prime} 1.7 \mathrm{mm}$ VGF-grown CZTS single crystal demonstrated high bulk resistivity $\sim 10^{10} \Omega-\mathrm{cm}$ and consequently a very low leakage current density of $2.8 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ at a bias of 100 V. The detectors showed excellent radiation detection performance with 100% charge collection efficiency at 200 V when exposed to Am-241 5486 keV alpha particles.
