The electron mobility-lifetime $(\mu \tau)$ product was measured to be $3 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}$ using a single polarity Hecht analysis which is at par with the recently reported values measured in CZTS grown by travelling heater method (THM). The electron mobility has been calculated to be $964 \mathrm{cm}^{2} \mathrm{V}^{-1} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ using a time-of-flight (TOF) method, a substantial improvement over that obtained from conventionally grown CZTS single crystals. Using a biparametric digital correction method, the detectors showed a robust peak corresponding to the 662 keV gamma photons when illuminated with a ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ radioisotope source.

articleTitle: Properties of TlCl scintillator with various dopants
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: TlCl emerges as a promising scintillation material for Positron-Emission-Tomography (PET), boasting a high density of $7 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ and an effective atomic number of 77, coupled with rapid Cherenkov emission. Its appealing attributes include a low melting point of $430^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and a straightforward cubic structure, suggesting potential for cost-effective production. Currently, the material is dually doped with Be and I, yielding a scintillation light yield ranging from 500 to 1000 $\mathrm{ph} / \mathrm{MeV}$, accompanied by a multicomponent decay profile. While this Be-I doping combination stands as the current benchmark, it presents certain production challenges and could benefit from enhanced prompt luminosity. Consequently, our research delved into alternative dopants for TlCl, aiming to optimize its scintillation properties. Our investigation encompassed various dopants (and doping levels), including $\mathrm{Ag}, \mathrm{Cu}, \mathrm{Hg}, \mathrm{Sm}, \mathrm{Eu}$, among others. Although some of these dopants exhibit emission under x-ray excitation, their light yield thus still falls short of the reference composition (Be, I). In this presentation, we present findings from our exploration, showcasing images of grown crystals, emission spectra, pulse height spectra, and, in select cases, decay times.

articleTitle: Deep Learning model for tumor segmentation in micro-PET/CT images of breast cancer specimens
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In curative breast cancer (BCa) surgery, complete tumor removal is vital to ensure no tumor cells remain within the breast. Recently, micro-PET/CT imaging of resected BCa specimens emerged as a promising technique for fast intraoperative margin assessment (IMA). This technique requires preoperative administration of [18F]FDG to the patient. As [18F]FDG may show nonspecific uptake in metabolically active benign tissue, like inflamed tissue, interpreting micro-PET/CT images can be challenging in some cases. We hypothesize that a decision-support system, based on deep learning (DL), can aid physicians to interpret micro-PET/CT images. We propose a DL model to segment micro-PET/CT specimen images, distinguishing malignant from benign tissue. We collected micro-PET/CT images of BCa specimens from 12 patients with invasive carcinoma of no special type and co-registered these images with the corresponding histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs). A pathologist annotated the WSIs, resulting in binary tumor segmentations that served as ground truth for our model. We split the data in a train and test set containing the images of 9 and 3 patients respectively. We optimized and trained a 2D residual UNet that takes the micro-PET/CT images as 2-channel input, and outputs a tumor probability map. When evaluating the model, we found a mean area under the curve of 0.90±0.04 for the receiver operating characteristic curve and 0.70±0.09 for the precision-recall curve across all test patients. For the binarized probability maps, we found a mean dice score of 0.70±0.08. Whereas the results are promising, additional data are required to further improve and validate model performance. In addition, the model needs to be tested in a clinical context, in terms of IMA accuracy and correct localization of positive margins in BCa specimens. The model is a first step toward a decision-support system to enhance micro-PET/CT-based IMA in BCa, facilitating its adoption in clinical practice.

articleTitle: PET motion correction using subspace-based real-time MR imaging in simultaneous PET/MR
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a motion-sensitive imaging technique. Patient motion, in particular respiration and cardiac motions, often lead to blurring artifacts in the reconstructed images, compromising diagnostic accuracy. Thanks to its excellent soft-tissue contrast and high spatial resolution, Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)-based methods have been applied to motion estimation in PET. This work presents a novel real-time MR-based motion correction method to mitigate artifacts caused by respiratory and cardiac motions in PET. We leveraged the low-rank property of dynamic MR images to reconstruct high-resolution, high-frame-rate images from sparse ($\mathrm{k}, \mathrm{t}$)-space data. The reconstructed dynamic images were then binned into respiratory and cardiac motion phases using EKG and respiratory motion navigator signals. The simultaneously acquired PET events were binned accordingly into sinograms, corresponding to each motion phase. The displacement fields for motion correction were estimated by registering dynamic MRI images to a reference image and then resampled to the coordinates of the PET images. To demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method, PET motion correction was performed by aligning the gated reconstruction in each motion phase to the reference phase. Gated reconstruction was performed using the Ordered-Subset Expectation Maximization (OSEM) algorithm with 12 subsets and 5 iterations. Future work includes improved dynamic MR image reconstruction using a manifold learning framework and direct motion-corrected PET reconstruction by incorporating the displacement fields into the OSEM system matrix.

articleTitle: A Proximity Focused RICH Detector for the ePIC Experiment at EIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new proximity focused RICH detector (pfRICH) is being developed for the ePIC Experiment at the future Electron Ion Collider at Brookhaven National Lab that will enable identification of pions and kaons up to $\sim 7 \mathrm{GeV} / \mathrm{c}$ at a $3 \sigma$ level in the Backward Endcap region. It will provide Ring Imaging Cherenkov information using an aerogel radiator and new improved High Resolution Picosecond Photon Detectors (HRPPDs) in a proximity focusing configuration. The HRPPDs will also provide a fast timing signal for the ePIC Time-of-Flight system with a resolution $\sim 10-20$ ps. This contribution will describe the overall design of the pfRICH detector and its particle identification capabilities, as well as initial performance tests of the first HRPPDs developed for EIC and other detector components. It will also describe the design of a prototype of the pfRICH detector that is currently being constructed and plans for future beam tests early next year.

articleTitle: Prism-PET II: Second prototype of the TOF-DOI Prism-PET brain scanner with tapered crystals and inverse rendering reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate PET quantification of tracer uptake in small brain structures is confounded by low sensitivity and the partial volume effect (PVE) caused by limited spatial resolution. In this study, we present the second prototype of the Prism-PET brain scanner (Prism-PET II), which overcomes the trade-offs among sensitivity, resolution, and cost. It employs TOF-DOI capable, single-ended Prism-PET detector blocks arranged in a compact and conformal decagon geometry. Compared to our first prototype, Prism-PET II features tapered crystals with a smaller cross-section at the crystal readout interface to mitigate light leakage, thereby enhancing both TOF and DOI resolutions of the module. Additionally, interleaved multiplexing (iMUX) readouts are used, where four anodes from every other SiPM pixel are connected to the same application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) channel. Combined with Prismatoid light guides that provide a 4-to-1 crystal-to-SiPM ratio, a total 16-to-1 crystal-to-ASIC readout ratio is achieved, substantially reducing the complexity, heat output, and cost of the scanner without compromising the performance of the detector blocks. Our imaging studies using ultra-micro hot spot and Hoffman brain phantoms demonstrate the ultra-high-resolution performance with fine structural details and the ability to resolve features as small as 0.8 mm in the axial direction, showcasing its potential to significantly improve the accuracy of PET neuroimaging in both clinical and research settings.

articleTitle: Evaluating Room-Temperature Semiconductor Technology for Nuclear On-site Verification
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Traditional high-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors, known for their high energy resolution, require long cooling times and are bulky, limiting their practicality in field applications. The new electrically cooled HPGe aims to address these issues with faster cooling and reduced size, but challenges remain in field deployment. Recent advances have emphasized the development of RTSDs such as cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) and cadmium telluride (CdTe), which offer moderate energy resolutions but are more suitable for field use because they operate at room temperature, eliminating the need for bulky cooling equipment. Over the past two decades, these technologies have improved significantly, with the latest models achieving energy resolutions close to those of cooled detectors. The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has begun to replace HPGe with MCCM for field applications. This shift indicates a significant move towards more portable and convenient verification tools in nuclear safeguards. This study systematically examines the energy spectra of several commercial RTSDs to assess their feasibility for nuclear material analysis using gamma-ray imaging. Instruments such as H3D’s H420 and Mirion’s I-PIX are characterized by their ability to perform simultaneous imaging and spectral analysis, aiding nuclide identification. This research is vital in supporting the development of field deployable non-destructive inspection equipment that can meet stringent verification standards. The results could lead to wider adoption of RTSDs in regulatory frameworks, thereby improving the efficiency and effectiveness of nuclear material verification on a global scale.

articleTitle: GOSS: GPU-based Optical Simulator of Scintillator Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scintillator-based detectors are essential components in various radiation imaging systems, particularly for positron emission tomography (PET). The optical transport of scintillation photons plays a critical role in determining key performance characteristics, such as timing and spatial resolution. This paper presents GOSS, a GPU-accelerated simulator for optical photon transport in scintillator crystals, developed using NVIDIA CUDA Fortran. The simulator achieves remarkable performance, processing up to 1e7 optical photons per second. GOSS accounts for the roughness of surfaces, the refractive index of materials, and the geometry, including edge effects. The simulator was evaluated against measurements of a detector block, consisting of 4x4 small LYSO scintillator crystals with different diffusive widths between the crystals and the SiPMs matrix. The results generated by GOSS were compared with actual data acquired with the detector. The realistic simulations allow assessing detector performance characteristics such as depth of interaction (DOI), energy, timing, and positioning information, which are crucial for the development and optimization of next-generation PET systems.

articleTitle: CT-based deep learning framework for analyzing brain PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Purpose: Quantitative analysis of PET/CT images relies on structural MR for accuracy, inducing unmet need for CT-based analysis. This study proposes CT-based deep learning framework for analyzing PET/CT images by synthesizing structural MR. Methods: In this retrospective study, 139 pairs of Brain 18F-FBB PET/CT and T1-weighted MRI images were acquired. FastSurfer was used to generate ground-truth annotations from MRI images. A two-dimensional residual U-Net was implemented to synthesize MR with CT. Subsequently, three independent U-Nets were trained in axial, sagittal, and coronal plane to segment the synthesized MR. Lastly, a composite standardized uptake value ratio (SUVR) was calculated in the cortical regions. Normalized root mean squared error (NRMSE), peak signal-to-noise ration (PSNR), and structural similarity index (SSIM) were calculated to assess the quality of synthesized MR. Model segmentation performance was evaluated by calculating the mean dice coefficient score (DSC) and was compared against CT. Linear regression analysis was performed to assess correlation between the SUVRs from synthetic MR and those from ground-truth MR images. Results: The mean NRMSE, PSNR, and SSIM was $0.206 \pm 0.072$ (mean ± standard deviation), $30.23 \pm 1.64$, and $0.974 \pm 0.005$ respectively. The segmentation model achieved a mean DSC of 0.733 across 95 regions, while CT segmentation model showed a mean DSC of 0.716. Regression analysis revealed a strong correlation (R-squared=0.997) between SUVRs from synthesized MR and SUVRs from ground-truth MR images. Conclusion: Our study highlights the potential of CT-based deep learning framework for PET/CT analysis. By eliminating the need for MR imaging, our framework is immediately applicable to diverse clinical settings. Further validation with other radiotracers and external scanners is warranted.

articleTitle: Performance of a Multiplexed DoI-Encoding PET Detector Using the TOFPET2 ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High resolution narrow-bore PET applications require detectors capable of measuring the depth of interaction (DoI) of the gamma ray interactions. Dual-ended readout PET detectors can provide excellent DoI performance, however to reduce manufacturing costs from the two-fold increase in the number of photodetectors, multiplexing schemes are commonly used. Although the field has seen an increase in the number of application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for photodetector signal digitization, almost all the current work integrating ASICs with PET detectors has involved 1:1 (not multiplexed) photodetector readout. The potential of multiplexing schemes has not been thoroughly explored. This work investigates the implementation and performance characterization of a dual-ended and multiplexed PET detector integrated with the PETSys TOFPET2 ASIC. The results indicate energy, DoI and coincidence performance well-matched with sub-millimeter resolution applications.

articleTitle: Acceleration of Radiological Mapping by Image Super Resolution
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Mapping and estimation of the absolute intensity distribution of radioactive materials in diverse environments see important applications in various fields. A mapping analysis models the environment as a 3-dimensional (3D) grid of voxels, and reconstruct the activity in each voxel based on radiation measurement by a detector that moved across the environment. A high-fidelity reconstruction uses more voxels, which is computationally expensive and difficult for real-time processing. Here, we investigated the application of machine learning method for the acceleration of radiological map reconstruction process. Specifically, instead of reconstructing a high-fidelity map, we first reconstructed a low-fidelity map with fewer number of voxels. Then the image super resolution technique is used to upscale the low-fidelity map to high-fidelity map with more voxels. We adapted and trained a super resolution model with synthetic and real radiological map data. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluation, the super resolution model produced promising performance for the image upscaling. Our approach here can reduce the computational cost significantly, which can enable real-time or near real-time reconstruction of high-fidelity map with lower computer memory and battery usage required.

articleTitle: Characterization of Diamond Pixel Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report on the hybrid diamond pixel detector for charged-particle monitors in the COMET experiments. To demonstrate a single MIP detection capability and sensor segmentation technique, a Single-Crystal CVD diamond with a die size of 5 mm by 5 mm was processed into 12 x 12 diode arrays with a pixel pitch of 270 um. We combined those diodes with a low-noise pixel readout chip by flip-chip bonding. In the testing, we successfully detected the signals of a Sr-90 beta-ray source from all pixels, however, a certain amount of pixels shows severely low charge detection efficiency (CCE). The location of the lattice defects can be determined in a polarized optical image. In this presentation, we discuss the origin of such low CCE with the pixel-by-pixel spectral properties and mitigation techniques of the polarization effect for the realistic application.

articleTitle: PCCT Detector-domain Material Decomposition Using FPGA-Based Edge Computing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) has emerged as a potential technology revolutionizing clinical CT imaging. PCCT utilizes Photon-counting Detectors (PCDs) that can count each x-ray event and measure the corresponding energy above the noise floor with much higher spatial resolution. However, the multiple energy bin setting and much smaller pixels (resulting in much higher spatial resolution) increase PCCT’s data flow rate by 20-160 times compared to traditional CT. With the current data processing flow, all the raw data are directly passed out of the CT gantry through the CT slip ring and processed outside the gantry. The data bandwidth of the slip ring struggles to process such large-scale data in real-time. To address these problems, we propose a new data processing flow and high efficient data process (material decomposition) algorithm is developed. The raw data are processed, and material decomposition is done in real-time using FPGA on the detector blade inside the CT gantry. The experimental results show that the proposed method can significantly reduce the data rate by 2 to 4 times with sufficient accuracy.

articleTitle: Time-Resolved 3D Imaging with Capacitively Coupled GaAs SAM-APD and Cross-Delay Lines for Hard X-Ray Photon Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-resolved ultrafast phenomena with hard X-ray radiation are among the groundbreaking research fields underlying scientific applications like pump-and-probe spectroscopy. Research on detectors and studies of new multichannel acquisition techniques are continually driven by increasingly stringent requirements. This motivates our proposal of an innovative detector designed for a fully digital 3D (x-y-time) imager for hard X-rays. From the detector’s perspective, the aspects in need of improvement include time resolution, spatial resolution (limited by the multipixel approach in most of the solutions), and quantum efficiency, particularly poor for silicon-based detectors in the case of hard X-rays. In this context, a Separate Absorption and Multiplication Avalanche PhotoDiode (SAM-APD) based on III-V semiconductors will be employed. Specifically, GaAs-based alloys feature a higher atomic number and mobility, making them much more efficient and faster than silicon in absorbing hard X-rays. Considering acquisition systems, the multichannel approach adopted by modern applications and the reduction of power and area budgets dedicated to individual channels shift the read-out electronics from the classical pixelated voltage-mode approach, involving analog waveform acquisition and digital processing, to time-based acquisition where both spatial (i.e., x and y) and timing information are tied to the time of the detection event. Temporal and spatial resolutions less than tens of picoseconds and hundred micrometers will be achieved by capacitive coupling of a large area (a few mm in diameter) GaAs SAM-APD to two Cross Delay-Lines (CDLs) connected to a 4 -channel 15-ps precision FPGA-based Time-to-Digital-Converter (TDC). This presents a powerful alternative to pixelation from both a technological and a processing standpoint; notably, it requires no aggressive lithography and only four channels, as opposed to one per pixel.

articleTitle: Statistically-based inter-crystal scatter event positioning method for a 3D position sensitive TOF detector based on side readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates a statistically-based method for positioning inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events in a 3D position-sensitive TOF detector using a side readout scheme. The experimental setup utilized a side readout with a 130 ps coincidence time resolution (CTR) and an energy resolution of less than 10%. Various methods were explored to accurately position ICS events, primarily using energy information and crystal identification via multiplexed signals. ICS events were defined as having two crystal identification signals per event, whereas photoelectric events only had one. The results showed that assigning the first interaction position using the maximum energy deposited method yielded an accuracy of 54.98%, while the minimum energy method resulted in 45.02% accuracy. We also introduced the proportional ICS positioning method to this side readout which utilize the ratio between the photoelectric event and the ICS event. The proportional ICS positioning method demonstrated high consistency, with $\mathrm{R}^{2}$ values above 0.97, indicating a strong predictive ability for the number of ICS events based on the number of photoelectric events. This method suggests an effective approach to maintaining sensitivity and accurate line-of-response assignment in PET systems. The findings are pivotal for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of PET imaging, with future research aimed at applying these methods to multi-layer block configurations to address ICS occurring between layers.

articleTitle: Dedicated Image Reconstruction with Elongation Correction for a Dual-Panel Prostate PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Prostate cancer represents a significant health challenge among men, necessitating sensitive and accurate imaging modalities for early detection and diagnosis. Efficient early detection is pivotal for timely treatment and improved patient outcomes. The dedicated ProVision PET scanner, featuring dual-panel high-resolution PET detectors, has been developed to meet this demand. However, the limited angle coverage inherent in its design presents a challenge, resulting in elongation artifacts in reconstructed images. To address this issue, we employed a methodology leveraging Lucy-Richardson Total Variation (LR-TV) filtering to optimize image reconstruction and mitigate elongation artifacts in the ProVision PET scanner. The efficacy of this approach was evaluated through a comparative analysis of classic Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) algorithms, with and without elongation correction, following full convergence. The convergence behavior of the MLEM algorithm was assessed through analyses of point source reconstructions. The analysis demonstrates the complete recovery of 2.5 mm elongated point sources to their original size of 1.5 mm. These results demonstrate improved image quality and convergence, confirming the effectiveness of LR-TV optimization in reducing elongation artifacts and enhancing accuracy in prostate cancer imaging.

articleTitle: Experimental survey of AC-LGAD sensor design parameters towards optimal 4D tracking in collider experiments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the performance of centimeter-scale AC-LGAD devices including strip sensors with varying pitch (coarse and narrow), and pixel sensors of varying metal electrode size and geometry. Strip sensors with narrow pitch provide good position reconstruction capabilities, however coarser pitch may offer better cost and performance for applications where channel count or electrical power density should be economized. Pixel sensors with a higher metal area fraction and smaller active thickness provide faster signal risetimes, leading to better time resolution capabilities. We studied the impact of various design parameters on the time and spatial resolution of these sensors and identified the guiding principles for designing sensors optimized for future collider experiments, such as the EIC.

articleTitle: Imaging of a 14.8 MeV neutron source via a hybrid neutron/gamma ray camera for applications in particle therapy range verification
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The highly localized nature of the dose deposition in proton therapy (PT) can be exploited for more conformal and less toxic treatments. However, this also makes PT highly sensitive to range uncertainties. To this end, the NOVO collaboration aims to develop a multi-particle imaging system for verifying the proton range in real time via the simultaneous imaging of secondary prompt gamma rays (PGs) and fast neutrons (FNs) emitted from patient tissues during treatment. In this work we present the first experimental imaging of a neutron source using a prototype NOVO detector - an interwoven array of 14 organic scintillator bars. Measurements were conducted at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt Braunschweig, where a point-like source of 14.8 MeV neutron was produced from accelerator-induced $3 \mathrm{H}(\mathrm{d}, \mathrm{n}) 4 \mathrm{He}$ reactions. Images of the source were produced via simple back-projection of double-scattered neutrons with the detector array position shifted via its mounting to a 2 -axis motor table. The extracted centroids of the images reveal that source shifts of 1 cm are reliably identified, while shifts on the order of millimeters should be identifiable with sufficient statistics and more sophisticated imaging algorithms.

articleTitle: Discovery of Biomarkers and Tumor Subtypes of Prostate Cancer on PSMA PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) has a high detection rate of prostate cancer and can predict response to systemic therapies including, chemotherapy and ${ }^{177} \mathrm{Lu}$-PSMA therapy. Automated tumor quantification and subtype characterization on PSMA PET/CT are important clinical needs to optimize early treatment. Retrospective data, including ${ }^{18}$ F-DCFPyL PSMA PET/CT scans from 408 patients with prostate cancer, were randomly partitioned into discovery and validation cohorts using a 70%/30% split. PSMA reporting and data system (PSMA-RADS) scores of 1-5 were assigned to segmented lesions, with higher scores having a greater likelihood of prostate cancer. Tumors on PSMA PET/CT scans were automatically detected and segmented using a nnU-net, and radiomic features were extracted. Molecular tumor phenotypes were identified using k-means clustering on latent features learned by a variational autoencoder optimized on the radiomic feature space. Predicted risk scores were derived for each tumor via trajectory inference with minimum spanning trees. The nnU-net yielded a true positive rate of 0.75 and a Dice similarity coefficient of 0.73 on the tumor segmentation task. Three tumor subtypes were discovered. Subtype 1 was associated with PSMA-RADS-1/2/3, indicating a low probability of prostate cancer. Subtype 2 was associated with PSMA-RADS-4. Subtype 3 was most closely associated with PSMARADS-5, indicating a high probability of prostate cancer. Distance zone matrix features had the highest discriminatory ability and yielded an overall accuracy of 0.90 for the subtype classification task on both the discovery and validation cohorts. Increasingly aggressive tumor subtypes were associated with higher predicted risk scores and higher PSMA-RADS scores. The developed unsupervised learning approach elucidated three distinct molecular subtypes of prostate cancer with varying levels of tumor aggressiveness on PSMA PET/CT.

articleTitle: Muon detection with an opaque scintillator detector prototype
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: LiquidO is an innovative scintillator-based radiation detector concept. The core idea is to achieve the self-segmentation of a detector by exploiting stochastic light confinement in a highly scattering medium. Key components include an opaque scintillator with short scattering and long absorption lengths, along with a wavelength-shifting fibre lattice for efficient collection of scintillation light, enabling confining and collecting light near its creation point. At the University of Sussex, the focus is on investigating the performance of the LiquidO technology on cosmic-ray muons detection. We developed the design of a 3D-printable 64 fibres cube. The cube has a length of a few centimetres and contains an $8 x 8$ grid of optical fibres along one direction, with a 3-millimetre pitch, read-out by silicon photomultipliers. Wax-based opaque liquid scintillators are used to fill the cube. Using this LiquidO detector, ‘ light cylinders” produced by cosmic-ray muons in a LiquidO detector are observed. The distinct LiquidO event topology is used to identify and reconstruct the muons track. A sub-millimetre one-dimensional position resolution is demonstrated, surpassing the capability of a physically segmented detector with identical pixel pitch. Room for improvements to further enhance the position resolution of the 64 -fibre cube comprises tuning the scintillator properties, supported by the study of the setup in Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, a ten times larger prototype with 256 fibres along two perpendicular directions is being commissioned and will soon be used to acquire cosmic-ray muons data. These results demonstrate the potential of LiquidO detectors in muons imaging techniques and advance the understanding of the novel LiquidO technology. Finally, these prototypes constitute a fundamental step towards the first large-scale detector under development by the LiquidO consortium, CLOUD (Chooz LiquidO Ultra-near Detector).

articleTitle: A Mathematical Model for the Investigation of Combined Treatment of Radiopharmaceutical Therapy and PARPi
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: As radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) continues to evolve and the need for mathematical optimization techniques in cancer treatment planning grows, this study introduces a mathematical model that facilitates in silico investigations of combined treatments involving RPT and poly (ADPribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi) The proposed mathematical model uses probabilistic statuses as average to simulate cells in different stages of the cell cycle. The model predicts therapeutic outcomes based on the absorbed radioactive doses by DNA and the resulting radiobiological responses, with DNA double strand breaks being the critical determinant of cancer cell fate. Rucaparib radio-sensitization reduces tumor cells after 3 days of lutetium therapy by 99.2%. Presented model predicts relative tumor shrinking after 14 days clinical protocol of Olaparib (250 mg) combination treatment according to the body weight of the patient (e.g. 60 kg: $99.6 \%; 90 \mathrm{~kg}: 98.0 \%$). This study significantly contributes to enhancing patient specific cancer treatment tailoring.

articleTitle: IMAS: a full-body PET system with enhanced TOF and DOI capabilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Total-Body Positron Emission Tomography (TB-PET) technology and designs have become very popular in the recent years. These systems are very attractive because of their high sensitivity resulting from their extended axial Field of View (FOV) and potential Time of Flight (TOF) capabilities, allowing for the simultaneous study of the kinetics of multiple organs. Most of TB-PET designs and implementations are based on LYSO crystal pixels without Depth of Interaction (DOI) capabilities. In this work we present a TB-PET system, named IMAS, based on semi-monolithic crystals to simultaneously enable TOF and DOI capabilities. Our design makes use of a reduction of signals without compromising performance. The system geometry is based on 5 rings of 10 cm in the axial direction each, and gaps of about 5 cm, resulting in a total axial length of 71.4 cm. The system has been constructed and installed (June 2023) at the largest hospital in Valencia named La Fe. Very preliminary experimental tests already predict an almost homogeneous spatial resolution below 4 mm in the whole FOV (as far as at 30 cm off-radial), outperforming any other scanner with a long axial FOV. The system sensitivity is $7.6 \%$ with a source at the Center of the FOV (CFOV). The detectors reached a TOF of about 350 ps FWHM. We aim to report a full characterization of the scanner during the conference.

articleTitle: Detector-Pixel Interactions via Transformer Encoders: A Direct Approach for PET Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Reconstructing images from positron emission tomography (PET) scans is challenging due to their complexity and high noise from limited data. Traditional methods like model-based iterative reconstruction (MBIR) are effective but require significant computational resources and time. Deep learning offers a promising alternative, especially with its ability to generate images directly from sinogram data. However, the use of transformer models, successful in language processing and some computer vision tasks, remains under explored in this area. In our study, we introduce a new approach using transformer encoders to reconstruct images effectively. This method can learn from small datasets and adjust to different object types, noise levels, and data variations in sinograms.

articleTitle: An Efficient Dual-Domain Deep Learning Network for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, several deep learning-based dual-domain sparse-view CT reconstruction methods have been proposed that significantly improve image quality. However, there are concerns about the large number of training parameters of the network and considerable computational time. Besides, few studies have evaluated the reconstruction performance on real CT projection data acquired on commercial scanners in the clinic. We designed two lightweight networks, Sino-Net and Img-Net, to restore the projection and image signal from the DD-Net reconstructed images in the projection and image domains, respectively. The proposed network has small training parameters and comparable running time among dual-domain based reconstruction networks and is easy to train (end-to-end). We collected clinical thoraco-abdominal CT projection data from a Siemens Biograph 128 Edge CT scanner to train and validate the proposed network. Further, we quantitatively evaluated the CT HU value on organ and anatomic structures, such as the liver and lungs. Besides, two radiologists conducted the subjective evaluation including diagnostic confidence, conspicuity of anatomic structures, and the overall image quality using a 1-5 scoring system. Objective and subjective evaluation showed that the proposed method achieves competitive results in eliminating noise and artifacts, restoring fine structure details, and recovering edges and contours of anatomic structures under 384 views (1/6 sparse rate). The proposed method exhibits good computational cost performance on real clinical projection data.

articleTitle: Pre-therapy dose prediction in targeted radionuclide therapy using semi-supervised learning: An in-silico preliminary study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Targeted Radionuclide Therapy (TRT) is a modern strategy in radiation oncology that aims to administer a potent radiation dose specifically to cancer cells using cancer-targeting radiopharmaceuticals. Accurate radiation dose estimation tailored to individual patients is crucial. Deep learning, particularly with pre-therapy imaging, holds promise for personalizing TRT doses. However, current methods require large time series of SPECT imaging, which is hardly achievable in routine clinical practice, and thus raises issues of data availability. Our objective is to develop a semi-supervised learning (SSL) solution to personalize dosimetry using pre-therapy images. The aim is to develop an approach that achieves accurate results when PET/CT images are available, but are associated with only a few post-therapy dosimetry data provided by SPECT images. In this work, we introduce an SSL method using a pseudo-label generation approach for regression tasks inspired by the FixMatch framework. The feasibility of the proposed solution was preliminarily evaluated through an in-silico study using synthetic data and Monte Carlo simulation. Experimental results for organ dose prediction yielded promising outcomes, showing that the use of pseudo-labeled data provides better accuracy compared to using only labeled data.

articleTitle: Achievable Resolution for Scalable Waveform Digitizing PET Readout and Comparison with Ideal TDC-based Readout with an Application of DNN to Optimal Estimation Including DOI.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time Of Flight PET (TOF-PET) is a transformative technology for PET systems, but reaping its fullest potential requires achieving very high spatial and timing resolution, and overcoming dependency on signal variability at the level of the individual pixels. In this study, we try to quantify the advantage of using custom waveform sampling devices versus TDC methodology using realistic estimates of noise and other non-idealities. With the use of DNN methodology we show achievable gain for current and future acquisition systems, and also demonstrate the feasibility of DOI estimation from single side readout. We conclude by arguing for the scalability of such a system based on our experience with compact waveform digitizer design.

articleTitle: Photoresponse and Deep Levels in Semi-insulating SiC Studied by Fourier Transform Photocurrent Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fourier Transform Photocurrent spectroscopy offers a powerful approach to characterize photodetectors, enabling high-resolution (up to $1 \mathrm{~cm}^{-1}$) measurement of their spectrally resolved photoresponse across various materials. The method allows the detection of very low photocurrents, and it provides valuable information about deep levels in semiconductors and their interband transitions. This study focuses on the photoresponse of semi-insulating SiC of 4 H and 6 H polytypes. In addition, we also show examples of the spectral photoresponse measured using other standard detector materials (CdZnTe and CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>). Additionally, a responsivity scaling procedure facilitates the evaluation of detector performance. While potential Fourier Transform artifacts and noise from the ambient can occur, these issues are readily addressed. This versatile technique holds promise for further investigation of detector behavior, including temperature dependence and time-resolved dynamics.

articleTitle: Light Output-Dependent Integration Gating for Optimized Pulse-Shape Discrimination
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) is a common technique that enables the identification of neutron and gamma-ray events in organic scintillators, PSD typically makes use of the charge comparison method. Other methods have been proposed and demonstrated, but many of these methods are computationally complex and not well suited to hardware implementation and field applications. In this work, we present a modified charge comparison method in which the short and long integration gates are allowed to vary with the light output rather than being fixed. This is anticipated to improve the discrimination quality while not increasing the computational complexity. We show the measured PSD performance of a liquid organic scintillator exposed to a ${ }^{252} \mathrm{Cf}$ neutron and gamma-ray source using this technique as well as the traditional charge comparison technique. The optimal short and long gates are shown to increase with increasing light output, whereas the optimal constant short and long gates are shown to be equal to the optimal short and long gate at the mean light output of the total distribution. The figure of merit improves at all light outputs when applying light outputdependent integration gates, and the degree of improvement increases at light outputs dissimilar to the mean light output.

articleTitle: Correction of Heel Effect on Imaging System for X-ray Irradiator: Simulation Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray source is the oldest and most commonly source used for diagnostic purposes. However, Xray tube produced X-ray source presents the heel effect on the imaging and dosimetry system due to the reflection geometry of X-ray tube target. This phenomenon should be corrected before performing the irradiation to improve the probability of diagnostic and therapy. In this present work, a compensation filter was investigated to address the heel effect and to improve the probability of irradiation using MCNP6 simulation. The results showed that the heel effect was effectively corrected through a wedge filter made by Aluminum leading to improve the uniformity of X-ray intensity distribution within the irradiation field. In the future study, this compensation filter will be designed by 3D printing with various materials, geometries, and thicknesses of the compensation filter for different irradiation purposes.

articleTitle: FPGA-Based Single-Input Time-to-Digital Converter with Rise Time Correction and Sub-2 ps Resolution for Precision Timing Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In numerous fields, including physics, industry, and medical technology, the precise measurement of extremely short time intervals, such as those below 100 ps, is essential. This research introduces an innovative FPGA-based time-to-digital converter (TDC) implemented on the UltraScale+ platform (VCU118, Xilinx). The UltraScale+ platform improves upon timing resolution by incorporating a CARRY8 primitive cell as a delay element, an improvement over the CARRY4, which was widely used in previous platforms. Through the novel end-of-propagation (EOP) technique, the implemented TDC achieves an average bin size of 1.11 ps, demonstrating significant resource efficiency compared to other reported FPGA-based TDCs. This study details the design, implementation, and empirical validation of the TDC. Additionally, a unique feature of the proposed TDC is its ability to measure the input pulse width and apply rise time correction without requiring additional inputs. To demonstrate its practical applicability, the developed TDC was connected to the output of an ultrafast Cherenkov-Radiator-Integrated (CRI)-MCP-PMT after evaluating its electrical performance. The preliminary coincidence timing resolution of a pair of CRI-MCP-PMTs shows improvements from 107 ps to 73 ps (FWHM) with the proposed rise time correction. These advancements highlight the potential of the TDC not only for next-generation medical applications but also for its transformative impact in applications demanding ultra-precise timing.

articleTitle: An Area- and Power-Efficient 32-channel Multi-Energy Photon Counting Readout ASIC Using Successive Approximation Register Logic
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In computed tomography (CT) X-ray imaging technology, the multi-energy window setting offers greater advantages in material decomposition and image quality. A traditional multi-energy discrimination photon counting circuit is typically implemented by a multiple-discriminator scheme, which employs multiple comparators to generate pulse signals and drives multiple counters for photon counting, within a single channel to implement the division of different energy windows. However, area overhead and static power consumption of each channel are significantly increased when the number of energy windows increases. This paper presents a novel circuit scheme based on peak detector voltage signals digitized by a successive approximation (SAR) analog-to-digital converter (ADC). The number of comparators will not increase with the extension of energy windows. A 32-channel front-end readout application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is designed in $0.35 \mu \mathrm{m}$ CMOS process with a die area of $4.8 \mathrm{~mm} \times 4.8 \mathrm{~mm}$. A charge-sensitive amplifier, a CR-RC pulse shaper, a gain amplifier, an event-driven peak detector and a 4-bit SAR ADC are integrated into each channel to discriminate and count incoming photon information through eight energy windows with a dynamic range of from 3 keV to 80 keV. The simulated equivalent noise charge is $53 \mathrm{e}^{-}$(rms) plus $4 \mathrm{e}^{-} / \mathrm{pF}$. The count rate is up to 1 Mcps under the power dissipation of about $4.9 \mathrm{~mW} /$ channel with a supply voltage of 3.3 V. The area overhead of the proposed circuit is shrunk by 5 times, and power consumption is reduced by 22%, compared with traditional multiple energy discrimination counting circuits.

articleTitle: The new PETsys TOFPET3 ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new PETsys ASIC in the TOFPET series, named TOFPET3, has been developed aiming at high performance PET applications. The new chip has a 64-channel analog front-end with baseline stabilization, pulse tail cancelation, dark noise rejection and gain configuration. In each channel, three 10-bit digitization of pulses above a configurable threshold are performed (2 TDC, 1 QDC). The maximum event rate per channel is 500 kHz, and the output bandwidth is $3.8 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ matching the input rate. The new timing and energy circuits have outstanding performance: 1) the TOFPET3 contribution to CTR is 26 ps FWHM, implying that a CTR =80(120) ps due to crystal and SiPM, increases to 84(123) ps with TOFPET3; 2) the contribution to 511 keV photopeak resolution is 1.1% and the deviation to linearity is $\pm 1 \%$ in the range 300-3000 p.e for SiPM gain $3.5 \times 10^{6}$. Charge integration of single photons is possible with $\mathrm{S} / \mathrm{N}\gt10$. The chip includes four additional channels with sums of 16,32 or 64 cannels (configurable) suitable for light sharing applications, as well as advanced triggering features allowing the selective readout of a group of channels triggered by the energy of one channel. The power consumption is 8 mW per channel. In this summary we present simulation results of the chip performance. At the conference, measurements with the prototype chip will be presented.

articleTitle: Anatomical Brain Segmentation from CT Images in Brain PET/CT Imaging for the Purpose of Partial Volume Correction in PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study explores the segmentation efficacy of computed tomography (CT) images for partial volume correction (PVC) in positron emission tomography (PET). Employing three deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs), we conducted supervised segmentation of multiple brain regions to ensure accurate anatomical information. A dataset of 100 CT images and their corresponding labels derived from magnetic resonance (MR) images from the “OASIS-3” database was utilized [1]. The UNet, VNet, and SegResNet models were implemented within the medical open network for artificial intelligence (MONAI) framework for each predefined region. Evaluation metrics, including the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and intersection over union (IoU), were employed to assess segmentation efficiency. Results demonstrate satisfactory segmentation of large regions despite the limited soft tissue anatomical information in CT images, with DSC scores reaching up to $75 \%$. However, smaller regions proved challenging to segment successfully, even with the incorporation of an attention mechanism during training. These findings contribute valuable insights into DCNN performance in medical image segmentation and offer guidance for further advancements in specific applications and datasets.

articleTitle: A Study in Generalization of Deep Learning-based Image Denoising Methods for non-FDG PET tracers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Supervised learning typically dominates in PET image denoising, primarily focusing on 18F-FDG images due to the high expense of training data collection, particularly for non-FDG tracer and new tracers. To address this limitations, some researchers have suggested training the network by utilizing self-supervised approach such as deep image prior, noise2noise, and noise2self. While this approach eliminates the need of additional training data, it comes at the expense of low efficiency. This paper aims to investigate the generalization of deep learning-based methods across diverse PET tracers and introduces a novel plug-and-play self-supervision paradigm specifically designed for this task. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness.

articleTitle: Reactor-Neutron Irradiation Effectson Gallium Oxide Based Rectifiers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the effects of reactor-neutron irradiation on the electrical characteristics of Ni/Ga<inf>2</inf>O<inf>3</inf> heterojunction diodes (HJD) and Ni/Ga2O3 Schottky barrier diodes (SBD) for a range of 1 MeV-Si equivalent fluences from 10<sup>12</sup> to 10<sup>16</sup> n/cm<sup>2</sup>. The novel contribution of this research is the comparison of SBD and HJD devices, with and without edge termination. Capacitance-voltage (C–V) characterization enabled the determination of the spatially dependent carrier removal rate. The forward current-voltage (I-V) characteristics were used to compare the changes in turnon voltage and specific on-resistance. The on-off ratio provides additional information by incorporating both the forward and reverse I-V characteristics.

articleTitle: Integrated Deployment of Unmanned Ground Vehicles and Compton Cameras for Hazardous Area Monitoring
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in the development of autonomous ionizing radiation detectors, particularly in response to the Fukushima Daiishi Nuclear Power Plant disaster. This advancement addresses the pressing need for Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs) to replace human workers in hazardous environments, as emphasized by the nuclear security community. Various methods for mapping radiation sources have emerged, ranging from basic dosimeters to sophisticated cameras like coded aperture detectors and Compton cameras. This paper presents an integrated approach to optimize the deployment of UGVs equipped with Compton cameras for efficiently measuring hazardous areas while ensuring accurate nuclear radiation measurements. Our proposed approach is resolved through exact methods, employing two mixed integer programs in an integrated and sequential manner. The findings of this study have significant implications for enhancing nuclear security measures and minimizing human exposure to radiation in hazardous environments. By leveraging advanced technology, such as Compton cameras mounted on UGVs, we offer a comprehensive solution that improves the efficiency and safety of radiation measurement in hazardous areas. Moreover, our integrated approach ensures the timely and precise collection of data, enabling better decision-making in nuclear security operations. Overall, this research contributes to the ongoing efforts to enhance safety protocols and mitigate the risks associated with ionizing radiation exposure.

articleTitle: Experimental Study: Scanner-level Inter-crystal Scatter Recovery for TOF-DOI Prototype Prism-PET Brain Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Inter-crystal scatter (ICS) poses a significant limitation to the quantitative accuracy of reconstructed images in positron emission tomography (PET), as gamma photons scatter among scintillation crystals before complete absorption within the detector. This phenomenon leads to mispositioning of the line of response (LOR), thereby compromising spatial resolution, which is particularly exacerbated in high-resolution PET systems with small crystals. In this study, we introduce an ICS recovery framework that generates synthetic scatter SiPM patterns through simulated photon interactions and experimental photoelectric SiPM patterns. Two convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are trained using synthetic scatter patterns and ground truth DOI and crystal ID data from simulations for crystal ID and DOI recovery. The experimental hot spot data from the Prism-PET prototype brain scanner is utilized to evaluate the CNN models. Comparison of the reconstructed images without employing the ICS recovery model reveals lower background noise and higher spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Kernel SIMPLE: Positron Lifetime Image Reconstruction Using Kernel Method
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Ortho-positronium (o-Ps) lifetime has the potential to become a biomarker for quantifying oxygen concentration and micro-structural properties of human tissue in vivo. Several model-based lifetime image reconstruction methods have been developed. The most computationally efficient method is the Statistical Image Reconstruction of Positron Lifetime via Time-Weighting (SIMPLE) method. It can achieve a spatial resolution comparable to that of the standard positron emission tomography (PET) images with a computational cost equivalent to two standard PET image reconstructions. However, the method lacks effective regularization to suppress noise in the lifetime images. To address this issue, here we developed a kernel-based SIMPLE method. The kernel matrix is first constructed using either dynamic activity images or lifetime-thresholded images and then utilized to represent both the activity image and the lifetime-weighted image in the SIMPLE method. Computer simulations show the kernel SIMPLE method can substantially reduce noise in lifetime images compared to the original SIMPLE method. The dynamic-image-based kernel matrix demonstrates better noise-suppression capability compared to the lifetime-thresholded kernel matrix.

articleTitle: Design of a Sub-0.5 mm Resolution Mouse Brain PET - GATE Simulation Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Spatial resolution is the most important factor for mouse brain dedicated positron emission tomography (PET). Previously, we developed a small-animal PET scanner with 1 mm crystal pitch with 3-layer depth-of-interaction (DOI) detectors to achieve 0.55 mm resolution. However, our original goal of sub-0.5 mm resolution was not realized because of the relatively large crystal pitch and unoptimized crystal layer design. Therefore, the aim of this study was to clarify the system design to truly achieve sub-0.5 mm resolution. The newly proposed mouse brain PET design consists of a staggered 3-layer DOI detector using 0.8 mm crystal pitch. The geometry has a 48 mm ring diameter and 23.4 mm axial FOV. The PET has 2 rings each of which has 16 DOI detectors. We conducted GATE simulations to optimize the crystal layer design which can provide the best spatial resolution throughout the field-of-view. Three different crystal layer designs were used: (A) $4+4+7 \mathrm{mm}$, (B) $3+4+4 \mathrm{mm}$, and (C) $3+3+5 \mathrm{mm}$. To evaluate the spatial resolution, four NEMA ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ sources $(\mathrm{D}=0.25 \mathrm{mm})$ with spacing of 5 mm in the radial direction were used. With the optimized crystal layer design, we evaluated the imaging performance with a resolution phantom having six different rod diameters (0.45,0.50,0.55,0.6,0.7, and 0.8 mm). The PET images were reconstructed by using an OSEM algorithm. An energy window of 440-560 keV was used for the image reconstruction. Design $(\mathrm{C})(3+3+5 \mathrm{mm})$ showed the best spatial resolution (0.42 mm at the center and 0.46 mm at the 5 mm radial offset) among the three. The 0.45 mm rods of the resolution phantom could be resolved with a valley-to-peak ratio of $0.573 \pm 0.062$, which is under the Rayleigh criterion (0.735). In conclusion, our proposed mouse brain PET with the optimized crystal layer design provided sub-0.5 mm resolution. In the future, we plan to develop a prototype mouse brain PET scanner to validate the simulation results.

articleTitle: Design and performance of the FBCM23 ASIC for the CMS luminosity measurement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the design and evaluation of the FBCM23 ASIC designed for the Fast Beam Condition Monitoring (FBCM) system intended for the upgraded CMS experiment at CERN. The ASIC is implemented in a CMOS 65 nm node and consists of 6 front-end channels with a binary architecture optimized to work with 1.7x1.7 mm area and 290 or 150 μm thick silicon sensors. The presented ASIC will replace the existing system based on the BCM1F chip [1], to comply with new, challenging specifications concerning the time resolution (1 ns rms) and noise, the latter related to the expected radiation damages of the sensors located at a radius close to 14.5 cm. The expected TID and the fluence at the end of the experiment lifetime are 200 Mrad and 2.5x10<sup>15</sup> N/cm<sup>2</sup> respectively. We will present the design and a complete characterization of the ASIC including TID irradiation, SEU tests, thermal drifts, and performance of the ASIC connected to the sensor.

articleTitle: A system-level DOI discrimination method for PET imaging based on semi-supervised learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We propose a system-level DOI discrimination method based on semi-supervised learning, for developing a TOF-DOI human brain dedicated PET system using a multi-resolution detector. Existing DOI discrimination methods require the acquisition of side-irradiation data from each detector, which was difficult to achieve in the PET system. To obtain a pre-training CNN model for DOI discrimination, the top and bottom layer LYSO events was acquired from a base-detector using electronically collimated side-irradiation, with the corresponding data labeled according to ground truth DOI layers. Then, using regular top-irradiation data of the test-detector (the detector we intend to generate a model for) and the side-irradiation data of the base-detector, the pre-trained model was further trained with a semi-supervised learning algorithm to produce an adapted CNN model suitable for the test-detector. The method’s reliability and robustness were tested with multiple detectors from different manufacturers, as well as by changing the acquisition system parameters to mimic the variabilities between detectors. The method proposed was all able to accurately discriminate between top and bottom LYSO events for the top-irradiation data of the detector. This method significantly reduces the data acquisition time and the labeling cost associated with deep learning for system-level DOI discrimination: Simply by using top-irradiation data from all test-detectors and side-irradiation data from one (or a much smaller number) base-detector, DOI discrimination models can be acquired for each detector in a PET system. By used this technique, DOI discrimination methods based on deep learning are made more effective and practical.

articleTitle: Investigation of BGO Coincidence Time Resolution with Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Significant advancements in coincidence time resolution (CTR) of BGO scintillators have been made in recent years, driven by the enhanced capability of new SiPMs to detect Cherenkov photons. However, BGO also emits slower scintillation light, causing time walk and degrading CTR when measured with leading edge discrimination (LED). This can be partially counteracted by using a second, higher threshold to perform time walk correction (TWC). Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were also shown to provide enhanced timing estimation in other scintillators by training with digitized waveforms. The present study compares the CTR performance of LED, TWC, and CNN approaches in BGO scintillators read out by NUV-HD-MT SiPMs and high-frequency electronics. For BGO 2×2×3 mm<sup>3</sup> utilizing TWC produces a CTR of 129 ± 2 ps FWHM, whereas the CNN achieves 115 ± 2 ps, representing 18% and 26% improvements over LED, respectively. For BGO 2×2×20 mm3, both approaches produce comparable CTR (around 240 ps FWHM, ~15% improvement over LED), but the CNN shows superior tail suppression in the coincidence time distribution. The increased complexity associated with waveform digitization required for CNNs might be alleviated by adopting a simpler dual-threshold approach, which so far appears to recover the most crucial features of the signal for enhancing CTR in longer BGO crystals.

articleTitle: Anisotropy coefficient image reconstruction in double photon emission pH imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, several studies have been conducted on taking additional high-order information from radioisotope intensity distribution. One method is to use positronium lifetime, which measures the lifetime of ortho-positronium changed by the environment, such as oxygen concentration. Another method is to use angular correlation of cascade gamma rays, which measures the anisotropy of cascade gamma ray directions attenuated by the external environment, such as pH and electric/magnetic field. The measurement of anisotropy of cascade gamma rays was studied with independent point sources and proven feasible in the previous study. However, signals from extended sources contain interference from neighbors without an appropriate image reconstruction method. This study proposes a maximum likelihood-based method to reconstruct anisotropy coefficients of extended sources. Computer simulation with a sphere-shaped Compton camera composed of two layers of detectors was conducted. The inner sphere acted as a scatterer, and the outer sphere acted as an absorber of the Compton camera. The extended sources located at the center area of the spheres are successfully reconstructed. The results indicate that the proposed method has the capability to reconstruct anisotropy coefficient images. This method enables accurate in-vivo anisotropy coefficient imaging to measure additional environmental variables, which provides high-order information for physiology and disease study.

articleTitle: FASTIME: A Multi-Channel 130 nm CMOS ASIC for a Complete Fast and High-Resolution Time Measurement Chain
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: FASTIME is a multi-channel ASIC providing a complete time measurement chain with a precision of the order of 1 picosecond for 1 pC input charge and a dead time less than ten nanoseconds. Such resolution becomes necessary in various fields such as future particle physics experiments at FCChh to mitigate the expected pile-up of 1000, or in future generations of medical imaging (PET) to reduce significantly the dose injected into patients. It will also be needed to exploit a new type of sensors with high temporal resolution called NanoChannel Plate (NCP). To meet this need, a prototype was produced in the 130 nm CMOS process. It consists of 4 channels; each one comprises a Fast Front End (FFE) stage coupled with a discriminator followed by a Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) with double-level time interpolation. A 10-bit coarse counter provides 800 ns on-chip dynamic range. The first interpolation level of TDC is based on a Delay Locked Loop (DLL) with 32 differential delay elements operating at 1.28 GHz reference clock, which is generated by a sub-ps jitter on chip PLL, allowing a quantization step of 24.4 ps resulting in a theoretical accuracy of 7 ps rms. To refine the DLL temporal precision, a second level of time interpolation is added using two different TDC architectures, Vernier Ring-Oscillator TDC and a Time Amplifier TDC, both with an LSB of 3 ps. An intermediate circuit called Residue Pulse Maker generates the start and stop signals needed for the 2nd level interpolator. The FFE stage also integrates two preamplifier architectures: a Voltage Preamplifier and a Trans-Impedance one. The ASIC is fully configurable via slow Control (I2C). A digital readout block performs initial data processing and serializes TDC data in differential mode with an output clock of 160 MHz. Each channel measures both ToA and ToT, the latter is used to compensate for time walk. The circuit is currently tested. Preliminary results are promising and validate all circuit functionalities

articleTitle: Design Optimisation of a Dual-Headed Molecular Breast Imaging System at Different Photon Energies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our previous design for a stationary tomographic molecular breast imaging (MBI) system was optimised for 140 keV photons (${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$). The system consists of two planar CZT detectors and multipinhole collimators. The design allows for overlap of different pinhole projections on the detectors (multiplexing (MX)). This improves sensitivity and sampling but can lead to artefacts. This can be addressed by utilising depth-of-interaction (DoI) information from the detectors. The system performance depends on pinhole size, opening angle and separation. The photon energy ($E_{\gamma}$) also affects the performance, by pinhole-edge penetration and interaction depth in the detectors. In order to investigate the optimal system design for different radionuclides, including ${ }^{177} \mathrm{Lu}$ and<sup>111</sup> In, we have performed a series of computer simulations with a range of parameter values for $E_{\gamma}$ in the range $[113,245] \mathrm{keV}$. Projection data were simulated for a phantom with 6 spherical inserts, diam. 5-10 mm, TBR 10. The data were reconstructed using ML-EM, and the images were analysed in terms of contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). Our results show that CNR decreases significantly at higher $E_{\gamma}$, with $\sim 30 \%$ reduction at 245 keV compared to 140 keV. With respect to parameter optimisation, the main effect is related to pinhole separation. At 140 keV, the optimum separation is 8 mm, while for higher energies it tends towards $\sim 10 \mathrm{~mm}$. This is due to a larger degree of MX due to greater detector penetration. However, the difference is quite small, suggesting that collimators optimised for lower $E_{\gamma}$ would also be appropriate at higher $E_{\gamma}$. In conclusion, we have shown that, as opposed to standard $\gamma$-cameras, it would not be necessary to change collimators on our novel MBI system for use with radionuclides with $E_{\gamma}$ up to 245 keV.

articleTitle: FPGA-based single board computer for data acquisition and trigger of the Muon g-2 laser calibration system
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Single Board Computers (SBCs), based on microprocessor component with several expanding ports ensuring full integration with sensors and peripherals, are mainly used in embedded applications to perform a specific task (i.e. slow control operation). The increasing of computing power and the use of reconfigurable FPGAs on these modules guarantee a high level of flexibility and allow the execution of different extensive functions such as real-time signal processing, data collection and trigger purposes.In this work, we present the hardware architecture and software platform of a custom general purpose SBC hosting an FPGA and an ARM-based processor, specifically designed to control and monitor the laser calibration system of the calorimeters for the Muon g-2 experiment. In particular, we describe its implementation, the system operation and the performance during six years of data taking (from 2018 to 2023) to contain the gain fluctuations of the calorimeter photodetectors at the 0.01% level.

articleTitle: Enhancing Cherenkov photons fraction in BGO and TICl detectors using dichroic filters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Bismuth germanate (BGO) and thallium chloride (TlCl) doped with beryllium (Be) and iodine (I) (TlCl: Be, I) are promising scintillator materials for radiation detection due to their high stopping power. Due to their transparency and high refractive index, these scintillators also exhibit a significant fast Cherenkov component, which can be exploited to obtain a high coincidence time resolution in relatively slow scintillator materials for time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET). However, differences in the Cherenkov and scintillation light emission spectra make efficient detection of both components challenging. Therefore, current configurations to achieve high time and energy resolutions simultaneously are not optimal. To overcome this challenge, we explore the spectral separation of Cherenkov and scintillation photons using dichroic filters. These filters have the ability to reflect or transmit photons depending on their wavelength; thus, potentially classifying them with no photon loss. We employ dichroic filters and demonstrate that the relative fraction of Cherenkov light can be enhanced approximately two-fold using the optimal shortpass filter with a cut-off wavelength of 450 nm for BGO, and a longpass filter with a cut-on wavelength of 550 nm for TlCl. Basic characterization of several types of dichroic filters with scintillators, along with light yield, energy, and time resolution will be presented.

articleTitle: Dual-Ended Readout PET Detectors Based on 0.5 mm Pitch LYSO Arrays with Different Reflectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The performance of PET detectors is significantly influenced by the reflectors used to fabricate the crystal arrays, especially in high spatial resolution detectors that utilize dual-ended readout for depth-of-interaction (DOI) encoding. This study compared the performance of dual-ended readout PET detectors based on LYSO arrays that had the same 0.5 mm pitch and 20 mm thickness but employed five different reflectors: $80 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick barium sulfate (BaSO4), $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick Toray E60, and Toray E20 with thicknesses of $38 \mu \mathrm{m}, 50 \mu \mathrm{m}$, and $75 \mu \mathrm{m}$, respectively. Performance comparisons focused on flood histograms, energy resolution, timing resolution, and DOI resolution.

articleTitle: Python-based software tools for MCNP
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PyMCNP is a Python-based software toolkit designed to facilitate and automate the writing, reading, and running of input and output files of the widely-used radiation transport code Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP). Some of its features include reading a variety of output tallies including ptrac output files and the ability to easily extract ptrac data, reading standard information output tables, creating material cards from chemical formulas and mixture of elements, writing and automating complex source definitions, visualizing geometry including rotations and transformations, executing runs in parallel using computer clusters and/or multiple cores in a single CPU, etc. The repository will be made open source and publicly available before the start of the conference. We will present some of its capabilities and discuss the future of pyMCNP.

articleTitle: 3D-CBS: The first true paradigm change in biomedical imaging invented 23 years ago, confirmed by measured results to enable a safe, very early lifesaving cancer detection. Why hasn’t it been funded? Who is responsible for millions of needless deaths?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ultra-sensitive 3D-CBS (3-D Complete Body Screening) technology PET/CT based on the 3D-Flow invention for particle detection is targeted to significantly reduce cancer deaths and healthcare costs and is the first true paradigm change in biomedical imaging because it offers four advantages no other device can offer simultaneously: 1) an effective early detection of anomalous biological processes and diseases such as cancer at a highly curable stage, including improved diagnosis, prognosis and effective monitoring of treatments, as it is capable of detecting less than 150 Bq activity in humans; 2) a radiation dose 1% of current PET devices, 3) a 2 -minute effective screening examination covering all organs of the body, and 4) a very low examination cost, less expensive, and more effective that can replace mammograms, PAP tests, colonoscopies, PSA tests, and others. It is capable of extracting ALL valuable information from radiation (spatial, time and energy resolution and sensitivity) related to biological processes at the lowest cost per valid signal captured from tumor markers.
