This task is achieved with the technology-independent 3D-Flow system, feasible in a 16 cm cube of electronics consuming less than 2 kW, and costing less than ${\$}$ 18 per channel; it has an input bandwidth of $2,949 \mathrm{Gbps}, 2,304$ electronic input channels, $14,400 \times 3 \mathrm{D}$-Flow processors and the capability to execute up to 40 × 26 operations on each processor. Based on the measurements of 5.7 MBq radiation dose or 18.75 second exam time on the EXPLORER device using 18.1 mm thick LYSO crystals to obtain “Diagnostic quality” images, the 3DCBS with its 30 mm thick BGO crystals and 1.5 m FOV can claim 1/7 the radiation dose or 1/7 the examination time at 1/44 the cost of the EXPLORER per valid signal captured. A study shows the 3D-CBS invented in 2000 and suppressed for 23 years could have saved 39 million lives and ${\$}$ 10 trillion and could save over 100 million lives and ${\$}$27 trillion in the next 30 year

articleTitle: Optimized acquisition using spectral photon counting CT for calcium crystals discrimination
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Inflammation in joints from calcium crystal arthropathies stems from various crystals like hydroxyapatite, octacalcium phosphate, and calcium pyrophosphate Dihydrate. Distinguishing them with dual-energy CT poses challenges due to spectral similarities in attenuation profiles, noise, and artifacts. This study utilizes the MARS multi-energy spectral photon- counting CT (SPCCT) for superior energy and spatial resolution. We simulated calcium crystal scans using the default energy setting of the MARS SPCCT scanner, revealing indistinct profile variations. To enhance identification and quantification, we propose optimizing the acquisition protocol to advance personalized diagnostics and treatment strategies. We investigated scenarios involving different tube voltages, various starting energy levels, and subsequent bin sizes. Our results show that the 7-12, 12-15, 15-18, 18-21, and 21-120 keV acquisition protocol achieves maximum distinction among calcium-based crystals. Using this protocol, we conducted experimental and simulated scans of various hydroxyapatite concentrations, establishing correction factors between experimental and theoretical attenuation values. Validation of these factors through a blind scan confirmed the efficacy of our optimized protocol, indicating its potential for accurate crystal identification and quantification.

articleTitle: The ATLAS ITk Strip Detector System for the Phase-II LHC Upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: ATLAS-ITK Strip Collaboration (the speaker to be selected by the ITk Speakers Committee after the contribution acceptance) ATLAS is currently preparing for the HL-LHC upgrade, with an all-silicon Inner Tracker (ITk) that will replace the current Inner Detector. The ITk will feature a pixel detector surrounded by a strip detector, with the strip system consisting of 4 barrel layers and 6 endcap disks. After completion of final design reviews in key areas, such as Sensors, Modules, Front-End electronics and ASICs, a large scale prototyping program has been completed in all areas successfully. We present an overview of the Strip System, and highlight the final design choices of sensors, module designs and ASICs. We will summarize results achieved during prototyping and the current status of production and pre-production on various detector components, with an emphasis on QA and QC procedures.

articleTitle: A Novel Diffuse Laser System for Calibrating the sPHENIX TPC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A gaseous time projection chamber (TPC) is the main tracking detector for the sPHENIX experiment, which recently began data taking at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) at Brookhaven National Laboratory. To precisely measure energetic particles emanating from heavy ion collisions, the TPC must rely on several independent calibration schemes to correct for non-uniformities in both the electric and magnetic fields in the drift region, including local field distortions from the build-up of space charge. Such field abnormalities modify particle tracks and impose errors in the tracking analysis unless they are corrected for. This work focusses on corrections due to space charge distortions resulting from positive ion backflow into the active volume of the detector caused by the gas amplification process. We have adopted a calibration scheme utilizing a high rep. rate laser to produce a well-defined pattern of photoelectron clusters, used to monitor small, localized changes in the drift field in between physics events. Consequently, a time evolving distortion field may be reconstructed to enable a reliable distortion-correction model. At the conference, the hardware implementation of this calibration scheme will be discussed, along with some initial measurements taken with this system.

articleTitle: Assessing the Use of Transfer Learning in Neural Networks Used to Assist in the Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The analysis of neuroimaging data by means of computer systems has become a general practice in the diagnosis and monitoring of Alzheimer’s disease. In recent years, different systems based on neural networks have been proposed to aid in the diagnosis of this disorder. These systems usually contain millions of parameters that must be adjusted during the training process. This requires large datasets, often not available in most studies. The use of pre-trained systems (also known as transfer learning) would help to alleviate this problem, however these systems are often pre-trained with data of a very different nature than neuroimaging data, so their use could be counterproductive. In this work we evaluate the use of transfer learning for the development of a computer-aided diagnosis system for Alzheimer’s disease. To this end, we compared the performance obtained by different systems with and without transfer learning. The results show that transfer learning improves the results in some cases, reaching higher performances than other systems, however, the improvement depends largely on the optimizer used. In addition, we propose a novel method to convert neuroimaging data from 3D volumes to the 2D images used as input for most pre-trained systems.

articleTitle: Impact of the Block-PairWise Dead Time Correction on the Quantitative Accuracy of BrainPET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our improved dead-time correction (DTC) method uses random coincidences from block pairs of the Siemens 3T MR/BrainPET insert at Forschungszentrum Jülich GmbH to accurately estimate dead time (DT) losses in the true coincidence counts. The method provides dead time correction factors (Df) from the random coincidences on the level of the block pairs. The block-pairwise DTC was validated by using a decay experiment to sample a large dynamic range. Then, we evaluated the time activity curves (TACs) using different radioactive tracers, i.e., $\left[{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right] \mathrm{ABP688}$, and $\left[{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ Flumazenil. The quantification bias introduced by the block-pairwise DTC method was significantly smaller than for the global DTC method supplied by the manufacturer. The block-pairwise DTC shows a better agreement between the ground truth (ideal behavior without DT losses). For the $\left[{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ ABP688 the observed relative difference ratios between both DTC methods ranged from 1.4 to 1.1 in a non-linear manner. These differences could lead to a misinterpretation of results, e.g., the masking of the effects that cognitive tasks have on the TACs in the ROI and the reference region. The validation of the $\left[{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ Flumazenil measurers has shown a difference in bias behavior between the different DTC methods ranging from .05 to 0.1%.

articleTitle: Towards the LHCb PicoCal: R&D on radiation-tolerant SpaCal technology with picosecond time resolution
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The aim of the LHCb Upgrade II is to operate at a luminosity of up to $1.5 \times 10^{\wedge} 34 \mathrm{~cm}^{\wedge}-2 \mathrm{~s}^{\wedge}-1$ to collect a data set of $300 \mathrm{fb}^{\wedge}-1$. This will require a substantial modification of the current LHCb ECAL due to high radiation doses in the central region and increased particle densities. A consolidation of theECAL already during LS3 would reduce the occupancy in the central region and mitigate substantial ageing effects there after Run 3. Two spaghetti calorimeter (SpaCal) ECAL technologies are planned as baseline solutions for the inner regions. This contribution focuses on results from a test beam campaign of SpaCal technology with polystyrene scintillating fibres. A full prototype with tungsten absorber was produced and tested using radiation-hard materials. An energy resolution with sampling contributions of about $10 \% / \sqrt{E}$ was observed. Above 20 GeV, the time resolutions are found to be better than 30 ps with polystyrene fibres in tungsten. The results are in agreement with detailed Monte Carlo simulations.

articleTitle: Monte Carlo Evaluation of the Ultra-High Physical Performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) scanner with semi-monolithic detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Brain PET has demonstrated its unique value for human neurological disorders [1], and in neuro-oncology [2]. However, most studies employ body PET scanners not optimized for the high spatial and temporal resolution requirements in brain imaging. In this study we are employing Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the physical performance of the Ultra-High performance Brain PET (UHB-PET) scanner prototype utilizing (i) a compact (31-cm diameter, 26.4 cm axial FOV) geometry of large solid-angle coverage for high sensitivity, (ii) semi-monolithic LYSO slabs for optimal events positioning and timing, (iii) a “right trapezoidal” slab shape for minimal transaxial gaps, and (iv) machine learning event positioning algorithms for upgradeable spatial resolution via software updates. UHBPET is equipped with 5 detector rings, each of 20 blocks, each forming a 2×2 mini blocks array, each comprised of an array of 1 (transaxial) × 16 (axial) LYSO slabs attached along their larger sides. Assuming a current experimental 295ps coincidence time resolution, all acquisitions were simulated with GATE [3] based on NEMA NU2-2012 standards and reconstructed with CASToR [4]. Each event’s transaxial (Tx) position-of-interaction and depthof-interaction (DOI) was modeled based on the average intrinsic Tx (2.9 mm) and DOI (4.2 mm) resolution attained with machine learning (ML) using experimental data. The system sensitivity was 51.54,39.05, and $33.97 \mathrm{cps} / \mathrm{kBq}$ for 250-650, 350-650 and $450-650 \mathrm{keV}$ energy windows respectively. The average transaxial and axial resolution was 2.04 and 1.76 mm FWHM and 2.33 and 1.42 mm FWHM at 1 cm and 20 cm radial offset, respectively. Contrast recovery increased from 64% to 81% while background variability dropped from 1.7% to 0.5% from 10 mm up to 37 mm regions. New ML positioning models from preliminary MC optical data suggest intrinsic Tx resolutions down to 1 mm to significantly improve above NEMA results.

articleTitle: Novel Embedded Wire Electrode Approach for High Spatial Resolution X-ray and Gamma-Ray Imaging Detectors Using Methylammonium Lead Tribromide (MAPbBr3)Perovskite Single Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study addresses challenges posed by the high cost of traditional high-Z materials, difficulties with conventional electrode deposition methods, and limited availability of large single crystals for X-ray and Gamma-ray imaging spectrometer applications. The research introduces a groundbreaking method for fabricating high-resolution detectors using metal-organic Perovskite single crystals. In this study, we are focusing on MAPbBr 3. We have attempted to embed gold-coated wire electrodes during crystal growth, to improve detector’s charge collection properties and spectral performance and simplify the manufacturing process. Strategic enhancements such as including a 3D mesh wire, continuous saturated solvent flow to optimize the crystal growth process are highly challenging. Despite a multitude of challenges, ongoing optimization efforts have shown promising results, enhancing detector performance. Further refinement is crucial to fully exploit these enhancements and address manufacturing challenges. Collaborative efforts between DTU Space, DTU Chemistry, and Nagoya Institute of Technology, NiTech, Japan, are expected to drive significant advancements in detector technology. Future work will optimize larger crystal growth with different perovskites and enhance spectral performance using advanced simulation models, highlighting the immense promise of this pioneering technique for compact, efficient, and high-resolution detectors in medical imaging and high-energy astronomy applications.

articleTitle: A Novel Computed Tomography-Based Automated Computational Framework for Individualized Radioactive Particle Deposition Modeling in the Human Respiratory Tract
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a comprehensive and automated framework for personalized particle deposition assessment in the human respiratory tract (HRT), overcoming the limitations of traditional models and offering a method for subject-specific studies. We introduce a novel computational framework, generating individualized particle deposition profiles and detailed dose maps leveraging 3D reconstructed HRT from Computed Tomography (CT) scans and advanced Computational Fluid and Particle Dynamics (CFPD) simulations. The work integrates 3D geometry reconstruction from CT scans using computer vision algorithms, geometry preprocessing for CFPD simulation readiness, pre-converged CFPD parameters for modeling airflow and particle simulation, and Monte Carlo source card generation for internal dose assessment from inhaled radioactive particles. Validation and verification of CFPD simulations confirmed convergence using a mesh with a base size of 1 mm. The workflow was tested on 14 different HRT geometries under various breathing conditions. The impaction parameter was used in our analysis to compare particle deposition efficiency results to those of previous literature, confirming our workflow accuracy. Particle and Heavy Ion Transport code System (PHITS) source cards were automatically generated using activity-weighted point sources from the CFPD-informed particle distribution profile. Our results showed a difference as high as 90 % in the absorbed fraction by specific organs compared to PHITS simulations using uniform particle distribution in the HRT. The presented automated workflow allows researchers to reduce the human hours spent on this task, typically spanning several hours or days, to a matter of minutes. This approach addresses the anatomical and physiological variations inherent in HRT, which are crucial for drug delivery systems, targeted respiratory therapies, and assessing inhaled radioactive particles at a subject-specific level.

articleTitle: Positron Emission Tomography Kinetic Modeling Using a Cascaded Neural Network with Long Short-Term Memory (KM-LSTM)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Kinetic modeling (KM) has been widely applied for quantifying dynamic Positron Emission Tomography (PET). Aside from a region-based analysis, the generation of parametric maps is of interest to allow a voxel-wise comparison between PET data of different patient groups. However, this voxel-wise analysis is usually affected by the inherent noise of dynamic PET, resulting in biased KM parameters. Meanwhile, image-based deep-learning approaches have emerged, outperforming filtering methods in terms of preserving resolution while reducing noise. This study developed a cascaded neural network with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to estimate KM parameters of a 1 Tissue Compartment Model (1TCM), using the Time Activity Curve (TAC) and plasma input curve as input. For training and testing with noise-free input data, KM parameters were estimated with high accuracy. While an estimation error of around 10% was observed with moderate noise level, the performance was limited for processing very noisy data.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-based Filtered Back Projection Reconstruction of Attenuation and Scatter Corrected PET Images Using Multiple-energy-window Data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Current iterative image reconstruction algorithms for PET are computationally intensive. This paper proposes a novel, fast, deep learning-based PET image reconstruction method that utilizes simple back-projection of multi-energy window TOF PET data to enable attenuation and scatter correction without the need for CT or MR images. We investigated both 2D and 2.5D convolutional U-Net architectures that process high-, mixed-, and low-energy back-projection data to generate attenuation and scatter corrected PET images. Our method was validated using voxelated phantoms from clinical PET scans, and comparisons with traditional OSEM reconstructions demonstrated significant improvements in image quality: PSNR increased by 26%, SSIM by 27%, and NRMSE decreased by 55%. The proposed model shows potential for increased lesion contrast, evidenced by a 26% higher Contrast Recovery Coefficient (CRC) and a 16% higher Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) from incorporating data from multiple energy-window PET data. Future work will focus on refining these deep learning techniques and evaluating them on clinical PET systems to further study the utility and accuracy of this novel deep learning-based back projection reconstruction method.

articleTitle: A 50-Gbps 4-Channel DWDM Transceiver in monolithic 45-nm CMOS Si-Photonics SOI Technology - Concept and Design
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A concept and design of a 50-Gbps 4-channel dense wavelength division multiplexing (DWDM) optical transceiver is being developed. It is designed in a 45-nm monolithic silicon-photonics CMOS technology. The design targets to meet the rising data throughput requirements of high-resolution detectors in high-energy physics and photon science. We discuss the key components of the transceiver, emphasizing high-speed ring modulators, ring resonators and their electronic circuitries, highlighting the advantage of the monolithic integration. The transmitter concept is based on multi-wavelength light coupled into a single waveguide to be modulated by cascaded ring modulators at their resonant wavelengths within free spectral range of 9.3 nm. The dedicated electronic circuitry to modulate ring modulators contains custom-designed 10-to-1 multiplexer followed by a dedicated driver with asymmetrical differential voltage of 1.5 V. The multiplexer and driver consume only 0.7 pJ/b at 12.5 Gbps. An array of four 2<sup>nd</sup> order ring resonators are cascaded to demultiplex the transmitted spectrum at the receiver side. The spacing between the channels is designed to be 400 GHz (2.1 nm) to ensure the device peformance. We examine the temperature dependencies of ring modulators and resonators to determine the tuning range available by biasing the heating element. Furthermore, the correlation between crosstalk among the channels and channel spacing is addressed. Through comprehensive electrical-optical co-design simulations, we present the feasibility and performance potential of our proposed optical transceiver paving the way to realize efficient and compact detector systems.

articleTitle: THOR-SR: TGF and High-energy astrophysics Observatory for gamma-Rays on board the Space Rider
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: THOR-SR (TGF and High-energy astrophysics Observatory for gamma-Rays on board the Space Rider) mission is a high-energy astrophysics pathfinder mission designed to explore a range of phenomena that includes gamma-ray astrophysics’ emissions, space weather and terrestrial gamma-ray flashes (TGFs). The mission’s scientific payload is based on CdTe and Si detectors with a large field of view (up to 2π sr) provided by a four-layer CdTe stack detector. The detector operates in the 0.1-10 MeV energy range and will be used to perform spectroscopy, imaging, time variability, and polarimetry. THOR prototype performance tests will be performed, presented and discussed. In particular, tests under ESRF polarized beam and ICNAS proton beam facilities, that will allow to validate THOR operation and performance potential during the Space Rider two months flight.

articleTitle: Patlak-Guided Self-Supervised Learning for Dynamic PET Denoising
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dynamic PET imaging delivers crucial FDG metabolism data for diagnosis and treatment response assessment. Count limitations pose challenges to existing methods for estimating Ki images. We proposed a deep-learning framework that integrates the Patlak model into UNet-LSTM without imposing image size constraints. The study used a dynamic PET dataset with 28 patients, employing a three-fold training scheme. Training from scratch was challenging due to noise and weak supervision, soa pre-trained 3D UNet model on prompts-matched static images from 100 subjects was utilized. The pre-trained model was then used to initialize the downsampling and upsampling blocks of the UNet-LSTM network, facilitating convergence. After weight initialization, two approaches were used: Model A utilized raw dynamic frames as the input, while Model B utilized denoised dynamic frames by the pre-trained model as the input. Evaluation of 28 patients with 54 lesions reveals that the proposed approach achieves superior noise reduction and lesion detectability compared to both the prompts-matched model and direct reconstruction methods. Overall, Model B exhibits the most promising outcomes, as indicated by the enhancement in lesion Signal-to-Noise Ratio from 20.6 ± 13.6 (Indirect Recon), 33.7 ± 25.9 (Prompts-Matched), 34.5 ± 22.2 (Model A) to 47.6 ± 40.2 for 14 -frame prediction and from 20.9 ± 13.5 (Direct Recon), 14.2 ± 9.3 (Indirect Recon), 24.8 ± 18.1 (Prompts-Matched), and 26.9 ± 17.9 (Model A) to 32.9 ± 26.6 for 6 -frame prediction. In conclusion, we propose the Patlak-Guided Self-Supervised learning method, which integrates spatial and temporal data for dynamic PET denoising, enhances noise reduction and preserves lesions. The superior lesion SNR highlights its potential clinical utility and imaging quality improvement.

articleTitle: Leveraging Afterglow in Scintillation Detectors for Multi-Frame High-Speed Radiography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents an innovative approach to multi⃉frame high-speed flash radiography that utilizes slow decay, high⃉efficiency scintillators paired with flash X-ray sources to enhance image quality for capturing high-speed events. By leveraging the afterglow of the scintillator to maximize signal, this work redefines a traditonally direct imaging system as an indirect imaging system resulting in radiographs that exhibit significant ghosting across each frame. To extract the useful signal, this work presents a novel time-encoded approach and statistical estimators for image processing. Simulation studies presented in this work indicate promise and potential for significant advancements in high-speed imaging applications. This approach not only challenges conventional imaging techniques but also sets a foundation for further research into optimized data collection methods for dynamic events.

articleTitle: A Real-time Multiplicity-based Event Validator for Detector Arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The paper describes the implementation of an online, multiplicity-based second-level event validation system for high-granularity arrays of scintillation detectors, such as the PARIS array. Signal acquisition and processing for the PARIS detector array is based on the CAEN 1730 DAQ system (500 MHz, 14 bits). As the reconstruction of multiplicity information is not directly available from the DAQ, an external implementation in a dedicated digital system capable of collecting all the trigger signals of the PARIS array detectors (about 250) is necessary. Based on the specific multiplicity conditions associated with each experimental setup, the multiplicity estimator provides in real-time a unique validation return signal to all the DAQ modules, so that only the signals corresponding to the physical events of interest would be considered. As an example, all the events with multiplicity > 2, half of the events with multiplicity equal to 2, and just a 10 percent of the single events could then be processed. The events multiplicity selection logic has been implemented in a programmable logic device (AMD Zynq FPGA) within a “commercial on the shelf” evaluation board (Zedboard) for a limited number of channels (16, corresponding to a single DAQ module), aiming at extending the connectivity to the whole set of 16 digitizers by suitable interconnecting cables.

articleTitle: A Smart Readout ASIC with Real-Time Digital Waveform Processing and Machine Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent work has proposed the integration of machine learning (ML) algorithms within the frontend ASICs used for charge detection and readout in high-energy and nuclear physics experiments. The main goal is to alleviate data transfer bottlenecks to back-end field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) by only transmitting higher-level signal features. The latter may either be continuousvalued (e.g., amplitude, time constant, time of arrival) or discrete (e.g., particle ID). Several types of artificial neural networks, such as multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have been optimized for this purpose. Here we combine an array of MLPs with charge-sensitive analog front-ends (AFEs), analog-to-digital converters (ADCs), and digital signal processors (DSPs) to realize a complete multi-channel smart readout ASIC for a variety of segmented radiation detectors. The chip, which was designed in 65 nm CMOS technology, contains 23 independent sensing channels. Each channel features a low-noise analog front-end, single-ended to differential converter, ADC driver, high-speed 12-bit ADC, custom DSP, and MLP with programmable on-chip weights for performing either regression or classification tasks. The DSP was realized using a high-level synthesis design flow. Each channel contains 1.8 kb of onchip memory and consumes approximately 14.3 mW at the nominal sampling rate of 25 MS/s.

articleTitle: Coincidence Timing Performance Optimization of the Detector for the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome scanner is a high-spatiotemporal-resolution dedicated brain PET insert integrated with a 7T MRI system. The scanner is designed for unprecedented PET sensitivity ($\gt10 \mathrm{x}$ compared to commercial PET/MRI systems) to enable imaging of neurochemical dynamics on similar timescales (and simultaneous) to functional MRI. The PET insert comprises 872 high-performance detectors arrayed in a sphere with a 32 cm inner diameter for $\sim 70 \%$ solid angle coverage. Each detector is a $10 \times 10$ array of $1.6 \times 1.6 \times 26 \mathrm{~mm} 3$ LSO scintillator crystals coupled to a $4 \times 4$ array of $4 \times 4 \mathrm{~mm} 2$ silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). Light-sharing properties encode depth-of-interaction (DOI) information, and custom readout electronics provide precision timing. In this study, data acquisition (DAQ) parameters and post- processing corrections were optimized for coincidence timing. The time-to-digital converter (TDC) capability was validated down to $\sim 50$ ps precision using a pulsed laser system, and correction methods for TDC nonlinearity were evaluated, showing $\sim 20$ ps timing advancement. DAQ parameters in the timing chain were optimized for 511-keV gamma coincidence timing resolution (CTR), retaining good crystal identification (ID) and energy resolution of $16 \pm 2 \%$ full- width half max (FWHM). For each crystal, a 2-FWHM energy cut was taken around the photopeak and inter-crystal scatter events (ICSE) were rejected based on the □2 value from the mean photodetector signal. Crystalpair offsets were corrected, and a preliminary DOI-based correction was implemented. This analysis improved detector CTR from $\gt1.2$ ns to $617 \pm 20$ ps FWHM across 7 block pairs, best timing 586ps, enabling time-of-flight (TOF) PET.

articleTitle: Advanced 128-cha Front End Electronics for PET Detector Evaluation based on dual-polarity QDC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) was increasingly applied in nuclear medicine imaging development in recent years, especially in positron emission tomography (PET) scanner. To achieve a costeffective, power-efficient signal processing circuit for the SiPM array, a compact 128-channel front-end electronic (FEE) system based on dual-polarity charge-to-digital converter (dQDC) was proposed. For analog part, each channel of the FEE consists of two resistors, a commercial amplifier, and an integration capacitor. For digital part, only one FPGA is needed, in which a voltage-referenced receiver serves as an analog comparator. The hardware of the 128 -channel FEE consists of an analog board and an FPGA board. In the analog board, 128 channels of dQDC analog circuits are implemented. The FPGA board is based on a low-cost FPGA, instantiating 128 SSTL receivers that serve as 128 voltage comparators. The SSTLII standard is used to maximize the dynamic range of the dQDC circuit. The electronics performance of the FEE is evaluated in terms of noise, linearity, and uniformity. A PET detector is used to verify the readout capability of the 128 -channel FEE system. The PET detector is made up of a $15 \times 15$ lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) array and two SiPMs. The LYSO array is coupled with the two SiPM array at two ends. With the 128 -channel FEE, the energy resolution (ER) of the PET detector is about $13.2 \%$, and Peak-to-Valley Ratio (PVR) is 6.02. A time-to-digital converter (TDC) achieves about 50ps full-width at half maximum (FWHM) time resolution for the PET detector. All the results of the performance evaluations including electronics and detectors will be presented in the meeting.

articleTitle: RadSim: A Modular Open-Source Gamma-ray Detector Simulator
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes a simulation toolkit, RadSim, that will provide the capability to simulate radiation source emissions, interpolate results from radiation transport tools into a common format to prepare incident flux, and model radiation detector response to rapidly produce synthetic radiation measurement templates. The development and implementation of advanced algorithms and analysis methods to improve radiation detection necessitates detector modeling capability. The number of benign and threat sources, along with the number of possible shielding materials and variations in environmental scattering, is too great to be covered by physical measurements. Any development, testing, and deployment of analysis methods and algorithms requires accurate modeling that can be performed quickly with high fidelity. Users have several tools to choose from for solving radiation transport problems, but GADRAS [1] is the only tool that currently fulfills the critical role of detector modeling capability but has limited availability in its full form. RadSim is being developed as an open-source simulation framework linking existing source generation and transport tools (both deterministic and stochastic) with a newly engineered detector response module to meet the increasing demand from advanced algorithm and new detector development activities. The modeling methods are transparent, and the underlying code is being published as open source. RadSim will provide an alternative tool for building template libraries that can quantify uncertainties arising from using different decay calculators and radiation transport models. Additionally, RadSim can help tackle potential issues arising from characteristics unique to one tool in spectral analysis applications including overtraining in machine learning based radiation analysis.

articleTitle: In-Vivo Detector Arrays for Time-Dependent Inhalation Radiation Contamination Assessment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In response to radiological or nuclear emergencies, prompt assessment of internal radiation contamination is critical for triage assessment and medical countermeasures administrations. The NAIS-2’2 NaI(Tl) scintillation detectors were selected to construct a scanning system to measure internalized gamma-ray emitting radionuclide contamination in warfighters. A mesh-type adult female anthropomorphic phantom of 165 cm height and 65 kg weight was used, and an eight-point detector grid was implemented covering critical body areas (head, neck, chest, abdomen, and hip) implemented in the Monte-Carlo simulation tool, PHITS. The gamma depositions from critical radionuclides were simulated across all organs of interests. Biokinetic modeling data of each radionuclide were incorporated to determine the time-dependent retention in these organs and the gamma depositions in the detectors. To optimize the number and position of detectors for contamination characterization, a scoring algorithm was developed by analyzing the pseudo planes across the anterior and posterior of the phantom. These planes were subdivided into fine meshes to simulate the gamma flux, which were then integrated with biokinetics to compute the detector counting efficiencies at various times post-inhalation. This integration will enable the identification of the optimal detector array configuration, achieving the best counting statistics for various combinations of radionuclide sources, times post-exposure, and phantom morphologies, and the reconstruction of total contamination patterns.

articleTitle: The triggerless DAQ system for the Neutron Veto of the XENONnT Dark Matter experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The XENONnT dark matter detector, operating at the INFN Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (Italy), consists of a dual-phase liquid-gas xenon Time Projection Chambers (TPC) with a mass of 5.9 t of xenon (about three times larger with respect to its predecessor XENON1T) constituting the active target for particle interactions. This current implementation relies on an upgraded purification system, a new online cryogenic Radon distillation column and, finally, the development of Neutron Veto sub-detector around the cryostat to readuce the neutron background. The Neutron Veto is designed as a Gadolinium-doped water Cherenkov detector (made by an octagonal structure, 3 m-high and 4 m-wide) to tag neutrons by means of a capture on gadolinium or hydrogen. A total of 120 Hamamatsu 8” high-QE PMTs with low-radioactivity windows are placed along the lateral walls to detect the Cherenkov photons. A triggerless data acquisition system allows a continuous data stream of independent channels facilitating the searches for dark matter and other rare events. In this talk, the implementation and the performance of the Neutron Veto DAQ system during the first science runs will be described.

articleTitle: Quantifying the Impact of Lead and Neodymium Concentration Variations on V2O5 – Pb3O4 – TeO2 – Nd2O3 Glass through Monte Carlo Simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The study aimed to evaluate the shielding effectiveness of a material comprised of 15V2O5-(55-x) $\mathrm{Pb3O} 4-30 \mathrm{TeO} 2-\mathrm{xNd} 2 \mathrm{O} 2$, with varied molar concentrations (x) from 0 to 40, against gamma rays. Assessments were made regarding the influence of increasing Nd2O3 concentrations and decreasing Pb3O 4 concentrations on key attenuation parameters, encompassing the tenth-value layer (TVL), half-value layer (HVL), mean free path (MFP), mass attenuation coefficient ($\mu \mathrm{m}$), effective atomic number (Zeff), and buildup factor (BF), spanning an energy range of 50 to 1500 keV. Monte Carlo simulation (MC simulation) techniques were utilized for precise evaluation, incorporating variance reduction methodologies like importance sampling, Russian roulette, and the Russian rule for geometry to enhance computational accuracy and efficiency. Simulation outcomes were rigorously validated against the XCOM database, revealing an error rate ranging from 0.631 to 0.00207 percent. Additionally, a curve-fitting approach was employed for the $\mu \mathrm{m}$, demonstrating an error rate of less than $0.96 \%$ when compared to XCOM data. The analysis indicated that neodymium presents a promising alternative to lead for the development of gammaray shielding glass.

articleTitle: A Comparative Study of in Vivo Dosimetry Approaches for Mid-Plane EPID Dose Calculation: MCNP Simulation vs. Practical Measurements
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Ensuring high-quality treatment outcomes in radiation therapy for cancer patients relies heavily on quality assurance and control measures. This study explores the use of real-time dosimetry with an electronic portal imaging device (EPID) to obtain midplane dose during radiation therapy. Intracorporeal dosimetry, a crucial quality control method, directly monitors the dose delivered to the patient, thus addressing a significant challenge in the field. Comparative analysis with clinical data demonstrated that EPID dosimetry is an effective and reliable method, meeting acceptance criteria when compared with practical and simulated data. Three methods were employed to calculate midplane dose: arithmetic mean, geometric mean, and transmission dose via Monte Carlo simulation. The results of profile curves obtained using each of the three methods with 6MV photons have shown good agreement between the doses calculated by TPS, simulation, and EPID dosimetry, with a Gamma index of less than 1%. These findings suggest the feasibility of implementing a comprehensive system for precise dosimetry calculations in radiotherapy centers equipped with EPID. In conclusion, the practical and simulated results affirm the viability of EPID dosimetry, with gamma index results for midplane dose consistently below 1%.

articleTitle: The Exotic Adventure of CdZnTe Detectors at the DAΦNE Collider: Measurement of Kaonic Aluminium Transitions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the last year, we explored the potentialities of quasi-hemispherical CdZnTe (CZT) detectors for X-ray spectroscopy of kaonic atoms. Kaonic atoms are formed when a K-, stopped in a dedicated target, replaces one of the outer electrons and forms an exotic atom in a highly excited state. The measurement of the radiative X-ray transitions is very helpful to provide key information about the kaon nucleus interaction. In the framework of SIDDHARTA-2 experiment (funded by the National Institute for Nuclear Physics, INFN, Italy), we proposed the development of quasi-hemispherical CZT detectors for measurements of hard X rays from intermediate kaonic atoms. The detectors covered a detection area of 8 cm<sup>2</sup> with interesting room-temperature energy resolution of 4.4% (2.6 keV), 3% (3.7 keV), and 1.4% (9.3 keV) FWHM at 59.5, 122.1, and 662 keV, respectively.The results from measurements of X-ray emission from kaonic aluminium transitions, at the DAfNE collider in Frascati (Italy), will be presented.

articleTitle: Super-Resolution Tomographic Image Reconstruction Using Latent Diffusion Models
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Super-resolution (SR) techniques enable high-resolution (HR) image reconstructions from low-resolution (LR) image data. While acquiring HR medical image reconstructions is expensive and complex, preserving fine details remains crucial for accurate clinical diagnostics. Deep learning (DL) has emerged as a promising SR approach, but the application of recently introduced denoising diffusion probabilistic models for enhancing medical images through SR remains unexplored. This work introduces a conditional latent diffusion model (LDM) for SR image reconstruction. Our dataset comprises a subset of 3930 abdominal CT and brain MR images from the RadImageNet dataset. The resolution of the images were altered by applying Gaussian blur equivalent to a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 5mm, with a physical pixel resolution of 1.75mm per pixel. Subsequently, we down-sampled the image from 256 ×256 to 128×128 before up-sampling it back to their original size, thereby introducing variations in resolution quality. Our LDM was conditioned on the LR images. Image quality was assessed using two metrics: Laplacian variance and Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). The average Laplacian variance for the input images, ground truth, and predictions were 26, 554, and 549, respectively. Similarly, the average FFT values were -58, 4, and 3, respectively. This work showcases the potential of LDMs for SR tomographic reconstructions. Future research will explore their application in specific clinical settings, potentially leading to improved disease detection and patient outcomes.

articleTitle: Application of an electromagnetic motion tracking system in [18F]-MK6240 PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Head motion is inevitable and significant during the PET acquisition using $\left[{ }^{18} \mathrm{F}\right] \mathrm{MK} 6240$, primarily due to the prolonged duration of acquisition and the health status of the patient. To address this issue, a high resolution electromagnetic motion tracking (EMMT) system has been developed for PET-CT scanners, enabling real-time monitoring of the head movement and an event-by-event motion correction. This study presents a pilot clinical evaluation of the EMMT system’s performance in $\left[{ }^{18} \mathrm{F}\right]$ MK6240 PET imaging. Results indicate that the proposed EMMT system effectively mitigates motion-induced artifacts, thus recovering the spatial resolution performance of the PET scanner and improving the accuracy of PET quantification in the reconstructed images.

articleTitle: An autoencoder for non-invasive arterial input function estimation in pre-clinical dynamic PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An arterial input function (AIF) is essential for the quantitative evaluation of dynamic Positron Emission Tomography (PET) data. Here we demonstrate how an estimate of the AIF, an image derived input function (IDIF) can be found from the reconstructed PET image using a type of neural network called an autoencoder. The performance is evaluated for pre-clinical data from 15 rats scanned using the inflammation tracer [<sup>18</sup>F]LW223 compared to an IDIF estimate from a manually placed region of interest (ROI) and the gold standard determined using blood sampling. The autoencoder provides IDIFs in good agreement with the gold standard and outperforms IDIFs from a manually placed ROI. Future work will further explore this approach for other tracers and for data from human subjects.

articleTitle: Towards Standardised and Unified Image Reconstruction in Preclinical PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In preclinical PET imaging, achieving consistent quantitative accuracy and standardisation across various systems is hindered by the absence of imaging standards and open-source reconstruction packages capable of matching the resolution and quantitative accuracy of vendor-based methods. This work addresses these challenges by proposing a unified modelling methodology for cylindrical PET systems, aimed at harmonising system modelling used in image reconstruction and thereby enhancing system-wide quantitative accuracy. Building upon the proven modelling of clinical PET systems with NiftyPET, we demonstrate the proposed unified modelling approach for the Siemens Inveon preclinical PET scanner, while adopting a novel raw PET data standard proposed by the Emission Tomography Standardization Initiative. This integrated framework enables multisite and system-wide advanced analytics and machine intelligence applications by mitigating inter-scanner measurement variability and ensuring robust resolution and quantitative accuracy comparable to vendor reconstruction.

articleTitle: Cascaded Neural Networks for Image Registration, Synthesis and Segmentation in PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging faces challenges such as low spatial resolution and sensitivity, which can significantly impact diagnostic accuracy. Traditional deep learning methods often struggle with these challenges due to limitations in handling complex, spatially variant noise patterns. To address this, we introduce a novel cascaded network approach specifically tailored for PET image applications, focusing on rigid registration, attenuation map synthesis, and organ segmentation. Our cascaded network architecture enhances each task by leveraging iterative refinement and progressive learning, where each layer’s output informs subsequent layers, leading to more precise adjustments and improved overall accuracy. Evaluation of our method demonstrates performance improvements over traditional models, particularly in handling high-motion scenarios and low-sensitivity regions. Future research will focus on further testing these networks across a broader array of baseline models and clinical applications.

articleTitle: Experiment on Estimating the Depth of a Gamma-ray Source Using Stereo Gamma Imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we performed a mathematical modeling of the acquisition of two-dimensional position coordinate into three-dimensional image position information using two gamma-ray imagers, EPSILON-Gs. Two gamma-ray imagers were arranged in parallel to construct the experimental setup. The data obtained from each camera were used to calculate the depth estimation of the gamma-ray source from the camera using triangulation. The optimal distance between the two cameras was determined to be 11.5 cm. Using this distance, we applied two methods to estimate the depth of the gamma-ray source. Experiments to estimate the depth of the gamma-ray source from the center of the two cameras showed that the minimum and maximum values of the error were $1.2 \%$ and $5.4 \%$, respectively. In addition, in the depth estimation method of fixing the left camera and adjusting the angle of the right camera, the minimum and maximum values of the error were observed to be $0.4 \%$ and $14 \%$, respectively.

articleTitle: A Feasibility Study of Increasing Temporal Resolution in Cardiac-gated SPECT Acquisitions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In cardiac-gated studies in myocardial perfusion imaging with SPECT the number of gate intervals is typically kept to be small as a trade-off between motion blur and noise level in the reconstructed images. In this study we investigate the effect of increasing the number of gate intervals by quantifying the noise level and functional measurements based on a set of clinical acquisitions. To suppress the increased noise owing to lowered data counts with more gate intervals used, we employ a deep learning (DL) denoising network pre-trained on ungated cardiac SPECT images derived from reduced-dose studies. In the experiment we evaluated the gated images from 20 clinical acquisitions where the number of gate intervals was doubled from conventional 8 gates. The quantitative results indicate that with 16 gates the gated images can more accurately capture functional measurements near the ED or ES phase compared to 8 gates, while the increased image variability caused by lowered data counts can be effectively suppressed with DL denoising.

articleTitle: Comparative analysis of scintillators for detecting hydrogen capture γ rays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A comparative analysis of thallium-doped sodium iodide, europium-doped strontium iodide and cerium bromide scintillators for the detection of $2.223 \mathrm{MeV} \gamma$ rays, indicative of hydrogen presence in spent nuclear fuel via neutron capture on hydrogen is presented. The detection of this full-energy peak might serve as a proxy for water ingress in spent nuclear fuel which is important for the assessment of spent fuel storage integrity and safety. Experiments have been performed to explore hydrogenous foams as analogues for dispersed water in fuel-containing materials. Each scintillator’s efficiency, energy resolution, and potential application in a field setting are evaluated to determine the most effective detection system for monitoring hydrogen levels.

articleTitle: Initial Result of Low-dose PET Image Recovery using Cycle Denoising Adversarial Convolutional Network
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Reducing the radiation dose in a PET scan can alleviate the patient’s radiation burden. However, the quality of the reconstructed image may be compromised by a low radiation dose. Therefore, restoring full-dose PET images from low-dose PET images is of great clinical value. In this study, a Cycle-Denoising Adversarial Convolutional Network (Cycle-DCN) is proposed to enhance the quality of PET images while maintaining their reliability. Cycle-DCN consists of a noise predictor and two adversarial discriminators. The noise predictor aims to extract noise from low-dose images, while the discriminator distinguishes between processed low-dose images and full-dose images. The discriminant results serve as an adversarial loss to improve the performance of the noise predictor. Additionally, a cycle consistency loss is incorporated into the loss function to ensure that the predictor’s output solely consists of noise and does not include any other information from the image. PET brain images from 240 patients scanned with a Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner were utilized for the development of our method. Images were reconstructed with different acquisition time to mimic the situations of full-dose and low-dose images. The results indicate that the proposed Cycle-DCN effectively preserves image details and enhances Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), and Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NRMSE) values by up to 17%, 41%, and 76%, respectively, while also exhibiting a faster inference speed.

articleTitle: Investigating μSiPMs to overcome the limits of BGO in ToF-PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fast timing in ToF-PET improves the signal-to-noise ratio for better patient comfort through either a lower dose or a shorter scan time. Recent clinical PET scanners using lutetium-based crystals, like LYSO, reach a coincidence time resolution (CTR) of around 200 ps. Their CTR is mainly limited by the scintillation process. Thus, crystals with a significant emission of Cherenkov light, most prominently BGO, are being investigated as an alternative. BGO cannot reach its full potential due to a too low bandwidth of the electronics and too low time resolution of the photosensors. We investigate the segmentation of the photosensor into an array of individually-read-out $\mu \mathrm{SiPMs}$ to allow a better use of the Cherenkov photon’s prompt time information through an effectively higher bandwidth. In this work, we simulated the optical photon production with Geant4 and applied a signal model with a leading-edge threshold to determine timestamps and calculate the CTR from the first $\mu$ SiPM timestamp. Detectors with either 3 mm or 20 mm BGO or LYSO crystals were examined with varying photosensor segmentations. Segmenting the photosensor resulted in a significant improvement of the CTR for BGO crystals of both lengths, reducing it to $29 \pm 15 \mathrm{ps}$ (FWHM) for 3 mm and $80 \pm 21 \mathrm{ps}$ (FWHM) for 20 mm. BGO benefits from the segmentation due to its higher Cherenkov-to-scintillation ratio, while the same does not apply to LYSO with its lower Cherenkov and higher scintillation light yield. Adding noise factors, we validated the simulation of a full SiPM with measurements. For the 20 mm BGO crystal, we found that the CTR of the highest segmentation deteriorated slightly, but stayed in the range of 100 ps. For a more realistic model, further simulations with more noise factors are planned. Finally, first measurements with test structures will be used to verify our simulation results.

articleTitle: A 64-channel, 130-nm CMOS Front-end Readout ASIC with Charge Measurement and Time-stamp Digitizer for SiPM Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) detector with scintillator crystals is widely employed for γ-ray imaging domain such as γ-ray camera, positron-emission tomography, and dark matter detection. The benefit of such detector is that the dynamic range of generated charges is very large, generally, from 100 pC to ~ 1000 pC. Designing a large-dynamic range readout ASIC with fast charge and time measurement for scintillator/SiPM detector is a great challenge. In this paper, we propose a new-generation of readout application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) in 130-nm CMOS technology with the power supply of 1.2/3.3 V. In this ASIC, 64-channel analog front-ends (AFE), a 64-channel time-to-digital converter (TDC) and a global digital control block has been integrated. A regulated common-gate (RGC) trans-impedance amplifier (TIA) is proposed to achive the maximum input dynamic range of 1500 pC. A current-mode fast discriminator with a flash TDC is designed for the generation of triggers and time-stamp digitizing to achive an event rate of 1 Mcps. The inconsistency between channels of AFE is lower than 3%. The shaping time of the pulse shaper is 250 ns. The differential nonlinearity (DNL) and the integral nonlinearity (INL) of TDC are simulated as -0.1/+0.04 LSB and -0.1 LSB/+0.05 LSB. The power dissipation is evaluated as ~ 10 mW/channel. The chip is now under fabrication and the samples will be come back in this June. For future work, the ASIC will be tested. In addition, a high-resolution ADC will be integrated for all-digital output.

articleTitle: Perovskite Advancements Using Depth Correction and Trapezoidal Shaping Parameters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr3 is a room-temperature semiconductor perovskite crystal. This research employs depth of interaction corrections (DOIC) and improved shaping time optimizations to study gamma-ray spectroscopic properties of prototype CsPbBr3 detectors. The aim is to provide benchmarks on their performance and operational stability over time. By applying these techniques, we observed differences in electron and hole transport properties between different pixel signals and over operation periods. These differences in charge transport and collection necessitated different optimal shaping times. The experimental results have shown an energy resolution of 1.04% FWHM at 662 KeV from eight working pixel electrodes, with the best energy resolution of 0.85% FWHM at 662 KeV observed on pixel electrode 3 on a 0.5 cm thick CsPbBr3 detector with a 9x9 pixel electrode and one planar cathode.

articleTitle: Real time Pulse Shape Discrimination in nanoparticle ZnS:Ag/6LiF neutron detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron detectors with the ability to discriminate between neutron and gamma radiation are required in a wide range of industries. Given the expense and limited availability of ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$, scintillation detectors are becoming increasingly prevalent. $\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag} /{ }^{6} \mathrm{LiF}$ based neutron detectors are commonly employed at neutron scattering facilities worldwide. These have numerous benefits including excellent pulse shape discrimination (PSD), however $\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag}$ is rate limited by its inherent afterglow. With the ongoing development of new, high flux neutron scattering facilities, there is a growing need for neutron detectors with significantly higher rate capabilities that still possess good PSD. Nanoparticle ZnS:Ag scintillator has recently been identified as a promising candidate for use in the next generation of high rate capability neutron detectors. It has been demonstrated to have scintillation decay approximately 20 times faster than standard $\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag}$, and significantly reduced afterglow. However to be a realistic candidate for use in scattering facilities, ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ gamma sensitivities on the order $10^{-5}$ are required. In the current work we present the development of a new signal processing procedure to achieve gamma sensitivities $\lt10^{-5}$ and rate capabilities >1Mcps in nanoparticle $\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag} /{ }^{6} \mathrm{LiF}$ based detectors. This signal processing algorithm is implemented in real time on a NI DAQ 121 digitizer. This system allows for the programmatic adjustment of all variables in the PSD algorithm which can be used to determine the optimal operating conditions for use in the nanoparticle detector. The optimization of signal processing parameters to achieve the best neutron detection efficiency, gamma rejection and count rate capabilities will be shown. The PSD system could be similarly applied to other materials which require novel signal processing procedures. The real time PSD demonstrated is an important step in the development of realistic high performance nanoparticle $\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag}$ neutron detectors.

articleTitle: Data-driven application of the Wasserstein distance to scaleable detection of inter-crystal scatter in light-sharing PET detector modules
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In finely-pixelated PET detectors, Compton-scatter of the incident annihilation photon generates a spatial blurring known as inter-crystal scatter (ICS). This blurring is particularly exacerbated in light-sharing depth-encoding detectors - a design that is otherwise an excellent candidate for cost effective high-resolution imaging. Accurate identification of ICS in these detectors is crucial to establishing their viability as a high-performance imaging platform. We, therefore, developed a pair of data-driven ICS identification algorithms - a contour-based method that utilizes only the centroid position of the event and a Wasserstein distanced-based method that incorporates the full dimensionality of the detector response pattern. As a proof-of-concept, both algorithms were tested on experimental calibration data acquired from the Prism-PET brain scanner, and each event was classified as ICS or photoelectric (PE). Results of the classification were evaluated by inspecting distributions of the energy and the DOI estimation parameter (w) for both ICS and PE-classified events. Excellent classification performance was demonstrated by both methods via suppression of high-energy components of the energy distribution and shaping of the DOI-parameter distribution to align with expectations from the Beer-Lambert relation. However, the Wasserstein-based classification outperformed the contour method, indicating the importance of utilizing the full dimensionality of the input detector response data.

articleTitle: Novel FPGA-embedded SEU Monitors for the Belle II Experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Belle II detector is installed at the interaction region of the SuperKEKB ${ }^{+}{ }^{-}$collider (Tsukuba, Japan). Since the machine commissioning, its luminosity is increasing aiming at the design value of $8 \cdot 10^{35} \mathrm{~cm}^{-2} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Consequently, single event upsets (SEUs) are observed in the configuration static random-access memories (SRAMs) of on-detector field programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). While present SEU rates are tolerable, higher rates are a potential issue for a stable data acquisition. In fact, some of the subdetectors now include on-the-fly SEU-correction circuitry. Moreover, dedicated sensors have been installed at the interaction region to further understand this effect of beam backgrounds. In this conference contribution, we describe the usage of novel FPGA-embedded SEU monitors we designed, and their deployment around the Belle II volume. Conventional monitoring solutions require dedicated SRAM chips to sense SEUs and additional components to read and transfer data off the radiation area. Differently, our sensors use the FPGA configuration SRAM cells as sensitive elements and a radiation-hardened-by-design readout logic programmed in the fabric. These SEU sensors are the first integrated in a single commercial-off-the-shelf device, which made it possible to implement a compact system with low power consumption (0.7 W). We discuss how to distinguish the contribution to SEUs from thermal versus non-thermal neutrons, and present supporting experimental results from irradiation at the TRIGA reactor of the Jozef Stefan Institute (Ljubljana, Slovenia). We will delve into the details of the sensor readout system architecture at Belle II, providing insights into the implementation of our solution in other experiments. Eventually, we will present the measurements of the radiation environment at the interaction region during the operation of the collider in the year 2024.

articleTitle: Comparative analysis of two parametric imaging programs for NeuroEXPLORER studies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study evaluates and compares the performance of parametric imaging using the United Imaging PET Reconstruction Toolbox (URT) and Yale in-house kinetic modeling toolkit for images acquired on the NeuroEXPLORER, a state-of-the-art PET/CT scanner designed for human brain imaging. Four healthy volunteers participated in dynamic PET scans with different tracers: ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ FDG, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-SynVesT-1, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FE-PE2I, and ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}-(+)$-PHNO. Data were processed using both software packages for three models, i.e., Patlak analysis, one-tissue compartmental model (1TC), and simplified reference tissue model (SRTM2). Consistent parametric imaging results were found for all conditions, including low-dose applications (10% counts) and reconstructions with and without head motion correction. Minor quantitative differences (0-3%) between the toolkits were found.

articleTitle: CASPER-AI: a Machine Learning Method for Enhanced Active Collimation in Multichannel SDDs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Monolithic arrays of Silicon Drift Detectors (SDDs) are gaining interest in X-ray spectroscopy and imaging due to their excellent energy resolution and high count rate capability. However, they suffer from charge sharing, where a single X-ray event deposits energy in the boundary of multiple pixels. This creates background events and reduces overall efficiency.This work builds upon a previously presented reconstruction algorithm that performed electronic collimation by mitigating charge sharing in SDDs without sacrificing active area. We introduce CASPER-AI (Charge-sharing Analysis and Spectroscopic Performance Enhancement via Reconstruction through AI), a significant advancement that employs Machine Learning (ML) techniques, and specifically Decision Trees, for a more robust and highly adaptable active collimation, leveraging rise time and coincidence information between adjacent channels. Unlike our previous algorithm, which relied on user-defined thresholds, CASPER-AI requires minimal training on the user’s side, making it adaptable to various sources with improved performance. Experimental results demonstrate that CASPER-AI significantly improves peak-to-tail ratio (5 x) with respect to its predecessor, and recovers 8% more useful events compared to the uncollimated case. Additionally, the use of Decision Trees is compatible with real-time implementation within a Digital Pulse Processor (DPP), possibly leading to improved performance in SDD-based spectroscopy detectors.

articleTitle: Design and Preliminary Studies of a 1 mm3- resolution, MR-compatible, and Multiplexed Breast-dedicated PET Insert
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Existing PET systems can only study a single tracer per session due to the indistinguishability of 511 keV photons. Visualizing and quantifying biomarker heterogeneity of breast cancer with PET is also currently not possible owing to the relatively poor spatial resolution. This study introduces the design and preliminary studies of a high-resolution, MR-compatible, breast-dedicated PET insert capable of distinguishing signals from more than one tracer in the same PET/MR imaging session, as well as the ability to visualize biomarker heterogeneity, enhancing the ability of PET to characterize breast cancer. The development of this innovative PET system focuses on employing <sup>44</sup> Sc, a positron+prompt gamma ray emitter, to differentiate it from a pure positron emitter using its prompt gamma emission of 1157 keV that results in a triple coincidence. We utilized Monte Carlo simulations to optimize the LYSO crystal length for detecting the high energy prompt gammas and assess the sensitivity of 511 keV coincidences and 1157 keV singles. A semitrapezoidal detector design was proposed and evaluated, combining rectangular and wedge-shaped crystal elements. Through simulation, we opted for a LYSO crystal length of 35 mm. The simulation showed that the peak sensitivity of the proposed PET system reaches $21.4 \%$ for 511 keV coincidences and $35.4 \%$ for 1157 keV singles. A flood image of the proof-of-concept LYSO crystal array using a ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source as a surrogate for $\mathrm{Sc}-44$ showed all 210 array crystal elements ($\sim 1 \mathrm{~mm}$ width) could be resolved, indicating that high resolution is achievable. The energy resolution ranged from 12-13% FWHM for 511 keV and 6-10% FWHM for 1274 keV. Future work will focus on refining detector designs, enhancing signal processing techniques, and developing specialized algorithms.

articleTitle: Long-term polarization of depleted CdZnTe
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CdZnTe is prominent materials investigated due to its excellent ability to directly detect and perform energy-dispersive spectroscopy of high energy radiation with devices operating at room temperature. In spite of significant progress at the material technology and detector manufacture, the bias-induced polarization of Schottky-barrier-type detectors manifested by gradual warping of electric field throughout the detector and depreciation of spectra detected in a steadily biased sensor is still an unresolved problem. In this presentation, we investigate the polarization phenomena in CdZnTe equipped with hole blocking anode, which induces a negative charging in the detector’s bulk. We measure Laserinduced transient currents excited on the cathode side in different bias and a very wide time range $0.1 \mathrm{~ms}-5 \times 10^{4} \mathrm{~s}$ after detector’s biasing. We show that the polarization does not saturate at any specific time. It continuously slows down but proceeds without tendency to the stabilization. The ongoing polarization cannot be explained by a charging of a set of discrete defect levels. We thus propose more complex model of defect structure defining multivalent states positioned near the middle of the band gap. Such states are populated continuously in time with a decreasing detrapping rate of holes depending on the progressive occupation of these states by electrons. Despite very simple model, the theory allowed us to depict both the onset of the polarization and the slope of the charge density v.s. time. We deduce that corresponding defect states could be related with small tellurium precipitates with diameter less than $1 \mu \mathrm{m}$ or with dislocation network. We also discuss possible contribution of such states to the defect self-compensation and the pinning of Fermi energy near the middle of the band gap that is necessary for the formation of stable semi-insulating material in parallel with very low deep level doping.

articleTitle: Source finding strategy of a spatial directional detector working with a quadruped robot
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Currently, the primary approach to locating radioactive sources is to use dosimeters carried by personnel or robots. It is possible to reconstruct the location of a radiation hotspot by analyzing the radiation dose at several measurement points. Efficiency and safety are of great importance in the search for radioactive sources. In this work, we present the feasibility of using a novel spatial directional detector as an alternative to conventional dosimeters for the efficient search of sparse radioactive sources. We designed and implemented a spatial directional detector by coupling a $2 \times 2 \operatorname{CsI}(\mathrm{Tl})$ crystal array to a silicon photomultiplier array, and then mounted the detector on a quadruped robot. By combining the source spatial direction of the source given by the detector with the position determined by the robot, the spatial position of the source can be reconstructed from only two position measurements. This strategy provides an approach to reconstructing the spatial hotspot of a radioactive source without traversing measurements in three-dimensional space

articleTitle: Fast and precise timing with resistive μ RWELL-PICOSEC detector technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The $\mu$ RWELL-PICOSEC detector, which is based on Resistive Micro-Well ($\mu$ RWELL) technology, is a novel concept for fast timing gaseous detectors. It can provide timing resolution in the tens of picosecond range, making it suitable for use as a time-of-flight (TOF) technology in the fields of particle physics and medical instrumentation. The $\mu RWELL-PICOSEC$ technology employed a Cerenkov radiator to convert energetic charged particles into Cerenkov photons, a photocathode to produce primary electrons from generated photons and utilizing $\mu$ RWELL foil to multiply the electron density as consequence of a strong signal on the pad segmentation readout. Timing performance of single channel uRWELL detector carried out at CERN SPS H4 beamline is presented. Preliminary timing performance with order of 23 ps has been measured with the single channel uRWELL-PICOSEC detector

articleTitle: Using principle component analysis to identify isotopes in gamma spectra collected in urban environments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Sigma dataset consists of approximately 1.5 billion gamma spectra collected in London throughout 2018. The dataset was collected to explore the feasibility of a multi-sensor network to locate illicit radiological material and provide real-time information to the relevant authorities. This work uses a 10 day subset of this data to assess the viability of using principle component analysis (PCA) to accomplish these objectives. Initial results have shown that PCA is capable of discriminating between isotopes, identifying F-18 and Tc-99m within the data analysed. Principle components from sodium iodide (NaI) datasets were also used to identify these isotopes in a different caesium iodide (CsI) datasets showing at least some degree of detector invariance.

articleTitle: A 4-Channel Microstrip RF Coil for a 7T Whole-Body MRI to Shield PET-Insert Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We developed a 4-channel microstrip RF coil that integrates the RF shields of PET detectors as an integral part of the individual coil. We call it an MS PET coil. A conventional 4-channel microstrip coil (MS coil) was also developed for comparison. The coils were tested with a 7T whole-body MRI system (Siemens MAGNETOM 7T, Siemens Healthineers, Erlangen, Germany) for a homogeneous cylindrical phantom (NaCl + NiSO<inf>4</inf> × H<inf>2</inf>O). MR images were measured for both gradient-echo (GRE) FLASH and turbo spin-echo (TSE) sequences. Signal-to-noise ratios (SNR) for the GRE images were 203.1±28.2 and 202.4±34.2, and for the TSE images they were 80.2±27.0 and 75.1±29.8 respectively, for the MS coil and the MS PET coil, whereas the corresponding homogeneities were 39.5±19.6% and 60.3±15.6% and 13.2±12.3% and 29.2±13.9%. The MS PET coil showed relatively high performance compared to the MS coil.

articleTitle: Al alloy phase recognition through neural networks using X-ray transmission
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This project outlines a methodology for analyzing aluminum alloys through transmission imaging using an X-ray cone beam and a hyperspectral detector. This approach aims to enhance the aluminum recycling process by improving sorting and effectively controlling phases during re-solidification to reduce the material degradation. Samples are prepared with homogeneous thickness and aligned using a rail system for varying magnifications, able to resolve the alloy microstructure on a $\sim 10 \mu \mathrm{m}$ scale. The experimental setup includes temperature control to prevent energy bin shifts or image blurring due to thermal expansion movements and a diode to monitor the X-ray tube flux. The system is validated by attenuation curves of reference samples, which show the k-edges of the expected elements and consistency with theory.
