Nevertheless, the agreement is not complete for absorption effects below 10 keV. A neural network classification model was trained on theoretical curves to distinguish between measured alloys. The performances are presented for various equivalent fluxes to determine the required count rate for conducting this process efficiently. The observation of an $\mathrm{AlCu}(20 \% \mathrm{wt})$ alloy reveals its dendritic structure, confirmed through spectral analysis and comparison with EDX information. A method for automatic elemental composition determination is explored to create a labelled dataset and train a neural network. Results are returned in a fraction of a second and this is expected to be the same when increasing the number of elements in the alloy. This comprehensive method demonstrates the potential of spectral transmission imaging and the limitations to be overcome for characterizing aluminum alloys during real-time applications, taking advantage of the benefits introduced by neural networks.

articleTitle: Chalcohalide Tl6SeI4 crystal for application in radiation detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Ternary chalcohalide materials are a promising candidate for semiconductor gamma-ray detector applications. Chalcohalides combine chalcogenides and halide, such as Tl<inf>2</inf> Se and TlI, to produce a semiconductor structure with a suitable bandgap for semiconductor detector. Crystal growth of thallium based chalcohalide Tl<inf>6</inf> SeI<inf>4</inf> was carried out using the Bridgman technique for application in radiation detection. The Tl metal was purified by zone refining to reduce background impurities. The orthorhombic structure of the grown crystals was verified using XRD and the diffraction peaks were well-matched with published JCPDS data. The elemental compositional uniformity was checked using energy-dispersive X-ray mapping and found to be nearly stochiometric with a uniform distribution of elemental components Tl, Se, and I. The resistivity of the crystals showed a very high value of in the range of $10^{12}-10^{13} \mathrm{ohm}-\mathrm{cm}$ with a leakage current of 5-10 nA/cm<sup>2</sup> using back to back gold electrodes. The Tl<inf>6</inf>SeI<inf>4</inf> detectors fabricated using Au contacts showed a clear response to all gamma-ray<sup>241</sup> Am,<sup>57</sup> Co,<sup>137</sup>Cs and ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ and alpha radiation with good proportionality for these energy lines. The detectors were also able to resolve the 5.4 MeV peaks of the alpha particle $\left({ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}\right)$.

articleTitle: 2D Hybrid Perovskites for Alpha Particle Spectroscopy: from Single Crystals to Thin Films
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The work here reported discusses spectroscopic alpha particles detection based on 2D hybrid perovskite (phenylethylammonium lead bromide, PEA<inf>2</inf>PbBr<inf>4</inf>) single crystals and enlights its extension to thin film devices of thickness in the micrometer scale. Solution-processed active materials are demonstrated to exhibit temporal stability and extremely low dark current ($\lt10 \mathrm{pA}$) at high applied electric field (1000V/mm), thus making them valid option for spectroscopic radiation detection applications. Although thickness being considered a limitation, the high performance of these devices leads to resolving alpha particles $(5.5 \mathrm{MeV})$ from ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}$ radioactive isotope. We propose a comparison of physical properties and responses of single crystals and thin films on interdigitated pixels (channel length $30 \mu \mathrm{m}$), from which we extract a Hecht-like behaviour and holes mobility-lifetime product of both the configurations (1.52 $\pm 0.3 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}$ and 6.0 ± $0.7 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} / \mathrm{V}$ respectively), these corresponding to the 2D-perovskite parameters obtained with optical techniques from previous works. As alpha particle spectroscopy is crucial for radiation detection and advancements in various fields, the results here reported open to a wide range of novel applications as thin films grant both high performance and interesting mechanical properties to be exploited for spectroscopy-grade detectors.

articleTitle: A Parallel Cross-Domain Reconstruction for PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Parallel Cross-Domain Reconstruction Deep Neural Network architecture for PET imaging. Unlike conventional PET reconstruction methods, which often operate exclusively within the image or sinogram domain or attempt a joint approach without fully harnessing their intrinsic correlations, our approach effectively combines complementary information from both domains by integrating multiple stages and incorporating cross-attention mechanisms. Evaluations conducted on synthetic data illustrate that our approach surpasses two deep-learning algorithms, including the proposed architecture lacking the cross-attention mechanism and the LPD algorithm, both in qualitative and quantitative assessments.

articleTitle: A Python-based open source toolkit for gamma ray spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: NASA-gamma is a Python-based open source analysis software toolkit designed for gamma ray spectroscopy. Some of its features include advanced peak fitting, energy calibration, efficiency calibration, peak finding, peak identification with specialized databases, and advanced visualization. We present a progress update from last year and an overview of its basic and advanced features so that researchers and students around the globe can make use of them. NASA-gamma has a Graphical User Interface (GUI), which allows for advanced analysis without any programming knowledge.

articleTitle: Calibration for TDC Offset Delay in Fully Wearable Brain PET System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) is essential for high Time-of-Flight (TOF) resolution in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems. We perform a calibration to correct TDC offset delay in SmartBrain, a fully wearable brain PET system. The calibration phantom consists of six glass tubes filled with <sup>18</sup>F-fluorodeoxyglucose(<sup>18</sup>F-FDG). The TOF for each line of response (LOR) is measured by TDC circuitry implemented on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and compared to the analytical TOF values based on the reconstruction image. A set of overdetermined equations representing time delay differences between arbitrary channel pairs is solved using LSQR, an iterative least-squares method, to estimate TDC offset delay. Calibration was evaluated through a TOF resolution experiment using modified NEMA NU4 2018 standard, achieving a system TOF resolution of 252.89 picoseconds.

articleTitle: Shorten scan duration for multi-parametric imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Parametric imaging based on dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) scan provides better quantification and improve specificity for cancer detection. The lengthy one-hour dynamic PET scans discomfort patients, add motion artifacts, and inflate costs, highlighting the need for tech advancements to reduce scan times. Therefore, we attempted to reconstruct multi-parametric imaging with only 20 min dynamic PET frames through deep learning techniques. We aimed to reduce the discomfort and costs associated with one-hour dynamic PET scans by reconstructing multi-parametric images from 20-minute scans using deep learning techniques. Our method, incorporating dynamic PET frames prediction, parametric linear fitting, and GAN, yielded high-quality images that closely resembled full-time parametric images. The reconstructed images achieved average PSNR values of $35.5535 \pm 7.1764 \mathrm{~dB}$, along with SSIM scores of 0.9798 ± 0.0122, respectively. Our approach is effective for imaging cancer-affected areas and was validated using actual FAPI datasets. We plan to test our method using total-body PET/CT scanners in a broader range of clinical practices in the future.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of DOI-PET Detector Inserting Quasi-monolithic Scintillator between Pixelated Crystal Array
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A depth of interaction-positron emission tomography (DOI-PET) detectors inserting a quasi- monolithic scintillation crystal between the pixelated crystal layers was proposed and examined. Sixteen LYSO discrete crystals with a size of 3 × 3 × 10 mm<sup>3</sup> were assembled into a 4 × 4 array. Two sets of pixelated crystal arrays were stacked in the depth direction. A quasi-monolithic LYSO scintillator with 1 × 4 array of 3 × 12 × T mm<sup>3</sup> was employed to allow the light spreading along the Y-direction. A Monte-Carlo simulation was conducted to investigate the scintillation light distribution pattern. A total of 1.16M γ-ray interactions was generated and post-processed for ten DOI-PET detectors. Position estimation algorithm was employed to sequentially determine the X-, Y-, and Z-position for each γ-ray interaction. All the X-Y positions were clearly identified for proposed DOI-PET detectors. The interaction layers could be identified with high accuracy (>93%) for the DOI-PET detectors by inserting the quasi-monolithic scintillator with a thickness of 4-10 mm. Simulation results confirmed that it was possible to identify the 3D interaction positions with high accuracy for incident γ-ray events. Further investigations should be include studying the improved position estimation algorithms with excellent accuracy (>99%). Moreover, future experimental studies will be followed to confirm the simulation results by using real DOI-PET detector.

articleTitle: Beyond Bootstrap: Enhancing Uncertainty Assessments of Metabolic Parameters through Gaussian Focused
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Inherent uncertainty in metabolic parameters substantially hinders the precision of positron emission tomography (PET) imaging diagnostics. Heterogeneous radiopharmaceutical uptake and model-based interpretations impact clinical decision making. Current dynamic PET image uncertainty assessment typically uses bootstrap, which depends heavily on the estimator used and does not always yield asymptotically valid results. In order to overcome these limitations, we introduce the Gaussian Focused Markov Sampling (GF-MS) method integrating it with an agglomerative clustering strategy. The clustering process derives self-generated prior knowledge, which provides a robust candidate set for model fitting and parameter estimation. Consequently, it enhances search efficiency and reduces computation time. The proposed GF-MS method significantly improves resistance to noise and offers a less biased predictor of parametric accuracy than the bootstrap method.

articleTitle: Multimodality Molecular Imaging of Brain Tumor Using Simultaneous [18F]FET-PET/MRSI
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Structural MR signals not as sensitive or specific for the definition of the borders of tumoral involvement. To address this issue, we propose a novel multimodality molecular imaging method using simultaneous [18F]-fluoroethyltyrosine ([18F]FET) and high-resolution MR spectroscopic imaging (MRSI). [18F]FET is an amino acid radiotracer that penetrates the intact blood-brain barrier via the amino acid transport pathway. MRSI has been proven useful in many gliomarelated applications, i.e. differentiating tumor infiltration from normal tissue. Exploring the synergistic molecular imaging from [18F]FET-PET and MRSI can lead to more accurate brain tumor delineation. However, the conventional MRSI is limited by spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio, and imaging speed. We addressed this challenge by leveraging our recent breakthroughs on development of a rapid high-resolution MRSI method that integrates fast sequence, subspace modeling and MR physics. To demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed method, 6 glioma patients were recruited for simultaneous [18F]FET-PET/MRSI scan using a whole-body 3T PET/MR scanner. The study was approved by the local IRB. The MRSI data were acquired with a spatial resolution of $3.8-\mathrm{mm}$ isotropic resolution and imaging time $=7 \mathrm{~min}$. [18F]FET SUVr was calculated using list-mode data acquired between 20-30 min after the injection. Our preliminary results show that the NAA/Cho map from MRSI indicated regions with possible infiltrations different from the tumor margin defined by the T2w signal. High-uptake of [18F]FET were found within the tumor, indicating areas with high proliferation activities. These preliminary results highlight the complementary metabolic heterogeneity information brought by PET/MRSI, which can be used along with the conventional structure MR for improved treatment planning.

articleTitle: Performance evaluation of the modular J-PET detector in conventional PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The utilization of organic scintillator strips in the construction of J-PET represents a remarkable departure from the conventional PET methodology that relies on inorganic crystal scintillators [1, 2]. This innovative approach not only holds the potential for cost-effectiveness but also facilitates the development of stand-alone detection modules, making PET imaging accessible to non-specialized laboratories [3]. The J-PET scanner, recently commissioned for research imaging on clinical patients at the University Hospital in Krakow, has undergone rigorous evaluation. This work is based on the study in which a single-bed position scan was performed on patients injected with [$\left.{ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}\right]$-DOTA-TATE. This study evaluates the performance of human imaging in J-PET with particular attention to incorporating various corrections, including attenuation, normalization, random and scatter corrections. Attenuation correction was applied using the kVp-dependent transformation [4]. Normalization corrections were calculated using the component-based approach [5]. Random coincidences were corrected using the delayed time window method [6]. A Monte Carlo-based scatter correction (SC) method was implemented using SimSET to simulate the scatter contribution and calculate the SC factors in between each OSEM iteration of the image reconstruction [7]. In this contribution, the reconstructed images of patients scanned with the JPET, the first scanner based on plastic scintillators, and supplemented with the necessary corrections, will be presented.

articleTitle: MR-based synthetic CT generation using continuity characteristic of adjacent slices
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In radiotherapy, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used for target volume and organs-at-risk delineation due to its superior soft-tissue contrast compared to computed tomography (CT) imaging. However, MRI lacks the electron density information needed for dose calculation. The aim of this study is to generate the MR-based synthetic CT that can be utilized for dose calculation using artificial intelligence. Different MRI scan protocols such as T1 weighted (T1W) image and T2 weighted (T2W) image were evaluated to optimize synthetic CT (sCT) generation process. We proposed a method to increase accuracy by applying adjacent slice information to a GAN-based generation algorithm. The dataset consisted of 2,100 registered MR images and 2,100 CT images. A total of 2,100 pairs of MR images and CT images were divided into training set, validation set, and test set at ratios of 64%, 16%, and 20%, respectively. The performance indicators of MAE, SSIM, and PSNR, which are general performance indicators of the sCT generation model, were calculated for the test set. The values of the basic GAN model and the proposed model were evaluated at a similar level: MAE 19.975 HU, SSIM 0.957, PSNR 31.096. However, upon visual inspection of the image analysis results, it was confirmed that the proposed algorithm more accurately generates bones and surrounding tissues similar to reality. Although the accuracy of radiation dose calculation using synthetic CT and additional algorithm validation using external data are needed, this study serves as a foundation for further research on MR-only radiation therapy.

articleTitle: Progress on the Development of Spectroscopic Polymer Organic Glass Scintillators for Radiation Portal Monitors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multi-mode radiation detectors capable of gamma-ray spectroscopy are needed as the next generation of radiation portal monitors (RPMs) at ports of entry along the nation’s borders. Plastic scintillators that are currently used in RPMs can be produced in very large volumes at low cost, but due to their low density and low effective atomic number (Zeff), are limited to gross gamma-ray counting. To meet the performance and size requirements needed for RPMs, RMD and SNL are developing tin-loaded Polymer Organic Glass Scintillators (tin-POGS). In this work we show progress on the development of tin-POGS. We have fabricated high quality samples of tin-POGS up to 6” x 6” x 1.5” and compared them to similar size EJ-200 PVT slab. We have performed GEANT4 simulations to establish detector response of tin-loaded POGS to Cs-137 with an objective of optimization of the final design of the detector configuration.

articleTitle: Quantification of 18F-FDG Delivery Rate for Liver Inflammation using Shortened Dynamic PET Imaging Protocols
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Liver inflammation is a diagnostic hallmark of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a severe form of chronic steatotic liver disease that affects a very large part of the general population. ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG delivery rate K<inf>1</inf> in the liver measured by dynamic PET with tracer kinetic modeling has the potential to assess liver inflammation and diagnose MASH noninvasively. However, a full one-hour scan protocol was required to generate liver K<inf>1</inf>, which is less practical for clinical use. In this study, we investigate two shortened scan protocols in combination with appropriate tracer kinetic models: a 15-min dynamic scan with a two-tissue reversible model and a 10-min dynamic scan with a two-tissue irreversible model, using 82 human subjects. K<inf>1</inf> generated from the proposed shortened scan protocols are approximately equal to K<inf>1</inf> from the full one-hour protocol and can equivalently differentiate healthy vs low vs high inflammation groups with statistical significance. In combination with liver CT that assesses steatosis, the two proposed shortened scan protocols achieved an AUC of 0.95 for ROC analysis of differentiating MASH vs non-MASH, very comparable to the performance of the full scan protocol. The results indicate it is possible to reliably estimate liver FDG K<inf>1</inf> using an early dynamic PET scan with an appropriate kinetic model. The proposed two shortened protocols are more efficient than the one-hour protocol for measuring liver FDG K<inf>1</inf> to evaluate liver inflammation and combine it with liver CT for diagnosing MASH.

articleTitle: Neutronic Analogues for Water Detection Studies in Spent Nuclear Fuel
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The identification of benign (not radioactive) materials to serve as neutronic analogues for prompt gamma activation analysis specifically relating to the identification of water in spent nuclear fuel is described. Production of $2.223 \mathrm{MeV} {\gamma}$ rays via the ($\mathrm{n}, {\gamma}$) reaction can be indicative of the presence of hydrogen and hence water. Using a simulated ${ }^{252} \mathrm{C f}$ neutron field, this research compares the neutronic properties of $\mathrm{U O}_{2}$ and capture $\gamma$-ray spectra to those of several candidate analogue materials. Of the tested materials, molybdenum yields the closest correlation to UO<inf>2</inf> in terms of its neutron transmission and $(n, y)$ reaction rate.

articleTitle: Preliminary Results of the Performance Characteristics for the New Digital uMI Panvivo PET/CT System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The newly developed uMI Panvivo PET/CT system utilizes a SiPM- and ASIC-readout-based uExcel UDP detector platform. The integration of application-specific integrated circuit has notably enhanced the system’s counting performance and improved quantitative accuracy in various applications. This study evaluates the performance of the first uMI Panvivo prototype in accordance with the NEMA NU 2-2018 standard. The PET system demonstrates a transaxial spatial resolution of 2.81 mm at full width at half maximum with a 1.0 cm offset from the center, a sensitivity of $16.9 \mathrm{cps} / \mathrm{kBq}$ at the center of the field-of-view, a peak NECR of 366.14 kcps at 37.04 $\mathrm{kBq} / \mathrm{cc}$, and a maximum relative count rate error of less than 4% across all slices for activity concentrations at or below the NECR peak activity. Furthermore, the timing resolution at peak and $5.3 \mathrm{kBq} / \mathrm{ml}$ were 234 ps and 224 ps, respectively. The overall image contrast assessed with the NEMA image quality (NEMA-IQ) phantom ranges from 65.3% to 93.7%, while the background variability ranges from 4.5% to 1.5%. Phantom imaging results suggest that the system exhibits a uniform distribution of background noise.

articleTitle: Effect of trace-element of TlBr semiconductors and charge transport properties of TlBr detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thallium bromide (TlBr) is an attractive material for the fabrication of gamma-ray detectors due to its high photon stopping power resulting from its high atomic number and high density (7.56 $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$). TlBr detectors fabricated from TlBr crystals grown by the traveling molten zone method using materials purified by the zone-purification method have demonstrated high performance. In this study, we evaluated the trace-element concentrations and charge transport properties of front-, middle-, back- parts of a TlBr crystal purified 408 times by the zone-purification method. The trace-element analysis for each part of the TlBr using multiple-spot laser ablation-inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (msLA-ICP-MS) revealed the accumulation of $\mathrm{Mg}, \mathrm{Sr}, \mathrm{Cs}, \mathrm{Ba}$ in the back part and Ca in the front part of the TlBr crystal, respectively. TlBr detectors fabricated from the front part of the TlBr crystal showed the best charge transport properties for electron. From the above, it is revealed that the front part of TlBr crystal has the lowest trace-element concentration and the best detector characteristics.

articleTitle: Improved Reconstruction Quality of PGET Using a Linear-Inverse Approach
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Passive Gamma Emission Tomography (PGET) instrument has received authorization from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for inspecting spent fuel assemblies (SFAs) to detect any diversion of fuel rods. The accuracy of fuel rod identification hinges critically on the quality of the reconstructed image. In comparison to the traditional filtered back-projection (FBP) method, the linear inverse approach has demonstrated superior image quality and identification accuracy. This approach frames the image reconstruction process as an inverse problem, relying on a precise forward model of the PGET system. In this work, we have built upon our previously developed forward model, which accounts for the gamma-ray down-scattering in the SFA, and developed a new point spread function model incorporating collimator septal penetration and detector scattering effects. A unique benefit of our approach is the direct estimate of the source strength, unattainable otherwise. This information can be directly compared with the operator’s declaration. The enhanced forward model was validated by comparing against MCNP simulation, and a 2.95% relative difference between the counts obtained using MCNP and our new forward model was achieved. Using this enhanced model, we successfully reconstructed the image of a simulated hexagonal assembly, identified 100% of the fuel rods, and achieved a 2.87% uncertainty in activity estimation. Additionally, we applied the model to an actual measured fuel assembly, successfully imaging all the rods, including the innermost ones, and identifying the water channels within.

articleTitle: List-Mode PET Image Reconstruction Using Dykstra-Like Splitting
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Efficient convergence of the block iterative method in image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) requires careful control of the relaxation parameters [1], which is a challenging task. Automatic determination of optimal relaxation parameters for list-mode reconstructions [2] also remains challenging. Therefore, an approach other than relaxation parameter control would be desirable for list-mode PET reconstruction. In this study, we propose a maximum likelihood listmode PET reconstruction using Dykstra-like splitting [3], [4] (LM-MLDS). LM-MLDS adds the distance from an initial image as a penalty term to an objective function for convergence. LMMLDS uses a two-step approach because the quality of the initial image affects performance. The first step uses a uniform image as the initial image, and then the second step uses a reconstructed image after one main iteration as the initial image. We evaluated LM-MLDS using simulation and clinical data on a brain PET scanner with four-layer depth of interaction information [5]. LMMLDS provided a better tradeoff curve between noise and contrast than the other methods. In a clinical study, LM-MLDS removed the false hotspots at the edge of the axial field of view and improved the image quality of slices covering the top of the head to the cerebellum. LM-MLDS showed different noise properties than the other methods due to Gaussian denoising induced by the proximity operator [6], [7]. These results suggest that LM-MLDS may be useful for improving the robustness of geometric sensitivity variations in the 3D PET scanners, and that list-mode proximal splitting PET reconstruction is useful not only for optimizing nondifferentiable functions such as total variation but also for converging block iterative methods without controlling relaxation parameters.

articleTitle: Residual Convolutional Neural Network-Based Automated Segmentation of Organs at Risk in Pelvic CT Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate delineation of organs at risk (OARs) is critical for radiotherapy planning but traditionally entails manual and time-intensive efforts. To address this challenge, our research introduces a robust convolutional neural network (CNN) for automated segmentation of OARs, including the bladder, prostate, rectum, right femoral head, and left femoral head, in pelvic CT scans. Utilizing SegResNet model, optimized specifically for semantic segmentation tasks. This model features a U-Net-like architecture with downsampling, upsampling, residual blocks, and transposed convolutions. It includes a variational auto-encoder (VAE) branch to ensure image fidelity. Our study encompassed 238 patients for prostate segmentation and 218 patients for the remaining four organs. Evaluation of the model’s performance against expert segmentation masks utilized metrics such as the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Jaccard Index (JI), Precision, and the 95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (95HD). The obtained DSC values, along with their standard deviations, were as follows: $0.956 \pm 0.036$ for the bladder, $0.832 \pm 0.071$ for the prostate, $0.864 \pm 0.052$ for the rectum, $0.980 \pm 0.021$ for the left femoral head, and $0.985 \pm 0.016$ for the right femoral head. These results underscore the high-quality segmentation achieved and the significant efficiency improvement compared to manual contouring methods. In summary, our research demonstrates the capacity of convolutional neural networks to streamline OAR segmentation in radiotherapy planning. The automation of this crucial process not only enhances accuracy but also accelerates planning, offering a promising avenue for optimizing treatment strategies in clinical settings.

articleTitle: Development and validation of an optimal GATE model for simulation of photon beam from linier accelerator
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this investigation, we assess the effectiveness of the Geant4/Gate Monte Carlo (MC) code as an independent dose commissioning system for Intensity Modulated Radiation Therapy (IMRT) facilities. We established a comprehensive framework for dose planning, utilizing MC simulation techniques to improve accuracy and computational efficiency through variance reduction methods, including threshold cuts, step size limiters, and the Russian rule for geometry. Specifically, we simulated a Varian Clinac $2100 \mathrm{c} / \mathrm{d}$ with a 6 MeV nominal energy using the Geant4/Gate toolkit to irradiate a $50 \times 50 \times 30 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$ water phantom at various field sizes of $3 \times 3$, $6 \times 6,10 \times 10$, and $15 \times 15 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, with and without a flattening filter(FF). The accuracy of the beam modeling was verified by comparing off-axis profiles and integral depth dose (IDD) distributions obtained from simulation with experimental measurements. Our results demonstrate excellent agreement between MC simulation and measurements for the depth-dose curve in flattening filter-free (FFF) mode, with maximum relative errors of 1.95% for $6 \times 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ field size, 2.9% for $10 \times 10$ $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ field size, and 2.4% for $15 \times 15 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ field size. Additionally, comparison of off-axis profiles for $3 \times 3 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}, 6 \times 6 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$, and $10 \times 10 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ in FFF mode, and $15 \times 5 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ in flattening filter mode, revealed maximum differences of 2.36% across all examined field sizes. These findings highlight the potential of GATE simulation as a reliable tool for quality assurance in photon therapy facilities.

articleTitle: System testing and integration preparation aspects of the silicon pixel detector of the ATLAS experiment for the Phase-II upgrade of the LHC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The entire tracking system of the ATLAS experiment will be replaced during the Phase-II upgrade of the LHC. It is foreseen to install an all-silicon detector comprised of a strip and pixel detector. The new pixel detector will consist of five layers in the central region and multiple forward layers. In order to cope with the demanding conditions at the HL-LHC, new silicon sensors of n-in-p type which are read out by the new ASICs developed within the RD53 Collaboration, will be used to have a high tracking performance. Moreover, high-rate capable services and stable, low mass mechanical structures are essential to have a low mass detector with high tracking performance. The system is further complicated by the need for low bit error rates on electrical links and the limited ability to conduct repairs both during integration and operational phases as well as its sheer scale. The detector comprises multiple custom-designed components, presenting unique challenges. As the project transitions to the production phase, an extensive testing and qualification program has been completed with different system configurations, as is expected for the central outer layers, the Outer Barrel, and will be presented in this contribution, focusing on the detector services and the full electronics chain validation. Such validation was completed also using irradiated services components and the effects of the irradiation were studied and will be shown. Developments related to production quality control testing of different components will be covered along with results from the testing of first production units. The ongoing efforts to achieve electronics systems connectivity and functionality validation at the different stages of detector integration will be outlined, illustrating the project’s unique difficulties and the strategies eventually used to overcome them. This includes grounding and shielding measures employed in order to achieve a low noise final detector system.

articleTitle: Design and testing of a 48 channel waveform digitizer card for the ALERT TOF detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ALERT-TOF detector (AtoF), to be installed in CLAS12 at Jefferson Lab, aims at detecting low momentum recoiling ions through scintillator coupled SiPM-generated pulses with excellent time resolution. The experimental capability and systematics can be greatly enhanced by the availability of waveform data from the scintillation process, especially during the high luminosity experimental configuration. For this reason, we developed a novel readout board using Nalu Scientific custom digitizing asics (ASoCs) that is capable of acquiring waveform data at ~2.2Gsps or more from 48 independent channels. The board is currently under testing and it is expected to be incorporated in the experiment in the near future.

articleTitle: Preliminary Study of X-ray Ghost Imaging Reconstruction with a Deep Neural Network Constraint
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Unlike typical imaging techniques that collect photons reflecting or transmitting an object with a multi-pixel photo detector, ghost imaging (GI) is an indirect imaging technique by correlating the intensity of two beams. One of the beams that does not interact with an object provides the spatial distribution (2D information), and the other beam that actually interacts with the object provides the intensity information from the interaction (1D information). Separation of detection and imaging parts in GI could resolve the limitation of conventional imaging techniques in harsh environments such as strong turbulence. GI was perceived possible only with entangled photon pairs in quantum correlation, however; later studies have shown that classically correlated lights such as pseudo-thermal lights are also applicable. Recently, GI using classical correlation covers X-rays, and it is expected that it will bring lower exposure to radiation and higher image quality. There have been several algorithms for GI, but the nature of GI reconstruction relies on the number of random speckle patterns and measurements, making a typical ghost image blurry. GI does not have a standardized point-spread function (PSF), making the deconvolution an ill-posed problem. There are studies to cope with the problem in GI using pseudo-thermal lights with deep learning techniques, but little studies were done regarding the improvement of quality in X-ray Ghost Imaging (XGI). In this study, we attempted to resolve the quality issue in XGI using a deep learning model called GIDC (GI using Deep neural network Constraint). This model enhances the quality of pseudo-thermal light GI effectively without any training, but has not been implemented on XGI. We calculated SSIM and PSNR values to demonstrate the impact of GIDC on XGI.

articleTitle: Quality Control for DUNE Cryogenic FEMB Production
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), the Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) is chosen as the far detector (FD) solution. The first two 10 kton DUNE FD modules will employ anode planes with cold electronics (CE) installed inside the cryostat. The CE developed for cryogenic temperatures (77-89K) operation is an optimal solution that achieves excellent noise performance and decouples the electrode and cryostat design from the readout design. There are 384,000 channels from FD1 and 245,760 channels from FD2 to be read out by CE, which requires 4,920 Front-end Motherboards (FEMBs). DUNE is expected to be operated for 20 to 30 years, which requires FEMBs to stay in liquid argon (LAr) for 30 years without the possibility of any replacement and maintenance. Therefore, a stringent quality control (QC) method is studied to assure the robustness and reliability of FEMB. It requires that all system aspects are considered starting from the early design phase to the detector commissioning phase. We summarize the design of cryogenic FEMB, experiences gained from pre-production, and QC testing method optimized for batch production.

articleTitle: Review and Strategy for Implementing Criteria of DNA Damage in an Atomistic Model using Geant4-DNA
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our project has been developing a Monte Carlo simulation tool using Geant4-DNA for assessing radiation-induced DNA damage in the atomic level. Radiation damage consists of direct effects caused by direct energy transfer from charged particles, and indirect effects starting from hydrogen abstraction reactions by OH radicals through water radiolysis. These effets induce damages in the atomic structure of DNA molecules. We have introduced molecular structures from the Protein Data Bank database into our simulations to evaluate DNA strand breaks by both direct and indirect effects. For the indirect effect, we employed a mechanical approach to determine damage sites at the atomic level by examining the correlation between post-diffusion coordinates of OH radicals after an average reaction time and the atoms in the DNA molecules. The results showed that the portion of strand breaks correlates with experimental data [1]. In addition, we evaluated the activation energy for hydrogen abstraction reactions using the semi-empirical quantum chemical calculation program MOPAC and assessed the accessibility of OH radicals to DNA molecule hydrogen using the molecular dynamics simulation program Amber. These results illustrate that the proportion of strand breaks’ sites can be explained from a chemical reaction process [2]. Meanwhile, it is desirable to incorporate the results from these quantum chemical and molecular dynamics calculations into the Monte Carlo simulation. This presentation reports on our strategy to implement the DNA damage models to utilize the parameters achieved from the quantum chemical and molecular dynamics calculations.

articleTitle: Flat Panel TOF-PET Detectors: a Simulation Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Flat panel detectors for positron emission tomography carry the capability to deliver a cost accessible, compact, flexible and modular alternative to standard cylindrical scanners. The modular nature means that a scanner could be assembled by combining the detectors in any number of ways, such as using two or four panels to achieve different angular coverages or placing panels consecutively to achieve total body coverage. This new geometry also comes with significant challenges in image reconstruction. Sufficient coincidence timing resolution is required to avoid artifacts in reconstructed images due to limited angular coverage and to compensate for the reduced sensitivity. In this work, flat panel scanners were simulated using GATE software and images were reconstructed using CASToR. Over a million core hours were utilised to obtain these results, making heavy use of high-performance computing. Various phantoms and metrics were used to compare the performance of the flat panel scanners to a reference scanner based on the current state-of-the-art clinical scanner, Siemens Biograph Vision. The results demonstrate that with improved timing resolution, flat panel scanners can achieve image quality comparable to the reference scanner while using less than a third of the scintillator material or achieve long axial coverage (1.2 m) while using the same amount of material and achieving homogeneous contrast across the axial length of the scanner.

articleTitle: Results from the Timepix4 Telescope at the CERN SPS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A beam telescope based on the recently developed Timepix4 ASIC has been built in order to perform tests of synchronous multiple-detector readout and track reconstruction with fast timing capability. The Timepix4 is a readout ASIC for hybrid pixel detectors that is designed to record both the time of arrival (ToA) and the time over threshold (ToT) of each discriminated signal. It has a 448 ×512 pixel matrix with square pixels at a 55 μm pitch. The ToA is digitized by a TDC with time bins of 195 ps, while the ToT is proportional to the charge collected by the silicon sensor, and is used to achieve sub-pixel spatial resolution. The ToT is also used to correct for time-walk and thereby improve the ToA resolution. The telescope consists of eight planes with n-on-p silicon sensors. Four of these planes are instrumented with 300 μm thick planar sensors, which are tilted and rotated by 9° with respect to the beam incidence to provide highly accurate spatial measurements. The other four planes have 100 μm thick sensors to achieve a better time response. Each detector assembly (sensor + Timepix4 ASIC) is cooled by circulating chilled glycol through a 3D-printed titanium block that is directly attached to the carrier PCB. The cooling block has a circular cut-out to minimise the amount of material traversed by incident particles. The assemblies are readout by SPIDR4 systems that send the data via 10 Gbit ethernet to the data acquisition (DAQ) computers. Three scintillators and two micro-channel plate (MCP) detectors provide precise time-reference signals that are recorded by a PicoTDC chip, which has time bins of 3ps. The time references are used to characterise and calibrate the time measurements of the telescope and fast-sensor prototypes.

articleTitle: Energy spectrum and counting test of secondary particles in heavy ion therapy based on orthogonal strip CZT detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The high sensitivity and low energy deposition characteristics of semiconductor materials contribute to the increased accuracy of dose distribution measurement for heavy ion beams. This study involved testing the response of heavy ion therapy using an orthogonal strip CZT semiconductor detector with an electrode width of 0.9 mm. During the experiment, a heavy ion beam bombarded the PMMA target to produce secondary particles, and the cadmium telluride zinc detector was able to detect the positron annihilation of gamma photons with an energy of 511 keV. The resolution of CZT single-anode events reached 5.7% in the in-beam process and 3.7% in the off-beam process, respectively. The effective counts per unit time during the beam and beam separation period were statistically analyzed. It was observed that the effective count during the beam period is positively correlated with time, while the effective count during the off-beam period follows an exponential decay rule. These findings verify the feasibility of using CZT semiconductor detectors for testing secondary particles and provide a basis for the dose monitoring of CZT semiconductor detectors during heavy ion therapy.

articleTitle: Progress of High Precision TPC Detection Technology for the Future Circular e+e-Collider
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Circular Electron Positron Collider (CEPC) was proposed as a Higgs and high-luminosity Z factory in the Chinese High Energy Physics community, with the Technology Design Report (TDR) released at the end of 2023. The baseline detector design features a high-precision (approximately 100 ${\$}$ \mu m ${\$}$) spatial resolution Time Projection Chamber (TPC) as the main tracking device surrounding a 3.0T solenoid field, even when operated at Tera-Z. The TPC technology requires a longitudinal time resolution of 100 ns, and the physics requirement of PID resolution should be less than 3%. This presentation will discuss the feasibility and status of the high precision TPC as the main track detector for an e+e- collider. The TPC detection aims to achieve good separation power with consideration for cluster counting, and the simulation results of the pad/pixelated TPC technology for the e+e- collider will be presented. Compared with the pad readout using the simulation, the high granularity readout TPC option will achieve better spatial resolution for single electrons, high detection efficiency in excellent tracking, and good PID performance (less than $3 \sigma)$. The results of track reconstruction performance and dE/dx are presented. The presentation will also review the results of track reconstruction performance and summarize the next steps towards TPC construction for CEPC physics and the detector TDR.

articleTitle: Radiography image quality and stability with Timepix-family detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Semiconductor detectors with Timepix-family chips exhibiting high spatial resolution, sensitivity and count rates in orders of $100 \times 10^{6}$ counts $\cdot \mathrm{mm}^{-2} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$ are an intriguing tool for radiography. The detectors utilizing CdTe and GaAs sensors, favoured for their sensitivity spanning broad energy spectra, face challenges due to crystal defects impairing image quality and stability. Two solutions mitigating image artefacts caused by crystal structure defects are introduced: a hardware approach based on pulsed bias voltage switching and a software solution based on adaptive flat field correction.

articleTitle: The H2M project: Porting the functionality of a hybrid readout chip into a monolithic 65 nm CMOS imaging process
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Monolithic active pixel sensors (MAPS) are attractive candidates for the next generation of vertex and tracking detectors for future lepton colliders. Especially an only recently accessible 65 nm CMOS imaging technology, that allows for higher logic density at lower power consumption compared to currently used imaging processes, is of high interest. To investigate this technology, explore the design challenges of porting a hybrid pixel detector architecture into a monolithic chip and to exercise the digital-on-top design methodology, the H2M (Hybrid-to-Monolithic) test chip has been developed and manufactured. It features a $64 \times 16$ pixel matrix with a pitch of $35 \times$ $35 \mu \mathrm{m} 2$, resulting in a total active area of approximately 1.25 mm 2. The sensitive pixel matrix is designed in the so called n-gap layout to optimise charge collection and to minimise charge sharing between pixels to boost the detection efficiency. This contribution introduces the first H2M chip, with a focus on the active pixel cell electronics and the different operation modes (time-of-arrival, time-over-threshold, counting and triggered) as well as an overview of the readout that is based on the Caribou DAQ system. Laboratory optimisation of the settings will be presented, including threshold equalisation. Test beam results, obtained with electrons at the DESY-II test beam, show a high detection efficiency of $\gt99 \%$ at moderate noise occupancy in the triggered mode. All other modes have also proven to be functional. In-pixel studies show a nonhomogeneous charge collection pattern, which will be discussed, alongside laser based laboratory measurements to confirm and understand findings at test beam.

articleTitle: Next Generation SOlar Neutron TRACking(SONTRAC) Instrument Encoded Readout Concept
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Next Generation (NextGen) SOlar Neutron TRACking (SONTRAC) instrument is based on a scintillating-fiber bundle and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). SONTRAC is designed to detect and track recoil protons from double scatter neutron events in the 20-200 MeV range to be able to measure solar and magnetospheric neutrons. The NexGen SONTRAC employs an encoded compressed readout that groups the SiPMs into fine and coarse segments and requires reconstruction. We present the concept and status for the NextGen SONTRAC instrument electronics for the encoded readout.

articleTitle: Temporal Response of GaAs:Cr X-ray Detector Under Intense Irradiation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study focuses on the temporal response of chromium-compensated gallium arsenide (GaAs:Cr) [1] under different X-ray fluxes. GaAs: Cr could be manufactured with mature technology and is regarded as a promising material used for detector in a photon counting CT (PCCT) due to its high electron mobility, high resistivity, and low cost. A common problem faced by various materials for photon counting detectors is polarization under high-flux X-ray irradiation. To validate the performance of GaAs:Cr, we tested the detector under different X-ray flux, energy spectra, and working bias voltage conditions. This study can help us evaluate the feasibility of GaAs material as a PCD and provide a guide to improve material properties and detector device design.

articleTitle: 16-Channel High-Precision FPGA-Based Detection Setup for High-Speed Time-Resolved Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The increasing accessibility of cutting-edge photon sources, such as the latest generation of FreeElectron Lasers (FELs) and synchrotron facilities, has substantially broadened research horizons, particularly in the investigation of chemical and physical dynamics like time-of-fligth mass spectrometry. Consequently, there is a need for a new generation of precise and flexible timeresolved acquisition systems. Two-dimensional particle detectors play a crucial role in this paradigm shift, evolving from mere pixelated imaging sensors to time-based devices capable of encoding the spatial coordinates of detected events into time delays, in addition to associating temporal information with each received event. In this sense, Cross Delay-Lines (CDLs) detectors play crucial roles. In addition to the information provided by the CDL, which can be obtained with a simple acquisition system based on 4-channel Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC), it becomes increasingly necessary to provide auxiliary measurement channels in order to acquire additional information to correlate with the CDL data. The acquisition electronics of these setups rely on TDCs based on Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), followed by Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) for data processing. However, the lack of adaptability and flexibility inherent in ASICs prompted us to explore a fully FPGA-based approach aimed at achieving outstanding precision at high measurement rate retaining the unparalleled flexibility that only an FPGA can offer. In the following work, we propose a system based on a 16-channel TDC with a precision of 12 ps r.m.s., 5 ns of dead-time, and 4 ps of integral non-linearity. In this regard, 4 channels of the TDC are connected to a CDL, achieving a spatial resolution up to $30 / 40 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ FWHM, while the remaining 12 channels are used for detecting auxiliary events to be correlated with the spatial information.

articleTitle: A Radiomic Cox Proportional Hazards Deep Neural Network Model to Predict Survival in Patients with Brain Metastases
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Estimates suggest that up to one-fifth of patients diagnosed with primary cancer will develop metastases to the brain. Metastases suggest a high cancer stage and are often an ominous sign. It is the physician’s responsibility to inform the patient of a rough estimate of survival times. A predictive model can help physicians make better, objective decisions and have accurate, informative interviews with the patient. We propose a new radiomic Cox proportional hazards model to predict survival in patients with brain metastases. We used open-source magnetic resonance imaging data from 200 patients from the Yale New Haven Health database, the Yale tumor board registry, and the Yale gamma knife registry to build the model. A multi-layer perceptron neural network is used to implement the Cox proportional hazards survival model. Our model performed well on a test set with a time-dependent concordance index of 0.874. It also demonstrated an integrated Brier score and integrated negative binomial log-likelihood of 0.02 and 0.065, respectively. A local interpretable model-agnostic explanations model indicated that first-order and neighboring gray-tone difference matrix features using local binary pattern and wavelet filters best explained model predictions. Our results suggest robust predictive accuracy using select hand-crafted radiomic features. Moreover, it demonstrated good reliability and precision in predicting survival over time. After adding imaging data from multiple centers and different imaging scanners, as well as further refining and fine-tuning, this model has the potential to be deployed in clinical settings to enhance and improve personalized medicine and patient care.

articleTitle: Time-Resolved X-Ray Luminescence Setup to Evaluate Thin Nanophotonic Super-Scintillator Samples
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Achieving sub-100 ps coincidence time resolution (CTR) in time-of-flight positron emission tomography could significantly improve image quality. Enhancing scintillation time constant and light yield is crucial for improving CTR. Recent developments in nanomaterials and nanophotonics offer promising methods to fine-tune optical and material properties at the nanoscale, maximizing light yield and scintillation properties. To provide an acceptable interaction rate for studying performance of thin nanoscintillators integrated with metallic plasmonic nanoparticles to substantially enhance scintillator radiative decay rate, we investigated a high flux tabletop x-ray ionizing radiation source. We developed a time-resolved x-ray luminescence measurement setup utilizing a sub-nanosecond, pulsed x-ray source along with microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (MCP-PMT) and avalanche photodiode (APD) array to identify potential requirements for evaluating performance of very thin nanoscintillators. With MCP-PMT, we conducted time-correlated single-photon counting and measured a decay constant of 227 ns from YAG:Ce. To accommodate the anticipated lower event rate from thin ($\lt1 \mu \mathrm{m}$) nanoscintillators, we studied the use of APD array. Benefiting from the higher spatial coverage of the APD array, we obtained higher contrast between x-ray-induced scintillation and the background. As the MCP-PMT provides superb timing and the APD array achieves higher sensitivity, choosing an alternative detector that can optimize these trade-offs will be important for characterizing light yield and decay time of nanoscintillators. By developing a dedicated detection system with a highly synchronized radiation source, we identified critical factors to consider when characterizing novel nanoscintillators. This gives us a basic experimental setup for understanding proposed photonic enhancements in scintillation with integration of plasmonic nanoparticles.

articleTitle: Data-driven respiratory motion correction of dual-gated cardiac PET/CT for coronary plaque imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Complex dual cardiac and respiratory movement is a challenge for PET/CT imaging of coronary plaques. When using dual-gating, respiratory motion correction (RMC) is essential to reduce blurring, but this is not yet available in vendor software. Moreover, existing vendor methods for RMC either ignore attenuation mismatch or require external devices to obtain matched PET and CT. This study investigates a method for cardiac PET/CT motion estimation and motion correction that uses gated PET in combination with cine-CT obtained without external monitoring. This methodology will be incorporated into an open-source software platform. 68GaDOTATATE PET/CINE-CT were acquired for 24 patients with identified coronary plaques. A respiratory motion model was derived from the cine-CT data after sorting via intensity analysis. Motion parameters were derived from respiratory gated non-attenuation corrected PET images. The resulting deformations were then applied to the CT data, which were used to obtain respiratory motion and attenuation corrected PET images. The effectiveness of our method was verified by comparing key metrics Root Mean Squared Error and Foot-to-head profiles in liver dome before and after the application of the motion model.

articleTitle: Multi-Energy Mapping of CZT Gamma-Ray Imagers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Coded-aperture gamma-ray imaging is an indirect imaging technique that allows one to create images of radioactive materials at radiation energies where lenses and mirrors are not practicable. The technique encodes the scene as a shadowgram onto a position-sensitive detector by positioning a shadow mask between the scene and the detector. When used with position-sensitive cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) detectors, it was found that sensitivity scans of an imager’s response to sources scanned across its field of view did not achieve the sensitivity expected. This has been traced to small distortions in the detector’s spatial response function that reports event locations laterally offset from the true location. These distortions are unique to individual CZT crystals and have been mapped using multi-pinhole masks and radiation sources at multiple energies. This paper reports the results of those mappings and how they have been used to correct the overall coded-aperture imaging response function.

articleTitle: The Effects of Two Confounding Variables on Radiomic Features in PET Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Medical imaging is crucial for diagnosing and treating cancer. Radiologists and clinicians assess medical images visually. Although medical images contain a wealth of information, they have not yet been fully explored to their full potential. Utilizing “radiomic features” through texture analysis can be one avenue for this exploration. Traditionally, texture features are calculated using a complex workflow that introduces many confounding variables, such as acquisition imaging time (post radiopharmaceutical administration) and variability in the method of delineating region of interest (ROI). To this end, we suggest evaluating the impact of these two parameters on the stability of radiomic features using the coefficient of variation. Using the coefficient of variation for feature consideration can serve as a promising method to assess parameter redundancy in radiomics models. For this purpose, PET images of a phantom with 4 tumors inserts with different level of heterogeneity were binned into different acquisition times, 20 minutes intervals from 0 to 80 minutes post injection. The impact of variation in segmentation volume was also explored by incrementally increasing contour size for each tumor inserts. Seventy-eight radiomic features were extracted for analysis. The stability of features measured by the coefficient of variation when considering post injection time was 5.8; for contour size this value was 14.9. From this analysis we conclude that both post injection imaging time and contour size (segmentation volume) affect the measurement of radiomic features and that texture features are less stable to varying contour size than to varying acquisition time.

articleTitle: The ScIDEP Muon Radiography Project at the Egyptian Pyramid of Khafre
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ScIDEP (Scintillator Imaging Detector for the Egyptian Pyramids) Collaboration is constructing a new muon telescope based on scintillator technology to investigate with the cosmic-ray muon-based muography technique the internal structure of the Egyptian Pyramid of Khafre at Giza near Cairo. Although slightly smaller than the Great Pyramid, the known internal structure of the Khafre Pyramid appears to be much simpler, which could point to the existence of yet unknown hidden rooms or structures inside this monument. The first and only muography campaigns conducted at this pyramid were actually performed already in the 1970s by Alvarez et al. but did not, at that time, reveal any hidden structures. The ScIDEP project aims to install a new muon telescope either inside the king’s burial chamber, located at the base of the pyramid, or on the outside of the pyramid. The initial base detector comprises two plastic scintillator planes measuring $61 \times 61 \times 2 \mathrm{~cm} 3$ each, with wavelength shifting fibers embedded orthogonally in both faces to capture X-Y hit information for the muon trajectory reconstruction. The scintillation light is measured by Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) connected to each individual fiber. The first version of the data-acquisition system is based on the commercial CAEN DT5550W module equipped with Petiroc2A-ASIC boards. In addition, custom-made readout electronics based on Weeroc ASICs in combination with FPGAs is under development. Simultaneously, a detailed Geant4-based simulation framework for the full setup is being developed, including a very detailed detector model and a CAD model of the pyramid containing its currently known internal structure. The cosmic ray spectrum is derived from either the CRY or EcoMug cosmic muon generator coupled to the Geant4 code. An overview of the project is provided, including the detector prototyping studies, the development of the data-acquisition system and the development of the detailed simulation framework.

articleTitle: Designing a Compact API System for 3D Compositional Object Imaging and Mapping
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma Reality Inc. is designing a compact Associated Particle Imaging system capable of real-time 3D mapping the isotopic composition of materials. Advancements in DT-API neutron generators by companies like Adelphi, now make compact systems that can be deployed on robotic platforms possible. We have developed Geant4 simulations to demonstrate the ability to image material objects underground and inside of objects. We will present initial results from simulations showing the ability to image multiple distinct objects and the ability to differentiate those objects from surrounding clutter objects. We will provide updates on designing and building a compact API system capable of 3D imaging objects and their material compositions. We will provide updates on optimizing systematic effects to improve signal-to-noise ratio and scan times. Our goal is to build an API system with compact components, including detectors, readout electronics, neutron generator and controls to enable a range of dynamic deployment options.

articleTitle: Skew Error Mitigation Technique for Pulse-Train Time Amplifier Used in Radiation Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents a design of an advanced pulse-train time amplifier (A-PTTA) that utilizes an active off-state time control to minimize the skew error and conversion rate in the radiation environments. Three D-flip-flops are employed to provide an overlap code (O-code), determining whether overlap occurs between the first input pulse and subsequent pulses. The output of the time amplifier is determined by selecting one of the delay chains based on the O-code. The proposed A-PTTA was verified using an electronic design automation tool, demonstrating the maximum improvement of 70% in conversion time. The proposed circuit was fabricated using general-purpose $0.18 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ CMOS technology, and the test results will be discussed at the conference.

articleTitle: Design and Initial Experimental Evaluation of the Alpha-SPECT: A Full-Body Clinical SPECT System with High-Performance CZT Imaging Spectrometers and Micro-Rotating Dual-Aperture Collimation for Imaging Therapeutic Radionuclides
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this paper, we report the design, development, and initial experimental evaluation of the Alpha-SPECT system, a full-body clinical SPECT scanner equipped with state-of-art CZT imaging spectrometers ideally suited to simultaneous imaging of therapeutic alpha-emitters (e.g., Ac-225, Ra-223, Lu-177, etc.) and their daughters (e.g., Fr.221, At-217, Bi-213, and Po-213 from the decay of Ac-225) in patients. Besides the potential for imaging alpha-labeled radiopharmaceutical therapy (a-RPT), the Alpha-SPECT system is intended to be a general-purpose clinical SPECT scanner for a wide variety of diagnostic and therapeutic applications. The system is equipped with a dual-aperture collimator that is installed on a CT-scanner-derived rotational gantry to allow the real-time switching between the two aperture configurations, as well as micro-swing of aperture in front of the CZT detectors with a sub- 15 mm precision to provide a variable FOV of 20-50 cm diameter and facilitate super-resolution sampling for further improved imagign resolution.

articleTitle: A DOI-TOF Detector Prototype based On U-shaped LYSO crystal and Ultrafast Laser Processing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The NeuroEXPLORER (NX), developed by Yale, UC Davis, and United Imaging, have successfully demonstrated fine spatial resolution, high sensitivity. We propose a novel U-shaped single-ended light-sharing detector with discrete depth of interaction (DOI) and time-of-flight (TOF) capabilities, achieved through Ultrafast Laser Processing technique. The combination of U-shaped LYSO crystals with Ultrafast Laser Processing is a promising approach, offering potential for high geometrical accuracy, reduced fabrication costs, and the elimination of the need for a complex DOI calibration process. We validate the feasibility of the discrete DOI capability by applying Ultrafast Laser Processing to segment transparent LYSO crystal bars into 2, 3, and 4 segments. A Monte Carlo (MC) simulation tool, encompassing scintillation, light transmission, and SiPM response processing, is constructed. We analyze the main factors affecting the performance of U-shaped crystals with Ultrafast Laser Processing by simulation and experimental comparison, and discuss the optimization of Ultrafast Laser Processing on LYSO to achieve simultaneous fine TOF and DOI resolution. Experimental results indicate that a fine discrete DOI resolution can be achieved without a DOI calibration process for both 2, 3, and 4 segments configurations. The measured TOF resolution at the micro-block level (four U-shaped LYSO slabs read by 22 array of 3mm SiPMs) was 186 ps and 205 ps for 2, 3 segments, respectively. Furthermore, by optimize the Ultrafast Laser Processing parameters, such as the density of microvoids and uniformity, a system with discrete DOI capability and sub-200 ps TOF resolution can be constructed.

articleTitle: Enhancing Overall Survival Prediction in Head and Neck Cancer with CT Peritumoral Radiomics and Machine Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Predicting the prognosis after treatment could be beneficial for patient selection and treatment optimization of head and neck malignancies. Machine learning (ML) proved to have the potential to predict overall survival after treatment using imaging textures and radiomics features extracted from gross tumoral volume (GTV). However, medical images from peritumoral tissue may contain information that enhances further the prediction power. The aim of this study was to explore possible improvements in ML algorithms using peritumoral tissue radiomics on a large-scale data. A total number of 2926 head and neck CT images and GTV segmentation pairs from the RadCure dataset (2327 males, and 599 females) were collected. A total of 107 radiomic features, including first order, shape, and textures were extracted from CT images on GTV segmentations and GTVs dilated by a margin varying from 1 to 22 mm with 3 mm steps using PyRadiomics python library. These nine different feature sets were fed to five different models after undergoing six feature selection (FS) methods to predict the overall survival in a ten-fold data split strategy. The model performance was measured in terms of Concordance index (C-Index). The ten-folds overall C-Index averaged over all FS and models were $0.64 \pm 0.023,0.65 \pm 0.02,0.65 \pm 0.03,0.65 \pm 0.03,0.66 \pm 0.03$, $0.66 \pm 0.03,0.67 \pm 0.03,0.67 \pm 0.03,0.68 \pm 0.02$ for GTV with no dilation, $1,3,4,7,10,13,16,19$, and 22 mm dilations respectively. We investigated the added value of peritumoral radiomics in the prediction of overall survival using 30 combinations of FS and models and 9 different inputs. Our results revealed the importance of tissues surrounding GTV CT radiomics in head and neck cancer prognosis prediction using ML algorithms.

articleTitle: Self-Supervised Deep Learned 3D Filtered Backprojection for Image Reconstruction Objectives with a Poisson Likelihood
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Filtered backprojection (FBP) is a widely known direct one-step PET reconstruction method that has been surpassed by alternative iterative methods with superior physics and noise modelling. However, iterative image reconstruction for fully 3D sinogram data can be computationally demanding. With the recent arrival of long axial field of view PET scanners, direct (non- iterative) deep learning (DL) based approaches have gained appeal due to their speed advantage when dealing with large datasets. Most data-driven DL based reconstruction methods to date have primarily used supervised learning for optimisation; if these methods were to be used on patients who are outliers of the training set, erroneous reconstructions could occur. In contrast, with this work we propose a model that uses self-supervised DL to model the filtering process within FBP to execute 3D reconstructions, while using a Poisson noise model and a more general forward model than just the Radon transform. Preliminary experiments of bias-variance trade-off show comparable results with our method against OSEM when reconstructing noisy data. The methodology will need expanding to utilise fully 3D data, explore generalisation of the learned filters, investigate the degree of self-supervised fine tuning, and explore other maximum a posteriori objective functions. These optimisations could result in overall speed benefits for training and final image reconstruction. Then, the next steps would be to use real-patient data to compare the reconstruction quality and speed of our method to that of vendor supplied reconstruction methods and state-of-the-art data-driven methods.

articleTitle: Neural Network-Asissted Dual-time-window Acquisition: Modeling Incomplete Input Functions for Patlak Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) imaging is an advanced molecular imaging technique that provides dynamic process of metabolism. Compared to static imaging, the net influx rate K<inf>i</inf> derived from dynamic imaging has shown better specificity under similar sensitivity for cancer detection, making it clinically valuable. In dynamic modeling analysis, a necessary requirement is measuring the time-activity curve (TAC) in arterial plasma as input function (IF) across the entire process. However, the tedious process hinder the application of dynamic imaging in clinical practice. Our study leverages the nonlinear, universal approximation capabilities of neural networks to enhance the estimation of incomplete input functions (IFs) through a multi-branch sampling method. By adding a 3min short scan after tracer injection, this approach not only abbreviates the scan protocol but also enables accurate Patlak analysis.

articleTitle: A novel standalone muon drift-tube trigger for the ATLAS HL-LHC upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The goal for the first level muon trigger of the ATLAS experiment at the High-Luminosity LHC is an unprescaled 20 GeV single muon trigger. The required selectivity is achieved by combining the coarse tracking information of the fast trigger RPC and TGC chambers with the precision tracking information from up to 400 times slower muon drift-tube (MDT) chambers.The baseline muon trigger algorithm utilises the fast trigger chambers for the precise determination of the bunch crossing reference time and for the determination of MDT detector regions from which the MDT hits are extracted and further processed.We propose here for the first time a next generation MDT trigger designed for standalone operation at the ATLAS HL-LHC or future hadron colliders. This marks a paradigm shift, addressing challenges stemming from the absence of a pre-trigger from the fast trigger chambers. These challenges consist in the accurate identification of event bunch crossings and the execution of pattern recognition throughout the entire MDT chamber volume. As for the baseline option approach, this new design must also operate within a stringent latency budget, while delivering good trigger performance, in terms of reconstruction efficiency, rate reduction, and momentum resolution.This paper introduces the inaugural design of the standalone MDT trigger, implemented in VHDL firmware for the Xilinx Virtex Ultrascale+ VU13P FPGA, currently deployed on the ATLAS MDT Trigger Processor prototype hardware. The implementation demonstrates reasonable resource utilisation, and the feasibility to implement such a system already at the present stage, without requiring any hardware modification.

articleTitle: Unlocking Diamond’s Potential Beyond Charge Collection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Diamond is an ideal solid-state detector material for harsh radiation environments. Historically, diamond detectors were operated in the charge-collection mode.
