As a result, their application in safeguards has stalled because of the small device size and availability. We present a new approach using diamond’s excellent scintillation properties as a detector for both fast and thermal neutrons. By integrating polycrystalline diamond (layers, powders, films) acting as a scintillator detector of charged particles, and thin layers of material containing 6Li or 10B, diamond acts as an efficient neutron detector. Photodetectors such as SiPMs, APDs, or PMTs are used to capture the scintillation light. This proven but not practically used approach utilizes inexpensive, readily available diamond material and is suitable for making thermal and fast neutron detectors. The method of utilizing scintillation from diamond offers great versatility, potential for superior radiation tolerance, large effective areas (approaching 100% efficiency for thermal neutrons), and easier production compared to conventional Si-based detectors.

articleTitle: Calculation of Response Matrices for GRID CubeSat Gamma-ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Gamma-Ray Integrated Detectors (GRID) mission aims to monitor high energy transients in space with multiple CubeSats carrying compact gamma-ray detectors as payloads. Reconstructing the energy spectra of detected bursts from the measured detector output energies requires detailed knowledge of the detector response characteristics, which are represented by response matrices. We calculate the response matrices for each GRID detector that has been launched and verify their accuracy using in-orbit data. In this work, Monte Carlo simulations with Geant4 are employed to calculate the energy deposition of gamma-ray photons in the detectors under various conditions. The response matrices are then generated by adjusting the simulation results based on the energy resolution obtained from on-ground calibrations. In addition, we establish a database of response matrices designed for interpolation, enabling efficient generation of matrices for any incident direction. The generated response matrices are verified through spectra fittings of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) observed by GRID detectors in orbit. Building on the calculation method described above, we provide a response matrix generation tool alongside the release of GRID scientific data, enabling convenient scientific analysis for the GRID mission.

articleTitle: MOSkin dosimetryfor very high-energy electron FLASHat Australian Synchrotron PEER.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: FLASH radiotherapy (RT) is an emerging cancer treatment modality that utilises much higher dose rates than conventional RT [1]. Delivering radiation with ultra-high dose rates (UHDR) has been shown to spare healthy tissue while providing an equal or greater dose to the tumour. Current research suggests the use of very high-energy electrons can provide further benefits, such as treatment of deep-seated tumours [2]. The MOSkin detector, designed at the Centre for Medical Radiation Physics at University of Wollongong is used in conventional radiotherapy and considered dose-rate independent over a limited range. The Australian Synchrotron uses a linac to inject pulsed 100 MeV electrons, with expected dose rates of $10^{7} \mathrm{~Gy} / \mathrm{s}$. The linac lacks beam scanning or positioning equipment so an array of five detectors was designed, built, and manually positione. An x-ray intensifier screen was positioned behind the array and imaged with a camera, to collect spatial data and relative beam intensity between pulses. 13 beam currents were used to deliver 300 pC pulses from 20 ns to 400 ns in length. With estimated dose rates as high as $2.5 \times 10^{7}$ Gy/s, a drop off in response was observed at beam currents below 2 mA. Beam profiles were created using the camera data to determine relative intensity between pulses at the detector’s estimated location. The amplitude was extracted from the distributions and normalised to 1, which enabled plotting against normalised MOSkin data to evaluate detector response against the charge delivered. The MOSkin response is consistent with the x-ray intensifier screen and indicates pulses are being delivered to the experimental stage at lower beam current than that measured by the linac diagnostics. The experiment has shown that further investigation is justified as the MOSkin appears suitable for dosimetry in UHDR VHEE environments. Future experiments will be conducted to gain better spatial information as well as an independent measurement of dose.

articleTitle: Study of resolution along a 10 cm length LYSO crystal with dual-ended SiPM readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The concept of using long scintillation crystals arranged axially for small animal PET was proposed over 10 years ago. This configuration can significantly reduce the number of photodetectors and electronics. However, the best-reported axial resolution was around 1.5 mm standard deviation, with variation along the length; this was inferior to state-of-the-art small animal PET scanners. With the advent of advanced photodetectors, electronics, and algorithms, we revisit this concept and aim to achieve an axial resolution of sub-millimeter for a 100 mm length LYSO crystal element.Using Geant4, the simulation setup involved a 100 mm length LYSO crystal element optically coupled to Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) at each end. Key optical properties like the refractive index, scintillation yield, and absorption length were considered. A beam of 511 keV annihilation photons irradiated the side of the crystal element at a step size of 0.2 mm. After selecting the photopeak events at each position, two million samples were acquired for analysis.A neural network with two hidden layers was used to estimate interaction position, achieving an average spatial resolution of 0.69 mm standard deviation, highly consistent with the theoretical limit calculated via the Cramer-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB) of 0.65 mm.Results indicated improved spatial resolution for interaction occurring along a long crystal element and validated the neural network’s effectiveness in approximating the theoretical resolution limit. Future efforts will focus on experimental validation and detector optimization.

articleTitle: Long-term stability study of CsPbBr3 for room temperature semiconductor detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cesium lead bromide (CLB) is a leading candidate for the next generation of room temperature semiconductor detectors. We recently improved the purification and crystal growth process to obtain high quality crystals with excellent gamma spectroscopy performance. Even though new records in the performance of fabricated devices are consistently set, instability in long-term performance is a major challenge in the commercialization of CLB. This is due to the reactivity of halide ions with metal electrodes, a common issue among halide semiconductors. An extensive investigation of electrode materials has been conducted to achieve the best electrode materials for CLB. In this study, we report progress in crystal growth and the long-term performance of fabricated devices with the Schottky barrier operated under reverse biasing. A $10 \times 10 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}$ pixelated device exhibits excellent energy resolution of $2.1 \%$ FWHM at 662 keV without depth correction. For long-term stability, a device with Pb anode performed stable for over a month.

articleTitle: Effect of inter-crystal scattering events on the spatial resolution of SIAT aPET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The probability of the inter-crystal scattering (ICS) events for 511 keV gamma rays in all current scintillation crystals is high and the ICS events degrade the spatial resolution of PET scanners, especially for the small animal PET scanners with high spatial resolution. In this work, the effects of the ICS events on the spatial resolution and image quality of SIAT aPET that uses high resolution dual-ended readout detectors were investigated by imaging a point source, two Derenzo phantoms, and an image quality phantom. Raw-data mode was used during the data acquisition. The ICS events were removed by selecting only events falling to a small circular region around the spot of each crystal in the flood histogram of the detector. The images were reconstructed by using an ordered subsets expectation maximization (OSEM) algorithm with point spread function (PSF) modeling. First, the spatial resolution of the scanner was evaluated by using a Na-22 point source placed at center axial field of view (FOV) with different radial offsets. Then, the image quality of the scanner was evaluated by using two Derenzo phantoms and a NEMA image quality phantom. The spatial resolutions obtained using the data with the ICS events were ∼ 20% worse than that obtained without the ICS events. The resolvability of the 1.0 mm diameter rods was improved by ∼40% and 60% when the ICS events were rejected for the standard and small Derenzo phantom images, respectively. The contrast recovery coefficients of the hot rods of all diameters were significantly improved, but the signal-to-noise ratio of the uniform region was significantly reduced for the image quality phantom when the ICS events were rejected.

articleTitle: Imaging Studies using PhytoPET, a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanner developed for Plant Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Utilizing Positron Emission Tomography-Computed Tomography (PET-CT) for three-dimensional imaging of plant dynamic rhizosphere phenomena presents a promising avenue for quantitative analysis of soil structure challenges. Integrating such imaging technology into Earth System Models (ESMs) could enhance the precision of soil structure data. Here, we are reporting the evaluation of PhytoPET, a PET scanner developed at the Thomas Jefferson National Accelerator Facility, designed for studying rhizosphere dynamics. PhytoPET features adaptable PET detector configurations, including 5 cm x 5 cm Hamamatsu H8500 position-sensitive photomultiplier tubes (PMT) coupled to $48 \times 48$ LYSO:Ce scintillator arrays, with individual pixel dimensions of $1 \mathrm{~mm} \times 1 \mathrm{~mm} \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}$. To assess and optimize PhytoPET’s imaging performance, three data sets were acquired and reconstructed for mini-resolution phantom scans. These included scenarios without experimental sensitivity maps, with detector sensitivity map correction using experimental data, and with multi-angle scanning to mitigate limited-angle tomography artifacts present due to the relatively large gaps between detectors. The average peak-to-valley ratio (PVR) for selected line profile data with analytical sensitivity, experimental sensitivity, and experimental sensitivity correction plus multi-angle scanning were measured to be 1.90, 1.93, and 3.0, respectively. Reconstructed images from all scenarios are presented, showing that experimental sensitivity map correction combined with multi-angle scanning outperforms the other two approaches.

articleTitle: Comprehensive Evaluation of the novel SiPM in a 110 nm CMOS process
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: RAYQUANT Ltd. has recently developed a novel SiPM in the 110 nm CMOS process with an area ranging between $1 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ and $16 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. In this paper we present the first evaluation of the properties of these sensors and validate their potential application to the readout of scintillation detectors. These sensors achieved a photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 60% at 420 nm with a dark count rate of $170 \mathrm{kcps} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$. We measured an energy resolution of 11.0% in response to 511 keV by reading out the scintillation light of a LySO crystal. The novel SiPMs are obtained at a CMOS process node and are thus compatible with the development of on-chip integrated sensors.

articleTitle: Exploring Lead-Free Perovskite-Inspired Materials as Pressed Pellets for X-ray Detector Application
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Highly sensitive X-ray detectors based on materials containing high atomic-number elements, such as metal halide perovskites (MHPs), would enable reduced dose rates, which is vital for medical applications. However, the instability and the potential toxicity of conventional lead-based MHPs constitute a challenge for commercialization, which prompts the use of alternative perovskite inspired materials based on less toxic elements, such as bismuth and silver to replace lead. Furthermore, to enable large-area, highperformance, detectors, it is paramount to employ methods to produce high-quality, millimetre-thick, layers of the detector material, which currently remains a challenge for MHPs. In this work, different lead-free, perovskite-inspired, materials, which include fully inorganic compounds, such as the double perovskite Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf>, as well as novel organic-inorganic ones were investigated as X-ray detectors. The materials were synthesized using ball-milling and polycrystalline pellets produced through scalable cold isostatic-pressing were used to assemble X-ray detectors. X-ray-based spectroscopic and diffraction methods were used to determine the composition and structural properties of the pellets. The detector performance was evaluated by measuring the photocurrent response under X-ray illumination. The results show that the selection of composition, additives, different post-treatment methods of the pellets as well as device architecture significantly affect the properties, potentially improving detector performance for various applications. The obtained sensitivities and detection limits are comparable to or even higher than those reported for similar perovskite-inspired materials. The work demonstrates that the materials are very promising, and could thus pave the way for future application of these materials as X-ray detectors.

articleTitle: Data Correction and Imaging Studies for PETCoil: A Second-Generation RF-Penetrable Brain TOF-PET Insert for Simultaneous PET/MRI
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A dedicated Positron Emission Tomography (PET) system optimized for organ imaging offers compact yet highly sensitive geometries, enabling superior spatial resolution and image signal-to-noise ratios (SNR). The Molecular Imaging Instrumentation Laboratory (MIIL) at Stanford is currently developing the PETCoil Gen II, a magnetic resonance (MR) compatible radio-frequency (RF)-penetrable Time of Flight Positron Emission Tomography (TOF-PET) a brain-dedicated PET insert for simultaneous PET/MR imaging. This study presents some key developments to prepare PETCoil Gen II for clinical use, including ongoing data correction algorithm development to improve image quality and accuracy. We assess the accuracy and impact of data corrections, including normalization, random subtraction, and timing skew correction. Imaging performance is evaluated through the acquisition and reconstruction of resolution and Hoffman brain phantom images, both with and without TOF information incorporated. A spatial resolution of $\leq 2.8 \mathrm{~mm}$, along with energy and coincidence timing resolutions (CTR) of 11.74 ± 0.03% full-width-half-maximum (FWHM) and $238 \pm 0.5 \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM, respectively, was observed. The incorporation of TOF information yields a significant SNR increase, with TOF achieving an initial 1.34-fold enhancement compared to non-TOF imaging. Similarly, for the 3-D Hoffman Brain phantom, measured SNR of the TOF-reconstructed images was 29.47, 1.32 times higher than non-TOF (22.44). Additionally, contrast to noise ratio (CNR) for TOF and non-TOF reconstructed images were measured as 17.18 and 13.10 respectively, indicatinga 1.31-fold improvement with TOF.

articleTitle: Direct Conversion Flat Panel Detector Utilizing TlBr Film for X-ray Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The direct conversion Flat Panel Detectors (FPDs) have garnered extensive attention in X-ray imaging due to its enhanced image quality. In this study, a novel direct conversion FPD using Thallium Bromide (TlBr) film is developed and characterized. TlBr film, with a thickness of $25 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and sensitive area of $29.61 \times 39.48 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$, was deposited using the evaporation method. A pixelated sensor matrix, featuring $168 \times 126$ pixels with a pixel size of $235 \times 235 \mu^{2}$, was developed using Low-Temperature Polysilicon Thin-Film Transistor (LTPS TFT) technology. Spatial resolution was evaluated using the slanted edge method with the TlBr layer biased at 1.00 V, capturing 100 frames for each experiment. The X-ray tube was operated at a voltage range of 25.0 kV to 35.0 kV with a constant current of 2.00 mA. The imaging performance of the TlBr FPD was assessed by imaging an anchovy object with a TlBr bias voltage of 0.75 V, capturing 1000 frames. The X-ray tube was operated at 23.0 kV with a current of 0.75 mA. The spatial resolution, determined from the Line Spread Function (LSF) profile, ranged from 222 to $280 \mu \mathrm{m}$ Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM), constrained by the pixel size. In the X-ray imaging demonstration, the shape and structure of the anchovy were distinctly discerned. TlBr FPDs hold promising potential as room temperature X-ray imagers for both industrial and medical applications.

articleTitle: MRI-guided PET reconstruction using a convergent plug-and-play approach
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dual modality Positron Emission Tomography (PET)/Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) systems provide seamless hardware-based image coregistration, making MRI-guided PET reconstruction a natural approach. In this work, we investigate the adaptability of the plug-and-play (PnP) paradigm for MRI-guided PET reconstruction. Inspired by proximal optimization algorithms and fixed point theory, the PnP approach proposes to replace the proximity operator of the regularization with a more general denoiser. Precisely, we integrate a deep denoiser - a DRUnet - into the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) algorithm such that convergence of the iterates to a controlled set of fixed points is ensured. Results on simulated [18F]-FDG PET scans demonstrate that multibranch architectures are more compatible with the PnP framework than multichannel architectures and that the PnP fixed-point solutions have high likelihood and a lower mean squared error than the reconstruction obtained with a classical MRI-guided Bowsher regularization and without MRI guidance.

articleTitle: Data-driven Gating for PET Using a Population-based Encoder
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Respiratory motion is one of the main sources of motion artifacts in positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. In a previous study, we proposed a data-driven approach using an unsupervised deep clustering network that employs an autoencoder (AE) trained with patient-specific short-frame images to extract latent features for respiratory gating. The extracted latent vectors could subsequently be clustered for automatic gating, resulting in better performance than traditional phase gating. However, the patient-specific training is time consuming. In this work, we investigate a new, population-based AE that is pre-trained using an ensemble of patient data and compared it with the patient-specific AE. Once pre-trained, the population-based AE does not require any patient-specific training and thus reduce the computation time for respiratory gating. Experiment results show that a pre-trained AE with $N=42$ patients training dataset can achieve the same performance as the on-the-fly AE

articleTitle: Target Design and Optimizations for Spent Fuel Transmutation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: There are six long-lived fission products (LLFPs) identified in nuclear spent fuel, which are responsible for at least 99% of the long-term radio-toxicity once actinide recycling has been completed. This paper discusses the feasibility of using proton beams to transmute the LLFPs into shorter-lived or stable isotopes. Although long-term storage for high-level waste would still be required, transmuting the LLFPs can reduce the volume of waste material stored. PHITS, a Monte Carlo transport code, is utilized to computationally model the interactions between the LLFP materials and the proton beam. PHITS is used in this paper to estimate the flux-energy spectrum and number of atoms irradiated in the LLFP target when interacting with the beam. This data is then post-processed in a 0-dimensional analysis in FISPACT to estimate the transmutation rate for each LLFP. Analysis of the performance of commercial cyclotrons with energies of 18-70 MeV has shown that transmutation rates will increase when the proton beam energy is increased. A cyclotron with a beam current of 10 mA and beam energy of 70 MeV running continuously can transmute 7.51 ± 1.19 g/year of technetium-99. However, technetium-99 is produced at around a rate of 1kg/year inside a 1 GW reactor, suggesting that commercial cyclotrons are not viable for transmutation purposes. Studies are ongoing on modeling 1000 MeV proton beams to cause spallation reactions inside the LLFP targets. The spallation process burns the LLFP target while producing many secondary neutrons that can be further used for transmuting the LLFPs. A preliminary analysis suggests that a 1000 MeV beam with a 10 mA current can transmute around 1kg/year of technetium-99 due to nuclear reactions without accounting for spallation reactions.

articleTitle: Enhancing the time resolution for discriminating between multiple contrast agents using 2-dimensional SiPM-based photon counting CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon counting (PC) detectors revolutionize medical CT imaging by precisely tallying individual photons and simultaneously gauging their energy, enabling tailored multi-energy imaging. This capability proves invaluable in discriminating between contrast agents based on their distinct energy signatures, elevating their potential as future tools for drug delivery systems. An established SiPM-based PC-CT, combining a multi-pixel photon counter (MPPC) array with a yttrium-gadolinium-aluminum-gallium garnet (YGAG) scintillator array has been expanded from a 1-dimensional to a 2-dimensional configuration, significantly reducing imaging time and enhancing temporal resolution. The 2-dimensional PCCT utilizes a 256-channel pixel array, with a pixel size of 1 × 1 mm2, arranged in a 16 × 16 configuration. Signal processing involves four large-scale integrated circuit boards, with each board handling signals from 64 channels across six energy thresholds. Concentration estimation using multiple-energy CT images obtained with a 2-dimensional PC-CT system of iodine and gadolinium mixture samples, followed by material decomposition of each composition, was successfully conducted. As a result, 3-dimensional visualization of sample concentration estimation was achieved. The time resolution increases more than 10 times faster compared to the 1-dimensional system due to the simplicity of sample rotation with the 2-dimensional detector in similar sample and configuration. Additionally, a simple demonstration of dynamic imaging was obtained, simulating the significant potential of the 2-dimensional PCCT system for future clinical imaging applications.

articleTitle: Automated in-silico Phantoms for Atherosclerotic Plaque Classification Models from Spectral CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a novel approach to study atherosclerotic plaque classification models in spectral computed tomography. We propose an end-to-end pipeline for automatically generated, realistic synthetic phantoms of coronary and carotid plaques. Motivated by the need for a more precise coronary artery disease diagnosis, we aim to overcome current limitations such as inaccurate tissue quantification capabilities by conventional methods and insufficient real-world data availability for model validation. The phantoms from our pipeline are based on clinically validated parameters and material compositions to mimic real anatomical conditions. Our approach leverages a state-of-the-art, physics-based ray-tracing framework for simulated data acquisition, which is then processed using calibrated reconstruction software to ensure highly realistic simulated imaging. We conduct an experimental validation consisting of qualitative and quantitative analyses. Comparing signal-to-noise ratio and contrast-to-noise ratio shows similar values for both synthetic and real-world data. The clinical impact of this work is relevant, as it may enable the bootstrapping of deep learning models for plaque classification, potentially enhancing diagnostic accuracy and allow more differentiated treatment strategies.

articleTitle: Self-Aware, Communicating and Cognitive Digital Twins for Cybernetic Detector Technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A digital twin concept [1] is presented for enhancing digital capabilities of radiation detection equipment. The twin transforms common detector into cybernetic units or cybernetic spectroscopy detectors (CSD). Here the term cybernetic refers to a sensorial unit that seamlessly integrates into large-scale detection solutions. It interacts, communicates and even controls other detectors or components, while providing models and data for the interplay with these units. Such a smart detector is elementary for realising portal solutions or robotic process automation (RPA). The paper presents an architecture to implement such a system. Its build upon a digital twin that a) contains knowledge models [2] about itself and its surrounding environment, b) runs a communication system that allows rapid data streaming and slow batch processing, thus fulfiiling the definitions of the lambda-architecture [3] and c) is cognitive, meaning it has access to predictive models [4], [5], that extend its view on the environment and the own state. With this architecture, detectors can be easily swapped or integrated into complex, overarching technical solutions. Often, the detectors need to communicate and correspond with several other agents, like annunciators, actuators like robot arms or retrieve additional information from secondary sensors.Several pilot demonstrations are presented, including a vehicle based mobile search system and fixed portal installation with more than 10 detector units. It is also shown, how the digital twin is combined with further automation infrastructure such as occupancy sensors, camera and motion tracking and supplementary data streams, e.g. from GPS localizers.

articleTitle: Monte-Carlo-Informed Shape Learning for Gain Shift Correction based on LaBr3:Ce,Sr Intrinsic Activity
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Coincidences in La-138 are simulated with the Monte-Carlo solver tRAYcy, modelling the intrinsic activity $\mathrm{LaBr3}: \mathrm{Ce}, \mathrm{Sr}$ detector [1] and the influences of additional potassium K-40. Based on this data, a decision tree regressor [2] is trained to estimate a numerical value for contribution of additional K-40, to improve retrieval of the peak position. Lanthanum bromide, typically doped with Cerium or Strontium ($\left.\mathrm{LaBr}_{3}: \mathrm{Ce}, \mathrm{Sr}\right)$ has become a versatile detector material in the high resolution market of scintillators. With an FWHM often better than 3%, the material is a notable attractor for homeland security applications [3]. Due to its intrinsic activity of La-138 [4], this scintillator shows a complex background radiation spectrum containing many features - a fact thoroughly discussed in literature. Some users understand this background radiation as distortion, yet it is also known to be exploitable for automatic calibration against peak shifts. The most prominent feature of the LaBr3:Ce,Sr intrinsic background is a peak structure at between 1435 keV and 1468 keV. It is due to a coincidence of the La-138 gamma line at 1435.7 keV and its series of X-rays emitted between 4 keV and 37 keV. The 1460 keV gamma line of natural K-40 usually overlaps with this LaBr3 structure, even increasing the complexity of the spectroscopic structure. The paper presents a novel technique that decomposes the overlapping to find an accurate gain prediction for stabilisation. The proposed decision tree uses the Gini-Impurity as measure for splitting its nodes and yields reasonable performance on finding the right K-40 amount just based on shape analysis. The stabilisation is further tested with a detector in a laboratory climate chamber during temperature ramps to emulate real-life usage e.g. for nuclear security scenarios.

articleTitle: Graphene-Silicon Charge Amplifier for Nuclear Science Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In various nuclear science experiments, sensors equipped with diode-based detectors, such as High Purity Germanium detectors, play a central role. These detectors generate faint, high-impedance signals that necessitate specialized amplifiers for voltage conversion. Operational amplifiers, serving as integrators, efficiently handle this task by converting charge pulses into voltage pulses and subsequently amplifying them with low impedance output amplifiers. Charge Sensitive Amplifiers (CSA), often comprising multiple stages, employ high-gain, low-noise transistors like FETs or JFETs in the initial stage to preserve signal integrity. The subsequent stage acts as a low-impedance buffer to ensure successful signal transmission. To mitigate noise, typical techniques such as employing low-noise transistors and implementing active refrigeration are utilized. This study advocates for the substitution of traditional transistors with Graphene Field Effect Transistors (GFETs) in charge amplifiers. GFETs harness graphene’s superior electrical and thermal conductivity, resulting in reduced resistance losses and improved heat dissipation compared to silicon. Moreover, GFETs exhibit higher carrier mobility than regular FETs. Graphene’s zero-gap semiconductor nature enables the adjustment of the Dirac point via the top gate, akin to the threshold voltage in conventional FETs. The mobility of GFETs typically ranges between 500 to $5000 \ \mathrm{cm}^{2} \mathrm{V}^{-1} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$, influenced by factors such as graphene purity and substrate material.

articleTitle: PIN photodiodes made of cascade perovskite single crystals for gamma-ray detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We reported a new structure of PIN photodiodes made of solution-processed perovskite single crystals ($\mathrm{MAPbX}_{3}, \mathrm{MA}=\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{NH}_{3}, \mathrm{X}=\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}$) for gamma-ray detection. To decrease the dark current of the PIN photodiodes by energy barriers, we choose 1 mm -thickness Bi-doped MAPbCl<inf>3</inf> perovskite single crystal as substrate, as well as n-type layer. Then nearly $200 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thickness of intrinsic MAPbCl<inf>3</inf> perovskite single crystal was epitaxially grown on the substrate as intrinsic layer, as well as protection layer. To absorb enough high energy photons, $2 \sim 4$ mm-thickness intrinsic MAPbBr<inf>2.5</inf> Cl<inf>0.5</inf> perovskite single crystal was epitaxially grown on MAPbCl<inf>3</inf> layer. Then, 1 mm -thickness $\mathrm{MAPbBr}{ }_{3}$ perovskite single crystal was grown on the MAPbBr<inf>2.5</inf> Cl<inf>0.5</inf> layer. Finally, Ag-doped MAPbBr<inf>3</inf> perovskite single crystal was grown on the intrinsic MAPbBr<inf>3</inf> perovskite single crystal as p-type layer. Consequently, the PIN photodiode is consisted of n-type layer (Bi-doped $\left.\mathrm{MAPbCl}{ }_{3}\right)$, intrinsic layer $\left(\mathrm{MAPbCl}_{3} / \mathrm{MAPbBr}_{2.5} \mathrm{Cl}_{0.5} / \mathrm{MAPbBr}_{3}\right)$ and p-type layer (Ag-doped $\left.\mathrm{MAPbBr}{ }_{3}\right)$ by solution-processed epitaxial growth.Due to mismatch rate between (Bi-doped MAPbCl<inf>3</inf>)/ (intrinsic MAPbCl<inf>3</inf>) and (Ag -doped $\mathrm{MAPbBr}{ }_{3}$)/ (intrinsic MAPbBr<inf>3</inf>) is below 0.1%, the defect density near the interfaces is extremely small. The charges from high voltage would be blocked by the n-type and p-type layers. And all the electrical field would be applied on the intrinsic layer.Besides, the intrinsic layer made of cascade perovskite single crystal of $\mathrm{MAPbCl} / 3 / \mathrm{MAPbBr}_{2.5} \mathrm{Cl}_{0.5} / \mathrm{MAPbBr}_{3}$ could have a large mobility-lifetime product. Due to the halide gradient, the cascade perovskite single crystal could naturally suppress the halide ions migration under large bias.Finally, the PIN photodiodes made of cascade perovskite single crystals, the energy resolution is measured as nearly 5%@662 keV.

articleTitle: Helium-beam radiography for precise cancer irradiation: Impact of scatter rejection on image quality
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Compared to conventional cancer radiotherapy with photons, ion-beam radiotherapy can be beneficial for patients with e.g. head and neck tumors. Currently, ion-beam radiotherapy treatments are planned for each patient individually based on X-ray images. However, conversion errors from the photon-related to ion-related physical quantities can impair the precision of these treatments, which is why ion-beam radiography is a very promising imaging alternative without these conversion errors.In this work, we investigate the impact of scatter filtering on the image quality of helium-beam radiographs acquired with thin silicon pixel detectors. Estimating a path for each single ion based on the tracking information of Timepix detectors, we want to omit ions, which were affected by large angle scattering events. Using the path length as a measure for the extent of scattering, we filter different percentages of ions out. Then, the impact on the spatial resolution (SR), the contrast to noise ratio (CNR) and the mean detector signal is investigated. Also, a small region of a helium-beam radiograph of a human-like phantom is shown for different filtering percentages. We show that the SR improves by a maximum of $31 \%$ if $50 \%$ of the ions are filtered out. The CNR worsens by $30 \%$ in the same interval. The mean energy deposition is constant for a filtering of up to $1 \%$ and then steeply decreases indicating a strong dependency on the percentage of omitted ions.

articleTitle: First imaging study for a brain PET scanner with a ring of detectors using a semi-monolithic design
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we built and evaluated a prototype brain-dedicated positron emission tomography (PET) system using a semi-monolithic detector design. The system had a ring diameter of 364.6 mm and an axial field of view of 40 mm. The imager consisted of 24 detector modules arranged in one ring. Each detector module was built with one $40 \times 40 \times 3.72 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ scintillator slab, side readout by four $1 \times 8$ silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays. Signals from the 768 SiPMs in the system were digitized by the TOFPET-2 FEM128 system from PETsys. A pre-trained neural network was used to estimate the gamma ray interaction locations. The spatial information combining with the energy and timing information from the digitizer were used to form list mode data for image reconstruction. Maximum-likelihood expectation maximization iterative reconstruction was used for the imaging studies, in which we used both a ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source and a Phantech Derenzo phantom to evaluate the performance of the system. By placing the point source at radial positions of 0 mm and 101.6 mm, the tangential/radial/axial spatial resolutions were 2.15/1.87/2.01 mm and 2.70/2.02/2.51 mm, respectively, in terms of full width half maximum. For the Phantech Derenzo phantom, 1.5 mm rods could be resolved for the phantom placed at the center of the field of view, and 2.0 mm rods could be resolved for the phantom placed at a radial position of 101.6 mm. The ultimate system will consist of multiple layers of scintillators in both axial and radial directions to reach the necessary sensitivity, with the layers providing for depth-of-interaction and inter-layer scatter information.

articleTitle: A Dual-Modality PET and CT Image Generation Pipeline for Virtual Clinical Trials
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Virtual imaging clinical trials (VICTs) have emerged as a promising adjunct to clinical medical imaging studies. This development has been motivated by the cost, time, ethical considerations, and lack of ground truth in medical imaging studies. VICTs use population-based physical and statistical models of human subjects, pathologies, imaging devices, protocols, and analysis methods to simulate clinical trials. In this work we describe an image generation pipeline for VICTs. The pipeline uses as input the XCAT phantom, which contains anatomical objects defined by non-uniform rational B-splines (NURBS). The use of NURBS allows for families of phantoms of varying size, shape and sex, and temporal sampling of periodic motions (e.g. cardiac motion and respiration). The objects are classified by both material type (for x-ray and PET photon interaction probabilities) and radioactivity concentrations. The PET acquisition is simulated using ASIM (Analytic Simulator), though the codebase also supports the use of the photon-tracking SimSET package. Recent additions to ASIM have enabled the simulation of time-of-flight PET and the direct use of NURBS surfaces without voxelization. The PET simulation is done without discretization of the phantom, which avoids using similar projection processes in the simulation and the image reconstruction, since the latter is always voxelized. The CT acquisition is simulated using DukeSim. The simulated CT image is rescaled and used for attenuation correction of the PET data, allowing the simulation of biases introduced by material and positional mismatches from respiratory-induced misalignment and other effects. ASIM and DukeSim use ray-tracing methods with noise models for rapid generation of ensembles of independent data sets to enable statistical testing. The PET/CT pipeline demonstrated in this work will provide a vital tool in multimodality imaging research.

articleTitle: Estimation of population mean kinetic parameters for 64Cu-DOTA-rituximab single time point dosimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical therapy dosimetry requires multiple time points (MTP) scans to calculate the time-integrated activity (TIA), resulting in increased data collection efforts. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of ${ }^{64} \mathrm{Cu}$-DOTA-rituximab single time point (STP) dosimetry using mean kinetic parameters. Four micewere intravenously injected with $50 \mu \mathrm{Ci} / 100 \mu \mathrm{l}$ of ${ }^{64} \mathrm{Cu}$-DOTArituximab. post-injection gamma camera scans of heart, liver, lungs, spleen, kidney and small intestine were performed at 0, 1, 2, 6, 24, 48 and 72 hours. Mono and biexponential functions were fitted to the measured data. Each exponential function has different TIA equation. Activity at scan time was multiplied by the kinetic parameters in each equation. STP dosimetry was performed using population mean kinetic parameters. The accuracy of STP dosimetry for both functions was assessed by evaluating estimation mean error results from comparison with MTP. Both functions showed high TIA estimation errors in most organs at early $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$. The mean errors of monoexponential STP at $1 \mathrm{~h} \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ ranged from 3.9% to 21.5%. Similarly, biexponential STP resulted in errors range of 3.8% to 20.9%. Errors at $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ of 2 and 6 h were similar to those at 1 h. At $24 \mathrm{~h} \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ monoexponential exhibited errors ranging from 2% to 28.5%. Conversely, biexponential errors at $24 \mathrm{~h} \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ ranged from 6.4% to 15.8%. For monoexponential, errors were 28%, 25.7%, 36.3%, 26.5%, 12.7%, and 0.3% at $48 \mathrm{~h}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ and 34%, 31.5 %, 44.8%, 31.4%, 15.3%, and 2.7% at $72 \mathrm{~h} \mathrm{~T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ respectively. Biexponential demonstrated errors of less than 10% for all organs at $\mathrm{T}_{\mathrm{sc}}$ of 48 and 72 h, TIA estimation errors were 4.4%, 5.1%, 7.8%, 6.3%, 1.9%, and 1.4% at 24 h, and 1.8%, 1.5%, 2.7%, 2.2%, 0.8%, and 0.2% at 72 h, respectively. We conclude that ${ }^{64} \mathrm{Cu}$-DOTA-rituximab STP dosimetry using population mean kinetic parameters is feasible, particularly if the scans were performed after 48 hours post injection and biexponential function was fitted to data.

articleTitle: The testing and performance of the ETROC2 for CMS MTD Endcap Timing Layer (ETL) upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Endcap Timing Readout Chip (ETROC) is designed to process LGAD signals with time resolution down to $\sim 40-50$ ps per hit. The ETROC2 is the first full-size prototype design fully compatible with the final chip specifications for CMS ETL. The ETROC2 chips have been extensively tested over the past year since May 2023, with laser, hadron beam at CERN, and electron beam at DESY, with temperature vs voltage vs TID scan, with proton beam and heavy ion beams for SEU and wafer probe testing and stress testing using charge injections. Overall, the performance of ETROC2 is satisfying, the time resolution performance meets the ETL design specification (<50 ps per hit), TID has passed 400 MRad even though the specification is 100MRad, and the yield is very high reaching 97% based on wafer probe testing studies. So far, only few relatively minor issues identified, and all have been fixed with the ETROC2 wafers on hold. The ETROC2 design, test results, and design improvements using wafers on hold will be presented.

articleTitle: Design and Testing of the Endcap Concentrator ASICs for the CMS High-Granularity Calorimeter Upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A major upgrade of the High-Granularity Calorimeter (HGCAL) in the CMS detector is planned for Long-Shutdown 3 (LS3), currently expected to start in 2026. This upgrade will contain over 6 million channels and the electronics will be required to be low power and to withstand a radiation environment with a High-Energy Hadron flux of $3 x 10^{* *} 6$ particles per square centimeter per second. The solution to this significant challenge is the two Endcap Concentrator (ECON) ASICs, ECON-T and ECON-D, working in tandem with the HGCROC front-end ASIC. The two ECON ASICs provide critical on-detector data reduction for both the 40 MHz trigger path (ECON-T) and 750 kHz data acquisition path (ECON-D) of the HGCAL. The ASICs are fabricated in 65nm CMOS. They are rad-tolerant to 600 Mrad with low power consumption (<2.5 mW/channel). This presentation will be a comprehensive description of each ECON design, including the infrastructure that they share as well as the elements that make each unique. The presentation will also include functionality and radiation tests for both ASICs, and the first high statistics characterization results from the full production of 75 k ECON-D and ECON-T ASICs.

articleTitle: Deep-PRC: A Positron Range Correction Tool for preclinical and clinical PET/CT images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep-PRC is a deep learning-based Positron Range Correction (PRC) method for enhancing spatial resolution and accuracy in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scans using radionuclides with large positron ranges, such as 68Ga. Traditional PRC strategies often increase the noise in the final images and struggle with the anisotropic blurring caused by varying positron energies and tissue electron densities, yielding inaccurate results in non-homogeneous regions. Deep-PRC uses a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated data to offer a fast and effective alternative. This study elaborates on the methodology from the creation of the simulation dataset to the development and testing of the model, using preclinical (Inveon) and clinical data (Biograph Vision). Results demonstrate that Deep-PRC significantly improves image quality by recovering activity levels, increasing contrast up to 27% and 46% in the heart and bladder, respectively, and reducing noise by 11% with respect to images without PRC. This advancement represents a promising approach to obtaining more accurate quantitative PET images in both preclinical and clinical settings, particularly for non-standard PET isotopes.

articleTitle: Design and Characterization of a 12-Bit SAR-ADC for Charge Integrating Pixel Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: JUNGFRAU is a state-of-the-art charge-integrating detector for high performance experiments at synchrotrons and free-electron lasers. It is currently limited to a frame rate of 2.2 kHz. With the goal to increase the frame rate of the detector to $\gt10 \mathrm{kHz}$, we have designed a 3.125 Gbps high speed serial readout. Thus, the development of a fast Analog-To-Digital Converter (ADC) has become a priority. The design of the current rail-to-rail, fully differential ADC prototype will be presented along simulation results and laboratory evaluation. The prototype targets a sampling rate of $20 \mathrm{MS} / \mathrm{s}$ together with an effective number of bits (ENOB) of equal to or greater than 11 bits. Power and area requirements to reach this goal are currently under evaluation. To meet these demands, a 12-bit Successive Approximation Register (SAR) ADC has been developed and fabricated in the 110 nm UMC CMOS process. We present laboratory characterization results, verifying the design requirements together with a comparison to other ADCs targeting similar use cases.

articleTitle: Background reduction of Compton-camera based 3D imaging for range verification in proton therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low signal-to-background ratio and subsequent image degradation limits the performance of Compton cameras and hinder their application for range verification in hadron therapy. While several approaches have been explored to improve the signal-to-background ratio via event selection (e.g. with neural networks, energy cuts or using dedicated hardware), background reduction within the 3D image reconstruction process has been hitherto overlooked. In this work we present three such background reduction techniques, and show their potential for image-quality improvement by using simulated data. The explored techniques are shown to reduce image noise-edge artifacts, as well as improve the image contrast and/or be quantitatively closer to the ground truth spatial emission distribution. Such promising results encourage further study on their implementation and impact on range verification.

articleTitle: Inter-Crystal Optical Crosstalk in a Crystal Array
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-resolution radiation detectors involve using small scintillating crystals optically isolated from each other. Understanding inter-crystal crosstalk is of great interest to optimize detectors to avoid spatial and energy performance detriment but is difficult to characterize experimentally. Accurate optical Monte Carlo simulation plays a crucial role in this context. This work investigated inter-crystal optical photon crosstalk in a 9-crystal array. We simulated crystal scintillation and light transport in GATE using the experimentally validated look-up table Davis Model that incorporates optical photon refraction at crystal interfaces. The first results were obtained using nine LYSO crystals coupled to each other’s with ESR, and with optical photons emitted within the crystal at the center of the array. Results showed a mean optical crosstalk of 3.7% with lateral crystals and 0.4% with crystals at the edges. Simulations on different configurations (crystals, interfaces, reflectors) will be performed and validated against experimental measurements. These results and the model we developed are of great interest and valuable resources for researchers when optimizing radiation detector design to mitigate optical crosstalk for optimal detector performance.

articleTitle: Kernel-based image reconstruction for delayed PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The initial positron emission tomography (PET) scan performed after tracer injection provides fundamental metabolic activity information of the heart. However, conducting another PET scan after a certain period following tracer injection allows for observation of the tracer distribution in cardiac tissue and any associated metabolic changes. By comparing delayed imaging with the initial scan, doctors can achieve a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamic changes in cardiac function, enabling better assessment of the patient’s cardiac health status and the development of personalized treatment plans. Our research focuses on delayed imaging utilizing PET images from the initial scan, a crucial and challenging task aimed at reconstructing PET images acquired after a certain period following tracer injection. We propose a novel kernel reconstruction approach that integrates autocorrelation texture features from Gray-Level Cooccurrence Matrix (GLCM). This new kernel function considers the correlation between grayscale and texture features from previous images, thereby enhancing the accuracy of delayed imaging PET reconstruction.

articleTitle: Emulating Scanning Process for Stochastic Bone Scan Denoising
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Improving the quality of low-dose nuclear medicine images can reduce radiation exposure and acquisition time, and deep learning is a major trend in this area. Due to the nature of deterministic denoising, restored images are often blurred. In this study, we used the Generative Accumulation of Photons (GAP) method to stochastically denoise bone scan images by emulating the scanning process. The effectiveness of the method was evaluated using 99mTc MDP and DPD bone scan images from Seoul National University Hospital and compared with well-established deterministic denoising schemes - low-dose image to low-dose image training (Noise2Noise, N2N) and low-dose image to full-dose image supervised training (Noise2Full, N2F). The mean of stochastically sampled full-dose images using GAP showed higher structural similarity index measure (SSIM) and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) compared to N2F and N2N denoising results, along with good perceptual metrics calculated using Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). For denoising $50 \%$ dose images, GAP achieved SSIM of 0.938, PSNR of 36.76 dB, and LPIPS of 0.039. Additionally, for denoising 20% dose images, GAP achieved SSIM of 0.891, PSNR of 34.34 dB, and LPIPS of 0.086 (average of 41 images).

articleTitle: Toward the Detection of Prompt Neutrons from Photofission: New Developments in Threshold Activation Scintillation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Prompt neutrons from photofission are about a hundred times more numerous than delayed neutrons, whilst the detection of their signature is still under investigation. The photofission reaction is usually induced with an accelerator that converts electrons into Bremsstrahlung photons by slowing them on a target made of heavy atomic nuclei, such as tungsten. This reaction is involved in the Active Photon Interrogation (API), which is a non-destructive nuclear measurement technique that preserves the integrity of the object to be analyzed. Therefore, many applications ranging from characterization of nuclear waste package to homeland security exploit this technique. Yet, when an energetic photon interacts with actinides, photofissions occur and prompt neutrons are nearly instantly emitted, while the gamma flash saturates the electronics of the neutron detection system. Thence, in API, delayed neutrons and gammas are preferably detected. In the 2010’s, threshold activation detectors (TAD) have been described as promising to meet this need. They allow avoiding both the short measuring window, by delaying the detection in time, and a strong background noise due to photoneutrons created in the conversion target while producing the photon beam. Prompt neutrons interact with those detectors and activate radionuclide whose reaction products are thereafter measured. Using the Monte Carlo simulation code PHITS3.33, we design an optimized photofission prompt neutron detection system. For instance, we assess the impact of several parameters including the electron energy of the linear accelerator (linac) enabling to produce the interrogating photon beam, or evaluate the thickness of the fluorinated activation material overlaying the scintillating detector. Experimental tests are then conducted with a Linatron-M9 linac operated at 9 MeV at the SAPHIR platform, CEA Paris-Saclay (France). The results obtained are compared and discussed with those presented in the state of the art.

articleTitle: Modeling Prompt Gamma-ray Timing Spectra for Treatment Verification in Proton Therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Range verification is a key component of online adaptive proton therapy, and Prompt Gamma-ray Timing (PGT) is a promising candidate for its realization.Recently, the PGT method demonstrated that it can detect range deviations of a few millimeters under quasi-clinical conditions for individual pencil beam spots. However, results obtained so far have only been based on relative measurements. In everyday clinical practice particle transport calculations based on the treatment planning should provide this reference.This work reports on the development of a Geant4-simulation designed to generate PGT spectra for the irradiation of a homogeneous, cylindrical acrylic glass phantom. The effects of the accelerator (periodicity, bunch charge), the detectors (time resolution, detection threshold, dead time, pulse pile-up) and the post-processing (background subtraction, energy selection) were applied to the raw simulated data. The resulting spectra show a very good agreement with those measured experimentally. The sensitivity of the method was further investigated by introducing cavities of various thicknesses and materials into the phantom, the results of which align well with experimental measurements.

articleTitle: Performance of the Inner Tracking System of the ALICE experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Inner Tracking System (ITS2) of the ALICE experiment at CERN is a silicon vertex tracker, which is based on a Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor (MAPS) called ALPIDE. The detector has an active area of $10 \mathrm{~m}^{2}$ and is segmented into about $10^{10}$ pixels with a pitch of $27 \mu \mathrm{m} \times 29 \mu \mathrm{m}$. The ITS2 has been in operation since its installation to ALICE in 2021. In the talk, we will present the ITS2 detector and its current performance during the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) pp and $\mathrm{Pb}-\mathrm{Pb}$ campaigns in Run 3. The detector has about 3 times better impact parameter resolution w.r.t. the previous ITS at $1 \mathrm{GeV} /c$. In addition, it exhibits stable charge thresholds and a very low fake-hit rate. Finally, the upcoming upgrade for the innermost layers based on bent wafer-scale MAPS will be briefly outlined.

articleTitle: Improve DOI resolution for a human brain PET detector using convolutional neural networks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A novel detector design was proposed for high sensitivity and high spatial resolution human brain PET imaging in our previous work, and the detector had the ability to decode the depth-ofinteraction(DOI). To further improve the DOI resolution of the detector, we used NN-based algorithm to predict the DOI for the gamma ray events interacted at different depths of the detector. The detector consist of two layers of LYSO crystal array, top layer was a $16 \times 16$ array of LYSO crystals and bottom layer was an $8 \times 8$ LYSO array. Placed between the top and bottom layers of the LYSO array was a 2mm thick glass light guide for light sharing. The dataset of 15 different depths from DOI $=8.5-22.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ with a step size of 1 mm were acquired and input into the neural network for training, and a separate dataset at three depths of 10, 14, 19mm was acquired and input to the trained neural network for evaluating the DOI prediction accuracy. The DOI resolution was calculated for all crystals within a detector block at three DOI of 10, 14, 19 mm. A comparison was made between the DOI resolution obtained using the w-value method and the NN-based approach, and the average DOI resolution were 4.95 mm and 2.60 mm using the w-value and CNN, respectively. The proposed network provides a 1.9 times improvement in DOI resolution compared with the w-value method. Compared with other NN-based DOI estimation methods, our proposed network was trained with events from all crystals in a detector at multiple depths, instead of individual crystal events. Furthermore, the training process needs fewer epochs and has shown greater improvement on DOI resolution. Preliminary experimental results demonstrated the feasibility of the CNN method in estimating the DOI.

articleTitle: Development of a Double Scatter Time-of-Flight Technique for Fast Neutron Spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To fulfill the demand of applications utilizing accelerator-based neutron sources, techniques for characterizing neutrons with energies up to tens of MeV are essential. The time-of-flight (TOF) represents a straightforward method for measuring fast neutron spectra. However, the necessity of a long flight distance in conventional TOF to achieve a high time resolution for measuring neutrons with energies > 10 MeV tends to limit the use of TOF in compact spaces. Hence, we are motivated to develop a double scatter TOF technique suitable for installation in confined spaces to characterize fast neutrons. A double scatter TOF spectrometer, composed of a trigger and a record organic scintillation detector, was implemented to evaluate the accuracy of a measured spectrum for neutrons emitting from an AmBe source. The energy of an incident neutron, E<inf>n</inf>, is the summation of the energy of recoil proton, E<inf>p</inf>′, in the trigger detector and the energy of scattered neutron, E<inf>n</inf>′, determined by the TOF between the trigger and the record detector. As E<inf>p</inf>′ is estimated from the light yield in the trigger detector, our simulations indicate that events related to neutron multiple-scattering in the trigger detector can cause significant underestimation of neutron energy. Setting appropriate discrimination thresholds for signals from the two detectors can effectively remove multiple-scattering events in a measurement and improve the accuracy of a retrieved spectrum. When using discrimination thresholds of 0.125 and 0.5 MeVee for the trigger and the record detector, respectively, the experimentally measured spectrum for neutrons from the AmBe source exhibits good agreement with the ISO reference spectrum in the range of 5.5 MeV to 11 MeV. Our results emphasize the significance of setting appropriate discrimination thresholds for detectors in a double scatter TOF spectrometer, which is anticipated to facilitate the measurement of fast neutrons with energies exceeding 5 MeV in confined spaces.

articleTitle: Image Reconstruction via Linear Regression Fit of Coded-Aperture Gamma-Ray Imager Data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-ray imaging can be used to identify and localize nuclear material, making it well-suited for nuclear security applications. For position-sensitive detectors, the coded-aperture imaging technique may be utilized to generate radiation images with excellent angular resolution. However, the distance to a given source within a coded-aperture image - necessary for quantification of the source material - is often difficult to determine accurately. An alternative to the traditional coded-aperture approach, iterative imaging techniques seek to reconstruct the distribution of source material by finding a linear combination of pre-computed detector responses that best match the observations of one or more detectors. We present a novel implementation of linear regression fitting for radiation image reconstruction and its application to a commercial cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) gamma-ray imager. The methodology of this technique, its performance, and potential for 3D scene reconstruction are discussed.

articleTitle: Modelling and Performance Assessment of a CMOS Switched Capacitor Analog Neuron
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Incorporating signal processing into the front-end of radiation detectors presents a strategy to manage the rising complexity of nuclear imaging scanners, particularly as their field of view expands, leading to a higher number of channels. Machine learning presents an effective solution. Our research focuses on analog AI accelerators for the reconstruction of the position of interaction of gamma rays in the scintillator crystal of Anger cameras used in PET and SPECT applications. We designed and implemented a reprogrammable, in-memory-computing analog neural network ASIC on a $0.35 \mu \mathrm{m}$ CMOS process, performing the matrix multiplication in the charge domain with no ADCs or FPGAs. This chip is able to interface directly with the analog acquisition chain of the detector, processing up to 200,000 events per second. The network features 64 analog inputs, two hidden layers of 20 neurons and 2 output neurons. 8.81 Kbit of embedded SRAM are used to store 1762 5-bits weights. Our experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed analog NN accelerator, even if many non-idealities have deteriorated the expected performances. This work focuses on those non-idealities: an analytical model has been built and verified starting the study and modelling of low level, single neuron experimental measurements, and has been used to predict the full-network ASIC behaviour, improving the final ASIC performances.

articleTitle: A Prototype Coded Sensing SPECT designed for Ultra-high Sensitivity Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we discuss the design and development of an ultra-high sensitivity imaging system, Coded Sensing SPECT (CS-SPECT), dedicated to guide and optimize application of alpha particle-emitting radiopharmaceutical therapy ($\alpha$RPT). Alpha particles are highly potent and unlike conventional external beam therapy, they can be used in metastatic settings. Currently, the lack of information of radionuclide distribution hinders estimated internal absorbed dose from $\alpha$RPT, which calls for ultrasensitive SPECT technologies that can report reliable activity distribution under ultra-low count rate imaging conditions. The proposed CS-SPECT is based on an innovative design that incorporates the geometry of both conventional pinhole collimator and coded aperture. Aimed to decouple the dependence of resolution and sensitivity, the heavy metal collimator is replaced by scintillator crystals to serve dual purposes of increasing detected events and providing spatial information. The proposed detector module consists of a 9×9 array of crystal elements. Each crystal presents an alternating pattern of GAGG scintillator and acrylic. The depth of interaction (DOI) information is obtained through dual-ended readout system. Our experimental results are based on a working prototype CS module that has 8x8 detector columns and is fully functional under a broad range of energy (70 keV – more than 511 keV), which is well-suited for alpha particle emitter imaging applications. Furthermore, we performed a preliminary imaging study of Tc99m point source. The number of detected events by the whole detector module is 11-fold higher than that from the bottom detectors resembling a conventional pinhole camera alone, demonstrating a tremendous improvement in system sensitivity.

articleTitle: Motion correction quality control of markerless head motion tracking for ultrahigh performance brain PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Head movement in brain PET studies compromises image quality, leading to resolution degradation and bias in quantification results. For the NeuroEXPLORER (NX), an ultra-high-performance brain-dedicated PET system, the exquisitely high spatial resolution exacerbates the impact of motion, magnifying its effects during brain PET studies. This study presents a comprehensive motion quality control metric for United Imaging Healthcare Motion tracking system (UMT), combined metric (CM), tested in human scans, particularly in intentional facial expression experiments. CM proved effective in detecting and mitigating motion blurring caused by non-rigid movements and rigid motion tracking failure. Different gating strategies based on CM was developed for discarding corresponding low-quality PET data. Intentional motion experiment results showed that CM can detect facial expressions and rigid motion failure with high frequency, and the proposed UMT gating method yielded motion-free images and outperformed the original UMT motion correction (MC) method qualitatively, highlighting its potential for enhancing imaging quality in neuroimaging studies. In human ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FEPE-2I scan, the use of proposed gating strategy did not affect results for a study without large, planned motions. Moving forward, the study proposes future investigations involving the implementation of CM in a large-scale human cohort study utilizing the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) system. This next phase of research will focus on parameter fine-tuning to optimize motion quality control and ultimately improve the accuracy and reliability of neuroimaging analyses in clinical and research settings.

articleTitle: Quantifying scattering rate based on the similarity measurements of the quantum states of the two coincidence detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent developments in quantum physics have sparked interest in its application to medical imaging, notably in positron emission tomography (PET) scanners. This study presents a quantitative approach to assess the similarity and covariance matrix of quantum photonic states derived from two coincidence measurements, one of which involves scattering. Using CZT detectors positioned near a positron source within a thin plastic housing, we recorded positions and energy resulting from Compton scatterings. Our findings indicate a decrease in the similarity ratio between detectors with increasing scattering medium width, revealing predictive behavior linked to different medium widths. This study highlights the effectiveness of employing quantum mechanics as a measurable tool for characterizing scattering scales in medical imaging systems, with potential implications for PET scanners. Future investigations will expand this analysis to explore additional parameters, such as detector distance, size, and source type, to deepen our understanding of quantum phenomena in medical imaging technologies.

articleTitle: Sub-Pixel Position Sensing And Readout Electronics For Perovskite Low Energy (140 keV) Gamma-Ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High spatial and energy resolution gamma detectors are one of the key components for nuclear molecular imaging system. As a novel type of Low Energy Gamma detector, Perovskite detectors possess significant potential, with outstanding material properties such as high stopping power and excellent hole mobility-lifetime product. While it is application for high energy gamma ray detector(${\$}$\sim${\$}$ 661 keV) has been well investigated\cite{he2021cspbbr3}, this study focuses on the optimization design of CsPbBr 3 perovskite gamma ray position and energy sensing for low energy gamma ray (around 140 keV). Sub-pixel position sensing is investigated through simulation and experiments. To handle the low signal amplitude, we designed a front-end circuit comprising input buffering, charge-sensitive preamplification, and second-stage amplification circuits to effectively reduce noise, enhance gain, thus improving the detector’s spatial and energy resolution. Additionally, sub-pixel position sensing theory was validated through simulation experiments. The results demonstrate that by appropriate electronic circuit design and position sensing algorithms, the resolution of perovskite detectors can be significantly improved, promoting their applications in medical imaging fields.

articleTitle: Exploring the Impact of TiO2 Variations on the Gamma-Ray Shielding Properties of Bi2O3-ZnO-Pb3O4-Al2O3 Glass
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we employed the MCNP Monte Carlo (MC) code to assess the gamma-ray shielding properties of a glass system with a specific composition. The glass composition consisted of (55-x) Bi2O3-15Pb3O4-20Al2O3-10ZnO-xTiO2, where x varied (x=0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 35 mol percent) to represent different concentrations of TiO2. Various parameters related to photon attenuation, including Half-Value Layer (HVL), Tenth-Value Layer (TVL), mean free path (MFP), mass attenuation coefficient (□m), and buildup factor (BF), were examined across energy levels ranging from 0.1 to 1.5 MeV using the MCNP Monte Carlo code. To validate the simulation results, we compared them with experimental data from the XCOM database. Our analysis revealed a strong correlation between the NIST-XCOM database and the simulation results, with the percentage deviation (PD) for □m calculations mostly below 0.59%. The average difference between MCNP and XCOM data in terms of Z<inf>eff</inf> was 1% and 4%. Our results suggest that the novel glass composition demonstrates superior attenuation properties compared to conventional shielding materials like concrete and lead. Particularly, the glass variant with the lowest TiO2 content exhibited the most favorable density among the materials studied. The consistent agreement between the □m results and the XCOM database highlights the reliability and effectiveness of the MC modeling technique utilized in this investigation.

articleTitle: Bayesian Calibration of Feynman-Y distributions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In passive neutron multiplicity counting, the Feynman-Y parameter accounting for excessive variance-which is due to the correlated neutrons emitted by fissions or chain reactions-has to be ascertained with the utmost level of confidence. However, the measured distributions may not be entirely described by Feynman’s model—notably for short time gates-, depending on measurement conditions. The gate generation methods (incrementing and sequential) employed to build these distributions may also have an impact on their behavior. This paper describes how one can address this issue with statistical inference. The Bayesian calibration technique devised to correct faulty Feynman-Y curve fittings, which show chi-squares up to 8.15, implements bias through a model error. It involves two hyperparameters that are selected by calculating a likelihood function, which accounts for fitting residues and an extended uncertainty matrix. Provided that the subsequent regression is validated by the leave-one-out procedure, the Jacobian matrix and residues vector complete the relations for estimating the Feynman-Y mean and a posteriori variance. The resulting fits show valid chi-squares with a $95-\%$ confidence level, and therefore provide reliable uncertainty intervals on Feynman-Y. Correction of the experimental fit establishes the model difficulty in accounting for the curve growth, whose governing parameter is increased by $14.7 \%$, which results in a 1.4-% lowering of the convergence value. A parallel simulation-based study that corroborates the experimental diagnosis also indicates a potential physical meaning behind the model error, which turned out to be equivalent for all fit corrections. The Bayesian technique hence offers a robust tool to improve the accuracy of multiplicity data analysis. Directions for future research should involve extending this technique to a wider range of configurations and enhancing the physical interpretation of hyperparameter values.

articleTitle: Structure-activity relationship of LYSO:Ce crystal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Different sites mean different surroundings & crystal fields, thus leading to different luminescence wavelengths and also different decay time. In this talk, we will present our study on structure-activity relationship of $\left(\mathrm{Lu}_{1-\mathrm{x}} \mathrm{Y}_{\mathrm{x}}\right)_{2} \mathrm{SiO}_{5}: \mathrm{Ce}$ (LYSO:Ce) crystal. A series of LYSO:Ce crystals with yttrium content x ranging from 0 to 100 at% were grown by using Czochralski method. A systematic study has been carried out on how component affects crystal structure, ions’ location and distortion parameters of polyhedral, band structure, crystal-field splitting and coupling strength of 5 d state of $\mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ ion, electron trap depth and thermally stimulated luminescence, intrinsic radioactivity energy spectra, luminescence spectra and decay kinetics.The results show that $\mathrm{Y}^{3+}$ cations were found to have a preferential occupation for RE1 site (7oxygen-coordinated) over RE2 site (6-oxygen-coordinated), while $\mathrm{Lu}^{3+}$ cations were found to have an opposite preferential occupation. With the increase of Y content, crystal-field splitting and intrinsic radioactivity decrease<sup>1</sup>, while band gap, deep electron trap depth ($\mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{t}} \approx 1.00-1.21 \mathrm{eV}$) and decay time increase<sup>[2, 3]</sup>.Besides, we will also present our recent results on slow emission suppression and enhancement of scintillation properties by co-doping (Fig. 1) <sup>[4, 5]</sup>.
