articleTitle: Evaluation of a PET detector module composed of a BGO monolithic scintillator with SiPM readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report on the performance obtained with a positron emission tomography detector composed of a monolithic BGO crystal coupled to an $8 \times 8$ array of silicon photomultipliers with a 6.2 mm pitch. The detection module has a sensitive area of $50 \mathrm{~mm} \times 50 \mathrm{~mm}$, different scintillator thicknesses were tested, up to 20 mm. The detector’s performance was evaluated in terms of energy, 3 -dimensional spatial, and timing resolution, using Monte Carlo simulations and by scanning the detector with a collimated 511 keV photon beam and a LYSO pixel as a coincidence detector. A coincidence time resolution of 446 ps and 484 ps (full width at half maximum) was obtained with the coincidence detector, for 16 mm and 20 mm BGO thicknesses, respectively, using an energy-weighted algorithm for the reconstruction of the event timestamp. An improvement in the time resolution is expected to be achieved with the adoption of neural networks, that were already tested in simulation, achieving a coincidence time resolution between two modules of 350 ps for the $16-\mathrm{mm}$ thick crystal and of 390 ps for the $20-\mathrm{mm}$ BGO. The detector is intended to be used for the construction of a compact PET scanner with 16 detectors arranged in a double ring for intraoperative margin assessment of excised tumors.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study on the Discrimination of the Gamma Rays and Other Particles from the Thunderclouds and Lightnings with NaI:Tl Scintillator
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thunderclouds and lightnings are known to generate some gamma rays originating from accelerating electrons in electric fields within thunderclouds, and some research groups observed such gamma rays on the ground-based observatories. On the other hand, the observation of neutrons, muon and/or other particles from the thunderclouds is insufficient. In this paper, we discuss the detector we have developed for both gamma rays and particles consisting of two plastic scintillators and Tl-doped NaI scintillator (Tl:NaI). We show preliminary results of the demonstration test for this detector with gamma-rays.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-based Dynamic PET Intra-frame Motion Correction and Integration with Inter-frame Motion Estimation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In dynamic PET imaging, intra-frame motion poses a significant challenge, leading to blurred reconstructed frames. Current methods using respiratory gating and conventional image registration can correct intra-frame motion but suffer from computational inefficiency and limitations in integrating with intra-frame motion estimation. To address these challenges, we propose to utilize a deep learning-based spatial-temporal motion estimation framework for both gated image registration and inter-frame registration. On a whole-body FDG dynamic PET dataset, our preliminary results demonstrate the generalization ability of the model on gated images and its efficacy across different reconstruction protocols. With only 1/400 of the inference time, the deep learning-based registration approach significantly improves intra-frame motion correction compared with conventional registration, leading to enhanced spatial alignment in gated images and improved image sharpness and contrast in reconstructed dynamic frames. This deep learning-based work shows promise in accelerating motion estimation processes and improving image quality in dynamic PET imaging.

articleTitle: 3D Compton Imaging System Using Inertial Measurement Units
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-ray energy depositions and interaction positions within a three-dimensional (3-D) pixelated position-sensitive Cadmium Zinc Telluride detector, capable of imaging in 3-D via Compton imaging, are fused with the position and orientation (POSE) of the user operating the detector and the orientation of the detector, each provided by an inertial measurement unit (IMU), to localize and identify gamma-ray sources with respect to an operator’s POSE as a function of time. University of Michigan Imaging Software, programmed in the Orion Radiation Measurement Group at the University of Michigan, is used to simultaneously collect data from all 3 devices and do image reconstruction via 3-D Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization. Measurements were taken where the user walked a several meter linear path near a Cesium-137 source with the detector orientation either remaining the same for the duration of the measurement or rotating. In both instances the system was able to reconstruct the source estimation close to the true source location, with better performance in the former case, confirming its effectiveness as a tool in search and locate scenarios. Future work includes enhancing the source estimation accuracy and working on the real-time implementation of the system.

articleTitle: A Simulation Study of Monte Carlo Dosimetry in a Mouse Model for predicting the Injection Dose of Sn-117m Radiopharmaceuticals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Simulation-based small animal dosimetry is commonly used for new radionuclide therapy. In this study, therapeutic internal radiation was investigated in mouse tumor models to predict injection dose. The absorbed doses for internal radionuclides (Sn-117m and Iodine-131) were calculated using the mouse digital phantom and Monte Carlo simulation code MCNPX. The mean dose per cumulated activity, S-values (mGy/Bq*s) were simulated for different source target organ pairs for multiple radionuclides in the organ regions of interest. The voxel-based mouse digital phantom was designed using mouse whole-body(MOBY) Phantom, and the xenograft tumor mass of 1053 mg were additionally coded into the right flank of the voxel based mouse model. The physiologically based bio-kinetic factor results were obtained from actual bio-distribution tumor xenograft mouse measurement data at 1,2,3,5,7,14d post injection(n=5). The doses of 111 kbq/200ug/head were bolus-injected into normal and tumor xenograft mice. The average dose for organs itself and others were calculated as a function of fractional energy depositions. The results showed the effective doses of 10 organs, the blood, xenograft tumor, and remained body. In this study, we can support the estimated Sn-117m radiopharmaceuticals production yield plan. The calculated S-values of Sn-117m compared with I-131. It can be further applied to evaluate pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics research with dose calculation. We expect that the results can be used to determine the appropriate administrative injection dose for radiopharmaceuticals.

articleTitle: Towards Enhancing Auxiliary Lymph Node Detection Using a Breast Insert with a Whole-Body PET/MRI Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In general, breast PET inserts are designed to improve the detection capability for small lesions and early metastases. Expanding on prior research, the insert our group is developing aims to enhance the spatial resolution of axillary lymph nodes beyond the insert’s field-of-view (FOV) via the combination with a clinical whole-body (WB) PET scanner. To explore this potential, Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using Na-22 point sources positioned outside of the insert’s FOV to mimic real lymph node locations. A dedicated reconstruction was developed to accommodate different types of coincidences in this hybrid setup, and the system model was partially validated using a phantom of uniformly distributed activity. Results indicate that, while the WB-PET’s spatial resolution may degrade due to insert attenuation, the combination of conventional WB-PET coincidences and mixed coincidences from both systems enhances spatial resolution in terms of full-width at half-maximum in x-direction, and also helps to mitigate the negative effects of the insert in y-direction. Future steps include a comprehensive assessment of image quality, refinement of the reconstruction algorithm to include the solid angle effect, and evaluation of image performance with realistic phantoms.

articleTitle: Lessons Learned From Bump Bonding During the ETL Upgrade for the CMS Experiment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) will bring unique challenges to the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) collaboration with the sizable jump in instan-taneous luminosity. In order to mitigate the increase in the number of interactions per bunch crossing, CMS is adding a new layer of timing detectors to measure minimum ionizing particles (MIPs) with a time resolution of 40-50 ps per hit. This MIP timing detector (MTD) will have extended coverage in the endcap region (up to $|\eta|=3$) thanks to the Endcap Timing Layer (ETL). To survive the harsh environments of this region of CMS, ETL will implement silicon sensors with fast charge collection that are also radiation hard in the form of low-gain avalanche diodes (LGADs). In addition to the sensor technology, the front-end readout technology also needs to meet stringent design requirements. A new ASIC for ETL (ETROC) has been designed, produced, and is being validated with a variety of testing procedures. The ETROC and sensor are connected via bump bonds. To study the electrical yield and resistance to stresses, “dummy” components are bump bonded together with the same dimensions as will be used in the final detector design. This talk will cover results of bump bonding yields and tolerances to stresses of dummy assemblies, and comparisons to ETROCs bump bonded to sensors.

articleTitle: Three-dimensional response evaluation system for detectors using a wavelength tunable laser
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The development of a satellite named ‘LiteBIRD,’ which is intended to test the inflation theory of the early expansion of the universe, is currently being advanced in Japan. This satellite aims to verify the inflation theory through detailed observations of the polarization patterns in the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB). In particular, the inflation theory suggests that the early universe expanded exponentially and the gravitational waves produced during this process left traces in the CMB as B-mode polarization. The B-mode polarization that LiteBIRD aims to detect is extremely weak compared to the CMB’s temperature fluctuations of about 10 □□. To capture these minute variations, LiteBIRD utilizes highly sensitive superconducting detectors called Transition Edge Sensor (TES) bolometers. However, these sensitive detectors face issues with accidental effects (glitches) caused by cosmic rays colliding with the silicon of the detectors, making data utilization difficult. This research aims to maximize the limited observation time of the satellite and thus fully utilize the performance of the detectors. To address this, glitch evaluation tests using gamma rays have been conducted, but accurately pinpointing the origin of the phonon (heat) generation is challenging. To resolve this issue, glitch evaluation tests using lasers have been proposed. This method allows for easy identification of the laser irradiation site and provides a similar source of glitches as radiation. Additionally, the advantage of using lasers is that the wavelength can be set, allowing for a three-dimensional evaluation of the response function. By measuring while changing the laser wavelength and using the inverse Laplace transform of a function of penetration depth, the response function in the depth direction can be determined. The research target was to verify the principle of this new method. This approach enables improvements in detector design and data analysis methods.

articleTitle: A detection technique for low-energy gamma rays from alpha emitters in background radiation environment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station’s decommissioning requires thorough inspection of piping for contamination, including alpha nuclides. External alpha particle measurements are impossible, necessitating gamma-ray detection methods. A phoswich detector for low-energy gamma-ray detection was developed and validated experimentally at a nuclear fuel facility. The detector was designed considering energy deposition characteristics. The detector comprises YAlO3:Ce and Bi4Ge3O12 scintillators with a photomultiplier tube for signal amplification. Validation involved Geant4 simulation and actual radiation source measurements. Performance assessment at a nuclear fuel facility yielded a gamma-ray dose rate of $850 \mu \mathrm{Sv} / \mathrm{h}$. Measurement and simulation results show correlation between scintillator energy depositions for different gamma-ray energies. Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) plots distinguish alpha particles and gamma-rays, confirming simulation predictions. Nuclear fuel facility measurements exhibit higher energy deposition in the first scintillator layer. This suggests potential for developing a sensitive low-energy gamma-ray detector using scintillator combinations. Future work aims to optimize detector design and conduct field tests for validation.

articleTitle: Surface flattening of TlBr crystal by hot pressing to form small pixel electrodes
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes the capability of surface flattening of thallium bromide crystals by hot pressing. TlBr detectors are suitable for X-ray imaging applications because of the associated large attenuation coefficients and direct conversion behavior. In the process of developing X-ray imagers such as flat panel detectors, it is essential to form small pixel electrodes on the detector, which requires flatness on the detector surface. However, the TlBr crystal is relatively soft as a semiconductor detector material, and there is a problem in ensuring flatness over a large area using mechanical or chemical polishing. The softness is that the shape of the crystal can be changed by hot pressing, so by pressing the TlBr crystal with a sufficiently flat surface, the flatness of the surface can be improved by an area corresponding to the pressing area. In addition, the TlBr crystal maintains the property of detecting gamma rays in pulse mode even after pressing.

articleTitle: New Polycrystalline Based Semiconductors for Radiation Detecting Devices
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Bulk, polycrystalline-based semiconductors (PBS) show promise as a low-cost option for radiation detecting devices. To achieve the optimal radiation response, dense, phase-pure ceramics with large, uniform grains must be fabricated. $\mathrm{Ta}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{5}, \mathrm{InTaO}_{4}, \mathrm{BiTaO}_{4}, \mathrm{Bi}_{3} \mathrm{TaO}_{7}$, and Hf<inf>6</inf> Ta<inf>2</inf> O<inf>17</inf> were investigated as potential PBS candidates because of their high density ($\gt 8.0 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$), high effective atomic number (>60), and wide bandgap ($\gt2 \mathrm{eV}$). The compounds were synthesized into >90% dense, phase-pure ceramic pellets with a thickness $\sim 1 \mathrm{~mm}$ using the solid-state sintering method. The phase purity of the samples was confirmed with powder x-ray diffraction. The microstructures of Ta<inf>2</inf> O<inf>5</inf> samples that had undergone different sintering parameters were imaged with a scanning electron microscope. A slight increase in grain size with increasing sintering time was observed. Preliminary current-voltage characterization showed that Ta<inf>2</inf> O<inf>5</inf>, Hf<inf>6</inf> Ta<inf>2</inf> O<inf>17</inf>, and InTaO T<inf>4</inf> demonstrated relatively linear ohmic behavior with very high resistivities of $\sim 10^{11} \Omega-\mathrm{cm}$. BiTaO<inf>4</inf> and Bi<inf>3</inf> TaO<inf>7</inf> also demonstrated linear ohmic behavior and had resistivities of $10^{9} \Omega-\mathrm{cm}$ and $10^{14} \Omega-$ cm, respectively. The results from x-ray and gamma ray response measurements will be reported.

articleTitle: Photon Counting-Based Metrics for Soft Tissue Differentiation in Coronary Plaque Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon counting CT is a promising novel improvement for coronary artery disease diagnostics, bypassing limitations of traditional CT angiography such as calcium blooming. We introduce two new methods integrated into our clinical software: The dual energy ratio and the effective Z map. Both aim to enhance tissue differentiation and plaque segmentation, especially for soft and adipose tissue. The dual energy ratio is easy to compute, but requires careful noise reduction and calibration. The effective Z map offers a more robust alternative, potentially reducing susceptibility to noise, but is still vulnerable to overlapping tissue types. While these methods could potentially revolutionize coronary artery disease assessment, successful clinical implementation and evaluation relies on high quality image denoising and available ground-truth data. Overcoming these challenges yields significant improvements in clinical outcomes by aiding in early detection and treatment of vulnerable plaques.

articleTitle: A low-count quantitative SPECT method for Actinium-225-based alpha-particle therapies
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Actinium-225 (Ac-225) is a promising radioisotope for alpha-particle radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPTs). To facilitate clinical evaluations and subsequent clinical dosimetry with these therapies, there is a crucial need for methods to quantify dose deposited in lesions and at-risk organs. Ac-225 decay yields $\gamma$-emissions, enabling dose quantification via SPECT. However, traditional quantitative SPECT methods face challenges in reliably quantifying Ac-225 due to low counts, stray-radiation noise, SPECT artifacts and crosstalk with the daughter isotopes, Francium-221 (Fr-221) and Bismuth-213 (Bi-213), each of which may form their own independent bio-distributions. To address these challenges, we propose a generalized Multi-Isotope Low-Count Quantitative SPECT (MI-LC-QSPECT) method. The method jointly estimates the regional activity uptake of multiple isotopes (in this case, Ac-225, Fr-221 and Bi-223) directly from the SPECT projections and without performing reconstructions. The method was evaluated in clinically realistic simulation studies with anthropomorphic phantoms in the context of patients with neuroendocrine tumors treated with Ac-225-based peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). The proposed method yielded highly reliable quantitative estimates, achieving an average normalized mean square error (NMSE) $\lt 5\%$ for all three isotopes. Further, the method outperformed a conventional dual-isotope ordered subset expectation maximization (DOSEM) reconstruction method for Fr -221 and Bi-213, emphasizing the advantage of projection domain quantitation for low-count imaging. The method also outperformed a single-isotope projection-domain low-count quantitative SPECT method that does not model crosstalk emphasized the importance of modeling crosstalk. The performance of MI-LC-QSPECT motivates further clinical evaluation and application of this method to other alpha-particle RPTs.

articleTitle: An Overview on the micro-RWELL technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The challenges posed by the forthcoming High-Energy Physics experiments necessitate the development of particle detection technologies that are easily engineered and compatible with industrial-scale production. The micro-RWELL, a single-amplification stage resistive MPGD based on sequential build-up technology, effectively meets these demands. In this contribution, we provide an overview of the detector characteristics, its good spatial and time resolutions, and the stability under heavy irradiation, outlining the design and testing steps conducted at INFN-LNF. Additionally, we offer a schematic description of the construction processes performed at the ELTOS Company and CERN MPT Workshop. The experience detailed in this contribution indicates that a significant portion of the detector construction can be effectively carried out by the industry, providing substantial advantages in terms of production time and cost-effectiveness. Furthermore, it is crucial to highlight the significant effort invested in the production of large DLC (Diamond-Like-carbon) foils, a fundamental component of the detector amplification stage. The acquisition of the DC-magnetron sputtering machine, a fruitful joint venture between CERN and INFN, represents a crucial development, allowing a remarkable advancement in this technology. The results of the tests carried out with an X-ray gun at LNF and particle beams at the CERN North Area beam facility are then discussed in detail. The outcomes of most recent tests are summarized, indicating a production yield of approximately 90%. The fruitful experience gained in this phase of the technology transfer is a first step towards the construction of larger detectors, as envisaged for the forthcoming challenges in HEP.

articleTitle: Position and Anomaly Sensitivity for Multi-Variant Signature Analysis Utilizing a Natural Uranium Fresh Fuel Mock-Up
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The nuclear community does not currently employ a multi-variant detector system to discern between fresh nuclear fuel assemblies. This research examined a detection system consisting of four commercial off-the-shelf detectors: He-3 proportional counter, NaI(Tl) crystal scintillator, Eljen EJ-309 liquid scintillator, and $\mathrm{Cs}_{2} \mathrm{LiYCl}_{6}: \mathrm{Ce}^{3+}$ (CLYC) crystal scintillator; these detectors are capable of measuring either gammas and/or neutrons and this research applied the system against a natural uranium fresh fuel mock-up. The natural uranium fresh fuel mock-up was designed in CAD and machined out of aluminum. It is designed for multiple configuration variations; for this work it was adapted to ten different configurations of natural uranium. The detection system conducted measurements at three positions. Data was post-processed to be used to develop an initial machine learning algorithm capable of discerning between natural uranium fresh fuel mockup configurations. This algorithm will be modified and further developed in future experiments. It provides initial promise at successfully radiologically verifying and distinguishing between fresh nuclear fuel assemblies.

articleTitle: A Novel Gamma Camera Based on Joint-Self-Collimating-Compton Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The application of conventional SPECT in the field of high-energy gamma photon imaging is challenging, which severely restricted the range of selection of radionuclides. Recently we have developed the self-collimation (SC) concept for single photon emission imaging with a multilayered interspaced mosaic detector architecture. The new detector geometry makes Compton imaging with detector scatters a readily accessible pathway to further enhance imaging performance, especially for imaging high energy (e.g., 511 keV) photons. In this simulation study, we model the contributions from detector scattered events on a self-collimation gamma camera through the well-known Compton imaging approach and incorporate the model in the imaging generation process of the SC system. We show that Compton imaging significantly enhances the camera’s sensitivity and signal-to-noise ratio in imaging 511 keV single photon sources.

articleTitle: Development of Measurement Electronics Circuit Utilizing Radiation hardened H-diamond MOSFET(RADDFET)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Electronic devices with the capability of operating under high levels of radiation and high temperature environments are required to further ensure the safety of nuclear power plants. As a specific example, the decommissioning project of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant (1F) requires radiation detectors for criticality proximity monitoring and debris composition confirmation for fuel debris removal. Charge-sensitive pre-amplifiers (CSA) that do not require γ-ray shielding are also needed. In this research, we have developed hydrogen-terminated diamond MOSFETs (RADDFETs) with the capability of operating under high levels of radiation and high-temperature environments and demonstrated their voltage amplification performance. As part of the development of radiation-resistant CSA, we designed, fabricated, and evaluated a differential amplification unit using the improved RADDFETs, which have a lower amplification factor than conventional FETs. Therefore, we attempted to develop a CSA circuit using a different circuit system. We devised a CSA circuit with a negative feedback configuration by connecting three stages of unit amplifiers and confirmed the feasibility of the unit amplifiers as the core of the amplification section. The unit amplifier uses a differential amplifier circuit system utilizing pair characteristic FETs. To secure high open gain under limited mutual conductance and DC bias conditions, the load resistor was made an active load with FETs to increase the gain by taking out the output with high impedance. In the actual prototype circuit, a signal output of 563 mVp, equivalent to 35.3 dB, was confirmed for a 10 mVp, 1 kHz sine wave input. Furthermore, a GB product of 12 MHz was confirmed. The circuit achieved the frequency characteristic and the target gain, successfully demonstrating the ability of the operation at the practical circuit level using diamond FETs.

articleTitle: Ultra-low power, low-noise ASIC with 7-bit ADC and 24-bit histogram memory for radiation modules
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A personal radiation monitoring system requires a long-term measurement with highly accurate and real-time response. This study is the development of an ASIC connected to a photodetector (PD) for measuring radiation events, which has continuous energy distribution with ultra-low power consumption, and it can be operated by a small battery (e.g., coin battery) for more than 1 year.This ASIC has special circuits to achieve highly accurate energy detection and ultra-low power consumption, such as a function of data collection to memory that reduces the power consumption of the high-performance MCU, and it has an I/F for wireless communications. This ASIC has a low-noise, low-power first-stage analog part, a 7-bit ADC that makes it possible to acquire the spectrum, and a 24-bit wide histogram memory, and it is I/F-connected to the MCU with an I2C interface. The MCU connected to this ASIC can stand by in a sleep state for some minutes (e.g., 10 minutes or more) during the measurement interval and minimize power consumption. The evaluation results of the ASIC with PD showed that the low energy level (e.g., 15 keV) can be detected and the maximum non-paralyzed counting rate is over 30 kcps with 31 uA power consumption.

articleTitle: Amorphous Silicon Microchannel Plates: A New Photon Detector with 10 ps Timing and 15 μm Spatial Resolution
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we present the principle, development, functionality, and characterization of a new type of photon detector. The technology of amorphous silicon Micro-channel plates (AMCPs) uses a versatile approach to stack hydrogenated amorphous silicon in thicknesses up to 100 um, using plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition and etch microchannels of diameter 2 um, every 4.5 um, on a hexagonal pattern, by deep reactive ion etching. Five generations of these devices have led to significant improvements in specifications. The versatile fabrication process allows etching of funnel-shaped channels, leading to an active area close to 100%. Measurements have shown excellent timing resolution ($\sigma\lt10 \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM) for low incoming fluxes, along with a maximum single-channel gain around 1500, in reverse voltage of 500 V. The flexibility of the fabrication processes allows to grow the detector directly on top of a CMOS cascade of low-noise amplifiers with a spatial resolution of 15✗15 um<sup>2</sup>, offering 350000 channels on chip.

articleTitle: Updates on the Gantry Design and Manufacturing for the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present advancements in the design of the PET gantry for the Human Dynamic NeuroChemical Connectome (HDNCC) scanner. This system integrates an ultra-high-sensitivity PET camera with a 7-T MRI scanner to image dynamic processes in the brain with high temporal resolution. Our key goal is maximizing PET sensitivity while ensuring compatibility with ultra-high-field MRI. We leveraged additive manufacturing to optimize the gantry design for cost-effectiveness and versatility. The novel design provides mechanical support and water cooling for PET detectors and readout electronics. Additionally, the gantry is designed to conform to the complex inner geometry of the MR bore and bed rails. Stereolithography (SLA) printing enabled us to achieve intricate support structures quickly and at a low cost while meeting design specifications. We evaluated various SLA resins and selected UTR8220 for its combination of toughness, affordability, and minimal B0 field distortion. Furthermore, we are developing an outer shell for the gantry to provide robust mechanical support, light-proofing, seamless integration with the MR patient bed, and electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding to minimize interference with the MR scanner. We are currently constructing the shell using a combination of carbon fiber for structural integrity and Kydex for easy shaping. Two options for EMI shielding are under evaluation: a flexible printed PCB and a fine phosphor-bronze mesh. With the gantry design finalized and manufacturing ongoing, we are moving toward assembly and testing in the coming weeks.

articleTitle: Surface Passivated Perovskite Single Crystals for X-ray Detectors with High Sensitivity
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Perovskite single crystal-based self-powered direct X-ray detectors demonstrate promising performances that rival those of commercial technologies in terms of sensitivity and detection limit. However, surface defects, particularly those induced via post-polishing, detrimentally limit the performance of direct X-ray detectors. In this study, we synthesized perovskite single crystal with composition of $\mathrm{FA}_{0.85} \mathrm{MA}_{0.1} \mathrm{Cs}_{0.05} \mathrm{~Pb}\left(\mathrm{I}_{0.85} \mathrm{Br}_{0.15}\right)_{3}$ and implemented a chemical passivation approach to mitigate defects and improved detector performances. We employed a double-side passivation strategy, wherein we deposited a reactive organic salt of phenethylammonium iodide. This salt exhibits reactivity specifically towards the defective perovskite sites, facilitating the formation of lower-dimensional perovskite layers on both the bottom and top surfaces of the crystal. Chemical passivation leads to a significant reduction in defects, resulting in low dark current with high sensitivity of $3.7 \times 10^{3} \mu \mathrm{C} / \mathrm{Gy} \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ to X-ray responses in the X-ray detector. The detector shows an indicative response for single-photon gamma-ray detection. These findings highlight the practical applications of chemically passivating defects in perovskite single crystals for high performance $\mathrm{X} / \gamma$-ray detectors.

articleTitle: Development of a GEANT4 Model for a 6LiInP2Se6 Semiconductor Neutron Imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a GEANT4 simulation model for the <sup>6</sup>LiInP<inf>2</inf>Se<inf>6</inf> (LIPSe or LIPSE) thermal neutron semiconductor imaging system. Meticulous C++ programming defined key components including detector geometry, material properties, source configuration, and data extraction methods. Analytical calculations of neutron detection efficiency, especially near thermal energy, aligned well with simulated results across various semiconductor materials and thicknesses. The model’s framework emphasized scalability and multifunctionality in model development over processing. Preliminary findings suggest potential for accurately simulating neutron detection in <sup>6</sup>LiInP<inf>2</inf>Se<inf>6</inf> semiconductors, advancing detection technology.

articleTitle: Characterization of TlBr Films for X-Ray Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Room temperature semiconductor materials provide important performance advantages in photon-counting X-ray imaging applications. This paper presents preliminary results on columnar thallium bromide (TlBr) films directly deposited on TimePix readout chips. This paper presents the current-voltage data for $\sim 100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick, $1^{\prime \prime} \times 1^{\prime \prime}$ or larger area, TlBr films deposited on ITO glass. The TlBr films exhibited resistivities $\gt1 \times 10^{9} \Omega \cdot \mathrm{cm}$. The work also shows the effect of thin barrier layers, intended to protect the electrode from parasitic electrochemistry, between the TlBr film and the electrode on the IV curve and X-ray response. The IV curve from barrier layers deviates from linearity, however, the magnitude of the current indicates the transport of charge across the barrier. All devices respond to a 70 kVp X-ray pulse, where the bare TlBr film device generated the most signal current, and with the barrier was lower by a factor of 2 to 4. A TlBr film was directly deposited on a TimePix chip and photon-counting events from the irradiation by a ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}$ source were imaged.

articleTitle: Integration and Testing of the Background-Subtracting Gamma-Ray Spectrometer for the MAMBO CubeSat Mission
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The origin of the cosmic diffuse gamma-ray (CDG) background in the $0.3-10 \mathrm{MeV}$ energy range is a mystery that has persisted for 50 years. The best existing measurements have large systematic uncertainties and sparse sky coverage. Intriguingly, the latest theoretical models based on emission from active galactic nuclei and supernovae differ significantly from these data below $\sim 1.5 \mathrm{MeV}$. The Mini Astrophysical MeV Background Observatory (MAMBO) is a new CubeSat mission under development at Los Alamos National Laboratory with the goal of making highquality measurements of the MeV CDG to help solve this puzzle. Scheduled for launch in late 2025, the concept is motivated by the fact that the sensitivity of space-based MeV gamma-ray instruments to the CDG is limited not by size, but by the locally generated instrumental background produced by interactions of energetic particles in spacecraft materials. Comparatively tiny CubeSat platforms provide a uniquely quiet environment relative to previous gamma-ray science missions. The MAMBO mission will provide the best measurement ever made of the MeV CDG spectrum and uniformity across the sky utilizing an innovative shielded spectrometer that simultaneously measures signal and background. Primary detector, background monitor, and active shield volumes made of bismuth germanate (BGO) scintillator are read out by custom silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays to enable an efficient, compact instrument suitable for CubeSat deployment. A tagged calibration source maintains constant gain across detector elements despite expected temperature variations. We describe the integration and testing of the MAMBO instrument and present calibration measurements which verify the required energy range, energy resolution, and stable performance over the expected operating temperature range. These measurements validate a Monte Carlo simulation model, enabling prediction of counting rates and the instrument’s scientific performance.

articleTitle: Dual-Ended Readout TOF-DOI PET Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Two types of time-of-flight (TOF) and depth-of-interaction (DOI) positron emission tomography (PET) detectors based on the dual-ended readout method and LYSO arrays with two different pitches were introduced. Both detectors were equipped with $8 \times 8$ silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays with a 3.2 mm pitch coupled to both ends of $8 \times 8$ lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) arrays with a 3.2 mm pitch or $16 \times 16$ LYSO arrays with a 1.6 mm pitch. All crystals in the LYSO arrays were clearly resolved. Detectors based on the $8 \times 8$ LYSO arrays achieved an average coincidence time resolution (CTR) of $198.3 \pm 4.3 \mathrm{ps}$ and an average DOI resolution of $3.9 \pm 0.6$ mm across the crystals. In contrast, detectors with the $16 \times 16$ LYSO arrays provided an average CTR of $211.2 \pm 5.9 \mathrm{ps}$ and an average DOI resolution of $2.6 \pm 0.3 \mathrm{~mm}$. The TOF-DOI PET detectors developed in this work are promising candidates for whole-body PET and brain PET scanners, which can offer uniform spatial resolution across the field-of-view (FOV).

articleTitle: Effects of Angular Sampling in Deep-Learning based PET Reconstruction for Total-Body PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In recent years, deep-learning (DL) has shown significant promise in positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction. Initially, the use of single view histo-images as input for end-to-end DL reconstruction offered easier handling by convolutional neural networks. Thereafter, the use of multi-view histo-images in DL-based PET reconstructions demonstrated better performance. Especially for Total-Body PET or dynamic imaging, DL-based reconstruction is useful in handling large data sizes since it decreases reconstruction speed when compared to classical tomographic approaches. For example, the PennPET Explorer data is sampled to a total of 180 views ie., 20 azimuthal-angular and 9 polar-angular samples. In this work, we investigate the effects of angular sampling strategies of PET data in DL based reconstruction approaches, which are quite different from the classical tomographic approaches following angular sampling requirements.

articleTitle: Advancement of Anthropomorphic Thorax Phantom for Multimodal Imaging: Integration of Organs Synchronized with Respiratory Motion
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In continuation of our prior work on thorax phan tom development, we here present the advancement of a novel anthropomorphic thorax phantom based on a cardiovascular blood flow system. This phantom is capable of simulating motion of the left radioactivity-filled myocardium while providing a pulsatile blood flow. The objective of this study is to integrate organ compartments, such as liver, stomach, kidneys, and spleen, which move along with respiratory motion. It is further intended to facilitate the delivery of blood flow to tissues and organs. Consequently, this advancement enables the execution of dynamic tracer studies, thereby simulating perfusion-related tracer uptake under realistic conditions encompassing organ, cardiac, and respiratory motion.

articleTitle: Frequency Selective Flux Focusing Passive Lenz Resonators for Substantial MRI Signal-to-Noise Ratio Amplification
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The need for increased sensitivity in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for its advancement as an imaging modality. The amplification of MRI signal will lead to more efficient diagnosis and patient treatment. While there are methods that exist to amplify the signal from specific nuclei in MRI, such as hyperpolarization, a general solution will be more advantageous and would work in conjunction with these preexisting methods. While the Lenz Lens proposed such a general solution based on the reciprocity principle, it came at the cost of minimal signal enhancement. In this work, the first-in-kind prototype Lenz Resonator was conceived and examined as a general frequency selective passive flux focusing element for significant MRI signal enhancement. A 3T Philips Achieva MRI was used to compare signal from samples in the presence of Lenz Lenses, Lenz Resonators, and control trials with neither component. An MRI investigation demonstrated an experimental amplification of the signal-to-noise ratio up to $80 \%$ using an MRI insert of two coaxial square Lenz Resonators. Resonators displayed consistent amplification, nearly independent of their position on the axis of the target within the MRI bore. This behavior demonstrates the feasibility of imaging large objects of varying shapes without penalties for signal amplification.

articleTitle: CZT strip detector exposed to outer space from the ISS-Alpha
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The effect of the Low Earth Orbit (LEO) environment on future high energy instrument sensors is essential to optimize their performance, by minimizing orbital background noise. In the framework of the CNES-ESA European Material Ageing program (EMA), the ageing effects on critical components of a Laue lens telescope in the LEO space environment will be investigated. Since more than a decade, the group has been developing CZT drift strip sensors to meet the stringent requirements of a Laue lens focal plane detector for high-energy photons. As part of the EMA proposal, they plan to expose two simplified samples of drift strip CZT detectors on the CNES Bartolomeo external platform for 6 to 12 months. The objective is to test the robustness and reliability of the surface passivation and metallization processes in the LEO space environment. In this work we present the realization of the simplified CZT detector samples, and the results of laboratory characterization measurements.

articleTitle: Analysis of Characteristic Gamma Spectra Originating from Neutron Activation of Steel Scrap Materials
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The detailed analysis of characteristic gamma lines observed in neutron activated spectra of steel scrap samples is presented. The samples content represent the key chemical elements in steelmaking processes, such as $\mathrm{Fe}, \mathrm{Cu}, \mathrm{Cr}$ and Ni. The samples activation is performed by means of a DT neutron generator, emitting 14 MeV neutrons. The background in the recorded spectra is significantly reduced due to incorporation of the associated particle imaging technique and data acquisition in coincidence with alpha particles detection. The gamma detection system comprises of 14 large scintillation detectors of three types: 4 cylidrical 3.5x8 inch LaBr, 4 cylindrical 5x5 inch BGO and 6 cuboid $5 \times 5 \times 10$ inch NaI(Tl). The analysis of characteristic gamma spectra is mainly performed on measurements with LaBr and later compared to NaI and BGO data. The aim of the analysis is understanding of intensities of the observed peaks, the proper identification of the characteristic gamma lines as well as understanding of their origin due to interaction channels and changes in intensity due to possible overlapping.

articleTitle: A Monte Carlo Simulation for Prompt Gamma Time Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We develop a Geant4 Monte Carlo (MC) simulation of the TIARA detector dedicated to Prompt Gamma Time Imaging (PGTI) used to monitor dose deposition in protontherapy. The Time-of-flight Imaging Array (TIARA) consists of a beam monitor and thirty PbF2 Cherenkov radiators placed around a phantom head. Computed Tomography (CT) scans of the setup tested at the Mediterranean Institute for Protontherapy of the Centre Antoine Lacassagne (CAL) in Nice are used to define precisely the geometry of the simulated setup. The simulated proton beam reproduces the beam specifications that are used at CAL. The phantom that is used is a RANDO phantom head described by taking into account the materials it is made of using DICOM data of the phantom scan. The purpose is to compare results obtained with the simulation to the experimental data. We describe the Monte Carlo implementation of the PGTI setup and preliminary simulation results against experimental data.

articleTitle: Fabrication and characterization of Heteroepitaxial Diamond Radiation Detector with Ti/Pt/Au electrodes
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Diamond radiation detector with $\mathrm{Ti} / \mathrm{Pt} / \mathrm{Au}$ electrodes was fabricated from a heteroepitaxial diamond grown on a Ir/sapphire substrate. The diamond substrate measured $4 \mathrm{~mm} \times 4 \mathrm{~mm} \times$ 0.5 mm was cut and polished. The $\mathrm{Ti} / \mathrm{Pt} / \mathrm{Au}$ electrodes were deposited on the polished surfaces by spattering method. Thin gold wires were bonded between the electrodes and a printed circuit board. The device was irradiated with high-energy X-rays from a radiation therapy treatment system at room temperature. The X-rays at 6 MV were irradiated for 12 seconds. The total amount of absorbed dose was about 1 Gy. The device exhibited linear response corresponding to the applied bias voltage between the electrodes of the front and back sides. The higher bias voltage resulted in higher charge amount and less standard deviation. The charge amount per unit volume was about 14000 times higher than that of a conventional ionization chamber at maximum. The results indicated that the heteroepitaxial diamond detector with $\mathrm{Ti} / \mathrm{Pt} / \mathrm{Au}$ electrodes had a capability for high energy X-ray radiation detection with high sensitivity and high reproducibility.

articleTitle: Effect of inter-crystal events inclusion on high resolution small-animal PET scanner performance
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Inter-crystal scattering (ICS) events cause mispositioning of annihilation events, leading to contrast degradation of Positron-Emission-Tomography (PET) images. In Depth-of-Interaction (DOI) detectors for high resolution PET scanners the ICS events rate increases due to the smaller size of the crystals. This results in uniformly distributed counts of photon hits on flood histogram of the detected events (flood-map) in the detector, increasing the probability of crystal misidentification. DOI detectors with Anger-type calculation exhibit areas on the flood map not referable to any crystal. In our system, events in such areas represent ICS events and reach 25% of the total number of events detected, resulting in ~50% of the coincidence events being discarded, as they contain at least one event unassignable to any pixel. We developed a method based on most likely position to include such ICS events in the PET reconstructed images to improve the sensitivity of the scanner. The method is being developed in the context of the “Small animal proton Irradiator for Research in Molecular Image-guided radiation Oncology” (SIRMIO) project, which succeeded at developing a prototype in-beam PET system for image-guided small animal proton irradiation at clinical facilities. The scanner features 56 staggered 3-layer DOI detectors, each of them comprising a LYSO pixelated (0.9 × 0.9 × 6.67 mm<sup>3</sup> crystal size) scintillation block coupled to an 8 × 8 SiPM array, light-sharing method and Anger type calculation with a 4 channels output for crystal identification. The signal of a <sup>22</sup>Na source and the activation produced by a 30 MeV proton beam were measured. The events outside the crystal response areas were assigned to one of the closest pixels according to a probabilistic computation and later used for image reconstruction. The results support the feasibility of the method for online PET applications, resulting in a doubled sensitivity and a minimal spatial resolution degradation.

articleTitle: Experimental Qualification of a Germanium Drift Detector Built in Planar Technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Semiconductor Drift Detectors (SDDs) allow the joint achievement of low electronic noise and high-rate capability due to the low output capacitance independent of the active area thanks to the sideward depletion technique, introduced by Gatti and Rehak in 1982. Till nowadays SDDs are mainly in silicon, with an endingless variety of applications mainly in high precision X-ray measurements. To overcome the energy barrier of 20 keV X-rays, thicker SDDs in silicon were produced, but only high-Z materials can provide sufficient detection efficiency and Ge is a natural candidate for drift topologies given the superior properties of carrier transport. On the basis of the established high-quality fabrication capability of planar Ge detectors (strips, pixels), we started a R&D program towards the implementation of Ge drift topologies in a fully planar fabrication process. Simulation studies allowed us to tackle all the constraints arising from the very high resistivity of the substrate, the limitation on the drift field due to the punch-through between adjacent p+ strip and the optimization of electrode geometry according to the substrate doping and thickness. We designed a 3-inch wafer with 3 main Ge drift detectors and some test structures. Great technological effort allowed the setup of a reliable double-sided and multi-mask process able to guarantee the presence of p- and n- contacts on the same surface. We qualified the performance of the designed detectors both with an IR laser and with radioactive sources. Mapping of the amplitude and collection time of the generated charge along the radial direction clearly showed the expected relationship drift time vs. drift distance. To our knowledge, it is the first evidence of a Germanium drift detector in planar technology.

articleTitle: Tests and implementation of the voltage measurement using noise distribution algorithm
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the implementation and evaluation of the voltage measurement using the noise distribution algorithm within the SMAUG1 application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC). The implemented algorithm is based on the measurement of the distribution of the noise superimposed with the measured signal. Thanks to the presence of the circuit noise, the signal is “blurry”, which allows the noise histogram measurement, from which we can extract the signal value with a precision better than it might result from the circuit noise performance. The presented algorithm is similar to the widely used threshold scan procedure (used in radiation imaging systems). However, instead of using a single comparator with a variable threshold, it combines information from multiple comparators with fixed thresholds and performs measurements on a single pulse rather than a series of pulses. The prototype SMAUG1 ASIC, designed in CMOS 28 nm technology, provides algorithm implementation as a part of a single-photon counting radiation imaging system. The chip includes a matrix of 7×7 pixels with 68x68 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ area. Each pixel comprises an input amplifier with a calibration pulse generator and eight comparators with counters. The prototype evaluation covers the extraction of base parameters like gain and noise ($165 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{fC}$ and 2.5 mV, respectively) and calibration of the comparators’ offset and speed. The measurements show some problems with the number of counts for the comparators working with low overdrives of several millivolts (only the noise is toggling the discriminators). Nevertheless, the tested algorithm improves the precision by x4-8 compared to standard measurements.

articleTitle: Correction of Attenuation and Scattered Photons in a Three-detector Multi-pinhole SPECT System Using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A three-detector multi-pinhole SPECT system can obtain the projection data necessary for image reconstruction without moving the detectors, so it has the potential to visualize the dynamic distribution of radiopharmaceuticals. In this study, we corrected the effects of gamma ray attenuation and scattered photons in an 11 pinhole SPECT system using a convolutional neural network(CNN). The correction by the CNN(UNet++) was performed on the projection data. In order to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, we compared the image corrected by CNN with that corrected by conventional methods incorporating attenuation correction into the ML-EM method after the correction of scattered photons with the triple energy window(TEW) method. As a result, although the proposed method did not use the distribution of attenuation coefficients, it was able to achieve correction accuracy that is almost the same as that of the conventional correction method. ⃉

articleTitle: Evaluation of an MR-compatible Power Supplying Solution for a Second-Generation RF-Penetrable Brain TOF-PET Insert for Simultaneous PET/MRI
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the development of a modular power supply unit (MPSU) tailored for the PETCoil Gen II, a magnetic resonance (MR)-compatible radio-frequency (RF) penetrable Time of Flight Positron Emission Tomography (TOF-PET) insert with substantial power demands ($\approx 1000 \mathrm{~W}$). The MPSU integrates off-the-shelf switching power supplies, custom MR-compatible coaxial cables, a linear power-regulating unit (LPRU), and an RF shielding cage. A liquid cooling system was implemented to address the overheating issues and maintain optimal detector performance. Our stability test shows consistent PET scanner performance, with an energy resolution and coincidence time resolution (CTR) of $11.74 \pm 0.03 \%$ full-width-half-maximum (FWHM) and $238 \pm 0.5 \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM, respectively, over a 10 -hour-long stability test. Stable temperatures of $20 \pm 0.1 \circ \mathrm{C}$ and $45 \pm 1.4{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ are recorded for PET detector modules and LPRU, respectively, during a 10-hour study. The developed power system offers a modular, MR-compatible, low-noise, and high-power solution for our second-generation RF-Penetrable Brain TOF-PET Insert for simultaneous PET/MRI scanning

articleTitle: Comprehensive Study on Dose-Rate Realtime Monitoring System with an Optical Fiber for the Decommissioning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Real dose monitors under the high dose-rate condition are required to remove the debris in the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant as the decommissioning step. We have proposed a doserate monitor consisting of a scintillator, optical fiber and photodetector, and scintillation materials are required to have the long-emission-wavelength (550 - 1000 nm) and high light output. We have developed several novel materials such as Cs<inf>2</inf>HfI<inf>6</inf> and Rb<inf>2</inf>HfI<inf>6</inf> for gamma-ray detection, and Li<inf>2</inf>HfBr<inf>6</inf> had sensitive to both gamma rays and neutrons. Additionally, the noise spectrum is expected to have position information for the hot-sopt along the fiber, and we found fiber noise has rate information in one-dimensional imaging. In this paper, we show the scintillation properties, calibration system and evaluation of the noise.

articleTitle: Data-driven non-rigid motion detection and correction for NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Patient movement in PET studies can lead to image blurring and inaccurate tracer concentration estimates. The next-generation brain PET system, NeuroEXPLORER (NX), has an integrated UIH markerless motion tracking system (UMT), which provides rigid head motion data by registering the upper facial surface. Additionally, the NX’s extended axial field of view increases sensitivity, aiding in extracting image-derived input functions (IDIF) from the carotid arteries (CA) and improving quantification in oncological studies. The lower face and neck areas, which include the CA or lesions, are prone to complex non-rigid motion patterns that cannot be expressed by rigid transformations and exceed UMT’s tracking capabilities. Therefore, effective MC is particularly vital for these areas. In this study, we introduced a data-driven non-rigid motion correction framework for the NX (NX-NRMC) to address non-rigid motions and assessed the effectiveness of UMT-derived rigid motion data in non-rigid regions. Our NX-NRMC, tested in two human studies, demonstrated promising results in improving quantification in non-rigid areas such as carotid arteries and tumors, areas where UMT-based rigid motion correction was inadequate. For the quantification of the tumor ROI, NX-NRMC yielded $\operatorname{SUV}_{\text {mean }}$ and $\operatorname{SUV}_{\text {max }}$ of 4.7 and 8.4, respectively, which were close to the motion-free reference values of 4.9 and 8.8. In the future, we will integrate the captured non-rigid motion estimates into an event-by-event motion correction reconstruction as well as combine both UMT-based rigid motion and NX-NRMC-based non-rigid motion to represent patient movement more accurately.

articleTitle: The Development of the SBND LArTPC Cryogenic Readout Electronics System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Short Baseline Near Detector (SBND) is one of three liquid argon (LAr) neutrino detectors sitting in the Booster Neutrino Beam (BNB) at Fermilab as part of the Short Baseline Neutrino (SBN) program. The detector is in a cryostat holding 260-ton of LAr and consists of four 2.5 m (L) $\times 4 \mathrm{~m}(\mathrm{~W})$ Anode Plane Assembles (APAs) and two Cathode Plane Assemblies (CPAs), which leads to 11,264 Time Projection Chamber (TPC) readout channels and two separate 2 m long drift regions. In order to achieve optimum noise performance, minimize feedthrough penetrations and lower construction complexity, the front-end electronics is placed close to the wire electrodes, which detects, amplifies, digitizes and gets the charge signals multiplexed to high-speed links in LAr at 87 K. In addition, the warm interface electronics is placed on the feed-through flanges outside of the cryostat at room temperature, which further organizes and transmits the digitized signal to the DAQ system via fiber optical links. The large number of readout channels and high-performance specifications required robust electronics system design following with a large-scale production and rigorous quality control, careful installation, and detector commissioning efforts. SBND LAr filling was completed in early March 2024 and the detector turned into the early phase of commissioning, cryogenic readout electronics has exhibited performance exceeded expectations. We summarize the cryogenic readout electronics system design, production and quality control, installation, and commissioning efforts that enabled this excellent electronics performance.

articleTitle: Direct reconstruction of multiplexed PET acquisitions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multiplexed PET imaging offers the possibility to capture the diverse physiological and pathological characteristics of tissues by employing multiple radiotracers simultaneously. This study introduces a method for direct reconstruction and separation of images from mixed sinograms. The approach aims to be generic and unsupervised in order to be suitable for future clinical applications. The proposed method is compared to the indirect method previously published and found to have better performances closer to those obtained with separate singletracer acquisitions

articleTitle: 3-D position reconstruction in CZT drift strip detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, great efforts have been made in the development of room temperature gamma ray spectroscopic imagers, aiming to compete with the superb energy resolutions of high-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors (0.3% FWHM at 662 keV) obtained after cryogenic cooling. Cadmium-zinc-telluride (CZT) detectors equipped with particular electrode structures demonstrated to be a possible solution for room temperature measurements. In this work, we present the performance of new high-resolution CZT drift strip detectors (0.8% FWHM at 662 keV), recently fabricated at IMEM-CNR of Parma (Italy) in collaboration with due2lab company (Reggio Emilia, Italy). The detectors, used in planar transverse field (PTF) geometry, are able to perform 2D positioning through cross-strip electrode patterns on the cathode/anode electrodes and the third coordinate with the C/A ratio and/or drift time. The analysis of the zoo of collected and induced-charge pulses from CZT drift strip detectors allows sub-millimetre 3-D spatial resolution. These activities are in the framework of an Italian collaboration on the development of spectroscopic gamma ray imagers (10-1000 keV) for medical and astrophysical applications.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Approach for Positron Range Correction in PET Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Range correction is a crucial step in PET image reconstruction when dealing with data acquired with high energy radionuclide, such as <sup>68</sup>Ga. The correction of positron range in reconstruction typically involves the use of a convolution kernel, the complexity of which is a trade-off between accuracy and computational efficiency. In this work we propose the use of a deep-learning approach, trained on a Monte-Carlo simulated database comprising annihilation images derived from reconstructed images of varying resolutions and variances. The architecture is integrated in the iterative reconstruction and applied to the current estimation of the image prior to forward projection. In order to train the deep learning model, we generated a database of images reconstructed from simulated acquisitions of geometrical phantoms. Theses reconstructed images were used as <sup>68</sup>Ga distribution to produce employing maps depicting positron annihilation locations using Monte-Carlo simulations. These maps were then used alongside attenuation maps to train the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture to model positron range blurring accross different mixture of materials. Subsequently, the GAN architecture was integrated into the MLEM reconstruction algorithm to account for the blurring effect of positron range on the current image estimations before the forward projection steps. The proposed method was evaluated using two phantoms, demonstrating enhanced contrast recovery in comparison with the use of a tissue-dependent convolution kernel reconstruction approach, particularly in tissues with lower attenuation, albeit with a trade-off of increased noise in the areas with higher attenuating materials. This study demonstrates the feasability of the proposed approach to correct for positron range. Current work focuses on training the approach with anthropomorphic phantoms and assess its potential to correct for positron range for <sup>68</sup>Ga clinical data.

articleTitle: A Low-Power Analog Readout Circuit Assisted by The Pseudo Thyristor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) are integral to modern high-energy physics experiments, but as the number of detector elements or pixels increases, there is a growing need for power-efficient read-out circuits. Addressing this, a novel CMOS discriminator called the Pseudo Thyristor, consuming zero static current, was proposed. Leveraging this innovation, we introduce a low-power analog read-out circuit tailored for precision timing detector applications for particle physics and nuclear physics experiments. The circuit begins with a low-impedance, high-slew-rate transimpedance amplifier to capture the input signal, which is then converted to current and further amplified by a discrimination input stage before being injected into the Pseudo Thyristor. The timing information of the particle hit event is derived from its flipping time. Schematic simulation results validate the effective detection of hit events. In addition, 27% power consumption is saved compared to the traditional readout circuit. This work will be implemented in the layout and fabricated in TSMC65nm process, and measurement results will be presented in the future. This development provides a power-efficient solution for future high-energy physics read-out Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs).

articleTitle: Attention-Guided U-net Framework for Automated Pulmonary Embolism Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) poses a significant risk to patients and often presents with nonspecific symptoms, challenging its timely detection during visual examination of computed tomography (CT) scans. Leveraging convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can aid radiologists in precise PE detection, potentially averting delayed treatment and associated complications. This study presents a novel neural network architecture, an augmented U-Net framework, tailored for detecting emboli in CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) images sourced from publicly available datasets (CAD-PE and FUMPE datasets). The network architecture, comprising 103 layers with self-attention (SA) blocks and a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layer, aims to enhance feature representations and capture spatial dependencies critical for accurate embolism detection across individual slices. Our modified attention-based U-Net demonstrates a specificity of 0.78 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.81) and maintains an acceptable false positive rate (FPR) of 0.22. Notably, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) attains 0.81 (95% CI, 0.79 to 0.83), affirming the reliability of our network’s embolism detection outcomes. With a high sensitivity of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.83 to 0.87) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.60 to $0.66)$, our model demonstrates effectiveness and accuracy in identifying emboli presence. Furthermore, the Cohens’ kappa score of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.59 to 0.67) indicates substantial agreement in embolism detection. This network exhibits promising results in accurately identifying emboli, offering potential advantages for enhancing PE diagnosis and patient management. The integration of attention mechanisms within the U-Net architecture represents a significant step forward in improving PE detection efficiency and ultimately patient care outcomes.

articleTitle: Quality Control for DUNE Cryogenic FEMB Production
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE), the Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) is chosen as the far detector (FD) solution. The first two 10 kton DUNE FD modules will employ anode planes with cold electronics (CE) installed inside the cryostat. The CE developed for cryogenic temperatures (77-89K) operation is an optimal solution that achieves excellent noise performance and decouples the electrode and cryostat design from the readout design. There are 384,000 channels from FD1 and 245,760 channels from FD2 to be read out by CE, which requires 4,920 Front-end Motherboards (FEMBs). DUNE is expected to be operated for 20 to 30 years, which requires FEMBs to stay in liquid argon (LAr) for 30 years without the possibility of any replacement and maintenance. Therefore, a stringent quality control (QC) method is studied to assure the robustness and reliability of FEMBs. It requires that all system aspects are considered starting from the early design phase to the detector commissioning phase. We summarize the design of cryogenic FEMB, experiences gained from pre-production, and QC testing method optimized for batch production.

articleTitle: MR Compatibility Evaluation of a BrainPET Insert for UHF-MR Systems and Neuroscientific Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, the results of a mutual MR/PET interference evaluation for an UHF-MRI compatible BrainPET insert for multimodal and multiparametric neuroscientific imaging applications are presented. The BrainPET insert has spatial resolution of 1.8 mm over the entire brain, peak sensitivity of 57.2 kcps/MBq (with transceiver array), and a peak NECR of 414 kcps at 12 kBq/ml when operated outside the MR scanner. For MR imaging, a Siemens Magnetom Terra 7T MR scanner together with a PET-compatible 8-channel self-shielded transceiver array is used. First RF interference measurements showed that the power supply and PET modules design seems appropriate and potentially does not lead to RF power emission within the relevant frequency band of +/- 250 kHz around the Larmor frequency. A complete assessment of MR interference between the 7T MR system, the coil array and the PET system, including MR image quality and PET subsystem performance with running MR system will be shown at the conference.

articleTitle: Inverse Rendering for PET Image Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Differentiable rendering (DR) is an emerging field that facilitates the calculation and propagation of gradients of 3D objects through images. In contrast to deep neural networks (DNNs), which generally lack the understanding of 3D objects that form the image, DR mitigates the need for extensive 3D data collection and annotation, thereby offering a higher success rate across a range of applications. In this work, we introduce a new approach in positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction, leveraging inverse rendering (IR) techniques which aim to reconstruct the highest resolution image from the measured sinograms, outperforming other algorithms based on DNNs or maximum likelihood expectation maximization (MLEM).

articleTitle: Upgrade for the Hyperion Detector Platform: Calibration Methods for the TOFPET ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The TOFPET ASIC from PETsys Electronics is a promising candidate to use for SiPM signal digitization in PET systems. Our group is currently integrating the ASIC in the MRI-compatible Hyperion PET detector platform. During this process, the calibration of the ASIC’s time- and charge-to-digital converters to register the timestamp and energy of an SiPM signal have to be considered both in firmware and in software routines. We present the calibration process we will use in our systems and compare to the PETsys-provided routines used in their hard-, firm-, and software. The TDC calibration method we propose uses randomly generated triggers. We could show that the method is reliable and even produces slightly better timing accuracy compared to the vendor provided method and does not rely on generating test pulses with specific phase shifts relative to the clock edge of the reference signal.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of Gamma-Ray Detector Comprising Monolithic NaI (Tl) Scintillator and SiPM Array
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The NaI (Tl) scintillator is widely utilized in gamma-ray detection due to its low cost, mature production processes, and reasonable performance. The traditional photomultiplier tubes (PMTs) are experiencing a trend of being replaced by silicon photomultiplier tubes (SiPMs). Pixelated NaI (Tl) may result in better spatial resolution, but it can also lead to additional cost increases. The aim of this study was to design and evaluate a cost-effective yet high-performance gamma-ray detection module. We developed a gamma-ray detection module consisting of a single $50.44 \times$ $50.44 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ detector block, including a $41.88 \times 41.88 \mathrm{~mm}^{2} \mathrm{NaI}$ (Tl) crystal, coupled with an $8 \times 8$ SiPM array. We adopted a 64-channel independent signal readout scheme in hopes of extracting more information from uncompressed SiPM signals. And corresponding front-end amplifier board was designed. Collimators for radioactive source and multi-axis translation stages were also constructed for evaluation with experiment. We utilized ${ }^{57} \mathrm{Co}$ and ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$ flood sources to evaluate the energy performance of our gamma-ray detection module, whiles the collimated ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$ source was employed for evaluating spatial resolution performance, which was obtained by the Anger logic calculation and the statistical-based positioning (SBP). Experimental results indicate that the energy resolution of the detector module is 16.19% at 140 keV, and the energy resolution exhibits reasonable uniformity across different positions. The results point to that the intrinsic spatial resolution of our detector module is approximately 2.32 $\mathrm{mm} \pm 0.26 \mathrm{~mm}$, which is superior to the typical value of 3 mm for conventional. Anger cameras The detector shows potential for gamma detection and medical imaging applications.

articleTitle: Quantifying Uncertainty in SPECT Imaging Using a Gamma Statistical Model with Spatial Covariance
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PurposeUncertainty assessment improves radiopharmaceutical dosing accuracy, aiding clinicians in predicting therapeutic outcomes and minimizing side effects. It ensures that scanner performance aligns with design specifications through routine quality checks on sensitivity, bias, and 3-D capabilities. Building on research that normalized PET data with the Gamma model, we aim to extend this method to SPECT, analyzing statistical distributions and spatial covariance in reconstructed images to refine noise recalibration and enhance uncertainty estimates.MethodsThe method involves two main steps: data analysis within the ROI and simulated data generation.
