Initially, voxel-level shape and scale parameters in the ROI are estimated through multiple scans or by re-binning List-mode data from a single scan to adjust for changes due to radioactive decay and biological clearance. We used 5 images to normalize data and construct a spatial autoregressive matrix, which scales simulated Gaussian white noise accordingly. The white-noise variance equals the mean voxel value, consistent with Poisson distribution. These images help calculate the ROI’s relative error, defined as the standard deviation divided by the mean value. Validation involves using the XCAT phantom and SIMIND software to simulate a patient scenario with a liver tumor post 6.85 GBq 177Lu-DOTATATE injection. OSEM reconstructions are performed with 10 to 30 iterations across 6 subsets.Results and DiscussionThe covariance from 600 noise realization images guided the selection of a 5-order neighbor model for the spatial autoregressive matrix, optimizing accuracy and simplicity. Results showed symmetric covariance, allowing us to limit optimization to 5 coefficients and speed up computations. This model application significantly reduced autocorrelation and showed that relative error in total counts across the ROI or tumor area increases with the number of OSEM reconstruction iterations.

articleTitle: The Synthesis and Electronic Properties of Cs2AgBiBr6 Double Perovskite Single Crystals for Radiation Detector Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the synthesis, comprehensive characterization, and application of all inorganic Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> double perovskite single crystals with a focus on their use in radiation detection technologies. Through the use of an effective synthesis method, we successfully produced high-quality Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> crystals and performed a detailed analysis of their structural and electronic characteristics. Techniques such as Optical Microscopy, Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX) were utilized to elucidate the morphology and chemical composition of the crystals. Furthermore, the electronic properties were systematically investigated through current-voltage (I-V) measurements, revealing their potential for high-sensitivity radiation detection. Notably, the stability of these crystals was also rigorously tested under various environmental conditions to evaluate their practicality in real-world applications. The results indicate that Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> double perovskite single crystals exhibit a combination of excellent material stability and outstanding electronic properties, making them ideal candidates for the next generation of efficient and cost-effective radiation detectors. This study not only broadens the understanding of Cs<inf>2</inf> AgBiBr<inf>6</inf> as a remarkable semiconductor material but also confirms its significant promise for technological applications in the field of radiation detection.

articleTitle: A Porous Metal Foam Collimator for Robotic Tasks
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An evaluation of graded density, metal foam collimator plates for use with single-detector localization systems on robotic platforms is described. Linear attenuation measurements have been made of three foams of different bulk densities, and a combination of these has been used to manufacture a barrel-type collimator. The angular responses obtained with this device reveal the distinct shape consistent with the response of a conventional, higher-density, homogeneous alternative which enables localization of radioactivity at gamma-radiation energies up to and potentially exceeding 2.5 MeV. This suggests that the use of low-density metal foam collimators might reduce the payload demand in nuclear robotic applications to enable a range of new nuclear characterization tasks.

articleTitle: Characterization of Superconducting Nanowire Single Photon Detectors to Search for Axions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Superconducting nanowire single photon detectors (SNSPD) are low threshold quantum sensors that have been widely used in quantum communication. They have been demonstrated to have a high detection efficiency of 98% at 1550 nm (0.8 eV), time jitter below 3 ps, low energy threshold of 0.1 eV, and dark count rate of ∼10<sup>-5</sup> count per second. Recent advancement have enabled the fabrication of large-area SNSPDs (mm<sup>2</sup>), allowing its application in high energy physics experiments. SNSPDs have been proposed to search for dark-matter by efficiently detecting the photons produce by its interaction with the experimental apparatus. The BREAD (Broadband Reflector Experiment for Axion Detection) experiment is currently looking to focus these converted photons into SNSPDs using a novel reflector design. The use of SNSPDs allow us to extend the target axion mass to 0.04 eV to 1 eV, which is a mass range currently unexplored by the traditional resonator experiments. We will report on the characterization of a state-of-the-art 4-channel 1×1 mm<sup>2</sup> SNSPD in an adiabatic magnetization refrigerator. The dark count rates of each and photon count rates for all 4 channels and their correlations have been characterized and will be analyzed extensively. Additionally, the temperature dependence of the dark count rate will also be reported.

articleTitle: Parametric Maps of Kinetic Heterogeneity and Ki in Dynamic Total Body PET using Approximate Bayesian Computation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The quantification of [18F]Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) metabolism in oncology via positron emission tomography (PET) is essential for accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Traditional semi-quantitative methods like the Standard Uptake Value (SUV) and Patlak plots, although widely used, often fall short in addressing the complexities of tissue heterogeneity. We introduce a voxelwise Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) for total body PET (TB-PET) imaging heterogeneity study and kinetic parameter estimation, demonstrating high accuracy in simulation and distinguishing reversible from irreversible FDG phosphorylation using real TB-PET data. The study successfully computed model probability maps and kinetic parameters (Ki) across an extensive real dataset of over 44 million voxels, achieving a significant computational speed-up. Future work will expand on these findings by exploring additional heterogeneities and their clinical implications, as well as incorporating spatial correlations.

articleTitle: An Investigation on Cross-Tracer Generalizability of Deep Learning-based PET Attenuation Correction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction (AC) is a critical step to ensure accurate quantitative PET imaging. To eliminate the radiation dose from CT, deep learning (DL)-based methods have been extensively investigated to generate the CT-equivalent attenuation map (μ-DL) directly from the PET signal. However, almost all previous studies only focus on <sup>18</sup>F-FDG due to its extensive data availability which is suitable for DL model training. In this work, we explored the cross-tracer generalizability of μ-DL generation DL models - primarily focusing on whether a model trained on a commonly used tracer like <sup>18</sup>F-FDG can be effectively applied to less common tracers such as <sup>68</sup>Ga-DOTATE and <sup>18</sup>F-Fluciclovine, and vica versa. Our preliminary results found that the DL model trained on one specific tracer can be adapted to other tracers with competitive performance when compared to the tracer-specific trained DL model. Immediate future works include analysis of PET reconstructed images using μ-DL from these cross-tracer models for AC and its impact on PET tumor quantification.

articleTitle: A phoswich detector for direct measurement of alpha and beta contamination in the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Understanding and assessing alpha and beta contaminations are crucial for the safe decommissioning of nuclear sites like the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station (FDNPS). However, conventional methods face challenges, particularly in high-gamma dose-rate environments. This study presents a novel approach utilizing a phoswich detector for direct in-situ detection of alpha and beta particles. The phoswich detector design is tailored to the anticipated higher beta radioactivity at the FDNPS site, comprising a ZnS(Ag) scintillator for alpha detection and a plastic scintillator for beta detection. The distinctive decay times of the scintillators enable discrimination between alpha and beta particles. Experimental measurements involved both radiation sources and on-site measurements within the FDNPS reactor building. Results demonstrate successful discrimination of alpha and beta particles, with clear separation of clusters in Pulse Shape Discrimination (PSD) maps. The counting efficiency for alpha particles reached 55.6%, while beta particles were separated. Simultaneous measurement of alpha and beta particles further validates the detector’s efficacy, with distinct clusters observed for both types of radiation. Field measurements conducted within the FDNPS site confirm the phoswich detector’s effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Future studies will report detailed measurements from the site. Overall, the developed phoswich detector offers a promising solution for direct and accurate alpha/beta contamination detection, facilitating enhanced radiation protection and internal exposure assessment in nuclear decommissioning efforts.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of SmartBrain for Real-Time Imaging in Free Movement
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Background. Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a vital medical imaging tool for studying in vivo metabolism. However, conventional PET system are limited in their inability to image during free movement. Therefore, we have developed a portable brain PET system for real-time imaging, which names SmartBrain. In this study, we evaluated imaging performance of SmartBrain. Methods. The SmartBrain used 192 detectors and the detector consists of a 6 x 6 LYSO crystal $\left(3.1 \times 3.1 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right.$) array with $3 \times 3$ SiPM array. We evaluated the physical performance of SmartBrain according to the NEMA NU 2-2018 standards. In addition, we performed ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG imaging in smaller Hoffman and mini Derenzo phantom. Results. Spacial resolution is 2.0 mm in center of FOV. The sensitivity was $3.943 \mathrm{kcps} / \mathrm{MBq}$. Additional, the SmartBrain showed the structure of Hoffman phantom and high resolution for separating 1.7 mm rods. Conclusion. The SmartBrain still can clearly showed brain structure, which is fit to clinic brain research.

articleTitle: Benefit of Improved Scanner Performance on Monitoring Therapy Response in Oncology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Quantitative positron emission tomography (PET) is increasingly employed for cancer therapy response assessment. We conducted a virtual clinical trial (VCT) using patient data from the PennPET Explorer to monitor therapy-induced changes in standardized uptake value (SUV). Two patients with high and low BMI were studied, each with 20 small lesions (1 cm diameter) embedded in lung and liver organs. Multiple scans were generated via bootstrapping and reconstructed using list-mode time of flight ordered subset expectation maximization (TOF-OSEM) for varied scan durations and SUV changes. The resulting SUVs were utilized to construct receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, enabling the quantification of the system’s capability to assess response. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) was used as a metric to assess our ability to accurately measure changes in SUV. Our results demonstrate that long axial field of view (LAFOV) PET scanners with high sensitivity can effectively detect early tumor response to therapy, even with very brief scan durations. Moreover, our findings suggest that extending the imaging times, while remaining practical, enhances sensitivity to measuring smaller changes in tumor uptake, making it feasible to detect patient therapy response at an earlier time point.

articleTitle: Pediatric Neuroblastoma: Estimating Radiation Dosimetry of [124I]-Metaiodobenzylguanidine (mIBG) Dynamic PET/CT Using Animal-to-Human Extrapolation and MCNPX Code with OLINDA/EXM Software
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) using iodine-124 metaiodobenzylguanidine (mIBG) is a well-established modality for imaging and pre-therapeutic dosimetry in neuroblastoma. This study investigates the biodistribution of [124I]-mIBG by extrapolating data from animal models to humans and estimates radiation doses using Monte Carlo (MC) dosimetry, specifically tailored to a pediatric model. Utilizing the Monte Carlo neutron particle (MCNPX) code, dosimetry of [124I]mIBG was conducted within a 10-year-old pediatric Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) phantom. Human organ-specific time-integrated activity coefficients (TIACs) were derived from a previous animal study, incorporating a relative mass scaling factor. These TIACs were then employed to calculate absorbed doses (ADs) in various target organs, including the liver, kidneys, lungs, pancreas, stomach wall, spleen, urinary bladder wall, and brain. To validate our approach, we compared our MCNPX-based results with those obtained using OLINDA/EXM v1.1, utilizing relative percentage error (RPE). Furthermore, we compared our findings against a previous study employing adult-to-pediatric extrapolation. Organ-specific MCNPX-derived doses ranked highest for the liver ($1.00 \mathrm{mGy} / \mathrm{MBq}$), followed by the kidneys $(0.51 \mathrm{mGy} / \mathrm{MBq})$ and lungs $(0.36$ $\mathrm{mGy} / \mathrm{MBq}$). Our results closely aligned with those from OLINDA/EXM v1.1, demonstrating RPEs of less than 7% across most organ targets. Compared to adult-to-pediatric extrapolation, RPEs were generally below 6% for the majority of organ targets. Leveraging animal-to-human extrapolation in pediatric dosimetry yields valuable insights into absorbed doses, overcoming challenges associated with direct dosimetry in this population. Our findings underscore the reliability and applicability of [124I]-mIBG PET/CT imaging and dosimetry, thereby enhancing confidence in clinical decision-making and treatment planning.

articleTitle: Development of a Dynamic Mouse Heart Phantom for Multimodal Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We propose a novel cardiac phantom that mimics the left ventricle of a mouse heart. Motion in medical imaging procedures such as CT, MRI, PET or SPECT can impair the images and lead to blurring effects or artifacts. The phantom enables the validation of static and dynamic cardiac imaging of a beating left ventricular myocardium. The phantom is made of double-walled, elastic silicone. It comprises an outer myocardial volume of approximately $70 \mu \mathrm{l}$ and an inner residual blood volume of approximately $20 \mu \mathrm{l}$ with a variable ejection volume of 10-50 $\mu \mathrm{l}$. The heart was produced by casting with 3D printed molds. It allows the separate filling of myocardial and blood volumes with radioactive or/and contrast agent based fluids. A pneumatic piston system is developed that can simulate physiological heart rates of up to 400 bpm which is a typical rate for mice under anesthesia. As demonstrated in a preliminary study, the newly developed heart phantom is suitable for multimodal imaging for simulating different tracer uptake situations under variable cardiac motion. The mouse heart phantom can be operated in static and dynamic mode and thus has a wide range of potential applications in preclinical imaging studies.

articleTitle: FlexiBlock: a high-resolution self-collimation gamma camera with an adaptable modular design
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma cameras are vital tools for detecting, characterizing, and localizing gamma emission sources in complex nuclear security scenarios. However, the diverse environmental conditions necessitate gamma cameras with varying capabilities. This study presents the development of a novel modular gamma camera system for diverse environmental imaging. The system utilizes block modules composed of BGO and GAGG(Ce) scintillators and needle-shaped tungsten blocks to construct a self-collimation gamma camera. Configuring these modules in different arrangements offers flexibility to meet various imaging requirements. Simulation studies were conducted to assess the system’s feasibility, demonstrating its effectiveness in resolving dual point sources, multiple point sources, and phantom structures across different scenarios. The results highlight the system’s suitability for diverse environmental imaging applications in nuclear safety and security contexts.

articleTitle: Application of Digital Pulse Processing Code to Organic Scintillator Outputs for Pulse Shape Discrimination
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Organic scintillators are frequently used for radiation detection in mixed gamma-ray and neutron environments due to their pulse shape discrimination capabilities and fast timing. These properties allow for differentiation between gamma-ray and neutron pulses. Digital signal processing of the pulses generated by the scintillators requires a well-verified method to perform this pulse discrimination. The digital pulse processing code DualRead (gamma-ray and neutron), developed at the University of Michigan, is being verified for the purpose of making it available as an open-source tool for pulse processing. In this work, three 2.54 cm diameter by 2.54 thick organic scintillator detectors were measured using a Cf-252: an EJ309 liquid scintillator, an organic glass scintillator and a trans-stilbene crystal scintillator. The resulting data were collected using CAEN’s data acquisition software CoMPASS. DualRead was then used to process the pulses from each detector and perform pulse shape discrimination. DualRead’s pulse processing methodology is discussed as is the resulting pulse shape discrimination for each type of detector. Trans-stilbene displays the best PSD, EJ309 has the next best PSD, whereas organic glass exhibits the worst PSD.

articleTitle: Improving Performance of Inorganic Scintillators with Optimized Photonic-Crystal Nanostructures
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Many inorganic scintillators are widely used in gamma spectroscopy applications due to their relatively high light yield, good energy resolution, and detection efficiency. However, most inorganic scintillators have a high refractive index, which leads to significant light loss due to total internal reflection. This project investigates using photonic crystals, which are repetitive nanostructure arrays, to reduce such light loss. Photonic crystals can enhance the amount of light collected from a scintillator via constructive light interference. Optimization simulations were performed in Geant4 and OptiFDTD codes to improve the scintillator’s energy and time resolution by improving light extraction. Specifically, optimization simulations were performed for 10x10x3 $\mathrm{mm}^{3}$ LYSO and 10x10x2.5 $\mathrm{mm}^{3}$ BGO scintillators, which resulted in $63 \%$ and $92 \%$ light output improvement for LYSO and BGO, respectively. The optimization simulations were done for a single pass of light through the scintillator photosensor interface, which did not include reflections from the scintillator surfaces. Additional simulations were performed for LaBr<inf>3</inf> using Geant4 to assess the light loss due to the total internal reflection. For a cubic $25.4 \mathrm{~mm}^{3} \mathrm{LaBr}_{3}$ scintillator, $67 \%$ of the light yield is lost due to the total internal reflection. Thus, LaBr<inf>3</inf> would benefit from coupling with optimized photonic crystals to improve the light collection and energy resolution. In future work, the optimized photonic crystal geometry will be manufactured using electron beam lithography and assessed through radiation measurements. The experiments will validate the simulations and demonstrate the effectiveness of photonic crystals in improving the energy and time resolution of various inorganic scintillators.

articleTitle: Design and Performance Optimization of SiPM Array Multiplexing Readout Circuit
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In order to achieve high spatial resolution performance positron emission tomography (PET) detector with time-of-flight (TOF) capability, the time summation circuit and the symmetric charge division (SCD) method are employed to multiplex the fast and standard outputs for acquiring both time and energy information. To address the deterioration of time information extraction caused by multiplexing, a 470pF capacitor is employed for analog filtering, a BGA2869 chip is utilized for signal amplification, and the diode operating voltage is carefully chosen to mitigate signal shaping. The best overall coincidence timing resolution (CTR) is 272.6 ps, and the position resolution is clear, meeting the system requirements.

articleTitle: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for LOR Identification of Positron + Prompt Gamma Ray Emitters in Multiplexed PET (mPET)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: For many diseases applications, it is beneficial to simultaneously observe multiple biomarkers at a time. However, current PET systems are unable to image multiple tracers in one session due to annihilation photons being indistinguishable across radiotracers. However with the utilization of one or more positron emitting radionuclides that also emit a prompt gamma (positron + prompt gamma ray emitter), the latter signal can be used to unmix the tracer signals and facilitate multiplex PET or mPET. With the use of prompt-gamma-positron emitters, an issue arises with the correct identification of the two annihilation photons in a triple photon coincidence. In this work, we present a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) framework that uses spatial, timing, and energy information to return the most probable line of response (LOR). We validate our method using simulated data. Results indicate we can achieve > 99% accuracy at identifying the correct LOR for a <sup>22</sup>Na source.

articleTitle: Current status and recent scientific results of GRID: a student-driven NanoSat constellation for GRB observation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma-Ray Integrated Detectors (GRID) is a student project designed to deploy multiple gammaray detectors carried by nanosatellites (CubeSats), forming a full-time and all-sky gamma-ray detection constellation to monitor the transient gamma-ray sky in the multi-messenger astronomy era. As of 2023, eight GRID detectors onboard 6 commercial nanosatellites were launched into Sun-synchronous orbits. The detector design follow two base-design types and small improvements, especially in firmware, have been made continuously. Six of these detectors are in normal observation state and accumulating data. Currently, first dozen of gamma-ray burst events have been successfully observed and published.

articleTitle: Simultaneous High-Resolution and High-Sensitivity Brain Dedicated PET system: Design optimization and performance evaluation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a brain-dedicated PET system with high resolution and sensitivity, aiming to offer dynamic brain imaging. The design concept is based on maximizing solid angle coverage of the human head. The system comprises elliptical cylinder covering with neck cutout, supplemented by front and back panels to improve sensitivity and line-of-response (LOR) sampling. Simulation results from a previous study have demonstrated higher sensitivity than any current existing brain PET systems, with varying sensitivity in different locations of the field of view (FOV) ranging from $23.42 \%$ to $15.99 \%$ with a 15 mm thick staggered LYSO:Ce crystal arranged with 3 depth of interaction (DOI) levels. This work presents improvement on system design, and resolution-sensitivity metrics with detector configurations with varying DOI level with a 20 mm thick detector and timing resolution values varying from 50 ps to 200 ps. The goal of this study is to determine the best achievable system performance with varying detector configurations while keeping the design practical.

articleTitle: Utility of Total-Body PET for Range Verification and Tumor Diagnosis in Carbon Ion Therapy: A Rat Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET has been studied for range-verification in charged particle therapy, in which positron ($\beta^{+}$) emitters are produced through nuclear fragmentation reactions in a patient. Due to the short physical and biological decays, PET scans during and/or immediately after irradiation have been thought to be necessary. On the other hand, the recently appearing technology of total-body PET may enable PET imaging in an ‘off-line’ mode due to its ultrahigh sensitivity. In this work, we demonstrated the utility of total-body PET in monitoring carbon ion therapy by conducting a rat irradiation study using our original total-body small-animal PET (TBS-PET) that covers the whole body of a rat. A rat tumor was irradiated by a ${ }^{12} \mathrm{C}$ ion beam, and off-line PET imaging was performed. ${}^{18}\mathrm{F-FAZA}$ tumor hypoxia PET imaging was also performed to observe the tumor pathological conditions, which we expect can also be diagnosed by the washout rate in PET. The acquired PET data were divided into 15-30 s duration time frames, and image quality was investigated by changing the time frames to a sum. Additionally, the washout rate were derived from two different data sets: the whole phase (0-30 min) and a late phase (10-30 min). Image quality of the late phase was almost the same as that of the whole phase. The washout rate derived from the late phase exhibited the same tendency as the rate from the whole phase. Also, a heterogeneous intensity distribution in the tumor was observed in the PET image even with the late phase; the high intensity region corresponded to the hypoxic region that was observed in hypoxia PET. In conclusion, the utility of total-body PET in monitoring carbon ion therapy was demonstrated in rats not only for range verification but also for tumor diagnosis. It was suggested the washout rate obtained by total-body PET can be a biomarker for tumor hemodynamics to assess the therapy effect.

articleTitle: Deep-learning based real-time KSTAR fusion neutron energy spectrum unfolding with TRIASSIC and MCNP simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes deep-learning based real-time neutron energy spectrum unfolding method that handles fusion neutrons from KSTAR tokamak entering stilbene scintillator. Neutron energy spectrum unfolding with organic scintillators such as stilbene requires knowledge of the neutrons response function which correlates the neutrons energy with pulse heights. Despite the presence of likelihood maximization-based neutron unfolding techniques, necessity of deep-learning appears in that calculation time is reduced by time complexity order which leads to the feasibility of real-time neutron energy spectrum unfolding. Convolution-based deep learning model structure was constructed with pairs of fusion neutron energy distribution of KSTAR plasma and neutron light output energy spectrum acquired from end-to-end simulation: from generation of fusion neutron in KSTAR tokamak to stilbene scintillator-based detection system. Through TRIASSIC (Tokamak reactor integrated automated suite for simulation and computation), calculation of temporal fusion plasma power which corresponds to the temporal probability of neutron emission was executed. MCNP (Monte-Carlo N-particle transport) code simulates the transport of fusion neutrons entering the stilbene scintillator. Stilbene scintillator is widely utilized for fast-neutron spectroscopy in many applications due to its decent property for real-time unfolding. Through real-time neutron energy spectrum unfolding, immediate recovery feedback of unstabilized plasma would be possible.

articleTitle: Dynamic micro RI Imaging System Using Eutectic Scintillation Crystal with Micro Fiber Structure
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Studies on cell regulation are attracting worldwide attention in the push to realize regenerative medicines. Therefore, development of dynamic micro imaging techniques based on nuclear medicine is desired. Conventional nuclear imaging techniques are not suitable for cell regulation studies. For example, PET and SPECT scanners cannot achieve spatial resolutions smaller than $100 \mu \mathrm{m}$. Autoradiography cannot obtain dynamic images. In this research, we developed a new micro RI imaging system for dynamic cell observations. This system use a plate eutectic scintillator which has a micro fiber structure smaller than $1 \mu \mathrm{m}$. Compared to previous imaging systems, an important feature of the new system is the eutectic scintillator which can suppress the scintillation photon spread due to the micro fiber structure to improve imaging resolution.We made a prototype of the imaging system consisting of a Tb: $\mathrm{GdAlO}_{3} / \alpha-\mathrm{Al}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ eutectic scintillator, imaging lenses and an EM-CCD camera (C9100-23B). The dimensions and thickness of the eutectic scintillator were $3 \mathrm{~mm} \times 4 \mathrm{~mm}$ and $\sim 1 \mathrm{~mm}$, respectively. The scintillation lights were detected with the EM-CCD camera from which we obtained scintillation light images of the $\beta$-rays of ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ irradiation. The time variation of scintillation light intensity during the 840 min measurement matched the half-life of ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$. This result meant that the obtained scintillation images were exactly derived from the interactions between the $\beta$-rays of ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ and the eutectic scintillator. As the next step, we will evaluate resolution of the scintillation imaging while optimizing the thickness of the eutectic scintillator.

articleTitle: A Fast Transient Fully Integrated LDO With Improved PSR for SiPM-MVT System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The SiPM-MVT system has been proven to be an efficient photoelectric detection and signal processing system, which is widely used in PET. As the system is highly sensitive to noise and has fast load transitions, its power supply must possess high PSR and fast transient response. This paper proposes a fully integrated low dropout regulator (LDO) for SiPM-MVT system. The LDO uses feedforward ripple cancellation technology to gain PSR, and a recycling folded cascode structure error amplifier is utilized for better transient response. The LDO also provides frequency compensation to ensure stability. The LDO is designed using CMOS 180 nm 3.3 V standard CMOS technology. The PSR of LDO can better than -55 dB in the range between 100 kHz-1 MHz. The voltage overshoot of the LDO is less than 55 mV even the load current is varied from 1 to 20 mA within 100 ns.

articleTitle: Limits of the time resolution and avalanche build-up analysis of FBK NUV-HD-MT SiPMs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) timing performance, in particular the Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR), is of paramount importance in applications like Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (ToF-PET). In turns, the CTR strongly depends on the Single Photon Time Resolution (SPTR) defined as the time jitter when a single photon is detected by the SiPM. In this study, we performed a characterization of the recently introduced FBK Near Ultra- Violet-High Density with Metal-filled Trenches (NUV-HD-MT) technology in terms of its timing performance by measuring the SPTR of single Single Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs) with different cell sizes. We used a femto-second laser with a wavelength of 390nm and a custom-made high frequency amplifier. The single SPADs show an excellent SPTR of $(17.63 \pm 0.04) \mathrm{ps}$, $(22.5 \pm 0.1) \mathrm{ps}$, $(24.4 \pm 0.1) \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM for the $30 \mu \mathrm{m}, 40 \mu \mathrm{m}, 50 \mu \mathrm{m}$ microcell respectively. We performed a signal shape analysis to study the influence of the avalanche point injection in the microcell active area on the SPTR.

articleTitle: Deep Learning-powered CT-less Organ Segmentation from 68Ga-PSMA/Dotatate PET Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Organ segmentation and quantification can help to improve the diagnostic and prognostic value of PET/CT imaging. The use of widely available CT-based organ segmentation approaches inherently suffers from limitations owing to the high prevalence of mismatch between CT and PET images, mainly due to respiratory phase differences. This study aimed to develop a CT-less organ segmentation pipeline using only emission Ga-68 PSMA/Dotatete PET images. A total number of 570 patients injected with Ga-68-PSMA or Ga-68-Dotatate were included in this study. After excluding images presenting with mismatch, CT, or PET artifacts, 185 PET/CT images were retained. A total number of 14 organs were delineated automatically employing previously developed deep learning algorithms in our lab for CT image segmentation. Subsequently, the segmentation masks were resampled to PET resolution. The PET non-corrected and segmentation masks were used to train self-configuring nnU-Net models in five-fold data split strategy using 2000 epochs. Dice and Jaccard metrics were used to compare the predicted and reference segmentations masks. Average Dice values of $0.82 \pm 0.04,0.93 \pm 0.03,0.69 \pm 0.12,0.86 \pm 0.06$, $0.81 \pm 0.04,0.83 \pm 0.09,0.87 \pm 0.08,0.90 \pm 0.03,0.62 \pm 0.12,0.56 \pm 0.07,0.81 \pm 0.04,0.81 \pm$ $0.10,0.82 \pm 0.09,0.82 \pm 0.02$ was achieved for the aorta, brain, eyeballs, heart, hips, kidneys, liver, lungs, pancreas, ribs, sacrum, spleen, urinary bladder, and vertebrae, respectively. Ga-68 PET image quantification using segmentation masks generated on CT images is limited to available and reliable co-registered CT images which is not always the case due to mismatch between PET and CT images. We developed a robust and fast organ segmentation pipeline to tackle this issue using non-corrected PET images.

articleTitle: Transitioning neural network isotope identifiers to real-world deployment scenarios
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Real time identification of radioisotopes can aid law enforcement in the interdiction of illicit radiological material. AWE have collected the Sigma dataset, consisting of approximately 1.5 billion, 1 s spectra collected around London in 2018 which is used in this work to explore the effect of background radiation of convolutional neural network isotope identifiers. A neural network was trained on simulated data augmented with background radiation from this dataset and optimised using a hyperband tuner. A testing set was created consisting of a simulated Co-60 spectrum augmented with $0 \mathrm{~s}-100 \mathrm{~s}$ of background spectra. Gradient class activation mapping was then used to determine which parts of the convolutional neural network were being used to predict the presence of Co-60. It can be seen from these results that the neural network is largely ambivalent to the decrease in signal-to-noise ratio despite the training set containing no spectra with more than 1 s acquisition time of background radiation. The aim of this work is to train more neural networks with intentionally bias or unrepresentative training data to develop tools for identifying these traits in algorithms intended for deployment.

articleTitle: A Forward Model For Minimum Detectable Activity
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The analysis of Minimum Detectable Activity over complex environments is a valuable tool for radiological search and survey personnel. Clearance maps can be created to inform operators of potential risk while search parameters and detector designs can be optimised. To enable such analysis in complex scenes a radiation transport model must be used to estimate detected radiation. This work presents a fast forward propagation model that efficiently transports radiation through a complex scene. The model uses pre-computed libraries of detector response functions combining solid angles and full energy photopeak efficiencies interpolated for all possible detector orientations for chosen gamma energies. Attenuation through air and blocking bodies is calculated and combined with detector response to obtain detected photopeak energies that are used in the analysis. A synthetic survey task using the SPIR-Pack at 1.2 m high with an attenuating human surrogate and the SPIR-Explorer at 15 m flying height was modelled. A single clearance map combining the responses of the two detectors was created for ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$. A clearance map for a range of isotopes used in a real-world survey, as well as model validation, will be presented.

articleTitle: Over 39M lives needlessly lost from cancer in the past 23 years, and 69 M more over the next 7 years because scientists’ goal for PET is to take beautiful pictures and crushed my invention to cost-effectively measure biophysiology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Background - From the year 2000 articles, funding and presentations to conferences of my inventions targeted to save many lives have been suppressed and continue to be suppressed. Materials and methods - My calculations of the year 2000 that the 3D-CBS could detect tumors with only 100 cancer cells was proven with measurements by a third party in 2019 on a copy of my idea.
