Conclusions - The scientific truth cannot be suppressed forever, Galileo’s book was suppressed for 100-years, how long will it take and how many additional people will die before I am allowed to present my book, the Table and the TB-CAD?

articleTitle: New Kinetic Model for Coronary Artery Disease for Positron Emission Tomography using 82Rb
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cardiac PET is currently used as a method to accurately diagnose coronary artery disease (CAD) through both qualitative and quantitative analysis of tracer uptake (e.g. ${ }^{82} \mathrm{Rb}$) in the heart. Using computer simulations, we have tested how a standard approach to quantitative analysis would perform on time-activity curves modified due to an occluded artery. We find that flow values derived under CAD rest conditions are substantially biased due to the influence of the occlusion; the bias is smaller under CAD stress conditions. Our work strongly suggests that quantitative analysis of ${ }^{82} \mathrm{Rb}$ data from the ischemic myocardium can provide misleading results if the model used does not capture the diseased state of the patient.

articleTitle: Performance of High-Resolution PET Detectors based on Long Semi-Monolithic Scintillator Slabs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Current high-resolution PET scanners use either pixelated or monolithic scintillator detectors. Depth of interaction (DOI) encoding detector is vital for PET scanners for high imaging quality. Semi-monolithic scintillators have DOI encoding of monolithic scintillator, and improve spatial resolution by reducing edge effect. In this work, performance of 4 lutetium yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) semi-monolithic detectors was measured. Detector 1 consisted of 12, $0.96 \times 56 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ slabs with BaSO<inf>4</inf> reflector between slabs and the front and two end faces painted black. Detector 2 was same as detector 1 but without black paint. Detector 3 was same as detector 1 but with enhanced specular reflector (ESR) instead of BaSO<inf>4</inf>. Detector 4 was same as detector 1 except consisting of 14 slabs $0.81 \times 56 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$. A $4 \times 16$ silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array with row and colum readout circuit was used. Different positions of monolithic (y) and DOI directions of the array were irradiated using a $0.3 \mathrm{~mm}^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source and a single $1 \mathrm{x} 1 \mathrm{x} 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LYSO coincidence detector. Energy square COG method improved y resolution by sim 30% compared to COG method. Black paint improved y and DOI resolutions, but degraded energy resolution. Detector with ESR had similar y and DOI resolutions, better energy resolution and slab identification compared to detector with BaSO<inf>4</inf>. The detector with thinner slabs provided similar y, DOI, and energy resolutions, but poorer slab identification compared to detector with thicker slabs. The detectors provided a good identification of slabs of 0.96 and 0.81 mm, y resolutions of 1.67 to 1.87 mm, DOI resolution of $\sim 2.3 \mathrm{~mm}$ and energy resolutions of 14.9% to 17.7%, and can be used in high resolution small animal and organ specific PET scanners. Machine learning positioning algorithms will be used in upcoming work to improve the results.

articleTitle: Long-Term Stability of NaOCl Passivation on CZTS Crystals Investigated via SEM-EDS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the efficient passivation of CdTe-based semiconductor crystals, focusing on the long-term stability and underlying mechanisms of NaOCl passivation. CdZnTeSe crystals were grown, processed, and passivated with NaOCl, and their surface characteristics were studied using SEM-EDS and XPS. The passivation was found to significantly enhance the surface resistance, with a sustained effect for more than 90 s, attributed to the formation of a tellurium oxide layer. The passivation process was further elucidated through detailed morphological and compositional analyses. The NaOCl-passivated crystals exhibited improved electrical and spectroscopic properties in radiation detection, with a prolonged stability of 60-90 days, which are longer compared to other passivants. Additionally, the feasibility of NaOCl passivation on a CdZnTeSe detector was explored, showcasing enhanced resistivity and spectroscopic performance. The study concludes with insights into the potential industrial application of NaOCl passivation for CdTe-based radiation detectors.

articleTitle: Performance of scintillator-based detectors for photon counting x-ray computed tomography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon counting detectors (PCDs) for x-ray computed tomography (CT) are the future of CT imaging. They improve the spatial resolution by a factor of 2 and make it possible to access spectral data retrospectively. At present, two main sensor materials either being used or investigated for PCD-CT are cadmium telluride (or cadmium zinc telluride) and silicon. Unfortunately, both have major challenges, including high cost and poor signal-to-noise ratio of spectral data. Fast scintillators such as $\mathrm{LaBr}_{3}: \mathrm{Ce}$ are inexpensive in comparison and could be excellent alternative materials for PCDs. In this study, we study the expected performance of $\mathrm{LaBr}_{3}: \mathrm{Ce}$ for PCD-CT and show the potential for higher performance in K-edge imaging than CdTe PCD-CT.

articleTitle: Artificial Neural Network for 3D Event Positioning in a Monolithic PET Detector with Integrated Corner Reflectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Monolithic scintillators are a promising alternative to standard pixelated crystals in positron emission tomography as they can be more cost effective, reduce dead space, and capture the full light distribution which can be crucial for depth of interaction estimation. This study explores how the use of an artificial neural network can further enhance 3D positioning capabilities. Using GATE simulations, we compare the standard Anger Logic event positioning to a neural network approach in order to analyze the performance of several commonly seen entrance face surface finishes on monoliths. We focus on the improvements seen by using an array of integrated corner reflectors (ICR) machined directly into the entrance face of the monolith, which we previously showed to improve light collection and preserve light distribution. Our findings show that the use of an artificial neural network provides stable spatial resolution below 1mm outperforming Anger Logic which suffers from edge effects and is sensitive to electronic noise. These improvements are most evident in the use of an ICR which has the best spatial resolution when compared to the standard black and flat specular approaches.

articleTitle: Can PET FDG Deep Texture Representations Be Made Robust?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The efficacy of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in recognizing cancerous textures in PET scans is well acknowledged, yet model generalizability across different cancer types, imaging acquisitions, and reconstruction protocols remains largely unexplored. This study evaluates a 3D CNN originally trained on esophageal cancer data, applied to lung cancer and lymphoma. We test the model using organ-specific PET data from four glycolytic volumes with high Standardized Uptake Values (SUV), acquired from different scanners and acquisition protocols. Through Principal Component Analysis (PCA) of the network’s sub-logit layer activations, we demonstrate its ability to distinctly identify textural features across different cancers, scanners and acquisition protocols, highlighting its robust cross-cancer applicability and potential for enhancing diagnostic precision.

articleTitle: High Multiplicity Trigger for Long-Lived Particles in the CMS Muon Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Searches for long-lived particles (LLPs) have attracted much interest lately due to their high discovery potential in the LHC Run-3. Signatures featuring LLPs with long lifetimes and decaying inside the muon detectors of the CMS experiment at CERN are of particular interest. In this talk, we will describe a novel Level-1 trigger algorithm that significantly improves CMS’s signal efficiency for these exotic signatures. The implementation has been done at multiple stages of the Level-1 trigger processing, considering limited FPGA logic resources and tight latency requirements. Events satisfying the Level-1 requirements are passed to a High-Level Trigger (HLT) algorithm that further reduces the rate to the target few Hz level. The developed trigger algorithms have been taking CMS data since 2022. Their performance, implementation, commissioning results, and potential future developments will be reported.

articleTitle: Evaluation of a depth encoding hybrid semi-monolithic detector using optical coupling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Most clinical PET systems do not have DOI capability, but the significance of DOI is rising in clinical PET imaging, especially in total body PET with a long axial field of view and greater DOI effect. In this work, performance characteristics of a depth encoding hybrid semi-monolithic detector using coupling were evaluated in terms of energy resolution (ER), DOI resolution, intrinsic spatial resolution (ISR), and coincidence time resolution (CTR). The detector was comprised of a hybrid semi-monolithic LYSO scintillator read out by a 64-channel multi-pixel photon counter (MPPC) (S14161-3050HS, Hamamatsu Photonics, Bridgewater, NJ). The hybrid semi-monolithic scintillator consists of a row of a 1 × 8 array of 3.1 × 2.1 × 20 mm<sup>3</sup> LYSO crystals (3.2 mm pitch) coupled to a monolithic slab of 25.5 × 1 × 20 mm<sup>3</sup> using high-refractive (n=1.7) optical adhesive (NOA170, Norland170). Both the coupling surfaces of the pixelated crystals and the monolithic slab are unpolished. The pixelated crystals are separated by enhanced specular reflector (ESR; 3M, St Paul, MN). The top and lateral surfaces of the detector were covered with ESR. Preliminary experimental results show that the pseudo-pixels (defined as the section of a pixelated crystal element along with the neighboring part of the monolithic slab it couples to) can be clear resolved from the measured flood image. The average ISR in FWHM and FWTM are 1.99±0.06 and 3.65±0.11 mm. An average DOI resolution of 4.0±0.5mm and a CTR of 282 ps are achieved. The detector also provides a good ER of 10.3%. In conclusion, this work demonstrated a depth encoding hybrid semi-monolithic detector design suitable for developing high-performance human body PET scanners.

articleTitle: Deep learning for Proportion Estimation of Target Radionuclides in Extreme Environment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We propose a deep learning-based approach utilizing a 1D Convolutional Neural Network to accurately estimate the proportions of target radionuclides, 137Cs and 133Ba, within mixed gamma-ray spectra, even under extreme conditions of high temperature and radiation. Our results demonstrated high precision, with Mean Absolute Error (MAE) values below 5% for each target radionuclide in standard testing conditions. Remarkably, even when 54Mn-a radionuclide not included in the training phase-was introduced as noise, the model’s performance remained robust, with error rates kept below 9%. This underscores the model’s capability to deliver accurate radionuclide quantification, despite the presence of unfamiliar spectral noise, affirming its substantial utility for nuclear safety in complex environments.

articleTitle: Results from a Beam Test Analysis of a Large-Area GEM detector with Low Mass and Zigzag-strip Readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this report, the assembly and analysis of a low cost, low mass GEM detector is presented. The detector we designed is optimized for use in the upcoming Electron Ion Collider (EIC) as a forward tracker due to its low material budget and reduced cost. Our design showcases a standard CMS Triple GEM (TGEM) detector with a few modifications which reduce the overall material budget by seven times and reduce the manufacturing cost. Internally, our design utilizes modified GEM foils to replace the PCB of the drift and readout board. With the PCB removed, the structure of the TGEM was reinstated by adding carbon fiber frames to the exterior. These frames include a central window made of aluminized polyimide foil to allow radiation to enter the inner volume as well as enclose the working gas. To reduce electrostatic forces between the drift foil and the outer window, the external polyimide window was connected to HV and held at a similar voltage. Another modification to the TGEM was to optimize the readout board strip geometry to test different possibilities. Our readout board compares the historical straight strips with two ZigZag designs as well as a method to combine strips across multiple sectors. These changes optimize the space read out by a single strip such that the manufactured board only needs one third of its original strips - thus reducing the overall cost. Once manufactured, this design was tested at the FermiLab test beam facility with a 120 GeV proton beam and has shown similar or improved characteristics to a mass produced CMS TGEM.

articleTitle: Design of a Highly Flexible TOF-PET Detector Module with FESA Readout ASICs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Flexibility of the detector module to construct various TOF-PET systems is always limited by its large number of channels with complex readout electronics. Based on our newly developed 64-channel SiPM readout chip FESA, a highly flexible detector module is designed and performance evaluated. Six $8 \times 8$ SiPM arrays are closely aligned to share a data processing board, so that the detector module supports up to 384 readout channels with a compact structure. Multiple identical such modules can be easily combined to form a flat panel detector or a ring detector to construct customized TOF-PET scanners. The performance of the detector module is evaluated by coupling a $24 \times 24$ LYSO crystal array, each crystal element with a size of $0.99 \times 0.99 \times 15 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, to each $8 \times$ 8 SiPM array. Preliminary test results show that the detector module can achieve a positioning resolution of 1.0 mm and an average coincidence time resolution of approximately 461 ps.

articleTitle: Direct pre-amplifier sampling ADC for high-count rate and high-resolution X-ray spectroscopy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel technique for digital signal processing from X-ray detectors, such as silicon drift detectors, aimed at supporting high rates while maintaining excellent resolution. Traditional high-rate detectors for X-ray or gamma applications, connected to transistor reset preamplifiers, face challenges in signal acquisition due to the large voltage ramp produced, which greatly exceeds the amplitude of the signal of interest. To address this, we utilized a 20-bit SAR ADC capable of sampling the signal directly from the preamplifier with a dynamic range of 1 to 1 million, allowing effective capture even with the presence of a voltage ramp. We designed a system using four ADCs in interleaving mode to achieve a combined sampling rate of 160 Msps. The readout and control logic were managed by a Zynq SoC, interfacing with the ADCs. The firmware developed includes phase and gain correction for interleaving ADC, trapezoidal filter and readout PC interface logic. Preliminary measurements were conducted with the Ardesia detector at the Polytechnic University of Milan. The tests, although initial, have shown that the resolution achieved surpasses that of traditional methods using analog reshaping. We performed measurements at both low and medium rates, achieving an optimal resolution (FWHM) of 128 eV at a peaking time of $2 \mu \mathrm{s}. \mathrm{A}$ faster peaking time configuration tested for reduced dead time yielded a resolution of 140 eV at 1 Mcps. These findings highlight the potential of our digital processing approach, which could offer improved resolution and efficiency in X-ray detection systems, especially beneficial for high-count rate applications in scientific environments such as synchrotron facilities.

articleTitle: < 2mm Continuous DOI Positioning in Arrays of Side-Coupled Crystals for a Highly Compact 100 ps FWHM CTR TOF-PET Detector Design
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To achieve more accurate depth-of-interaction (DOI) response and 3D positioning of photoelectric or scattered events in our highly compact 100 ps CTR TOF-PET detector design, we have replaced a previously CPLD-based 3DPS approach with a 3D position sensitive charge-division scalable readout which better preserves our ∼100 ps FWHM CTR results. To validate the performance and compatibility of the readout with our mixed-signal TOF-PET design, we used $2 \times 4$ arrays of $3 \times 3 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LGSO crystals side-coupled to $4 \times 6$ arrays of $3 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPMs. By embedding this 3DPS readout in our scaled-up TOF-PET system, we resolved 3D interaction positions along the crystal array with an average 1.6 mm FWHM DOI resolution while easily preserving our 100 ps CTR and also saving the components, footprint, and subsequently the cost, power dissipation by 32% and at least 40% compared to our previous 3DPS CPLD-based and the common 3D Anger-based readouts, respectively.

articleTitle: Theoretical Calculation of Optimal Thickness for Boron-Containing Neutron Converter Layer under Various Low-Level Discrimination Conditions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a novel theoretical algorithm for calculating the optimal thickness of boron-containing converter layers under different LLD settings. We base this study on previously established relationships between neutron detection efficiency and boron-containing converter layer thickness. Thin-film semiconductor neutron detectors consist of a converter layer and a semiconductor layer. The thickness of the converter layer directly impacts neutron detection efficiency. Motivated by the limited research on a direct calculation for the optimal thickness of the converter layer under various low-level discrimination (LLD) conditions. This research introduces a new, rapid, and direct calculation method for determining the optimal thickness of boron-containing converter layers suitable for various materials under different LLD conditions. Monte Carlo methods were used to conduct simulations as a comparative reference to theory and shows good correlation. The inverse correlation between the converter layer thickness and LLD values suggests that a higher LLD threshold permits a reduction in the converter layer thickness.

articleTitle: Slit-Wall Differentiation Method for Depth-of-Interaction Measurement for PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET), accurately measuring the Depth-of-Interaction (DOI) of 511 keV gamma ray interactions is essential for improving spatial resolution in small animal PET, especially at off-center detector positions. DOI resolution can be improved by modifying crystal structures, reflectors, or by using dual readout techniques. Most methods, except for the more electronics-intensive dual side readout, increase light sharing among pixels, thereby reducing photon availability per pixel. This study introduces a novel Slit-Wall Differentiation (SWD) method, designed to restrict light sharing to just four adjacent pixels, thus enhancing DOI accuracy. The SWD method involves placing strategic slits on the adjacent faces of each pixel, controlling light sharing depending on the DOI position. DOI information is calculated from the output patterns of Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays. The effectiveness of the proposed method was validated through GATE simulations (vGATE 9.2) using a $3 \times 3$ Lutetium-Yttrium Oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) array with enhanced specular reflectors (ESRs). An LYSO array fabricated based on the proposed configuration was successfully prepared. For practical validation, an experimental setup using a 4 $\times 4$ NUV-HD-MT (Broadcom) SiPM array is also configured.

articleTitle: Development of A Charge Sensitive Preamplifier Using Silicon-Germanium Heterojunction-Bipolar-Transistors for Fast and Low-noise Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A fast and low-noise charge sensitive preamplifier (CSA) was developed for both fast timing and high-resolution spectroscopy applications. This charge sensitive preamplifier used commercial silicon germanium heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) as the main power consuming devices, based on a resistive-capacitive feedback network for charge readout. This design utilizes the low-power characteristics of HBTs, making it possible for the preamplifier to operate in extremely low temperature environments. We intend to use this for cryogenic semiconductor readout, however, within the current scope of work, a 10mm cubic GAGG coupled to a 10mm SiPM (HAMAMATSU) was used as the detector for feasibility verification. The read spectra of standard gamma sources <sup>22</sup>Na, <sup>57</sup>Co, and <sup>137</sup>Cs clearly showed characteristic peaks with resolutions of 19%@122keV, 10.9%@511keV, 10.2%@662keV and 5%@1275keV. The output voltage signal had a rise time of 500ns level and a baseline noise of around 5mV rms.

articleTitle: PET reconstruction using a generative model based on physical simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Radon projector used in most PET reconstructions does not incorporate Compton scattering and other important physical effects that affect the PET process, resulting in biases despite the use of corrections. In our work, we define the projector from the generative model of a Monte-Carlo simulator, which encompasses many of these effects, including scattering. From the implicit simulator model, we propose to learn a continuous surrogate of the projector using a neural density estimator, thus avoiding the discretization bottleneck and lowering simulation cost. Our work is carried out in the two-dimensional PET configuration and compared with the reconstruction using the Radon projector, in which corrective terms are factored into the PET matrix. We observed reduced noise at match bias with our method, illustrating the interest of this simulation-based approach.The principal objective of this work is to establish a proof of concept for the SBI approach in PET.

articleTitle: System design to realize functional and conventional images during single X-ray irradiation using a photon counting detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Energy-resolving photon-counting detectors (ERPCDs) have the potential to extract functional diagnostic information such as the effective atomic number ($\left.\mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }}\right)$ from X-ray images. Our study aims to construct an imaging system for obtaining both functional and conventional images during single X-ray irradiation. Taking advantage of the characteristics of EPRCD to analyze multiple energy information, we propose an optimal system that fully guarantees the performance of both $\mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }}$ image and conventional image. Our previously developed imaging simulator was used, which takes the following into consideration: (a) attenuation for polychromatic X-rays, (b) detector response, and (c) statistical fluctuation. Virtual phantoms with mass thickness ($\rho$ t) values of 0.1-80 $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ composed of aluminum (bone) and polymethyl methacrylate (soft tissue), and digital phantoms of the hand and pelvic region generated from computed tomography images were analyzed. The accuracy of $\mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }}$ images and the contrast-to-noise ratio of conventional images were evaluated. As a result, a high tube voltage setting of 120 kV was found to be the optimal condition. The accuracy of $\mathrm{Z}_{\text {eff }}$ images was drastically improved under this condition compared with that under low tube voltage conditions. The contrast of conventional images for certain objects ($\rho$ t $\lt2$ $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$) was slightly worse when using all energy images, but when using low and middle energy images, the contrast of all objects was improved systematically. Furthermore, it was found that high-quality pre-clinical images could be generated even when the optimal condition was determined based on single-element phantoms of bone and soft tissue. In conclusion, we proposed a novel ERPCD system using high tube voltage imaging and verified its clinical applicability through a simulation study.

articleTitle: CT-free PET for Pediatric Patients with Metal Implants
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal implants in pediatric sarcoma patients pose an inherent challenge for deep-learning (DL) based attenuation and scatter correction (ASC) in PET imaging. To address this issue, we developed a maximum a priori joint activity and attenuation (MAP-AA) PET reconstruction technique to integrate DL-generated $\mu$ map as the regularization. We first trained an nnU-net using 287 pediatric PET/CT examinations between time-of-flight non-ASC (TOF NASC) PET images and corresponding CT-based $\mu$ map ($\mu^{\mathrm{CT}}$). In MAP-AA, the activity image $\lambda$ and the attenuation map $\mu$ were alternatively updated, with the DL model generated $\mu$ map ($\mu^{\mathrm{DL}}$) regularizing the transmission reconstruction together with a smoothness prior. We tested the proposed method on two pediatric sarcoma patients with metal implants in legs and a patient with no metal implant. The $\mu$ maps generated by the DL model ($\mu^{\mathrm{DL}}$) and from the MAP-AA algorithm without and with the $\mu^{\mathrm{DL}}$-based prior ($\mu^{\mathrm{MAP}}$ and $\mu^{\mathrm{DL} \text {-MAP }}$), following with the PET images reconstructed using them for ASC, were evaluated with the $\mu^{\mathrm{CT}}$ and $\mu^{\mathrm{CT}}$-based ASC PET image as the reference. Normalized mean squared error (NMSE, in $10^{-5}$) was calculated on the PET images and standardized uptake values (SUVs) were measured in the most focused lesion(s). Metal implants in two sarcoma patients were better recovered by the MAP-AA in both $\mu^{\mathrm{MAP}}$ and $\mu^{\mathrm{DL} \text {-MAP }}$ than in $\mu^{\mathrm{DL}}$. Cross-talk artifacts were better mitigated in $\mu^{\mathrm{DL} \text { MAP }}$ than those in $\mu^{\mathrm{MAP}}$. The overall similarity of $\lambda^{\mathrm{DL}-\mathrm{MAP}}$ to $\lambda^{\mathrm{CT}}$ is comparable to that of $\lambda^{\mathrm{DL}}$, with NMSE as $1.21,2.97$, and 1.32 for $\lambda^{\mathrm{DL}}, \lambda^{\mathrm{MAP}}$, and $\lambda^{\mathrm{DL}-\mathrm{MAP}}$, respectively. Furthermore, $\lambda^{\text {DL-MAP }}$ exhibits lower errors in metal-affected areas, with NMSE as 1.49, 2.67, and 1.25; $\operatorname{SUV}_{\text {max }}\left(\operatorname{SUV}_{\text {mean }}\right)$ relative difference as $4.8 \%(1.8 \%),-4.3 \%(-7.1 \%)$, and $2.1 \%(-0.7 \%)$, for $\lambda^{\mathrm{DL}}$, $\lambda^{\text {MAP }}$, and $\lambda^{\text {DL-MAP }}$, respectively. We conclude that the proposed DL regularized MAP-AA reconstruction leads to the potential of using CT-free PET imaging for pediatric sarcoma patients with metal implants.

articleTitle: Crosstalk between SiPMs in dual-ended readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Coupling multiple photodetectors around a gamma-ray sensitive volume maximises light collection and reduces photon time spread to increase photon detection efficiency and thereby improved energy and timing resolution. However, uncorrelated and correlated noise of neighboring detectors can produce optical photons that, when detected, can counter the aforementioned advantages. We investigated the amount and role of silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) crosstalk in a dual-ended readout configuration with and without scintillation light. A 20 mm thick bismuth germanate (BGO) crystal was coupled to AFBR-S4N44P014M SiPMs from Broadcom and SiPMs were biased individually at various over voltages. Switching the second SiPM on increased the dark count rate in the first one up to 50 %. At the same time, the crosstalk probability increased more than 2-fold at high overvoltage due to detection and re-emission of avalanche photons, limiting the operational range and causing an up to 5-fold increase in the total number of detected photons. The results of this study may have implications beyond dual-ended SiPM readout as they can be of importance for any detector system with multiple photodetectors. Possible applications range from High Energy Physics Experiments, to (semi)-monolithic crystals, and neutrino / dark matter experiments with SiPMs at cryogenic temperature.

articleTitle: Experimental Validation of the Directional Radiation Monitoring System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Currently, radioactive materials are used in various fields such as medicine and energy, and the demand for facilities that utilize radiation is increasing. In these facilities, various types of radiation accidents can occur, such as radiation exposure of workers and environmental contamination. If an accident occurs, the radiation source must be removed quickly to protect public health and the environment. Therefore, the development of a radiation monitoring system that can determine the location of the radiation source is essential. In a previous study, we proposed the system that can provide source direction information. The proposed system consists of four NaI:Tl detectors arranged in a square and an externally attached wall-type collimator, and each detector measures different counts for one source. The source direction is predicted by analyzing the count ratio through an ANN-based algorithm. The ANN used the ReLU activation function and had a structure of a single input layer with 4 neurons, 2 hidden layers with 256 neurons, and an output layer with 1 neuron. The purpose of this study is to verify the principle of the directional radiation monitoring system through experiments. The system was fabricated using a MIRION detector with a NaI:Tl scintillator($\Phi 3^{\prime \prime} \times 3^{\prime \prime}$) and the collimator(Lead, $20 \times 100 \times 180 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$). System verification experiments using the ${ }^{137}$ Cs source were performed by moving the source from 0 to 90 degrees at 10-degree intervals at a distance of 6 m from the system. The obtained count ratio was input into the ANN to predict the source direction. The system performance was evaluated by calculating the degree of error in the predicted value. As a result, it was verified that the system can monitor the source with an average error of 4.48 degrees in all directions.

articleTitle: A CUDA Accelerated Time Alignment for uMI Panorama GS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) utilizes timing information to pair two 511keV photons into a coincidence event, assuming that the timestamps assigned to each detector are synchronized. In practical systems, time delays occur due to clock skew and optical pathway length. As timing resolution improves, time calibration becomes crucial as timing offsets can quickly become the primary error source. UIH has developed the uMI Panorama GS PET/CT scanner with a 78cm ring diameter and 148.2cm axial length. Previous work introduced a time alignment method using through CPU parallel computation. CUDA, Compute Unified Device Architecture, is a parallel computing platform and programming model developed by NVIDIA. It allows developers to use NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs) for general-purpose processing. CUDA enables significant performance gains for computing tasks by harnessing the parallel processing power of GPUs alongside traditional CPUs. In this study, we extend the time alignment method using L1-norm minimization and CUDA acceleration, suitable for low statistics and the long axial FOV of the PET system. The wider coincidence window required by the long axial FOV leads to the necessity for a wider coincidence window during initial time calibration. We can perform fast time calibration using this method due to high sensitivity and low statistics handling capabilities of the total-body PET system. The new CUDA-based time alignment approach is suitable for this scenario. We have tested the accuracy and convergence of this method in the uMI Panorama GS PET/CT, observing improvements in time resolution.

articleTitle: Single-view SPECT with a high-performance self-collimating gamma camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) serves as an important tool in both clinical and preclinical molecular imaging. The conventional SPECT system utilizes rotating gamma cameras to gather multiple projections, which are then reconstructed into 3D images. Our group recently developed a novel self-collimating gamma camera (SCGC), employing a multi-layer mosaic-patterned detector array alongside a high sensitivity large opening ratio coded-aperture plate. The SCGC system can offer a 3D volumetric image from a single view point due to its scintillator structure, which permits sampling across multiple viewing angles. We evaluate the volumetric imaging performance with phantom and animal imaging results. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the SCGC’s superior spatial resolution and depth positioning capabilities, suggesting it is feasible to generate a high-quality 3D volumetric image with only single-view scan with SCGC camera. This study represents a potential paradigm shift in SPECT system architecture.

articleTitle: Energy Resolution and Charge Sharing Improvements in High-Flux CdZnTe Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The development of energy resolved photon counting (ERPC) detectors for next-generation X-ray imaging is rapidly growing. Among room temperature semiconductor detectors (RTSDs), cadmium zinc telluride (CdZnTe or CZT) detectors represent the key standard, allowing high detection efficiency, sub-millimetre imaging and room temperature energy resolution below 2 keV up to 150 keV. Charge sharing is a well-known critical issue in sub-millimetre CZT array detectors. In this work, we will present the performance enhancements, in terms of energy resolution and charge sharing, in new high-flux HF-CZT detectors, recently developed at IMEM-CNR Parma (Italy). The spectroscopic response of linear array detectors (pixel pitch of 500 μm and inter-pixel gap of 25 μm) was measured taking into account the mitigation of the effects of incomplete charge collection, pile-up, charge sharing and high flux radiation induced polarization phenomena. Preliminary tests showed excellent room temperature energy resolution FWHM of 1 % (0.6 keV) at 59.5 keV and low charge sharing distortions.

articleTitle: 3D segmentation guided PET to MR synthesis via deep learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multimodal medical images, such as magnetic resonance (MR) and positron emission tomography (PET), have been widely used to diagnose brain diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease due to the variety of information they can provide. PET images can reflect metabolic changes before structural abnormalities are found, which is of great significance for early diagnosis. And the scanning time of PET is shorter than that of MR. Considering the limited clinical applications of PET/MRI systems, we propose a 3D segmentation guided deep learning network to synthesize MR images from PET images. To preserve structural semantic information, we introduce structural semantic loss to guide the network learning. Experiments demonstrate that our method has yielded superior visual and quantitative outcomes with a Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) of 23.03 dB, a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) of 0.7911 and a Mean Square Error (MSE) of 0.0052. Compared with methods without introducing structural semantic loss, the PSNR and SSIM have increased by 0.16 dB and 0.0061 respectively, and the MSE has decreased by 0.0001. In addition, we also performed brain segmentation on the synthetic MR images. The MR synthesized by our method obtained an overall Dice score of 0.7313, which is higher than the results of other methods. All experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of our method on PET to MR synthesis tasks.
