articleTitle: Mitigating Limited Angle Artifacts in a Dual-Panel Positron Emission Mammography Scanner Using Deep Learning Regularization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A dual-panel Positron Emission Mammography (PEM) scanner is a dedicated breast imaging device with higher spatial resolution and enhanced sensitivity, in comparison with conventional Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners. However, one of the main challenges this scanner faces are the limited angle artifacts that arise in the cross-planes. To mitigate such artifacts, deep learning regularization has been included in the List Mode Ordered Subsets Expectation Maximization (LM-OSEM) reconstruction algorithm. Regularization has been applied using a U-Net trained with Monte-Carlo simulated data. Network training was achieved using slices of cross-plane images of a PEM scanner as input and corresponding slices from a dedicated breast-PET ring scanner as target, since this scanner does not have the limited angle problem. In the regularization stage, the trained U-Net is employed to process the cross-plane slices of the preceding image estimation. Subsequently, the resultant output is fused with the former image estimate utilizing Forward-backward splitting expectation maximization (FBSEM). This image reconstruction framework has demonstrated a notable enhancement in image quality when assessed from the cross-plane perspective, while maintaining the quality of images when assessed from the in-plane perspective. With this approach, PEM images may be effectively analyzed as three-dimensional images.

articleTitle: High Responsivity (p+)diamond/(n)4H-SiC Schottky Barrier Radiation Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a groundbreaking advancement in radiation detection technology with novel ($\mathrm{p}^{+}$)diamond/(n)4H-SiC heterojunction Schottky barrier diodes (HSBDs). The HSBDs are poised to revolutionize harsh environment radiation detection applications where detectors with metal electrodes become unreliable over prolonged use. These HSBDs integrate a thin, transparent nanocrystalline $\mathrm{p}^{+}$boron-doped diamond layer with high-quality n-type $4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ epitaxial layers, yielding exceptional self-biased (zero biased) detection performance. The HSBD showed a very strong Schottky behavior with a rectification ratio of $6 \times 10^{8}$ at a bias voltage of $\pm 1.4 \mathrm{~V}$. When exposed to a ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}$ alpha particle source without any external bias, the HSBD detector produced a robust peak corresponding to the 5486 keV alpha particles in the pulse height spectrum with a full-width-at-half-maximum (FWHM) of 210 keV and a charge collection efficiency of 40%. The HSBDs also exhibited superior responsiveness to UV radiation compared to traditional metal/4HSiC Schottky diodes. We observed a photo-to-dark-current ratio (PDCR) of $1.12 \times 10^{5}$ and a responsivity of $0.01 \mathrm{~A} / \mathrm{W}$ at 0 V with the HSBDs exposed to 365 nm UV radiation having a power density of $3 \mathrm{~mW} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. Both diamond and $4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ being harsh environment compatible, the novel device structure addresses challenges in harsh environment radiation detection.

articleTitle: Timing Response of a Novel Rad-Hard Fast Detection System for Radioactive Ion Beam Tagging and Diagnostics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) are a unique tool to study the properties of nuclear structure, exploring also regions of the nuclei chart, located far from the stability valley. At the Laboratori Nazionali del Sud of INFN in Catania (Italy), the construction of a novel high intensity Radioactive Ion Beams (RIBs) facility named FRAISE, calls for novel detection systems for the diagnostics and the tagging of RIBs along the transport line. To this aim we are developing a novel detection system, based on an array of SiC diodes, readout by an optimized fast frontend electronics. The choice of SiC is dictated by its superior performance in terms of radiation hardness. In fact, the full detection system is designed to be housed in a DN160 spherical cross to be inserted along the beam path. $100 \mu \mathrm{m}$ - $180 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick monolithic detector tiles, duly segmented in pads, will be arranged to cover a detection active area of about $30 \mathrm{~mm} \times 60 \mathrm{~mm}$ as required to reconstruct typical RIBs profiles in the high dispersion point of the fragment separator. As a consequence, it is critical to provide experimentally the detector response matrix and in particular the mapping of the timing response, particularly relevant as the ToF technique provides particle identification. The proper identification of “close” nuclei requires time resolutions of the order of 100 ps -200 ps. This contribution deals with the study and the experimental qualification of the timing response of the proposed detection system, through a detailed qualification of the timing properties of the developed frontend electronics and the map of the detector response at different beams in small format demonstrators carefully developed to mimic the different situations we will have to face in the final system.

articleTitle: CZT Detector Calibration for Neural Network based Subpixel Positioning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Subpixel positioning is an interesting technique to improve spatial resolution of semiconductor detectors while minimizing the impact of charge sharing. As electron cloud size has a typical size of hundred micrometer, the use of pixel pitches above millimeter is preferable to get a correct spectrometric response. Moreover, as moving charges simultaneously induce signals on several electrodes, data processing techniques enable precise subpixel positioning. In general, subpixel positioning is achieved either by center of weight approaches or model-based maximum likelihood techniques. Recently, neural network approaches have been proposed to get higher processing flexibility. However, the concrete use of neural network for CZT imaging device faces two challenges. First, a FPGA implementation is required to integrate such feature in real systems. We will show how to address this challenge. Second, labeled data is required for doing the supervised learning of neural network weights: typically, one has to pair observed signals and incident photon position and energy, which are not known in general. After discussing standard approaches based either on detector modeling or experimental calibration protocols, we will present an unsupervised learning technique that permits to combine modeling and experimental calibration.

articleTitle: Partial Volume Correction on 177Lu-SPECT sinogram with Deep Learning trained on synthetic data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces PVCNet, a deep learning-based method for Partial Volume Correction for ${ }^{177}$ Lu-SPECT imaging, aimed at improving quantitative accuracy and image resolution prior to reconstruction. The method utilizes a large synthetic dataset derived from real patient images. PVCNet employs a dual neural network architecture, processing sinograms and projected attenuation maps as inputs. Its performance is evaluated using both real experimental phantom data and Monte Carlo simulations, and it is benchmarked against conventional Resolution Modeling (RM) and Iterative Yang (iY) methods, demonstrating promising results. On phantom data, PVCNet demonstrated superior performances ($0.80 / 0.93 / 1.00$ for Recovery Coefficients on 22/28/37 mm diameter spheres) than $\mathrm{RM}(0.52 / 0.66 / 0.77)$ but slightly lower than iY (0.96/0.99/1.06) which benefits from exact object segmentation, not required by PVCNet. On patient simulation, PVCNet showed the best results both in terms of Normalized Root Mean Squared Error (2.786/2.635/2.345 for RM/iY/PVCNet respectively) and mean Recovery Coefficients in background (1.05/0.95/1.03 for RM/iY/PVCNet respectively), kidneys ($0.93 / 1.16 / 0.97$ for RM/iY/PVCNet) and lesions ($0.66 / 1.14 / 0.91$ for RM/iY/PVCNet).

articleTitle: Low dose PET image reconstruction using diffusion sampling with posterior iterative correction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low dose PET image reconstruction is a crucial technique in functional imaging, addressing both patient safety and diagnostic needs by minimizing radioactive exposure. However, as dosage is reduced, the increasing noise makes reconstruction challenging. This study leverages a diffusion model in a pre-training mode to learn PET image priors from existing PET data, establishing a sampling framework for low-dose PET reconstruction. By constraining the sampling process with a data fidelity correction term through iterative reconstruction and implementing posterior iterative correction, we achieve 50x down-sampled PET reconstruction without the need for training with paired data. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves excellent performance compared with MLEM, EMTV and DeepPET method.

articleTitle: Radiation-Induced Leakage Current Measurement of CMOS MOSFET for Dynamic Modeling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work is measurement of radiation-induced leakage current for dynamic modeling on metal oxide semiconductor field effect transistor (MOSFET) based on complementary metal oxide semiconductor (CMOS). The main contributors of radiation-induced leakage current are charge buildup due to trap at gate and interface of the shallow trench isolation (STI). The drain current for leakage current is measured with P/NMOS, including variations such as width, finger and 1.8 V/ 3.3 V bias type, during the radiation exposure. The leakage current is obtained to a maximum of $6 \ \mu \mathrm{A}$ at NMOS with width of $1 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ and 1 finger. From these results, we have been presented modeling approach for dynamic model which track charge trapped buildup as radiation exposure time.

articleTitle: Development of a Super High Resolution Self-Collimating Industrial Gamma Camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Gamma cameras are valuable tools for nuclear safety, nuclear security and nuclear emergency response scenarios. In many scenarios, imaging of high-energy radionuclides and complexly distributed radiation sources is necessary. However, existing gamma camera, including Compton camera and coded-aperture-based gamma cameras, could not achieve high-resolution imaging of complexly distributed high-energy sources. Recently, we introduced the self-collimation concept, which the spatially distributed scintillator elements play a dual role of both collimation and detection. In this study, we develop a self-collimating gamma camera (HESCGC) system to enable high-resolution imaging of radioactive materials with complicated shape. Experimental evaluation was conducted on the prototype using a $^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ point source. The average sensitivity at a distance of 1.0 m from the camera was $(1.00 \pm 0.24) \times 10^{-5}$. We use a point-source-array phantom, a dual-line source phantom, and a “Nuclear” alphabetical phantom to evaluate the performance of HESCGC. Projection data from the $^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ point source $(4.77 \mathrm{mCi})$ at various positions were collected, and selected projection data were combined to mimic the phantom. The camera accurately located single point sources and effectively resolved a $3 \times 3{ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ point source array (Total activity: $4.77 \mathrm{mCi}, 45 \mathrm{~s}$) with a 1.25° point-to-point separation in three distinct regions. The dual-line sources spaced 1.25° apart and 20° in length successfully separated. The reconstructed image of the “Nuclear” alphabetical phantom faithfully depicted its shape with clear details and minimal artifacts. The HESCGC system demonstrated exceptionally high-resolution performance in gamma imaging, holding significant promise for industrial applications.

articleTitle: First Measurements with On-Chip PET Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents the initial real-world evaluation of a dedicated On-Chip PET scanner designed for functional imaging of Organs-on-Chips (OOCs). OOCs provide a promising alternative to conventional in vitro and animal models for drug development, disease modeling, and toxicity testing. Our previous work has focused on optimizing the scanner’s design through simulations, developing deep-learning techniques for positron range correction, and demonstrating its capability to dynamically image OOCs. The On-Chip PET scanner consists of two detectors, each made up of a monolithic LYSO crystal optically coupled to four 8 x 8 SiPM arrays, which are individually read out by PETsys’ SiPM readout system. Following the ASICs calibration, several data acquisitions were conducted with the point source positioned at different locations within the field of view for 60 seconds each. Analysis of flood maps and energy spectra confirmed expected variations based on source positioning, demonstrating the functionality of the scanner. These preliminary results represent a first step towards enabling functional imaging for OOCs. Future work will involve further detector calibration and phantom measurements before transitioning to imaging actual OOC devices.

articleTitle: An Automatic Calibration Method Applied to the VDL Delay Chain of MVT Chip
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Multi-Voltage Threshold (MVT) method is an approach to digitizing scintillation pulses by sampling a set reference voltage. This method has been demonstrated to be effective for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) systems under field programmable gate array (FPGA). To enhance integration and reduce system costs, we designed an 8-channel MVT22 chip using application specific integrated circuit (ASIC) technology, capable of achieving a bin size of 19.5 ps. However, due to consistency issues between different channels, we propose a method for automatic on-chip calibration of the Vernier delay line (VDL) measurement for the MVT22 chip. The performance before and after calibration have been evaluated and the results indicate a significant improvement in the consistency of VDL distribution among channels after chip calibration. On average, in homogenous tests, the standard deviation is reduced to 28.3 ps, with an optimization of approximately 4.4 ps, and full width at half maxima (F WHM) is reduced to 50.6 ps with an optimization of approximately 14 ps. In heterogeneous experiments, the standard deviation is reduced to 27.9 ps, with an optimization of approximately 5.9 ps, and FWHM is reduced to 56.6 ps with an optimization of approximately 7.8 ps.

articleTitle: A Custom 2x2 inch SiPM Array with Temperature Sensor and Readout Electronics for Thermal Compensation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The measurements with Phoswisch CeBr-NaI scintillators, which were read with an OnSemi J60035 64P SiPM matrix and a readout electronics manufactured by us, showed a clear thermal drift. This is in contrast to the considerable insensitivity to magnetic fields. Systematic measurements of the gamma peak shifts as a function of temperature show a linear behavior. This allows its compensation as long as the measured temperature is as close as possible to the actual temperature of the SiPM sensors. For this purpose, we have built a custom version of the SiPM array with a temperature sensor directly on the back of the board in conjunction with a diffuse plane and a new redout circuit that compensates for the thermal drift by varying the Vbias voltage.

articleTitle: SparkPix-RT2: The design of a 192 × 168 pixel detector ASIC with on-chip data processing for ultra-fast photon science
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: SparkPix-RT is a pioneer mixed-signal ASIC for the development of the next generation high frame-rate X-ray detectors featuring continuous real-time on-chip data compression. We present the design of SparkPix-RT2 (RT2) which is full-reticle 192 x 168 pixel detector ASIC. RT2 increases the size of the pixel matrix from 8-pixel cluster columns of 4 clusters each to 32 pixel cluster columns of 14 clusters each. This increases the total pixel array from 48x48 to 192x168 pixels, the same as ePixUHR ASIC. This requires 32 compressors and an increase in the number of high-speed serial transmitters from 2 to 16. The main design challenge is that the FIFO and Dark SRAMs must be scaled up in size, occupying more area. This has been accommodated by increasing the balcony area slightly in the vertical direction. The RT2 design was frozen April 1, 2024 and verification (RTL simulations, emulations and mixed-signal verification) will continue until tape-out in July 2024.

articleTitle: Ground Calibration and In-Orbit Operations of the MASS-Cube Gamma Ray Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: MASS-Cube is a Compton telescope project aimed at achieving higher line sensitivity to gamma ray detection in the MeV energy range, employing high-performance three-dimensional position-sensitive pixelated CdZnTe(CZT) detectors. Utilizing the Compton effect, MASS-Cube reconstructs the direction of gamma ray sources. To achieve optimal imaging performance, precise calibration of gamma ray energy deposition and three-dimensional positioning within the crystal is necessary. Additionally, comprehensive in-orbit monitoring and real-time calibration strategies will be proposed to address challenges posed by the variable space environment, such as temperature fluctuations, bias voltage adjustments, and radiation damage, ensuring the detector’s optimal functionality. These efforts lay the groundwork for obtaining reliable data from MASS-Cube during its orbital operations.

articleTitle: 4pi-directional radiation monitoring system using single crystal detector and depth-of-interaction method
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: As the number of facilities using radioactive materials increases, the risk of radiation accidents such as radioactive material leaks is also increasing. In accident situations, it is important to quickly identify contaminants and their locations, so gamma cameras and multi-detector systems based on measured count ratio have been developed. However, those systems have limitations, including limited field of view(FOV) and difficulty monitoring multiple radiation sources. In this study, we proposed a single crystal-based monitoring system that can provide radionuclide and direction information for multiple sources in real time with a 4 pi-FOV. The proposed system consists of a cylindrical single crystal(CsI:Tl, $\Phi 1^{\prime \prime} \times 4^{\prime \prime}$), two photomultiplier tubes(PMTs, $\Phi 1$ “) attached to both ends of the crystal, and a collimator. The collimator is made of 10 mm thick lead surrounding the crystal and contains eight independent slots designed in different directions depending on the height. The system interacts with the incident radiation at a specific height in the crystal for each source direction, and obtains direction information through the depth-of-interaction(DOI). The PMTs are connected by a coincidence circuit, and each PMT signal is used to obtain the DOI(ratio between two PMT signals) and radiation energy(sum of two PMT signals). The feasibility of the proposed system was verified using the GATE toolkit. Simulations were performed by moving the ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ source from 0 to 360 degrees at 22.5-degree intervals at a distance of 50 m from the system. As a result, each energy spectrum along the source direction was measured at s specific crystal height. Additionally, the slots partially share the FOV, allowing sources to be detected by separating them into 16 directional sectors. The system is expected to be able to acquire independent energy spectra depending on the slot height, enabling nuclide identification and direction monitoring for multiple sources in real time.

articleTitle: Introduction of High-Performance Gamma-ray Measurement Probes for Nuclear Inspection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents an in-depth analysis of innovative $\operatorname{CsI}(\mathrm{Tl})$-based gamma-ray measurement probes designed for effective detection and analysis of hidden nuclear materials within undeclared nuclear sites. These technologies address the deficiencies in current nuclear verification practices, especially in states with enhanced secrecy such as North Korea. The gamma-ray probes, equipped with multiple detectors made from CsI(Tl) scintillators, offer high photon yield and efficient gamma-ray detection. The probes operate over a broad dose rate range, enabling detection of minute quantities of radiation indicative of illicit nuclear materials. TCP/IP-based wireless communication technology enables the probes to transmit measurement data instantly over distances up to 100 meters. Field tests in simulated environments resembling undeclared nuclear facilities have validated the probes’ effectiveness. The probes demonstrated an ability to detect radiation levels as low as $0.001 ~ \mu \mathrm{Sv} / \mathrm{h}$. The probes achieved an energy resolution of approximately 9%. In a controlled test simulating an undeclared nuclear site, the probes successfully identified and quantified Cs-137 isotopes. The probes operated continuously for over 5 hours on a single charge during field operations. Bayesian inference algorithms allowed for accurate localization of radiation sources. Future enhancements will focus on improving energy resolution and expanding communication capabilities.

articleTitle: Better Than the Total Variation Regularization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The total variation (TV) regularization is popular in iterative image reconstruction when the piecewise-constant nature of the image is encouraged. As a mater of fact, the TV regularization is not strong enough to enforce the piecewise-constant appearance. This paper suggests a different regularization function that is able to discourage some smooth transitions in the image and to encourage the piecewise-constant behavior. This new regularization function involves a Gaussian function. We use the limited-angle tomography problem to illustrate the effectiveness of this new regularization function. The limited-angle tomography situation considered in this paper uses a scanning angular range of 40°. For two-dimensional parallel-beam imaging, the sufficient angular range is 180°.

articleTitle: Quantification and Identifiability of Molecular Blood-Brain Barrier Permeability-Surface Area Product with Total-Body Dynamic PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability dysfunction has been observed in many disease states. Measuring the BBB permeability of PET molecular tracers generally requires the target tracer’s BBB transport rate K<inf>1</inf> and cerebral blood flow (CBF) obtained from a second flow-tracer PET scan. This enables quantification of the permeability-surface area (PS) product, a widely-used kinetic measure of BBB permeability. Here we propose a single-tracer multiparametric PET method with high temporal resolution kinetic modeling to eliminate the need for the flow-tracer PET scan and characterize the identifiability of PS herein. Our method applies the adiabatic approximation to the tissue homogeneity (AATH) model on the first two-minutes of high temporal resolution ($60 \times 1$ $\mathrm{s}, 30 \times 2 \mathrm{~s}$) dynamic PET data to estimate CBF and the tracer-specific K<inf>1</inf> from a single dynamic scan. The extraction fraction $E=K_{1} / C B F$ was computed to quantify $P S=-C B F \ln (1-E)$ based on the Renkin-Crone equation. To demonstrate our method can measure the spectrum of BBB permeability, BBB PS was quantified in fifteen subjects scanned on the uEXPLORER PET/CT system with either ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-fluciclovine, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), or ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}$-butanol, with known low, moderate, and high BBBK<inf>1</inf>, respectively. Image-derived input functions were obtained from the ascending aorta. Mean ± standard deviation (SD) of grey matter BBB PS was $0.017 \pm 0.003 and 0.142 \pm 0.011 \mathrm{ml} / \mathrm{min} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$ for fluciclovine and FDG, respectively. Butanol PS was indeterminately high as the median extraction fraction was 100% for this flow tracer. Practical identifiability analysis suggested that the mean ± SD error of PS was 0.2 ± 11.5% and -0.1 ± 3.4% for fluciclovine and FDG, respectively. Further simulations varying E from 1 to 99% showed that error mean and SD were <5% and <10%, respectively, for E between 2.5 to 75%. Our new single-tracer multiparametric PET method may enable non-invasive studies of BBB permeability at the molecular level.

articleTitle: Motion-Corrected Brain PET on a PET/MR Scanner using MR Volume Navigators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Head motion will blur PET brain images for patients unable to keep their head still during a $\mathrm{PET} / \mathrm{MR}$ scan. This is a concern for patients with neurodegenerative disorders or diseases, limiting the use of PET/MR brain imaging. In this work a method to correct for motion in PET/MR brain scans is developed and evaluated. Head motion is tracked using a 3D volume navigator (vNav) inserted into the inversion recovery time (TI) of the parent T1-weighted MP-RAGE sequence. New 3D vNav images are obtained at the repetition rate (TR) of the MP-RAGE scan and registered with the starting 3D vNav reference image to determine rigid body head motion. Motion information is used to adjust MP-RAGE scan planes and navigators in real time and is recorded for retrospective PET image reconstruction. PET processing begins by determining time frames for histogramming. The first vNav image becomes a reference and frame 1 ends when motion relative to this pose exceeds a given threshold. For subsequent frames the pose at the end of the previous frame becomes the new reference, and the frame ends when motion relative to this new reference is exceeded. List-mode data are histogrammed into sinograms for each time frame. PET images are reconstructed and realigned to the initial head position using the average vNav pose information for each frame. The method was evaluated using PET/MR scans of a 3D Hoffman brain phantom filled with F-18 FDG and attached Na-22 point sources. The phantom was scanned with and without a variety of motions. Navigators were acquired approximately every 2 sec. Motion correction was successfully performed in all cases. Point sources were relocated to their starting positions and motion blurring was removed from PET images. This method for PET motion correction using MR volume navigators is non-invasive, does not require additional hardware and can be implemented with many clinical 3D MR sequences. Human studies are planned.

articleTitle: Development of a Nuclear Material Weighing System Based on Fast Neutron Multiplicity Counter
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The international community uses safeguards agreements to prevent nuclear facilities or nuclear materials from being diverted to nuclear weapons or nuclear explosive materials. Nuclear material accountancy for nuclear material verification typically uses the nondestructive assay and are divided into neutron multiplicity counting and fast neutron multiplicity counting for neutron multiplicity measurements. Conventional neutron multiplicity counters use thermal neutron-sensitive He-3 tubes, but due to the scarcity of He-3 and the loss of energy and time information, fast neutron multiplicity counters using organic scintillators such as stilbene, anthracene and plastics are being investigated. In this study, a fast neutron multiplicity counter was modeled and fabricated by arranging five 20 mm thick stilbene arrays in a pentagonal shape. MCNPX-PoliMi simulations were performed on the fabricated system using ${ }^{252} \mathrm{Cf}$, and the simulated and measured data were linearly fitted to the simulated data. Two-parameter assay were used to estimate the mass, and both methods were able to estimate the mass with an error within $1.5 \%$.

articleTitle: Advances on Compton camera technology with a 5mm thick CdTe photon-counting detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In search of more sustainable alternatives for energy production, countries like France and Finland heavily rely on nuclear power. Furthermore, nations such as Italy and Germany are actively phasing out nuclear energy in favor of safer alternatives. These shifts require solutions for the nuclear waste management prob-lem. The storage of mid- to low-level radioactive waste presents a challenge, as it must be precisely identified and differentiated from non-radioactive material. Current methods for classifying radioactive waste include radiochemistry treatment of samples, which, it is time-consuming. Alternative methods include the usage of Geiger-Muller counters and coded-aperture gamma cameras, for pre-screening of samples before radiochemical analysis. These methods require either proximity to the sample or extended exposure times and suffer from limited field-of-view and energy sensitivity. Thus, the use of Compton scattering-based systems has surged as an alternative for precisely identifying radiation sources and radionuclides, especially when based on pixelated photon-counting detectors such as those from the Timepix family. The Timepix3 detector allows for studying single events at high fluxes (38Mhits/cm2/s) due to its data-driven out-put. It also records the energy and time-of-arrival for each event, providing the required information for reconstructing the location of the source of radiation, based on Compton scattering kinematics, as well as its energy spectrum. This work investigates the usage of a Timepix3 photon-counting detector, bump bonded with a 5mm CdTe sensor, in a single-layer camera configuration. The general characterization of the ensemble is presented, as well as its performance in the localization of radioactive sources in different control environments, including multiple radiation and surface sources. The performance of the device relative to a 3mm CdTe sensor will also be discussed.

articleTitle: The Impact of MRI-based Attenuation Correction on Lung Fibrosis Quantification in 68Ga-CPB8 PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The negative impact of MR-based attenuation correction (MRAC) in PET quantification is known. However, it has yet to be investigated in depth with an emphasis on fibrotic lung tissue. Lung fibrosis is a common radiological finding in interstitial lung diseases (ILD). Recently, ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}-\mathrm{CPB}$, a novel positron emission tomography (PET) radiotracer for Type I collagen detection, was introduced, and several ongoing studies aim to evaluate this tracer for different applications. As integrated PET and magnetic resonance imaging (PET/MRI) scanners are used for some of these studies, one critical factor that needs to be evaluated for this novel radiotracer is the MR-based attenuation correction (MRAC) effect on the uptake values. In this simulation-based study, we generate pseudo-emission images based on the ${ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}$-CBP8 PET PET images of a 19-subject cohort. The pseudo-emission images were paired with the Subject’s high-resolution CT scans, accurately representing the disease. Then, we simulated the data using SIRF and reconstructed them using MR- and CT-based correction, comparing them with the ground truth PET images. The method allowed us to accurately isolate the effect of MRAC in the fibrotic tissue.We show that collagen-rich accumulation in the lung affects the attenuation and scattering properties of the tissue, reducing the mean measured uptake in the fibrotic tissue and the aorta. In addition, se show considerable bias on the aorta when fibrosis has developed in the neighboring area. However, the effect is not easily quantifiable as each subject’s personalized disease stage can introduce strong bias focally, even when the global effect is not strong. We plan to address the issues identified in this work by generating R2* images from a combination of multi-echo UTE images. Then, we will convert them to linear attenuation coefficients based on data obtained from transmission and CT scans.

articleTitle: A New Method for Thoron Radon Individual Detection from Same Air
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Due to the shorter half-life, it has been assumed that thoron has negligible health hazards on humans compared to radon. However, it is possible to get a higher concentration of thoron gas compared to radon depending on the detector’s position or thorium concentration in the building material. As most radon detectors can not differentiate radon and thoron count, they show the total count of both gases as a single radon count. This in turn results in a biased estimation of lung cancer risk in epidemiological studies. For a continuous and discriminative measurement of the gases from the same air, a new method was suggested where two detectors and a pipe were used. To check the thoron measurement capability of the system, a closed chamber condition was applied. It was observed that the thoron count rate was exponentially dropped according to the thoron half-life and the decay curve matches with the theoretical calculated value. In the proposed system, the first chamber measures radon and thoron gas while the second only measures radon gas. It was observed that for a 2 liter per minute air-flow rate, it needs a 20 m long pipe to remove all thoron ($840 \mathrm{~Bq} / \mathrm{L}$) present in the examined air. In this study, a surface barrier detector and a collimated alpha source were used to calibrate the proposed system. The proposed system could be a cheap solution for thoron and radon individual detection.

articleTitle: Optimization of Single-ended Continuous Photon Depth-of-Interaction Positioning Scheme Based on Novel Light Sharing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study focuses on enhancing the DOI resolution in PET systems by optimizing a single-ended continuous DOI positioning scheme using a 2 mm pitch $12 \times 12$ LYSO crystal array with varying boundary models. Three models were evaluated for DOI resolution at different depths using SiPMs with a 3.16 mm pitch. Results showed that Model 2, which features a central fully blocked boundary, provided the best DOI resolution of $1.87 \mathrm{~mm}(\sigma)$, equivalent to a FWHM of 4.40 mm. Experiments utilized PETsys module to read the SiPM array individually, and applied row / column sum method manually. With the row / column summed data, the optimization involved comparing and refining four metrics: variance, max/sum ratio, flood map position, and the difference between sums of even and odd entries. Additionally, the coefficients between the row values and column values were optimized. These findings highlight that strategic placement of boundaries within the detector array substantially enhances DOI accuracy, making Model 2 particularly effective for precise PET imaging, and also employing a variety of metrics, rather than a single unified metric, can lead to improved depth of interaction (DOI) resolution.

articleTitle: A next generation preclinical PET/EPRI: performance evaluation of the complete PET subsystem
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report on a PET system that has been recently completed after the last several years of development work. The PET system is a sub-component of PET/EPR hybrid imaging system for investigating tumor hypoxia in small animal, and will be deployed to replace the current PET subsystem of the PET/EPR imager. The new PET system possesses several superior features over the existing system for small animal imaging: the axial field-of-view is increased 4 times from $\sim 25$ mm to $\sim 106 \mathrm{~mm}$, and constituent scintillator pixel size is reduced from 3.0 mm to 1.0 mm to achieve sub-millimeter image resolution. The PET system is modularized and built by using 14 detector modules (DM). Each DM consists of 8 detector units (DU) in a row, and each DU in turn is a 12 x 12 array of $1 \mathrm{x} 1 \mathrm{x} 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LYSO crystals coupled to a Hamamastu 14161-3050HS-04 MPPC array. The PET system employs a new signal readout method to efficiently handle a greatly increased number of detector outputs by combining a conventional resistive network (RN) and a strip-line (SL) method. Due to the highly multiplexing feature of the readout, each DM generates the total of 6 outputs only (2 SLs and 4 RNs) for digitization. After the evaluation test, BASP-10011 readout board (Brightonix Imaging, Korea) was adopted for high throughput and performance data acquisition needed for routine animal imaging studies, and was incorporated into the PET system. Following successful development and integration of all components, we started to conduct phantom imaging for performance evaluation of the PET system before installing it inside the EPR magnets. $\mathrm{A}^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source image shows 0.8 mm FWHM resolution in both transverse and axial direction. Image of a NEMA image quality phantom was acquired to assess the imaging performance of the PET system. We present the completed PET system and initial results on phantom imaging. More thorough performance results from on-going systematic evaluation will be reported at the conference.

articleTitle: Exploring Various Neural Networks for Interaction Localization in Semi-Monolithic Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Semi-monolithic scintillators for PET detectors offer an excellent trade-off between pixelated and monolithic scintillators. Interaction positioning techniques have been explored in these detectors, including machine learning approaches that have demonstrated high prediction accuracy by analyzing the signal distribution among the photosensor array. In this work, we explore whether this accuracy can be further improved using different neural network architectures and number of input signals. To this end, we performed measurements of semi-monolithic scintillator arrays with a 64-channel SiPM readout used in the total-body IMAS PET scanner, and in a forthcoming brain-dedicated scanner (UHB). We compare the positioning performance of a multilayer perceptron (MLP) fed with 16 signals obtained from a summation of the rows and columns of the readout to a convolutional neural network (CNN) fed with all $64(8 \times 8)$ signals. The CNN seems able to exploit some of the light sharing observed to occur between the semi-monolithic slabs, resulting in an improved accuracy compared to the MLP. This study contributes to quantifying the performance disparities among machine learning models when provided with varying levels of signal information.

articleTitle: Generation of Synthetic brain PET images of synaptic density from MRI and FDG-PET using a Multi-stage U-Net
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) in human brains is an important biomarker of synaptic loss associated with several disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease (AD). However, SV2A tracers, such as [$\left.{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ UCB-J, are less available in practice due to constrains that include cost and the need for an onsite cyclotron. Therefore, we investigated the possibility of using a 3D Multi-stage U-net (MS U-net) to generate synthetic [$\left.{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ UCB-J SV2A PET images based on T1-weighted Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and/or [${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$]FDG PET imaging. In our study, we used paired data from 54 participants including 22 healthy controls (HC) and 32 participants with AD. Our results demonstrate that the MS U-net was able to generate desirable SV2A PET images that are visually similar to true images in terms of contrast and tracer distribution, quantitatively with low bias and high similarity. Thus, synthetic SV2A PET images can provide additional pathological insights into AD and other neurological disorders without increasing radiation exposure and cost. Our experiments show that through progressive learning MS U-net achieved less bias and outperformed U-net. Adopting residual connection, cross-stage feature fusion and supervised attention strategies contributes to better gradient flow, mitigates information loss and enables selective focus, leading to better generation results. Additionally, combining MRI and FDG PET images as the network input provides the best prediction performance, whereas having FDG PET alone produces better synthetic [<sup>11</sup> C]UCB-J SV2A PET image than using MRI alone. We also evaluated our model performance for 18 typical brain regions and MS U-net achieved less than 5% bias in almost all regions. Furthermore, the differences between AD and HC in certain regions (e.g., hippocampus) are still significant in generated images. We conclude it is feasible to produce robust SV2A PET images for HC and AD from MRI and FDG PET.

articleTitle: Initial studies of high resolution PET detectors using a novel dual-ended readout for organ-dedicated imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To image smaller organs such as the breast, heart and prostate using PET, there is a need for developing organ-dedicated PET systems that offers higher spatial resolution, high sensitivity, and low cost. This study will focus on developing the PET system with a dual-panel geometry. This study proposes a novel duel-ended readout method with an asymmetric SiPM design: the front end of the crystal array couples to a 4×4 SiPM array of 6×6 mm<sup>2</sup> size without optical light guide for optimal timing resolution, and the back end couples to an 8×8 SiPM array of 3×3 mm<sup>2</sup> size for high spatial resolution. High DOI resolution can be achieved using the ratio of signal energy detected by the SiPM at one end to the total energy from both ends, with a crystal thickness of 20mm to ensure high detection efficiency. The dimension of the crystal arrays studied is 25×25×20 mm<sup>3</sup> with the end area matches the area of the SiPM arrays. The TOFPET2 ASICs of PETsys Electronics were used to individually digitize and process the 64 signals coming from an SiPM array. All crystal can be clearly resolved in the flood image. The average energy resolution of the detectors was 14.0% and 16.3%. The event timing was determined using energy-weighted averaging method, resulting in CTRs of 242 ps and 282 ps for the two arrays with an energy window of 410-610 keV, respectively. The dual-ended readout detectors developed in this work provide good CTRs and a high three-dimensional position resolution, suitable for developing organ-dedicated PET scanners, capable of achieving simultaneously uniform and high spatial resolution, high sensitivity and high timing resolution.

articleTitle: Front-end Electronics of a LiInP2Se6 Neutron Detector for Single Crystal Diffractometer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work reports on the development of a double-sided strip $\operatorname{LiInP}_{2} \mathrm{Se}_{6}$ neutron detector for single-crystal diffractometer (SCD) facilities. The detector aims to improve overall detection performance by achieving a spatial resolution of less than $500 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and ensuring high detection efficiency. To meet our objectives and challenges, a double-sided cross-strip configuration with a strip pitch as small as $300 \mu \mathrm{m}$ is patterned on a $\operatorname{LiInP}_{2} \mathrm{Se}_{6}$ substrate and coupled to our detection system. The data collected from each strip necessitated the development of a specific and suitable readout system, described in this paper. The front-end electronics of the detection system consist of a custom daughter board with two VATAGP7 Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs), which is in turn connected to an already developed main acquisition board for readout process control.

articleTitle: Small Field Measurement using a Commercial Amorphous Silicon Flat Panel Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With the development of precision radiotherapy, the minimum radiation field of radiotherapy can reach a magnitude of 1 mm. For 6 MV linear accelerators, radiation fields smaller than $3 \times 3 \mathrm{~cm} 2$ could be referred to as small fields. Compared with conventional radiotherapy fields, the unique dosimetry characteristics of small fields, such as high dose gradient on the edge of the radiation field, loss of lateral charged particle equilibrium, the overlapping between the radiation source and multi-leaf collimators, and the size of the detector is larger than the area of the radiation field, would significantly increase the difficulty of precise dose measurement. Consequently, the uncertainty of clinical dose measurement would also increase, far exceeding the measurement error requirement of <5% proposed by the International Commission on Radiation Units and Measurements(ICRU) 24 report<sup>[1]</sup>. Therefore, the development of small field dosimeter becomes a research hotspot. Due to its ultra-high detection resolution (about 0.2 mm), commercial X-ray flat panel detectors could be a potential choice for small-field measurements. However, due to the flat panel detector’s side-scattering and radiation energy response effects, the detector’s dose conversion factor must be finely corrected to ensure sufficiently low dose measurement errors. In this paper, for a commercial amorphous silicon flat panel detector, the detector acquisition mode tuning and detection parameters correction are completed. At the same time, based on the Elekta 6 MV linear accelerator, the ghost effect correction factor, radiation field size correction factor, and off-axis distance correction factor of the flat panel detector were calculated using the EBT3 radiochromic film measurement as the reference value. Hence, the detector image-dose calibration model was built. Furthermore, the average measurement error was lower than 3% for a typical small field.

articleTitle: Development progress of N-PET, a high-sensitivity and high-resolution TOF-DOI PET prototype dedicated for human brain imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To achieve high sensitivity and high spatial resolution for human brain PET imaging, the N-PET project is developing a range of methodological advancements from the innovative multi-resolution TOF-DOI detector to multiple machine learning methods that can enhance DOI discrimination and improve DOI resolution. We aim to develop an N-PET prototype system that offers a ${\lt}1.5 \mathrm{~mm}$ spatial resolution, at least 4 levels of DOI discrimination and ${\lt}300 \mathrm{ps}$ TOF resolution. The major innovations include a multi-resolution TOF-DOI detector with two-layer LYSO crystal arrays and lightguide that can achieve high spatial and TOF resolution as well as DOI decoding capacity, an efficient and practical DOI discrimination method at the system level using semi-supervised learning to reduce labeling costs while maintaining reliability, and a CNN method trained by detector side-irradiation data acquired at different depths that can further improve DOI resolution by 48%. Currently, preliminary experimental results show that the detector is able to achieve a TOF resolution of 260 ps and a DOI resolution of better than 4.2 mm at bottom layer. The impact of TOF and DOI information on image quality is evaluated using GATE Monte Carlo simulation. A specialized image quality phantom suitable for evaluating brain-dedicated PET systems has been designed, and image reconstruction and normalization algorithms has been developed. The simulation results demonstrate that the imaging quality of the multi-resolution detector-based system is enhanced by using its TOF and DOI information. The development of a single-ring prototype is in progress, with more detectors and electronics are being delivered. We plan to present the prototype’s initial performance at the conference, including spatial resolution, CTR, and results from phantom and animal imaging.

articleTitle: Motion Correction for Cardiac PET via Parametric Image Optical Flow
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Motion correction (MC) is crucial in cardiac positron emission tomography (PET) to mitigate artifacts caused by cardiac, respiratory, and body motion. Motion correction not only improves image quality also leads to accurate quantification of cardiac health. In this study, we explore the effectiveness of optical flow based motion correction for gated cardiac PET. We present a novel method of joint estimation and denoising of parametric images.We also present preliminary results of parametric image based optical flow MC, a novel MC method. By jointly denoising and estimating parametric images we see a $\lt4 \mathrm{~dB}$ increase in PSNR for Patlak $K$ image compared to no denoising and see at least a 1 dB PSNR gain with our MC method over all noise scenarios.

articleTitle: 3D-CBS: Features, Implementation and Usage Targeted to Reduce More than 50 percent of Premature Cancer Deaths and Costs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Background - 3D-CBS (3-D Complete Body Screening): first true paradigm change in biomedical imaging invented 23 years ago, confirmed by third party measured results on a 3D-CBS copy as able to safely detect clusters (tumors) of 100 cancer cells instead of millions of cells. Materials and methods - 157 cm -FOV 3D-CBS capable of detecting all possible 511 keV -pairs of photons from the tumor markers at the lowest cost/valid pair captured, with components costing less than ${\$}$2,000,000/device, ${\$}$200/2-minute screening test, and ${\$}$1,200/15-minute clinical exam, in two 8 -hour shifts can safely perform 360x2-minute tests, 8x15-minute exams. It is estimated 48 professionals/day are needed: 8 administrators, 4 logicians, 8 nurses, 8 technologists and 20 doctors; each doctor reading 16-20 screening tests/day for 22 minutes each, and 1 clinical exam for 68 minutes. People must perform several screening tests on the same machine, using the same protocol and radiation dose. To avoid false positives, the diagnosis will not be based on a single screening test but on the Total-Body Computer-Aided Diagnosis (TB-CAD) tool calculating the trend of anomalies in several screening tests and radiologists’ experience. Several screenings tests reveal unique hotspots showing increased activity/size of an anomalous biological process requiring deeper investigation (15-minute clinical examination). Screening tests before/after surgery detect if any cancer cells have been left over and monitor for recurrences at an early curable stage. Results - 90,000/test/year/device, 57billion tests/30-year on 57,000x3D-CBS devices built gradually over 30 years can save over 100,000,000 lives and over ${\$}$27 trillion. Conclusions - Because early cancer detection can save up to $98 \%$ lives, an experimental test on a sample population using this approach based on the TB-CAD trend calculated over several 3D-CBS screening tests will prove definitively that we can save millions of lives and trillions of dollars

articleTitle: The Origins of Unstable Properties in X-ray Imaging Sensors and Their Compensation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Semiconductor hybrid pixel detectors with Timepix-family chips with CdTe pixelated sensors are widely used for the detection of various types of ionizing/non-ionizing radiation in applications ranging from radiography imaging, non-destructive testing, particle radiotherapy to electron microscopy. It is important to achieve a higher long-term stability of the sensor chips and a lower occurrence of overall malfunctions. The polarization of the sensor to which a bias is applied, and the associated deformation of the electric field profile is the main cause of the instability of the detection properties. Better stability of the detector and limitation of the effect of its polarization opens the way to ultra-high-dynamic-range image capture. Results of implementing the pulsing bias voltage method in the MiniPIX detector with CdTe pixelated sensor and the study of stabilization of the degree of polarization by illuminating the sensors using LEDs are shown. A vein-like structure is observed in the image of the detector surface uniformly illuminated by a defocused Gaussian intensity profile laser beam. This structure is identical to that which can be observed under X-ray irradiation. Laser-Induced Transient Current Technique is used to characterize the electric field profile and examine the vein structure in detail by scanning a focused laser beam. We evaluate the time evolution of the electric field profile at the border of the veins and outside to find the difference. Obtained current waveforms in mapping the pixelated detector chip and the distribution uniformity of the collected charge will be shown. The properties of the sensor will also be evaluated when combined with the display readout chips. With the use of the X-ray diffraction method, the causes of the vein-like structure can be more closely identified. The obtained data are also shown.

articleTitle: Dynamic PET Image Reconstruction Using Spatiotemporal Kernel Method With Deep Image Prior
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) image reconstruction is challenging due to the inverse problem is ill-posed and low counts statistics. Spatiotemporal kernel method highly improves the quality of reconstructed images by implicitly introducing a spatial temporal prior information into the forward projection model. Deep image prior (DIP) demonstrates the ability of convolutional neural networks to denoise PET images without pre-training. In this work, we proposed a dynamic PET image reconstruction method using spatiotemporal kernel with deep image prior denoise. The composite image prior was constructed by rebinning the original 24 frames into three temporally averaged groups, then reconstructed using MLEM for 200 iterations to generate a high-count composite image for building the spatial kernel and neural network inputs, frame number information was then used to construct the temporal kernel, spatiotemporal kernel obtained by the Kronecker product by spatial kernel and temporal kernel. We employ the U-net architecture to simultaneously denoise the kernel coefficient images of all frames during each iteration, to suppress noise levels during reconstruction, and enhance the reconstructed image quality. The Zubal head phantom simulation results demonstrate the proposed method achieve a better performance on data from different time frames, and more robust across different iterations than MLEM, KEM, STKEM. In conclusion, the proposed method represents a highly improvement over conventional techniques for dynamic PET imaging, the unsupervised learning nature of DIP allows for easy generalization to different datasets and potential extension to accommodate various reconstruction algorithms.

articleTitle: High-Resolution X-ray Imaging with Hybrid and Inorganic Perovskite Flat Panel Imagers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With the advent of flat panel detector technology, flat panel x-ray imagers (FPXIs) are now the cornerstone of digital X-ray imaging. Commercial medical FPXIs commonly employ scintillator-based systems or amorphous selenium (a-Se) semiconductor films that directly convert X-rays into electronic signals. While scintillator-based FPXIs offer high detective quantum efficiency (DQE) up to 140 kV, their spatial resolution is compromised due to isotropic light propagation. Conversely, a-Se-based panels, although excellent in spatial resolution and DQE at lower X-ray doses, are less effective at higher energies, limiting their use to soft-tissue imaging like mammography. Recently, low-cost perovskite semiconductors, known for their application in solar cells, have shown excellent potential as highly sensitive and defect-tolerant X-ray sensors. This study evaluates both hybrid and fully inorganic perovskite semiconductors to determine their suitability for X-ray imaging in terms of spatial resolution, contrast, and stability. Our findings reveal that fully inorganic perovskites exhibit superior contrast and resolution, approaching the performance of commercial a-Se panels.

articleTitle: Long-Axial Field-Of-View Limited-Angle PET System with Ultra-High Time-Of-Flight and Depth-Of-Interaction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent developments in PET instrumentation, including advances in silicon photomultipliers and electronics, are fueling the development of novel PET systems improving flexibility and reducing costs. Among the improvements, ultra-high resolution time-of-flight (TOF) enables the use of limited angle geometry without sacrificing image quality. In this work, we present simulation results for a PET system under development, with ultra-high TOF resolution and depth-of-interaction (DOI). The proposed system is arranged for long axial field-of-view scanning using flat detector panels. We evaluate the performance of the system for varying TOF and DOI resolutions while incorporating geometric corrections during reconstruction. Results demonstrate the promising performance of a 2-panel, 70 ps TOF resolution system with 2.5 mm DOI resolution, as evidenced by traditional and task-based image quality metrics.

articleTitle: Development and Comparison of DOI capable Detectors for a Dedicated Breast PET/MRI Insert
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our group is developing a PET/MRI insert for enhanced breast imaging with a clinical 3T whole-body PET/MRI scanner. The small bore-diameter in combination with long, thin scintillation crystals promotes parallax error, which we aim to mitigate by determining the depth of interaction (DOI) for incident gammas. We therefore developed and compared two different DOI capable detectors based on a modified version of the C13500 TOF-PET modules (Hamamatsu Photonics K.K). A $4 \times 450 \mu \mathrm{m}$ S13546H MPPC array (Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.) was coupled to the following LSO crystal blocks separated by ESR and a 1.6 mm crystal pitch: a $10 \times 10$ crystal 15 mm high single layer block or a dual layer block with $10 \times 10$ crystals of 9.8 mm height (bottom layer) and $9 \times 9$ of 5.2 mm height (top layer). DOI information was extracted from the light spread pattern for the single layer block using a $380 \mu \mathrm{m}$ top light guide. DOI profiles were obtained using a tungsten collimated coincidence setup with defined irradiation depth at $3 \mathrm{~mm}, 8 \mathrm{~mm}$ and 13 mm with a 1.2 GBq F-18 line source. Both configurations showed a good crystal identification (peak to valley ratio of $7.3 \pm 3.3$ (single layer) and $4.3 \pm 1.6$ (dual layer)). Mean energy resolutions of $13.6 \pm 2.2 \%$ (single layer) and 13.3 $\pm 2.0 \% / 14.3 \pm 3.8 \%$ (dual-layer bottom/top layer) were achieved. The DOI resolution for the dual layer block inherently was limited to two DOI bins, with the single layer a DOI resolution of $5.3 \pm 2 \mathrm{~mm}$ was obtained. These preliminary evaluations demonstrate the suitability of both configurations for the breast insert and currently we prepare a timing related comparison. The higher DOI resolution of the single layer configuration requires a detector individual DOI calibration. Therefore, we are currently setting up a ring configuration with 8 detector modules and precise automated translational stages to develop system-applicable DOI calibration methods.

articleTitle: Ultra-High-Resolution Material Decomposition for Photon-Counting CT Using Physic-guided Foundation Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PCCT can measure the energy of each detected X-ray photon and can differentiate between materials and tissues in ultra-high-resolution (UHR) mode. However, while current material decomposition methods have been evaluated at the standard resolution, material decomposition in UHR mode has not been fully explored. The performance of UHR material decomposition could be degraded in practice due to the non-uniform detector spectral response from the misalignment between the anti-scatter grid and the detector pixel array. In this paper, we propose a material decomposition method in UHR mode based on a physics-guided foundation model, including pixel-specific quantum sensitivity, charging sharing effect, pulse pile-up effect, and scattering.

articleTitle: A new generation of HPGe hybrid pixel detectors: the concept of micro thermal-divider
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This project addresses the challenge related to the operation of High Purity Germanium (HPGe) sensors in hybrid pixel detectors for the detection of hard X-rays. Usually, the operation of cryogenic sensors like HPGe sensors in hybrid pixel detectors is related to the development of cryogenic Application Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs). This is somehow still a niche technical area restricting the range of applications and resulting in high development costs. Instead, it is proposed an alternative concept aimed at popularising the use of HPGe sensors with any available pixel ASIC which is designed for room temperature operation. This approach is based on the technical capability of managing an extreme temperature gradient between the ASIC and the sensor, while maintaining outstanding electrical performance and mechanical stability. We called “micro thermal-divider” the combination of the micro-fabrication technologies and the micro-electronics interconnection techniques enabling the control of extreme temperature gradients in a hybrid pixel detector. This contribution introduces the rationale and the requirements for the micro thermal-divider.

articleTitle: Total Lesion Glycolysis-weighted Non-rigid Registration for Respiratory Motion Correction in PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET with 18F-FDG is crucial for cancer diagnosis, but respiratory motion (RM) artifacts can cause image degradation. To correct RM, respiratory motion compensation (RMC) is performed, where registration is needed to align PET images at different respiratory gates. However, existing intensity-based image registration methods struggle with small lesions, particularly those with low tracer uptake. This work proposes a novel segmentation-augmented registration framework that incorporates total lesion glycolysis (TLG), a pathologically meaningful information, to improve small lesion motion estimation in PET. For each individual lesion, a adaptive weight is calculated, and integrated into the loss function. The proposed method is capable to work with existing registration algorithms, including deep learning-based method and conventional method.Extensive evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance for small lesion motion estimation without sacrificing registration accuracy for other anatomy.

articleTitle: CT Scout Scans with Deep Learning for Ultra-low Dose Attenuation Correction in PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Most clinical PET scanners integrate a CT for anatomical correlation and PET data corrections. However, when there is a spatial mismatch between PET and CT due to respiratory or gross body motion, CT-based attenuation correction (AC) results in image artefacts and quantification biases. Deep learning (DL) shows promise for CT-less AC, particularly when trained on specific organ regions. We propose to use non-corrected (NC) PET and scout images (= dual-view localizer radiographs acquired at the start of PET/CT scans) as inputs to a dual-branch network with the goal to extract complementary, modality-specific features. While scouts are routinely used for scan planning, the 2D projection images contain anatomical tissue density information that can be leveraged by a neural network for AC in PET, potentially precluding the need for the full CT scan. Our proposed approach aims to optimize a DL framework for a variety of tracer studies in long axial field-of-view PET which currently presents a challenging case for DL-based AC methods. Evaluations on ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FNOS, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FTT and ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}$-CFN studies showed that the co-learning strategy with NC PET and Scout data helps to reduce quantitative biases. We will also explore the utility of spectral CT scout scans, offering diagnostic benefits over conventional scouts by using projection-based material-specific maps to further fine-tune the DL-AC methods.

articleTitle: The Study of prototype Frontend Readout ASIC for the Muon Detector of STCF
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work is primarily focused on the prototype design of the front-end readout Application Specific Integrated Circuit(ASIC) for the Muon detector(MUD) of the super t-charm facility(STCF) based on CMOS 130nm technology. The STCF is an electron-positron collider with a peak luminosity of no less than $0.5 \cdot 10^{35} \cdot \mathrm{cm}^{-2} \cdot \mathrm{s}^{-1}$. Therefore, the MUD, which located in the outmost part of the STCF detector system is composed of plastic scintillator and Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC). Through simulation of muon measurement reconstruction, it has been ascertained that the muon detector necessitates a spatial resolution of approximately 2 cm. Consequently, the dimensions of the plastic scintillator strip and the spacing between RPC readout strips are established at 4 cm. The RPC module reaches a maximum length of about 1.1 m, while the plastic scintillator strip extends up to 2.4 m. The plastic scintillator will be optically coupled to Silicon Photomultipliers(Si- PM) for signal detection. The prototype ASIC with 4-channel mainly accomplishes the functions of the charge collection, shaping, and discrimination for the Si-PM equipped with a plastic scintillator. This prototype ASIC provides variable gain, with a maximum value of 24mV/fC. The prototype ASIC’s input charge ranges from 2fC to 400fC and the pulse width is above 20 ns. The electronic system, consisting of the prototype ASIC and FPGA TDC will achieve a time resolution better than 100 ps and the event rate exceeding 100 kHz to meet the physical requirements of the MUD. Considering the output signal characteristics of the RPC, Modifications to the prototype ASIC could also potentially involve reading out the inner layer RPCs of the MUD.

articleTitle: Anatomically and Metabolically Informed Deep Learning Low-Count PET Image Denoising
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent progress in deep learning (DL) positron emission tomography (PET) image denoising has shown great potential for generating high-count images from low-count data, thus minimizing radiation exposure during imaging. However, DL models typically over-smooth images with details blurred, leading to quantification underestimation. In this study, we propose leveraging both organ and lesion priors obtained by auxiliary segmentation tools to make denoised images more anatomically and metabolically credible. Specifically, the DL training process is adjusted by semantic-weighted guidance. This approach forces class-wise alignment of standard uptake values and histogram distributions, and adaptively assigns weights to each semantic class. Experiments were performed on a dataset with 200 cases acquired by a Siemens Biograph mCT PET/CT system. Results showed that incorporating semantic information improved image quality and reduced the normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) on liver, lung, and lesion by 7.06%, 5.58%, and 1.21% on average, respectively, compared to the DL baseline without segmentation guidance.

articleTitle: Design and Construction of Thin-Gap GEM-uRWELL Hybrid and Cylindrical μ RWELL MPGD Prototypes for Tracking at the EIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Micro-Pattern Gas Detectors (MPGDs) offer the capability of providing space-point measurements for tracking and pattern recognition and momentum determination at the Electron Ion collider. These detectors are designed to cover a wide pseudorapidity range, encountering tracks at various incidence angles at the outer regions of the tracking volume. For tracks at large incidence angles relative to the normal, standard MPGD’s show deterioration in spatial resolution. The thingap MPGD (tg-MPGD) has a smaller gap between the ionization gas volume that the particle traverses before reaching the amplification stage allowing higher spatial resolution to be achieved for large track incidence angles. A mechanically stretched double-sided thin-gap GEM- $\mu$ RWELL hybrid detector and a cylindrical $\mu$ RWELL (C- $\mu$ RWELL) prototype have been designed as prospective next-generation MPGD detector improvements. The hybrid employs a structure with a 0.5 mm gap between gas volumes and purely mechanical stretching of GEM foils and drift foils, while the C- $\mu$ RWELL design features two independent half-cylindrical sections with a drift gap of 3 mm. To our knowledge this is a first adaptation of micro resistive-WELLs in either structural arrangement. Since for both prototypes, multiple Coulomb scattering of tracks should be minimized, the material budget for this tracking detector is critical. To minimize that, this detector implements drift, gain elements, and readout electrodes on thin foils resulting in total detector material of not more than $0.4 \%$ radiation lengths in the active area.

articleTitle: Development of a High-Resolution (< 1.5 mm) Brain PET with Diode-based Multiplexing Readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Most brain PET scanners consist of highly pixelated crystals to achieve high spatial resolution and employ multiple readout schemes to reduce the complexity and development costs of the readout circuits. The spatial resolution of commercial PETs still remains approximately 2-3 mm FWHM. Additionally, utilizing resistor-based multiplexing circuits causes noise increase and signal distortion, resulting in degradation of the detector performance, such as energy and time resolutions. In this study, we developed a brain PET achieving a high spatial resolution of less than 1.5 mm and utilizing a diode-based symmetric charge division circuits reducing the degradation of the detector performance.A high-resolution detector module was designed to utilize a 14 × 14 array LYSO size of 1.75 mm × 1.75 mm × 16 mm coupled to an 8 × 8 array SiPM size of 3 mm × 3 mm and a detector block consisted of a 2×2 matrix of detector modules. The PET consisted of 20 detector blocks with an inner diameter of 340 mm and axial length of 52.6 mm. Two hundred fifty-six output signals from each detector block were sent to four multiplexing circuits, which reduced the 64 SiPM signals to 16 output signals. The 1,280 signals from 20 detector blocks were transferred to ASIC-based readout electronics.All crystal pixels were clearly resolved in the flood histograms. Average energy resolution and coincidence timing resolution were 14.4±1.5% and 507 ps, respectively. Spatial resolution and sensitivity were 1.4 mm and 1.4% at the center field-of-view, respectively. The smallest rods were clearly resolved in a hot-rod phantom image, and activity distribution patterns between the white and gray matters in the Hoffman brain phantom were well imaged. Experimental results indicated that the PET proposed in this study could provide high spatial resolution with a modest compromise in time resolution by taking the advantage of the high resolution detector combined with the diode-based multiplexing circuit.

articleTitle: ARDESIA-64: a Novel High-Throughput SDD-based X-ray Spectroscopy Detector
