articleTitle: Diffusion Model-based Lu-177 Dose Rate Mapping From Single-Time-Point SPECT/CT Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate voxel-level dosimetry is crucial for assessing the effectiveness of Lu-177 PSMA therapy for prostate cancer. Current dosimetry practices based on the MIRD schema rely heavily on approximations, limiting their personalization and accuracy. Monte Carlo simulations provide high accuracy but are computationally expensive. This paper proposes a diffusion probabilistic model to predict dose rate maps from single-time-point SPECT/CT imaging. Our DPM operates by simulating a diffusion process of dose rate images and learning their distribution, resulting in accurate dose rate predictions. We compare our approach with a U-Net architecture, demonstrating the efficacy of diffusion models in improving dose estimation accuracy while handling grainy Monte Carlo simulations as targets. The proposed method offers a promising approach for achieving personalized and efficient dosimetry in Lu-177 PSMA therapy.

articleTitle: A Real-Time Embedded Digital Processing Architecture for a Modular Time-of-Flight Computed Tomography Readout Using PETsys TOFPET 2C ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-flight (TOF) in computed tomography (CT) can lead to an increase in image quality with no loss of sensitivity. To implement this approach a modular 256 channels time-of-flight CT using four PETsys TOFPET 2C ASICs is actively being developed. One of the challenges with this system is the quantity of raw data needed to produce the image. On a full-scale CT scanner with the current TOF limitations, up to 120 Tb/s can be generated. To solve this problem, a Zynq-based system on module is used to deserialize the data coming from the four ASICs, do real-time correction and computation of TOF and generate one histogram per channel in a dedicated dual port RAM. With the help of a custom device driver, the histogram data is read directly from the memory and is sent through an Ethernet link to a monitoring PC. The histograms generation and transmission has been tested using simulation data and has been able to handle a data rate superior to the TOFPET 2C ASIC maximum with no dead time for reading the histograms.

articleTitle: A Simulation Framework to Establish Ground Truth for Motion Correction in Total-Body PET: Initial Evaluation for Complex Respiratory Motion
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The enhanced sensitivity of total-body PET/CT scanners substantially decreases noise, however the full potential for spatio-temporal resolution is still hampered by artefacts and quantification degradation due to patient motion. To compensate for this, a variety of different motion correction methods were developed, but lack a motion free reference. To this end, our group developed a framework enabling Monte Carlo simulations of patient-like phantoms with motion modelling that accurately resembles event processing and image reconstruction of the Biograph Vision Quadra total-body PET/CT scanner. Simulations were performed with the XCAT phantom to mimic a clinical 5 min $\left[{ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}-\mathrm{FDG}\right]$ scan, with modelling of breathing motion with various breathing frequency/amplitude. To evaluate the impact of motion correction, an elastic motion deblurring approach, OncoFreeze AI, was used. Image quality, quantification of 5-20 mm lesions in lung and liver, and lesion line profiles were compared for a static (no motion) reference and for modelled motion with and without correction. Motion induced blurring in the images and could be compensated by the motion correction. The respiratory curve could be recovered by OncoFreeze AI with high precision (difference $\mathrm{Hz} \pm 0.5 \%$ over all motion segments). The motion correction helped to increase the recovery of the static activity concentration, e.g. for a 10 mm lung lesion: $9.4 \mathrm{kBq} / \mathrm{ml}$ (static no motion), $7 \mathrm{kBq} / \mathrm{ml}$ (motion) and $8.3 \mathrm{kBq} / \mathrm{ml}$ (motion corrected) and recovery of the lesion size 8.0 mm FWHM (static no motion) to 13.4 mm (motion) and 8.6 mm (motion corrected). This work underlines the need for motion correction and confirms the suitability of our framework to provide ground truth information on patient motion for total-body PET scans. Future work will extend this initial evaluation to more motion correction methods and a larger, more diverse data set with different scan durations, activities, and lesions.

articleTitle: Development of a Fast Detector for Associated Particle Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In an Associated Particle Imaging (API) neutron generator, a neutron and an alpha particle are emitted back-to-back and detecting the alpha inside the vacuum chamber will help reconstruct the trajectory of the neutron which, after escaping the chamber, can be used – for example - for tomography of a high-Z material. We are developing pixelated detectors able to accurately determine the hit position and time of the alpha particle. The first detector is based on a large area monolithic silicon sensor sitting in vacuum and read-out by an ASIC which is mounted onto a board external to the vacuum chamber. Signals from the ASICs are then processed by FPGAs placed on the same boards for timing and amplitude extraction. The second detector mounts the ASICs inside the vacuum of the neutron generator, to decrease the parasitic capacitance due to the long connections and therefore to increase the timing resolution of the system. This is a multifaceted activity which requires the development of many parts, including the silicon sensors, a vacuum-compatible assembly, a fast ASIC, a FPGA firmware among other aspects. At the conference, we will detail the status of each single part of the detector development.

articleTitle: 2.5D Multi-view Averaging Diffusion Model for 3D Medical Image Translation: Application to Low-count PET Reconstruction with CT-less AC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is an important clinical imaging tool but inevitably introduces radiation hazards to patients and healthcare providers. Reducing the tracer injection dose and eliminating the CT acquisition for attenuation correction can reduce the overall radiation dose, but often results in PET with high noise and bias. Thus, it is desirable to develop 3D methods to translate the non-attenuation-corrected low-dose PET (NAC-LDPET) into attenuation-corrected standard-dose PET (AC-SDPET). Recently, diffusion models have emerged as a new state-of-the-art deep learning method for image-to-image translation, better than traditional CNN-based methods. However, due to the high computation cost and memory burden, it is largely limited to 2 D applications. To address these challenges, we developed a novel 2.5D Multi-view Averaging Diffusion Model (MADM) for 3D image-to-image translation with application on NAC-LDPET to ACSDPET translation. Specifically, MADM employs separate diffusion models for axial, coronal, and sagittal views, whose outputs are averaged in each sampling step to ensure the 3D generation quality from multiple views. To accelerate the 3D sampling process, we also proposed a strategy to use the CNN-based 3D generation as a prior for the diffusion model. Our experimental results on human patient studies suggested that MADM can generate high-quality 3D translation images, outperforming previous CNN-based and Diffusion-based baseline methods.

articleTitle: Comparison of two new methods to measure the sensitivity of total-body and long-axial field-of-view PET scanners
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Several of the NEMA NU 2 standard measurements are not suitable for characterization of total-body or long-axial field-of-view (LAFOV) PET scanners ($\gt65 \mathrm{~cm}$ axial FOV), however there is no agreed upon standard for characterization of these recently developed PET scanners. This work outlines two suitable methods for sensitivity characterization of LAFOV PET scanners and provides a comparison to the NEMA NU 2 standard. The methods introduced here include using a point source stepped through the axial FOV and a 2-meter line source which fully characterize LAFOV PET sensitivity. We present here our evaluation of the methods’ suitability for LAFOV sensitivity assessment, the methods’ complexity and difficulty, and make a quantitative comparison between them. We discovered that the 2-meter line source sensitivity method provided a full characterization of the PET scanner sensitivity profile, and when interpolating to the central $70-\mathrm{cm}$ was within 0.4% agreement with the NEMA NU 2 method validating its accuracy. The point source method was the easiest to perform, however, it could not provide an absolute sensitivity measurement without cross-calibrating with a standard line source method. This cross-calibration procedure revealed a close (+1.2%) agreement with the 2-meter line source measurement indicating its suitability for LAFOV sensitivity assessment.

articleTitle: First validation of a trimodal imaging and therapy system: PET-FUS-MR
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Combining Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scanners with Magnetic Resonance (MR) and/or Focused Ultrasound (FUS) equipment has emerged as a leading approach in different medical areas. Such trimodal systems are not commercially available. Aiming to provide simultaneous PET-FUS-MRI imaging, we have designed, assembled, and validated a small-animal preclinical PET insert based on monolithic LYSO crystals of 33 25.4 8 mm<sup>3</sup>. The scanner has outer and inner diameters of 113 mm and 72 mm, respectively, and is compatible with both high-field MRI and commercial FUS systems. This work details the initial performance evaluation of the PET system, following the NEMA NU 4 2008 standards. We have found a spatial resolution of 0.98 ± 0.06 mm at ¼ of the axial Field of View (FOV), and a sensitivity at center of the scanner of 3.1% (30% energy window). The NECR peak is 92 kcps for an activity of 22200 kBq. Regarding image performance, the Recovery Coefficients (RCs) values measured for the Image Quality phantom, were 0.17, 0.38, 0.90, 1.08 and 1.04 for rods with diameters ranging from 1 mm to 5 mm, and Spill-Over-Ratios of 22.9% in water and 15.1% in air. In addition to this, we present for the first time, a simultaneous PET-MRI-FUS study. Using a costum FUS device, we heated a gelatin-filled phantom containing FDG in a specific area. Simultaneously with the heating process, different MR sequences were running with a low-field MRI, while PET data was acquired. As the gelatin melted, the FDG was distributed within the entire phantom volume. This dispersion was observed in the reconstructed PET-MRI images, thus validating our trimodal system.

articleTitle: A New Monolithic Pixel Sensor in a 65 nm CMOS Imaging Process
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This contribution will discuss the development of new monolithic active pixel sensors for future lepton colliders which are implemented in an only recently available 65 nm CMOS imaging process. The investigation of a new process, which is not meant to be used as a particle detector, requires detailed studies of basic charge collection properties for which a generic workflow for sensor simulations has been set up. It is built around detailed device simulations based on generic doping profiles which are combined with Monte Carlo simulations of charge deposition and collection to predict charge collection properties of different sensor geometries and designs. In parallel, three prototypes (MLR1, APTS and DESY ER1) have been designed and tested in laboratory and test beam campaigns. This contribution is going to summarise the simulation and testing efforts of the three different test chips. The simulation workflow is introduced and test beam results of APTS samples are compared to the results from simulation, showing good agreement. Additionally, a detailed transient simulation is compared to measurements. Finally, the revised design of a charge-sensitive amplifier-based chip (ER1) is introduced and laboratory characterizations are going to be shown alongside the first test beam results. It is concluded, that the investigated 65 nm CMOS process is well-suited for high energy physics applications.

articleTitle: Unsupervised Learning of Multi-modal Affine Registration for PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Affine registration plays a crucial role in PET/CT imaging, where aligning PET with CT images is challenging due to their respective functional and anatomical representations. Despite the significant promise shown by recent deep learning (DL)-based methods in various medical imaging applications, their application to multi-modal PET/CT affine registration remains relatively unexplored. This study investigates a DL-based approach for PET/CT affine registration. We introduce a novel method using Parzen windowing to approximate the correlation ratio, which acts as the image similarity measure for training DNNs in multi-modal registration. Additionally, we propose a multi-scale, instance-specific optimization scheme that iteratively refines the DNN-generated affine parameters across multiple image resolutions. Our method was evaluated against the widely used mutual information metric and a popular optimization-based technique from the ANTs package, using a large public FDG-PET/CT dataset with synthetic affine transformations. Our approach achieved a mean Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.870, outperforming the compared methods and demonstrating its effectiveness in multi-modal PET/CT image registration.

articleTitle: A 32-Channel Cryo-CMOS ASIC for SNSPD Biasing and Readout with Picosecond Timing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors (SNSPD) are a promising technology for particle detection. Although SNSPDs have demonstrated picosecond timing accuracy, scaling up large arrays has proved challenging. In this work, we introduce a 32-channel cryo-CMOS application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) that can be tightly integrated with SNSPD arrays. The ASIC is designed to operate at a temperature of 4K and can perform up to 32 simultaneous timing measurements with a root-mean-square (RMS) accuracy of 8.0ps. The ASIC includes on-chip circuitry for externally biasing superconducting devices, low-noise amplifiers for reading superconducting devices, high-resolution time-to-digital converters (TDC) for time-tagging events, and serializers for transmitting data to room-temperature electronics. The ASIC is manufactured in a 22nm FDSOI process and occupies an area of $4.0 \mathrm{~mm} \times 1.0 \mathrm{~mm}$. The performance of the ASIC was verified using custom cryogenic device models internally developed for the 22nm SOI process. Measurement results will be presented at the conference.

articleTitle: Accurate Replication of a Gamma Decay Cascade Using Mechanical Adjustable Arm
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes an experimental system that adjusts the positions of two gamma sources in a manner such that the observed activities with a gamma detector are similar to those of a decaying series, also known as a parent-daughter decay. Two sets of 1-meter-long mechanical arms were used to control the source-detector distances with a precision of ${\lt}1 \mathrm{~mm}$. The mechanical arms are given 1-second interval instructions to create an accurate non-linear motion. Recordings are performed with a digital acquisition system to collect list-mode data streams containing relevant timing information. Decay chains with half-lives of as low as 5 seconds were accurately replicated, measured, and analyzed. This experimental system allows for the observation of highly dynamic radioactive effects in a manner that does not require the possession of an irradiation or chemical separation system, and it is flexible in accurately replicating a wide range of parent-daughter scenarios.licating a wide range of parent-daughter scenarios.

articleTitle: Ultrafast High Light Yield Spectroscopic Scintillators Based on a Rugged Semiconductor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Despite extensive research into scintillator materials, the quest for an ideal scintillator combining ultrafast decay times (akin to BaF<inf>2</inf> and Yb -doped scintillators such as $\mathrm{Lu}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}: \mathrm{Yb}$), high light yields (exceeding 2000 photons per MeV), spectroscopic capabilities, and exceptional radiation hardness remains unfulfilled. Achieving these features within a single scintillator could dramatically improve many applications. Our research has explored various wide band gap semiconductor-based scintillators, including doped Lutetium oxide, Yttrium oxide, and Gallium oxide. This presentation will focus on a groundbreaking gallium oxide-based scintillator that embodies all these critical attributes, showcasing light yields up to 8 k photons per MeV and decay times as fast as 2 nanoseconds. To test the radiation hardness of the scintillators, we subjected twenty-six scintillators made from the grown $\beta-\mathrm{Ga}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{3}$ crystals to a ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ gamma irradiation rate of $14 \mathrm{krad} / \mathrm{h}$, with a total radiation dose of 2 Mrad, and found that their scintillation properties remained unchanged. These cost-effective, robust, and high-density scintillators hold the promise of superseding current technologies in diverse fields such as physics research and nuclear security.

articleTitle: Comparative Study of Convolutional Neural Network and Particle Smoother-Based Expectation Maximization for Estimation of 82Rb Myocardial Perfusion PET Kinetic Parameters

articleTitle: Experimental evaluation of rigid patient motion detection and correction in SPECT with exponential data consistency conditions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Rigid patient motion may cause artifacts in the reconstructed SPECT images. This study evaluated a fully data-driven method exploiting exponential data consistency conditions (eDCCs) -equations describing redundancies in SPECT measurements - to estimate and correct for rigid patient motion on experimental data. We minimized the pairwise inconsistency of projections with a noiseaware metric implementing eDCCs. The method led to a significant improvement in image quality. For instance, for a 20 mm motion in the middle of the acquisition in the axial or vertical directions, the activity recovery coefficient (ARC) for the biggest sphere (37 mm diameter) of the NEMA IEC phantom was improved from 0.41 (non-corrected projections) to 0.58 (motion-corrected projections), i.e. the same ARC as the one obtained with reference motion-free projections.

articleTitle: Comparison of crystal quality and two-dimensional carrier transport properties in TlBr crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thallium bromide (TlBr) is being developed as a semiconductor detector material that can operate at room temperature with high detection efficiency and energy resolution. To fabricate high-quality and large-size detectors, it is necessary to grow crystals with uniform charge transport properties. We have previously evaluated the crystal quality of TlBr using neutron Bragg dip imaging and electron beam backscatter diffraction (EBSD). In this study, we fabricated a detector using the sample for which crystal quality evaluation was performed. We also evaluated the carrier transport property by using a time-of-flight method of the carriers induced by pulsed laser irradiation. By scanning the laser irradiating position, the two-dimensional distribution of transport properties was measured. Although the crystal orientation of the samples was slightly distorted, no clear difference in electron mobility was observed within the fabricated detector. In a future work, we will prepare several samples and compare their orientation distributions and charge transport property distributions.

articleTitle: Evaluation of a 3D Position Sensitive Time-of-flight PET Detector Unit with CPLD-based Frontend Electronics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces and evaluates a stackable side-readout detector unit with second-generation frontend electronics for near 100 ps CTR Time-of-Flight 3D Position Sensitive (TOF-3DPS) detectors. This design utilizes a timing signal multiplexing scheme based on RF amplifiers and summing circuits to achieve 24:1 timing multiplexing and employs complex programmable logic devices (CPLDs) to facilitate high-precision energy measurement, and photon depth of interaction (DOI) positioning for single and multi-interaction inter-crystal scatter (ICS) events across different crystal elements within a detector unit. Experimental results with a single layer sub-unit comprising a $4 \times 2$ array of $3 \times 3 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ LYSO:Ce crystals side-coupled with a $4 \times 6$ array of $3.16 \times 3.16 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPMs yielded a 9.88 ± 0.86% energy resolution and a Coincidence Timing Resolution (CTR) of $121.28 \pm 3.35$ ps FWHM. Electrical collimation measurements performed at different positions along the 10 mm length of one crystal element produced a $1.44 \pm 0.44 \mathrm{~mm}$ FWHM DOI resolution. Additionally, electronic collimation of different columns in a detector unit revealed ICS event ratios for scatter to adjacent columns from the collimated column of 6.90%, 10.46%, 10.85%, and 5.33%, respectively. The side-readout detector layer sub-unit and the corresponding frontend circuitry have a footprint of only $27 \mathrm{~mm} \times 95 \mathrm{~mm}$, making it easy to stack and form a multi-layer TOF-3DPS block detector.

articleTitle: Overlaying Feature Lines on Volume Rendering for Improving Structure Perception
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray CT scanning is a nondestructive measurement technology, and is used in a variety of situations ranging from medical care to manufacturing. The CT volume is a three-dimensional array of voxels with CT values. Volume rendering is a method of visualizing a CT volume by projecting the voxel set onto a two-dimensional display. It can display an object transparently by specifying the color and transparency for each CT value, thus it can color-code each material of the object. However, because the internal structure of the display is layered, it is difficult to intuitively grasp the shape and depth of the object. We purpose to improve the visibility of the volume rendering by generating and displaying feature lines that represent the shape of the object on the volume rendering and changing the color and thickness of the lines. Using a CT volume as input, the shape index which is derived from the gradient of the CT values is used to detect feature points. Next, feature lines are generated by connecting the feature points along the directions they spread. Finally, the colors or/and thickness of the feature lines are varied to improve the visibility of the volume rendering. We conducted a questionnaire survey to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. It showed that changing the color and thickness most improved the visibility of the volume rendering among the other variations. However, currently, there are still over/under detection of feature lines due to complexity of the object or discretization error in CT volumes. In the future, we will focus on such problems, evaluate the accuracy of the detected feature points and propose more efficient visualization of feature lines.

articleTitle: DIANA - Detectability Investgations using Artificial Nodal Additions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) imaging often encounters challenges in quantifying lesion detectability and contrast recovery due to the absence of known in vivo ground truths. To address this, we introduce DIANA (Detectability Investigations using Artificial Nodal Additions), a Monte Carlo-based tool designed to improve lesion detectability analysis. DIANA permits the insertion of artificial lesions into human subject list-mode data with precise activity concentrations, thereby enabling a detailed assessment of image quality metrics. In this study, we demonstrated DIANA by analyzing the influence of image smoothing and the number of iterations on image contrast and the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) in PET scans. The tool was tested using data from the uEXPLORER total-body PET/CT scanner, with artificial lesions between 4 mm and 8 mm in diameter introduced into the scans of a 73-year-old female. Images were reconstructed using an in-house OSEM algorithm, and lesion detectability was quantified through the lesion-to-background ratio (LBR) and the contrast recovery coefficient (CRC) across different count densities and frame lengths. Results demonstrated a dependency of CRC on frame length and lesion size, with notable degradation at shorter frame lengths. The study also explored the effects of Gaussian smoothing on contrast to noise ratio (CNR), highlighting the expected trade-off between lesion visibility and image noise. Overall, DIANA proved effective in validating PET imaging techniques and enhancing the quantitative accuracy of lesion detectability, paving the way for further applications in varied clinical scenarios and dynamic imaging. Future work will extend the utility of DIANA by incorporating patient motion and diverse body mass indices to reflect more realistic clinical conditions.

articleTitle: Impact of DL HYPR4D Kernel Method on Detection of Task-Induced Neurotransmitter Release
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We describe an investigation on the impact of the recently proposed deep learning (DL) assisted HYPR4D kernel method (DL HYPR4D-K) on detection of task-induced neurotransmitter release which is highly sensitive to the 4D PET image quality. Human $\left[{ }^{11} \mathrm{C}\right]$ RAC data (a subject with Parkinson’s Disease) with $\sim 15 \mathrm{mCi}$ bolus injection were acquired on GE SIGNA PET/MR for 71 mins. A finger tapping task was introduced at 36 mins post injection. The acquired dynamic data were reconstructed using standard HYPR4D kernel method and DL HYPR4D kernel method. IHYPR4D post processing was applied to the images reconstructed with standard HYPR4D kernel method to further reduce noise (i.e. HYPR4D-K + IHYPR4D). A recently proposed Residual Space Detection (RSD) method was applied to the images reconstructed with DL HYPR4D-K and HYPR4D-K + IHYPR4D to produce neurotransmitter release maps as well as histograms of release amplitudes. Simulations were also performed to see if the trend observed from human data agrees with simulated results. It was observed that better preservation of release amplitude (~ 60%) can be achieved by the DL HYPR4D-K as compared to HYPR4D-K + IHYPR4D, and this resulted in additional detection of voxels likely with release. In addition, DL HYPR4D-K enables detections of smaller clusters of release and clusters with lower release amplitudes compared to HYPR4D-K + IHYPR4D.

articleTitle: Solution-Processable Perovskite-based Flat Panel Imagers (PEROXITM) for Direct X-ray Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray radiography via flat panel X-ray imagers (FPXIs) is widely used in the medical and industrial fields for non-destructive evaluation and testing. Though scintillator-based indirect FPXIs currently dominate the market for higher X-ray energies, they suffer from poor spatial resolution due to the optical cross-talk between the pixels of the coupled photodetector arrays. On the other hand, highly sensitive semiconductor-based FPXIs that directly convert X-ray photons to charge carriers are capable of yielding radiographs with high spatial resolution. Nevertheless, the only commercial direct imager that is integrable with large-area active pixel array (APA) backplanes, amorphous selenium (a-Se), is limited to low X-ray energy (${\lt}30 \mathrm{keV}$) applications (e.g. mammography) due to its poor charge carrier transport properties and its low stopping power to high-energy X-rays. Compared to a-Se, solution-processable polycrystalline metal halide perovskites (MHPs) such as methylammonium lead iodide (MAPI) have higher X-ray attenuation coefficients, larger mobility-lifetime ($\mu \tau$) products, greater defect tolerance, and are more sensitive to high-energy X-rays. Still, a common issue of high background noise and large leakage from perovskite-based FPXIs has resulted in radiographs with inferior contrast and poor spatial resolution. Using a vertically integrated approach, we have systemically optimized MAPI perovskite-based FPXIs (PEROXI ${ }^{\mathrm{TM}}$) to realize radiographs with better contrast, high spatial resolution, and long-term environmental stability. The PEROXI ${ }^{\text {TM }}$ that have been developed will help to pave the way for the next generation of low-cost, low-dose, high-efficiency commercial FPXIs.

articleTitle: Image-Derived Input Functions on an Ultra-High Performance Brain PET Scanner: Minimizing the Carotid Partial Volume Effect
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Image-derived input functions (IDIF) are non-invasive alternatives to arterial blood sampling for PET kinetic modeling. However, partial volume effects (PVE) limit their applicability in brain PET. The NeuroEXPLORER (NX), a next-generation PET scanner with unprecedented sensitivity and spatial resolution, may allow for better IDIF extraction from carotid arteries. Six studies were performed on the NX (three tracers: ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG, ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-SynVesT-1, ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}$-PHNO). Arterial input functions (AIF) were acquired. Standard motion correction (MC) and MC based on a markerless motion-tracking system (UMT) were compared. Common carotid (CC) and internal carotid (IC) arteries were manually segmented on an early summed image. Region centerlines were generated, and dilated to 1-6 mm diameter to evaluate PVE. Percent IDIF-to-AIF area under the curve bias was calculated at different time intervals to estimate IDIF ability to recover whole-blood AIF. Using AIF and IDIF, kinetic modeling was applied to brain regions to estimate tracer uptake/binding ($K_{\mathrm{i}}$ for ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG, $V_{\mathrm{T}}$ for ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-SynVesT-1 and ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}$-PHNO) and inflow $\left(K_{1}\right)$. The percent bias of IDIF-to-AIF-based estimates was calculated. Using this simple segmentation approach, good recovery of AIF AUC was obtained for small centerline diameters (% bias < 5-10% for 1-2 mm). Kinetic parameter bias was very small for FDG $K_{\mathrm{i}}$ (% bias < 5%) and larger for ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-SynVesT-1 and ${ }^{11} \mathrm{C}$-PHNO $V_{\mathrm{T}}$. UMT MC provided lower bias. Overall, the usually challenging IC artery was equivalent or superior to CC. These results highlight how the NX helps minimize PVE in IDIF extraction.

articleTitle: Development of Multi-Chain Tapped-delay Line Based TDC Using Down Sampling Method for Minimizing FPGA Resources
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multi-chain tapped delay line (TDL) architecture has been widely employed in FPGA-based Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) to minimize the bubble errors and to improve the linearity of TDC. However, this structure requires a large FPGA resource usage causing high cost. The purpose of this study was to develop multi-chain TDL based TDC using down sampling that can minimize the FPGA resource usage while maintaining the performance of the TDC. The proposed TDC was composed of multi-chain TDL using down sampling, flip-flops, encoders and calibration look up table (LUT). Multi-chain TDL with three lines was designed to improve the precision of the TDC and each TDL was cascaded using CARRY8 logics which had two kinds of output logic (OUT and COUT) with down sampling. Down sampling method alternately selecting OUT and COUT was implemented to reduce FPGA resource usage. The encoder was converted to the corresponding calibrated fine time by the LUT. The fine time was combined with the coarse time which was generated by a counter running at the system clock to produce the final timestamp. Multi-chain TDL based TDCs were implemented on the UltraScale+ FPGA and 8 cases were designed to optimize the down sampling pattern. DNL, INL and RMS precision were measured to evaluate the performance of the proposed TDC and compared to those measured using the multi-chain TDL based TDC without down sampling. The best result was obtained in the CASE5(O-O-C) and DNL, INL and RMS precision measured using the CASE5 were decreased by 5%, 4% and 5%, respectively, however, FPGA resource usage was improved by 47% compared to that of the TDC without down sampling. The results indicated that multi-chain TDL based TDC using down sampling developed in this study could effectively minimize the FPGA resource usage with the modest compromise of the TDC performance. Multi-channel expansion and performance evaluation of the TDCs are currently in progress.

articleTitle: A Shielding Free PET Insert for High Sensitivity PET/MRI of the Brain
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work outlines MRI compatibility tests of a shielding free PET insert for high sensitivity, cost effective PET/MRI imaging of the brain. The MRI compatibility of silicon photomultiplier based PET detectors, originally developed for an organ targeted PET camera, was explored through MRI and PET performance. To analyze the effect of passive and active PET modules on MRI performance, T1-weighted gradient echo images and B1 maps were acquired. The effect of passive and active MRI on PET performance was evaluated using, crystal maps, energy spectra, and images of a 22-Na point source. The average mean squared error between central slice B1 maps with and without passive PET detectors was 0.003 and the structural similarity index was 0.975. For the active PET experiment, these values were 0.054 and 0.891, respectively. There was no significant change in coefficient of variation of B1 intensity due to the active state of PET detectors. The PET crystal map results showed that the spatial distribution of events was not affected by the passive B0 field of the MRI or a simultaneous MRI acquisition. The same result was found for the peak position and full width at half maximum of the energy spectra in PET data. No difference was observed between trials in the reconstructed images of a 22 Na point source. Despite the lack of shielding, the MRI compatibility of Radialis PET detectors was supported by our results, suggesting they will be usable in the proposed PET insert for high sensitivity PET/MRI of the brain.

articleTitle: Learned Primal Dual Reconstruction with Dual-Domain Transformers for PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is a prominent technique for studying metabolic activity and is commonly used for cancer diagnosis. The presence of noise affects the measurements severely, resulting in the need for specialized reconstruction algorithms. By employing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), the Learned Primal Dual (LPD) algorithm has achieved impressive results for image reconstruction. The nonlocal nature of the sinogram domain could imply that CNNs are ill-suited for use. In light of this, we propose a transformer-based architecture for solving the reconstruction problem. Additionally, we present a synthetic data generation process designed to mimic features of a preclinical system. Our results show that the proposed architecture outperforms the CNN based model on all reported figures of merit. Furthermore, the reconstruction quality on unseen data from a preclinical system is higher for the transformer architecture than the CNN based model. The results indicate impressive transfer learning from system specific synthetic data to the preclinical data.

articleTitle: OrdinalNet: A Deep Learning-based Relative Image Quality Metric for Motion Compensation in CBCT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Interventional C-arm cone beam CT significantly reduces time-to-therapy for patients suffering from acute stroke. Extended acquisition times as compared to modern helical CT systems make rigid patient motion more likely, introducing a mismatch with the geometry alignment presupposed during reconstruction, leading to typical blurring or streaking artifacts. Different autofocus methods exist which aim to find a compensation trajectory and reestablish a motion-free reconstruction by optimizing a quality metric on the reconstructed images. However, depending on the type of implemented metric, these methods show diminished performance for larger motion amplitudes, often converging into local minima. To overcome these drawbacks, we present OrdinalNet, a deep learning model predicting a pseudo-binary score to assess motion artifact deterioration or improvement between two reconstructions resulting from slightly different motion trajectories. Our method eliminates the necessity for absolute artifact quantification in each image, along with establishing a relative ordering among data points which is sufficient for effective simplex-based optimization. The model is trained and evaluated on simulated motion applied to motion-free clinical acquisitions. When presented 1000 motion-affected pairs from previously unseen patients, it shows superior performance on a threshold-dependent binary classification task when compared to an entropy-based metric, resulting in areas under the curve of $\mathrm{AUC}_{\text {ONet }}=0.9295$ and $\mathrm{AUC}_{\mathrm{Ent}}=0.6366$

articleTitle: A 64-channel, 80 e-(rms), 10.5 Mcps, Energy-Resolving Photon-Counting Readout ASIC in 130-nm Technology for Silicon X-ray Imaging Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A silicon-strip detector is a good candidate for energy-resolving photon-counting detectors in next-generation computed tomography (CT) imaging scanners with an energy range of 2 to 140 keV. A full-customized multichannel readout application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) is required to read out the detector signals and generate the photon count with energy classification. The challenges of such an ASIC lie in low-noise analog front-ends to meet the energy detection limitation of less than 2 keV, as well as a high-performance multi-energy discriminator-counter circuit to achieve a count rate larger than 10 Mcps. In this paper, we propose a novel multichannel energy-resolving photon-counting readout ASIC in 130-nm technology for such application. The first prototype ASIC includes 64 readout channels, 2 testing channels, peripheral blocks, and a global digital part. Eight energy bins are implemented by employing eight comparators and counters in each channel. The die size is 4.3 mm × 3.5 mm. The simulated results are listed below. The input dynamic range is 0.08 fC ~ 7 fC. The best equivalent noise charge of the analog front end is 79 e- (rms) plus 22 e-/pF under the power dissipation of about 2.5 mW/channel. The count rate is up to 10.5 Mcps. The inconsistency between channels is less than 4 %. The chip has been submitted for fabrication. The samples will come back in June. For future work, the overall performance of the prototype chip will be evaluated and a 192-channel ASIC will be developed.

articleTitle: Scatter correction based on time-of-flight measurements for radiography and photon counting CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-flight (ToF) CT and radiography are explored as a novel method for scatter estimation and correction for state-of-the-art medical X-ray imaging with increased sensitivity. By measuring the ToF of X photons from the source to the detector, the scattered contribution can be estimated in each pixel individually, owing to the longer paths taken by scattered X photons. While an entire scan can be made this way, there is some concern about the duration of the acquisition since measuring ToF requires a pulsed X-ray source with a very low duty cycle (1-5%). As an alternative, this paper explores the use of ToF-CT to correct for scatter contribution in a regular photon counting projection image. It is validated at different timing resolutions and for different ToF scan durations using Monte Carlo simulations performed with GATE. The results show that with a 10 ps FWHM timing resolution, the method is capable of accurately estimating and correcting for $98 \%$ of the scatter while keeping a sensitivity to primary photons over $98 \%$ in photon counting mode. Between 50 and 150 ps, the scatter correction performance is comparable to an anti-scatter grid’s, but without any loss in sensitivity.

articleTitle: Development of a HEXITEC-based Compton Camera for Spatially Resolved Dose Deposition Studies in Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates the feasibility of utilising HEXITEC (High Energy X-ray Imaging Technology) detectors as the fundamental component of a compact and lightweight Compton camera, with potential applications in Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT). BNCT, an emerging radiation treatment modality, holds promise for targeting cancer cells through boron-enriched agents interacting with an epithermal neutron beam. Leveraging Geant4 simulations, we explore the implementation of HEXITEC detectors for both layers of the Compton camera, harnessing their inherent advantages in energy and spatial resolution. Through the optimisation of detector parameters such as scatterer and absorber thicknesses, optimal values of 15 mm for the scatterer and maximum achievable thickness for the absorber were determined. By employing a Stochastic Origin Ensemble (SOE) algorithm for image reconstruction, even preliminary geometries yield promising results, demonstrating the ability to reconstruct point and volumetric sources. Experimental validation, including comparative analyses with commercial detectors, provide further insights into the efficacy and applicability of the proposed Compton camera system. Additionally, efforts are made to establish a quantitative relationship between gamma counts in the reconstructed image and boron concentration within the patient, advancing our understanding of BNCT dosimetry.

articleTitle: Detector Performance Results on Prototypes of 65nm CMOS Stitched Sensor Structures for ALICE ITS3
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The ALICE collaboration is currently developing a new vertex detector (“ITS3”), foreseen to be installed in 2026 - 2028 during LHC long shutdown 3 to replace the three innermost layers (Inner Barrel) of the current Inner Tracking System as from Run 4 onwards. ITS3 comprises the use of ultra-thin (down to $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$) silicon wafers and stitching technologies in 65nm CMOS imaging process to produce large area ($9.8 \mathrm{~cm} \times 26.7 \mathrm{~cm}$) Monolithic Active Pixels Sensors sensors which will be bent to half-cylindrical shapes of $19,25.2$ and 31.5 mm bending radii for layer 0, 1 and 2 respectively, and kept in place using slices of carbon foam. The very low power consumption of about $40 \mathrm{mV} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ allows for air cooling, thus no further mechanical and electrical support structures are required. The very low material budget of less than 0.07% of a radiation length per layer provides extremely good tracking and vertexing capabilities.Within the comprehensive R&D program for the ITS3 different large area stitched prototype structures with various pixel pitch and matrix sizes have been produced and are tested before and after irradiation with TID and NIEL to validate the ITS3 technology approachIn this contribution we present an overview on detection performance measurements obtained for such prototypes in test beams using various chip settings.

articleTitle: Progress report on PETSIRD: a standard for PET raw data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The recent advancement of data science methods in emission tomography (ET) has highlighted the need for standardization in the access, use, and sharing of the unprocessed raw list-mode acquisition data to exploit their high fidelity spatio-temporal information before the production of the respective DICOM images. The Emission Tomography Standardization Initiative (ETSI) was founded in 2022 from an international consortium of academic and industry experts to define open, extendable, and vendor-agnostic ET data formats. ETSI is now focusing on the development of the PETSIRD (“PET Emission Tomography Standardization Initiative’s Raw Data”) prototype: an open standard format for Positron Emission Tomography (PET) list-mode raw data. The components of PETSIRD are (i) its data elements (coincidence events, geometry, correction factors, physiological signal etc.), (ii) a container of the data elements architecture and its access protocols built with the investigational prototype YARDL (Microsoft Research) meta-language, and (iii) a use-cases software toolkit facilitating the basic utility of the standard.In this contribution, we provide a status report of the initiative. Results will be shown of the first ETSI hackathon held in November 2023 as well as progress made on the definition of PETSIRD prototype since then. Up-to-date information can be found on our website https://etsinitiative.org/.

articleTitle: Evaluation of High-Z Sensors for Synchrotron Sources and FELs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High-Z compound semiconductors aim to replace silicon as sensor material for X-ray energies above 15 keV thanks to their superior absorption efficiency. Compared to silicon, high-Z sensors are still lacking in several aspects such as response uniformity, charge transport properties, charge trapping (leading to polarization and afterglow effects), long ranged fluorescence photons, and others. The aim of this study is to identify sensor materials that can widen the usable energy range of our detector systems at synchrotron sources and free electron lasers (FELs) towards higher photon energies using the charge integrating $75 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pitch JUNGFRAU detector with various high-Z sensors (GaAs:Cr, Ohmic/Schottky type CdTe and CdZnTe). As charge integrating detectors allow the direct measurement of the collected charge of every single photon with a high spatial resolution, these detectors offer interesting insights into temporal as well as spatial sensor effects which affect the charge collection. One of the major challenges of current light sources, such as diffraction limited light sources or free electron lasers, are very intense photon beams or photon pulses, that require a prompt linear sensor response which ideally shows no signal afterglow. Over the last years, an extensive measurement campaign has been performed at the Material Science (MS) beamline of the SLS using photon fluxes up to $5 \times 10^{10} \mathrm{ph} /\left(\mathrm{mm}^{2} \cdot \mathrm{s}\right)$. Additionally, pulsed signals have lately been investigated at free electron lasers, namely SwissFEL (Switzerland) and EuXFEL (Germany), mainly focused on understanding the dynamic behavior (like signal stability, polarization and afterglow effects). New sources of chromium-compensated GaAs sensors have emerged, which allow the production of full scale detector modules of $8 x 4 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$. The presentation will show the results from the evaluation of the novel GaAs:Cr sensors and put them in perspective with high-flux CdZnTe from Redlen.

articleTitle: Tumour Margin Thickness Inference for 99mTc Radioguided Surgery Using Internal Conversion Electrons
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In radioguided surgery (RGS), a cancer-targeting drug labelled with a radioactive isotope, such as ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$, can be detected using an intraoperative probe to locate cancerous tissue. In this study, the feasibility for tumour thickness and depth inference using a 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) was explored for tumour margin evaluation. Training data were experimentally collected with ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$ sources of different thicknesses and depths using a CMOS intraoperative probe optimised towards the detection of internal conversion (IC) electrons. For thicknesses between $500 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and $1250 \mu \mathrm{m}$, the network trained for thickness inference was able to achieve a root mean square error (RMSE) of approximately $90 \mu \mathrm{m}$. For a depths up to approximately 20 mm, networks trained to infer depth thresholds were able to achieve an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) score of above 0.7. Overall, the proposed methods were able to infer source characteristics that may be valuable for intraoperative tumour margin evaluation using ${ }^{99 \mathrm{~m}} \mathrm{Tc}$ RGS. Future work may focus on evaluating the proposed methods with data that reflects clinical conditions by using more realistic radiotracer distributions.

articleTitle: Characterization of Stilbene scintillator for neutron metrology and spectrometry from 100 keV to 22 MeV
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thanks to new crystal growth method, pure stilbene scintillators can now detect neutrons from 100 keV. For neutron metrology purposes, two 2”x2” stilbene scintillators were characterized as secondary reference detectors for neutron field measurements in the energy range from 100 keV to 22 MeV. Photon sources were used to determine the electron calibration and resolution. Calibration was performed using the “second derivative” method to determine the Compton edges, assimilated to the inflection point. Resolution function was determined using adjustments at each Compton edge between a broadened MCNP simulation and the measurement. For neutron characterization, due to the anisotropic response, only a full experimental characterisation is possible for now. The neutron response function in the energy range of scintillators was determined using a white neutron spectrum and the Time-of-Flight technique. Reference neutron fluence measurements were used to adjust the scintillator fluence response at calibration point. This method leads to a complete characterization of these scintillators for neutrons field from 100 keV up to 22 MeV.

articleTitle: Design and Simulations of a Collimator for SPECT Measurements in a BNCT Facility
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents the development of a new collimator design for a BNCT-SPECT system, tailored to overcome limitations that could be encountered in a BNCT clinical facility. BNCT-SPECT systems aim to quantify and localize the dose administered to a patient during Boron Neutron Capture Therapy (BNCT) by detecting the 478 keV gamma rays emitted from ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}(\mathrm{n}, \alpha)^{7}$ Li reactions. The presence of boron also inside the irradiation room walls in most of the clinical BNCT facilities, brought us to reconsider a collimator already designed ad hoc to fullfill all the requirements of this treatment. Helped by FLUKA simulations, we define the main drawbacks of our current system in a clinical scenario, and propose a new configuration to overcome this limitations. We report the specifics of the new design, highlighting the capability to distinguish a boron source from the background radiation over 10 ppm concentration.

articleTitle: Improving Brain SPECT Image Quality Using Noise2Void
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is a vital medical imaging modality for evaluating various physiological functions. However, in SPECT, there exists a trade-off relationship between spatial resolution and detection efficiency: as spatial resolution improves, detection efficiency decreases, leading to an increase of noise within images. This study aims to improve the image quality of brain SPECT images using Noise2Void (N2V), a denoising method based on self-supervised learning, which can denoise only a noisy target image. We evaluated the effectiveness of N2V in improving image quality using both simulated data obtained from a numerical brain phantom and actual data acquired by imaging a physical brain phantom with a high-resolution SPECT device under development. We denoised projection images using a N2V network trained on 180-directional projection images and reconstructed images from the denoised projection images using the ordered subset expectation maximization (OS-EM) algorithm. Additionally, we compared the reconstructed images processed with N2V to those processed with a similar method, deep image prior (DIP). In the reconstructed images of the numerical brain phantom obtained through simulation, noise was reduced while preserving edges, resulting in a significant improvement in peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) from 6.69 dB to 20.04 dB and structural similarity (SSIM) from 0.443 to 0.836. The PSNR of the reconstructed images processed with DIP was 18.96 dB, and the SSIM was 0.734. Moreover, in the reconstructed images of the brain physical phantom acquired by our high-resolution SPECT device, noise was significantly reduced, and the phantom structure was clearly depicted. These results suggested that N2V effectively reduces noise in SPECT images and improves image quality. Furthermore, compared to DIP, N2V was indicated to have equivalent or superior performance.

articleTitle: Short Acquisition Optimisation for Deep Learned Dual-Tracer PET Image Separation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multiplexed positron emission tomography (mPET) imaging can simultaneously observe multiple targets of interest using different tracers in a single scan. Separation of mPET signals within a single PET scan is challenging due to the fact that each tracer gives rise to indistinguishable 511 keV photon pairs, and thus no unique energy information for differentiating the source of each photon pair. The majority of separation methods in mPET imaging primarily focus on dynamic mPET images for separation due to the assistance provided by the differing tracer dynamics. Short-duration static imaging is more routinely used in diagnosis and treatment monitoring due to its convenience and relative simplicity compared to dynamic imaging. Separating static mPET images, however, is more challenging than dynamic ones as the separation process relies solely on spatial information. Nonetheless, PET list-mode acquisition during a regular “static PET” protocol allows for flexibility in dynamic time framing prior to reconstruction. This motivates us to consider separating single-tracer images from multiplexed data arising from a standard “static” data acquisition interval by using dynamic framing of the data. Given a target static window for single tracer scan information, in this work, we investigate the best mPET acquisition start time Δa for a fixed delay time Δf before injecting 2nd tracer, for best prediction of single tracer separation in target window. We propose an adapted version of a kinetic model-informed deep network (KM-net) which allows investigation of the impact of Δa. The results showed that for Δt = 15 mins, using the entire mPET dynamic data (Δa = 0 mins) for separation achieves better performance compared to Δa = 15 min (simultaneous dual-tracer information only) and Δa = 25 mins (target window information only). Future work will focus on investigating the impact of Δt and the separation performance at the ROI level.

articleTitle: A high-brightness low energy positive muon beam for future precision muon-based experiments
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The muCool project aims at developing a novel device that reduces the phase space of a standard low energy positive muon beam, $\mu+(\mathrm{E} \sim$ few MeV), by a factor of ten orders of magnitude with $\mathrm{O}\left(10^{-4}\right)$ efficiency. The phase space compression is achieved by stopping a standard $\mu+$ beam in cryogenic helium gas. The stopped $\mu+$ are manipulated into a small spot using complex electric and magnetic fields in combination with gas density gradients. The muons are extracted from there into the vacuum and in a field-free region. Various aspects of this compression scheme have been demonstrated. They include the proof of the longitudinal and transversal compression, obtained first in two stages. The combination of the measured longitudinal and transversal compression stages corresponds to a phase space compression factor of $10^{10}$ with an efficiency of $10^{-3}$, as predicted. We will present the achieved results, where the combination of the transverse and longitudinal compression has been obtained, and measured using scintillators coupled to siliconphotomultipliers. We will discuss the next steps focused on studying the extraction and reacceleration scheme. The integration of such a cooling scheme into the incoming High-Intensity Muon Beam Lines at PSI, aiming at delivering up to $10^{10}$ muons/s will represent a major milestone for future precision experiments based on muons.

articleTitle: Energy Characteristics for High-Sensitivity Fiber Optic Radiation Monitor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fiber optic radiation monitors allow detection points to be located in high temperature and high dose rate environments; thus, they are particularly suitable as dosimeters for monitoring nuclear environments since the optical measurement system can be placed several hundred meters away from hazardous areas. However, a reduction in the variation of the energy characteristic is required to comply with IEC 60532. In this study, we used a numerical simulation to investigate a method that reduces variation of the energy characteristics and we evaluated a prototype fiber optic radiation monitor based on the investigation results. We found the prototype monitor can selectively detect an energy range by placing two metal housings of different densities outside the scintillators and it can reduce the variation of the energy characteristics by adding both sets of counts for the two housings. From an irradiation test done at the standard calibration site of the National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, we demonstrated the relative sensitivity of the high-sensitivity fiber optic radiation monitor ranged from -16% to +28% and that was within the target range of -25% to +40%.

articleTitle: Theoretically and Experimentally Driven Noise Model for X-ray Fluoroscopic Image Synthesis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fluoroscopic and digital angiography (DA) images are both acquired during x-ray image guided interventions. Fluoroscopic images are acquired at lower radiation dose and therefore have higher image noise. The purpose of this work is to develop a method for fluoroscopic image synthesis from DA images. The developed noise model leverages measured system parameters to determine a mapping from DA images to fluoroscopic images without requiring knowledge of the system parameters that the DA images were acquired with. The noise texture between simulated and real fluoroscopic images was found to be similar with a mean absolute percent difference between normalized noise power spectrums of 0.7±0.7%. The noise magnitude was also similar, with a mean absolute percent difference between noise-curves acquired at 70, 90, and 120 kVp of 4.2±6.4%, 3.9±4.6%, and 1.9±1.3%, respectively. This method facilitates fluoroscopic image synthesis from DA images for the training of deep learning algorithms or testing of denoising algorithms with a known reference.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of Automatic Classification Algorithm for Acquisition Fast Neutron Radiography with Multi-Channel Pulse Shape Discrimination Results
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dual-modal imaging is widely utilized in both industry and the medical field for distinguishing various materials. Dual X-ray imaging or dual particle imaging is predominantly employed, utilizing differences in the attenuation coefficient ratios within materials for differentiation. In this study, we define materials by utilizing the difference in transmission of fast neutrons and gamma rays to calculate the R-value. Methods for obtaining fast neutron images include thermal neutron measurements via moderators and fast neutron measurements via recoil protons. Particularly, fast neutron measurements via recoil protons involve methods of measuring light using scintillator-based SiPMs or CMOS/CCD cameras. In situations where neutrons are prevalent, gamma rays inevitably accompany them as a by-product. To acquire images reflecting the attenuation of fast neutrons, pulse shape discrimination is necessary. Hence, to acquire fast neutron radiography, SiPM array-based sensors are more suitable than CMOS camera-based sensors. In this research, we utilized the EJ276G organic scintillator and the Onsemi MicroFJ-SMA-60035 model. Automatic classification combined unsupervised learning methods of K-means clustering and Gaussian Mixture Model with supervised learning method Support Vector Machine to distinguish between fast neutron and gamma-ray signals from pulse shape discrimination results. We validated our findings by obtaining and verifying labeling data through Time-of-Flight, demonstrating excellent automatic classification performance with an AUC of the ROC curve value of 0.9504. In future studies, we plan to investigate the feasibility of material identification through R -value using a multi-channel Radiography system.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Deep Learning-based Partial Volume Correction on Clinical 99mTc-TRODAT-1 SPECT Using a No-gold Standard Technique
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: 99mTc-TRODAT-1 SPECT is effective for the early detection of Parkinson’s disease (PD) but is compromised by the partial volume effect. Previously we have proposed a deep learning (DL)based partial volume correction (PVC) method for PD SPECT based on Monte Carlo simulation data, using original phantoms as the training label and show superior results as compared to the standard PVC method Van-Cittert (VC). In this study, we further applied this DL-PVC to clinical data. We retrospectively use 227 realistic digital PD brain phantoms, with data augmentation by aligning the head direction of each phantom to a randomly selected clinical data. Thus, 320, 44 and 90 phantoms are used for training, validation, and testing. DL-PVC is implemented using the attention generative adversarial network (AttGAN) and U-Net using simulated data, which are then directly tested on 100 clinical data. VC method is also implemented for comparison. Mean activity (MA) for the whole striatum and striatal binding ratio (SBR) are measured using a no-goldstandard technique (NGST), which applies a maximum likelihood estimator on both simulation and clinical data. The noise-to-slope ratio (NSR) is assessed as a figure-of-merit for NGST over 100 noise realizations. The MAE of MA and SBR are calculated in simulation data to verify the NGST. Results demonstrate that for the simulation data, the NSR rankings are consistent with the MAE rankings for both MA and SBR, where AttGAN has the best PVC performance, followed by U-Net, VC, and non-PVC. For the clinical data, the same NSR rankings are obtained as with the simulation data. DL-PVC based on a training model from simulation data is feasible for clinical PD SPECT and is superior to standard PVC methods like VC. NGST is feasible for evaluating PVC in clinical SPECT where ground truth is unavailable.

articleTitle: Assessing the Performance of the TOFPET2c ASIC at X-ray Energies for Time-of-Flight Scatter Rejection Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The addition of a time-of-flight (ToF) measurements to radiography and computed tomography (CT) opens the door to an anti-scatter grid-free approach to scatter rejection in imaging systems, potentially increasing system sensitivity and image quality. Previously developed hardware limited to a few channels showed that the ToF scatter rejection is possible, but lacked in scale and density. A medium-scale ToF scatter rejection detection module was developed, allowing for the evaluation of off-the-shelf ToF ASICs, as well as the future development of dedicated devices. The TOFPET2c ASIC designed by PETSys showed good potential for the first detector, offering high integration and pixel count. The evaluation of the TOFPET2c ASIC at X-ray energies (20 keV to 140 keV) showed a 414 ps FWHM detector timing resolution. Such a value is slightly over the 300 ps FWHM limit sufficient to reach scatter-rejection similar to anti-scatter grids and requires further investigation. An energy resolution bellow 50% was also reached for all desired energies.

articleTitle: The Relationship between Dose-Averaged LET and In-Beam PET Imaging in Carbon Ion Radiotherapy: A Study of Prostate Cancer Patients
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The study investigates the application of in-beam PET imaging in Carbon Ion Radiotherapy (CIRT), exploring its advantages and correlations in tumor treatment. The distribution of dose-averaged LET and PET imaging in CIRT is simulated using Geant4/GATE tools. A case study of prostate cancer patients undergoing pass-through irradiation irradiation is employed to assess the impact of LET<inf>d</inf> on PET imaging. Results indicate a stronger correlation between LET<inf>d</inf> and PET imaging’s Bragg peak positions compared to physical absorbed dose. PET imaging enables inference of biological effects within tumors, offering new insights and guidance for optimizing treatment strategies. This study provides clinical references for precision carbon ion radiotherapy in prostate cancer patients.

articleTitle: Novel collimator Compton camera for high contrast and wide-band imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray and gamma-ray imaging is essential in nuclear medicine. Recently, various therapeutic radionuclides have been proposed, increasing the need to visualize their pharmacokinetics. In addition, gamma-ray imaging of neutron-activated gold nanoparticles (AuNPs), which are promising drug carriers, has been proposed. Although various X-rays and gamma rays are emitted from radioactive drugs and drug carriers, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is limited to low-energy ($\lt \sim 200 \mathrm{keV}$) X-ray/gamma-ray imaging, and positron emission tomography (PET) specializes in 511-keV annihilation gamma-ray imaging. The use of Compton cameras capable of high-energy broadband gamma-ray imaging is a promising way to visualize various drugs and drug carriers; however, the relatively low contrast of images obtained using Compton cameras has hindered their clinical use. To improve the contrast, we attached a tungsten collimator to the front surface of Compton camera and applied signal weighting based on the distance that the gamma rays penetrated the collimator walls. Aiming at future high-contrast imaging of neutron-activated AuNPs, we demonstrated contrast improvement by imaging neutron-activated gold plates with and without a collimator. The image showed a higher contrast with the collimator than without it. In addition, low-energy X-ray/gamma-ray imaging, which is challenging for conventional Compton cameras, is achieved using the collimator and the scatterer of the Compton camera as SPECT. Broadband imaging was demonstrated by visualizing the ${ }^{133} \mathrm{Ba}$ source using its $81-\mathrm{keV}$ and $356-\mathrm{keV}$ gamma rays based on the principles of SPECT and Compton cameras, respectively. The contrast improvement and wide-band imaging demonstrated in this study could pave the way for the clinical use of Compton cameras and the visualization of various radioactive drugs/drug carriers.

articleTitle: Demonstration of Muon Tomography at an Archaeological Site in Ancient Jerusalem
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a novel underground imaging system using cosmic ray muons for scanning the underground environment. The first results of measurements at the archaeological site of the City of David in ancient Jerusalem are presented. The system is designed to locate and map underground hidden voids and unexpected deviations in the ground. This is demonstrated by describing initial studies of mapping Jeremiah’s Pit, next to the archaeological excavations at the City of David’s site using muons from cosmic rays. The muons, generated in the atmosphere, penetrate through the ground and reach the particle hodoscope, which is placed inside the pit. This work is the result of an interdisciplinary effort involving archaeologists and physicists who are utilizing this technology to deepen our knowledge and understanding of the biblical period in ancient Jerusalem.

articleTitle: Preliminary Investigation into Geometry Optimization for Omnidirectional Gamma-Ray Imager Using Detector Response Patterns
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We are developing a gamma-ray imager, the ‘Coded Cube Camera for Gamma-Ray’ (C3G), which offers an omnidirectional field of view, and is compact and lightweight. The C3G consists of irregularly arranged shielding and detector cubes. The C3G has demonstrated the ability to image a <sup>137</sup>Cs source at a distance of 3 meters with an angular uncertainty of 5 degrees. In the current prototype, the arrangement of shielding and detectors has yet to be optimized. Since the imager geometry influences the angular resolution and accuracy of position estimation, identifying a metric for geometry optimization has become a pressing challenge. This study analyzed the relationship between imaging accuracy and detector response patterns. A Simulation was conducted to search for parameters that affect imaging accuracy. As a result, it was found that the coefficient of variation (CV) of the detector’s response patterns affects imaging accuracy, and the simulation confirmed that performance can be improved by changing the imager geometry to enhance the CV. The results obtained will be an essential indicator for future imager design. We plan to develop an algorithm that can select the optimal geometry.

articleTitle: SUV-guided PET Attenuation Correction for Delayed Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Compared with conventional PET scan protocol, delayed images (e.g., 90 min post-inject of 18FFDG) could reduce background activity and clearly characterized the lesion activity. However, the multiple CT scans may significantly increase the risk of ionizing radiation for the delayed images. In this study, we proposed a direct generation method for PET attenuation correction of delay imaging by introducing the first SUV images, which would greatly eliminate the need for a second CT scan. By using data from two PET scans before and after, it has great potential in fully exploring the temporal variation association of tracers in human metabolic signals for delayed images. In terms of the network architecture, a 3D U-net is employed to predict the attenuation-corrected delayed images using second non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET images and first reconstructed SUV images. Experiments are conducted on a delayed PET datasets with 32 clinical patient data from Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center. The experimental results demonstrated that the excellent generation performance rather than the direct attenuation-corrected model. What’ more, the quantitative results proves the better performance in terms of PSNR and SSIM. In the future, we would seek further studies in more patient data and different tracers.

articleTitle: Compton camera image reconstruction with sparse data via U-Net and SwinIR for prompt gamma imaging during proton therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Prompt gamma (PG) imaging has been proposed for in-vivo range verification during proton therapy (PT), which is promising to reduce the impact of range uncertainty and improve the clinical effectiveness of PT. Compton camera (CC)-based PG imaging has attracted extensive attention and research due to the CC’s advantages such as high detection efficiency, direct three-dimensional imaging, etc. However, limited by the delivered dose in most spot-mode treatments and the CC detection efficiency under the clinical dose rate, the PG images obtained by the CC are degraded by the sparse data and finite resolution of the detectors. In this study, we investigate CC-based PG reconstruction via deep learning (DL) algorithms with sparse simulation data. For simulation, a proton pencil beam with energy from 90 MeV to 160 MeV irradiated a three-layer box phantom consisting of human tissues. A developed two-layer LYSO CC prototype was modeled and detected the PGs. 107 protons were used in each irradiation to obtain the sparse projection data which only contained several hundred events. A representative CNN-based method U-Net and a proposed modified SwinIR were used for PG image restoration from the original reconstruction images with sparse projection data obtained by the CC. Simulation results show that the DL algorithms can restore the PG distribution from the degraded images caused by the low statistics and finite position and energy resolution of the CC. Meanwhile, the PG distributions restored by U-Net are over-smooth and the proposed modified SwinIR has average PSNR gains of 3.14dB over U-Net. The preliminary simulation results show that the DL-based algorithm is promising to solve the sparse data problem in CC-based PG imaging in clinical and can realize a more accurate and rapid PG distribution reconstruction in terms of range monitoring during PT.
