articleTitle: TID analysis of LVDS receivers with impedance spectroscopy for the ATLAS muon trigger
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the framework of the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) program, the ATLAS muon barrel trigger will undergo significant upgrades, including the installation of new front-end electronics. The new Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) readout system will be based on Data Collector Transmitter (DCT) on-detector boards, that collect RPC data and send them to the off-detector boards through optical fibers. Low-Voltage Differential Signaling (LVDS) receivers are hosted on the DCT boards and are used to receive detector front-end signals. In this work, we study the Total Ionizing Dose (TID) damage on LVDS receivers also through an approach based on impedance spectroscopy. Our experimental setup includes a suite of three boards, and it allows testing ten LVDS receivers and four Si pn diodes. To this aim, two TID tests are being carried out, the first one at the ATLAS target dose of 100 Gy at 25 Gy/h and the second one at ~ 10 kGy with a dose rate of 360 Gy/h. Irradiations are presently underway at the CC60 facility at CERN, equipped with a ~ 10 TBq 60Co source. The impedance spectroscopy analysis performed pre- and post-irradiation will be benchmarked with diodes. Such analysis will reveal microscopic alterations caused by irradiation in a non-destructive way.

articleTitle: First Evaluation of Novel Ultra-dense and Transparent Lutetium Oxide Doped with Lanthanum Ceramic Scintillators for PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scintillators are central to the performance of positron emission tomography (PET) scanners. Lutetium-yttrium oxyorthosilicate (LYSO) has emerged as a leading scintillator due to its appropriate attributes for PET, yet it presents challenges such as high cost. In this study, we explore the potential of a novel ultra-dense transparent ceramic scintillator: lutetium oxide doped with lanthanum as an alternative for PET imaging. Ceramic scintillator samples with a size of 3 × 3 × 5 mm<sup>3</sup> were fabricated and compared with LYSO in terms of timing and energy resolution characteristics. The experimental setup involved two Near Ultraviolet High-Density Silicon Photomultipliers (NUV-HD SiPMs) connected to readout boards for extracting timing and energy signals. Energy resolutions and coincidence timing resolutions (CTRs) at different thresholds were calculated using digitized waveforms. Results indicated comparable light yield and energy resolution between LYSO and the ceramic scintillators. In terms of timing properties, the new ceramic scintillators showed appropriate timing performance for the use in Time-of-Flight (TOF) PET applications.

articleTitle: Correlative analysis of CsPbBr2Hal (Hal = Cl, Br, I) melt-crystallization parameters
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal halide perovskites (MHPs) are an exciting research topic as they have the potential to make solar cells that are both more efficient than current silicon-based designs and have a wider range of applications. In this work the crystallization of $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_{2} \mathrm{Hal}(\mathrm{Hal}=\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}, \mathrm{I})$ halide perovskites melts were studied by the differential thermal analysis method. It was established that the crystallization of the $\mathrm{CsPbBr}_{2} \mathrm{Hal}(\mathrm{Hal}=\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}, \mathrm{I})$ melts can be “hot” (at temperatures above the starting temperature for alloy melting) or with supercooling. The replacement of the bromine atom with another halogen atom leads to a shift of the dwell temperatures range, at which point the “hot” crystallization takes place, from 830-846 K for CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> to 807-832 K for CsPbBr<inf>2</inf> Cl and 741-768 K for CsPbBr<inf>2</inf> I. The activation energy of “hot” crystallization decreases in this order. A linear dependence between the pre-exponential factor ($\ln V_{\text {cryst, } 0}$) and the activation energy $\left(E_{\mathrm{a}}\right)$ of the crystallization process is revealed from experimental data, proving the compensation effect.

articleTitle: Enhancing Precision in Proton Therapy: Monte Carlo Simulation Modeling and Validation of FLASH Proton Therapy for Accelerated Treatment Delivery
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the landscape of radiation therapy for cancer treatment, mitigating damage to healthy tissues surrounding tumors poses a significant challenge. FLASH Proton Therapy (FPT), characterized by its ultra-high dose rate ($\gt40 \mathrm{~Gy} / \mathrm{s}$), presents a promising avenue to address this concern. This study aims to develop and validate a Monte Carlo (MC)-based model for FPT and integrate it into human treatment planning protocols. Initially, the Proton Therapy System (PTS) utilizing spot scanning was simulated using GATE software. Dosimetric and optical beam parameters were derived from subsequent simulations irradiating a homogeneous water phantom. Parameters such as range, Bragg Peak (BP) location, mean point-to-point, and Spread-Out Bragg Peak (SOBP) curve were investigated within the energy range of 70-240 MeV. Validation procedures encompassed irradiation of a Head and Neck (H&N) heterogeneous phantom within the 70-150 MeV energy spectrum. Comparisons between GATE simulation and experimental measurements for depth-dose curves revealed a mean point-to-point difference parameter of approximately $0.015 \%$. Key parameters, including BP location, range, and SOBP modulation region length, demonstrated excellent agreement with experimental measurements, deviating by less than $1 \%$. The simulated spot size closely mirrored measurement data, exhibiting a discrepancy of under 3%. Furthermore, comparative analysis between FPT and Conventional Proton Therapy (CPT) showcased a nominal difference of $0.590 \%$. These findings underscore the potential efficacy of FPT, offering comparable treatment quality to CPT while potentially minimizing collateral tissue damage.

articleTitle: Real-time radiation beam monitoring by flexible perovskite thin film arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Real-time and in-line transversal monitoring of ionizing radiation beams is crucial for various applications, ranging from medical treatments to high-energy physics particle accelerators. Here, we introduce a flexible, large-area device based on 2D hybrid perovskite thin films (phenylethylammonium lead bromide, PEA<inf>2</inf>PbBr<inf>4</inf>) deposited on a thin and flexible polyimide substrate. This device can accurately map in real-time and in-line the transversal profile of high energy radiation beams. The here reported performance is compared to standard commercial large-area technology, specifically radiochromic sheets. We demonstrate its effectiveness by real-time mapping of a 5 MeV proton beam, with fluxes ranging from $10^{8} \mathrm{H}^{+} \mathrm{s}^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^{-2}$ to $10^{10} \mathrm{H}^{+} \mathrm{s}^{-1} \mathrm{~cm}^{-2}$, without signal saturation issues in high radiation environments. Moreover, we showcase the versatility and scalability of this detecting system by developing a multipixel array capable of realtime mapping a 40 kVp X-ray beam spot (dose rate $=8 \mathrm{mGy} \mathrm{s}^{-1}$). Perovskite thin film-based detectors emerge as a promising class of thin, flexible devices for real-time, in-line, large-area, conformable, reusable, transparent, and cost-effective transversal beam monitoring across various ionizing radiation types.

articleTitle: Simulation of Noise Signals in Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Front-End Amplifier Circuit
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) are highly sensitive, fast-response single-photon detectors increasingly used across various fields. In the pursuit of optimizing time resolution, challenges arise due to SiPM signals having low amplitude, short duration, and noise interference from dark avalanche rates, crosstalk, afterpulsing, and thermal noise in the front-end circuit. This paper simulates pulse voltage sequences from a lutetium oxyorthosilicate scintillator with a Analog SiPM, incorporating thermal and dark noise using LTspice and Python. Various shaping circuits and voltage-sensitive preamplifiers were simulated to test signal outputs. Experimental measurements and analysis were conducted to validate the simulation results. The findings offer helpful insights for future designs and optimizations of front-end amplifier circuits.

articleTitle: Experimental Evaluation of DE-SPECT: A Hyperspectral SPECT System for Region-Selective 3-D Gamma-Ray Spectroscopy of Molecular Theragnostics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Dynamic Extremity SPECT (DE-SPECT) system employs state-of-the-art technology for precise, region-selective gamma-ray spectroscopy using Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) imaging spectrometers and dynamic dual-field-of-view (FOV) collimators. This clinical system is designed to enhance the diagnostic accuracy of Peripheral Vascular Disease (PVD) assessments in the lower extremities by providing comprehensive, multifunctional molecular imaging. The CZT detectors used in the system offer an excellent energy performance (2.6 keV FWHM at 220 keV, 3.3 keV at 440 keV) spanning a wide energy range of up to 600 keV. The uniquely designed dual-FOV aperture system enables region-selective imaging capabilities with two configurations: a 28-cm diameter FOV for dual-leg imaging and a 16-cm diameter FOV for focused, high-resolution, and high-sensitivity imaging. The system’s unmatched capability facilitates in vivo simultaneous multi-tracer theragnostics within user-selected targeted regions. We have fully assembled the system and conducted phantom studies using a series of uniform phantoms, custom-made image quality (IQ) phantoms, and a resolution phantom filled with multiple radiotracers (Tc-99m, I-123, In-111, etc.) to evaluate the imaging performance of the DE-SPECT system.

articleTitle: A Study on Time Resolution Performance of TOF-PET Detector Based on Simulation and Analytical Modeling
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study delves into the gamma-ray detector system in Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (TOF-PET). Using LYSO:Ce scintillators and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), we evaluated system performance through simulations and analytical modeling. Light propagation simulation reveals how scintillator crystal size affects Energy Resolution (ER) and Coincidence Time Resolution (CTR). We introduce an analytical model to resolve single photon electron response from SiPM to study the influence of SiPM intrinsic parameters on output signal shape, especially the slew rate and its impact on time resolution. Through light simulation and electrical modeling, an overall signal from the SiPM is obtained. Here we present a preliminary result on CTR with respect to the scintillator length and SiPM parameters

articleTitle: Multi-stage Diffusion Modelfor Fast PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Fast PET imaging is vital in both practical and clinical contexts, improving patient comfort and reducing motion artifacts. However, shorter scan times often lead to compromised image quality and increased noise. To overcome this challenge, we propose an advanced diffusion model tailored for efficient and accurate fast PET imaging. Unlike traditional methods, our approach directly utilizes fast PET images (30 s) as the endpoint of the diffusion process, eliminating the need for numerous reconstruction iterations. We employ progressive learning and a multi-stage diffusion model architecture to ensure an accurate representation of real PET scan distributions at different time points. Additionally, we integrate a Phase Error Correction Net to enhance image quality, correct cumulative errors, and prevent artifacts. Experimental validation on a dataset of $68-\mathrm{Ga}$ FAPI PET images demonstrates the effectiveness of our method, achieving PSNR values of 36.2 dB and a mean SSIM exceeding 0.97 for all tested patients. These results highlight the potential of our model to significantly improve diagnostic accuracy under fast PET scanning conditions.

articleTitle: Detector Performances of Large Area Scintillator / Wavelength Shifting Fiber Neutron Detectors for SENJU Upgrade at J-PARC MLF
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Detector performances of large area two-dimensional neutron detectors produced for upgrade of SENJU diffractometer at Materials and Life science experimental Facility at J-PARC have been evaluated. The detectors are developed based on a ${ }^{6} \mathrm{Li}: \mathrm{ZnS}(\mathrm{Ag})$ scintillator and wavelength-shifting fiber technology. The protype detector has a neutron-sensitive area of $512 \times 768 \mathrm{~mm}$, which is six-fold of the original detector installed in the SENJU. The pixel size is $4 \times 4 \mathrm{~mm}$, which maintains the same as that of the original detector. The prototype detector exhibited a detection efficiency of $40 \sim 50\%$ for 2Å neutrons and ${ }^{60} \mathrm{Co}$ gamma-ray sensitivity of $\sim 10^{-6}. 9$ detector modules have been produced for the planned SENJU upgrade. The produced detectors exhibited similar detector efficiencies and gamma-ray sensitivities to that of the prototype detector. Neutron counts of these detectors with a ${ }^{252} \mathrm{Cf}$ source varied within 5% to the average. The experimental results of the prototype and the produced beamline detectors are presented.

articleTitle: Development of the Engineering Model of the Solar Neutron and Gamma-ray Spectrometer (SONGS)
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We are developing the solar neutron and gamma-ray spectrometer (SONGS) with small size (10 cmx15 cmx15 cm), light weight ($\sim 3 \mathrm{~kg}$) and low power ($\sim 6 \mathrm{~W}$) for microsatellite to clarify particle acceleration mechanisms in the solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs). This detector consists of two parts. One is fast neutron detection part consisting of 16 plastic scintillator (3.95 mmx3.95 mmx64 mm for each) bars with 16 layers, and the other is gamma-ray detection part composed of $12 \mathrm{x} 12 \mathrm{GAGG}(\mathrm{Ce})$ scintillator array. Fast neutron in $30-120 \mathrm{MeV}$ can be detected via elastic scattering and incident energy can be determined assuming the Sun direction, while gamma-rays in 0.1-3 MeV can be detected via either photo-absorption or Compton scattering process in plastic scintilators. Both scintillators are read out individually by Hamamatsu silicon photo-multipliers (SiPMs), and their 704 signals are processed by 45 IDEAS ASICs and 6 Xilinx FPGAs. In this geometry and configuration, we can track the particle trajectory in three dimensions. We also attached the low-power wide-area network (LPWA) antenna and transceiver to send an alert of occurence of giant solar flares to public people for space weather purpose. After verification of bread-board model (BBM) in previous years, we are now testing and constructing the SONGS Engineering Model (EM) which has almost the same detector configuration as flight model (FM) aiming at the launch around 2026 by the JAXA innovative satellite technology demonstration program. In this paper, we will introduce our SONGS project and report on the current status and performance of the SONGS EM.

articleTitle: Measurement of Fast to Thermal Neutron Flux Ratio under D-T Neutron Irradiation using a LaBr3Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Many active neutron interrogation systems use D-T neutron generators and take advantage of modern high-resolution scintillators such as LaBr<inf>3</inf> and CeBr<inf>3</inf>. In this work, we use the internal activation of a LaBr<inf>3</inf> crystal to determine the ratio of fast and thermal neutron flux in an operating D-T generator environment. The basis for the measurement is the difference in cross-sections for the production of ${ }^{80 m} \mathrm{Br}$ and ${ }^{809} \mathrm{Br}$ isomers in thermal ${ }^{79} \mathrm{Br}(\mathrm{n}, \gamma)^{80} \mathrm{Br}$ and fast ${ }^{81} \mathrm{Br}(\mathrm{n}, 2 \mathrm{n})^{80} \mathrm{Br}$ reactions. Measurement of the variation in the isomeric cross-section ratio with the incident particle energy may be used to determine the properties of the incident neutron energy spectrum. The relative production of these isomers can be determined from the time-dependent count-rate evolution after irradiation. We identify the main $\beta$-spectrum components and estimate the relative production rates of ${ }^{78} \mathrm{Br}$ over ${ }^{82} \mathrm{Br}$, which are respectively related to the fast and thermal portions of the incident neutron energy spectrum.

articleTitle: pin-diode type GaN X-ray imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report on the development of a high-sensitivity Gallium Nitride (GaN)-based X-ray detector, specifically engineered for low-energy X-ray applications targeting energies below 25 keV. This study introduces two types of diode-based detector structures, pn-type and pin-type, fabricated on high-mobility n-type GaN substrates. Our experimental results demonstrate that both detector types exhibit favorable characteristics, with enhanced output counts proportional to the X-ray dose, thereby confirming their efficacy for medical imaging purposes. A comparative analysis of the pn-type and pin-type detectors revealed a preference for the pintype configuration due to its superior performance metrics, establishing it as the basic design for further development. This preference is largely attributed to the structure of the pin-type detector which features a thick depletion layer, essential for the effective operation of X-ray detectors. The required thickness for this layer ranges from 100 to $1000 \mu \mathrm{m}$, significantly greater than the several micrometers necessary for visible light photodiodes. This thickness is crucial to ensure stable, recombination-free carrier transport across the detector, which is vital for maintaining high charge collection efficiency. Notably, the intrinsic layer (i-layer) of the pin-type detector contains fewer defects compared to the p-layer, further contributing to its higher charge collection efficiency. The advancements highlighted in this research are promising for the enhancement of low-energy X-ray applications, potentially leading to significant improvements in medical imaging technology. This work lays the foundation for future studies and development of GaN-based detectors, steering the field towards more sophisticated and efficient X-ray imaging solutions.

articleTitle: A New Tool for Evaluating the Spatial Resolvability in Hot Spot Phantoms
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Hot Spot phantoms are widely used to assess the spatial resolution performance and image quality of PET scanners. Conventionally, a simple visual examination is conducted to determine whether hot spots of specific sizes are discernible. However, the lack of quantitative assessment could lead to different conclusions based on the observer’s perception of spot resolvability. To address this, some groups have recently reported valley-to-peak ratios (VPRs) of line profiles drawn across the spots to determine whether they are resolved using the Rayleigh criterion. We propose an opensource tool for semi-automatic drawing of line profiles through all possible directions of sections in Hot Spot phantoms to determine the VPRs and fraction of discernible spots. Various techniques are available to the users for extracting the valleys and peaks, for instance with fitting or region-averaging to mitigate the influence of noise. This tool can help the nuclear imaging community to complement the conventional qualitative assessment of Hot Spot phantoms with a more robust quantitative evaluation of the resolvability.

articleTitle: Precise charged particle timing with robust PICOSEC Micromegas detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Future high-luminosity experiments require timing precision of the order of tens of picoseconds for pileup mitigation while aiming at instrumenting large active areas. PICOSEC Micromegas detectors combine a Cherenkov radiator with a photocathode and a two-stage gaseous amplification structure to achieve timing precision of $\lt25 \mathrm{ps}$ for minimum ionising particles [1] while allowing for economic area coverage. We present the development of tileable detector modules achieving high timing precision and optimisations in detector construction and signal routing which improve the achievable resolution to better than 20 ps. In parallel, new developments towards maintaining performance in challenging environments are pursued including alternative photoconversion layers which tolerate higher levels of ion back flow and resistive amplification structures. Carbon-based photocathodes including diamond-like carbon and $B_{4} C$ are evaluated and timing resolution values in the range of $30-40$ ps were obtained. Resistive detector technologies including resistive Micromegas and $\mu$ RWELL detectors were implemented to withstand high-rate environments. To profit from efficient protection against discharges and minimise the influence of delayed signal components on timing performance, high resistivity electrodes are used and comparable time resolution to non-resistive prototypes is demonstrated. The performance of different scalable readout approaches is compared to demonstrate the availability of suitable electronic readout schemes for multi-module detector systems. Dedicated preamplifiers coupled with waveform-digitising TDCs are used for constantfraction discrimination while a threshold-based timing ASIC is shown to allow for timewalk correction with complementary energy information. The presented developments illustrate the versatility of PICOSEC Micromegas precise timing detectors and their compatibility with challenging environments for high-pileup environments as well as photo detection.

articleTitle: Quantum-Inspired Denoising via Adaptive Planck Constant and Image Patching
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Traditional denoising methods face challenges in environments where images are corrupted by high noise levels, due to limitations in learning intricate patterns and capturing complex structures. To overcome these limitations, recent efforts have explored learning-based approaches and especially deep learning. However, in addition to their long training time, these approaches face the lack of labeled data in many applications area such as medical imaging. A recent appealing alternative is the integration of quantum principles into denoising techniques, showing promise in improving performance. However, current approaches often entail high computational costs and manual hyperparameter setting. Our study introduces an adaptive Planck constant formulation to quantum-inspired denoising, reducing computational overhead and streamlining the process. By incorporating this adaptive approach alongside image patching, we achieve improvements in denoising efficiency. This advancement not only eliminates the need for manual intervention in hyperparameter settings but also enhances the usability of quantum-inspired methods.

articleTitle: Organs and Systems Glucose Metabolism Analysis in Different Smoking Groups for Lung Cancer Patients using Total-body PET/CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Smoking history has been an important indicator in lung cancer (LC) screening as it damages lung function. However, whether smoking is harmful to other organs and what abnormalities may occur among various organs have not yet been studied since total-body imaging is not feasible for previous scanners. With the emergence of the total-body PET/CT, we may explore the correlation between abnormal glucose metabolism among various organs and systems for smoking. This work investigates if the smoking intensity plays a role in the metabolic abnormalities among different organs and systems in different smoking groups for LC patients. ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG PET and CT images from 60 anonymized subjects with 40 LC patients and 20 healthy controls (HCs) are retrospectively recruited and scanned from a uEXPLORER PET/CT. Among LC patients, their smoking intensities were surveyed (non-smokers: light smokers: heavy smokers $=21: 4: 15$). For each scan, 17 regionsof-interests are outlined. To analyze the abnormal metabolism of different smoking groups, we construct individual and group abnormal metabolism networks respectively based on a reference network with HCs. Pearson correlation coefficients between standardized uptake values of each organ pair and system pair are calculated to analyze their connectivities. Results show that more significant abnormal metabolism is observed in smokers as compared to non-smokers. Besides, heavy smokers have a substantially greater proportion of metabolic decline compared with others for lungs, heart, kidneys and esophagus. In addition, the abnormal metabolism connectivity of the lungs-esophagus and lungs-thyroid gland increases significantly along with the increased intensity of smoking, while stronger abnormal metabolism connectivity is also observed between the nervous system and other systems for heavy smokers. The proposed analysis method is feasible for LC patients using total-body FDG PET/CT and has the potential to be applied to other systemic diseases.

articleTitle: Study of CsPbBr3Perovskite Crystals for X-Ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The paper presents the results of studies of CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> perovskite crystals which are promising for the creation of semiconductor X-ray detectors. Crystals with dimensions of 5.5x5.5x2.0 mm<sup>3</sup> are grown using the ITC (Inverse Temperature Crystallization) technology. A thorough investigation of CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> crystals was carried out using Raman spectroscopy, transmission/reflectance spectra analysis, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS) and reflection electron energy loss spectroscopy (REELS). The combination of these techniques provides a comprehensive understanding of the structural and electronic properties of CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>, crucial for its application in the field of radiation detector devices. The spectrometric characteristics of crystals in the simplest test detectors of X-ray and gamma radiation with metal-crystal-metal contact structures, hemispherical and drift ring structures were evaluated. The volt-ampere and capacitance voltage performance of detectors in the range of voltage supply from 0 to 600 V, as well as the spectra of standard radioisotope sources in the energy range from 5.9 to 1332 keV are presented.

articleTitle: Diagnosis of chest X-Rays images with Deep Learning enhanced with discrete wavelet transform
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Deep learning (DL) is increasingly used in medical imaging to improve image acquisition technology and aid in disease diagnosis and classification. In this work, we present an enhancement of DL applied in lung chest X-rays (CXR) imaging first to enhance lung image segmentation, and second to accurately classify images based on their status of normal, or with tuberculosis, viral pneumonia, or COVID-19 induced pneumonia. The images were obtained from public datasets: 247 from the Japanese Society of Radiological Technology and the Japanese Radiological Society; 138 from the Health and Human Services, Montgomery County (MC), Maryland, USA; 800 from Shenzhen and Montgomery; and 33,920 from Qatar University. For the segmentation, we replaced the Max-Pooling in U-Net++ with the Discrete Wavelet Transform (UNet++-Rand-DWT) integrated with Attention Gates. Prior to U-Net++-Rand-DWT, the images were normalized with the Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE) and augmented with the Progressive Growing Generative Adversarial Networks (PGGAN) by generating synthetic images to balance the different image classes. For image classification, the DenseNet-201 model was enhanced with Rand-DWT (DenseNet-201-Rand-DWT). The results for the segmentation obtained with U-Net++-Rand-DWT demonstrated greater accuracy, both qualitatively and quantitatively, compared to U-Net++ with Max-Pooling and to four other models, as evaluated by accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, Dice coefficient and Jaccard Index. For pathology classification, DenseNet-201-Rand-DWT outperformed the traditional U-Net++ and U-Net, and the synthetically generated images with PGGAN significantly enhanced classification accuracy, as determined by precision and F1-score metrics. Furthermore, DenseNet-201-Rand-DWT demonstrated an enhanced performance in discriminating pneumonia and COVID-19 CXR images, even without data augmentation.

articleTitle: Quantum C100: Wafer Scale CMOS Sensor for Direct Detection of 100keV Electrons for CryoEM
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Developed at the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) in partnership with Quantum Detectors ltd. and the Rosalind Franklin Institute, Quantum C100 is a wafer-scale monolithic CMOS image sensor optimised for the direct detection of 100 keV electrons in the field of Cryo-electron Microscopy (cryoEM). Custom designed by STFC Technology Department, C100 features a full, uninterrupted 11 x 11 cm sensitive area, with a resolution of $2048 \times 2048$ pixels on a pitch of $54 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and is capable of a full frame rate of over 2000 fps at 12 -bit pixel depth. This paper will describe the development of the device, the technology within, and the challenges associated with the design of a wafer-scale image sensor. We will also present simulations and results from the small-scale test structure and full-size sensor currently in fabrication.

articleTitle: A universal activity painting phantom for positron emission tomography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work describes a novel phantom for positron emission tomography (PET) consisting of a single high-statistics dataset produced by traversing the volume of interest with a point source in the field-of-view (FOV) of a scanner. The dataset can be sampled to model arbitrary static and dynamic distributions of various complexities within any body region. Uniquely, random and scattered events can be separated from true coincidences based on the distance between their line of response (LOR) and the source, and if the scatter fraction is low, the randoms fraction in the phantom can be varied. Initially, we acquired a planar dataset by raster-scanning a $220 \times 180$ $\mathrm{mm}^{2}$ coronal plane with a 27.5 MBq 1-mm ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source mounted on a robotic arm in the FOV of the uEXPLORER PET/CT scanner. The source moved continuously along the axial direction at $10 \mathrm{~mm} / \mathrm{s}$; adjacent lines were 1 mm apart. The equations of motion were defined by dividing the dataset into 1-s frames and computing the source position in each frame. Finally, we constructed a simple geometric distribution and a high-resolution ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) distribution in the brain by defining activity concentration in every voxel, and randomly sampled the phantom dataset to achieve the desired concentrations. There is good agreement between the target patterns and the reconstructed phantom images, and line profiles through the geometric phantom show very good quantitative accuracy of the approach. We also modeled a dynamic ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-florbetaben study by extracting grey and white matter activity concentrations from the time activity curve (TAC) of a human study and assigning them to the tissues in a segmented brain phantom. Overall, the planar data demonstrated significant promise, and work is under way to extend the phantom to 3D. Using a similar experimental setup, we collected data over a $180 \times 200 \times 110 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ volume and will use it to model realistic activity distributions in the entire human brain.

articleTitle: Development of A Multi-Layer Silicon Betaray Spectrometer for CANDU Environment and Preliminary Characterization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To echo the growing demand of precise assessment dose to lens of eye from beta radiation at Canada Deuterium Uranium (CANDU) power planet, we present a silicon-based beta-ray spectrometer that is able to measure the in situ beta-ray fluence spectrum and real-time dose monitor with a high gamma rejection ratio avoiding overestimation of beta dose in the beta-gamma mix environment at CANDU sites. A prototype has been developed that features one 500 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ and three $1500 \mu \mathrm{m}$ silicon detectors in series to measure a beta energy range of 70 keV to 3000 keV using the $\Delta \mathrm{E}$ vs. E method, which enables temporal coincidence and energy logic for electron channel binning. GEANT4 simulation was extensively conducted for the geometric factors and instrument response functions to facilitate the instrument design and characterization. The silicon beta spectrometer prototype was characterized under a beta-gamma mixed field consisting of ${ }^{90} \mathrm{Sr}$ and ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$ sources to evaluate the beta/gamma discrimination ability. In this paper, we report the project motivation, hardware description, GEANT4 modeling and preliminary characterization of the prototype system.

articleTitle: Results from the First Neutron Reflectometry Application of a Fast Photon-Counting Camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A detector based on Timepix3 readout of image-intensified light from a scintillator ($\mathrm{ZnS}: \mathrm{Ag}: \mathrm{LiF})$ has been applied and tested in neutron reflectometry for the first time. The detector has been characterized at a monochromatic beamline with lambda $=4.2 \mathrm{AA}$ at HFIR reactor at ORNL. It was then installed on the Time-of-Flight (ToF) reflectometer ASTERIX at LANL and compared to a conventional ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ reflectometry detector. The search for faster reflectometer detectors has been underway using multiple technologies around the world. Our new detector has made a successful entry into this field. This paper presents the measured reflectivity profiles for several standard samples - Ni, Ir and quartz. The detection efficiency and signal-to-background were nearly indistinguishable from ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ detector. Reflectivity profiles for these samples are presented in comparison to ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ demonstrating excellent performance of the detector. The rate that could be used before the onset of non-linearities was significantly greater with instantaneous rate of 100 kHz and above, presenting no issues already in the current build of the detector. Several improvements are already underway. These will further increase the detector rate performance by reducing the scintillator afterglow as well as alleviate the rate limitations of the image intensifier. The eventual upgrade to Timepix4 is promising to unlock yet another order of magnitude in rate capability. We further propose handling even more intense direct beams using a smaller lens aperture. This serves as a controlled adjustment of the detection efficiency in place of the necessarily wavelength-dependent beam attenuation typically used on for direct beams with current ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ detectors. Further design and prototyping will be performed for the QIKR reflectometer at the Second Target Station at ORNL.

articleTitle: Compton imaging of therapeutic radionuclides with a CZT camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiopharmaceutical therapies (RPT) have shown a great promise treating numerous types of malignancies. Within this modality, targeted alpha therapy (TAT) is emerging as a more potent cancer therapy than beta therapy due to the higher linear energy transfer of alpha particles. A very popular candidate to alpha RPT is ${ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$, which has shown great therapeutic efficacy in recent clinical trials. Many of these RPT radionuclides exhibit photon emissions that can be imaged via single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT). However, gamma-ray imaging of therapeutic isotopes is not always easy due to the low injected activities, low branching ratio of emitted gamma-rays, and the high energy of some gamma-ray emissions. We propose to use a pixelated dual-layer collimatorless cadmium zinc telluride (CZT) camera to provide Compton imaging of the high-energy gamma-rays as well as proximity of low energy gamma-rays at the same time. We have conducted tests on a highly compact, single-layer CZT gamma camera with 3D positioning that enables internal tracking of the gamma-ray. We measured an energy resolution of $0.82(1) \%$ FWHM at 440 keV, much superior to scintillator detectors. We obtained the ${ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$ images by selecting 440 keV gamma-ray (decays from ${ }^{213} \mathrm{Bi}$) having $\sim 0.13 \%$ sensitivity. The detector is capable of imaging and identifying a $\sim 1 \mu \mathrm{Ci}^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$ source in less than 5 minutes at a distance of 4 cm. However, employing multiple detectors and extending the acquisition time in close distance allows us to image significantly lower levels of activity. In addition to Compton imaging, work is underway on proximity imaging using low-energy (218 keV) techniques to enhance sensitivity, with future plans for in vivo imaging.

articleTitle: A Performance Upgrade for the EUDET-type Test Beam Telescopes
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The EUDET-type beam telescopes are provided by several test beam facilities around the world to their users. They are required to record particle tracks mainly as reference data for beam tests of detectors for high energy physics experiments. In the approximately 15 years of their operation, the requirements for particle detectors have increased significantly. To remain able to provide adequate reference measurements, the EUDET-type beam telescopes are due for an upgrade. ALPIDE was chosen as the best available option of a pixel sensor on which to base the upgrade on. A first prototype is already in continuous user operation at the DESY II Test Beam facility. Device under test integrations with the old system can be reused with the upgraded version, requiring only minimal changes, which was an essential design specification. The 10 us readout time of ALPIDE, which is an order of magnitude smaller than that of the previously used MIMOSA26 sensor, allows for more efficient data taking. In addition, users profit from the ease of use, the very stable operation, and a high tracking efficieny. While the first prototype proves the feasibility of an upgrade of the EUDET-type beam telescopes based on ALPIDE sensors, we still aim to improve on the long-term maintainability of the new system. Thus, a second prototype is currently in production, which uses open-source components wherever possible and an architecture that is more flexible regarding specific models of central off-the-shelf components (e.g. FPGAs).

articleTitle: Ion migration: an approach to enhance the performance of perovskite CsPbBr3 γ-ray detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Uncontrolled ion migration in perovskite semiconductors is well known. Ion migration, which is often considered to be deleterious, may actually be used to improve the performance of perovskite CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> semiconductor gamma-ray detectors, as shown by our findings. In asymmetric electrode devices, ion migration may be actively managed to modify the metal-CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> interface barrier height. This is accomplished by the purposeful application of electrical biasing. The contact potential difference measurement, thermally induced current spectroscopy, and photoluminescence studies all provide evidence that ion migration plays a significant part in the process of eliminating bulk defects. The data suggests that biasing-induced ion migration in $\mathrm{C s} \mathrm{PbBr}_{3}$ leads to fewer electron traps. Higher temperature biasing accelerates ion migration, so preconditioning CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> crystals with reverse biasing may enhance performance.

articleTitle: Development of a spectral unmixing method for gamma-ray spectra analysis: application to airborne measurements.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The CEA develops and uses airborne detectors to carry out gamma mapping missions for various private and public entities, and various national and international authorities. The main objectives of these missions are: site monitoring (natural and anthropic contributions to environmental radioactivity), mapping contaminated areas, detecting and identifying radionuclides and radioactive sources. Methods for analyzing the spectra acquired during these missions are being studied, with a view to improve decision thresholds and detection limits for various radionuclides of interest. A spectral analysis method called “spectral unmixing” has been developed, using more information than the reference method based on regions of interest. This algorithm takes into account the response of the detector under study to an individual radionuclide, and estimates the proportions of the different radionuclides using a likelihood estimator. This method was shown to be accurate for reconstructing radionuclide activities, with improved sensitivity compared to the reference method [1], [2], [3]. The application of this algorithm to airborne detectors raises a number of challenging problems, such as taking into account the variability of spectral signatures linked to the environment and source shielding. Improvements linked to these themes are actually under study. The use of this method to airborne detectors should not only improve sensitivity for radionuclides of interest, but also enable full spectra analysis in real time, allowing in flight automatic nuclides identifications.

articleTitle: Study of environment-friendly gas mixtures for Resistive Plate Chambers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Resistive Plate Chambers (RPC) are gaseous detectors with excellent timing performance and are used for triggering on muons in the LHC experiments. They operate with the standard gas mixture, composed of C2H2F4/i-C4H10/SF6, because it allows the detector operation in avalanche mode, as required by the high-luminosity collider experiments. The gas density, the low current and the comfortable avalanche-streamer separation guarantee high detection efficiency, rate capability and longevity. This gas mixture has a high Global Warming Potential (GWP) of 1430 due to the presence of C2H2F4 (GWP ∼ 1450) and SF6(GWP ∼ 22400). These two gas components are not recommended for industrial uses anymore, thus their availability will be increasingly reduced over time and the search for an alternative gas mixture is of absolute priority. The LHC experiments are meanwhile adopting an intermediate solution in order to reduce C2H2F4 emissions. It consists of the addition of a small fraction of CO2(GWP=1) to the standard gas. The most critical component to replace is the SF6, because it acts as streamer suppressor, thus allowing for RPC operation at low current, for high rate capability and longevity. In this work the SF6 is replaced with the Chloro-Trifluoropropene (C3H2ClF3, GWP ∼ 5), never been tested in the RPC detectors before. The RPC performance in terms of efficiency, streamer probability, time resolution have been studied in the Gamma Irradiation Facility (GIF++) at CERN at high $\gamma$ irradiation rates, as expected at the High Luminosity LHC and at future colliders like FCC. The status of the aging campaign performed using the new gas is reported. The possibility to operate the RPCs in future experiments for the first time with a totally environment-friendly gas mixture with a total GWP ∼ 10, by replacing the C2H2F4 and SF6 with C3H2F4 and C3H2ClF3 respectively has been also studied.

articleTitle: Enhancing Particle Identification and Energy Resolution through Chromatic Calorimetry: a Proof-of-Concept Study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Calorimetry, in particle physics, involves precise energy measurement from particle interactions with detectors, offering insights into their properties. Recent advances in material science, notably in nano-material scintillators with tunable emission bandwidths, have led to chromatic calorimetry. This method tracks electromagnetic or hadronic shower progression within a module, enhancing particle identification and energy resolution by layering scintillators with varying emission wavelengths. Our study validates this method using inorganic scintillators, strategically stacked by decreasing wavelength maxima. Using electrons and pions with up to 100 GeV, we achieved analytical discrimination and longitudinal shower measurement. This proof of concept underscores chromatic calorimetry’s potential for broader applications and optimization.

articleTitle: Weight-Adjusted SBP-Based LM-MLEM Algorithm for a High-Resolution Prototype Compton Camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Objective: This study aims to address the challenges associated with the traditional image reconstruction algorithms such as the numerous artifacts and poor spatial resolution for the simple back-projection (SBP) method, as well as the lengthy iteration times and extensive noise levels for the list mode maximum likelihood expectation maximization (LM-MLEM) method. A specialized reconstruction algorithm was developed and evaluated using data from a prototype high-precision Compton camera. Methods: The Compton camera incorporates two layers of detectors. The scatter detector consists of an array of $21 \times 21$ GAGG crystals of $0.68 \times 0.68 \times 2 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ single-ended readout by an $8 \times 8$ SiPM array with an active pixel area of $2 \times 2 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. The absorber detector consists of an array of $23 \times 23$ LYSO crystals of $1.0 \times 1.0 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ dual-ended readout by $8 \times 8$ SiPM arrays with an active pixel area of $3 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$. The proposed image reconstruction algorithm utilizes an inverse projection technique to incorporate prior image data and employs parallel computing along with a weight adjustment strategy. It is named the weight-adjusted SBP-based LM-MLEM algorithm (WA-SBP-MELM). This facilitates the computation and quantification of the weights of Compton projection rings at varying positions, thereby supporting the iterative calculations required for MLEM. Data acquired with the prototype Compton camera using a 0.3 mm diameter ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ point source will be used to compare different algorithms. Results: The proposed WA-SBP-MELM algorithm resulted in improvements in spatial resolution, noise performance, and reconstruction speed compared to previous algorithms. A spatial resolution of $\sim 0.9 \mathrm{~mm}$ was achieved for the point source. In the future, data of multiple point sources and phantoms will be acquired to further evaluate the proposed algorithm.

articleTitle: Liroc and Poproc: 64-channel Fast Photon-Counting Read-Out Chips
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: LIROC and POPROC are pin-to-pin compatible read-out chips designed to read-out respectively SiPM and MCP-PMT or MA-PMT. The two read-out integrated circuits embed for each channel a preamplifier followed by a discriminator and a differential output buffer. LIROC features a RF voltage amplifier including an input DC adjustment to correct for SiPM non-uniformity. POPROC features a current-conveyor more suitable for low capacitance detector such as PMT, MA-PMT or MCP-PMT. The two read-out chips output each channel trigger signal allowing time of arrival (TOA) and time over threshold (TOT) measurements. Both read-out chains have a bandwidth in the GHz range to allow photon counting over 300 MHz, double-pulse separation below 3 ns and jitter on TOA better than 20ps FWHM. Trigger outputs are very low voltage differential CLPS (CERN low power signaling) and are compatible with the CERN PicoTDC and most of the FPGAs on the market allowing a large panel of solution for the data acquisition to cover all scientific instrumentation requirements.

articleTitle: The Hardware implementation and Testing of the Full-function Global Common Module prototype for ATLAS Phase-II upgrade
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC) is set to become operational in 2029, aiming to achieve instantaneous luminosities 5-7.5 times of the nominal value of the LHC. This poses significant challenges to the design of the Trigger and Data Acquisition systems. To address these challenges, a baseline architecture has been chosen for the ATLAS Phase-II upgrade, relying on a single-level hardware trigger known as the Level-0 Trigger. This trigger has a maximum rate of 1 MHz and a latency of $10 \mu \mathrm{s}$. The Global Trigger performs complex algorithms, akin to those currently used in Phase-I high-level trigger software (such as Topoclustering), on full-granularity calorimeter data. The Global Trigger is divided into three sublayers: the Multiplexer Processor (MUX) layer, the Global Event Processor (GEP) layer, and the Global to Central Trigger Processor interface (gCTPi). A full-function Global Common Module (GCM) hardware prototype has been designed to fulfill the requirements of all three sublayers of the Global Trigger, featuring different firmware loads. This GCM prototype, based on the ATCA form factor, incorporates two of the latest AMD (Xilinx) Versal Premium devices VP1802 and twenty Samtec 12-channel 25 Gb/s FireFly optical engines. These devices double the density of the Virtex UltraScale+ FPGA VU13P used in the previous design and include an integrated System-on-Chip (SoC) with a completely new architecture. The development of an ATCA blade with two large FPGAs and about 240 optical links running at $25 \mathrm{~Gb} / \mathrm{s}$ is a very challenging task. The power integrity, signal integrity, and thermal simulations, hardware design considerations, functionalities, and performance test results of this GCM prototype will be presented.

articleTitle: Development of pixelated TlBr detectors with self-trigger pixel ASICs for Compton-PET hybrid camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Although simultaneous multi-nuclide imaging technology has been required in nuclear medicine, the conventional imaging technologies, such as positron emission tomography (PET) and single photon computed emission tomography (SPECT), are difficult to integrate into a single system. For simultaneous PET and SPECT nuclides imaging, we have proposed and developed a Compton-PET hybrid camera that can visualize PET and SPECT nuclides simultaneously using PET and Compton imaging, respectively. Highquality PET and Compton imaging require a high time resolution and a high energy resolution. Therefore, we have been developing pixelated thallium bromide (TIBr) semiconductors detector to realize both high time and high energy resolutions in a single detector as an absorber. TlBr semiconductor detectors are suitable for Compton-PET hybrid camera due to its good characteristics: high energy resolution (1-2% FWHM for 662 keV), high time resolution (300 - 400 ps) by detecting Cherenkov photon. In this study, we developed a self-trigger energy-resolving pixel application specific integrated circuit to bond with the pixelated TlBr crystals. The pixel size is $200 \mu \mathrm{m} \times 200 \mu \mathrm{m}$ and pixels were arranged in $16 \times 16$ arrays. Each pixels comprises an analog circuit and a digital circuit and trigger signals are generated from a gamma-ray hit pixel. The simulated maximum energy of dynamic range of a pixel was approximately 800 keV. The simulated equivalent noise charge was 57.0 e rms at a sensor capacitance of 25 fF.

articleTitle: Handheld Backscatter Imaging for Security Forces Detector Characterization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With advances in single sided handheld backscatter imaging and their incorporation into security applications, detector characterization is essential to operator feedback, image enhancement, and decision making. While a well-trained operator has the ability to discern contraband materials during inspections, understanding the limits of an imager’s resolution at varying distances inform additional inspections or advise threat scenarios. This research characterizes the detector response of a Nighthawk handheld backscatter imaging device developed by Viken Detection in laboratory conditions utilizing High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE) phantoms. The Nighthawk uses a collimated millimeter-sized pencil x-ray beam that scans 150 times per second laterally along a fan arc to generate a series of 1D linear images and then compile to a 2D image of the phantom. Sampling occurred using line pair bar slits of different interval frequencies and the straight edges of the HDPE phantoms at different separation distances from the NightHawk front surface ranging from 10 centimeters to 1 meters. The Nighthawk was placed on a moving table while phantom was kept stationary to maintain consistent scan speed during image capture. Image processing relied on analyzing the contrast visibilities of line pair phantoms and edge responses of a slanted edge phantom. The slanted edge image allowed over-sampling a sharp edge and then an Edge Spread Function and Modulation Transfer Function were derived to characterize system resolutions at different imaging distances.

articleTitle: Time-of-Flight Requirements to Reduce the Effect of Acollinearity on PET Spatial Resolution
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Spatial resolution in positron emission tomography (PET) is degraded by the acollinearity of annihilation photons (APA), resulting in a blurring of the order of 2 mm FWHM for whole-body PET scanners. We have previously shown that perfect Time-of-Flight (TOF) resolution can effectively mitigate this blurring and overcome the conventional (i.e., TOF-less) theoretical spatial resolution limit. However, the TOF resolution and coincidence event statistics required to achieve a noticeable improvement in spatial resolution remain unexplored. The purpose of this study is to investigate these requirements, specifically for whole-body and total-body scanners. Using a hypothetical $81-\mathrm{cm}$ diameter scanner with $2-\mathrm{mm}$ wide detectors, we show that ultrahigh TOF resolution (e.g., 13 ps FWHM) yields observable improvements in spatial resolution over a range of event statistics. Furthermore, this study reveals that lower TOF resolutions (e.g., 26 or 65 ps FWHM) may suffice to mitigate APA effects on spatial resolution, especially for the oblique tubes of response of large 3D systems, which are subject to more significant APA blurring. Therefore, ultrafast TOF would not only reduce APA blurring, but also alleviate the non-stationary nature of spatial resolution in long axial FOV total-body PET scanners.

articleTitle: A deep learning-based technique to for crystal identification of PET detector utilizing LYSO background: A monte carlo study
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the modern Positron Emission Tomography (PET), the utilization of 2D arrays of scintillation crystals in conjunction with Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays is prevalent. Accurate segmentation of the characteristic flood map response is essential for the precise determination of the interaction site of annihilation photons within the scintillation crystals. This crystal identification is not only crucial for system modeling but also for comprehensive detector characterization and performance analysis. Traditionally, the identification process relies on flood maps acquired from a radiative source, which can be both time-consuming and prone to inaccuracies. In this study, we introduce an innovative, deep learning-based technique for the automatic crystal identification of flood maps, harnessing the inherent radiation from the LYSO background. Our approach employs a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to enhance the process, offering a more efficient and accurate alternative. To substantiate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted Monte Carlo simulations, exploring various CNN configurations, including layer arrangements and kernel dimensions. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed CNN-based method is highly effective, offering an advancement in PET detector calibration.

articleTitle: A Cost-effective Dual-ended DOI PET Detector Based on BGO Crystal Array and 45-degree Tilted SiPMs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Depth-of-interaction (DOI) encoding capability is essential in positron emission tomography (PET) scanners, especially for high-resolution imaging such as small animal and organ-dedicated PET. A dual-ended readout scheme provides accurate DOI estimation and easy calibration among the DOI encoding approaches. Our previous study introduced a cost-effective DOI-encoded PET detector using LSO crystals and 45-degree tilted SiPMs. This study investigates a combination of 45-degree tilted SiPMs with BGO crystals, leveraging its benefits of higher stopping power, lower radiation, and cost-effectiveness. The performance of this configuration with BGO and LSO was comparatively evaluated. To minimize the timing performance of our detector, the timing signal was generated by a fast-timing readout circuit using a balun transformer and RF amplifiers. Additionally, the triggered signals of our detector were generated by the energy signals. The timing, energy, and DOI resolution with the LSO crystal were 262 ps FWHM, 12.3% FHWM, and 2.7 mm. The timing, energy, and DOI resolution with the BGO crystal were 1.8 ns FWHM, 32.0% FHWM, and 5.4 mm. The timing and energy performance of our detector with LSO crystal improved, while the DOI performance slightly decreased. The performance of our detector with BGO crystal was worse than that of the LSO-based configuration due to lower light yield and slow decay of the BGO crsytal. Further study will optimize the parameter of the fast-timing signal readout circuit to enhance the performance of the BGO-based configuration.

articleTitle: Optimization of a Row-Column Multiplexing Circuit Dedicated to the TOFPET2 ASIC Module
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multiplexing is a key technology for development of clinical positron emission tomography (PET) scanners to minimize the complexity of their electronics and data acquisition systems. Therefore, various multiplexing techniques have been proposed. In this study, we present the optimization results of a row-column summing multiplexing circuit dedicated to the TOFPET2 ASIC module for our next generation whole gamma imaging systems. We used two different detector designs, the one-to-one coupling detector and the crosshair light sharing (CLS) detector. The one-to-one coupling detector consists of an $8 \times 8$ array of fast-LGSO crystals $\left(3.1 \times 3.1 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right)$ and an $8 \times 8$ silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array (Hamamatsu, S14161-3050HS). The CLS detector consists of a $14 \times 14$ array of fast-LGSO crystals $\left(1.45 \times 1.45 \times 15 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right)$ and the same type of $8 \times 8$ SiPM array. The TOFPET2 ASIC module was used for data acquisition. For coincidence detection, a pair of two identical detectors was used. A ${ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$ source (1 MBq) was placed at the center of the detectors and data were taken for 1 min. The optimal resistor value of the row-column summing multiplexing circuit was investigated. Then, the effects of the multiplexing circuit on the detector performance were evaluated. The experimental results showed that the optimal resistor value of the multiplexing circuit was $300 \Omega$ in terms of crystal map quality. For the one-to-one coupling detector, the energy resolution and coincidence timing resolution (CTR) were degraded about 11% ($11.7 \pm 0.5 \%$ to $13.0 \pm 0.4 \%$) and $45 \%$ ($343 \pm 33$ ps to $497 \pm 21$ ps) with the multiplexing. For the CLS detector, the energy resolution and CTR were degraded around 11 % (11.7 ±0.5 % to $13.0 \pm 0.4 \%$) and $45 \%(343 \pm 33 \mathrm{ps}$ to $497 \pm 21 \mathrm{ps})$ with the multiplexing. In the future, we plan to further enhance the CTR by implementing the pole-zero cancellation circuit or diode-based multiplexing.

articleTitle: Characterization of High-Temperature SiPM Noise
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper investigates the response of two silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) (the MicroFJ-30035 by Onsemi and the ASD-NUV3S-P by Advansid) as a function of temperature. Their breakdown voltage and gain are measured at five different temperatures and compared, and their performance at room temperature is compared. SiPMs are solid state photon detectors with small form factor, low-voltage power requirements, and excellent time resolution. However, their performance depends on several different parameters and changes dramatically with temperature, which impedes their use in high temperature environments. Their response must be further studied and characterized before SiPMs can be employed in harsh environments. We found that the breakdown voltage of the Advansid is 33.3% more sensitive to temperature than the Onsemi and that the change in gain as a function of temperature was comparable between the technologies. However, the Advansid displays a lower level of noise, with a 24.6% reduction in optical crosstalk and 34.2% decrease in dark count rate, when compared with the Onsemi. The Onsemi was found to have a 154% increase in gain compared with the Advansid.

articleTitle: A 3D-printed Thick-GEM as sole gain element
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A small 3D-printed Thick-GEM (THGEM) is used as the sole active gain element in a $10 \mathrm{~cm} \times 10$ cm micropattern gaseous detector (MPGD). The THGEM features three separate board sectors, each with 0.7 mm diameter holes that have rim annuli of different sizes ($0.1,0.15,0.2 \mathrm{~mm}$). We comment on various challenges encountered with the 3D-printing process for this board. Together with a drift electrode and a standard strip readout board, the THGEM is assembled into an MPGD. When exposed to an alpha source and with HV applied across the THGEM, a pulse signal is clearly established on the readout. No additional gaseous pre-amplification stage is required for operation. The sector with 0.15 mm rims achieves $10^{4}$ gas gain. We study the gain behavior over time up to two days. In the first hours of operation, the gain varies considerably, presumably due to charging up of the THGEM structure, but stabilizes after about 24 hours when continuously powered and irradiated.

articleTitle: 3D list-mode surrogate-MLEM for dual-scanner PET image reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) plays a crucial role in cancer diagnosis and monitoring despite its comparatively lower resolution to CT and MRI. Limited-angle, high-resolution PET scanners attempt to balance system cost with high-resolution. In this study, we propose a novel approach using a dual-system setup constituting a low-resolution 2π PET scanner and a high-resolution limited-angle PET scanner. We introduce a 3-D list-mode Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization (MLEM) algorithm, termed Surrogate MLEM, which incorporates data from non-synchronous imaging on both scanners. We perform a Monte Carlo simulation of this experimental setup using the high-resolution UCSC 2-Panel PET Scanner (2P) and the lower-resolution GE Discovery 690 WB PET Scanner, comparing the images from each system and the surrogate model. Our results demonstrate the Surrogate Scanner significantly reduces limite-dangle artifacts of the 2P Scanner and enhances contrast recovery over both systems. This approach shows promise for enhancing PET imaging in challenging anatomical regions like the head and neck of asynchronous coincidences.

articleTitle: Half-Volt Power Supply Charge-Sensitive Amplifier - Discriminator Chain for Binary Readout in Small-Footprint Pixel Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A signal processing chain, comprising of a chargesensitive amplifier, discriminator and interface to the event-driven readout network tailored for small footprint O(20 micrometer pitch) pixel detectors with binary readout is presented. The circuit operates with only 0.5 V power supply, delivering high sensitivity of 1 mV/electron and ENC below 10 electrons. The design is based on the self-cascoded field effect transistor topology in the CSA’s first stage for efficient charge multiplication, using translinear pole-zero cancellation effect. The second stage is an integrator, realizing charge to voltage conversion with a currentchoked source follower that enables resetting. The final stage is a discriminator in the form of a simple Schmitt gate with an unconventional threshold setting given by the power supply of the Schmitt gate. The design was carried out to consume about 75 nW of power, but providing response with TimeWalk not exceeding a couple of hundreds nanoseconds. The design was realized in a 65 nm process suitable for Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors on the increased resistivity substrate and uses highly minimized number of bias lines to increase immunity to mismatches.

articleTitle: Development of a 256-to-4 signal multiplexing readout for high resolution PET detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We developed a small animal PET named S-PET, which features LYSO/BGO phoswich detector (crystal size, LYSO: $0.79 \times 0.79 \times 5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$; BGO: $1.22 \times 1.22 \times 7.5 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$). The system utilized ASIC that enables the individual reading of each MPPC pixel, providing more detailed information for event detection. Nevertheless, this readout approach comes with a relatively high cost. In this work, a multiplexing readout circuit was developed capable of reading 256 signals from 4 MPPCs and converting them into 4 position encoded signals. This approach only needs 40 electronic channels to read the 40 detector blocks in the S-PET system, leading to significant savings on hardware costs. Our preliminary tests demonstrated the feasibility of using this readout method to interpret data from the LYSO/BGO phoswich detector, and delayed charge integration (DCI) technique is used to discriminate between the LYSO and BGO events. Both the LYSO and the BGO flood images demonstrated high-quality position decoding in the central region, but a slight degradation was observed in the edge areas, indicating the need for further optimization in our next step. The average energy resolution was 14.3±4.6% and 15.2±4.7% for the LYSO and BGO crystals, respectively. In conclusion, preliminary results support the feasibility of the developed signal multiplexing method in reading LYSO/BGO phoswich detector, which introduces an alternative, cost effective approach for data acquisition in the S-PET system.

articleTitle: Performance of a Small Animal PET Detector Based on Dual-Ended Readout and Multicycle-Encoding FPGA ADC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Developing high performance detector with compact and robust readout electronics for small animal PET systems is crucial to preclinical molecular imaging and biological studies. In this study, dual-ended readout depth-of-interaction (DOI) PET detectors were developed utilizing our recently developed low-noise and compact readout electronics based on multicycle-encoding FPGA-ADC. Each detector consists of two $8 \times 8$ arrays of $2 \times 2 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPMs coupled to both ends of a $20 \times 20$ array of $0.73 \times 0.73 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ polished LYSOs with a 0.8 mm pitch. The performance of the detector in terms of flood histogram, energy resolution and timing resolution were measured at various bias voltages ranging from 52.25 to 53.75 V with 0.25 V intervals, and two different temperatures, $5{ }^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ and $15^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. All crystals in the detectors were clearly resolved under these conditions, with optimal performance achieved at a bias voltage set to 53.0 V and a temperature of $5^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Under the optimal condition, the average energy, timing, and DOI resolutions across all crystals were $23.16 \pm 7.62 \%, 4.54 \pm 1.21 \mathrm{~ns}$, and $2.98 \pm 0.51 \mathrm{~mm}$, respectively. These results demonstrate the developed PET detectors are suitable for use in high-performance small animal PET system.

articleTitle: Imaging at Extremes: How do High-Z Sensors Perform at Modern Light Sources?
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent upgrades to synchrotrons [1] and the arrival of XFELs [2] mean, within the photon science community, the need for detectors capable of imaging with high spatial resolution (100 mm), at hard X-ray energies ($\gt10 \mathrm{keV}$) and extreme fluxes ($\gt10^{9} \mathrm{ph}. \mathrm{s}^{-1} \mathrm{~mm}^{-2}$) has never been greater.Historically, the development of materials such as CdZnTe have focused on a drive for ever higher electron mobility-lifetime with the aim of delivering high energy resolution in thick detectors $(\gt1 \mathrm{~cm})$ for nuclear imaging applications. Today, spectroscopic grade CdZnTe material routinely has $\mu_{\mathrm{e}} \tau_{\mathrm{e}}$ values in excess of $10^{-2} \mathrm{~cm}^{2} \mathrm{~V}^{-1}$ delivering spectroscopic performance at 662 keV of <1% FWHM [3]. The cost of this impressive performance? A reduction in hole transport properties with significant implications for imaging at extreme fluxes.The lifetimes of holes in these materials are typically orders of magnitude lower than that of electrons ($0.2 \mu \mathrm{s}$ compared to $11.0 \mu \mathrm{s}$) [4]. This low hole lifetime combined with an intrinsically low mobility, leads to dynamic polarisation effects under synchrotron-relevant levels of flux [5]. These polarisation effects limit the application of these detectors at photon light sources.The development of colour CT for medical/security imaging has broadened interest in high-Z sensors. These applications typically use X-ray energies $\gt50 \mathrm{keV}$ and fluxes of the order $10^{8} \mathrm{ph}. \mathrm{s}^{-1} \mathrm{~mm}^{-2}$, very similar to the requirements of photon light sources. The development of materials, such as the HF-CdZnTe [5], for use in these commercial application areas have potentially significant benefits for the photon light source communities.In this contribution, an appraisal of the status of the most promising high-Z detector materials for photon science (Cd(Zn) Te and $\mathrm{GaAs}: \mathrm{Cr})$ will be given. Drawing upon recent measurements made at STFC/Diamond [6] and ESRF [7], this talk aims to address the question, are these high-Z materials ready for use at a new generation of photon light sources?

articleTitle: Neural network based event selection on FPGA for COMET Phase-I
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A neural network based online event selection is being developed for the COMET (COherent Muon To Electron Transition) Phase-I experiment. This experiment employs the world’s highest intensity muon beam and a detector system comprising a drift chamber and a trigger hodoscope. Such a highintensity muon beam would generate significant backgrounds, leading to high trigger rates. Thus, we are developing a machine learning-based online classification algorithm on FPGA, that utilizes information from both the drift chamber and the trigger hodoscope. The neural network is constructed using COMET Phase-I Monte Carlo simulation data and will be implemented on an FPGA board developed for COMET Phase-I. We are investigating the classification performance and latency of this algorithm. We plan to present its expected trigger efficiency and contribution to the experimental sensitivity.

articleTitle: Development of Multi-Channel DXA Detector for Cone Beam Data Acquisition
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Linear-type fan beam detectors have been commonly used in dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), which requires long scan time and high radiation exposure when imaging a large area. These problems could be resolved by employing array-type cone beam detectors that could provide a wide field-of-view with a single exposure. The purpose of this study was to develop an array-type multi-channel cone beam DXA detector consisting of SiPM based scintillation detector, analog signal processing circuit and FPGA based TOT. The detector was composed of an 8 × 8 array of 1 × 1 × 2 mm<sup>3</sup> LYSO coupled with an 8 × 8 array of 1 × 1 mm<sup>2</sup> SiPM. Analog signal processing circuit consisted of a resistor-based symmetric charge division readout to reduce the 64 signals of SiPMs to 16 and a diode-based time-over-threshold (ToT) to measure the time and energy information. A 16-ch tapped delay-line TDC was implemented in FPGA to measure the rising edge and the width of the ToT output. To evaluate the energy resolution of the cone beam DXA detector, the energy spectra were acquired using Am-241 and Co-57 point sources. The 64 energy spectra were also acquired using X-ray generator with 83 kVp and 0.2 mA and a Ce filter with K-edge absorption at 40.4 keV. The count variations of the low- and high-energy regions were measured for 5-minutes intervals over 30 minutes to evaluate the uniformity and stability of the detector.
