The energy resolutions were 25.6% and 18.1% at 60 keV and 122 keV, respectively. Two energy peaks in low- and high-energy regions were clearly discriminated in the 64 energy spectra. Average count variations of the low and high energy regions were 2.4% and 2.3%, respectively. These results indicated that the proposed cone beam DXA detector had sufficient energy resolution, uniformity and stability to discriminate low-energy X-rays and could be useful for cone beam DXA detector. For further study, expansion to 256-ch consisting of 4 modules of 64-ch detector is being studied.

articleTitle: MCNP Modeling of Gratings-based Phase Contrast X-ray Imaging for Nuclear Security
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The characterization of materials is an essential aspect of nuclear forensics and safeguards. Verifying and examining materials is one way to help prevent proliferation. It is important to determine small changes that can indicate the diversion of special nuclear material. Conventionally, nuclear forensic examinations have been carried out through destructive imaging techniques. Because of this, the availability of a nondestructive image acquisition technique would help preserve samples for further examination and attribution. Traditional X-ray imaging has failed to differentiate between similar materials in a sample due to relying solely on transmission through the object. Gratings-based phase contrast X-ray imaging (GBX), on the other hand, allows for the extraction of three different signals: absorption, differential phase contrast that highlights edges in the material, and dark-field that measures scattering in the material. The application of GBX to characterize materials is explored. A sensitivity study was conducted on Monte Carlo N-Particle Transport Code (MCNP) in order to investigate the use of GBX on forensics applications.

articleTitle: A Comparison of Various Attenuation Map Generation Methods for MR Coils in PET/MR
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: To achieve quantitatively accurate PET images, careful consideration of photon attenuation and scatter is essential. In PET/MR, patient attenuation and scatter correction (ASC) factors are often estimated using pseudo-CT images derived from MR images. Additionally, ASC due to MR hardware is addressed by registering a previously calculated attenuation map for MR coils to the patient attenuation maps given their positions. In this study, we investigate various methods for calculating MR coil attenuation maps and demonstrate their effects on PET quantification. Attenuation maps of an MR head and neck coil were calculated using single-energy CT, dualenergy CT, photon-counting CT, and 511 keV transmission imaging. PET images of a uniform phantom inserted within the head and neck coil and reconstructed using different attenuation maps were compared against the case of ignoring the coil in the attenuation maps. Analysis of the reconstructed PET images revealed an average quantitative error of $(5.4 \pm 3.1) \%,(2.0 \pm 2.7) \%$, $(-1.1 \pm 1.8) \%,(-2.6 \pm 1.1) \%$, and $(-15.3 \pm 5.4) \%$ when using single-energy CT, dual-energy CT, photon-counting CT, transmission-based, and ignoring coil attenuation maps, respectively. Analysis of the reconstructed PET images suggested that visual artifacts and quantitative errors appear when using standard single and dual-energy CT attenuation maps, and that photoncounting CT is likely the most reliable approach for estimating hardware attenuation maps in PET/MR.

articleTitle: Comparison Between the 3D-CBS Screening and the Liquid Bio and Other Screening of Cancer Procedures
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This article provides the comparison between the expected results in cancer deaths and costs reduction from non-invasive cancer screening procedures. These two screening procedures are the 3D-CBS (3-D Complete Body Screening) and the Liquid Bio (Liquid Biopsy). A comparison will also be made on the efficacy of the officially approved and currently used mammography, colorectal and PAP-smear screening procedures in many countries. We should all face the same challenges against cancer, not a competition between each other, and should accept the efficacy test on a sample population in a specific location with respect to the mortality rate of the previous 20 years in the same location. The author’s 3D-CBS invention from the year 2000 can provide the features of a non-invasive, 2-minute, safe, low-cost, efficient, cancer-screening test, that can detect tumors with only 100 cancer cells that no other device can provide simultaneously. It revolutionizes medicine by recording anomalous biological processes simultaneously of the entire body, by basing the diagnosis on the trend of anomalies rather than from a single exam, by extracting patterns of pre-diseases formation, however the 3D-CBS was never funded. The Liquid Bio is a blood test aimed to detect a tumor’s mutational profile. It was announced in 2007 as a breakthrough in Time magazine. In 2012 at the WCC in Montreal was announced to provide a sensitivity greater than $94 \%$ and specificity greater than $91 \%$ in the early detection of the 4 big cancer killers, but the test was later abandoned. Liquid biopsy received conspicuous funding but did not produce results in cancer deaths reduction, although it has recently gained a lot of traction. Mammography and colorectal screening are not effective because there is no significant mortality rate difference between countries who do or don’t. PAP smear screening is effective but is a small percent of the total 10 million/year cancer deaths.

articleTitle: Future LASE Plans to Characterize WbLS for BUTTON Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Livermore Attenuation and Scattering Experiment (LASE) system was designed to quantify the attenuation and scattering of diverse candidate fill materials throughout the visible spectrum. LASE is an optical property measurement device for candidate liquids for neutrino detectors. It is designed as a horizontal and adjustable path-length attenuation and scattering system that operates in complete isolation from the atmosphere with a high degree of vibration insensitivity. Scattering measurements are available at multiple angles and adjustable beam polarization angles which allows for reliable quantitative scattering measurements and phase-function reconstruction. Attenuation measurements are made by measuring changes in laser beam intensity as a function of liquid column length. The performance of the device was benchmarked using deionized (DI) water. and found to accurately determine the optical properties of candidate fill materials for neutrino detectors. In the near future, a similar device will be installed at the Boulby Underground Technology Testbed Observing Neutrinos (BUTTON). BUTTON is a technology testbed for evaluating liquids and purification systems for neutrino and dark matter detectors.

articleTitle: Large Size Fast Decay YSO Scintillation Crystal
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present in this work Ca doped large size YSO crystal with fast decay. YSO crystals with diameter of 85 mm and 200 mm in length was grown by CZ method at different doping level. Samples with dimension of 20X20X5 mm were made. Optical and scintillation properties including transmittance, scintillation spectrum, light output (L.O.), decay kinetics and scintillation afterglow (AF) were investigated. No obvious absorption band was found within wavelength interested. The L.O. was determined to be 30000 photons/MeV for a $\mathbf{0. 0 4 \%}$ Ca doped sample. The decay time was found to be 33 ns measured by time correlated single photon counting method for the 1% doping. The AF, with Ca doping, was found a little bit higher than un-doped sample, yet at a very low level. With high L.O., fast decay, low afterglow and non-radioactive the Ca doped YSO is promising for space application and nuclear imaging.

articleTitle: Direct image reconstruction using deep image prior in limited-angle SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Detecting the gamma-ray emitted from the radiopharmaceuticals in the body, the projection data for SPECT image reconstruction can be acquired. If the projection data are insufficient in the cases, such as restricting the projection angle range to shorten the scanning time or suppress the exposure dose of patient, the reconstructed image is distorted. Since no image reconstruction method has been established for the limited-angle problem, therefore we proposed the novel method using deep image prior (DIP) in last year’s conference. The purpose of this study is to clarify how accurate the proposed method can reconstruct images without dependence on a limited-angle range. The numerical simulation was performed to compare the image quality among the proposed method, ML-EM and MAP-EM. The BrainWeb numerical phantom was used, and the pixel values of gray matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid were assigned to 1, 0.25, and 0.05 to simulate the relative concentrations observed in blood flow pattern. The projection is assumed as ideal and parallel beam, and the projection angle range was changed from 30 degrees to 60 degrees. The images reconstructed by ML-EM and MAP-EM were distorted in the limited-angle range of directions. On the other hand, the proposed DIP method was able to reconstruct the image more accurately than the other methods. We found that proposed method allows images to be more accurately reconstructed with little dependence on limited-angle range.

articleTitle: Development of methods for industrial-scale production of Resistive Plate Chambers for large-area muon detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) represent a cost-effective detector technology for efficient muon detection over large areas, providing sub-nanosecond response and excellent time resolution. Their background rate capability and longevity in the context of hadron colliders have been enhanced by an order of magnitude through the reduction in gas gap thickness between the high-pressure phenolic laminate (HPL) electrodes from 2 mm to 1 mm. The ATLAS muon spectrometer will undergo a major upgrade for operation at the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) by installing triplets of such thin-gap RPCs in the inner layer of the barrel muon system of the ATLAS detector in LHC’s long shutdown 3 to maximize the detector’s muon trigger acceptance and efficiency. Almost 1000 RPC gas gaps have to be produced for the ATLAS upgrade. In order to avoid the dependence on a single gas gap supplier and to increase the overall gas gap production rate, the construction and certification of the RPCs have been established at two new companies in Germany, as well as at the Max Planck Institute for Physics in Munich. This was made possible by adapting the gas gap assembly procedure to the infrastructure and tools available at industrial manufacturers. Two RPC gas gap prototypes per manufacturer were used to certify the methods. The efficiency and time resolution were measured in a high energy muon beam at CERN Gamma Irradation Facility (GIF++) at different gamma background rates and found to be in agreement with the requirements. Real-size prototypes for ATLAS also passed an aging test at the GIF++ where they were exposed to the maximum photon dose expected at the HL-LHC. The gas gap manufacturing procedure and the results of the certification will be presented.

articleTitle: Impact of Re-framing High-Dose Scans for the Training of Neural Networks for Denoising Low-Dose PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In PET, patient radiation exposure is mainly determined by the administered amount of radiotracer and its metabolism. By lowering the activity, the radiation dose is minimized at the cost of increased statistical fluctuations in the data; the latter increases the image noise level. Many artificial intelligence (AI) approaches have been proposed for image denoising of low-dose PET scans. Supervised AI algorithms require the use of labeled datasets, with the high-dose PET image as the target and the low-dose image as the input. This approach assumes that the performance of the PET systems is the same in the two activity regimes. However, the contribution of random coincidences, pile-up and dead-time effects depend on event rates. This study focuses on comparing two approaches to generating the training pair and their impact on the performance of a 3D U-Net using Monte Carlo simulations. The package GATE, v.9.1, was used to simulate a standard BMI XCAT phantom and a Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT. Digital twins of 5-min <sup>18</sup>F-FDG-PET scans for an activity of 3 MBq/kg were obtained to simulate two low-dose scenarios: injected low-dose, and injected high-dose re-framed to low-dose. The results showed that both methods of generating low-dose datasets yield comparable results without degradation in image quality. However, differences were observed in the random fraction for the high-dose dataset, i.e., the texture of the data noise changed. This study shows that using high-dose data is suitable for training of AI-based denoising algorithms on image space; nevertheless, denoising algorithms working on the projection space might overestimate the noise level within the data. Future work will include other activity concentrations and scan durations, incorporating motion, and the use of other radioisotopes.

articleTitle: The properties of SiPM signal with passive quenching
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) is an advanced photon detector consisting of multiple Single Photon Avalanche Diodes (SPADs) connected in parallel, with each SPAD equipped with quenching elements. When photons arrive, SPADs trigger avalanches, generating a substantial number of charge carriers. These carriers encounter impedance from the quenching elements, leading to their accumulation in the depletion layer and reduction of its electric field, thus terminating the avalanche process. After quenching, the quenching elements restrict the charge carriers from exiting the device, thereby shaping the single-photon response signal. This study employs transient simulations of passive quenching circuits in SiPMs with varied quenching elements to investigate the impact of the quenching element parameter selection on the SiPM output signal characteristics.

articleTitle: 3D-FLOW OPRA: A Revolutionary Electronic Instrument Maximizing Performance, Flexibility And Cost-Effectiveness For Detection And Imaging Technology
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The 3D-Flow OPRA is a new electronic instrument and device targeted to solve problems of Detection and Imaging Technology. It has the capability to detect multi-dimensional objects in real time on data arriving in parallel from a matrix of thousands of transducers at ultra-high speed sent to an equivalent matrix of thousands of 3D-Flow processors which execute programmable Object Pattern Recognition Algorithms (OPRA) with neighboring data exchange (3x3, 5x5,..). The bypass switch of the 3D-Flow architecture allows the execution of uninterruptable algorithms for a time longer than the interval between two consecutive input data sets. The 3D-Flow pyramid provides reduction from thousands of input channels to one or a few output channels. The 3DFlow processors can execute in one “OPRA step” up to 26 operations in less than 3 ns. It compares the reference object (shape) with billions of objects per second while sustaining an input data rate of several million frames per second with zero dead-time. It can measure all kinds of phenomena and identify all kinds of objects in 3-D that create an electrical signal in response to physical stimuli (e.g. from CCD, APD, PMT, SiPM, PADs, etc.). It provides advanced triggering capabilities. A 3D-Flow system with max 12,800 Gbps input bandwidth, 10,000 electronic input channels, 50,000 x 3D-Flow processors and the capability to execute up to 40 “OPRA steps” on each processor is technology-independent, feasible in a 36 cm cube of electronics consuming less than 6 kW at a cost of less than ${\$}$15 per channel. The 3D-Flow conceptual design allows to increase input data rate and the complexity of the real-time algorithm to satisfy the most stringent requirements. The inventor has faced many adversities and suppressions that have delayed its implementation. This caused a monetary burden on taxpayers and curbed the advancement of science that calls for an investigation to fix science as stated in the Oct. 2018 issue of Scientific American.

articleTitle: Effect of Fractional Glandular Breast Composition on Synchrotron Breast CT Dose
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With clinical breast imaging trials fast approaching at the Australian Synchrotron using phase contrast CT, characterisation of surface radiation detectors such as MOSkins are necessary to determine safe radiation doses during the screening of patients. A GEANT4 study was conducted to comprehend the effects of different beam energy, different glandular fractions and breast radii on the dose delivered to the breast. The results were compared to experimental measurements using MOSkins in water-equivalent breast phantom to validate the experimental and simulated results, and we obtained agreement within 95% confidence between the simulation and experimental results. We simulated glandular fractions of 0%, 50% and 100% with different breast cup sizes at 32 keV to optimise the applications of synchrotron CT for patients. The results distinguished a difference between a homogeneous composition of 0% and 100%, and heterogeneous composition of 50% glandular fractions, as an anthropomorphic phantom. 0% and 100% agreed with the homogenous water-equivalent phantom, whereas 50% glandular fraction present with a necessity of further studies of the anthropomorphic phantom.

articleTitle: Energy resolution of the GRAiNITA protoype detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We will present the outcomes of a GEANT4 simulation study of the energy resolution that can be achieved with a GRAiNITA detector. GRAiNITA is a new-generation sampling calorimeter based on the use of high-stopping power inorganic scintillator grains evenly distributed in a volume of high-density liquid, as absorber. As in a shashlik detector, the scintillation light produced by the grains, can be collected to the photodetectors by means of wavelength-shifting fibers. The characterization of a GRAiNITA prototype, filled with ZnWO<inf>4</inf> grains, proved that a stochastic fluctuation of $1 \% / \sqrt{E}[\mathrm{GeV}]$ on the energy resolution, due to photo-electron statistics, is at reach [1]. While this result is really encouraging, the estimation of the constant term contribution to the energy resolution, due the non-uniformity of the detector response and to the containment of the electromagnetic shower in the detection volume, remains crucial to demonstrate the real effectiveness of GRAiNITA.

articleTitle: Feasibility study of a LYSO-SiPM based prototype for hybrid Compton and PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a prototype for hybrid Compton and PET imaging system aiming to enhance data utilization and enable concurrent imaging of multiple radiopharmaceuticals. The prototype comprises two existing detectors utilizing LYSO-SiPM in our laboratory. One detector consists of a $50 \times 50$ array of LYSO crystals, each measuring $0.9 \times 0.9 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ with 1 mm pitches, while the other detector comprises a $25 \times 25$ array of LYSO crystals, each measuring $1.9 \times 1.9 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ with 2 mm pitches. These detectors are mounted on a rotational stage, allowing them to function as either a Compton camera or a PET detector pair. The 64-channel signals from the SiPMs of each detector are processed through a capacitive multiplexing circuit to yield four position-weighted outputs. Distinct energy windows were utilized for discriminating Compton events from PET events. Energy resolution and energy-channel relationships were calibrated using multiple sources. The measured average energy resolution (Full width at half maximum, FWHM) for both detectors were 17.5% and 15.2%, respectively. Initial experimental results indicate an angular resolution (FWHM) of 8.6° for the system working in Compton imaging mode. A V-shaped tube injected with ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ solution were clearly reconstructed to further verify the system’s imaging capability in Compton imaging mode. Simulation as well as experimental imaging studies show that the system can detect tumors as small as 1 mm in diameter when working in PET imaging mode. Mouse bone PET imaging was successfully conducted, with results matching well with CT images. This technology holds great potential in advancing the development of physiological function modalities.

articleTitle: Model-based Delays Estimation for Long-axial Field-of-view (LAFOV) PET/CT Scanners
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent developments in LAFOV PET/CT scanners have improved image quality by enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio, achieved through increased sensitivity with lower injected activity compared to traditional PET/CT scanners. Despite the significant enhancement in sensitivity with these new machines and the continuous trend towards lowering the dose, there remains some interest in administering higher activity for certain clinical applications. For instance, myocardial perfusion imaging using rubidium-82 (Rb-82), particularly for obese patients, might need higher injected activity to assess coronary artery disease more accurately. The administration of higher activity, thereby increasing statistics in the images, would also facilitate more precise quantification of myocardial blood flow in routine studies.However, LAFOV PET/CT scanners are limited to dose levels of approximately 400-450MBq, depending on the patient size. Previous research conducted on a Biograph Vision 600 (Siemens Healthineers) demonstrated a potential method to mitigate this limitation by reducing the measurement of delays, thus expanding the scanner’s bandwidth to allow for higher dose injections. In this study, model-based delay estimation has been prototyped on the Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT to double the system’s count rate capability, thereby preparing it for high-activity clinical studies.Initial results indicate that model-based delay estimation offers a viable alternative to delay measurement, with comparable performance in image quality. The method has been evaluated using patient data on the Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT system. The proposed method is planned to be tested more on phantom data, including NEMA scatter phantom, as well.

articleTitle: Investigation of Fast DOI TOF Image Reconstruction using DOI Rebinning and TOF Axial Fourier Rebinning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The integration of Depth of Interaction (DOI) and Time of Flight (TOF) measurements has significantly enhanced the spatial resolution and effective sensitivity capabilities of PET scanners. However, reconstructing full DOI TOF list-mode images poses significant computational challenges. In this study, we introduce a fast image reconstruction that leverage DOI rebinning and TOF axial Fourier rebinning, aimed at harnessing the full potential of both DOI and TOF data while significantly reducing data storage and computational time. The DOI rebinning is developed using two linear DOI equations, allowing mapping of DOI events to virtual detectors, thereby efficiently incorporating DOI information. The TOF axial Fourier rebinning method (axFRT) is designed to convert sinograms 3D TOF exactly and efficiently into 2D TOF sinograms without information loss. It features an embarrassingly parallel structure, making it suitable for implementation on massively parallel processors such as GPUs to substantially accelerate the rebinning process. In summary, we present an efficient DOI TOF image reconstruction, which not only maintains the high spatial resolution benefits of DOI and takes advantage of all TOF event statistics benefits, but also ensures exact reconstruction capabilities, even in PET scanners with large acceptance angles. Monte Carlo simulations with a generic DOI TOF PET scanner demonstrate significant improvements in processing efficiency and image quality, highlighting the potential of this approach.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of Cs3Cu2I5 Perovskite Scintillator Grown by Seedless SEST Method
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we utilized the seedless Slow evaporation solution growth technique (SEST) method to grow Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf>, a 0-D perovskite scintillator material, at room temperature. The growth was conducted under conditions of 23°C temperature and 40% humidity for 10 days, resulting in obtaining multiple crystals of 5 mm in size. Using single crystal Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf> detectors grown in our lab, we evaluated its performance using radioactive isotopes ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs},{ }^{241} \mathrm{Am},{ }^{54} \mathrm{Mn},{ }^{60} \mathrm{Co},{ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$, and ${}^{57}\mathrm{Co}$, and acquired energy resolutions of 8.55%, 23.35%, 7.59%, 6.49%, 9.38%, and 16.8%, respectively. In comparison with polycrystalline counterparts, single crystal Cs<inf>3</inf>Cu<inf>2</inf>I<inf>5</inf> exhibited superior performance, although both demonstrated excellent characteristics. By comparison, measurement using GAGG:Ce as a reference scintillator with the same setup showed an energy resolution of 10.00 %.

articleTitle: Inverse Rendering for PET Scanner Calibration
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The significant degradation of reconstructed image resolution and the presence of apparent artifacts can result from sub-millimetric misalignment of scanner configuration in high spatial resolution positron emission tomography (PET) systems. Therefore, ensuring accurate scanner configuration alignment is crucial for obtaining high-quality reconstructed images in such systems. Moreover, incorporating time-of-flight (TOF) technology has demonstrated its efficacy in enhancing image quality within PET. Achieving substantial reductions in statistical noise within reconstructed PET images via TOF information necessitates excellent timing resolution across the scanner’s entire field of view (FOV). This work aims to explore the impact of misalignment within the Prism-PET brain scanner system and to introduce an inverse rendering-based technique for geometric calibration. Additionally, with regard to time-of-flight (TOF), we update our iterative TOF offset calibration method and deploy it on GPU to expedite computation. The results of the proposed inverse rendering-based calibration method illustrate its capacity to rectify misalignment configurations of detectors on the scanner rings, aligning them with the ideal geometry configuration to effectively eliminate image artifacts. The GPU-accelerated TOF offset calibration maintains a consistent coincidence time resolution (CTR) of 320 ps full-width half maximum (FWHM) compared to the previous method. However, it achieves a remarkable acceleration, now completing the process approximately 240 times faster than before, requiring only about 12 minutes.

articleTitle: Geant4 simulation of Cherenkov photons in perovskite CsPbBr3 Gamma-ray Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Perovskite materials have recently attracted significant attention for hard X-ray and gamma-ray detection due to their ease of manufacture, yet are semiconductors, and therefore have potential for excellent energy performance. Cherenkov light generated by fast electrons due to gamma-ray interaction with the material could also yield extremely fast timing information. Here, we report Geant4 simulation results of Cherenkov photon generation, transport, and detection within perovskite CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>. The Cherenkov photon yield, energy spectrum and their temporal distribution are investigated under different gamma-ray energy deposition within CsPbBr<inf>3</inf>. A large refractive index and bandgap are desirable for high Cherenkov photon yield. CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> has a similar refractive index as that of TlBr, which has demonstrated fast-timing capability based on Cherenkov light. Although CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> has a bandgap of 2.3 eV, which is lower than the 2.68 eV of the TlBr, simulation shows that CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> has a similar Cherenkov photon yield to that of TlBr. With 511 keV energy deposition, the average Cherenkov photon yield is 9.54 photons for CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> versus 10.22 photons for TIBr for the simulated wavelength range of $300-954 \mathrm{~nm}$. The effect of crystal volume and surface finish on the timing performance of Cherenkov photon detection is also discussed. This work provides insights into Cherenkov photon processes of CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> and shows that it is promising to implement hybrid CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> semiconductor gamma-ray detector with direct charge collection for high energy resolution and simultaneous Cherenkov light collection for high timing resolution.

articleTitle: Comparison of network structures for deep learning-based cardiac PET scatter correction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, deep learning-based methods have emerged as potential alternatives to conventional scatter correction techniques, particularly in static PET applications. In this study, we evaluate the efficacy of two prominent deep neural network architectures, U-Net and ResNet, for dynamic cardiac PET scatter correction. These architectures are selected for their capacity to handle intricate data relationships and reduce noise, aiming to optimize PET reconstruction and improve diagnostic efficacy in cardiac imaging.We retrospectively selected three clinical Rb-82 myocardial perfusion PET scans: two datasets containing stress and rest scans were allocated for training, while the remaining dataset with only rest scans was designated for testing. Each dataset was reconstructed into 15 frames with and without model-based scatter correction. The frames without scatter correction served as inputs for the U-Net and ResNet networks during training, with the corresponding scatter-corrected frames serving as labels.During testing on the remaining dataset, we calculated the Mean Absolute Relative Difference (MARD) for the body region and assessed local relative differences (RD) in specific volumes of interest (VOI) for each frame. Across the 15 frames, the MARDs for U-Net and ResNet were 6.16% $\pm 3.14 \%$ and $5.45 \% \pm 1.61 \%$, respectively. For RDs in the left ventricle, U-Net achieved $5.91 \% \pm$ $38.8 \%$, while ResNet achieved $1.94 \% \pm 23.09 \%$. In the myocardium VOI, U-Net exhibited RDs of $-4.92 \% \pm 12.95 \%$, whereas ResNet showed RDs of $1.92 \% \pm 8.7 \%$.In conclusion, the ResNet architecture demonstrated lower quantitative error and superior edge preservationin the dynamic cardiac PET scatter correction task compared to the U-Net architecture in our testing dataset. Further studies are necessary to validate these findings with additional data and to explore the impact of these results on time-activity curves and parameter estimates derived from the dynamic images.

articleTitle: In-vivo carbon-ion radiotherapy monitoring by tracking of charged nuclear fragments: latest patient results
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The precision of carbon-ion radiotherapy in delivering radiation dose to the tumor while sparing adjacent healthy tissue surpasses that of conventional X-ray radiotherapy, offering a significant advantage in treatment. However, this comes with an increased sensitivity of the treatment quality to deformations and displacements of tissue, which can arise from morphological changes inside the patient or inaccuracies in patient positioning. To address this issue, we have been developing a non-invasive in-vivo treatment monitoring method based on the tracking of charged nuclear fragments produced by interactions of the carbon ions with nuclei of the patient’s tissue. The measured tracks allow the reconstruction of fragment origins, whose distributions can be compared between different treatment fractions. In this comparison, interfractional changes of the patient’s morphology or positioning may be uncovered. A unique detection system consisting of 28 Timepix3 silicon pixel detectors for usage during patient treatments at the Heidelberg Ion Beam Therapy Center (HIT) was developed and built. This detection system is being used in an ongoing prospective clinical trial named InViMo (In-Vivo Monitoring) with the purpose of detecting internal changes in the skull base region. This work presents the latest results from monitoring measurements during patient treatments. Changes in the distribution of charged nuclear fragments, which could arise from deformations and displacements of the patient’s tissue, were observed for several patients. These results pave the way towards increasing the benefits of carbon-ion radiotherapy for many patients through in-vivo monitoring, as reduced uncertainties could facilitate dose escalation and the reduction of safety margins.

articleTitle: Mif-PET: A multimodal approach to functional neuroimaging, integrating eye-tracking and heart rate monitoring with upright Prism-PET brain scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Functional [18F]-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-fPET) represents a revolutionary approach to mapping dynamic brain functions in response to stimuli during scans, revealing subtle variations in brain activity that are often undetectable in resting-state studies. To enhance the utility of fPET and overcome inherent limitations such as sensitivity, spatial resolution, and motion artifacts, we propose the Motion-tracked Immersive functional Positron Emission Tomography (MIf-PET) platform. This platform centers around the portable, upright TOF-DOI Prism-PET brain scanner and integrates immersive virtual reality (VR) headsets equipped with infrared eye tracking and electrocardiograms (ECG) to measure eye movements, heart rate, and heart rate variabilities-indicators of central and autonomic nervous system function. Brain stimulation through controlled, life-like augmented reality (AR) environments, which possess high ecological validity, enables us to conduct novel behavioral paradigms that challenge the brain and elicit responses from different neural networks. In this study, we simulated a brain activation study in GATE and evaluated the impact of different tracer injection methods and the sensitivity of Prism-PET to dynamically detect activation in small brain regions. Additionally, we employed Magic-Leap 2 AR headsets synchronized with ECG sensors to measure eye and heart parameters during oculomotor tests. The simulations and preliminary results confirm that the innovative Prism-PET scanner, combined with sophisticated injection strategies, significantly enhances the quality of functional PET imaging, providing detailed insights into brain function with high temporal and spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Preliminary Assessment of an Asymmetric Dual-end ReadoutDOI Detector for Preclinical PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a preliminary assessment of an optimized asymmetric dual-end readout depth-of-interaction (DOI) detector, specifically designed for preclinical positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. The detector employs a built-in light guide for precise positional encoding of the crystal array and is coupled to both multi-anode and single-anode silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) array board through custom-designed light collectors. This configuration efficiently captures comprehensive event information, including location, energy, time, and depth, while reducing the number of required SiPM channels and minimizing sensitivity losses associated with multi-array stitching. A detector platform was constructed using 3 mm and 6 mm SiPMs with an $8 \times 8$ crystal array of single-crystal pixels measuring $0.8 \times 0.8 \times 12 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, achieving an approximate DOI resolution of 2 mm. The floodmap revealed clear delineation of all crystals, and after calibration, an average DOI-ER of 12.5% and a DOI-TOF resolution of 278 ps were obtained. These results validate the feasibility of the detector for preclinical PET applications and offer a cost-effective and technically viable solution for DOI-PET imaging. Further detailed system performance analysis will be provided in the subsequent parts of this work.

articleTitle: A Count-Rate Recovery Method for Photon Counting X-ray Detectors Using Scintillator/SiPM
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Previously, we developed a photon counting detector for X-ray fluoroscopic imaging using a scintillation detector unit and an MVT digitizer. Due to the dead time in the detection channels, the counts will be lost when working in a high count-rate condition. To avoid the streak artifacts in the image, we normally adopt a low X-ray dose when imaging with the detector. However, a low X-ray dose always means a worse imaging signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) or longer imaging time. In this work, we model the response of the detector as a paralyzable processing and set up an X-ray imaging system with the detectors for validation. By analyzing the measured count rate of the detector when setting the X-ray tube’s voltage at 120 kV and varying the current from 0.1 mA to 1.2 mA, we estimated the dead time of each channel in the detector to be (112±11) ns. Having the dead time and the paralyzable response model, the lost counts therefore could be recovered according to the measured value. Typically, we measure the count rate of channel 81 to be 2.97 Mcps/pixel and recover it to be 6.20 Mcps/pixel when setting the X-ray tube’s voltage and current at 120 kV and 0.8 mA respectively. An image of the step phantom is further obtained and the streak artifacts in the image are gone after the count-rate recovery and uniformity calibration.

articleTitle: Hybrid motion correction in brain PET combination of external device and data-driven methods
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Motion artifacts significantly impact the accuracy of PET brain imaging, complicating clinical diagnoses and quantitative assessments. Traditional motion correction strategies rely either on data-driven methods or external devices, each with inherent limitations. This study introduces a hybrid head motion correction (HMC) method implemented on the NeuroEXPLORER system, combining an external camera-based structured light motion tracking system (UMT) with a data-driven strategy, Motion Corrected Centroid-of-Distribution (MCCOD). This method improves HMC by selectively excluding periods of unreliable motion data through quality control based on MCCOD. Additionally, we propose novel algorithms to convert continuous motion data captured by UMT into discrete dynamic frames, facilitating more efficient frame-based reconstruction. Preliminary results demonstrate that our approach effectively reduces motion artifacts and preserves high-resolution details in PET imaging. Future work will extend these methods to dynamic imaging scenarios.

articleTitle: Maximum-likelihood expectation maximization for dual-tracer PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Conventional PET imaging is restricted to image a single radiotracer at time. Knowledge about two metabolic processes can be acquired by performing two PET scans sequentially. However, the simultaneous imaging of metabolic targets could give new insights about the interplay of neurotransmitter systems and the causes for neurological disorders. For the simultaneous reconstruction of PET images of two radiotracers, a $\beta^{+}$-emitter emitting only annihilation photons and a $\beta^{+}-\gamma$-emitter emitting annihilation photons and an additional prompt $\gamma$ photon are combined. The $\gamma$-photon is used to identify events originating from the $\beta^{+}-\gamma$-emitter. However, due to e.g. attenuation the $\gamma$-ray is often not detected and not all events can correctly be associated with the $\beta^{+}-\gamma$-emitter. This makes an accurate separation challenging. In this work, we concentrate on tracers emitting a high-energy $\gamma$-photon ($\gt625 \ \mathrm{keV}$). In order to separate both tracers, a triple-to-’false double’ ratio of detected events belonging to the $\beta^{+}-\gamma-$ emitter is estimated. This ratio is dependent on the location of the annihilation in the field-of-view and the current attenuation map. In contrast to previous work, we estimate the triple-to-’false double’ ratio including the attenuation of the prompt $\gamma$ in the object and incorporate this estimation of ‘false double’ coincidences in the forward-projection of the ML-EM algorithm. For evaluation, we simulate two overlapping cylinders containing the $\beta^{+}$-emitter ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$ and the $\beta^{+}-\gamma^{-}$ emitter ${}^{44}\mathrm{Sc}$. To assess algorithm performance, we calculate the residual error of the $\beta^{+}-\gamma$-emitter in the reconstructed $\beta^{+}$-emitter image. The mean residual error remaining in the $\beta^{+}$-image is 7.2%. This result demonstrates that our approach can effectively separate both tracers and can reconstruct two separate images iteratively.

articleTitle: Characterization of Monolithic CMOS Sensors with Internal Gain in a 110 nm Technology Node
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This article presents the design and the characterization results of a first monolithic prototype with internal gain fabricated in a standard 110 nm CMOS technology for the third run of the ARCADIA project. The introduction of the internal gain in a commercial grade CMOS process represents an attractive solution for applications in which low power electronics and low material budget are required, such as radiation detectors for space experiments. In this prototype the sensor and the electronics are hosted in the same $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$ thick, n-type, epitaxial layer which can be fully depleted, thus establishing the charge collection by drift as the main mechanism. The in-pixel frontend is placed at the pixel border, and it is based on a cascoded common source stage implemented with 1.2 V transistors. This stage is then followed by an analogue buffer designed with 3.3 V transistors to drive the output analogue pads. The result of the characterization using an infrared laser and a Sr90 radioactive source will be presented.

articleTitle: Towards a scalable readout solution for large coverage BGO-PET scanners
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) constitutes the molecular imaging modality of choice for the study and diagnosis of different medical conditions. Current research focuses on increasing the sensitivity of PET systems to provide faster imaging or/and a reduction of the dose administered to the patient. With this objective, different approaches have been proposed such as constructing larger axial coverage PET systems and/or enabling accurate time-of-flight (TOF)-PET scanners. Implementing large coverage scanners is a major investment (high cost) challenge. Moreover, enabling accurate TOF capabilities requires fast and low-noise electronics. To mitigate these limitations, BGO-based systems may be an option since BGO scintillators are cheaper than Lubased scintillators, and their emission spectrum contains promptly-emitted photons (Cherenkov light, ($\sim 20$ above BGO’s absorption band and $\sim 9$ above LSO’s absorption band)) which can be exploited to boost TOF performance. However, detecting these Cherenkov photons is challenging and requires the implementation of specific readout able to discriminate the events based on their dynamics, at a reasonable cost. In this work we show our first steps towards designing and implementing a scalable readout for large coverage BGO-PET. Our readout is based on a balun transformer to split the photodetector signals combined with a two-channel method for event discrimination.

articleTitle: A DOI rebinning time calibration method for ultrahigh resolution TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-flight PET has demonstrated enhanced image quality compared to conventional PET. The calibration of time has been identified as a critical factor in timing performance, given that calibration errors can significantly contribute to time resolution. However, calibrating the time delays between detector voxels to a PET using multilayer DOI information presents challenges due to the increase in dimension of DOI data in proportion to the square of the number of DOI layers. In this study, we implemented a compressed method for DOI rebinning to reduce computational costs while maintaining high-quality time calibration. The method was applied to the practical data of The NeuroEXPLORER, a state-of-the-art brain TOF-PET/CT scanner that achieves ultra-high resolution through the utilization of 8-layer DOI information. Subsequently, an investigation into the comparison of TOF performance (in accordance with NEMA NU2-2018 standard) in no-DOI, rebinned-DOI, and 8-layer-DOI cases was conducted. The findings indicate that the DOI rebinning time calibration method effectively decreases computational expenses while maintaining the benefits of precise TOF performance.

articleTitle: Size Effects In The Luminescence Of CeF3 Nanoparticles
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A comparative analysis of the luminescent parameters of the CeF<inf>3</inf> nanoparticles and CeF<inf>3</inf> sing crystals was performed. CeF<inf>3</inf> single crystals exhibit characteristic luminescence attributed to the radiative emission of 5d-4f Frenkel excitons at 283 and 305 nm, and “perturbed” cerium ions with a maximum at $\sim 360 \mathrm{~nm}$. In the case of nanoparticles, the intensity of excitonic luminescence decreases and “perturbed” cerium ion luminescence becomes dominant. The maxima of the excitation spectrum of the excitonic luminescence for nanoparticles coincides with the dips in the excitonic luminescence excitation spectrum of single crystal. This feature of the excitation spectra is caused by the absence of saturation effects of light absorption in the thin layer of nanoparticle. A significant decrease of the decay time constant of the excitonic luminescence upon transition from single crystals to nanoparticles indicates a non-radiative mechanism of luminescence quenching mainly by the nanoparticle surface defects. For nanoparticles with $\mathrm{a}=8 \mathrm{~nm}$ the coincidence of dips in the excitation spectra of “perturbed” cerium luminescence with the maxima of the luminescence excitation spectra suggests the formation of free excitons even in the absence of excitonic luminescence. This indicates that excitons completely non-radiatively recombine with defects in the nanoparticle during their lifetime. The absence of efficient excitation of “perturbed” cerium centers in the $4 \mathrm{f}-5 \mathrm{~d}$ absorption region and no delay at the stage of increasing intensity of the luminescence kinetics curve for nanoparticles with $\mathrm{a}=8 \mathrm{~nm}$ indicate the radiative nature of the interaction between excitons and “perturbed” centers.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Radiation Tolerance of Neutron-Sensitive Semiconductor Lithium Indium Phosphor Selenide
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new lithium-containing compound semiconductor, LiInP<inf>2</inf> Se<inf>6</inf> (LIPSe), shows promise as a near-thermal neutron converter for imaging applications requiring excellent timing and spatial resolution. However, its potential lifetime in this application is predicated on the ability to retain performance after exposure to operational fluences of up to $10^{14} \mathrm{n} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$, representing several use cycles at a spallation facility such as Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL). Therefore, the tolerance of LIPSe after neutron irradiation was evaluated. Characterization tests involved examination using Raman, UV-Vis, and X-Ray diffraction to search for changes in bulk crystal properties as well as IV measurements and response to alpha particles, a surrogate for neutron response. Results from materials characterization studies do not indicate the presence of significant crystallographic damage. Results from exposure to alpha particles reveal distinguishable response with resolved peaks in samples exposed to up to $10^{15} \mathrm{n} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$ of reactor-spectrum neutrons. Systemic factors which make this likely to be an underestimation of the full capabilities of irradiated LIPSe are identified and discussed, ultimately concluding that thicker and more robust samples will likely exhibit better long-term stability.

articleTitle: Discharge Studies in a CMS ME0 GEM Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The LHC is undergoing a significant upgrade to boost its luminosity by half an order of magnitude. This requires upgrades to several detector systems, including the introduction of ME0 GEM detectors in the endcap muon system of the CMS detector, extending pseudorapidity acceptance for muons to |η|=2.8. However, during tests with an alpha source under a hole in the drift board of the chamber, it was found that the VFATs reset and become unconfigured due to discharges induced in the detector. The cause of these resets is unclear, as the discharge generates a large electromagnetic pulse, causing nearby voltage probes to act as antennas and pick up unreliable signals. To investigate further, simulations of discharge conditions have been attempted. A clamping circuit is used to inject pulses into the power rails of the VFATs, where a 7V pulse is reduced to a 100mV ripple. Gas Discharge Tubes are also used to manually inject a large amount of charge into the VFAT channels, resulting in damage to the readout channels but no reset of the VFAT itself.

articleTitle: Development of Radiation Monitor for Space weather measuring Electrons (RMS-e) for Himawari-10
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radiation Monitor for Space weather measuring Electrons (RMS-e) is an electron detector that will be installed on the next geostationary meteorological satellite Himawari-10 to provide continuous observations of high-energy electrons in the geostationary satellite orbit over Japan. Current space weather forecasting in Japan is based on observations from the GOES satellites, which have different conditions from the space environment around the geostationary satellite orbits over Japan. RMS-e will provide continuous observations of energetic electrons in geostationary satellite orbits over Japan, which are critical for improving the accuracy of space weather forecasts in Japan. RMS-e consists of two sets of layered solid-state detectors (SSDs) made of silicon semiconductors called RMS-e lo and RMS-e hi. RMS-e lo and RMS-e hi are designed to measure electrons with energies in the range of 50 keV to 1300 keV and 0.8 to 5 MeV, respectively. The energy resolution of RMS-e lo is less than $20 \%$ and that of RMS-e hi is less than $10 \%$ based on evaluation tests. Currently, we are completing the development of the engineering model (EM) of RMS-e and preparing for the development of the proto flight model (PFM) of RMS-e. In this presentation, we report the current status of the instrument development and test results of RMS-e.

articleTitle: First Patient Study of In-Beam OpenPET for Range Verification in Carbon-Ion Therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In-beam PET measurement is recognized as one of the most practical methods for range verification of particle therapy, in which fragmentation reactions produce positron emitters. As the positron emitters are produced in small amounts and have short half-lives, measurement during or immediately after the irradiation is required to obtain as many events as possible. Therefore in-beam PET is desired, but conventional in-beam PET systems with a dual-head geometry were designed mainly for 2D imaging. Therefore, we invented the OpenPET, which has an open space for the beam to pass through even with a full-ring geometry enabling 3D imaging. Last year, we installed the $5^{\text {th }}$ prototype of the OpenPET into a treatment room of the heavy-ion medical accelerator in Chiba (HIMAC) and we reported results of the first phantom study. Following the in-beam phantom measurement, here, we report the first patient study for head and neck cancers. The patients were treated with two-port vertical and horizontal irradiations for each fraction. Because the OpenPET system is designed only for horizontal irradiation, the vertical irradiation took place without the OpenPET, and the in-beam PET measurement was performed only for the following horizontal irradiation. The measurement, which started at the beginning of the beam irradiation, was continued for 10 min after finishing the irradiation. As the number of counts in the measured coincidence data is low, we employed a maximum a posteriori ordered subset expectation maximization algorithm with median root prior for image reconstruction. As a result, we could visualize the positron emitter distribution produced in the patient body by carbon-ion irradiation.

articleTitle: Design and Evaluation of a Partly Segmented Light Guide for High Resolution Solid-State Positron Emission Tomography (PET) Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Radialis organ-targeted PET camera utilizes planar detector technology based on tileable individual detector blocks. Each detector block consists of a 24×24 array of polished LYSO crystals with a pitch size of 2.4 mm, coupled to an 8×8 array of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). A borosilicate light guide is positioned between the scintillation crystal array and the photosensors for light sharing and multiplexed readout. However, LYSO crystal identification degrades at the block edges due to asymmetrical light sharing and reflection. To address this, we developed a partly segmented light guide with slits filled with barium sulfate to redistribute light spread near the detector edges. Block detector prototypes with partially segmented light guides were evaluated using a 4-channel readout and a 64-channel PETsys readout, demonstrating improved coordinate reconstruction and edge LYSO crystal identification, especially with 4.0 mm slits and Enhanced Specular Reflector (ESR) wrapping.

articleTitle: Measurement of D-T Neutron Source Flux by Self-Neutron Activation Analysis with a LaBr3 Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Special nuclear materials and other contraband interact with fast neutrons in a manner that emits characteristic radiation signatures. Fast neutrons can be conveniently produced by neutron generators; knowledge of their absolute neutron output is essential for predicting reaction rates in activated samples and for validating simulations needed to advance active interrogation techniques. However, measurements of the fast neutron production rate are often prohibitively complex or lengthy. This work uses a lanthanum bromide LaBr<inf>3</inf> scintillation detector to quantify the neutron output of the Thermo Fisher Scientific P211 D-T neutron generator using neutron activation analysis of the naturally occurring bromine isotopes within the detector medium. LaBr<inf>3</inf> is an attractive medium for this approach because the ($\mathrm{n}, 2 \mathrm{n}$) reactions leading to activation of ${ }^{79} \mathrm{Br}$ and ${ }^{81} \mathrm{Br}$ have thresholds of about 10 MeV, the detector has high efficiency for its own electron emissions, and the activation products of interest have half-lives on the order of minutes. The LaBr<inf>3</inf> detector was irradiated by DT neutrons for 30 minutes, and a multi-term exponential function was fit to the experimentally measured decay time profile. The fitted decay time profile shows a strong contribution from ${ }^{78} \mathrm{Br}$. The activity of ${ }^{78} \mathrm{Br}$ was used to estimate the neutron production rate, $5.54 \times 10^{7} \pm 8 \times 10^{5} \mathrm{~s}^{-1}$. Additional Monte Carlo analysis is needed to model the neutron transport and refine the initial estimate of the neutron production rate.

articleTitle: A frame prediction network for total-body dynamic PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Total-body dynamic PET holds high potential for diagnostic imaging of various malignancies. However, traditional dynamic PET scans typically require prolonged durations ($\geq 60$ minutes), potentially causing patient discomfort and resulting in artifacts in final images. In recent years, many deep learning studies have leveraged short-duration PET scans (typically 10-20 minutes) to generate dynamic parametric images, aiming to indirectly address this issue. These approaches overlook all the temporal information contained in the given dynamic PET scan and the real-time metabolic processes occurring in the human body. Therefore, we propose a generative adversarial network capable of predicting dynamic frames to directly reduce the scanning time. Experiments were conducted on two total-body dynamic PET datasets with different radiotracers ($\left.{ }^{[68} \mathrm{Ga}\right] \mathrm{Ga}$ PSMA-11 and $\left.{ }^{68} \mathrm{Ga}\right]$ Ga-FAPI-04) to evaluate the performance of the proposed method. Moreover, parameter images were generated to evaluate the performance of the model. Both visual and quantitative results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. In the future, broader experiments and improved solutions will be explored to minimize scan duration while attaining higher prediction precision.

articleTitle: Implementing a Simple Sigma-Delta ADC in Low-cost FPGA for SiPM-based Nuclear Imaging Systems
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper describes a simple, low-cost, and scalable readout electronics based on sigma-delta modulation for silicon photomultipliers (SiPM) used in nuclear imaging systems. For energy measurements, the proposed readout design needs only one resistor, one capacitor, and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) without using any external analog-to-digital convertor (ADC). In this paper, we introduce the new readout electronics and present our preliminary energy measurement results with CsI(Tl), LYSO, and GAGG crystals optically coupled to Onsemi’s J-Series SiPMs. Our preliminary measurement results show that the proposed readout electronics design is able to achieve energy resolutions (FWHM) of 7.2 %, 12.0 %, and 10.9% from 511 keV gamma-rays in $\operatorname{CsI}(\mathrm{Tl})$, LYSO, and GAGG detectors, respectively.

articleTitle: Integrating spectral photon counting CT and deep learning for metal artefact reduction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metal-induced artefacts in computed tomography (CT) images are caused mainly by beam hardening, scattering, and photon starvation. They obstruct the characterization of fine anatomical structures and compromise diagnostic value. This study introduces a novel machine learning approach called residual dense U-Net (RDU-Net) for reducing metal artefacts in spectral photon-counting CT (SPCCT) images. RDU-Net corrects artefacts across all energy bins simultaneously, leveraging the strengths of ResNet, DenseNet, and U-Net architectures. ResNet tackles the vanishing gradient issue with residual connections, DenseNet promotes feature reuse and gradient flow through dense connectivity patterns, and U-Net preserves spatial information with its encoder-decoder structure and skip connections. Assessment of metal artefacts before and after applying the MAR algorithm was conducted using the scanned images containing metal inserts (aluminium, stainless steel) and material inserts (Hydroxyapatite (HA) and iodine). Image acquisition was performed using Mars SPCCT, operated at 118 kVp, 80 μA, and 160 ms, with 981 circular projections. The images were reconstructed into five energy bins: 7-40, 40-50, 50-60, 60-79, and 79-118 keV. Results showed that the proposed MAR algorithm significantly improves image quality metrics such as signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), root mean squared error (RMSE), and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). After MAR, SNR and SSIM increased from 3.37 to 17.40 and from 0.56 to 0.75, respectively, and RMSE decreased from 0.016 to 0.001. Furthermore, material identification accuracy for HA and iodine improved from 86% to 91% and from 84% to 93%, respectively. Findings demonstrate the potential of our technique to mitigate metal artefacts and enhance diagnostic accuracy in SPCCT images.

articleTitle: Measurement of mixed samples of alpha and beta (gamma) nuclides using a high spatial resolution alpha-particle imager with Quantitative CMOS camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The measurement of alpha contamination, or alpha radiation, is important for the decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station (FDNPS). It is very important to verify whether alpha particles can be visualized in a situation where alpha, beta, gamma-rays are mixed together. In this study, we applied our newly developed alpha imager to the measurement of actual samples containing a mixture of alpha, beta, and gamma nuclides, and verified its effectiveness. The alpha imager consisted of a qCMOS camera (ORCA-Quest (C15550-20UP)) and an optical microscope (BX53MRF-S from Olympus). A ZnS(Ag) scintillator with a thickness of 3.25 mg/cm2 was used for alpha measurements by placing the scintillator closely over a sample. An 241Am alpha standard source was measured to verify whether alpha particles could be measured. In addition, samples containing a mixture of alpha, beta, and gamma nuclides were measured. Image processing was used to extract clusters of alpha particles. By applying image processing, clusters of alpha particles were successfully extracted. When measuring a sample with a mixture of alpha, beta, and gamma nuclides, clusters of alpha particles could be confirmed. Although the sample had a higher beta activity than alpha activity, only alpha particles were successfully extracted. The developed alpha imager will be useful for contamination measurement in the site of FDNPS.

articleTitle: Transformer-based Sinusoidal Curve Learning for Sinogram Denoising
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In few PET imaging application it can be relevant to be able to reconstruct images from low-count acquisitions. However, this often results in lower image quality, requiring specialized reconstruction methods or denoising algorithms to improve diagnostic accuracy. While many recent denoising techniques use Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), these architectures may struggle with capturing long-range non-local interactions, potentially leading to inaccuracies in global structure representation. Recognizing the advantages of transformer architectures over CNNs, our study introduces a novel sinogram denoising algorithm tailored to enhance PET sinogram quality. Additionally, we propose a sinogram transformer module specifically designed to learn sinusoidal curves, improving sinogram feature extraction. Leveraging a transformer architecture with a self-attention mechanism, this module effectively preserves sinogram inner structure, resulting in superior denoising performance and preventing noise from propagating into the image domain. Evaluations on synthetic data demonstrate that our sinusoidal curve learning transformer module outperforms methods learning projections from various view angles or radial positions, both qualitatively and quantitatively.

articleTitle: Autonomous Determination of Crystal Efficiencies using Data Consistency for 3D PET Normalization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate normalization is essential for artifacts-free quantitative 3D positron emission tomography (PET) imaging. The de facto method for PET normalization, component-based normalization, involves a dedicated data acquisition with known tracer distribution using a symmetric phantom, such as a uniform cylinder or a rotating line source. While time-invariant components like geometry and block profile are generally stable, time-variant components like intrinsic crystal efficiencies can fluctuate over time. Regularly updating of time-variant factors is crucial to prevent artifacts and maintain imaging quality. In this work, we present a novel approach to autonomously determine crystal efficiencies using PET data consistency. First, we derive a second-order partial differential equation, known as the John-Defrise equation, which characterizes the redundancy of 3D PET data in native coordinates. As an application of this equation, we then derive a crystal efficiency equation, modeling the relative line-of-response (LOR) sensitivity of each detector pair as the product of the two crystals’ efficiency factors. We further develop a numerical algorithm to solve for the crystal efficiency factors on a per-crystal basis. The proposed method allows autonomous crystal efficiency estimation using data acquired with any tracer distribution, eliminating the need for specialized data acquisition. To evaluate this approach, we conduct numerical simulations of a generic 3D PET scanner with a NEMA and cylinder phantom, showing that crystal efficiencies can be estimated with an NRMSE of 0.32%, leading to artifact-free image reconstruction. As next-generation TOF PET scanners improve imaging performance, requiring frequent calibration and performance monitoring, the proposed autonomous normalization method enables automatic estimation of residual crystal efficiencies using clinical data whenever computing resources are available.

articleTitle: A new approach in pulse amplitude measurement technique for radiation or particle detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In radiation detector signal processing usually, the charge sensitive pre-amplifier converts the small charge signal coming from the semiconductor-based detector into voltage form and then the signal is further amplified to measure the energy of the incoming radiation. The voltage pulse from CSPA is amplified with use of shaping amplifier which reduces the signal bandwidth. To have better energy resolution, precise measurement of peak amplitude of shaping amplifier output is required. In recent years, people have shown that the signal from the CSPA can be directly digitized using high-speed Analog to Digital Converters (ADC) and then further signal processing such as gain and shaping is carried out inside the Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA). This method requires higher sampling ADC which consumes more power. For multiple detector system these kinds of methods are quite power consuming and difficult to implement in FPGA. In this direction, we initiated the development of a technique which uses CSPA, Shaping amplifier, low sampling ADC and FPGA. The LaGrange’s interpolation technique is implemented in FPGA to precisely measure the peak of analog pulse. Results show that the implemented technique gives similar energy resolution compared to pulse processing and peak detector standered based technique. The details technique and comparative results will be presented in the symposium.

articleTitle: Visualization of alpha rays using a qCMOS camera and evaluation of the effects of beta rays, gamma rays, and neutrons on its camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: At nuclear facilities that handle plutonium, visualization of Pu particles in working environment is important for evaluating internal exposure doses for workers. Because the diameter of the Pu particles (activity median aerodynamic diameter) is important for the evaluation. In this study, a new type of Quantitative Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (qCMOS) camera with low noise signals and high readout speed has been used in the alpha imaging system to improve the spatial resolution for alpha rays and to visualize Pu particles. The system consists of a 3.25 $\mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{cm} 2 \mathrm{ZnS}(\mathrm{Ag})$ scintillator (EJ-440, Eljen Technology), an optical microscope (BX53MRF-S, Olympus Co.), and a CMOS camera (ORCA-Quest,Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.). The images were irradiated with alpha rays, beta rays, gamma rays, and neutron radiation, and the obtained images were analyzed using Image J. As a result, only alpha rays could be measured specifically, and beta rays, gamma rays, and neutrons had no effect. In some images, light spots were observed in the corners of the captured field of view that could be considered noise. Although the intensity of alpha rays and noise are comparable, the detected areas are different, allowing selective measurement of alpha rays.

articleTitle: Prediction of Mediastinal Lymph Node Metastasis in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Based on 18F-FDG PET Radiomics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Background: Lymph node metastasis (LNM) in lung cancer is a significant factor influencing both survival and recurrence rates. However, the relationship between radiomic features (RFs) and LNM remains unclear. This study aimed to develop and validate a radiomics signature for predicting LNM in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC). Methods: The study included 383 NSCLC patients, and RFs were extracted from PET images. A radiomics signature was constructed using a multivariate logistic regression model that incorporated clinical and PET parameters. Model performance was evaluated through the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results: Thirteen RFs were selected from 158 candidate features to construct a radiomics signature significantly associated with LNM. The model showed strong predictive ability, with an AUC of 0.794, sensitivity of $78 \%$, specificity of $66.2 \%$, and accuracy of $72 \%$. Conclusions: The radiomics signature derived from pretreatment PET images offers a noninvasive approach to predicting LNM in NSCLC patients.

articleTitle: Performance Evaluation of a Monolithic Crystal PET Detector with Six-sided Readout Scheme
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper aims to design a cubic monolithic crystal positron emission tomography(PET) detector with a six-sided readout scheme to achieve good position resolution and comparable depth of interaction(DOI) resolution with fewer readout channels. We used a monolithic LYSO crystal with a size of $14 \times 14 \times 14 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$. Each side of the crystal was polished and coupled with 4 SiPMs (Size: $6.4 \times 6.4 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$), resulting in 24 SiPMs for each detector. Compared with conventional single-ended readout schemes, the proposed design has excellent spatial symmetry. By taking advantage of this symmetry, a neural-network-based positioning algorithm was developed from Monte Carlo simulation. Then the detector was assembled and evaluated with a pencil beam experiment. The final results show that the proposed readout scheme achieves a spatial resolution (FWHM) of less than 1.57 mm both in-plane and in-depth.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study of a Collimator-less 4π FOV Imaging System using Pixelated GAGG(Ce) Scintillator and Deep Learning Method
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study explores the feasibility of a collimator-less 4 p field of view (FOV) imaging system using pixelated GAGG(Ce) scintillator and deep learning method. We proposed pixelated detection system that reduced the time for training the fully convolutional network (FCN) model because of its small data size and provided convenience in processing as training data, enabling real-time imaging applications. The FCN model was configured using the TensorFlow library 2.0. The train data and label data for FCN model were acquired by using Monte Carlo N-Particle (MCNP) simulations, and the standard isotopes were ${ }^{57} \mathrm{Co},{ }^{133} \mathrm{Ba},{ }^{22} \mathrm{Na}$, and ${ }^{137} \mathrm{Cs}$. The trained FCN model was validated using test data, and the images reconstructed by the FCN model were compared with the labelled data through the structural similarity index measure (SSIM) method. The results confirmed that the model could predict up to five sources with varying positions and isotopes. The method of estimating radiation source positions using deep learning offers substantial advantages in real-time imaging. Once trained, the model can rapidly and efficiently compute source positions, providing significant benefits in terms of speed and simplicity for various industrial applications.

articleTitle: High loading nanocomposites of cesium lead halide nanocrystals for fast timing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cesium lead halide nanocrystals are widely studied in many fields for their excellent luminescent properties. Recently, their potential for fast timing applications in radiation detection has been demonstrated [1, 2]. To ensure material stability, these nanocrystals are often embedded into a polymer matrix, forming nanocomposite scintillators. However, most research on nanocomposites focuses on low loadings (around 1% by weight)—insufficient for detecting high-energy X-rays or $\gamma$ rays, with only a few studies exploring materials with higher loading but with limited success in terms of transparency of the final material [3]. In our work, we present nanocomposites of cesium lead halide nanocrystals with loading up to 40% by weight.
