We employ copolymerizable ligands to enhance nanocrystal dispersion within the matrix, thereby improving the final material transparency. We characterise the radioluminescent properties of nanocomposites of cesium lead bromide and cesium lead bromochloride nanocrystals with varying chloride content and asses their timing capabilities under X-rays. Our findings reveal a significant improvement in time resolution under X-rays compared to previously published values for cesium lead bromide polymer nanocomposites [2]. When combined with increased stopping power of high nanocrystal content, this advancement holds great promise for practical applications in time-of-flight positron emission tomography and computed tomography or high energy physics.

articleTitle: Development of a Digital Miniature Cathode Ray Magnetometer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Our study presents a novel Digital Miniature Cathode Ray Magnetometer engineered to excel in key parameters crucial for modern applications, notably the characterization of insertion devices in light sources. Employing a charged particle beam and digital imaging, this magnetometer overcomes limitations such as accuracy, temperature sensitivity, and spatial resolution. The magnetometer’s core operation involves a low-energy electron beam interacting with a scintillator screen, captured by a CMOS sensor for precise magnetic field mapping. Optimization efforts focus on parameters tailored for specific applications, with particular attention to spatial resolution, sensitivity, and temperature range. Prototype testing demonstrates its viability, albeit with ongoing improvements required to meet stringent sensitivity targets. Strategies for enhancement include advanced signal processing techniques, exploration of alternative scintillator materials, and integration of electrostatic deflecting plates. Future developments, such as custom CMOS imagers and optical fiber bundles, promise expanded applications in extreme environments and enhanced robustness.Our research advances magnetic measurement technology, offering promising avenues for scientific, medical, and industrial domains. The Digital Miniature Cathode Ray Magnetometer stands as a testament to ongoing innovation in measurement technologies, poised to catalyze progress across various fields.

articleTitle: Performance Characterization of CdTe Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CdTe and CdZnTe detectors are widely used in X-ray photon counting applications. We report on performance characterization of CdTe photon counting detectors. Charge collection properties and obtained energy spectra over a range of energies will be presented for planar and pixelated detectors with ohmic and Schottky contacts.

articleTitle: Design of a Dual-End Depth-of-Interaction PET Detector Using Segmented GAGG:Ce Crystals with Multiple Decay Constants
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Depth-of-interaction (DOI) detector is widely used in high resolution positron emission tomography (PET) systems to reduce the impact of parallax error at the periphery of the field-of-view (FOV). However, the state-of-art DOI detector techniques shows limited DOI resolution. In this work, we propose to construct a DOI PET detector by integrating the phoswich detector technique into a dual-end-readout DOI PET detector We used Ce-doped gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG:Ce) scintillators with different decay constants and a combined DOI + pulse shape discrimination (PSD) method to improve the DOI resolution. We design a crystal bar of 1 × 1 × 20 mm<sup>3</sup> with a repetitive arrangement of 20 GAGG:Ce crystal units of 1 × 1 × 1 mm<sup>3</sup> with three decay constants. We test different crystal surface treatment choices. For crystal bars ground with the grit size of 14 μm (W14), an optimized energy resolution of 13.84% ± 1.65% can be achieved. We will further explore the best achievable DOI resolution with this approach.

articleTitle: Measurement of Neutron Active Interrogation Contraband Signatures Using Organic Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Active interrogation signatures of contraband and special nuclear material are often relatively weak, requiring the use of long measurement times and high radiation doses from the interrogating source. We are exploring new digital pulse processing techniques for active neutron interrogation to enhance the detection of concealed contraband and special nuclear material with a focus on prompt gamma-ray signatures for drug and explosive detection and fast neutrons for special nuclear material detection. In this work, we use organic scintillators as gamma-ray detectors to detector contraband. Maximum likelihood estimation maximization-based spectral reconstruction is applied to enhance gamma-ray spectroscopy in organic scintillators. Reconstructed activation spectra from hydrogen, carbon, oxygen, and nitrogen (HCNO) rich objects produced using a pulsed DT neutron generator and measured with liquid organic scintillators are shown to include many of the major HCNO signatures used for contraband detection. The signal-to-background ratio for certain signatures is shown to be enhanced using the pulsed timing information. Using these methods, combined spectro-temporal analysis is being developed for detecting shielded contraband with improved sensitivity. We additionally conducted Monte Carlo simulations to estimate the impact of pileup on the measurement sensitivity to motivate the need for fast detectors in pulsed fast neutron active interrogation.

articleTitle: A novel method to remove the stem effect in a fibre based dosimeter
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Real-time dose measurement is a crucial aspect for radiation therapy and optical fibre sensors represent an important tool. Because of their small size, flexibility, light weight and cost efficiency, together with immunity to magnetic fields, they are suitable for minimally invasive in vivo dosimetry. However, in some cases the response is affected by the “stem effect”. This effect consists of the production of Cherenkov radiation due to secondary electrons that travel through the fibre faster than the light in the medium, contaminating the dosimetric measurement. In this paper we introduce a novel method to remove the Cherenkov light contamination while preserving the original signal and we demonstrate its potential in High-Dose-Rate Brachytherapy.

articleTitle: Precision Renal Tumor Segmentation: Harnessing Prior Attention for Optimal Efficiency
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Kidney cancer ranks among the more prevalent forms of cancer in humans. Semantic segmentation offers a promising avenue for the accurate and quantitative analysis of tumors and kidney structures. Nonetheless, the manual segmentation of images is notably labor-intensive. Consequently, there is a pressing need for an automated or semi-automated segmentation technique to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of kidney tissue segmentation. This requirement can be fulfilled through the application of advanced deep-learning methodologies. In this study, we explored the utilization of the traditional U-Net model alongside the Prior Attention Net (PANet) for the task of kidney and kidney tumor segmentation. The attention map is created by applying a convolution, followed by normalization and a sigmoid function to highlight key features. The dataset employed in this research was sourced from the KITS19 challenge, comprising 200 cross-sectional CT images that include kidney tumors, alongside their corresponding annotations. From this collection, 140 images were allocated for network training, 20 for validation, and 40 for testing purposes. The outcomes of this study reveal that PANet markedly surpasses the performance of the conventional U-Net model in several key aspects. Specifically, in the case of kidney segmentation, PANet demonstrated a 7.41% improvement in the Jaccard index, a 4.5% enhancement in both the Dice coefficient and precision metrics, and a 3.45% increase in the IOU metric. When it comes to tumor segmentation, the superiority of PANet becomes even more pronounced, with improvements exceeding 42% across the mean Dice coefficient, precision, and IOU metrics, and reaching an impressive 52.27% in the Jaccard index. These findings unequivocally illustrate that PANet significantly outshines UNet, particularly in tumor segmentation tasks, where it delivers substantial advancements across all evaluated metrics.

articleTitle: Recent Progress of Inorganic Scintillators for Future HEP Calorimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Following the priority research directions for calorimetry documented in the DOE basic research needs for HEP instrumentation, the Caltech HEP Crystal Lab has been actively investigating novel inorganic scintillators along the following three directions. Fast and radiation hard inorganic scintillators to face the challenge of severe radiation environment expected by future HEP experiments at hadron colliders, such as the HL-LHC and a 10 TeV pCM collider, where radiation damage is induced by ionization dose, protons and neutrons. Ultrafast inorganic scintillators to face the challenge of unprecedented event rate expected by future HEP experiments searching for rare decays, such as Mu2e-II, and ultrafast time of flight (TOF) system at colliders. Cost-effective heavy inorganic scintillators for the homogeneous hadron calorimeter (HHCAL) concept to face the challenge of both electromagnetic and jet mass resolutions required by the proposed Higgs factory. We report recent progress in all these directions, such as LuAG:Ce ceramic fibers for the RADiCAL proposal, Lu<inf>2</inf> O<inf>3</inf>:Yb ceramics for TOF and ABS:Ce and DSB:Ce glass scintillators for HHCAL and the CalVision effort. The result of this investigation may also benefit nuclear physics experiments, GHz hard X-ray imaging, medical imaging and homeland security applications.

articleTitle: Investigation of the resolution requirement for propagation-based phase contrast imaging using inverse Compton scattering sources
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We conducted theoretical calculations and simulations to assess the resolution requirement for propagation-based phase-contrast imaging using an inverse Compton scattering light source. The theoretical width of the fringe primary peak associated with the edge enhancement effect was obtained, which could be a resolution guidance for the propagation-based phase contrast imaging applied in medicine and other fields.

articleTitle: Exploring the afterglow of GAGG:Ce scintillators for applications in space
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The recently developed cerium doped gadolinium aluminum gallium garnet (GAGG) has excellent scintillation properties for radiation detection such that it is suitable for a wide area of basic research and applications. However, the afterglow is a concern for deploying GAGG in space because of the harsh radiation environment. The effects of afterglow of GAGG was studied by irradiating several commercial off-the-shelf samples with a Co-60 source where the accumulated dose is equivalent to the daily average in orbit. The leakage current of the photodiode which was coupled to the scintillator, was measured for an extended period to examine the afterglow from the exposure. Because not all traps in the GAGG samples were filled up in one instance and the lower gain of the photodiode, the leakage current quickly decreased back to the baseline. It is concluded that the effects of GAGG’s afterglow due to cosmic radiation in orbit is manageable and can be mitigated by using photodiode as the readout device.

articleTitle: Ablation Study of Diffusion Model with Transformer Backbone for Low-count PET Denoising
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Diffusion models (DM) built from a hierarchy of denoising autoencoders have achieved remarkable progress in image generation, and are increasingly influential in the field of image restoration (IR) tasks. In the meantime, its backbone of autoencoders also evolved from UNet to vision transformer, e.g. Restormer. Therefore, it is important to disentangle the contribution of backbone networks and the additional generative learning scheme. Notably, DM shows varied performance across IR tasks, and the performance of recent advanced transformer-based DM on PET denoising is under-explored. In this study, we further raise an intuitive question, “{if we have a sufficiently powerful backbone, whether DM can be a general add-on generative learning scheme to further boost PET denoising}”. Specifically, we investigate one of the best-in-class IR models, i.e., DiffIR, which is a latent DM based on the Restormer backbone. We provide a qualitative and quantitative comparison with UNet, SR3 (UNet+pixel DM), and Restormer, on the 25% low dose ${}^{18}\mathrm{F-FDG}$ whole-body PET denoising task, aiming to identify the best practices. We trained and tested on 93 and 12 subjects, and each subject has 644 slices. It appears that Restormer outperforms UNet in terms of PSNR and MSE. However, additional latent DM over Restormer does not contribute to better MSE, SSIM, or PSNR in our task, which is even inferior to the conventional UNet. In addition, SR3 with pixel space DM is not stable to synthesize satisfactory results. The results are consistent with the natural image super-resolution tasks, which also suffer from limited spatial information. A possible reason would be the denoising iteration at latent feature space cannot well support detailed structure and texture restoration. This issue is more crucial in the IR tasks taking inputs with limited details, e.g., SR and PET denoising.

articleTitle: Probabilistic Sequencing for Compton Imaging using the General Klein-Nishina Cross-Section
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: For a three-dimensional pixelated position-sensitive Cadmium Zinc Telluride detector, the order of interactions for each recorded full-deposition gamma-ray must be determined using the energy deposition and position of each interaction. Sequence reconstruction is necessary for Compton imaging and is often done via the probabilistic method. After making changes in GEometry ANd Tracking 4 (GEANT4), simulations show that using the general Klein-Nishina (KN) cross-section in the probabilistic method, instead of the conventionally used unpolarized KN cross-section, yields improvement when determining the order of interactions for a gamma-ray originating from a polarized or unpolarized source. For a 511 keV polarized source, the most sequencing improvement was seen for gamma-rays undergoing a scatter of $\left(\theta=90^{\circ}, \phi=90^{\circ}\right.$). The method using the general KN cross-section sequenced 4.83% more events correctly compared to the method using the unpolarized KN cross-section, for 3-interaction events, and 2.23% more events for 4-interaction events. For an 511 keV unpolarized source, the most improvement was also seen in the same scattering geometry, with an improvement of 2.05% for 3-interaction events. There was improvement in other scattering geometries for both source polarizations, however not as much as expected. Simulation is being revised to look for errors and the sequencing algorithm runtime is being optimized to get statistical uncertainties. Currently this work shows a way to improve the probabilistic method of sequence reconstruction by considering a gamma-ray’s initial and final polarization for each scatter. Improvements in sequence reconstruction for polarized sources would aid in Positron Emission Tomography and imaging polarized objects in high-energy astrophysics.

articleTitle: Design of a DAQ for a Modular Detector for Dose Monitoring in Hadrontherapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present the development of the Data Acquisition System (DAQ) of a modular detector for dose monitoring in hadrontherapy based on pixelated LYSO scintillator coupled with 15 μm cell SiPM arrays. The detector and electronics are specifically designed for Prompt Gamma Imaging (PGI) in hadrontherapy applications. The modularity allows the system to be used in a variety of treatment plans, not being strictly limited by the physical constraints of the patient and beam position. The camera is organized in 64-channel module of 55×55 mm<sup>2</sup> area, each composed of two 32-channel front-end electronics system. Two 16 channel SITH ASIC are used to acquire the SiPMs current signals. This ICs are specifically designed for the readout of arrays of SiPMs and are able to process high input currents (tens of mA range) in order to be used with large-area photodetectors and high-energy gamma rays. The DAQ is based on two Analog Front-End circuits (AFE) and a FPGA for each 32-channel module. The ASICs energy outputs are converted by an octal-channel, 12-bit, 65 Msps ADC multiplexed 2:1 to read all the 16-channel of the ASIC. 32 Time-to-Digital Converters (TDCs) are implemented in a single FPGA to obtain the timing information with a precision better then 300ps (FWHM). Acquiring hit position, energy, and timestamp for each event is crucial for implementing time coincidence strategies that help to accurately reconstruct events, especially those involving Compton scattering and pair production, which are the dominant interaction mechanisms for high-energy gamma rays in PGI. We present preliminary experimental measurements acquired with two 16 and 32-channel prototypes obtaining a 511 keV energy resolution around 12% FWHM and a CRT of 200ps (FWHM) with 3×3 mm<sup>2</sup> SiPMs coupled with 3×3×5 mm<sup>3</sup> LYSO scintillators.

articleTitle: Large Diameter Fast and Bright Thallium-Based Ternary Halide Scintillators for High Energy Physics and Medical Imaging Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scintillator crystals play an important role in the radiation detection field. Widespread use of scintillators as gamma-ray detectors is largely generated by their extensive availability and tunable properties, such high light output, high stopping power, fast decay time, and good proportionality. Additionally, the cost for manufacturing a scintillation detector like $\mathrm{NaI}: \mathrm{Tl}$ is usually considerably lower than the cost for manufacturing a semiconductor detector. The vast variety of applications and requirements necessitates more research into new scintillation materials and/or better methods of producing existing materials. In this paper we present the investigation and development of bulk size, non-hygroscopic intrinsic Tl-based scintillation compounds for high energy physics particle detectors, growing these highd-ensity scintillators by incorporating heavy ions such as Tl-ion has been shown significantly increase material density. Our objective is to develop non-hygroscopic scintillators with high densities, high light yields, with a fast decay time component and sufficiently radiation hard. Up to 1-inch diameter ternary compounds TlAX<inf>3</inf> (where $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{Mg}, \mathrm{Ca}, \mathrm{Cu}$, or $\mathrm{Ba}, \mathrm{X}=\mathrm{Cl}, \mathrm{Br}$, I or mixed halides) are grown, processed, and characterized for their scintillation performance. Energy resolution, light yield, decay time, and proportionality behavior of these novel compounds will be presented.

articleTitle: 3D Reconstruction of Cerebral Aneurysm Geometry from 2D Angiographic Imaging using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The sudden rupture of a cerebral aneurysm can result in severe disability or death and is treatable with neurosurgical clipping or minimally invasive endovascular procedures (coiling or flow diverters) guided by angiography. However, the need for retreatment is relatively common. Clinicians rely on experience and 2D image techniques to lead and guide endovascular procedures. Cerebral vasculature is highly three-dimensional, with complex 3D curvature and tortuosity. Current imaging techniques are used during procedures to ‘flatten’ the complex vasculature. In this study, we developed a method for using 3 uniquely oriented angiographic images to reconstruct the 3D aneurysm geometry.We used open-source datasets of 149 aneurysm geometries consisting of patient-specific cerebral aneurysms and surrounding vasculature with a range of complex morphologies and sizes. After leaving 30 for unseen testing, we augmented the remaining dataset by orientation and scaling, yielding a dataset of over 24,000 unique geometries. We restructured the irregular point clouds into a regular grid. This 3D data functioned as the output to the neural network. Simulated angiographic images were obtained by using 2D projections of the gridded data in the XY, YZ, and XZ planes. These three projections were used as the input to the model.We developed a 3D convolutional neural network with a customized dice loss function to account for the surrounding padding. Initial results are promising, showing that complex vasculature can be identified in 3D; however, DARNN has trouble distinguishing multiple outlet vessels in a small region. Predictions are made in 0.1 s.

articleTitle: Use of CZT detectors for Non-Destructive Testing based on backscattered radiation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The vast array of technologies available for non-destructive testing (NDT) includes ultrasound, radiography, thermography, visual inspection, magnetic resonance, and computed tomography, among others. X-ray radiography stands out as a versatile and effective NDT method, particularly renowned for its remarkable depth of penetration into dense materials. Semiconductor-based detectors, and in particular CdZnTe, have gained traction for their ability to offer high energy resolution and facilitate the development of Energy Resolved Photon Counting (ERPC) Systems. This study focuses on X-ray backscattering-based NDTs, a novel approach that situates all instrumentation on one side of the analyzed material. Notably, this configuration promises cost reduction and minimized cleaning downtime from an industrial perspective. The envisioned applications span in-line wood and ceramic inspection, as well as quality control of plastic raw materials. The proposed system aims to extract comprehensive material characteristics, including density and effective atomic number profiles across various depths. Employing custom collimators and X-ray spectrometers based on CZT, this system enables precise material analysis at different layers. Through simulations, we demonstrate promising potential in achieving accurate density determination and depth resolution, bolstering its applicability in diverse material inspection scenarios.

articleTitle: CZT Characterization using a Novel Contactless Time Of Flight Technique
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work concerns process feedback and device characterization to aid the development of detector grade CZT detectors for the demanding high flux application of medical Spectral Photon Counting CT (SPCCT) imaging. In previous work (RTSD 2021) a novel Time of Flight method using Na22 511 KeV excitation instead of lasers or alpha particles was reported for estimating timing jitter for photon absorptions in CZT slab detectors. The technique is herein extended in 2 significant ways. First, the offline Digital Pulse Shape Analysis (DPSA) was further developed to be able to determine bulk material transport parameters including: the energy spectral response ($\varepsilon$), the depth of interaction (doi), the electric field (E) nonuniformity, mobility (m) and lifetime ($\tau$) for both holes (h) and electrons (e). These parameters are critical to the avoidance of material polarization and flux limitations, as well as to electronic signal design and count rate capability in SPCCT. The second development was to be able to perform the above measurements on bare CZT without applied metal contacts, so called contactless. Removable, reusable, resistive rubber contacts $\left(\mathrm{R}^{4}\right)$ were developed that permit the full DPSA analysis and thus sample comparison without the need for ‘fab’ in the research cycle and without the confounding measurement variability due to the fab contacts process. The current work shows the success of the technique using CZT Samples with applied metal Fab contacts compared to results with $\mathrm{R}^{4}$ contacts replacing them. Results for different samples with a single $\mathrm{R}^{4}$ contact are presented as well to show assay capability. The new measurement technique allows the separation of contact and bulk performance variables in the development and optimization of CZT for CT application as well as providing a new and effective alternative wafer screening technique to add to the current lineup of screening tests.

articleTitle: Benchmarking Monte Carlo codes for the modelling of low-energy neutron production target reactions
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accelerator-based neutron sources (ABNS) are gaining importance for applications such as neutron capture therapy (NCT) due to the decline in the number of nuclear research reactors that are in operation. Optimising ABNS design requires accurate modeling of low-energy neutron production target reactions. This study benchmarks Geant4, PHITS, FLUKA, and MCNP Monte Carlo codes for simulating the 7Li(p, n)7Be, 9Be(p, n)9B, 9Be(d, n)10B, 13C(d, n)14N, and $p(7 \mathrm{Li}, \mathrm{n}) 7 \mathrm{Be}$ reactions relevant to NCT. Simulated neutron yields and angular distributions are compared to experimental data. Results show general agreement for 9Be(p, n)9B neutron yield in the forward direction, with some variations at lower energies. Geant4 11.2.0 shows noticable improvement over 10.7.3 for 7Li(p, n)7Be. This work guides simulation tool selection for ABNS design and emphasises the need for ongoing benchmarking to ensure accurate modeling of low-energy neutron production target reactions.

articleTitle: Optimizing Event Graphs in Particle Discrimination for Neutron Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron-gamma discrimination ratios (NGD, or neutron- and gamma-efficiency ratios) for scintillator neutron detectors have improved to about 10<sup>7</sup>-10<sup>9</sup> using a graph-embedded nonnegative matrix factorization (GNMF) algorithm. But GNMF works only under the constant neutron-to-gamma flux ratio in the learning and testing stages. To generalize a graph-embedded algorithm, a multilayer filter structure is proposed to construct more generalized graphs. We present a framework, called graph-construction based NMF (GC-NMF), to identify neutron events exclusively and efficiently at various neutron-to-gamma flux ratios. An application-specified Figure-of-Merit (FOM) is defined to select model parameters and balance the bias and variance, which provides excellent generalizability, selectivity, and neutron detection efficiency. As an example, the GC-NMF algorithm allows a bright Eu-doped CaF<inf>2</inf>-AlF<inf>3</inf>-<sup>6</sup>LiF (Eu:CALF) neutron scintillator to provide a NGD ratio of 6E6, and a thermal-neutron detection efficiency of about 50% under the neutron-to-gamma flux ratios varied by 10 times. We will review the generalizability of GC-NMF for other two neutron scintillators, <sup>6</sup>Li-glass (GS20) and Ce: Gd<inf>3</inf>Al<inf>2</inf>Ga<inf>3</inf>O<inf>12</inf> (GAGG). This work indicates the development of generalized machine learning (ML)-based particle discrimination algorithms is critical for neutron detectors applied at different radiation environments.

articleTitle: Addition of detailed structures to the XCAT brain phantom for in-silico high-resolution multi-modal imaging system usage
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Advances in imaging techniques have enabled visualization of anatomical structures in the body and the brain at a higher resolution than previously known. In-silico multimodal high-resolution imaging research could both ‘benefit from’ and ‘be challenged by’ extending the XCAT anthropomorphic phantom feature set and functionality suitable for sub-mm resolution imaging. By adding anatomical objects of interest that have complex shapes and dimensions that are in the order of sub-mm to less than a few cm to the existing XCAT anthropomorphic model, image quality of the systems under development may be assessed and improved. Herein, we summarize our ongoing effort towards furthering in-silico high-resolution brain imaging by enhancing the XCAT digital anthropomorphic phantom via adding anatomical structures of small (<5 mm) dimensions, sub dividing previously existing organs to represent different nuclei, and asses the challenges in imaging these additions by using simulated multi-pinhole dedicated brain SPECT acquisition.

articleTitle: Development of a Configurable Photon-to-Digital Converter in 65 nm
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A photo-detector chain with a timing jitter below 10 ps will increase the resolution of high-energy physics experiments vertex reconstruction, quantum telecommunication and medical imaging. To achieve this, our team at Université de Sherbrooke is developing a Photon-to-Digital Converter (PDC), an array of single photon avalanche diodes (SPAD) coupled one-to-one by their cathodes to quenching circuits (QC). The prototype, designed in TSMC 65 nm LP technology, includes the full front-end chain required to detect and timestamp photons. The prototype time-to-digital converter (TDC) adopted in our design is a patented cascaded-stage Vernier TDC with reduced power consumption and area already validated in 180 nm technology. The circuit includes 2 arrays, one optimized for rad-hard applications, of $4 \times 4$ QCs connected to integrated CMOS 65 nm SPADs as the input and to TDCs at the output. The QC discriminator consists of an inverter chain capable of configuring its switching voltage to optimize the front-end’s timing jitter and reduce spurious counts due to the input noise. Furthermore, the QC follows the technology’s design for manufacturing rules to maximize the production yield. This work follows the design process and shows updates on PDC fabrication and preliminary results on the newly developed QC prototype.

articleTitle: In-vivo demonstration of activation imaging of gold nanoparticles
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, drug delivery using gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) has attracted considerable attention. In vivo visualization of AuNPs is crucial because some studies have shown that the biodistribution of AuNPs varies depending on various factors. However, methods that image AuNPs directly and with high sensitivity have yet to be established. Here, we propose the activation imaging of AuNPs. Activation imaging activates materials through neutron irradiation and performs imaging using X-rays and gamma rays emitted from the activated atoms. When gold is irradiated with neutrons, stable ${ }^{197} \mathrm{Au}$ becomes radioactive ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$, which emits $412-\mathrm{keV}$ gamma rays and has a halflife of 2.7 days. In this study, neutron-activated gold nanoparticles ($\left[{ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}\right] \mathrm{AuNPs}$) were synthesized, injected into tumor-bearing mice, and visualized using a wide-band X-ray and gammaray imager. Consequently, $\left.{ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}\right] \mathrm{AuNPs}$ retained in the tumor were successfully visualized 4 days after injection. In addition, we labeled an alpha-emitting therapeutic drug, ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$, with $\left[{ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}\right]$ AuNPs. The 79-keV X-rays emitted during the decay of ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$ and the $412-\mathrm{keV}$ gamma rays from ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ enable the individual imaging of ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$ and AuNPs. In addition, the 2.7-day half-life of ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ allows long-term tracking of ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$-labeled AuNPs, which has been difficult due to the short half-life of ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}(7.2 \mathrm{~h})$. Mice were injected with ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$-labeled $\left[{ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}\right] \mathrm{AuNPs}$, and ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$ and ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$ were imaged individually using the same measurement data and setting energy windows corresponding to 79 and 412 keV, respectively. Two days after injection, ${ }^{211}$ At could no longer be imaged because of its decay; however, we could still visualize the ${ }^{211} \mathrm{At}$-labeled $\left[{ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}\right] \mathrm{AuNPs}$ using gamma rays from ${ }^{198} \mathrm{Au}$. We believe the in vivo activation imaging of AuNPs demonstrated in this study can effectively contribute to developing drug delivery technologies that use AuNPs.

articleTitle: Analog Neural Network ASIC (ANNA) for Position Reconstruction in Anger Cameras
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents an analog neural network ASIC (ANNA) for embedded position-of-interaction estimation of gamma rays in Anger Cameras. The neural network features 64 input nodes interfacing with photodetector analog signals, two 20-neurons hidden layers, and two output neurons corresponding to the predicted x and y interaction coordinates. The multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) operations are performed in charge domain through programmable switched-capacitor crossbar arrays, in which network weights are implemented with 5-bit precision. Leveraging in-sensor processing of analog signals allows to reduce the amount of data to transmit, as well as eliminating the requirement for ADCs and FPGAs, with evident advantages in terms of costs, latency, throughput and power consumption, especially for detectors with large field of view and high density of channels (e.g. Total-body PET). Fabricated in a 0.35 um CMOS process node, this first prototype chip demonstrates an energy efficiency of $150 \mathrm{GOP} / \mathrm{J}$ at maximum frequency of 10 MHz. Its correct functioning is experimentally demonstrated on a simulated dataset of a PET detector based on $51 \mathrm{~mm} \times 51 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{x}$ 10 mm LYSO scintillator read out by an 8 x 8 array of SiPMs. We finally report a study regarding the optimization of neural network architecture for the next version of the ASIC.

articleTitle: A Study on Performance Evaluation of Prototype X-ray Backscatter Imaging Device for Discrimination of Low-Density Materials
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The backscatter X-ray imaging device demonstrates excellent capability in distinguishing lowdensity materials. Currently, we are developing a prototype of the backscatter X-ray imaging device and evaluating its performance to enhance the device further. To confirm the performance of the developed prototype and to find additional improvement directions, we utilized three testing methods. The first and second test methods utilized for performance evaluation are the assessment of Cu wire detection capability and the evaluation of spatial resolution through slit measurement specified in ANSI N42.46. The measurements revealed that wires up to 2mm in diameter could be detected, and a resolution of 7mm line pairs could be achieved. Furthermore, to evaluate the material discrimination capability, we tested the measurement capabilities on 16 types of materials. It was confirmed that the device could distinguish between high-density and low-density materials, with particularly high discrimination ability for aluminum. Overall, we were able to verify the performance level of the backscatter X-ray imaging device under development and obtain foundational data to determine development directions for achieving improved performance in the future.

articleTitle: Characterization of MIRA ASIC with a MCP and new version towards upscaling of UV sensor readout formats
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: MIRA (Microchannel Readout Asic) is a pixelated ASIC composed of a 2D matrix of $32 \times 32$ pixels. It has been realized in the PLUS project (PLanetary Ultraviolet Spectrometer) which aims to develop a novel dual channel FUV/EUV imaging spectrometer working in 55-200 nm spectral range. Within this context, the MIRA is designed to provide high counting capacity (100 Kcps/pixel), a low input Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) of $20 \mathrm{e}^{-}{ }_{\text {ms}}$ and an high Dynamic Range (DR). In this work, we present MIRA’s characterization of both the analog and digital sections including the measurements with a Micro Channel Plate (MCP). Finally, we present the work done on revising the circuit, in particular on power reduction of analog readout chain, with the goal to upscale the pixel matrix and therefore reducing the voltage drops on the power supply lines.

articleTitle: Improved Event Classification of Metascintillators: An Approach Using Time-over-Threshold Analysis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Metascintillators are complex scintillating heterostructures, that enhance the energy sharing mechanism from recoil electron events, employed to improve both stopping power and timing resolution. However, the analysis for classifying shared events requires complicated processes. The purpose of this study was to develop a method utilizing Time-over-Threshold (ToT) information to effectively identify shared events. A $3 \times 3 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ metascintillator comprising inorganic scintillator (BGO, $200 \mu \mathrm{m}$) and plastic scintillator plates (EJ-212, $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$) was designed, achieving a coincidence time resolution (CTR) of 279.3 ps FWHM for whole photopeak events. To discriminate shared events, the sum of dual-threshold ToT values was utilized to estimate deposited energy, enabling the identification of regions specific to 511 keV events. The difference between ToT values was used to calculate the ratio of rise to decay times of the pulses generated by BGO and plastic scintillator. By plotting these values and selecting events having similar ToT values with small ToT differences, it was possible to effectively distinguish shared events from those fully deposited in BGO. Shared events comprising 8.6% of the total were identified, achieving a CTR of 145 ps. The classification results were similar to those based on the rise time of the timing signal used in the previous studies, while requiring only simple ToTs for the classification. It was expected that this approach which could be implemented by hardware circuit, could facilitate the classification process of metascintillators.

articleTitle: The mobility-lifetime product of hole in CdZnTeSe depending on Se contents
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The charge collection efficiency (CCE) of a radiation detector greatly depends on the ratio of the electron to hole mobility-lifetime product. In order to improve the energy resolution of the detector, it is crucial to minimize the effects of hole tailing effect and the polarization effect. A recent study has shown that the addition of Se to CdZnTe (CZT) detectors can improve the mobility-lifetime product of holes by reducing the density of E<inf>c</inf>-1.1-eV traps (hole traps) [1]. To determine the optimal amount of Se, the mobility-lifetime product of holes in CdZnTeSe (CZTS) detectors was evaluated with Se contents ranging from 1% to 10%. The Zn content was adjusted accordingly to compensate for the decrease in bandgap at higher Se contents. The detector performance and mobility-lifetime products of holes at different Se contents will be presented.

articleTitle: Accurate resistivity measurement in low-mobility semiconductors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We demonstrate that the I-V characteristics measured shortly after biasing can be used to distinguish bulk and contact resisitivity in CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> detector with Cr contacts. This technique can be also to determine the drift mobility of the charge carries. We also conducted I-V measurements at various temperatures to determine the contact barrier height. Presented technique will be used to study the equilibrium resistivity in whole crystal ingot along the axis of growth.

articleTitle: High-Stopping Power Ceramic Scintillator Lu2O3: La for High-Resolution Brain PET Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Key characteristics of brain PET scanners include spatial resolution and sensitivity, requiring detectors to have both high 3D resolution and high detection efficiency. We are developing a high- density ceramic scintillator for brain PET applications based on lutetium oxide, Lu2O3:La (LO). Compared with state-of-the-art scintillators such as lutetium (yttrium) oxyorthosilicate (L(Y)SO), LO exhibits a higher density (9.4 g/cm3 for LO vs. 7.2 g/cm3 for L(Y)SO) and effective atomic number (Z) (68 for LO vs. 65 for L(Y)SO), providing higher stopping power and photoelectric ratio. Our results show that a ~ 11% energy resolution can be obtained from a 1 x 1 x 5 mm3 LO element. Currently, we are fabricating a 4 x 4 array of 0.9 x 0.9 x 15 mm3 LO crystals with a 1.0 mm pitch. The performance of a dual-ended readout detector based on this LO array and position-sensitive silicon photomultipliers (PS-SiPMs) will be reported and compared to a detector based on an L(Y)SO array with the same dimensions at the conference.

articleTitle: Smart Pixels: In-pixel AI for on-sensor data filtering
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present a smart pixel prototype readout integrated circuit (ROIC) designed in CMOS 28 nm bulk process, with in-pixel implementation of an artificial intelligence (AI) /machine learning (ML) based data filtering algorithm designed as proof-of-principle for a Phase III upgrade at the LargeHadron Collider (LHC) pixel detector. The first version of the ROIC consists of two matrices of 256 smart pixels, each $25 \times 25 \mu \mathrm{m} 2$ in size. Each pixel consists of a charge-sensitive preamplifier with leakage current compensation and three auto-zero comparators for a 2-bit flash-type ADC. The frontend is capable of synchronously digitizing the sensor charge within 25 ns. Measurement results show an equivalent noise charge (ENC) of $\sim 30 \mathrm{e}$ - and a total dispersion of $\sim 100 \mathrm{e}$ - The second version of the ROIC uses a fully connected two-layer neural network (NN) to process information from a cluster of 256 pixels to determine if the pattern corresponds to highly desirable high-momentum particle tracks for selection and readout. The digital NN is embedded in-between analog signal processing regions of the 256 pixels without increasing the pixel size and is implemented as fully combinatorial digital logic to minimize power consumption and eliminate clock distribution, and is active only in the presence of an input signal. The total power consumption of the neural network is $\sim 300 \mu \mathrm{W}$. The NN performs momentum classification based on the generated cluster patterns and even with a modest momentum threshold, it is capable of 54.4%-75.4% total data rejection total data rejection, opening the possibility of using the pixel information at 40 MHz for the trigger. The total power consumption of analog and digital functions per pixel is $\sim 6 \mu \mathrm{W}$ per pixel, which corresponds to $\sim 1 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{cm} 2$ staying within the experimental constraints.

articleTitle: Detection Efficiency and Imaging Performance of a 25.4×25.4×24 mm3 Compton Cameras based on a Single Voxelized Scintillator.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study demonstrated the enhancement of a Compton camera system through the expansion of the voxelized detector volume, aiming to increase its detection efficiency and reduce data acquisition times to reconstruct radiation sources. By doubling the size of the previous $4 \times 4 \times 4$ voxel detector $\left(12.6 \times 12.6 \times 12 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right)$ to an $8 \times 8 \times 8$ one $\left(25.4 \times 25.4 \times 24 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}\right)$, both the angular resolution and the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) were significantly improved. Simple back projection (SBP) and list mode maximum likelihood estimation method (LM-MLEM) were utilized for image reconstruction, and the expanded system showed a substantial decrease in measurement times up to a 40-times with equivalent image quality. This advancement makes significant improvement to deploy a lightweight and high-efficiency Compton cameras in unmanned measuring equipment, such as drones for various industrial applications.

articleTitle: A Study on Novel Scintillators for Interventional Multimodal X-ray and Scintigraphy Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Multimodal imaging systems are beneficial for the treatment of cancer with radionuclides, because they provide anatomical and nuclear information at the same time. With the combination of scintigraphy and fluoroscopic X-ray imaging, the hospital logistics and patient burden of e.g. radioembolization procedures could be reduced. One approach is to mount the gamma camera directly behind a flat-panel X-ray detector on a clinical C-arm. A compact design and a naturally good image alignment is obtained. However, several shortcomings still need to be addressed, especially the X-ray induced blinding effects in the gamma camera. To this day, most clinical gamma cameras use NaI(Tl) as the scintillator. NaI(Tl) has a relatively high afterglow, which gives rise to a background signal following each X-ray pulse. This high background obscures the signals generated by the gamma photons emitted by the radionuclide. This research focuses on finding a scintillator with similar properties as NaI(Tl), but with lower afterglow. GATE simulations of the interventional X-ray and scintigraphy imaging detector (IXSI) were performed. The most promising candidates were further studied in our lab. The selection was done using the simulated signal-to-background ratio at 100 ms after the X-ray pulse. For the in-lab measurements, afterglow, energy-resolution, non-proportionality and light yield were evaluated. Initial measurements are consistent with our simulation. The study includes novel compounds like NaI(Tl,Sr), CsI(Tl,Sb,Bi) and the most promising low-afterglow candidate so far, NaI(Tl,Sr,Y).

articleTitle: Deep Texture Analysis for Automated TNM Staging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The potential of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in detecting various forms of cancer has been widely recognized. However, the generalizability of metabolic signature-based results across the three categories of TNM staging using deep texture analysis remains largely unexplored. This study seeks to examine the cross-TNM category and cross-cancer relevance of deep textures identified by a 3D CNN model. Our methodology involves processing patches of PET data from various glycolytic volumes, including primary tumor, malignant nodes and metastases, from PETFDG data, with high Standardized Uptake Values (SUV) for patients presenting with clinically confirmed esophageal cancer. Activation values were calculated for each filter in the CNN, and a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is conducted to assess the model’s ability to generalize its learned metabolic signatures. Our results indicate that a CNN trained for esophageal cancer primary tumor detection can successfully demonstrate distinct patterns of cellular metabolism for primary tumor, malignant nodes and metastases that a CNN trained for esophageal cancer primary tumor detection can discern all parts of esophageal TNM staging categories.

articleTitle: The sPHENIX Data Acquisition System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: By the time of this conference, the sPHENIX experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) will have ended its second data taking run. sPHENIX is the first major upgrade to a Nuclear Physics experiment in the US in 2 decades, and will be the final experiment taking data at RHIC before the construction of the Electron-Ion Collider. In 2023, the experiment went through a commissioning phase with beam that was meant to be followed by a physics production period. However, that was cut short by a failure of a RHIC magnet that prematurely ended the beam operations for the year. sPHENIX still took about 12PB of data in various modes in 2023. At the time of this writing, the 2024 RHIC operations with proton-proton beams have been ongoing for less than 2 weeks. The experiment has already taken some physics-quality data. We will explain the design and show the performance of the sPHENIX data acquisition system, and describe the plan for future upgrades as we prepare for the $2025 \mathrm{Au}+\mathrm{Au}$ run.

articleTitle: Spectral Response of an Edge-on GaAsCr Detector for Clinical Photon Counting CT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel edge-on structure X-ray detector based on GaAs:Cr, designed to enhance the spectral response of photon-counting detectors (PCDs) used in clinical applications. The GaAs:Cr detectors offer superior electron mobility and resistivity, contributing to a significant reduction in the pile-up effect and scattering when compared to face-on CZT and edge-on Si. These properties ensure a higher signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and better energy resolution. To validate the performance of edge-on GaAs detector, we build a module with a specially engineered front-end amplification circuit, characterized by high gain and low noise.

articleTitle: Recent Advances in Cesium Lead Bromide Crystal Growth and Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> (CLB) is an emerging halide semiconductor suitable for gamma spectroscopy. We report on recent advances in purification and crystal growth of CLB crystals, and performance of gamma detectors fabricated from the grown crystals. The crystalline defects in the grown crystals, the plausible cause of the defects, and remedial approaches are discussed. We will also discuss the conditioning and polarization in CLB detectors and report on the influence of various growth and fabrication parameters on achieving high energy resolution and long-term stability.

articleTitle: Measurement of pulsed neutrons using real-time data display and storage module in neutron reflectometer at J-PARC MLF
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A data display and storage module has been developed for a gaseous two-dimensional neutron detector used in the Materials and Life Science Experimental Facility (MLF) at J-PARC, especially in the neutron reflectometer beamline 17. The developed module is fabricated in the VME standard widely used in MLF and designed for easy user operation. The module provides inputs for two-dimensional position data and T0 signals for time-of-flight measurements, and outputs for data storage and display. Users were only required to determine the measurement time and to start/stop the measurement. The image shown on the display in real time is a two-dimensional image and projections of the x - and y -axes. In addition, it displays elapsed time, count rate, and total counts. Irradiation tests were performed using high-intensity pulsed neutrons. The distance from the neutron source to the detector was 18 m, and the neutron beam was adjusted by changing the aperture width of the neutron slit equipped in the beamline. The measured counts increased with increasing aperture width, and the shape of the TOF was consistent. The developed module worked well without missing random signals from pulsed neutrons. The results show that the module has a counting rate capability of over 130 kcps and has the potential to make effective use of intense pulsed neutrons. It is expected that this module will become an important tool for neutron scattering experiments in the near future.

articleTitle: Spectroscopic and Imaging Performance of the H3DD_UM Array DAQ System Using the H3DD_UM ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The H3DD_UM ASIC is a new generation of waveform sampling ASICs, being developed at the University of Michigan, for pixelated semiconductor gamma-ray detectors, such as CdZnTe, TlBr and perovskites. This contribution summarizes the spectroscopic and imaging performance of the H3DD_UM array DAQ system based on the most recent version of the H3DD_UM ASIC. Using a $20 \times 20 \times 15 \ \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ CdZnTe detector, 0.40% FWHM was achieved at 662 keV for single-pixel events. With a larger $40 \times 40 \times 15 \ \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ CdZnTe crystal, 0.46% FWHM was obtained. Subpixel position resolution is about $600 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ at 80 keV, which gives about 1 mm coded aperture imaging resolution at 1 meter away.

articleTitle: Waveform Digitizing ASIC-based Radioisotope Identification Device
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Radioisotope Identification Devices (RIIDs) are essential tools for security experts, allowing for the localization and identification of nuclear material in the field. To achieve these objectives quickly and accurately, RIIDs must meet several criteria, including energy resolution and gamma ray detection efficiency. Operational deployment creates a number of other requirements, including ruggedization, robustness to a wide range of temperatures and humidity levels, and a sufficiently long battery life. We present the development of a RIID incorporating a waveform digitizing application specific integrated circuit (digital ASIC) at H3D. The digital ASIC, matured at the University of Michigan, achieves an energy resolution of 0.5% full-width-at-half-maximum at 662 keV with large volume (up to $24 \mathrm{~cm}^{3}$) pixelated CdZnTe detectors. The high resolution makes digital ASIC-based systems ideal for RIID applications where better resolution yields significant gains in sensitivity and accuracy. An architecture around the digital ASIC has been designed at H3D, with an emphasis on maintaining the high energy resolution while enabling high count rates up to 40 k cps. The ASIC is integrated into a handheld RIID with a compact design, weighing less than 2.5 lbs.

articleTitle: X-ray photon counting by perovskite CsPbBr3 detectors with resolved k-edge and improved count rate
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Traditional X-ray detectors work at energy integrating mode that does not resolve the energy of individual X-ray photons. X-ray photon counting is an emerging technique that aims at resolving single photon energy, which enables higher X-ray image quality with more information about scanned object at a lower X-ray dose. Recently, perovskite materials have demonstrated promising performance for hard X-ray and gamma-ray detection. In our previous work, we reported the performance of our perovskite CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> photon counting detectors that can count an incident X-ray photon rate of $0.099 \mathrm{Mcps} /$ pixel at 10% deadtime loss under reasonable pulse processing conditions. Here, we report further development of perovskite CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> photon counting detectors. When indium, barium, or lead was used separately as the scanned object, the transmitted X-ray energy spectrum acquired by the CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> detector clearly resolved the feature due to the k-edge discontinuity of their X-ray attenuation coefficient. Besides, with improvement on the crystal quality and device fabrication, we were able to operate the CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> detector at a higher voltage, e.g., 1200 V reverse bias for a 1 mm thick detector vs 350 V for 1 mm detector in our previous work. The higher bias voltage leads to reduced charge drifting time, and consequently, the count rate performance was improved compared to previous results.

articleTitle: Whole-Body PET Tumor Lesion Segmentation Using a Transformer-Based Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate segmentation of tumors in PET images is pivotal for cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. In this study, we employ a transformer-based model named MedSAM, a fine-tuned version of the Segment Anything Model developed by Meta [1, 2]. MedSAM comprises a vision transformer (ViT)-based image encoder for feature extraction, a prompt encoder for integrating user interactions such as bounding boxes, and a mask decoder responsible for generating segmentation outcomes and confidence scores. The base ViT model consists of 12 transformer layers, each block containing a multi-head self-attention block and a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) block with layer normalization, resulting in a feature size of 64×64 in the image embedding after passing through the image encoder (downscaled by a factor of 16). The prompt encoders map the corner points of the bounding box prompt to 256-dimensional vector embeddings. PET DICOM files were converted to SUV space and cropped from 400×400 to 250×250 pixels. Only a subsample of PET images from the Whole-Body FDG-PET/CT-lesions challenge dataset [3] was used in this study. The challenge dataset included 1014 whole-body PET/CT scans from 900 patients, publicly available on The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA). We utilized a subset of 120 patients (single = 74 and metastatic = 46) for training (200 epochs), with 57 patients (single = 42 and metastatic = 15) retained as a held-out internal test set. Our training strategy involved 200 epochs with an AdamW optimizer, a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 1e-4, and a loss function comprising Cross-entropy and Dice loss. Achieving a Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.78 for Single tumor segmentation, 0.71 for metastatic segmentation, and an average DSC of 0.76 when the network trained using 120 patients, demonstrates promising results for this segmentation challenge.

articleTitle: Improving Image Performance of Coded-aperture Gamma-ray Imager Under Relative High Dose Environment
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The EPSILON-G used in this study is a gamma-ray imager based on coded-aperture mask, capable of detecting the location of radiation sources and the distribution of radioactive contamination. It also allows for the representation of ambient dose equivalent rate and the identification of nuclides using energy spectrum. However, the EPSILON-G encountered issues with decreased image performance in environments with high ambient radiation levels. To improve image acquisition and performance by minimizing the influence of ambient radiation, the optimal detector system was determined by comparing different masks with additional tungsten shields and comparing the thickness of the scintillator. Then, the image acquisition performance was evaluated by simulating an environment where the ambient dose rate is larger than the dose rate of the target gamma-ray source, such as the primary system of a nuclear power plant. This demonstrated that the modified detector system can be utilized to acquire images in environments where the ambient radiation dose rate is higher than the dose rate at the target source.

articleTitle: High-Z Sensor Developments for High Energy Synchrotron Application
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Sensors providing high quantum efficiencies for hard X-rays are key to extend effective photon science beyond the reach of existing silicon sensors. To overcome this limitation, semiconductors with high atomic number (“high-Z”) are being investigated for use in hybrid pixel detectors. In this work, Germanium and Cadmium Zinc Telluride sensors have been explored and integrated to an MM-PAD readout ASIC. Germanium pixel sensors, fabricated at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and Redlen High flux CZTs have been adopted for this purpose. In this work, we discuss the sensors characteristics, fabrication, and initial results of detector performance.

articleTitle: Advanced Positronium Lifetime Imaging Reconstruction Using Two-Component Modeling in Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is a crucial imaging modality for the diagnosis of diseases such as cancer and Alzheimer’s, highlighting the uptake of radiolabeled molecules that target specific disease markers. Recently, positronium lifetime imaging (PLI), which supplements PET by examining the tissue microenvironment’s properties beyond tracer uptake, has been implemented using time-of-flight (TOF) PET with non-pure positron emitters. However, accurately reconstructing lifetime images from data captured by systems with limited TOF resolution remains challenging. This paper presents a novel approach to two-dimensional PLI using a maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method based on an exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) probability distribution to describe the positronium lifetime data from TOF PET. We assess our EMG-based MLE method’s effectiveness against existing methods that use exponential likelihood functions and penalized surrogate approaches. Our results from computer simulations indicate that the EMG-MLE method produces quantitatively precise lifetime images. Moreover, we introduce an advanced two-component model that enhances the accuracy of ortho-positronium (oP) lifetime images and accommodates data from multiple positron populations. Comparative studies with existing models reveal that our two-component model excels in capturing complex lifetime distributions more accurately, marking a significant advancement in PLI technology.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based PET image correction and optimization from CT-less PET data
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study aims to compare six distinct deep learning-based pathways for generating fully corrected PET images from low-dose PET images without attenuation and scatter correction, with the goal of reducing radiation exposure. By scrutinizing the effectiveness of these pathways in generating high-quality, corrected PET images from uncorrected low-dose PET data, the research seeks to identify the most efficient correction strategy. A dataset 240 patients’ brain scan from a Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT scanner were applied for this study. Of these, images from 200 patients were used as the training set, and images from 40 patients as the test set. Peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), Structural similarity index (SSIM), and Normalized root mean square error (NRMSE) metrics were employed to evaluate the ability of different pathways to produce high-quality full-dose PET images with attenuation and scatter correction from CT-less low-dose PET data. Among the six pathways investigated, the approach which utilized full-dose data with generated CT images for attenuation and scatter correction yielded the most promising outcomes. In the brain region of the test datasets, this approach achieved an average error of less than 1%. The SSIM was 0.9626 ± 0.0213, PSNR was 49.5288 ± 3.2620, and NRMSE was 0.0062 ± 0.0039. Of the remaining five pathways utilizing only low-dose data, the strategy involving the generated CT image and the original low-dose PET image without attenuation and scatter correction as dual-channel input to produce full-dose PET images with attenuation and scatter correction exhibited commendable performance. The SSIM, PSNR and NRMSE for this approach was 0.9325 ± 0.0279, 44.4489 ± 2.9297, 0.0295 ± 0.0072, respectively.

articleTitle: A Cryogenic readout integrated circuit with analog pile-up and in-Pixel ADC for high frame rate Skipper CCD-in-CMOS Sensors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Skipper CCD-in-CMOS Parallel Read-Out Circuit V2 (SPROCKET2) is designed to enable high frame rate readout of Skipper CCD-in-CMOS image sensors. The SPROCKET2 pixel is fabricated in a 65 nm CMOS process and occupies a 60um x 60um footprint. SPROCKET2 is intended to be heterogeneously integrated with a pixelated Skipper CCD-in-CMOS sensor, such that one readout pixel is connected to a multiplexed array of 16 active image sensor pixels, to match their spatial geometry. Our design benefits from the Skipper CCD-in-CMOS sensor’s non-destructive readout capability to achieve exceptionally low noise through multi-sampling and averaging while optimizing for total power consumption. The pixel readout utilizes correlated double sampling to minimize 1/f noise and includes “pile-up” of ten successive samples in the analog domain before digitizing at a rate of 66.7 ksps. Measurement results of in-pixel serial SAR ADC show DNL and INL of $\sim 0.44$ LSB and 0.58 LBS respectively. A large area array of 20,000 SPROCKET2 ADC pixels (multiplexed 1:16 to 320,000 sensor pixels) is currently under test. By reading out data over a 10 Gbps optical link, this pixel design enables a frame rate of $\sim 4 \mathrm{kfps}$ for large sensing areas with minimal sensing deadtime. In the highest gain mode, the pixelated ADC has an input-referred resolution of 10 uV with a simulated power consumption of 50 uW. The pixel operates with constant current draw to minimize power-rail crosstalk.

articleTitle: Instrument Performance of the Lunar-VISE Gamma Ray Neutron Spectrometer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The Lunar Vulkan Imaging and Spectroscopy Explorer (Lunar-VISE) mission consists of a suite of instruments to explore the Gruithuisen Domes located in the northern lunar hemisphere. One of instruments to be mounted on a rover is a gamma ray and neutron spectrometer. The spectrometer uses a $\mathrm{Li}-6$ enriched $\mathrm{Cs}_{2}{ }^{6} \mathrm{LiYCl}_{6}$ (CLYC) scintillator to detect both gamma rays and neutrons. The design of the instrument balances mass, power and performance to obtain high-quality gamma ray spectroscopy with a $6.4-\mathrm{cm}$ diameter CLYC crystal encased in a gadolinium shell to veto thermal neutrons. To obtain a measure of the thermal neutron albedo to assess the concentration of local neutron moderating materials, a $5.0-\mathrm{cm}$ diameter CLYC without a gadolinium shell is used to measure the full spectral neutron flux. To minimize power, the system design utilizes a multi-channel configuration to provide pulse shape analysis and spectroscopy using a single readout channel. The instrument design is completed, and the sensor heads are being assembled and tested to meet the design requirements.

articleTitle: Development of a Portable and Versatile PET System for Interactive Point-of-Care Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Current clinical PET/CT scanners are optimized for diagnostic accuracy & clinical throughput, primarily for whole-body FDG imaging in cancer detection & monitoring. However, these systems often cannot accommodate immobilized or intensive-care patients. The increasing availability of novel radio-theranostics underlines the need for versatile, accessible molecular imaging tools. This study introduces a Point-of-Care (POC) PET technology integrated with ultrasound (US), developed to enhance diagnostic capabilities in settings where conventional PET/CT scanners are impractical. The POC-PET incorporates a Kuka KR 10 R1100 sixx robotic arm, a rotation stage, & 8 time-of-flight (TOF) PET detector modules mounted on a trolley. It features Lutetium-Yttrium Oxy-orthosilicate (LYSO) arrays, Multi-Pixel Photon Counter (MPPC) arrays, & front-end electronics. A US transducer can be added between 2 front PET detectors, forming a combined PET/US probe. This system uses list-mode data acquisition & GPU-based MLEM reconstruction for rapid image processing. We evaluated the system using a tumor phantom mimicking Derenzo patterns & varying lesion sizes ($3.3 \mathrm{~mm}-11.4 \mathrm{~mm}$) & a tumor-to-background activity conc. ratio of 20:1. Ref. images were acquired using a Siemens Biograph Vision PET/CT for comparison. We imaged a silicone phantom containing ${ }^{64} \mathrm{Cu}$ solution & compared the PET/US images to standard PET/CT images. Initial results show that POC-PET images closely approximate the resolution of a clinical PET/CT. The versatility of the system was further validated at a proton therapy facility, where rapid imaging post-irradiation & real-time reconstruction illustrated its potential for clinical use. The development of the POC-PET technology with US integration marks a significant advancement in dual-modal imaging, providing bedside diagnostics and high-performance imaging on par with traditional systems, while also enabling real-time image-guided interventions like biopsy & ablation procedures.

articleTitle: Radiation damage and charge trapping in germanium cross-strip detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We present an investigation into the effects of high-energy proton damage on charge trapping in germanium cross-strip detectors. We calibrated and characterized the spectral resolution of a spare COSI-balloon detector in order to determine the effects of intrinsic trapping, finding that electron trapping due to impurities dominates over hole trapping in the undamaged detector. We then damaged the detector with a fluence of $2 \times 10^{8}$ proton $\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, which far exceeds the fluence expected during the prime mission. By measuring the depth-dependent spectral line shifts, we observed that the damage to the detector had drastically increased the amount of hole trapping, leading to significant degradation in the spectral resolution of the detector. We were able to perform a depth-dependent energy correction which vastly improved the spectral resolution of the damaged detector, bringing the hole signal much closer in resolution to the electron signal.

articleTitle: An Experimental Validation of a SiPM SPICE Model for Neutron-Gamma Discrimination
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron-gamma discrimination is crucial in nuclear instrumentation to detect both radiological and nuclear signatures. Handheld instruments based on scintillators and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) have been used for several years. In this context, simulation, including the SiPM model, is essential to design accurate front-end electronics for pulse shape discrimination (PSD). This work was carried out to build on the state-of-the-art SiPM models. This paper extends the model to commercial SiPMs based on parameters and characteristics extracted from the datasheet. Our parameterizable Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE) model can simulate any signal and thus fits real needs for instrumentation. The simulated single-photon response is then compared with the experiment. Finally, we measure pulses from Cs-137 and Cf-252 sources to gather experimental data. We successfully fitted these pulses to a three exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) model. This work provides accurate input data for the SiPM and allows us to define the theoretical discrimination performance of the SiPM.

articleTitle: Performance of SiC based neutron detector in high-dose gamma-ray field
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Neutron detectors are important for safe decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Plant as a criticality monitor. In this study, we focused on semiconductor based neutron detectors. Neutron detectors made of SiC, which has a larger band-gap energy than silicon, can be used in higher temperature environments and has higher radiation tolerance than silicon detectors. Against this background, we have been studying SiC neutron detectors that detect neutrons after converting them into charged particles such as alpha rays and protons with Li or B based conversion layer. We used a detector prototyped by Fuji Electric, attached with a B4C converter, or a LiF converter and irradiated it with thermal neutrons and $\gamma$-rays. As a result, the LiF converter can detect thermal neutrons with an efficiency of about $0.042 \%$, and even under $\gamma$ ray irradiation of about 200 Gy/h, the detection efficiency is considered to be about half of that in the absence of $\gamma$-rays. The simulation results show that thinning the surface electrode is effective in improving the detection efficiency.

articleTitle: Accelerating 3D Source Reconstruction with Gamma-Ray Imagers Using 2D Projections
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: 3D source reconstruction from multi-view measurements with gamma-ray imagers can suffer from large memory footprints and heavy computational cost from the construction and usage of large forward matrices that map the 3D image space to the detector space at each view. This problem can be exacerbated if the reconstruction uses list-mode data, such as 3D Compton reconstructions. This work explores a method for reducing the costs of 3D source reconstructions by separating the forward matrix into a product of two simpler matrices, one being a sparse sparse projection matrix that maps the 3D image space onto intermediate 2D image spaces for each view and the other being a 2D forward matrix that maps the 2D image spaces to the detector spaces at each view. This method is compared with the traditionally constructed forward matrices in terms of speed, memory footprint, and reconstructed activity for various problem sizes.

articleTitle: Dental Imaging with a Quantum-dot-based Direct Conversion X-ray Image Sensor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
