abstract: X-ray imaging has been extensively used in medical diagnosis thanks to the ability of X-rays to penetrate through our body or a part for non-invasive imaging of internal structures. Nowadays, most commercial X-ray detectors including dental imaging instruments rely on a cesium iodide (CsI) scintillator to convert X-rays into visible light. However, they normally suffer from a low spatial resolution due to optical crosstalk among neighboring pixels. Pixelated detectors made of cadmium telluride (CdTe) or cadmium zinc telluride (CdZnTe) have shown excellent performance for X-ray imaging. Nevertheless, they require flip-chip hybridization to connect to silicon readout, adding assembly complexity, increasing fabrication cost, and restricting achievable pixel resolution. We have developed a direct conversion X-ray imager with a high-Z lead-sulfide (PbS) quantum-dot (QD) based photon absorber monolithically and directly deposited on a CMOS readout chip. The silicon readout has been designed with a standard 180-nm CMOS process and the photon absorber with a 120- $\mu$ m layer of PbS QDs has been deposited from solutions at low temperature. This approach takes advantages of CMOS technologies for a high pixel resolution, low-power consumption, and complex readout electronics. It also benefits from high X-ray absorption efficiency and low-temperature solution-based fabrication of PbS QDs. To our knowledge, this is the first direct conversion X-ray imager with an absorber stack of PbS QDs on silicon readout. Following an introduction to sensor design and fabrication, this paper demonstrates the potential use of this imager in medical imaging particularly dental imaging. This novel radiation detector has been used to produce high-quality tooth images while presenting a low dark current, high linearity, a low noise equivalent dose, and a high spatial resolution. The validation of this solution-based monolithic approach benefits realization of low-cost high-performance X-ray imagers.

articleTitle: Deployment of a 7 MeV Mobile Photofission Inspection System at the Rijeka Seaport for the Detection of SNM in Cargo Containers
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Special Nuclear Material (SNM) such as uranium and plutonium isotopes could be potentially involved in a terrorist attack. To prevent illicit trafficking of SNM in Europe, inspection of cargo containers at borders is required. X-ray scanning is widely used by customs to control containers. However, the latter technology is not adapted for the detection of SNM. Therefore, a second line technology based on the photofission reaction could enable to detect SNM in a non-destructive manner. In the frame of the ENTRANCE European project, the CEA-List institute and Smiths Detection have developed an Active Photon Interrogation (API) system based on a 7 MeV X-ray scanner for the detection of SNM. The system is based on the use of a linear electron accelerator (linac). First, high-energy photons generated by Bremsstrahlung in the conversion target of the linac irradiate a suspect area of the cargo container. Secondly, if SNM is present, delayed particles emitted following photofission reactions are detected. In this paper, first, we give an overview of the global scenario of the ENTRANCE project. Then, we present the field tests of the project conducted at the Skrljevo inland terminal, which is owned by the port of Rijeka, Croatia, using a 7 MeV mobile photofission system. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of photofission at 7 MeV using samples of depleted uranium. Further, the deployment of mobile photofission systems would make it possible to strengthen security at Europe’s borders with regard to the SNM risk.

articleTitle: High-resolution Positronium Lifetime Imaging on the PennPET Explorer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Positronium lifetime imaging (PLI) has received growing interest because the lifetime of orthopositronium (o-Ps) can be affected by tissue microstructure and the concentration of certain molecules including O<inf>2</inf>. Previously we have developed several model-based lifetime image reconstruction methods and demonstrated their ability of reconstructing high-resolution lifetime images using point sources and small objects. In this study we leverage the high-performance of the PennPET Explorer scanner and its flexibility in singles data acquisition to perform highresolution PLI using ${ }^{82} \mathrm{Rb}$ on a large flow phantom and a cylinder phantom. The latter has a $6-\mathrm{mm}-$ thick polycarbonate insert to create lifetime contrast. List-mode data were acquired in singles mode with an extended energy window $[429,1533] \mathrm{keV}$. A software-based method was used to identify triple coincidence events with an annihilation photon energy window of [430, 560] keV and a prompt gamma energy window of $[700,835] \mathrm{keV}$ to capture the 777 keV gamma from ${ }^{82} \mathrm{Rb}$. The average positron lifetime images were reconstructed using the SIMPLE method. The reconstructed lifetime image of the flow phantom showed a uniform lifetime distribution inside the phantom, despite the very high randoms-to-trues (R/T) ratio. The cylinder phantom reconstruction showed the $6-\mathrm{mm}$ thick polycarbonate insert can be resolved in the lifetime image. These results clearly demonstrate the feasibility of performing high-resolution PLI for extended phantoms at activity levels relevant to clinical human imaging. In future work, we will extend the study to other radiotracers and perform in vivo animal and human imaging.

articleTitle: Investigating the Effect of Time Window on Cross-Strip CZT PET System
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The coincidence efficiecy is a fundamental aspect in positron emission tomography. A possible way to increase the line of responce detection efficiency is to select an optimal coincidence window leading to more accurate photoelectric coincidences and less random events. This study investigates the different coincidence windows and explore the performance of the positron emission tomography to explore the window size correlations with random rate and detection efficiency to provide a better understanding of the data aquizition and a possible advancement towards a more accurate coincidence detection in positron emission tomography.

articleTitle: Purcell enhanced “super-scintillator” using surface plasmonic nanoparticles coupled to a scintillator slab
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces a novel nanoscintillator concept incorporating plasmonic nanoparticles and ultra-thin scintillator slabs. By leveraging the surface plasmonic effect, the proposed nanoscintillator aims to maximize the Purcell factor, leading to a significant increase in scintillation radiative decay rate. Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) simulations were conducted to evaluate the performance of the nanoscintillator, revealing up to a 36-fold enhancement in emission rate for visible light. The simulation results demonstrate the feasibility and potential of the proposed concept, guiding further optimization through nanoparticle size, material, and shape variations.

articleTitle: Scatter compensation for dynamic brain PET using very fast Monte Carlo simulation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scatter compensation is a key part of image reconstruction in positron emission tomography (PET). It currently relies on tail-fitted single scatter simulations, which are prone to errors in low count frames. Up until recently, more accurate scatter estimation methods based on Monte Carlo (MC) simulation were not feasible due to their very long calculation times. We showed, using the newly developed MCGPU-PET simulator, that it is possible to get a reliable scatter sinogram estimate using just $3^{*} 10^{8} \mathrm{MC}$-simulated scatter coincidences, for dynamic emission frames as short as 1 second. This requires a simulation time of 5 minutes, but can be reduced even further, so that image reconstruction with Monte Carlo based scatter compensation can be done in clinically acceptable computation times.

articleTitle: Experimental Evaluation of the Alpha-SPECT-Mini System with Machine-Learning-based Energy Reconstruction and Dynamic Windowing for In Vivo Imaging of Ac-225-labeled Radiopharmaceuticals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: As one of the important multi-functional molecular imaging applications, the alpha-emitter radiopharmaceutical therapy attracts rising interest due to its great preclinical and clinical success. The Alpha-SPECT-mini system utilizes ultra-high energy resolution CdTe detectors to enable the ability to separate X- and gamma-rays emitted from the Ac-255 decay scheme. In vivo mice imaging studies with labeled Ac-225 injection has been demonstrated using Alpha-SPECT-mini. Energy peaks from Ac-225, Tl-209, Fr-221, Bi-213 can be used for tracing each element’s biological distribution. The Ac-225 washout processing and Bi-213 and Tl-209 accumulation in kidneys are observed during the In vivo mice imaging study.

articleTitle: Development of hybrid pixel detectors for MeV UED and UEM applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Mega-electron-volt (MeV) ultra-fast electron diffraction (UED) and electron microscopy (UEM) have gained more and more interests in recent years. Compared to electron microscopy in 100-300 keV, they have higher penetration power and less space charge effect. On the other hand, they can resolve much higher spatial resolution than X-rays at sub-picosecond timescale. The paper presents development of hybrid pixel detectors dedicated for MeV UED and UEM applications. Diamond (Micron, UK) and silicon (Hamamatsu, Japan) pixel detectors were fabricated and evaluated. According to simulation results, diamond shows much less scattering for MeV electrons and hence could potentially achieve better imaging resolution. Both diamond and silicon detectors have 128 x 128 pixels with pixel size in 150 μm x 150 μm. The thicknesses of the detectors were designed to be 200 μm for diamond and 500 μm for silicon, respectively. The detectors are flip-chip bonded to a readout ASIC (EMPIX2), which has a dynamic range of 24 bit and can operates at 100 kfps frame rate. Fast electron cameras have also been developed based on these detector modules, including TEC and water cooling and the data acquisition (DAQ) system. The bandwidth of the DAQ system was up to 80 Gbps. The cameras were installed in a MeV UED system and the performance of the detectors were evaluated and compared. At low flux, the diamond detector showed less multi-hit events than silicon detector due to scattering. But it also showed some polarization effect. The detailed design and test results of the detector will be present in the paper.

articleTitle: A Cosmic Muons Test Bench for the Characterisation of GRAiNITA
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The GRAiNITA project aims to propose a novel design for a next-generation calorimeter. This innovative approach uses a mixture of submillimeter sized inorganic scintillating crystals (around 1-2 mm) dispersed within a high-density, transparent liquid. This technology is expected to achieve excellent energy resolution at a significantly reduced cost compared to existing technologies. This paper presents the development and operation of a test bench designed to characterise the performance of the GRAiNITA prototyp. Its working principle is based on the reconstruction of the track of cosmic muons traversing the prototype. The length of the reconstructed track is directly correlated with the deposited energy within the detector. These measurements allow one to assess the light generation efficiency and its uniformity across the entire detector volume. The test bench incorporates a Timepix tracker to accurately reconstruct the muon trajectory within the detector. Additionally, a set of scintillators provides a trigger signal and a time stamp for each muon candidate event. This system is currently in operation and gives its first results, which will be presented in the upcoming conference. These measurements provide a first step before producing finer studies in test beams.

articleTitle: CT-free Attenuation Correction of Whole-body PET Images via Direct Diffusion Bridge
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation correction of PET images is a crucial step in obtaining accurate quantification in PET/CT and PET/MRI studies. Typically, structural images such as CT images are required to calculate attenuation coefficients and correct for the effects of gamma-ray attenuation. However, CT-based attenuation correction methods pose a concern due to CT artifacts and radiation exposure. Recently, there have been attempts to synthesize CT from MRI or non-attenuation corrected PET (NAC PET) using generative models, such as Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN). However, utilizing the synthetic CT for generating attenuation-corrected PET (AC PET) has resulted in significant errors in whole-body PET scans, thus limiting its clinical applications. In this study, we have adopted the recently proposed diffusion bridge model (DBM) [1] to address this issue, which learns the transition trajectory between two different distributions. We aimed to generate the attenuation map ($\mu$-map) from NAC PET and subsequently perform the PET attenuation correction using the $\mu$-map. We conducted a comparative analysis of $\mu$-maps generated using U-NET, conditional Generative Adversarial Networks (cGAN), and Diffusion Bridge Models (DBM). The evaluation metrics utilized were normalized mean squared error (NMSE), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM). DBM exhibited superior performance relative to the existing methods. Following this, we conducted attenuation correction of 18F-FDG PET using attenuation maps produced by each method. CT-based AC PET served as the ground truth for this comparison, using NMSE and PSNR as the assessment metrics. DBM achieved significant enhancements in performance across all metrics when compared to traditional approaches

articleTitle: Multi-MeV Gamma Interaction Position Estimation in Large Pure Cherenkov Emitter Crystals
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, we study the Cherenkov light created by prompt-gammas in a monolithic and pure Cherenkov emitter crystal to achieve position estimation for Prompt-gamma Imaging (PGI). This approach relies in the exclusive use of Cherenkov light and could lead to a novel system concept with an effective background discrimination at a relatively low production cost. The detector consisted of a $25 \times 25 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{\wedge} 3 \mathrm{PbF} 2$ crystal coupled to a $8 \times 8$ SiPM array and was mounted on a 2 D translation stage. Two tungsten blocks were used to form a 3 mm slit to collimate a 228 Th gamma source. The detector was shifted in increments of 3 mm in the Y -axis direction, while the collimation system and source were fixed. Four datasets were acquired at four different detector positions: $0 \mathrm{~mm}, 3 \mathrm{~mm}, 6 \mathrm{~mm}$, and 9 mm. The floodmaps from each dataset showed consistent distribution shifts across the four positions. However, the presence of noise/background in the results was significant and did not allow to achieve an accurate position estimation. The low signal-to-noise ratio and readout electronics used in the current setup pose limitations to the full potential of this approach. Next steps include the development of tailored readout electronics to enhance the Cherenkov light collection and testing the set-up in a proton beam line.

articleTitle: Baseline filtering to advance the timing limits with the FastIC ASIC for TOF-PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Time-of-Flight (TOF) has made significant progress in Positron Emission Tomography (PET) largely due to advancements in different areas such as electronics and scintillation materials, allowing an even more precise tracer location accuracy. However, correlated and uncorrelated Silicon Photomuliplier (SiPM) noise such as dark counts can limit the achievable timing performance by causing baseline fluctuations. This is particularly a challenge for systems where information to the original raw signal is not accessible. We have investigated the role of SiPM baseline fluctuations with the FastlC, a scalable multi channel ASIC developed for fast timing applications. By using the discriminator signal triggered by dark counts before the actual scintillation event, undesired events can be flagged. Coupling BGO crystals with different thickness to 4x4 mm<sup>2</sup> AFBR-S4N44P014M SiPMs from Broadcom, this method shows a 5% improvement in achievable coincidence time resolution (CTR). For small LYSO:CeCa crystals, up to 15% CTR improvement for high overvoltage is achieved. This study presents a new method capable of flagging undesired events toward a scalable system in TOF-PET and discusses the role of SiPM noise. In addition, we show how to incorporate noise events and correct for time walk effects in order to preserve sensitivity.

articleTitle: Simulation Study of a Panel-Type PET Geometry: Effect of TOF and Sensitivity on Image Quality
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In positron emission tomography (PET), measuring time-of-flight (TOF) of annihilation radiation is important to improve image quality. Recently, it was reported that a Cherenkov radiator integrated microchannel plate photomultiplier tube (CRI-MCP-PMT) with 30 ps TOF resolution enabled reconstruction-free imaging with a 1D pseudo dual-panel geometry. In this work, we investigated the feasibility of a dual-panel PET, anticipating new applications such as PET-guided surgery. Using Geant4 simulation, we compared the performance of the modeled dual-panel PET with a ring PET. Detectors of the 5.75 mm -pitch position-sensitive CRI-MCP-PMT with a bismuth germanate window were used considering a commercial multi-anode MCP-PMT geometry. Because lower sensitivity of the CRI-MCP-PMT than that of conventional scintillation-based detectors may cancel the benefit of TOF in image quality, we assessed the image quality using the signal-to-noise ratio. The TOF resolution was varied from 30 to 50 ps. The sensitivity was changed by reducing the number of counts. The radiator thickness was 5 or 1.5 mm. A numerical phantom composed of a uniform area (45 mm in diameter) and a multi-rod area with 21 MBq was modeled. Data acquisition time was 600 seconds. As a result, the percentage standard deviation (% SD) values of the dual-panel PET were improved by changing the TOF resolution from 50 to 30 ps and changing the count loss from 10% to 100%. The % SD of the dual-panel PET at 30 ps TOF with full counts (6.3%) was better than that of the 210 ps ring PET (7.6%). Regarding the count loss, for the 30 ps dual-panel PET, the % SD using half counts (6.8%) was still better than the 210 ps ring PET, which indicates the existence of tolerance to sensitivity. However, the % SD at the 30 ps TOF 1.5 mm radiator thickness (12.6%) was worse than that of the 40 ps TOF 5 mm radiator thickness (10.8%), which indicates that the TOF resolution and the radiator thickness have little room for compromise.

articleTitle: Advancements in Active Photon Interrogation through Photo-neutron Spectrometry: Unveiling Nitrogen Signatures for Illicit Materials Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Active photon interrogation (API) has been used for a long time in the detection of special nuclear materials and the characterization of nuclear waste, primarily relying on neutron counting from photo-fission reactions. However, recent advancements have opened new ways for extending the capabilities of API techniques. In this study, we introduce a novel approach aimed at broadening the scope of API by incorporating neutron spectrometry with an organic scintillator to unveil the signatures of light elements like nitrogen, oxygen, and carbon. These elements are commonly associated with conventional explosives, narcotics, and chemical weapons and can be identified through their photo-neutron spectra. This endeavor presents a significant challenge due to the intense and pulsed nature of the photon flux when using electron LINACs as interrogation sources. Our method entailed the utilization of a 22-MV electron linear accelerator (LINAC) in conjunction with a BC501A liquid scintillator, coupled with pulse shape discrimination and pile-up rejection algorithms. To assess the efficacy of our approach, we subjected to irradiation melamine powder (C<inf>3</inf>N<inf>6</inf>H<inf>6</inf>), a simulant for conventional explosives from the point of view of nitrogen content. The results of our investigation are very promising. We successfully detected fast neutrons originating from (γ,Xn) reactions, despite mixed short-pulse fields of photon and neutron radiation characterized by intense photon flashes. Moreover, we achieved the unfolding of energy deposited in the detector, enabling the extraction of photo-neutron spectra that highlight distinct nitrogen signatures from (γ,pn) reactions. This pioneering work represents the first experimental proof-of-concept for leveraging photo-neutron spectrometry within API techniques, offering a promising alternative for the enhanced detection of illicit materials.

articleTitle: A Versatile Data-Acquisition Platform for the Characterization of Low-Noise Analog Front-End ASICs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The front-end electronics of the ATLAS Liquid Argon (LAr) Calorimeter will be upgraded for High-Luminosity LHC. Low-noise analog front-end ASICs, including the ATLAS LAr Front-End (ALFE) and the LAr Upgrade Read-Out Chip (LAUROC), are under development for the upgrade. Each ASIC consists of four channels of pre-amplifiers and CR-(RC)<sup>2</sup> shapers with adjustable input impedance. Each channel implements two separate gain outputs to cover a 16-bit dynamic range with an optimal resolution. Each ASIC also includes a layer-sum output with CR-RC shapers and a switchable gain between 1 and 3. To characterize these ASICs, a Front-End Test Board (FETB), a versatile data-acquisition platform, is redesigned. The new design is still called FETB. Instead, the previous version is called FETBv1 to distinguish these two designs. The FETB integrates two octal-channel 16-bit ADCs ADS52J65 from Texas Instruments. The sample rate of the ADCs is up to 125 MS/s, allowing for high-speed data acquisition for the front-end ASICs. The FETB employs a System-on-Module (SoM) from Enclustra with a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ Multi-Processor Systemon-Chip (MPSoC). A PetaLinux operating system runs on embedded ARM processors, simplifying network management and software development. The FETB has been used to characterize ALFE2. The noise floor of the FETB was measured to be $86 \mu \mathrm{V}$ (RMS). The Equivalent Noise Currents (ENIs) of ALFE2, the second and final version of ALFE, were measured to be 168 nA and 50 nA for $25 \Omega$ and $50 \Omega$ input impedances, respectively. The Integral Non-Linearities (INLs) of the LG outputs are pm 0.21% in the 80% dynamic range and less than ± 0.72% in the full dynamic range, respectively, whereas the measured INLs of the HG outputs of ALFE2 are 0.13%. These test results demonstrate that both the FETB and ALFE2 fulfill the design goals for the characterization of front-end ASICs. The FETB is used for the production quality-control test of ALFE2 and other applications.

articleTitle: Adaptive Deep Image Prior Enhances Ultra-Low Dose PET Imaging with NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The dedicated brain PET system NeuroEXPLORER (NX) with high sensitivity, resolution, and continuous head motion correction holds the potential for ultra-low dose imaging. Low injected dose, however, still results in a decreased signal to noise ratio in the reconstructed images. The small number of scans available to date from NX poses a challenge for supervised learning-based denoising methods, which require a vast amount of training data. The goal of this study is to develop an adaptive deep image prior (ADIP) based post-processing technique for individual lowdose NX PET datasets. A reconstructed low-dose image served as the target of the ADIP network and the subject attenuation map was used as the input to provide structural information. To make the network adapt to the noise level of its target, we calculated the variance of a sequence of output within a running window to automatically determine the optimal stopping iteration and avoid overfitting. For evaluation, we generated list-mode datasets with different contrasts between gray matter and white matter ($8: 1,4: 1$, and $2: 1$) based on custom made brain phantoms scanned by NX. For each contrast, the full-count data was down-sampled to simulate $10 \%, 3 \%$, and $2 \%$ of the original counts. We calculated normalized standard deviation, relative error (RE) with respect to the full-count images, and contrast recovery coefficient (CRC) in a hot gray matter region to evaluate the lowdose images before and after ADIP processing. Achieving comparable CRC to the full-count images with all contrasts, the ADIP method reduces noise by $21 \pm 3 \%, 37 \pm 3 \%$, and $46 \pm 3 \%$ for the $10 \%, 3 \%$, and $2 \%$ count images. In addition, the ADIP method introduces negligible bias with the REs before versus after processing as $-.1 \pm.1 \%,-.2 \pm .1 \%$, and $-.2 \pm .2 \%$ versus $-.8 \pm .4 \%,-2.8 \pm 1.5 \%$, and $-1.9 \pm .3 \%$ for the $10 \%, 3 \%$, and $2 \%$ count images. We conclude that the proposed ADIP technique enables individual dataset based denoising for ultra-low dose PET imaging with NX.

articleTitle: Source Identification using Non-negative Matrix Factorisation on Gamma-ray Spectra
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Poisson non-negative matrix factorisation (PNMF) has been identified as a promising method to quantify and reconstruct gamma-ray spectra for detecting radioactive material using deployed scintillator detectors. Identifying threats represents an important goal to protect countries from illicit radioactive material being used for acts of nuclear terrorism. It is important for any deployed system to be sensitive to threats but also maintain low false alarm rates, which is complicated by fluctuations in background radiation levels. This work seeks to show the efficacy of PNMF at identifying isotopes using gamma-ray spectra from small-volume CsI(Tl) detectors. Although this technique has been proven using larger NaI(Tl) detectors, covering a larger area with many smaller detectors is desirable within the UK as these detectors are of lower cost and are more readily available. In this work, spectra containing data for five radioisotopes are injected into a sparse background dataset, and are identified using reconstructions with PNMF components. A comparison is made between the results of successful identifications for 2 different source activities.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Prompt Gamma Activation Analysis for Nuclear Forensic Characterization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: An experiment is being designed to investigate the capability of prompt gamma activation analysis (PGAA) for characterization of nuclear fuel cycle materials. This effort seeks to identify strong neutron capture resonances in the 0.5-40 eV energy region for rare earth elements (REEs) and leverage these resonances to amplify the prompt gamma response via PGAA. ${ }^{147} \mathrm{Sm}$ and ${ }^{145} \mathrm{Nd}$ are two isotopes that display strong neutron capture cross sections in this energy region, and remain stable upon neutron capture, making them prime targets for demonstrating the merit of PGAA. The experiment is being planned at the Detector for Advanced Neutron Capture Experiments (DANCE) at Los Alamos National Laboratory. DANCE is comprised of $\sim 160 \mathrm{BaF}_{2}$ detectors in a spherical geometry at the end of a neutron beam and offers an unparalleled capability for gamma spectroscopy. The objectives of the experiment are to characterize the prompt gamma response behavior of these isotopes upon neutron capture, to identify specific prompt gammas that may serve as signals of interest in a PGAA experiment, and to compare the prompt gamma yield from epithermal neutron capture events against known prompt gamma yields from thermal neutron capture reactions.

articleTitle: High Resolution Particle Tracker for In-vivo Carbon-ion Radiotherapy Monitoring
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The radiotherapeutic method of cancer treatment using precise beam of energetic carbon ions has demonstrated many advantages compared to the conventional X-ray radiotherapy. More precise dose delivery to the tumor spares the surrounding healthy tissue which makes this method especially suitable for brain cancer treatment. However, this comes with an increased sensitivity to deformations and displacements of the tissue within the patient body. To address this issue, our team has developed a non-invasive in-vivo treatment monitoring method based on the tracking of charged nuclear fragments produced by interactions of the carbon ions with nuclei of the patient’s body. The measured tracks allow the reconstruction of fragment origins, whose distributions can be compared between different treatment fractions. In this comparison, interfractional changes of the patient’s morphology or positioning may be uncovered. A novel high resolution particle tracking detector system has been developed, calibrated and successfully tested. The detector consists of 28 Timepix3 pixel detectors organized in seven units. Each unit consists of two layers (telescope) of two Timepix3 chips with single monolithic silicon sensor. All units are synchronized with nanosecond precision. The subpixel resolution of particle tracks registered in each layer allows for precise back projection reconstruction.

articleTitle: Low Noise High Frequency Electronic Readout for Large Area TOF-PET Detector Modules
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low noise, high frequency (LNHF) electronic readout for silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)-based time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) detectors preserves fast signal response intrinsically available from the ac-couped quenching capacitor of Geiger cells and minimizes the influence of electronic noise jitter to optimize time response. By facilitating fast impulse response for large area SiPMs, LNHF readout allows detectors to optimally exploit fast luminescence signatures and prompt optical phenomena for next-generation detector designs that aim to advance coincidence time resolution (CTR) for TOF-PET. Recent works have demonstrated single channel LNHF readout topologies that provide the benefits of this readout technique with footprints and power consumption feasible for scaling into prototype detectors and demonstration systems for advanced PET detector designs. In this work, we have scaled LNHF readout into a compact, 16 channel development board and demonstrated its ability to translate advances in CTR shown on the bench into multichannel detector designs. Identical CTR was observed between single channel readout boards and the 16 channel development board in single pixel coincidence studies with LYSO:Ce, Ca, LGSO:Ce, and BGO crystals (within 4 ps for all configurations). CTR measurements between 20 mm length LYSO:Ce,Ca and BGO crystal arrays demonstrated global CTR of $129 \pm 1$ and $255 \pm 16$ ps FWHM, respectively. Thus, this multichannel readout scheme offers a pathway to develop new LSO/LYSO and BGO-based TOF-PET detectors with significantly improved CTR, relative to that achieved in state-of-the-art commercial systems. Moreover, it serves as a test bed for novel detector concepts to further improve achievable CTR. We also present a further miniaturized readout scheme in a modular circuit block which fits within the area of a $4 \times 4$ SiPM array, in an edge-mounted readout configuration for tiling into readout for large area PET detector modules.

articleTitle: A Neutron-induced gamma ray imager with 3D resolution for in-situ planetary science applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We are designing an instrument based on the Associated Particle Imaging (API) technique that will allow, for the first time, non-destructive 3D elemental imaging of regions underneath a planetary rover or lander. The In-situ Nuclear Spectrometer with 3D Resolution (INSPECT3R) will open several new avenues for the in situ exploration of solid-surface planetary objects given its ability to measure the elemental composition of the near-surface with unprecedented resolution and sensitivity.

articleTitle: R&D of Low Gain Avalanche Diode with large area
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) has high-precision time performance, and the time resolution can reach 30 ps. The LGAD with a size of 1.3 mm×1.3 mm was used for the High Granularity Timing Detector (HGTD) in the upgrade of ATLAS and CMS on High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC). Compared with the HL-LHC, the future electron-positron collider (such as ILC, CEPC, FCC-ee and STCF) will have fewer charged particles in the final states. Large area LGAD will save electronics channels. This presentation will show the test results of the large area LGAD sensors, including beta source test, picosecond laser test, collected charge, signal-to-noise ratio, time resolution, etc.

articleTitle: A Reliable Setup for Measuring Light Yield Across a Large Range in Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study presents a robust setup for absolute light yield measurement across a wide dynamic range using GAGG Scintillators, which are known for their tunable light output and decay times through formula adjustments. Our system combines PMTs with reflectors and SiPINs to achieve high repeatability and stability in measuring light yields of large-range output crystals. The PMT, paired with a reflector, facilitates the relative measurements, while the SiPIN provides calibration for absolute measurements, ensuring precision across a broad spectrum of light yields. To address the impact of crystal size relative to the PMT and reflector dimensions, we conducted extensive Geant4 simulations which helped define the optimal crystal sizes for our measurement setup, offering guidelines for selecting crystal dimensions that maximize light collection efficiency. This setup aims to offer a practical reference for designing similar systems, potentially assisting in adapting this approach to various scintillation crystals.

articleTitle: Progress on a simultaneous photon counting and energy integrating detector for X-ray imaging applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The photon counting X-ray imaging system offers high spatial resolution, low noise, and reduced radiation exposure, but suffers degradation at high counting rates. We have developed a dual mode imaging readout chip suitable for cadmium telluride or cadmium zinc telluride crystals, capable of simultaneous integration and photon counting. Utilizing this chip, we designed an X-ray imaging camera system comprising four detector modules, each with a $32 \times 32$ array of readout channels covering a 16 mm by 64 mm imaging area in total. Electronic testing revealed the noise level of each counting channel in these modules to be approximately 860 electrons, with the integration channel’s leakage current measured at about 1 nA at $20^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. After correcting the non-uniformity for baseline and gain in the counting channels and the non-uniformity between the qpump and ADC conversion in the integration channels, imaging experiments were performed. Analysis of the concurrently gathered photon counting and integration data demonstrated a correlation between the dual-mode outputs. The system’s dual-mode imaging capabilities were validated by successfully reconstructing a basic water phantom computed tomography image using the filtered backprojection algorithm.

articleTitle: Signal Range Comparisons for a Trans-stilbene Detector Measuring Cf-252
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Dual-particle sensitivity and fast timing make organic scintillators an excellent candidate for the detection of prompt fission neutrons and gamma rays. When acquiring and analyzing radiation pulses, it is important to consider pulse height thresholds and resolution effects on the pulse-shape discrimination quality and effective neutron energy range. In this work, a Cf-252 spontaneous fission source was measured with one 5.08-cm-diameter by 5.08-cm-length trans-stilbene organic scintillator at four different high-voltage settings with variable pulse-height threshold values. Waveforms were acquired with a 500 MHz, 14-bit digitizer utilizing a 2-V dynamic range, 5% offset, and 400 ns record length. Each acquisition’s range for neutron energy deposition via proton elastic scatter is [490-13,000; 390-8,000; 310-5,100; 220-3,900] keV. The lowest high voltage setting caused deterioration of pulse-shape discrimination quality (40% decrease in figure-of-merit), which could be attributed to poor digital resolution of 0.45 eVee/bit in comparison to the higher amplification values. At an amplification of 1.1 mV/keVee, the pulse-shape discrimination figure-of-merit is consistently > 40% improved from 0-700 keVee compared to the lowest amplification of 0.3 mV/keVee. We recommend tuning the high voltage settings to preserve appropriate pulse height resolution (< 0.11 keVee/bit) and benefit pulse shape discrimination quality in the low-light-output (0-700 keVee) range. Once this resolution is achieved, increasing the amplification does not significantly improve the figure of merit, but the neutron efficiency is reduced.

articleTitle: Development of Resistive Plate Chambers with Optical Readout
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) are one of the crucial components of the muon systems in current and future collider experiments, as well as the (semi-)digital hadron calorimeter developed by the CALICE Collaboration. The RPCs are historically based on charge collection with an anode plane, which is segmented into pads or strips. With the development of one-glass and hybrid RPCs, the anode plane can be placed inside the chamber and can be made more functional by applying various coatings. It is also known that scintillation light is produced along with charge as a result of ionization in the gas layer. This light is typically in the ultraviolet range and possesses ionizing properties, which have been actively mitigated in traditional RPC applications. However, reading this light signal can provide additional high-time-resolution data beyond conventional RPC measurements. With this motivation, our team is in the process of making RPCs with optical readout with SiPMs directly coupled to the gas layer, and SiPMs coupled to in-chamber quartz fibers with wavelength shifter coating. Here we report on the progress in making the RPCs with optical readout and present preliminary results.

articleTitle: Preliminary study of image reconstruction from truncated CT data using hybrid image constraints
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In CT, data with transverse truncation arises when the transverse size of the X-ray beam’s field-of-view (FOV) received by the detector is smaller than that of the subject’s support. While existing efforts focus primarily on image reconstruction within the FOV, our work delves into achieving accurate reconstructions not only within the FOV but also within a substantially larger region. We investigate the reconstruction problem from truncated data by formulating it as a convex optimization program with hybrid constraints on image-region total-variation (TV) and imageregion L1-norm. To address this, we introduce the TVL1 algorithm, a primal-dual-based method aimed at achieving accurate reconstructions within the subject’s support. Simulated and real-data studies, covering various truncation degrees, validate the levels of algorithm’s performance and robustness. Our results showcase the TVL1 algorithm’s accuracy in reconstructing images within and beyond the FOV for various practical truncation extents. The methodology and TVL1 algorithm developed in this study hold promise for extending to cone-beam CT, thus broadening their applicability in medical imaging.

articleTitle: Measurements of the High Density Digitizer System on Chip (HDSoCv2): A 64 Channel 1 GSa/s Waveform Digitizer for High Density Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the measurements of the second revision of a waveform sampling ASIC (HDSoC), optimized for high density light detectors, such as Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) or MA-PMTs, suitable for large and high rate NP experiments such as the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and the future Electron Ion Collider.

articleTitle: Data-driven detection and correction of cardiac and respiratory motion in PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Cardiac PET images provide important diagnostic information on heart disease. Respiratory and cardiac movements of the heart can severely degrade image quality and impact the diagnostic accuracy of cardiac PET. The detection of respiratory and cardiac motions is essential to subsequently compensate the cardiac PET data for these physiological movements. In the literature, a robust approach to overcome this problem is motion gating, where only data acquired at a certain motion state are taken into account in the motion-compensated image reconstruction. The purpose of this study was to implement a data-driven dual-gating method to determine both respiratory and cardiac triggers directly from the list-mode (LM) data in order to produce motion compensated PET images. Two different motion correction methods were investigated to compensate for the heart’s physiological movements due to respiration and cardiac beating, as well as bulk patient movements. The assumption was made that the motion of the heart due to respiration can be modelled as a rigid body motion. 3D displacement vectors were calculated by rigidly registering the images of each cardiac cycle, and were subsequently integrated into an event-by-event LM-based iterative PET image reconstruction algorithm. The first method consists of producing a series of cardiac gated PET images corrected for respiratory movement, while the second method aims at producing two PET images compensated for respiratory movement at specific cardiac phases, namely diastole and systole. These methods were then compared with the image reconstructed using commercial data-driven respiratory motion gating, namely Q.Static. The results show that both correction techniques lead to improved image quality, with an increased contrast and better definition of cardiac structures.

articleTitle: The History and Prospects of Lithium-Containing Semiconductors in Neutron Scattering Facilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Historically, neutron imaging has mainly relied on indirect imaging modalities, such as imaging plates or scintillation screens. The advent of advanced readout systems, such as the Timepix ASIC, has opened the door for novel imaging conversion materials that may enhance both the throughput and outcomes of scientific studies. Recent advances in the development of lithium-containing semiconductors (LCSs) have provided the community with the opportunity to enhance the detection efficiency and gamma ray rejection capability compared to current imaging systems. In this presentation, we will overview the development and current results of the most promising LCSs over the last decade along with next steps for deployment.

articleTitle: The Performance of the Compact Model of the Position Sensitive Tissue Equivalent ProportionalChamber(PS-TEPC) using an ASIC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We are developing a position-sensitive tissue equivalent proportional chamber(PS-TEPC) as a dosimeter for the space radiation environment. The PS-TEPC is a three-dimensional time projection chamber using a position-sensitive charge collection device called as “ $\mu$-PIC” and tissue equivalent materials. The PS-TEPC can directly measure the linear energy transfer(LET) of each incident charged particle by measuring the energy deposition and the pass length in its detection volume. The LET is important amount to determine the dose equivalent due to the space radiations with high accuracy. In 2016, the performance of the PS-TEPC in an actual space radiation environment was demonstrated in the International Space Station(ISS). Currently, we aim to use the PS-TEPC in the “Gateway”, a manned lunar orbiting base. The PS-TEPC must be smaller and lighter because the transportation capability to the Moon is expected to be limited than that to the ISS. The objective of this study is to reduce the size and weight of the PS-TEPC by using an ASIC called as “LTARS2018K06A” as the signal readout circuit. In this study, a compact model of the PS-TEPC(CM PS-TEPC) was constructed by combining the detection part of the PSTEPC used in the ISS in 2016 with the LTARS2018K06A evaluation board. Then, we performed performance evaluation tests by irradiating the CM PS-TEPC with charged particle beams. From the tests, it was demonstrated that the CM PS-TEPC can acquire signals due to the incident particles and reconstruct those 3D track images. It was also demonstrated that the CM PS-TEPC can measure the LET of the incident particles with the almost lowest LET of the target LET range. From these results, it was concluded that the CM PS-TEPC has a certain feasibility as a space dosimeter.

articleTitle: Development of pn Junction CdTe Detector by Electron Beam for X-ray Photon Counting Imaging Devices
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CdTe used as a semiconductor detector has the advantages of high sensitivity to high energy and the ability to operate at room temperature. However, its charge collection efficiency is lower than that of Si and Ge. To ensure sufficient charge collection efficiency, it is desirable to use a structure that allows the application of a high voltage. Therefore, when used as a CdTe detector, it is desirable to use a diode with a pn junction, which has the features of leakage current suppression by rectification action, damage resistance, and heat resistance. As a doping method, laser doping using shockwave and heat is reported. We have developed a pn-junction CdTe detector by interface direct laser doping, but have not developed a CdTe detector with a pin junction; by having a pin junction, we aim to achieve full depletion at a lower voltage and improve the carrier collection efficiency. Since it is difficult to form a pin junction by direct laser doping at the interface, we propose to develop a pin junction CdTe detector by thermal diffusion doping using an electron beam to irradiate from the electrode surface. In this study, we first fabricate a pn-junction CdTe detector as a basic research, and aim to develop a radiation image detector with high spatial resolution.

articleTitle: Predicting Neoadjuvant Therapy Response in Breast Cancer Patients via Radiomics Analysis of Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced MRI Imaging Features
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study introduces an accurate approach to forecast neoadjuvant therapy response in breast cancer patients leveraging dynamic contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (DCE-MRI) features. Pre-operative DCE-MRI data were retrieved from the Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA), comprising axial breast MRI images acquired by 1.5T or 3T scanners, with sequences shared in DICOM format. Radiologist annotations facilitated accurate lesion location identification on DCE-MRI images, crucial for subsequent feature extraction. A comprehensive set of 529 computer-extracted DCE-MRI imaging descriptors, encompassing diverse tumor and tissue characteristics such as size, shape, texture, and enhancement, were derived using in-house software. To address class imbalance, oversampling techniques were implemented. Additionally, feature selection methods were employed to enhance model interpretability and efficiency. From the initial feature pool, the 40 most significant features were identified utilizing minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) analysis. Three distinct predictive models, namely Logistic Regression, AdaBoost, and XGBoost, were employed to forecast neoadjuvant therapy response. Evaluation of model performance revealed varying levels of accuracy, with XGBoost demonstrating superior performance metrics including accuracy (0.912), precision (0.917), recall (0.912), and area under the curve (AUC) value of 0.913, based on data from 416 patients, with a training-to-evaluation data split of 0.7:0.3. In conclusion, this study underscores the potential of DCE-MRI imaging features combined with comprehensive patient data for accurate neoadjuvant therapy response prediction in breast cancer patients. The findings highlight the promising role of imaging features in advancing personalized treatment strategies and ultimately improving patient outcomes.

articleTitle: A Deep Reconstruction Method for Limited-Angle and Low-Dose PET Imaging in Biology-Guided Radiotherapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging can locate tumor locations in real time by tracking radiation distribution and provide biological fiducial for biology-guided radiotherapy (BgRT), where the compromise of the PET system to beamlet delivery system leads to the incomplete detector and ultra-short scan. It brings a great challenge to the conventional image reconstruction that results in limited-angle artifacts and low-count noise in PET images. Researchers used deep learning such as Unet for image recovery and enhancement. But the resolution loss occurs in the sampling process in Unet, which is particularly noticeable in tumor lesions concerned by the BgRT system. In this work, we introduced the attention mechanism into Unet to improve the recovery of the target lesion area in PET images. The proposed network was trained and tested using Monte Carlo simulated wholebody phantoms to mimic the pre-scan stage during BgRT. The reconstructed images and quantitative analysis showed Unet with the attention module effectively recovered images from limited-angle PET data with artifacts suppression, organ structure restoration and noise reduction, and had a better lesion recovery than Unet.

articleTitle: High Resolution Cr/4H-SiC Radiation Detector for Harsh Environment Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We report radiation detection using $4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ Schottky barrier diodes (SBDs) with chromium (Cr) serving as the Schottky barrier contact. These SBDs are particularly suited for challenging conditions such as neutron detection near nuclear reactor cores. 4H-SiC SBDs have demonstrated a measurable neutron response, which varies linearly with the incident neutron flux and active area of the detector. Although $4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ is an excellent material for harsh environment applications, conventional metal contacts, and hence the junction properties, tend to deteriorate rapidly under such applications. In this article we investigate (Cr) a potential refractory contact material, as a Schottky contact on n-type 4H-SiC epitaxial layers for harsh environment applications. Compared to conventional Ni metal contacts, Cr offers a higher melting point and a lower work function, making it an excellent candidate for high-performance SBDs in high-temperature settings. The $\mathrm{Cr} / 4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ SBDs demonstrated excellent rectification behavior demonstrating a Schottky barrier height of 1.14 eV and a diode ideality factor of »1.0. The resultant built-in voltage was found to be notably high at 2.2 V, and the hole diffusion length measured $26 \mu \mathrm{m}$, surpassing conventional Ni based SBDs. The $\mathrm{Cr} / 4 \mathrm{H}-\mathrm{SiC}$ configuration exhibited an excellent energy resolution of 0.5% for 5486 keV alpha particles under optimized conditions. The SBDs also demonstrated an impressive energy resolution of 2.3% and a charge collection efficiency of 73% in self-biased (0 V applied bias) mode. Capacitance-mode deep level transient spectroscopy revealed the presence of titanium substitution, $\mathrm{Z}_{1 / 2}$, and EH<inf>5</inf> trap centers, with the latter two forming deep-level defects. This study underscores the untapped potential of highly stable Cr metal contacts on wide bandgap semiconductors such as SiC for highly efficient, self-biased radiation detection in demanding applications such as nuclear reactors and space missions.

articleTitle: Effect of Partial Volume Correction on Kernel-Based Dosimetry for Lu-177-PSMA Therapy with SPECT/CT Imagin
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Precision The precision of dosimetry plays a pivotal role in the efficacy of Lu-177-PSMA therapy, where accurate radiation delivery is essential for maximizing therapeutic outcomes. The aim is to quantitatively assess the impact of PVC on dose maps in Lu-177-PSMA therapy and ascertain its significance in radionuclide dosimetry accuracy. We analyzed SPECT/CT images from 10 patients undergoing Lu-177-PSMA therapy, applying PVC using the Richardson-Lucy iterative deconvolution method with ten iterations and a 3D Gaussian convolution kernel sized at 7.4 mm FWHM. Dosimetry calculations relied on Monte Carlo GATE version 9 simulations, involving 500 million particles in 2.21 mm voxels. Densities, determined from CT Hounsfield units and adjusted via the Schneider table, alongside 0.1 mm resolution calculations for gamma and beta radiation, facilitated precise dose estimations. To assess dosimetry accuracy, statistical analysis employed metrics including RMSE, MSE, ME, MAE, RE, and RAE. The application of PVC resulted in substantial adjustments in the SPECT dose maps. Quantitatively, the implementation of PVC led to improvements in dose maps, with RMSE decreased by 2.83% and MSE reduced by 8.36%. Additionally, PVC enhanced the mean absolute error (MAE) by $6.83 \pm 19.49$ and the relative absolute error (RAE) by $14.18 \pm 18$, indicating enhanced precision in dose delivery to targeted tissues. Visual representations of the dose maps further validated the quantitative metrics, demonstrating more defined dose distributions in the absence of tumor tissue and a more homogeneous distribution of dose throughout the targeted regions. Incorporating PVC into the dosimetric process significantly refines dose maps in Lu-177-PSMA therapy, enhancing treatment planning and delivery accuracy. This study advocates for the integration of PVC into clinical practice, marking a step forward in personalized radionuclide therapy.

articleTitle: A Deep Learning Approach for Robust Segmentation of Left Ventricular Wall in Cardiac SPECT Images
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate segmentation of the left ventricle is a necessary step in clinical assessment and quantification of the myocardium in myocardium perfusion imaging (MPI) with SPECT. Due to large inter-subject variability observed in clinical acquisitions, segmentation of MPI images using existing software tools is often assisted with manual intervention for correction of imaging anomalies that may be present. In this work we investigate the feasibility of applying a deep learning approach to improve the robustness in left ventricle (LV) segmentation, for which a generative network was employed to augment the image variability from subsequent training a segment network based on clinical acquisitions. Our preliminary results indicate that this approach can provide a reliable segmentation of the LV even in cases with elevated extra-cardiac activities near the myocardium. We envision that this approach could improve the clinic workflow by minimizing human interaction in quantification and analysis of cardiac SPECT studies.

articleTitle: A miniaturized CZ system for optimization of rare-earth aluminate perovskite scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The rare-earth aluminate perovskite (ReAP:Ce) scintillation crystals exhibit high density and fast decay time, rendering them promising candidates for PET detectors. Achieving component optimization of ReAP:Ce with superior comprehensive performance necessitates numerous experimental trials, which still remains a challenge. In this study, we developed a miniaturized Czochralski (CZ) system utilizing a solid-liquid surface model and achieved rapid growth of millimeter-scale ReAP:Ce scintillation crystals. Our system consumes approximately 20 grams of raw materials per growth cycle within 36 hours, making the exploration of numerous samples possible. Based on this system, we grew a series of (Gd<inf>x</inf>Y<inf>1-x</inf>)AP:Ce(x=0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) single crystals, achieving cost-effectiveness by excluding expensive element Lu. The as-grown crystals exhibit high quality with a minimum diameter of 4 mm. Through optical and scintillation tests, we found that Y<inf>0.5</inf>Gd<inf>0.5</inf>AlO<inf>3</inf>:0.5% Ce possesses the best performance among these compositions, with a density of 6.43 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, light yield of 12000 photons/MeV, and fast decay component of 8.72 ns (42.08%). In conclusion, the miniaturized CZ system showcases high efficiency in exploring new crystals. The optimized (Gd<inf>0.5</inf>Y<inf>0.5</inf>)AP:Ce exhibits potential for PET detector development, offering a cost-effective alternative to LYSO with only a tenth of the expense.

articleTitle: Investigating detector response and temperature dependence in the U.K. SIGMA dataset
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The SIGMA dataset comprises 1.5 billion spectra, collected from approximately 100 detectors deployed around London. The trial provided in-field measurements from a multi-sensor network, designed to measure radiation within an urban landscape. This contribution explores detector response as a function of surrounding ambient temperatures. One second spectra were filtered and organised into hour segments for each detector, the weighted mean energy of these hour segments were compared to historical temperature records. Spearman Rank coefficients were found for detectors located indoors and outdoors. Outdoor detectors show a correlation between weighted mean energy and temperature of R = 0.48 ± 0.08, with indoor detectors showing a correlation of R = 0.04 ± 0.07. Larger changes in temperature, over a day, resulted in stronger correlation with detector response. A laboratory setup has been established to simulate the collection of in-field SIGMA data, using an assortment of isotopes. The facility provides an environment allowing controlled radiological threats to be introduced, generating a training dataset for the purpose of training a neural network.

articleTitle: Plastic scintillator imaging of low-energy electron flash- and mini-beams
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This contribution describes our measurements with plastic scintillator sheets for dosimetry and beam verification of low-energy electron beams delivered at ultra-high dose rate and/or with spatial fractionation. Two $200 \mathrm{~mm} \times 200 \mathrm{~mm}$ plastic scintillator sheets, with thicknesses of 3 mm and 0.5 mm, respectively, were irradiated with $9-\mathrm{MeV}$ electron beams at the Pisa Center for Flash Radiotherapy and imaged with a scientific camera coupled to an objective. The following measurements were performed: 1) linearity of the scintillator response with increasing dose per pulse, 2) capability to measure the beam profile, to detect beam patterns (e.g. rows and point grids), and to measure their dosimetric parameters (e.g. peak to valley ratio, center to center distance, peak width, etc), 3) image the percentage depth dose curve, 4) estimation of the spurious Cerenkov luminescence. Results indicate that 1) the scintillator response appears linear with the dose per pulse up to $5 \mathrm{~Gy} /$ (intra-pulse dose rate of $\gt10^{6} \mathrm{~Gy} / \mathrm{s}$); 2) imaging of the beam transversal profile and dosimetric assessment is possible, but partially limited by the intrinsic spatial resolution of the imaging system; 3) the plastic scintillator sheets allow to obtain in a single acquisition a bi-dimensional map of the dose distribution, but Cerenkov correction is crucial as it is depth dependent and not negligible. The first tests suggest that plastic scintillator sheets may have satisfactory performance for imaging flash and spatially fractionated mini-beams.

articleTitle: Sub-mm resolution PET in case of long positron ranges using high and ultra-high energy prompts
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Sub-mm resolution preclinical imaging of PET isotopes with positron ranges of several mm is feasible using clustered multi-pinhole PET-SPECT (VECTor/CT, MILabs, The Netherlands). So far VECTor was experimentally validated for prompt energies up to 909 keV. VECTor performs positron range free imaging by magnified imaging of prompt gammas that are emitted next to positrons and are not subject to positron range. Here we investigate through simulations what resolutions may be obtained for a wider range of prompt energies, using ${ }^{52} \mathrm{Mn},{ }^{94} \mathrm{Tc},{ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr},{ }^{44} \mathrm{Sc},{ }^{86} \mathrm{Y}$, ${ }^{72} \mathrm{As},{ }^{124} \mathrm{I},{ }^{38} \mathrm{~K}$, and ${ }^{66} \mathrm{Ga}$. Images were iteratively reconstructed using system matrices that incorporate the energy dependent PSFs. Using the 603 keV prompt gamma from ${ }^{124} \mathrm{I}$, we achieved an imaging resolution of 0.65 mm. Prompt gamma energies of 703, 744, 834, and 909 keV emitted by ${ }^{94} \mathrm{Tc},{ }^{52} \mathrm{Mn},{ }^{72} \mathrm{As}$, and ${ }^{89} \mathrm{Zr}$ respectively yielded a 0.7 mm imaging resolution. Prompt gamma energies of 1.2 and 1.4 MeV from ${ }^{44} \mathrm{Sc}$, and ${ }^{52} \mathrm{Mn}$ resulted in imaging resolutions of 0.75 mm and 0.8 mm, respectively. Our findings identify three primary factors contributing to image degradation at higher energies: increased pinhole edge penetration, sensitivity reduction of the detector and isotope-dependent down-scatter issues. To conclude, our study indicate that VECTor is capable of achieving high resolution imaging of a wide range of PET isotopes with long positron range even when ultra-high prompt energies have to be utilized.

articleTitle: Free-Moving Gamma-Ray Imaging with a Rotating Coded-Aperture Mask
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A handheld coded-aperture imager equipped with SLAM sensors can form 3D radiation images as it moves. While detector motion provides multi-view data for image reconstruction, it also causes the distribution of unmodulated counts to vary over time, generating systematic noise in the image that is difficult to remove. Continuous spinning of a rotationally antisymmetric mask has potential to address this problem, provided the time between mask-antimask cycles is fast relative to the rate of change in unmodulated counts. In this work, we investigated this approach using a commercial, CZT-based imager. A method for least-squares image reconstruction from maskantimask data is presented along with experimental results from background subtraction with various detector motions and mask RPMs. A coded-aperture mask with a non-repeating, rotationally antisymmetric pattern was also designed for 3D imaging, showing good image quality for extended sources without aliasing.

articleTitle: MOLAR-NX: building a PET reconstruction framework for exploring the novel features provided by the NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this work, the PET reconstruction software, MOLAR (Motion-compensation OSEM Listmode Algorithm for Resolution-Recovery Reconstruction), is updated to support the NeuroEXPLORER (NX) - providing an advanced framework for investigating how the new features of the NX can be incorporated into the reconstruction process (MOLAR-NX). MOLAR’s detector masking feature seamlessly accounts for the detector blocks absent from the shoulder-cutout region of the system. Evaluation through phantom studies demonstrates the framework’s effectiveness as a tool for exploring the impact of depth of interaction (DOI), inter-crystal scatter recovery (ICS), energy and motion correction. Furthermore, MOLAR-NX introduces a new capability for merging listmode data, facilitating the integration of multiple listmode files with independent downsampling control during the reconstruction process. Future work focuses on refining scatter correction methods and assessing contrast recovery.

articleTitle: Multi-modality Based Low Dose PET Image Enhancement for Detecting Myocardial Fibrosis
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET is an effective tool for non-invasively quantifying myocardial fibroblast activation. However, ensuring high PET image quality requires high radiation dose or long scan time, which brings potential radiation risk or discomfort to the patient with myocardial infarction during the examination. In this paper, we proposed a low dose PET enhancement method for cardiac [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET images. The clinical applicability of enhanced PET images was evaluated with a polar map comparison to detect myocardial fibrosis. Our approach combines morphological and functional information from low dose PET and high contrast LGE MRI for enhancement. Using a Pixel-Net structure with five down-sampling and up-sampling blocks, we explored the impact of LGE MRI on enhancing low dose cardiac [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET images with various fusion methods. The performance was evaluated across five doses, including 50%, 25%, 10%, 5% and 1% of the clinical standard [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 dose. Through global and regional evaluation, we demonstrated that using LGE MRI as the reference modality can enhance [<sup>68</sup>Ga]Ga-DOTA-FAPI-04 PET images. At dose above 10%, the polar map distributions closely matched the ground truth, indicating the potential clinical utility of the polar map derived from our enhanced PET images for myocardial fibrosis analysis.

articleTitle: Scintillation Properties of Single Crystals of Cerium-doped Gadolinium Pyrosilicate at Temperature
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Scintillation detectors are crucial for nuclear well logging techniques in geological research and industrial subsurface exploration. Sodium iodide is the most common of five scintillators in widespread use. We study the properties of cerium-doped gadolinium pyrosilicate as a possible alternative for some applications. Gadolinium pyrosilicate growth had been attempted earlier by several groups, but its growth appeared difficult. However, over several years, crystals of up to 33 mm diameter and up to 69 mm length, with few inclusions, were grown. The weight measurements result in a density of $5.49 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$. A recent polished sample of 19 mm diameter by 69 mm length shows Gaussian-shaped peaks with $6.3 \%$ energy resolution for 661.7 keV gamma rays and $3.7 \%$ for 2615 keV gamma rays. Nine cylinders of $12 \mathrm{~mm} \times 12 \mathrm{~mm}$ showed an average cesium energy resolution of $5.7 \%$ with the best sample at $5.0 \%$. The material’s proportionality is better than that for thallium-doped sodium iodide. Exceptionally, the light output and scintillation decay depend only weakly on the temperature over a range from $0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $185^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. Two major decay components are present at around 70 ns and 160 ns. The faster component provides most of the light yield. Longer components in the microsecond range provide less than 1 to $2 \%$ of the light yield. In short, GPS meets the logging requirements of good light yield over a temperature range from $25^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$ to $175^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$, high detection efficiency and fast scintillation decay.

articleTitle: Optimized Monte-Carlo Scatter and Prompt Gamma Correction for WholeBody and Cardiac PET Imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Accurate scatter correction is of great importance for quantitative PET imaging. However, the current widely used model-based scatter estimation methods on clinical PET scanners is prone to correction errors at some scenarios and result in artifacts. This situation becomes even worse when the scans employ non-pure tracers which can emit the prompt gammas and formulate accidental coincidences while paring one or both 511 keV annihilation photons. Accurate estimation of the scatter and prompt gamma is particularly crucial for cardiac and oncological imaging with non-pure tracers. In this study we investigated and developed a multi-purpose Monte-Carlo (MC) simulation method to provide accurate estimation of the scatter and prompt gamma for quantitative correction. We implemented a simulator to generate accidental coincidences by recording the list-mode singles events with different energy emission and decay information, then sorting the coincidences of the two singles events (one from 511 keV & one from prompt gamma) by matching at the same decay location. To cover the scatter contribution from both inside and outside of FOV, we construct the extended body emission and attenuation images from the adjacent bed scans for estimation. We perform a fast ultra-low count simulation and process the MC histogram through down-sampling, up-sampling and interpolation to reach sufficient statistics, then via denormalization and scaling to match and align with the measured data. After a few iterative updates of the above steps and reconstruction, the scatter mean can quickly reach the convergence. The results demonstrate that our proposed approach can outperform the current model-based methods and lead to a greatly improved quantitative accuracy for clinical PET imaging. Our approach has been applied and validated in multiple phantoms and clinical studies on the GE HealthCare scanners involving various tracer tasks.

articleTitle: MACACO III Compton camera for imaging of targeted alpha therapy using 225Ac
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Actinium-225 $\left({ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}\right)$ is among the most promising alpha-emitting radionuclides employed in targeted alpha therapy (TAT). Treatments using this isotope may be monitored by imaging the gammas produced during its decay chain. MACACO III, a Compton camera based on continuous lanthanum bromide ($\mathrm{LaBr}^{3}$) crystals, has been proposed for the visualization of the biokinetics of ${ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$-labelled radiopharmaceuticals, through the detection of the 440 keV gammas emitted during the decay of its short-lived daughter nuclide, Bismuth-213 ($\left.{ }^{213} \mathrm{Bi}\right)$. Experimental measurements with MACACO III and a Derenzo-like phantom filled with ${ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$ have resulted in images that clearly distinguish 6 mm diameter rods. Monte Carlo simulations have shown that improving the spatial and energy resolution of the detectors can improve the angular resolution measure (ARM) of the system at 440 keV. Simulation studies have also demonstrated the improved image quality that can be achieved by increasing the dimensions of the second detector plane. This design upgrade has been implemented in an updated Compton camera, MACACO III+, developed by the IRIS group at IFIC-Valencia. Future measurements with ${ }^{225} \mathrm{Ac}$ will be made using the upgraded system, with improved sensitivity and detector performance.

articleTitle: Proof of Concept of the Prediction of Neutron Spectra using Solid Detectors via Machine Learning Approach
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Machine learning methods have recently emerged as promising tools in various nuclear applications, including fuel load pattern optimization, core design, and fuel management. Within neutron spectroscopy, machine learning approaches offer a unique opportunity to overcome measurement challenges inherent in current technologies, particularly in fast neutron spectroscopy. This study investigates a novel approach for predicting neutron spectra via machine learning algorithm using solid detectors data. Chemical Vapor Deposition diamond and 4H-Silicon Carbide detectors were employed, with simulations conducted using the PHITS code to populate the databases required to train and test the machine learning model selected. Experimental data were collected at the TOTEM facility of CEA Cadarache in March 2023, exposing the detectors to a 14 MeV neutron flux generated by a deuterium-tritium neutron generator and Am-Be neutron source. The capability of the detectors to reproduce the neutron flux energy distribution with the studied approach was assessed and reconstructed spectra were compared with simulations. The proposed machine learning algorithm, based on a Kernel Ridge model, predicted spectra with promising accuracy, showing potential for fast neutron spectra prediction. These findings highlight the utility of machine learning techniques in advancing neutron spectroscopy methodologies, offering insights into their applicability and performance in nuclear research contexts.
