This methodology is currently under investigation at Department of Nuclear Techniques and Department of Reactor Study, CEA departments, in order to check the feasibility of the technique in reactor pit environment and on site mixed neutron fields in nuclear facilities.

articleTitle: Non-destructive characterization of pure beta emitters using a PIPS detector and a MLEM deconvolution algorithm
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The non-destructive characterization of an arbitrary mixture of beta emitters is challenging in environmental monitoring, radiation protection, dismantling, and decommissioning (D&D) operations. Continuous spectra generated by beta decay require deconvolution techniques to extract meaningful information. This paper presents a non-destructive measurement method based on a CAM-PIPS (Continous Air Monitoring Passivated Implanted Planar Silicon) detector coupled with a MLEM (Maximum Likelihood Expectation Maximization) algorithm. The MLEM algorithm automatically analyzes measured spectra using response matrices derived from Monte Carlo simulation. A MCNP6.2 numerical model of the detector was developed and validated by comparing simulated and measured responses from standard beta sources. We assessed the performance of the MLEM algorithm for the deconvolution of <sup>14</sup>C, <sup>36</sup>Cl, <sup>90</sup>Sr, and <sup>137</sup>Cs mixed spectra. Finally, we conducted a sensitivity analysis by adding the response of <sup>60</sup>Co, <sup>133</sup>Ba, <sup>152</sup>Eu and <sup>154</sup>Eu, commonly encountered beta-gamma emitters, to the MLEM matrix. The validated method was employed to characterize beta emitters in nuclear graphite samples. This study confirms the potential of the proposed approach for real-time, non-destructive beta spectrometry applications

articleTitle: New frontiers of high-efficiency 4D particle tracking with monolithic AC-LGADs
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The simultaneous measure of space and time of a particle transit, the 4D-tracking, is the enabling key point in many fields, from high-energy physics to medical applications like proton tomography, and nowadays represents a technological challenge. On the one hand, trackers need a pixelated layout, on the other hand, sensors for precise timing like Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) incorporate an internal amplification mechanism to increase the SNR and have large and fast signals. However, LGADs require very homogeneous multiplication fields to provide good time resolutions over the whole sensor area, which is incompatible with high segmentations. To overcome the limitations of a pixelated layout and achieve a true 4D-tracking with a unique sensor, an innovative LGAD-based sensor was developed years ago: the Resistive AC-Coupled Silicon Detector. This device, using a thin dielectric layer over the sensor active area as a capacitive component for signal induction, features a continuous multiplication layer and a resistive n-type cathode to avoid segmentation and achieve a 100% fill-factor. Such AC-LGADs use the charge sharing to accurately reconstruct the track position (within few microns) even with a low channel density while preserving the time resolution of standard LGADs (20-30 ps). Since production costs per unit area, power consumption and material budget are becoming increasingly stringent requirements, including also the contribution of readout electronics, we propose an innovative sensor idea: the monolithic AC-LGADs, a combination of optimal coupling between sensor and electronics, and the most effective strategy to achieve the 4D-tracking. In this contribution we present an overview of a preliminary engineering run produced to test the CMOSLGAD compatibility. Then, we will describe the device figures of merit and the design strategies we are implementing to produce a first monolithic AC-LGAD prototype.

articleTitle: Characterization of a semi-monolithic BGO photon counting detector with Cherenkov identification capability
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A bismuth germanate (BGO) monolithic detector that counts optical photons detected in a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) array can derive unique timestamps for Cherenkov light, which is a pathway for fully exploiting this prompt signature for ultra-fast time-of-flight positron emission tomography (TOF-PET) detectors. In this work, we evaluated the coincidence time resolution (CTR) of a 16-channel, semi-monolithic BGO photon counting detector and investigated methods to classify the earliest detected photons as Cherenkov/scintillation in order to develop advanced 511-keV timing estimators. A $42.68 \times 2 \times 20 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ BGO was coupled to $16 \times 12 \times 2 \mathrm{~mm}^{2}$ SiPMs, where the signals were fed into low-noise high-frequency electronics that output digital photon timestamps. The time and energy signals from each channel were sampled by CAEN V1742 digitizers. The global single photon time resolution of the 16-channel board was quantified as 60 ps FWHM. Position calibration was performed to (1) train a neural network position estimator and (2) generate the first photon delay distribution (FPDD) that correlates the transit time of the first arrived photon on the SiPM pixel with the interaction position. The FPDDs exhibited clear distributions of both Cherenkov and scintillation photon arrival time profiles. A uniform irradiation dataset was acquired for evaluation, and we achieved a CTR of 176 ps FWHM in our setup (242 ps estimated for two identical BGO detectors), with 70% of the earliest photons being uniquely identified single photons. The FPDD was further used to quantify the probability of whether the earliest detected photons were Cherenkov light. Classified by this metric, a time-delay correction resulted in the achievable CTR of 113 ps FWHM (150 ps for two BGO detectors). This work shows breakthrough CTR for thick BGO slabs and provides opportunities to further improve CTR by leveraging Cherenkov photon classification.

articleTitle: DESY’s monolithic dSiPM: design and characteristics
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This contribution describes a monolithic digital silicon photomultiplier (dSiPM), designed and characterized at DESY. It consists of an array of single photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) arranged in a 32 x 32-pixel matrix at 70 μm pitch, with embedded CMOS circuitry for on-chip signal processing. The dSiPM is designed in LFoundry’s 150-nm CMOS process employing a fully characterized SPAD design provided by the manufacturer. It enables in-pixel sensor-signal digitization and masking, and provides the full hit map and time stamping at 3-MHz frame rate with a resolution better than 100 ps. Especially the availability of highly granular position information will be beneficial for applications like the readout of scintillating fibers, or the detection of minimum-ionizing particles (MIPs). Several measurements were carried out in the laboratory and at the DESY II test-beam facility using the Caribou readout system. The dark-count rate as function of the overvoltage and temperature, the TDC resolution, as well as their differential and integral nonlinearity are presented. The dSiPM was used to identify MIPs in the test beam and has demonstrated a detection efficiency of 30 %, limited by the fill factor. Comparing the time measurements of two dSiPMs installed at the test beam, show a time resolution on the order of 50 ps.

articleTitle: Mirai-PET: High-Resolution, Portable, Axially Long Small Animal PET with TOF-DOI Detection
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In preclinical PET, high spatial resolution is necessary to evaluate drug accumulation in a small region, and a long axial field-of-view (FOV) is required to visualize the systemic pharmacokinetics of newly developed drugs. To meet these needs, we developed a new high-resolution, large FOV small animal PET, Mirai-PET. The most prominent feature of the device is the crosshair lightsharing detector; fast-LGSO crystals of 15 mm in length are arranged in a 1.6 mm pitch, and depth-of-interaction information was decoded to three layers. The device has a ring diameter of 170 mm and an axial FOV of 156 mm. All the components are on a compact cart for portability so that one person can move the device easily. In this work, we evaluated imaging performance of the Mirai-PET. The filtered backprojection spatial resolution was 1.4 mm at the axial center with a 5 mm radial offset, and 1 mm rods were resolved with the ordered-subset expectation-maximization reconstruction. The peak noise-equivalent count rate (NECR) was 103 kcps at 28.3 MBq with the 440-620 keV energy window. The best time-of-flight (TOF) resolution was 231 ps, which was almost independent of count rate (246 ps at the peak NECR). TOF may not work well to improve image quality for mice, but it improves count rate performance. As imaging demonstrations, we measured a mouse and a rat for 60 min from 60 min after the injection of <sup>18</sup>F-sodium fluoride (20 MBq for the mouse and 37 MBq for the rat). As a result, we found the Mirai-PET visualizes the bone structure of the total-body uptakes in the mouse and the uptakes from the head to pelvis region in the rat. In summary, using the Mirai-PET we demonstrated 1 mm rod separation performance with a long axial FOV of 156 mm and excellent TOF resolution of 246 ps even at the peak NECR (103 kcps at 28.3 MBq).

articleTitle: DC-coupled resistive read-out silicon sensors for future 4D tracking: recent advancements and first laboratory characterization
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recent advancements in sensor technology have paved the way for the development of high-resolution 4D-tracking detectors capable of simultaneously measuring the position and time of passage of charged particles within a single sensitive device. The key point is the use of resistive read-out in thin Low Gain Avalanche Diode (LGAD) sensors, which introduces combined intrinsic signal sharing and internal gain. This contribution focuses on the development of a thin LGAD with a DC-coupled resistive read-out (DC-coupled Resistive Silicon Detector - DC-RSD). The aim is to achieve a spatial resolution of a few micrometers and an excellent time resolution of approximately 30 ps, using relatively large pixels (150-200 micrometers), which enables detectors with low channel density and low power consumption. A strong effort has been put into the simulation of the device, supported by experimental measurements of the AC-coupled resistive read-out sensors, which can be used to extrapolate the DC-RSD performance. This contribution describes the design and implementation strategy of the first DC-RSD production, presently in progress at Fondazione Bruno Kessler. Several test structures and application-oriented devices have been designed, which will enable detailed studies of the charge sharing optimization. The production is expected to be completed in early Fall 2024. The initial characterization of the production in the laboratory will provide us with immediate feedback on the soundness of the DC-RSD concepts.

articleTitle: Effects of Neighboring Modules in Compact 3D CdZnTe Detector Arrays
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: 3D CdZnTe detector modules can be tiled in tight-packed arrays to provide high efficiency in a compact form factor. In this work, the effect of neighboring modules on the CdZnTe detector response was investigated for an array with sub-millimeter spacing between modules.Measurements and simulations show that the air gap between detectors is small enough that both the cathode and anode weighting potentials are affected by the presence of neighboring modules. For regions of the detector near neighbor modules, the cathode weighting potential becomes nonlinear and the anode weighting potential improves in the near-anode region.

articleTitle: Comparative Analysis of Novel Time-Walk Correction Methods for Metascintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Development of novel scintillator materials and effective Time-Walk Correction (TWC) methods aim to improve coincidence time resolutions (CTRs) in Time-of-Flight Positron Emission Tomography (ToF-PET) systems. This study introduces an innovative approach using metascintillators coupled with advanced photodetector technologies to address the limitations of time-walk effects on CTR. We evaluated Linear (L-TWC), Differential (D-TWC), and Hyperbolic (H-TWC) TWC strategies, focusing on their impact on enhancing CTR in ToF-PET applications. The H-TWC method aims to mitigate long-tailed coincidence time distributions, thus leading to a more standardized Gaussian distribution and improving the CTR. Our experimental setup employed $3 \times 3 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ NUV-HD-MT photodetectors from Fondazione Bruno Kessler (FBK) coupled with $3 \times 3 \times 5$ $\mathrm{mm}^{3}$ LYSO:Ce,Ca reference crystals and novel $3 \times 3 \times 15 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$ BGO-EJ232 metascintillator heterostructures. Results indicate that while all the TWC methods do not improve the CTR values on the reference crystals measurements, the H-TWC demonstrates improvements from 50 ps up to 65 ps when metascintillator pixels are used. Our findings indicate that while L-TWC and D-TWC methods demonstrate similar improvements, the hyperbolic approach significantly enhances CTR values by effectively neutralizing heavy-tailed distributions.

articleTitle: Image-based Resolution Modeling for Spatially-variant PSF Deformation in a Dedicated Breast-PET Scanner
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Spatially-variant (SV) point-spread-function (PSF) deformation can hinder the ability of lesion detection and localization, as well as uptake estimation, in a dual-panel breast PET (BPET) scanner. In our previous work we showed that SV Image-based Resolution Modeling (IRM) method can improve the image quality of simulated BPET based on a grid of 250 simulated PSFs. In order to apply this methodology to measured data, it is necessary to characterize the SV PSF kernels as measured in the BPET scanner. Instead of performing several hundreds of PSF measurements, we propose an effective way to parameterize the spatially-variant PSF deformation by a polynomial quadratic panel fitting based on only a modest set of point-source acquisitions. A hot-rod phantom was measured and reconstructed by SV-IRM using the created PSF lookup table, leading to improved hot-rod identification and localization. Further evaluations are being performed on physical phantoms as well as research patient studies with quantitative metrics.

articleTitle: On the benefits of quantum entanglement information for semiconductor PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper studies the information carried by quantum entangled gammas resulting from positron annihilation, for application to Positron Emission Tomography (PET). The ~1 % energy and ~0.35 mm spatial resolution enabled by semiconductor detectors allows better measurement of the correlation in the difference of azimuthal angles in Compton interactions. We cross-compared Geant4 simulations and experimental results obtained with a two Cd-Zn-Te (CZT) head setup to check that the intensities of correlation induced by quantum entanglement are consistent. To extrapolate to a full system, we simulated with Geant4 a full-ring of CdTe detectors with 1 cm width, 15 cm inner radius and 30 cm in the longitudinal axis. A cylindrical water phantom with a radius of 7 cm is added at the center to generate gammas scattered in the patient. Events which do not produce at least two interactions in the detector for each annihilation photon are discarded. Two ways of identifying scatter in patients are used: the correlation of azimuthal angle in Compton scattering from entanglement and the combination of energy deposit and reconstructed incident energy. It appears that the information from energy is more valuable with an area under the curve (AUC) of the receiving operating characteristics (ROC) curve of 0.92 compared to an AUC of 0.52 for entanglement.

articleTitle: LCLS-II High-speed links reliability
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: LCLS-II (Linac Coherent Light Source II) is a cutting-edge X-ray free-electron laser facility located at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory. It aims to produce ultra-bright X-ray pulses for studying atomic-scale processes with unprecedented detail and speed. Going from 120 frame per second to up to 1 million requires major changes, including the way timing and data are distributed over the different experiments. Because of the number of optical links (up to 1000 links for a 16Mpixel 35kHz detector) the amount of data and the importance of trigger information, the optical link reliability is critical. This talk introduces the challenges we face going into production and the tools that had been developed to diagnose potential failures.

articleTitle: Development of an Isotropic-response wide energy range neutron spectrometer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: During the increasingly demand on neutron spectrum detection for various radiation application facilities, it’s significant to realize isotropic-response and wide energy range measurement of neutron spectrum. We developed an Isotropic-response wide energy range neutron spectrometer. Specifically, the spatially homogeneous arrangement of sufficient 56 micro detectors serve isotropic response of neutron radiation for the spectrometer. The introduce of lead to the composite-material nested-structure spherical moderator provides prominent moderation efficiency for high-energy neutron. Simulation and experimental results demonstrate that the custom-made neutron spectrometer has near isotropic response to different directional neutron radiation, efficient response to thermal neutron and neutron with energy up to $10^{3} \mathrm{MeV}$, and successfully acquired unfolded Cf-252 and Am-Be neutron spectrum with 0.91 and 0.97 similarity to standard spectrum.

articleTitle: Correction of Attenuation and Scattered Photons in a Myocardial SPECT Using Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Myocardial SPECT imaging has become an indispensable study for evaluating the viability of the myocardium. However, surrounding the heart are the lungs, liver, and soft tissues, and their attenuation coefficients differ greatly. In addition, since the energy of the radioisotope used is low, the influence of attenuation is large and its correction is essential. Furthermore, since many radioisotopes accumulate in the liver during myocardial study, it is also essential to remove scattered photons originated from the liver. In this study, we used deep learning with a convolutional neural network(CNN) to correct attenuation and scattering in myocardial SPECT imaging, and investigated the influence of scattered photons from radiopharmaceuticals accumulated in the liver. In addition, a conventional attenuation/scatter correction method with a $\mu$-map was also implemented at the same time, and the two were compared. The simulation results showed that the attenuation/scatter correction using a conventional method worked well in spite of the amount of activity in the liver. On the other hand, the results using the CNN affected by the liver activity even though the scattered photons from the liver were considered in the training data. To make a model which yields accurate scatter/attenuation correction, learning data should be carefully selected.

articleTitle: Proposal of performance evaluation methods for Compton cameras
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Compton imaging is expected to be the third imaging modality in nuclear medicine following SPECT and PET. Compton imaging can visualize various γ-emitters over a wide energy range without using a physical collimator. It is necessary to clarify the appropriate scatterer and absorber detector configurations and arrangements for future development of a clinical system. However, there is no standard method to characterize the performance of Compton cameras, which is a barrier in the investigation of promising detector technologies among various Compton cameras. In this study, we proposed performance characterization methods for Compton cameras, and we investigated the characteristics of four cameras: a dual ring GSO-GSO camera (the 3rd whole gamma imaging prototype), a GAGG-GAGG single-unit camera, a dual ring GAGG-GAGG camera, and a Si-CdTe single-unit camera. To clarify the performance characteristics over a wide energy range, we used 57Co (122 keV), 133Ba (356 keV), and 22Na (511 and 1275 keV) radioactivity sources. Sensitivity and angular resolution measure (ARM) were evaluated with these point sources. Image spatial resolution, contrast, and noise were measured with multi-rod phantoms and multi-contrast phantoms. These sealed radioactive phantoms could be easily transported between facilities where the Compton cameras were installed. For three systems using scintillation detectors, better ARMs were obtained as a function of γ-ray energy. For the other Si/CdTe system, the best ARM and sensitivity were obtained for 356 keV γ-rays (133Ba). Dual ring cameras outperformed single-unit cameras in terms of image spatial resolution, contrast, and noise. For 511 and 1275 keV γ-rays, 4-5 mm rods were resolved by the dual ring GSO-GSO camera (WGI-3) with ARM FWHM of 7.9-11.0°. We successfully characterized the performance of four Compton cameras according to our proposed methods. We concluded the dual ring geometry is a promising choice for a future clinical Compton camera.

articleTitle: Directional Detection of Multiple Gamma Sources using Mutual Shielding of Scintillators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Directional detection of gamma sources is crucial for various applications, such as decontamination, response to a nuclear incidents and radiological events, and as a preventive measures. For the low-energy range ($\lt200 \mathrm{keV}$, e.g. ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}$), Compton scattering cross section is neglectable, thus Compton cameras are not feasible. Therefore, traditional directional detectors use passive collimation [1, 2] such as coded aperture [3], with a narrow field of view, low sensitivity, and high weight. A few detectors based on mutual shielding [4, 5] propose a single gamma source locations estimation. We propose a 4π directional detector for multiple gamma sources, using the mutual shielding of scintillators. The detector comprises 64 sensors made of CsI(Tl) cubic scintillators, each side of 12.4 mm, coupled to Silicon Photomultipliers. The sensors are arranged in a spatial configuration which maximizes both directional accuracy and sensitivity. The sensor signals sampled by a commercial readout system. Employing an Expectation Maximization algorithm, we estimate the flux intensity from all directions simultaneously. This allows imaging and differentiation of multiple point-like sources or areas of spread contamination and background radiation. This work presents a comprehensive overview of the detector’s design, operational principles, and analytical methodologies. Initial measurements demonstrate the system’s capability to accurately determine the direction of gamma sources from any point within a 4π steradian sphere.

articleTitle: Development of a highly sub-pixelised CZT gamma detector array
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new technology for enhancing position resolution of CZT detectors using a high degree of sub-pixelisation has been developed by Kromek. The technology combines Kromek’s advanced D-Matrix rev.2 detector readout and a machine learning-based (ML) model used to analyse the raw detector data. The ML model provides a major improvement in the sub-pixel position resolution and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. The training of the ML model is based on high precision simulated data which simplifies the development process ensuring maximum flexibility in application and scalability of the new technology.The technology was developed within the framework of Kromek’s development of an ultra-low-dose molecular breast imaging camera. The technology was applied to the detector data acquired with the CZT camera comprising a 3x2 array of Kromek’s 5 mm thick CZT detector quad modules covering the total FOV of 132 mm x 88 mm. The detectors have an 11x11 pattern of 2 mm pixels. The performance was evaluated by collecting images produced by a parallel beam from a <sup>57</sup>Co source. The results demonstrate a major improvement in the position resolution allowing achievement of 5x5 sub-pixelisation with 2 mm pixel data. The resulting performance allows a balanced combination of excellent energy resolution typical for gamma detectors and high spatial resolution typical for x-ray imaging for the benefit of various nuclear imaging applications.

articleTitle: Multivariate analysis for signal pulse shape of TlBr semiconductor detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thallium bromide (TlBr) semiconductor detectors are developed as one of the alternatives of a high pure germanium semiconductor detector. Although the TlBr detector has relatively high mobility-lifetime products, one drawback is low mobility. Especially, the hole mobility is much lower than the electron mobility. Therefore, we usually apply the single-polarity charge sensing technique. When using this technique, the signal pulse shape depends on the weighting potential gradient along electron pathways in the detector. In this study, we consider the applicability of the multivariate analysis of the signal pulse shape of TlBr semiconductor detectors to analyze the signal pulse shape. By applying the principal component analysis, the pulse height spectrum can be improved.

articleTitle: Mobile Far-Field Gamma-Ray Imaging and Radiological Mapping Using CAMIS
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The detection and localization of radiological and nuclear materials at standoff distances of 20 m or more in urban and cluttered environments remains a challenge in nuclear security and proliferation detection. Previous approaches have explored large-area radiation imaging methodologies based on planar arrangements of detectors with passive masks, leading to limited field-of-view (FOV) and efficiency. We have developed the Cylindrical Active Mask Imaging System (CAMIS) which consists of $128(10 \mathrm{cm}) 3 \mathrm{NaI}(\mathrm{Tl})$ detectors arranged in a cylindrical configuration providing gamma-ray imaging capabilities with a 360 o azimuthal FOV. We have mounted this system within an electric van to detect and localize radioactive sources more than 100 meters away. Complemented with a multi-beam rotating LiDAR system, multiple large FOV optical cameras, and several contextual sensor data streams, this system will allow for the localization of these sources in dense urban landscapes. This system will also provide more detailed and sensitive mapping of background radiation fluctuations in the environment than previous large mobile radiation detection platforms. We present initial results in the detection and localization of sources in standoff distances of more than 100 m using a fully mobile platform

articleTitle: PET Image Denoising based on 3D Diffusion Models: Evaluations on 18F-FDG and 68Ga-PSMA-11 Datasets
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET image quality is often compromised by various physical degradation factors and limited photon counts received, especially during low-dose scans. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) have shown great promise in image generation tasks due to their capability of recovering image structures with high variability. However, DDPM is mainly developed in 2D mode, whereas PET is usually acquired, reconstructed, and analyzed in 3D mode. In this work, we presented a 3D DDPM-based PET image denoising approach which utilized a 3D convolutional network to train the score function, thus enabling the network to learn a 3D distribution. The 3D DDPM model was trained based on ${ }^{18} \mathrm{F}$-FDG datasets and further evaluated on both ${ }^{18} \mathrm{F}$-FDG and ${}^{68}{\mathrm{GA-PSMA-11}}$ datasets with different count levels from another scanner type. The proposed 3D DDPM method was compared with 2D DDPM, 3D UNet, and 3D GAN based on qualitative and quantitative assessments across tracers, scanners, and counts. Quantitative results showed that the proposed 3D DDPM framework outperformed other methods across different count levels for both ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG and ${ }^{68} \mathrm{GA}-\mathrm{PSMA}-11$ datasets.

articleTitle: Development of Thallium Bromide Detectors for Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a cancer treatment method based on the ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}(\mathrm{n}, \alpha)^{7} \mathrm{Li}$ reaction. The ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}$ distribution is requisite for the dose evaluation, which can be obtained by imaging 478-keV prompt gamma rays emitted by the neutron capture reactions. Thallium bromide (TlBr) is a compound semiconductor characterized by the wide bandgap energy of 2.68 eV and the high photon stopping power originating from its high atomic numbers (81 and 35) and high density ($7.56 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{cm}^{3}$). Zone-purified TlBr crystals exhibited high resistivity and good charge transport properties at room temperature. Thus, TlBr detectors are promising for constructing prompt gamma imagers for BNCT. In this study, TlBr detectors were fabricated from the crystals grown by the traveling molten zone method using zone-purified materials. The detector crystals measured approximately $12 \mathrm{~mm} \times 12 \mathrm{~mm} \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}$. Thallium electrodes were constructed on the facing two surfaces by vacuum evaporation using shadow masks. The cathode was a planar electrode with the dimension of $10 \mathrm{~mm} \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}$. The anode consisted of 4 circular electrodes (2 mm in diameter) and a surrounding electrode. The detector evaluations were performed at Kyoto university research reactor. A tungsten collimator matched to the 4 circular electrodes of the detector was attached to the TlBr detector. A mouse phantom with a tumor containing ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}$ was irradiated with thermal neutrons from the reactor. The prompt gamma rays from the phantom were measured by the TlBr detector. The detector exhibited sufficient energy resolutions for resolving peaks for 478 keV and 511 keV. The ${ }^{10} \mathrm{~B}$ distribution was successfully obtained by detecting $478-\mathrm{keV}$ gamma rays using the TlBr detector.

articleTitle: Phantom design to enable harmonisation of quantitative PET imaging for lung disease
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Current harmonisation efforts in PET-CT focus on oncology and brain studies. However, there is a similar need for studies of diffuse lung disease, where voxel-wise air fractions (AF) determined from (smoothed) CT can be used to correct for variable air content in lung. Resolution mismatches between PET and CT can cause artefacts in the AF-corrected image. In this work, we investigate the utility of modified thorax phantoms for determining the kernel to smooth the CT for AF correction, and assess its applicability in regions that approximate diffuse lung disease, as well as a hot lesion. A matched kernel approach was used to determine the kernel for clinical reconstructions of <sup>18</sup>F scans on three different PET-CTs. The relative difference between the optimally smoothed ground truth and reconstructed image was within 15% for all regions and reconstructions investigated. This phantom design allows kernel applicability to be investigated in regions of low density, fine-scale structure, as seen in diffuse lung disease, as well as for hot lesions. It therefore has potential utility for determining scanner-specific reconstruction recommendations, with a view to harmonisation of PET-CT lung imaging.

articleTitle: First Steps towards a Foundation Model for Positioning in Positron Emission Tomography Detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Lightsharing detectors, e.g., monolithic or semi-monolithic concepts, have raised broad attention in the PET community as combining good performance characteristics with depth of interaction information. Accurate determination of the gamma interaction position within the scintillation crystal can be achieved by machine learning-based algorithms such as gradient tree boosting (GTB). Varying experimental conditions, e.g. adapted surface coatings, still require new time-consuming calibration measurements. In this work, we make first steps towards developing algorithms with a generalized positioning capability. Such algorithms are potentially more robust against varied detector configurations. This implies the possibility of a single, universal model for all the detectors in a PET scanner irrespective of scintillator topology. For the initial investigation of this hypothesis, we simulate the calibration with an external reference (fan beam) and perform planar positioning. The detector configuration consisted of an array of 12 slabs of dimensions 2.66 $\mathrm{x} 32 \mathrm{x} 19 \mathrm{~mm}^{3}$, with read-out resembling an array of digital SiPMs with pitch 4 mm. The experimental conditions were varied by utilizing different detector wrappings, including various combinations of ESR foil and black tape. Simulation data labeled with the source position in monolithic direction were used as training data for GTB models. Two types of models were trained: Specialized models only trained on simulation data of one wrapping, and generalized models trained on data from all detectors. The generalized models demonstrated similar performances as the specialized models, with only slight deterioration in mean absolute error (MAE) on the test datasets. This provides an interesting outlook on generalized models that can adapt to different experimental conditions.

articleTitle: Efficient implementation of a data-based loss function in end-to-end deep learning PET reconstruction using the DIRECT framework
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: End-to-end deep learning PET reconstruction has gained popularity in recent years. However, it raises concerns about hallucinations (when the network creates artificial features), generalization capabilities, and the use of imperfect labels. Previous works have proposed using an unsupervised loss function operating on the sinogram domain. However, neural networks are usually trained with image patches to allow faster training and limit the memory requirement. Projecting these patches into sinograms is slow and under-optimal as it involves large sinograms. Replacing them with histo-images enables us to forward project a small image patch into a small histo-image patch very efficiently. Moreover, some studies have shown the superiority of histo-images over sinograms as the data representation input of the end-to-end reconstruction network. In this work, we implemented and evaluated this possibility. We found that adding the data loss in the training process on top of the image loss only slowed the training by a factor of three for the same number of epochs on a long-axial field-of-view scanner, which is very reasonable given the complexity of the forward projection process. Using the pure data loss function gave us a trend similar to the one observed in unpenalized iterative reconstruction, with the noise level increasing simultaneously with the contrast. When using a combination of data and image loss functions, the noise quickly reached a limit over which it was not growing anymore while the contrast was still increasing.

articleTitle: Characterization of an AI tool for identification of high-respiratory motion patients in cardiac SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Myocardial perfusion imaging (MPI) with SPECT is a common tool in the diagnosis of coronary artery disease. Image quality is degraded in the presence of respiratory motion (RM). Through a data-driven gating, retrospective motion compensation (MC) can be performed, but these methods are computationally intensive and time-consuming, making implementation in a clinical workflow impractical. In this work, an AI tool for rapid identification of patients that would benefit from MC is presented. This tool was trained on 2763 SPECT scans acquired from 1025 patients. Scans were retrospectively binned into respiratory gates and respiratory motion (RM) alignment vectors were found based on a minimized RMS difference between reconstructed gates. Using the AI model, extent of RM was estimated. An additional 773 MPI scans from 264 patients were reconstructed with and without MC. AI estimated motion extent was tested as a predictor of a change in perfusion score after MC. Using a motion cutoff of 10 mm, the tool showed an 80% true positive rate (TPR) for identifying stress scans that would show a significant change in perfusion score. Use of this tool takes less than 10 seconds. The tool was tested against sex- and state-based effects across rest, stress and prone SPECT MPI, and data were down-sampled to investigate the impact of noise on AI predictions. AI-estimated motion extent was shown to be best correlated to RMS values for stress scans (r<sup>2</sup> of 0.794 for stress compared to 0.683 and 0.629 for rest and prone). Predictions based on scans of female patients were also shown to have a weaker correlation with RMS values than male patients (0.662 averaged across states versus 0.696). The tool’s TPR rapidly decreased as noise increased. Overall, the tool was shown to reduce MC workload by up to 54% relative to correcting RM in all scans.

articleTitle: Spline-Initialized Factor Analysis in Dynamic Structures on Cardiac SPECT Sinogram
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we estimated myocardial blood flow (MBF) of a human subject by analyzing inconsitent projection data in dynamic SPECT from rotating camera heads. Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) was used for this purpose with forward and back-projection capability, employing an attenuation-corrected system matrix that embeds the point-spread function. The factorization process generated 1D factor-curves representing time-activity curves from corresponding tissue types, while the 3D coefficient maps depicted tracer dynamics (99 m Tc-tetrofosmin) according to the factor-curves. We performed four-factor analyses on retrospective anonymized clinical data, extracting tracer dynamics in the myocardium, liver, left ventricle (LV), and right ventricle (RV). The dynamic data used ranged from 1 to 9 minutes after tracer injection for four camera rotations. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of obtaining MBF from a short-duration dynamic SPECT scan and a more efficient data analysis pipeline than the conventional dynamic SPECT data analyses techniques.

articleTitle: Improvement of Coincidence Timing Resolution of PET Detectors using Transformer-based Deep Learning
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, convolutional neural network (CNN) has been studied to improve CTR of a PET detector. The improvement, however, was not considerable and the purpose of this study was to further improve the CTR by using transformer based on self-attention mechanism and the performance was evaluated by comparing with that by CNN. A detector composed of LYSO of 3′ 3′ 10 mm<sup>3</sup> coupled one-to-one to SiPM of 3.86′ 3.86 mm<sup>2</sup> was designed. A pair of detectors was placed at a distance of 100 mm, and a <sup>22</sup>Na point source was located at the center of the detector pair. A <sup>22</sup>Na point source was moved from -35 mm to +35 mm in 5 mm steps to acquire coincidence events. The signals were processed by an ultra-high frequency and fully-differential readout circuit, and the output signal waveforms were recorded using a 20 GSPS oscilloscope. Total 15 datasets were acquired, and each dataset consisted of approximately 35,000 coincidence events. For each event, a subset of 40 samples near the detected edge was selected from a pool of 1,000 samples. The transformer was composed of an input embedding, a positional encoding, and a transformer block with multi-head attention and feed-forward networks. The dataset was divided into training and test sets at a 7:3 ratio. The performance of each network was evaluated by the CTR and the R<sup>2</sup> value for the linearity of the peak positions of the timing spectra. The average CTRs were 185 ± 5 ps, 105 ± 14 ps and 87 ± 7 ps measured using LED, CNN and transformer, respectively. The R<sup>2</sup> values were 0.9998, 0.9020 and 0.9932 using LED, CNN and transformer, respectively. The transformer approach not only achieved the best CTR performance but also maintained excellent linearity due to the effective processing of global information by using self-attention mechanism. Experimental results indicated that the transformer-based deep learning can effectively improve the timing resolution of PET detectors while preserving the linear response.

articleTitle: Aerial Radiation Monitoring using Quadcopter
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have emerged as versatile platforms for various applications, including remote sensing and monitoring. This project presents the development of a novel miniature gamma radiation detection system mounted on a quadcopter for aerial radiation mapping and monitoring. The detector system features a compact sodium iodide (NaI) crystal coupled with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) technology, offering enhanced energy resolution and dynamic range for accurate radiation measurements. A custom-designed transimpedance amplifier and microcontroller facilitate real-time data acquisition and analysis, ensuring efficient detection capabilities. The integration of the detector with the quadcopter involves design considerations, including weight distribution, power management, and aerodynamic optimization, to achieve stable flight performance and maximize battery life. The proposed system aims to advance UAVbased radiation detection capabilities, enabling rapid and comprehensive surveillance of radiation sources in diverse environments. Deploying a swarm of quadcopters with NaI crystal-based gamma radiation detectors enables rapid and comprehensive radiation mapping of large areas. Potential applications include environmental monitoring, nuclear safety assessments, and emergency response operations. By leveraging UAV technology and innovative detector design, this project contributes to the advancement of radiation surveillance methodologies and fosters safer and more efficient monitoring practices. Innovations in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology have opened new avenues for remote sensing and monitoring applications

articleTitle: Ex vivo imaging of fatty liver using MPPC-based photon counting CT for evaluation of liver diseases
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: X-ray computed tomography (CT) is a non-destructive internal examination technology. Photon-counting CT (PC-CT) is its next-generation version, detecting X-rays in photon units to provide CT images with X-ray energy information. This enables quantitative investigation of material identification and density, promising new diagnostic methods and treatment visualization in medicine. We developed PC-CT by combining high-speed scintillators (YGAG:Ce) and multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs) as photo-semiconductor devices. To evaluate liver diseases, we utilized the developed PC-CT in our experiment. Specifically, we conducted ex vivo CT imaging on healthy and fatty liver rats, injecting them with gadolinium contrast agent (Gd-EOB), which selectively accumulates in healthy hepatocytes. This contrast agent is commonly used in MRI for liver disease assessment. Our study aimed to determine if PC-CT could produce images comparable to or superior to MRI, potentially offering diagnostic options for patients without access to MRI. Our findings revealed that gadolinium contrast agent accumulated throughout the liver in healthy rats ($1-5 \mathrm{mg} / \mathrm{ml}$), but not in those with fatty liver. This demonstrates the potential of PC-CT for evaluating liver diseases using Gd-EOB. Additionally, we estimated the fat fraction in fatty livers by analyzing the energy dependence of soft tissue and adipose attenuation coefficients. This revealed a fat fraction of $\sim 56 \%$, aligning closely with typical values. Such fat fraction estimation with PC-CT aids in assessing liver disease progression and understanding disease mechanisms, contributing to innovative diagnostics.

articleTitle: A multi-reader multi-case human observer study to evaluate CTLESS for cardiac SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Attenuation compensation (AC) is known to benefit performance on clinical interpretation tasks in myocardial perfusion SPECT (MPS) but typically requires an additional X-ray CT scan, posing challenges of increased radiation dose, costs, and potential SPECT/CT misalignment. Besides, many SPECT systems do not have CT capability. We recently proposed a deep learning-based transmission-less AC method for MPS (CTLESS) and, using numerical observers, showed that on the task of cardiac defect detection, CTLESS yielded similar performance as a CT-based AC (CTAC) method. Encouraged by the positive results, in this study, we objectively assess CTLESS on defect detection task in MPS with human observers. In this IRB-approved retrospective study with anonymized clinical MPS scans, we collected N = 180 MPS studies from two GE Discovery NM/CT 670 Pro SPECT systems with NaI and CZT cameras for the observer study. A multi-reader multi-case study was conducted. Three non-physician readers with training in detecting defects on cardiac SPECT images interpreted images obtained by CTLESS, a CTAC, and no-AC (NAC) methods. The study utilized a split-plot design, dividing paired samples into three groups. The performance was measured by the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve (AUC), and sensitivity and specificity at the optimal cut-point on the ROC curve. We observed that ROC curve obtained by CTLESS overlapped that with CTAC and consistently was above that from NAC. Moreover, CTLESS performed similarly to CTAC and outperformed NAC in terms of AUC, sensitivity, and specificity. These results demonstrate the capability of CTLESS method to achieve similar performance as a CT-based AC method on the task of defect detection in MPS images. This provides strong promise for the evaluation of this method by nuclear medicine physicians and nuclear cardiologists and demonstrates that the method has significant potential for transmission-less AC in SPECT.

articleTitle: Experimental Characterization of ESTHER: Expanded Source-based THERmal neutron field
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Thermal neutron fields based on sealed fast neutron sources, such as Am-Be or Am-B, embedded in large (few cubic meters) polyethylene or graphite moderator assemblies, are traditionally used for neutron dosimetry. ESTHER (Expanded Source-based THERmal neutron field) is a new thermal neutron irradiation facility at Politecnico di Milano. By housing a ${ }^{241} \mathrm{Am}$-Be neutron source within a cavity with reflecting polyethylene walls and incorporating a shadowing polyethylene bar to shield the irradiation volume from direct neutron exposure, the facility provides a nearly uniform thermal neutron field across the irradiation chamber. The experimental characterization of ESTHER was performed using gold foil activation applying the Westcott convention to measure the sub-cadmium cut-off fluence rate at different positions along th evertical axis. These were compared to Monte Carlo simulations using the FLUKA code. Results show good agreement between experimental measurements and simulations, demonstrating the facility’s effectiveness in achieving a consistent thermal field with significant fluence rates. The ESTHER facility also allows to create different irradiation scenarios by removing the polyethylene cap. This offers a range of applications in neutron metrology, dosimetry, and detector testing. ESTHER has a simple and effective design that combined with its capability to achieve substantial thermal fluence rates with modest neutron sources, makes it a promising resource for the scientific community. Future work aims to characterize the neutron spectrum within the irradiation chamber using a Bonner Sphere System.

articleTitle: The Fractal ASIC series of the IGNITE project: CMOS 28-nm technology for high-precision 4D-tracking
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The IGNITE project intends to develop technical solutions for the next generation of trackers at colliders, with special attention to the inner tracking systems, where extreme particle fluxes will be reached. The project is implementing an integrated module, comprising sensor, electronics, and fast readout, aimed at fast 4D-tracking. System pixels are required to have pitch around 50 $\mu \mathrm{m}$ and time resolution below 50 ps on the full chain (sensor to data readout). In the present paper we present measurement results concerning the performance of the first-born prototype ASIC (Ignite-0), which explores circuital solutions for high-performance Analog Front End and Time-to-Digital Converter circuits (time resolution below 30 ps). Such prototype structures have been tested before being integrated in a new design, featuring a 64x64 pixel matrix for the readout of pixelated sensors. Such device, having $55 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ pixel pitch and named Ignite-64, has been recently submitted. The subsequent and final ASIC of the project, presently under preparation, will have a larger matrix of $256 \times 256$ pixels, $45 \ \mu \mathrm{m}$ pitch, while keeping time resolution of 30 ps and a power consumption density below $1.5 \mathrm{~W} / \mathrm{cm}^{2}$. All the IGNITE devices are designed following an approach which we named Fractal Design. It relies on vertical integration and allows covering large areas with fully scalable structures.

articleTitle: Construction and performance of the small-diameter Muon Drift Tube Detectors for the upgrade of the ATLAS muon spectrometer at the High-Luminosity LHC
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In the next long shutdown of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) in 2026-2028, 96 new integrated muon tracking and trigger chambers will be installed in the innermost barrel layer of the ATLAS muon spectrometer. This installation aims to enhance trigger coverage and efficiency within the barrel region and improve the rate capability of the muon chambers in areas with the highest background rates during the High Luminosity-LHC era. The new chambers consist of the small diameter Muon Drift Tube (sMDT) chamber with 15 mm tube diameter and thin-gap Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) triplets with 1 mm gas gap thickness. They will replace the existing Muon Drift Tube (MDT) chambers in this area. The sMDT, like the MDT, chambers are used for precise muon measurements and will be included into the final level muon trigger at HL-LHC, increasing the selectivity, while the RPC chambers provide fast responce, ensuring efficient triggering of muon events in high-background environments. This combined sMDT and RPC detector system ensures efficient identification and fast triggering of muon events, crucial for the precision physics studies at the high luminosity conditions of the upgraded LHC. The sMDT chambers have the sense wire positioning accuracy better than $20 \mu \mathrm{m}$. A precision of $5 \mu \mathrm{m}$ has been achieved throughout the entire chamber construction period. The Max Planck Institute for Physics in Munich (Germany) designed the sMDT chambers and their mechanical integration with the RPC chambers in the ATLAS detector. MPI coordinated sMDT chamber construction at two sites: at MPI Munich and at the University of Michigan (USA) ensuring adherence to common quality control (QC) procedures In this contribution, we present the final results of the QC tests conducted for all sMDT chambers assembled at the MPI Munich production site and after their delivery to CERN.

articleTitle: Performance of custom fine-pitch indirect X-ray photon counting imager
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon Counting X-ray detectors attract great interest recently. They requires very high operating count rate up to $10^{7}-10^{8}$ photons $/ \mathrm{s} / \mathrm{mm}^{2}$. Pixelated energy resolving detectors are necessary and greatly of interest for the use in X-ray photon-counting computed tomography (PCCT) systems. While direct detectors, such as CdTe or CdZnTe, have been successfully studied and used in clinical PCCT scanner, the possibility of indirect fast scintillation detectors coupled with photosensors has been also proposed and investigated, however, the realistic fine-pitch (a few hundred micrometers pixel) SiPM+scintillator array are not demonstrated yet. In this study, we have fabricated a $250 \mu \mathrm{m}$ pitch indirect photon counting detector combining a custom-silicon photomultiplier array (pitch of $250 \mu \mathrm{m}$) with finely aligned GAGG/GFAG arrays ($200 \mu \mathrm{m}$) separated with $50 \mu \mathrm{m}$ reflectors by one-to-one coupling manner. The measured imaging performance shows the separation capability of $2 \mathrm{LP} / \mathrm{mm}$ while maintaining the energy resolving capability $\sim 25 \%$ @122 keV. The characterization combining high-speed (HS)-GFAG, GFAG,GAGG with $12,15,20 \mu \mathrm{m}$ devices shows the time response (FWTM) less than 100 ns and great potential for the use in high-flux applications.

articleTitle: Total-Body PET/CT Images Used for Generating Digital Phantoms as Training Data for Deep Learning Based Data Corrections
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Since the advent of total-body PET scanners, a large dataset of high-quality PET/CT images has become available for research, creating opportunities for employing deep learning (DL)-based methods for enhancing PET data corrections. This work proposes generating digital phantoms from total-body PET/CT images to be used in realistic simulations to create training data for DLbased data corrections. As a proof of concept, a set of phantoms was created from 14 lymphoma patient scans on the uEXPLORER. 10-min scans of the phantoms were simulated in GATE, including the scanner’s lutetium background radiation from ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}$ decay in the scintillators. ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}-$ based attenuation maps ($\mu$-maps) were generated from maximum likelihood for transmission tomography reconstruction. A 3D U-Net was trained to generate CT-quality $\mu$-maps using ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}$ and CT-based $\mu$-maps as network inputs and labels, respectively. Training, validation, and test data included images of 12,1, and 1 subjects, respectively. PET quantitative accuracy was evaluated in the test subject using the ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}$-, and DL-based $\mu$-maps, compared to CT-based $\mu$ maps. To demonstrate applicability of the network to experimental data acquired on different scanners, the network was also tested on a ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}$ scan of a healthy volunteer on the NeuroEXPLORER brain-dedicated PET scanner. PET quantification analysis showed improved performance of the DL-based $\mu$-maps compared to ${ }^{176} \mathrm{Lu}$-based $\mu$-maps by all metrics, with higher structural similarity index measure, lower normalized root mean square error, and lower regional biases in liver, lungs, bone marrow, and blood-pool. The network also successfully improved the ${ }^{176}$ Lu-based $\mu$-maps in 5-60 min transmission scans on the NeuroEXPLORER. With the promising results obtained, future work will focus on expanding the training data to enhance model generalizability and exploring broader applications, including scatter correction, motion correction, and integration with other imaging modalities.

articleTitle: Nondestructive Measurement Method for Fuel Debris Sorting
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The decommissioning of the Fukushima Daiichi Nuclear Power Station is currently in progress. In this process, one of significant issues is the measurement of the quantity of nuclear fuel material contained in materials retrieved from the primary containment vessel. For nondestructive measurement of nuclear materials, the use of neutron-induced nuclear fission reactions is effective. Moreover, nondestructive measuring method unaffected by neutron absorber materials is desirable since fuel debris may contain neutron absorber materials used in control rods. The fast fission neutron coincidence counting method (FFCC) is a nondestructive nuclear material measurement technique that utilizes fast neutrons less affected by neutron absorber materials. This method distinguishes between irradiation neutrons and fission neutrons by taking advantage of the simultaneous emission of multiple neutrons in nuclear fission reactions. Specifically, fast coincidence counting using multiple neutron detectors is conducted, counting only events when multiple fast neutrons are detected. In this study, a measurement system using liquid scintillation detectors as neutron detectors was constructed for simulation, and the performance expected when applied to fuel debris contained in a unit can φ210mm×H200mm) was evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation (Particle and Heavy Ion Transport code System: PHITS). As a result, it was found that measurements of fuel debris containing large amounts of neutron absorber materials are possible, while it is difficult to measure using the conventional methods based on nuclear fission reactions by thermal neutrons. Furthermore, it was found that overall measurement accuracy improves compared to the conventional methods.

articleTitle: Simultaneous Scintillation and Charge Induction Readouts for Gamma-Ray Detection in CsPbBr3
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: CsPbBr<inf>3</inf> is a promising semiconductor material for gamma-ray detection applications due to its ease of fabrication and for the symmetric $\mu \tau$ of both electrons and holes in certain applications. In this work we propose the use of a simultaneous light and charge induction readout based on previous work with TlBr utilizing scintillation light with a 11 mm X $8 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{X} 6 \mathrm{~mm} \mathrm{CsPbBr}_{3}$ crystal with a 1 mm X 1 mm cathode pixel. Such a measurement would allow for both fast timing and for depth-of-interaction correction of energy spectrum. Preliminary work has demonstrated the feasibility of the technique with simultaneous scintillation and semiconductor readouts. Future work will gather sufficient statistics for a thorough characterization of the hole drift and at several gamma ray energies to correlate scintillation light yield to incident gamma-ray energy.

articleTitle: Dynamic Whole-Body PET with Reduced Scanning-Time using Dual-Injection in combination with an IDIF Library
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Parametric whole-body PET images can be obtained with a conventional PET scanner using multi-bed multi-pass dynamic whole-body (DWB) acquisition protocol. The scanning time can be shortened by starting later, as the early tissue data is not required for kinetic analysis of irreversible tracers. However, the initial peak of the image-derived input function (IDIF) will be missed. We previously proposed a protocol, with a low-activity 2nd injection for measuring the peak. Here we propose an improvement of this method by using an IDIF-library. 24 patients were scanned, with a dynamic acquisition over the thorax directly after tracer injection, a DWB scan and a standard-of-care (SoC) WB scan at 60 min. IDIFs were obtained from the aorta. In one additional subject, a 2nd injection (I2) of 10% was given and another dynamic acquisition over the thorax was performed for 5 min. IDIFs were generated by fitting the data from I2 together with a sub-set from the DWB scan, a) using an analytical function, and b) by selecting one scaled IDIF from the library, that best fit the data. The results were compared with the data from the 1st injection in terms of MSE. We simulated data corresponding to a reduced I2 activity by factors of up to 8, with 1000 noise replicates. Data were analysed with 3- or 5-min scans after I2 in combination with DWB data from 30 or 40 min p.i. The results showed that, with a 10% I2, the two models gave similar results. With reduced activity, for the analytical model fit, MSE increased by factors of up to 2.5 and SD by factors of up to 5. The IDIF-library approach was much more robust, with MSE increasing by factors of up to 1.25 and SD by factors of up to 1.5. In conclusion, based on data from one single patient study, our results suggest the activity in the 2nd injection can be reduced significantly using our proposed IDIF-library approach.

articleTitle: Analytical calculation of the system matrix for a DC-SPECT system with square-hole collimators
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This work presents an analytical method for calculating the system matrix for a DC-SPECT system. The solid angle calculation is adapted for a square-shaped pinhole collimator. The calculated sensitivity map demonstrates consistency when compared to Monte Carlo simulations. Images reconstructed using our proposed model are compared with reconstructions using Monte Carlo simulated system matrix methods. Our results indicate that with the current system design, DCSPECT can achieve a resolution of 5.5 mm at a sensitivity of 0.07% over a 15 cm diameter FOV.

articleTitle: Development of structured optical guiding scintillators using Tl doped Cs3Cu2I5 for high resolution and sensitivity X-ray imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, optical-guiding crystal scintillator (OCS) fibers sing Tl doped $\mathrm{Cs}_{3} \mathbf{C u}_{2} \mathrm{I}_{5}$ were developed. It consists of single crystal scintillator cores and glass clads. The refractive index of the halide single crystals are higher than the glass in this system. Generated scintillation light above the critical angle is totally reflected at the interface with the glass and optically waveguided like an optical fiber. Owing to light guiding system, the OCS plate can show high sensitivity and high spatial resolution for radioactive particles. This study demonstrates that the diameter of the OCS core can be reduced to 7-8 $\boldsymbol{\mu m}$. Spatial resolution equivalent to the core diameter is expected. The presentation will include details on fabrication methods, crystal quality, luminescence properties, different combinations of scintillator and glass materials, radiation response, and imaging properties.

articleTitle: Neuromorphic Computing for Nuclear Safeguards
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Recently, ORNL, LSU and UTK have demonstrated the first use of neuromorphic computing for radiation anomaly detection. Neuromorphic technology is a cutting-edge field which promises to significantly revolutionize the ways in which advanced machine learning algorithms are designed and implemented across broad application spaces. In particular, neuromorphic computing enables traditionally power-hungry algorithms to be implemented in a way that significantly reduces their power consumption while simultaneously reducing the form factor of the computing hardware. Spiking neural networks were trained on data derived an extensive library of Monte Carlo radiation transport simulations and dynamic backgrounds collected in the field using evolutionally optimization methods developed by collaborators at UTK. This prototype system is composed of a commercial-off-the-shelf NaI(Tl) gamma-ray radiation detector, micro-channel analyzer and custom electronics which house a neuromorphic algorithm implemented on a fieldable programable gate array. This system uses three orders of magnitude less power than current edge computing systems while exceeding detection sensitivity of traditional anomaly detection methods (such as k-sigma) and approaching that over current high-performance machine learning algorithms. This system is now being extended to nuclear safeguards applications, including UF6 enrichment verification and cylinder monitoring.This effort includes developing new spiking neural networks to perform classification tasks, and integrating with higher resolution gamma-ray detectors as well as event driven cameras.

articleTitle: The beam test of lead tungstate calorimeter prototype with novel SiPM matrix readout at Jefferson Lab
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: The lead tungstate crystals are well-known radiator material for precise homogeneous electromagnetic calorimetry. In experimental nuclear physics, the typical way to read out the crystals is using conventional photomultiplier tubes (PMTs). If a magnetic field is present such a method has complications and requires a passive PMT shielding design. However, in the case of a strong field use of a PMT is almost impossible. The recent development of Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) with small pixel pitch sizes and relatively small noise levels presents an alternative to conventional PMTs. The SiPM-based readout is currently considered for the instrumentation of lead tungstate calorimeters for future nuclear physics and collider experiments. We present the beam test results of a 3x3 calorimeter prototype instrumented with SiPM readout performed at Jefferson Lab. The SiPM readout performance was compared with the PMT readout measured in the same experimental conditions. The prototype was successfully tested using a beam of photons in the energy range between (2.5--11.5) GeV in experimental Hall D. The detector performance was also studied using a secondary beam of positrons provided by the Hall D pair spectrometer.

articleTitle: Design benchmarks of the new NM-2023 ground level cosmic ray neutron monitor
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A new standardized Ground Level Enhancement (GLE) Event Monitor (GLEEM) designated NM-2023 has been developed to provide near continuous ground level neutron monitoring capability for the study and response to extreme space weather events. The design comprises a moderated array of ${ }^{3} \mathrm{He}$ proportional counters inside a massive Pb shell surrounded by an outer shield of polyethylene. The Pb acts as a cosmic ray spallation neutron target to boost the signal. Optimization of the design with respect to size, weight and overall economy was derived from Monte Carlo neutron transport simulations. Efficiency measurements using radionuclide sources enabled some aspects of the modelling to be validated but not the physics treatment of the spallation interaction. In this paper we describe neutron activation measurements performed at the ChipIR facility (ISIS Neutron and Muon Source, Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, UK) in a polyethylene-lead-polyethylene-lead-polyethylene assembly chosen to explore key features of the full-scale design. Comparison between experimental results and Monte Carlo predictions will be presented. Particular emphasis is given to the general end-to-end predictive and analytical framework used because it informed the process from the planning stages right through to the extraction of results. For example, the chain analysis for the radionuclide activities expected was unvaluable in planning irradiation sequences and foil handling, while the efficiency simulations of the HPGe detectors needed in the calculation of the true coincidence summing correction factors applied to the low-background high-resolution gamma-ray spectroscopy counting improved the quality of the experimental results at the backend of the measurement process.

articleTitle: Results from testing an ultrathick array module of 8×8×32 mm3 position-sensitive virtual Frisch-grid CdZnTe detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We characterized an ultrathick array module of 32-mm long position-sensitive virtual Frisch-grid (VFG) CdZnTe (CZT) detectors read out by an IDEAS GDS-100 data acquisition system. The array was designed for integration into large effective area gamma-ray telescopes AMEGO and GECCO that we recently proposed for imaging and spectroscopy of cosmic gamma-rays. The array employs the bar-shaped 8x8x32 mm<sup>3</sup> CZT crystals acquired from Redlen Technologies, Inc. and Kromek-eV Group PLC. The side-by-side mounted bars with minimum gaps in between allow for integrating arrays of different geometries and areas overcoming the size limitations of individual crystals while preserving the excellent performance of CZT detectors. The waveform sampling IDE3421 ASIC, developed by the University of Michigan and IDEAS for CZT pixel detectors, was employed in these tests. The same detectors were also tested as individual devices using hybrid chargesensitive preamplifiers. We measured the good spectral performance of the Redlen detectors with an energy resolution of <1% FWHM at 662 keV and the slightly poorer performance of the Kromek-eV detectors with a resolution of <2% measured at a temperature of $13^{\circ} \mathrm{C}$. We discussed possible explanations for this. One of them is the polarization in Kromek detectors that affects the electric field and the electron drift times.

articleTitle: Radiological characterization of decommissioned nuclear power plants: A case study utilizing a CeBr3 Compton camera
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In order to assist the process of dismantling inactive nuclear power plants innovative measurement techniques are required to assess the radiological situation of the building structure, remaining plant components and on-site low-level radioactive waste. Much of the material that remains after the spent nuclear fuel is removed is safe to be cleared from regulatory control and the challenge is to separate low-level radioactive waste from non-radioactive material. In-situ gamma spectrometry offers the ability to aim the detector at objects of different size, shape, and location, the collimation is still rather coarse. Compton scattering-based systems offer a better alternative to simultaneously achieve gamma-ray imaging and spectroscopy at reasonable exposure times. Two prototype Compton cameras have been built in which all detectors form a coplanar array [3]. The two Compton cameras feature groups of seven and four 3”x3” scintillation detectors, respectively, composed of two materials, cerium bromide as the absorbing scintillator [1, 2] and PVT as scattering scintillator. One of the prototypes is stationary, the other rotating. The Compton cameras are equipped with machine learning imaging software in which the training data are derived from Monte Carlo simulations [4]. The software is capable to reconstruct several images simultaneously. One prototype Compton camera was tested at the Rheinsberg nuclear power plant. At many locations the presence of three nuclides <sup>137</sup>Cs, <sup>60</sup>Co and <sup>152</sup>Eu was detected and those nuclides could be spatially located. This work presents the technical design of the Compton cameras, their performance characteristics in terms of resolution and sensitivity, and the imaging algorithms employed.

articleTitle: A High-Energy Transmission Imaging Measurement of a Varian M9 Linear Accelerator Using a 3D-CdZnTe Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: High resolution X-ray radiography, or transmission imaging, has a wide range of applications. 3D-CZT radiation detectors are capable of producing various types of radiation images with both photons and neutrons. In this work, a $40 \times 40 \times 10 \mathrm{~mm}^{\wedge} 3$ CZT detector was placed in the beamline of a Varian M9 Linear Accelerator (LINAC) behind a specifically designed lead, copper and tin shielding configuration. A tungsten block was positioned at an angle covering a fraction of the detector face in efforts to demonstrate an attenuation shadow. The resulting radiation image demonstrates an expected count gradient, albeit at a limited resolution. There is also an unexpected uniform waveform decay present in all anode signals during the LINAC pulse. Work will be continued to obtain a high resolution gradient image from future measurements.

articleTitle: A prototype multi-instrument quality assurance system for responsive nuclear fuel manufacturing
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: A prototype apparatus for in line quality control assessment of sintered uranium dioxide fuel pellets has been demonstrated. In this work we combine $\gamma$-ray spectrometer, laser profilometer, and hyperspectral and RGB cameras in a single system. The combination of instruments provides analytical data on uranium enrichment, pellet geometry, physical defects, and potential chemical contamination. The images and spectra are analyzed using a convolutional neural network and an automated quality control decision taken. The prototype was deployed at the National Nuclear Laboratory, Preston site to analyze Advanced Gas Cooled sintered UO<inf>2</inf> pellets. Results from the pellet analysis are added automatically to a pellet data library for future nuclear security and safeguards auditing and model-training to improve quality assurance decision-making.

articleTitle: Programmable Readout Electronics for Light Scintillation Detection in Liquid Xenon.
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
