abstract: This paper presents an investigation into the feasibility of a programmable electronic architecture specifically designed for reading out scintillations in a future iteration of a full-body version of Xemis, a three-gamma nuclear medical imaging system. This system employs liquid xenon (LXe) as the detection medium inside a time projection chamber (TPC - LXe), aiming to reduce the overall dose administered to patients. The main challenge for the readout electronics discussed here is about scaling the scintillation photon detection electronics over a 2 meter axial lenght system for clinical application, Xemis-3. The development of this programmable readout system, based on the light yield found in Xemis-2 simulations, aims replace PMTs with 16 VUV-MPPC (Multi-Pixel Photon Counters) arrays. This feasibility phase prepares for future design, with experimental validation to be done using the existing Xemis TPC test chamber. Initial simulation results indicate the effectiveness of Sigma Delta modulation readout electronics, achieving scintillation photon detection accuracy within ±1 photo. Upcoming experimental tests will evaluate this readout electronics with an FPGA at the temperature of liquid xenon.

articleTitle: Simultaneous multi-waveform clustering analysis for improving the spectral performance of CsPbBr3 detectors
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Perovskite CsPbBr (CPB) as a room-temperature gamma-ray detector has shown great potential for many applications. However, many CPB detector samples suffer from various types of material non-uniformity, and one of its influences is the charge collection efficiencies (CCE) for identical energy deposited at different locations in a detector vary with the location of interaction. This effect will affect the apparent energy resolution of the detector. Therefore, the development of methods for correcting the effect of non-uniform CCE would be beneficial. In this paper, we have explored a simultaneous multi-waveform clustering method to classify different interaction patterns and derive the variation of CCE accordingly. This information is then used to correct the energy spectrum and enhance the energy resolution. We validated this technique by using several CPB detectors. Our results showed that by employing this method, we can significantly improve the energy resolution of the sensors from $\sim 5.5 \%$ at 662 keV to $\sim 1.8 \%$ after the correction. The main advantage of our approach is that we can improve the spectral performance of a detector regardless of detector configuration and sources of changes in CCE.

articleTitle: PET-MOTUS: 500 ms non-rigid motion estimation and correction for PET imaging
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: PET imaging naturally suffers from motion-blur due to long acquisitions. As such, motion compensation provides a promising solution to improve image quality. Traditional methods for motion correction often fail to correct for a combination of periodic and random motion, as short timeframes are noisy and difficult to reconstruct. This study introduces a new method for high-frequency joint motion and image estimation (PET-MOTUS), with non-rigid motion estimation directly from very low-count projection data. It exploits the high compressibility and spatial smoothness of motion through a cubic B-spline motion model and spatial regularization. The algorithm is validated on the XCAT phantom and at a clinical scanner for an anthropomorphic torso phantom on a moving platform. The results show that periodic and random motion can be estimated and corrected for a high frequency (500 ms) with subvoxel accuracy at count rates typical of clinical examinations. This shows visually-significant image quality improvements. We conclude there is motion encoded in very short PET timeframes that can be estimated and corrected through PET-MOTUS, despite the very low counts.

articleTitle: Development of monolithic Germanium Drift Detector
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: There is a strong need for a spectroscopy detector for high-energy X-ray application where silicon, the material of choice for direct detection becomes X-ray transparent. Spectroscopic performance needs excellent noise performance and the Equivalent Noise Charge (ENC) in a simple model is directly proportional to the total capacitance at the preamplifier input. Efforts to minimize the pixel capacitance led to the invention of the Silicon Drift Detector (SDD) by Pavel Rehak and Emilio Gatti, at Brookhaven National Laboratory. SDDs are successfully implemented in spectroscopy beamlines at synchrotrons, electron microscopes, handheld devices, etc. However, implementing the drift topology in other semiconductors has been challenging. This has created a major hurdle for high-energy fluorescence experiments where there are clear advantages of using K - shell fluorescence lines. To address these, we propose to fabricate a planar germanium (Ge) drift detector (GDD) which has been attempted but never fabricated successfully. The detector would be fabricated with trenches separating the drift rings and the anode. Details of the sensor, and the spectroscopic performance of the GDD will be presented.

articleTitle: Fabricated heterogeneous head radiotherapy phantoms for Synchrotron and Linac X-ray radiotherapy: characterization and dosimetry
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Novel radiotherapy quality assurance phantoms are needed with the trend towards patient-specific medicine. Fabricating customizable phantoms can be done through additive manufacturing or 3D printing techniques. This study aims to fabricate and characterize heterogeneous 3D printed pediatric and adult head phantoms for Synchrotron radiation therapy and Linac X-ray dosimetry. 3D printed pediatric and adult head phantoms were designed and fabricated to simulate soft tissue, brain, and skull utilizing polylactic acid+, nylon, and hemihydrate plaster, respectively. Geometrical accuracy, Computed Tomography(CT)imaging, and uniformity were considered. In addition, synchrotron radiation treatment beams were delivered using 3 and 4 Tesla wiggler fields for four sets of synchrotron beam qualities by varying two sets of filters: $\mathrm{AlAl}, \mathrm{AlCu}, \mathrm{CuCu}$, and MoMo. Accumulated point dose and planar dose measurements were acquired using an ionization chamber, and films. In addition, a whole brain plan and a five-field intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) were delivered using a 6-MV Linac X-rays. Similar dosimeters were used to compare measurements with the calculated doses of the Varian Eclipse treatment planning system (TPS). The heterogeneous phantom has an excellent radiological tissue equivalence and visual similarity relative to pediatric and adult heads based on its measured CT number (in Hounsfield Units) with values 12.88± 7.65, 115.27±18.73, and 909.44±89.46 for brain, soft tissue head, and skull. Dose readings for both conformal lateral radiotherapy and IMRT match with the TPS calculated dose within ±3%. The fabricated heterogeneous head phantoms are useful in Synchrotron radiotherapy and Linac X-ray quality assurance.

articleTitle: A new active base of photomultiplier R4125 designed for the lead tungstate calorimeter
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper presents the design, performance, and results of radiation tests of an active base for a Hamamatsu 4125 photomultiplier tube. The active base was designed at Jefferson Lab and comprises a high voltage divider and an on-board amplifier. The photomultiplier with the active base is used to detect light from lead tungstate scintillating crystals of the forward electromagnetic calorimeter of the GlueX detector. The addition of the amplifier within the active base allows to operate the tube at lower high voltage, thereby limiting the photomultiplier anode current to a few microamperes even at a maximum counter rate of 1 MHz, while retaining the dynamic range of output signals. The performance of the active base and the calorimeter module assembly was studied using a bench test setup and a prototype positioned into a beam of photons. Measured key performance parameters such as linearity, high-rate capability, and the energy resolution verified that the active base design aligns with the detector specifications. Additionally, the resistance of the active base components to radiation was tested using a Caesium-137 source. Some damage observed during these tests required to make modifications to the original base design to improve its resilience.

articleTitle: Optimising Subset Selection in Synergistic Emission Tomography Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study investigates subset selection strategies for the synergistic reconstruction of Yttrium-90 PET/CT and SPECT/CT NEMA phantom data acquired on a triple-modality scanner. We previously introduced a smoothed directional total nuclear variation (TNV) prior, which extends the standard TNV prior with an anatomically informed, directionally dependent operator and can be used in gradient-based reconstruction algorithms. We used a modified block-sequential regularised expectation maximisation algorithm and its stochastic variants. Stochastic variance reduction improved convergence rates for PET but showed slower convergence in all but the smallest NEMA sphere for SPECT. Treating modalities as separate subsets yielded convergence rates comparable to joint updates, suggesting the number of subsets can be optimised for each modality. However, treating the prior as a separate subset was less effective, particularly for the largest sphere due to overshooting. This could be mitigated in future work with improved step size selection and preconditioning.

articleTitle: Therapeutic high-energy Radiation Characteristics Study for Verification of Flat-panel Detector without Semiconductor Conversion layer
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This study validates the adaptation of 2D Flat-panel Detectors (FPD), traditionally used in diagnostic KV ranges, for high-energy therapeutic imaging and radiation Quality Assurance (QA) with Linear Accelerators (LINAC). Our evaluation targeted dose characteristics including linearity, reproducibility, repeatability, beam uniformity, and energy dependence. We built FPD with semi-transmissive properties, and high-dose robustness, utilizing thick dielectric layers, deviating from standard semiconductor or photoconductor-based detector Structure. We assessed the characteristics of High Energy photon beams from a LINAC (Harmony Pro, Elekta, Sweden) adjusted for a $10 \times 10 \mathrm{~cm}^{2}$ field, capturing Pixel Data over time for analysis at a common 6 MV Photon Beam energy. Testing conditions spanned 50 to 300 Monitor Units (MU) and Gain values from 3Gain to 15Gain, with energy tests at 6MV to 15MV. Images were acquired with a Source to Surface Distance (SSD) of 100 cm. The Linearity with the increase in MU values showed an $R^{2}$ of 0.9805-0.9999. The Relative Standard Deviation of Reproducibility generally showing $1 \%-2 \%$. Repeatability was tested by conducting five consecutive measurements per day over three days, with an average error rate of 1%-2%. Uniformity in the horizontal axis showed beam output without error. Energy Dependency demonstrated a decrease with increasing MV due to the impact of Percentage Depth Dose (PDD), with an $R^{2}$ value ranging from 0.9959 to 0.9999. This study initiates with dose characteristic tests and aims to ascertain the potential for real-time monitoring of the QA of therapeutic devices such as LINAC using semi-transmissive detectors. It demonstrates a competitive edge over traditional detectors like Electronic Portal Imaging Device (EPID), particularly in terms of high-energy application, cost-efficiency, and mobility property.

articleTitle: Pixelized Thallium-Bromide Radiation Detector for Nuclear Medical Applications
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: We have successfully developed the first prototype of an $80 \mathrm{~mm} \times 80 \mathrm{~mm}$ 1024-channel Thallium-Bromide (TlBr) gamma camera module and achieved imaging of gamma-rays emanating from a thyroid phantom using that module. As radiation detectors for gamma camera applications, the combination of scintillator crystal, such as $\mathrm{NaI}: \mathrm{Tl}$, and photomultiplier tube (PMT), described as the “Anger Camera”, has long been used. Recently, semiconductor detectors such as Cadmium Zinc Telluride (CZT) detectors have started to be used instead. By applying these semiconductors for gamma-camera detectors, due to their higher energy and spatial resolution capabilities of gamma rays, it enables the acquisition of betterquality nuclear medicine images, ultimately leading to a reduction in the burden on Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) examinees. As of now, CZT and Cadmium Telluride (CdTe) are the only commercially available semiconductor detectors, but their much higher costs than conventional Anger type detectors are one of the issues to be solved to expand the use of the semiconductor detector-based modality. The TlBr detector has been developed with the aim of achieving cost-economized yet matching or even better performance than CZT’s or CdTe’s. Thanks to the higher effective atomic number and crystal density of TlBr, we observed a photoelectric interaction detection efficiency for 122 keV gamma-rays of 1.4 times higher than that of CZT and even higher efficiency for 356 keV or higher gamma-ray energies, the energy range required accurate measurement in “Radio-Theranostics” applications.

articleTitle: Polarization Modeling and Experimental Studies in GaAs:Cr Detectors under High X-ray Flux
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: GaAs becomes an attractive candidate material for photon counting X-ray detectors (PCDs), due to its high electron mobility, low characteristic x-ray energy, and high stopping power. However, the polarization issue in high flux becomes one of the major hurdle for clinical application. To understand the behavior of polarization, this study proposes a polarization model in one-dimensional semiconductor detectors, including X-ray energy deposition module, band structure module, electrode contact module, and charge carrier transport module. The energy deposition model simulates the X-ray photon interaction with the detector and generate non-equilibrium carriers. The band structure model simulates the defect levels acting as recombination center to dynamic adjust electric field and carrier concentration. The electrode contact model defines the boundary conditions. The material and electrode properties are directly measured from experiments. The temporal evolution of the system can be solved by charge carrier transport model. Final, the polarization model is validated with a series of experimental testing results of GaAs:Cr detector, such as current-voltage (I-V) characteristic curve, photocurrent, photon counting, and spectrum response.

articleTitle: A novel Concept for Prostate Dedicated PET scanner: A 4-layered Detector with Depth of Interaction and Time of Flight Capabilities
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: With the emergence of organ-specific PET scanners with smaller gantry size and non-cylindrical geometries, the need for specific PET detectors with high sensitivity and resolution is becoming more highlighted. Implementation of depth of interaction (DOI) and time of flight (TOF) capabilities in the detector appears to be the key solution for the simultaneous improvement of resolution and sensitivity. In this work, we introduce a 4-layer detector tower with a dual-sided readout scheme enabling DOI andTOF capabilities. The detector has dimensions of $18 \times 18 \times 30$ mm and is configured with 4 layers of eight $2.05 \times 4.4 \times 30 \mathrm{~mm}$ Lutetium Fine Silicate (LFS) crystals. Two arrays of 16 strip Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs) are attached to opposite sides of the detector, so that each crystal is read by 8 MPPCs (4 from each side). An in-house manufactured flood source, placed between two identical detectors, was used to calibrate energy, time, linearity, and later to evaluate the coincidence time resolution (CTR). The spatial resolution was measured using slit illumination of the detectors (${\lt}1 \mathrm{~mm}$ width). The detector showed excellent uniformity with less than 7% non-uniformity. The energy resolution was 87 keV (17%) full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) at 511 keV. The resulting CTRfor tower vs tower was 189 picoseconds, improved to 170 ps for layer vs layer. The DOI resolution and the resolution along the crystal pixelation are similar to the pitch of the crystals (4.5 and 2.25 mm, respectively). The resolution within the 30 mm elongation of the crystals was 4.7 mm FWHM. The this detector showed precise timing andspatial resolution, along with high sensitivity due to its 4-layer structure, making the proposed concept a potential candidate for organ-specific and noncylindrical geometry scanners.

articleTitle: Deep learning-based scatter correction for self-collimating SPECT
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: In this study, we investigated the impact of scatter on image quality and applied scatter correction on a full-ring self-collimating SPECT system based on GATE simulation. A deep learning-based scatter correction method with 3D U-Net was used, and compared with the conventional triple-energy-window (TEW) method. The training datasets were generated by GATE simulation of 24 different XCAT phantoms. Another two different XCAT phantoms were generated and simulated on GATE for U-Net testing. The reconstructed images without scatter correction, with true scatter correction, with conventional TEW scatter correction, and with U-Net scatter correction were generated and compared. The image quality was quantitatively assessed by comparing contrast recovery coefficient (CRC) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). The results showed that accurate scatter correction improved image quality both qualitatively and quantitatively for self-collimating SPECT. Compared to the conventional TEW method, the U-Net method showed a superior performance in terms of both CRC and CNR. In conclusion, deep learning-based scatter correction can improve image quality and quantification accuracy for self-collimating SPECT.

articleTitle: Image Reconstruction for 18F-FDG Delayed PET Imaging with multiplexed CT image
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Delayed PET imaging could improve the rate of lesion detection and provide more diagnostic information. However, the repeated PET/CT scans increase the time cost and expose the patients to the CT ionizing radiations again. Therefore, we have proposed a kernel-based image reconstruction method for ${ }^{18} \mathrm{~F}$-FDG delayed PET imaging. Moreover, considering that CT images could provide high-quality anatomical information, we extracted the gray features and texture features based on Grey Level Co-occurrence Matrix (GLCM) from the first CT scans and introduce the joint features as a prior to the image reconstruction process. Experiments were conducted on the abdomen PET/CT images from 32 patients, which contains dual time points: 50 min after injection and 110 min after injection. Several methods including MLEM+filter, EM+NLM and MLEM method were utilized for model performance evaluation. Our method yields superior quantification outcomes with a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of $32.60 \pm 3.44 \mathrm{~dB}$ and a mean square error (MAE) of $1.23 \pm 0.57$. Both quantitative and visualization results have shown that our method enable to improve the quality of delayed PET images and preserves high metabolic regions. In future works, we will try to introduce other priori information for image reconstruction for delayed PET imaging and apply our approach to clinical practice.

articleTitle: A Novel Reconstruction Method for Snapshot XRD System Based on Basis Function Representation
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: This paper proposes a novel method to extract the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of scanned objects in a snapshot fan beam XRD system with coded aperture. Although the use of coded aperture significantly improves the detection efficiency of the system, it’s difficult to reconstruct the XRD patterns due to the ill-posed nature of the inverse problem. Our method introduces a prior that XRD patterns could be represented as a combination of basis functions. The method reduces the impacts of noise and background, and improves the reconstruction of XRD patterns. It will facilitate material discrimination, and allow us to speed up XRD scan.

articleTitle: Self-Supervised Photon-Counting CT Denoising with Comprehensive Noise Propagation Model
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: Photon counting computed tomography (PCCT) is an emerging spectral CT technology with significant potential for revolutionizing clinical CT applications. However, noise amplification during signal decomposition significantly limits the utility of basis material images. While data-driven supervised learning has been successful in reducing noise in conventional CT images, applying this method to PCCT is challenging due to the early phase of clinical studies and difficulty in gathering sufficient clinical data for training. To solve this issue, this paper proposes a projection-domain noise propagation model for noise suppression during material decomposition. Firstly, an analytical model is derived from the decomposition of dual-energy materials to describe in detail the propagation of noise from the detector domain to the projection domain. Such model can accurately describe the variance of each pixel in the basis material images. Secondly, we incorporate this statistical model into self-supervised learning network and define a joint optimization strategy via maximizing the constrained log-likelihood with Gaussian statistics. For self-supervised learning, we suggest to construct pseudo training pairs to learn denoising solely from noisy samples. Extensive analyses on real data demonstrate that the proposed method is promising for improving the virtual monochromatic imaging (VMI) quality of PCCT. Our method uses a small amount of experimental data and could be implemented in a real clinical setting.

articleTitle: Evaluation of Depth-of-interaction Calibration for NeuroEXPLORER
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: NeuroEXPLORER (NX) incorporates a U-shape light-sharing detector design for depth-of-interaction (DOI) read out. The detector evolves from the dual-ended readout detector, its DOI encoding relies on proportion of light detections from different SiPMs, and its calibration based on known source distribution. The lutetium background radiation is used as an efficient DOI calibration source for NX (<10 mins’ data acquisition). However, calibration with uniform background count (UB) segmentation does not result in uniform DOI depths (UD) due to the unique detector shape. The optimized count segmentation for UD was obtained by measurement of front irradiation source experiments. In this work, we propose a system-level evaluation method for the calibrated DOI depths. A rotational <sup>22</sup>Na point source was used, and the consistency between PET images of different DOI layers serves as an indicator of whether the DOI depths used in reconstruction is correct. Depths were obtained by adjusting the assumed depths in reconstructions until all DOI layer’s results math each other. Two calibration setups, UB and UD, were evaluated. In the phantom study for validation, using the evaluated DOI depths improved the spatial resolution. The UD setup proved to have a smaller SD of 0.29mm for the DOI interval.

articleTitle: SAM+nnUNet: Deep-learning-based Head and Neck Tumor Segmentation on FDG PET
publicationTitle: 2024 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium (NSS), Medical Imaging Conference (MIC) and Room Temperature Semiconductor Detector Conference (RTSD)
abstract: FDG PET is a useful tool for diagnosis, staging and treatment monitoring on Head and Neck (H&N) tumors. Segmentation is usually performed for the tumors while the deep learning technique is emerging as an efficient yet precise alternate to manual segmentation. The performance of the conventional CNN-based segmentation networks is limited by insufficient training data. The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has been released by Meta, initiating a paradigm shift to a “smart” interactive segmentation that provides competitive performance when properly prompted. In this study, we proposed a SAM+nnUNet for H&N tumor segmentation on FDG PET to enhance the original SAM, in which the prompting process can be time-consuming and require a high degree of expertise. The HECKTOR2022 PET/CT dataset was used, with 420 patient images for training, 50 cases for validation, and 54 cases for testing. The training dataset of PET was used to fine-tune the mask decoder of pre-trained SAM, while both PET and CT were used to train an nnUNet. The trained nnUNet was first used to perform a preliminary segmentation of the tumors on the testing dataset, which was used to generate bounding box prompts for the SAM input after visual inspection and manual adjustment if necessary. Thresholding segmentation based on 42% of maximum intensity and various U-Net variants are implemented for comparison. Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Hausdorff Distance at 95th percentile (HD95), and SUVmean of segmented tumors compared to the ground truth were analyzed. Our results indicate that 5 out of 54 cases need manual adjustment for the nnUNet-based prompts for SAM. SAM+nnUNet performs best in all quantitative indices. We conclude that our proposed method is promising for H&N tumor segmentation on PET.
